I think that it is kind of holarious when people get really mad about bad game launches and post things like "I'm going to tell all the big Youtubers about this! Everyone is going to know and they're not going to buy your game! I'll never buy your games again". For one, no one cares. Two, yes, you probably will buy more of their games. You hopefully won't be naive and preorder with expectations of a perfect game, but you will buy more 2K games. Three, most games aren't perfect on launch, especially console games that are ported to PC, which this obviously is. It should have been delayed, but games aren't made for you to enjoy, they are made to sell. Enjoyment is an extra, sadly. If they can convince you that you will have fun, they have acheived their goal. That's not to say that they just made crap on purpose, though. I truly believe the devs tried to make a great game, and in a lot of ways it truly shows. So lets try to take an objective look at what is really here to judge it fairly.
The Good:
Graphics are actually decent. They are not perfect. They are actually REALLY glitchy. But what is working actually looks really nice.
Gun play is pretty solid.
Vehicle handling on "simulation" mode is awesome. Seriously, they could make an awesome driving game.
The world feels incredibly expansive. This is because the game is so rich with detail. It may be a smaller map, but you really cannot tell with how detailed and alive it feels.
The characters are incredibly interesting. You find yourself really wanting to get to know them.
The sounds are outstanding. The devs went out of their way for not only the best music, but awesome sounds like the reving of engines, the way tires sound on different materials like asphalt and gravel, and even the voice-over work is superb here.
The story is gripping.
The game has a fashion-forward, modern UI that fits well with the aesthetic of the game, though it shouldn't.
There are a lot more good things, but lets move on to the bad ones.
The Bad:
This game is a glitch fest.
A lot of people can't even get this game to launch.
It was locked at 30 FPS at launch, which is RIDICULOUS AND SHOULD HAVE NEVER HAPPENED. (Was patched within 48 hours to include framerate caps of 30, 60 and unlimited.)
There are TONS of texture glitches, including decently sized blurry boxes that hover around, oddly.
Game crashes at least once per two hours, if not more.
vehicles apear out of nowhere, which can be distracting, and feels cheap.
PC controls were not considered at all, as default keyboard controls are the worst I might have ever seen.
UI bugs that make it not apear correctly. (Like button promps not popping up when you are asked to either kill or recruit a racket boss, meaning the process times out and you accidentally kill the boss because if you do nothing for too long, because you can't see the UI, the character just kills the boss anyways.)
Tons more overlooked bugs and things simply ignored and not cared about at all.
Overall, this is a great game with an abyssmal launch. I don't know if patches can save this one, but I'm glad I got the game anyways. It actually is a really good game. I don't know if I should be giving this a positive review, but I'm going to look at it this way... It is a good game. It could be near perfect with some patches. If it is patched, then the game will be amazing. Maybe even GoTY. All it needs is patches, a lot of them. The game is already great, it just runs and looks like crap do to (what I assume is) greedy publishers who wanted this game to be the first huge release in Gametober. Lets be honest... 2K knows this game isn't going to compete with BF One, so it released before it even though the game isn't ready.
So lets call this what it is..
Mafia 3 is a really good game. It was pushed out WAYYY too ealy by a publisher who was afraid to compete with the bigger dogs releasing later in the month. The game could be patched to perfection, but as it stands, it's a pretty BS experiance.
If you buy this game, it might not run. If it does run and you can ignore all the glitches (which there are A LOT of) then you will have a really great time with the awesome story-telling and amazingly well done characters.

An okay mobile time killer type game but a mediocre at best game by normal standards.
The game had an alright if not overly original idea. A crafting game in an open map where you can gather materials improve your gear and build a base. The problem is execution completely neuters any real value the game could have had.
You start off like most games of this type gathering basic items to craft your tools, crafting stations, and building materials but unlike other games in the genre there isn't much beyond that to help hold your interest such as survival mechanics, fun combat, an interesting world to explore, or a really good story.
To start off from a survival perspective if that is what you are hoping for look elsewhere. This is not a survival game in any aspect. There is no hunger type meter and you are not fighting to survive. It's not that type of game simple as that.
So what about fun combat.... not in the slightest. There are three main components to the combat system. Core mechanics, pets, and gear. As far as core mechanics go you click on an enemy, your character attacks a couple times at which point a red highlight appears on the ground signalling the enemy attacking. You dodge out of the way of the attack and once it finishes you start the cycle all over again. The type of attack will vary from enemy to enemy but the core basis of that system is all there really is.
As to pets they don't add all that much to it as all they do is give you one or two passive buffs for having them follow you around and add a little bit of automatic damage. The only time my pet had any value was whenever I ended up having to fight multiple enemies at once. In that case the ground is buried by the red attack highlights leading to your new strategy being run around in circles avoiding the attacks while your pet does the combat for you (this is actually a pretty good tactic in general as from what I could tell your pet can't die). You can also stable your pets at your base and use them as a source for more items.
Which brings us to gear. You likely know most of what to expect here. It's normal crafting game fare where as you gather more materials you are able to make better armor and weapons which allows you to fight tougher enemies. But again this falls short as none of it really changes the combat up all that much. You are still doing the hit hit dodge hit hit dodge method regardless and the gear basically just allows you to do this with stronger variant of mostly the same enemies. There is some tactics to this as you get random buffs on the gear your craft which can be adapted based on the enemy you are fighting but when the combat still all comes down to the same repetitive slog it doesn't really help all that much.
So combats a dud what about the world? The story has you crashed on a planet surely that's interesting right? Nope. The first zone at least (six hours in and I hadn't made it to the second yet) consists of two or three types of terrain randomly generated into an obnoxiously large map. There's nothing all that interesting to see from it and aside from some hand crafted locations none of it is that interesting to look at. Even the hand crafted locations are mostly the same as the rest of the map just with maybe a building or some npc's added to it. And as mentioned this is a very large map which means you will spend a good amount of time walking around this repetitive uninteresting area. The saving grace here is that telepads are common enough allowing you to fast travel quickly back to your base without having to walk back but you have to find these first before you can use them meaning some repetitive walking is inevitable.
So that leaves story. This is actually the closest the game has to a bright side. The riding is actually decent. It's not amazing or anything. The story certainly isn't some great work of masterful storytelling that will keep you on the edge of your seat but it is decently funny. Except the drawback is that it is paired with generic uninspired quests. In between moderately amusing dialouge from NPCs and your character the quests all consist of the usual fetch so many of this item, kill this creature, or grind until you get this particular drop. It never goes beyond that meaning that for ever minute of amusing dialouge you will likely have at least 10-15 minutes of wandering around the dull world, with dull combat, and gathering materials.
And that's where my original statement comes in. For a mobile game that isn't so bad. What the game attempts to do works. It's functional and as such from the perspective of a mobile game it's not awful. It's works fine as a way to kill some time when you are stuck away from home and are just trying to fill the boredom. But as a PC game I simply can't recommend it. There are so many far better games (some of which for a lower price) that you could be playing instead.
If you just want a mindless non-stressful game to kill some time It can do the trick and is fine especailly if you get it on sale. I will probably play a bit more from time to time when I'm in that kind of mood. But if your looking for a really good engaging experience look elsewhere because this game simply isn't it.

It was a compelling and well-supported product during Early Access but around the time of proper launch there were big bugs which took far too long to fix, particularly on Vita and PS4 (patches failing Sony's certification numerous times was a running joke on the subreddit). It seemed like as soon as the game left Early Access the developers vanished and were done with it, completely in contrast to during development. Post-release support has been terrible.
Gameplay is fun on the face of it but soon wears thin due to a lack of depth and variation in the level design. Controller support has never worked for me. It is worth noting that the game is limited to a framerate of 30fps.
I'd personally not recommend buying the game primarily because of how Early Access supporters have been treated but irrespective of that, the game itself really does pale in comparison to others in this genre. Diehard fans of the game can probably look past the former but it left a bitter taste in my mouth which wasn't outweighed by the gameplay. I'd rather support developers with a more aligned moral compass.

I was looking forward to this game and I waited until it was released.  I feel sorry for the people that paid 59.95 for something that was then released for 39.95.  I am wondering what on Earth they used all that money for?  It is not the graphics as they are mundane at best even at the highest settings.  The graphic design is amateurish.  Although there are many games that are graphically impressive and the play value is less than satisfying.  Unfortunately this game fails at that as well.
One aspect of the game is it’s supposed to adhere to some kind of reality.  Such as a rifleman being unable to shoot well, if a target is pressing them with a melee weapon or the weapons being old and prone to jams in the middle of combat.  Now one aspect of reality is a human being can see in a 180 degree arc barring any physical problems.  Yet in this game the player has to constantly twist and turn, pan, zoom in an out and mouse over everything in sight so as not to miss anything that is obviously needed to complete the mission goal.
Another sore point for me is the random encounters that occur when traveling on the world map.  Every encounter is on the same one of three possible areas.  Every encounter drops the player at one seemingly random entry point.  The player might reach the enemy in two turns, but the enemy can cross the entire screen and still be able to attack multiple times.   Assuming the player survives, they loot and then get to pan all over the screen looking for the exit point.  There is nothing else in a random encounter aside from the NPCs to be killed. This game provides the real feeling of despair when you lose a friend. I first began my adventure on the hardest difficulty thinking, "hey I can easily win this". Two days into the game and I am here with half a squad of rangers, the others dead from a series of grenades, landmines, rocket launchers, bullets, and bad luck. It got to the point where I felt like loading my re-saves to attempt saving them. I quickly realized however that I enjoyed the game more when it was challenging and not easy. For this reason I am continuing forward within my adventure.
The pros of this game are very numerous:
FIRST OFF, THEIR IS NO DLC CONTENT (This is a pro for me because the game has all the content intended within it)
HOURS OF GAMEPLAY (we are not talking about an hour of gameplay here people, It took me 55 hours of gameplay to make me realize that I am about half way done).
DIFFICULTY SETTINGS (This option allows you make the game easier or tougher at certain parts throughout the game. This can help the user either complete the game early if they enjoy finishing the game quickly or long if they want to savor agonizing defeat).
CUSTOMIZATION (The option to customize the appearance of the soldiers within your squad helps in creating a unique group that you see fit in destroying the ranger's enemies. Saving the character template is also available so in the event that the player begins a new game. Basically, you can load an old character you created).
STORYLINE (The storyline is amazing within my opinion, there are numerous side quests and main quests but they tie in perfectly together. For example, a side quest might even have a side quest within it! So it gives you more options in obtaining a different experience).
Environment (The skills you pick within the game will determine how to deal with certain situations.  Let’s say that your squad stumble upon a locked safe. Nobody in your squad is a safecracker so you have no idea what to do. You can either ignore the safe for later or do what I do and blow it up with some good old TNT. Maybe a pipe bomb or grenade for the tougher ones though. Though last time I used a grenade it ended up blowing up the safe and its contents, so be careful with that. Anyhow, the point I'm making is that the game experience will reflect upon the skills within the squad).
EASTER EGGS: (Remember in good old halo days or other video games where the developers added something and you would say something along the lines of, "that shouldn't be here, but damn is it funny". The game provides exactly that with multiple references to certain lines and items you encounter. So enjoy and good luck finding them).
VALUE: (Though the game may appear to be high in price within first look. The true value of the game comes from the experience you will get from it. Not all video games are created with as many features as Wasteland 2. It is for this reason that I would highly recommend it to anyone in search of a fun game with lots of hours of gameplay).
Cons: A few minor bugs here and there but that is expected within most games and it does severely hinder the experience of the gameplay.

Often known as an alternative to Overwatch, Paladins actually has an edge over Overwatch in some cases.
I've played both games, 900 hours on OW and about 200 on this, being GM in OW, coming to Paladins was actually quite interesting.
Paladins succeeds in giving the community actual playable content meanwhile Overwatch is an extremely vanity game, more content being cosmetics than actually playable and worthwhile.
On average Paladins gets a new champion every month and Overwatch like what, every 4 months? Then the majority of OW's content is cosmetics, a new game mode locked behind a timed event, or the maps suck (nobody likes Eichenwalde Oasis or the newest one).
Competitive mode is pretty interesting in this versus OW. You can't have ditto champions and you can both ban a champion. You can actually carry in this game even with a thrower or two in a match where in OW it's borderline impossible. Should I mention healers in this game can actually carry games compared to OW?
You're also rewarded some actual good stuff for playing competitive mode, like skins and not some garbage spray, I should also mention we get balance patches quite often compared to OW (they're doing better but meh).
If you're coming from OW there are a few characters that have similar play styles, the classic Engineer, which is Barik, Fernando similar to Rein but they play much differently, Bomb King (JR0 but also plays extremely different, and Seris is kindaaa Mercy with the pocket heal.
TLDR:
OW - Better graphics and more cosmetics.
Paladins - Better playable content and regular releases of ACTUAL content, and arguably a better competitive mode.

I'll start this off by saying I really liked this game, I've always loved Lotr and everything about it /although I can say they mess with the lore quite a bit here, without spoilers, lol).  I also loved Shadow of Mordor. So a middle earth game centered around killing orcs for 40+ hours is something I'll be a bit biased about. I just love killing orcs as some kind of overpowered wraith/human thing, it's fun (really overpowered, I mean, even the highest difficulty is easy). But the game does have negatives too..
POSITIVES
-  Overpowered orc killing makes you feel like a god
.  Nice crafting/item system imo, albeit very simple
-  Creating your own army to become even more OP is really fun
- A lot of playing
- Even though lorewise it makes no sense, the story isn't TOO bad to play through.
- You get the "OP" and fun skills quite early on so you can be a god quickly
NEGATIVES
- Loot boxes
- Loot boxes...
- Why loot boxes in a full priced single player game Jesus Christ..
- The last act of the game (took me roughly 10 hours) is very repetitive and should honestly be significantly reduced gameplay wise or removed entirely. After completion, you see a "different ending" in a 3 minute cutscene that you could have easily googled and seen on youtube. From what I gather, the only reason they put this last act in the game is to make people frustrated with the difficulty/farming aspect and be forced to buy loot boxes. I died 2-3 times and difficulty wasn't really a problem for me neither was farming as I enjoy killing orcs for hours, but tbh I wouldn't even have bought loot boxes if I died 100 times.
- The last act was so repetitve that even though I love killing orcs and being this OP godlike character, I was getting sick of doing the same thing over and over. The last 2 hours I just wanted it to be over already, but I played through it because I love getting 100% game completion. So if you aren't so into 100% completion, and not so into killing orcs over and over, you're gonna hate this last act with a glowing passion.
OVERALL
I loved the game, I had so much fun with it, despite the flaws of the last act. That said I'm quite a biased lotr/orc killing fan. And the people who though loot boxes was a good idea should go and f**k themselves :)

There were some interesting moments in the main questline, but honestly most of the story in this game is disappointing.  There were some high impact moments early in the game, and then it transitions into almost generic kill/fetch type quests with some window dressing for story.  Honestly the Carnan questline, which is completely optional, was arguably the best part of the story since it seemed to have the most unique parts of the entire game.  It really just feels like the optional "collectible" questlines were just shoehorned in to accomodate the lack of story in the game.  However, at least there were things to work towards in this part of the game compared to the rest.
The biggest crime is the latter half of the story once you head into the "Shadow Wars".  I say latter half, but in actuality it may as well be 90% filler for virtually no reason.  All you do is defend/retake forts around 20 times. There were so many ways they could've made this Act IV more engaging.  There were zero unique boss fights, zero story cutscenes aside from the throwaway "this is what happened in the end" after the shadow wars, zero interaction between any of the characters introduced into the game, virtually zero dialogue by the main protagonist Talion.  I almost feel robbed and insulted by the lack of actual anything in Act IV.
If you enjoyed the gameplay of Shadow of Mordor then you'll likely enjoy what's on offer.
Traveling feels good and fast, although getting to a specific spot on and off walls is really finicky.  After unlocking all of the fast travel points on the map it usually takes you less than a minute to get to most places on every map.  For the most part it takes very little effort to get to anywhere on the map or on a battlefield.
Combat is engaging enough.  You have a number of combat options throughout the game, many of which will be required to be used given that many of the orcs will either have immunities to those options or develop them if you fail to dispatch them quick enough.  All the challenge in the game really just depends on what orcs you run into and how badly they screw with your established gameplan.  If you like vaulting and they're immune to vaulting, then you're just going to have to find something else.
Leveling lets you dominate high level orcs and gives you skill points to unlock various skills/abilities and variabilities on said skills/abilities.  However, by level 30/60 or so you will have unlocked virtually every skill and extention to each skill that you plan on using.  Every level and extra skill point after this can feel completely useless and leaves you with just unlocking skills just to use the skill points.  Once you get to this point all levels just let you dominate higher level orcs and use equipment.
As for equipment it feels somewhat shallow, but enough variation exists that people will definitely have their own favorites.  Depending on the rarity each equipment will have 0-3 different mods that are usually each part of their own set that will have values scaled to the item level.  Some of these mods can be quite useful like % chance to set enemies on fire, but honestly once you find something that works for you it really doesn't matter what level the item is because the modded values don't change very much aside from the main mods given by the items like damage and armor.  Even though numbers are given for virtually every stat mod, there is very little transparency in regards to what these numbers even mean.  200 armor compared to 500 armor?  How does that even change how much damage I take?  How much health do I really have? How much focus do my skills take?  The only other modifiers to equipment are the gems in which you can slot 1 gem for each type of equipment.  The gems are nice and all, but again very little transparency in regards to what these numbers do for you since they're just percentages added to vague numbers.
The main meat of the gameplay is the so called Nemesis system.  I have to say, that it is quite enjoyable.  There is enough variability and uniqueness to each orc that I can almost honestly say that no two orcs were ever the same.  Sadly, some doubles have definitely popped up not including the orcs that have unique names like "The Tower".  There are different archtypes, individual modifiers, and looks/personalities available to each orc.  Some orcs are more unique than others such as the bards, flame cannon ologs, spider orcs, necromancers.  I've found that these archetypes are a little too rare as I've only seen 1-2 of each of these types of orcs after seeing at least 100 individual ones.  One thing I've noticed is that although most orcs will not look the same you'll often see the same names pop up which can get annoying when you end up with 4 orcs with the same base name in a single army page.
There are a lot of neat little interactions in regards to the nemesis system.  You can have orcs randomly follow you between maps, ambush you, save you, humiliate you, betray you, return from the grave, etc.  Many of these seem to have small prerequisites to happening such as demoting orcs from warchief positions who will potentially betray you because of it.  Most orcs will have weaknesses or lack of immunities that will enable you to easily take care of them, but occasionally you'll run into an orc that may take you forever to deal with.  I've found that the dual wielding & shield orcs with sufficient immunities can provide the most challenge.  Otherwise, most orcs are easily dealt with with a combination of skills even up to levels 65.
The sound is ok.  Nothing bad, but nothing to particularly be excited about.  Explosions, weapon hits, grunts, etc all sound like what you would typically expect.  The music is forgettable.  Not much else to say.
There seems to be a lot of complaining about the loot system, but after playing through the game on Nemesis difficulty I can honestly say that it's completely redundant.  Unless your trying to get a fortress full of legendary orcs, which you can still do normally, I see no reason to buy anything from the market.  I hit level 60 around stage 8 of the shadow wars so if anything the XP boosters might be useful starting around Act IV to hit that level cap or at the very least level 55 as soon as possible.  I say level 55, because most of the orcs you run into will be at or under that level for most of the shadow war.  By the time I got to the Act IV I had around 40,000 natural Mirin so I was able to upgrade virtually everything, be it attacking or defending forces.  I only opened some free crates and just broke down every orc I got for more equipment since they were only decent in quality at best despite being epics/legendaries.
Defending a fort can either be significantly harder or take way more time than if you're attacking a fort.  This is because unless you have fully upgraded metal walls/door/spiked walls the attacking enemy force will usually make a breach and you'll often end up with 4 control points that you have to juggle because you'll have allied orcs going down every so often.  I found that unless I kept everyone outside it was very easy to have allied orcs bleed out.  I would suggest you lose the fort and retake it.  Plus you get significantly more XP just retaking the fort.
Game was decent, just wish the story and end game was actually something.

After 2 days I think I've fallen for this game. It's like Starcraft, Counterstrike, and Dead Space (if you're Marines) all rolled into a fun team based game. A great game if you're looking for a FPS that requires a little more thinking than Call of Duty or Battlefield.
That said there is some cons...the game is brutal to new players. The things that make you successful in most shooters will just get you killed in NS2. There are 'newbie friendly' servers marked out, but you'll find yourself getting slaughtered until you really learn to play. Marines aren't terribly complicated aside from learning how the aliens work. But aliens are very tricky to pick up since they don't play like a traditional FPS. There is a set of youtube videos detailing the gameplay...but it's 2 hours of video if you want to cover everything minus example matches. It's a lot to learn.
The RTS side is also frustrating for those new to the game. Commander is rather tricky to pick up (and far more challenging) even if you are accustomed to RTS. Memorizing hotkeys for everything is mandatory for any hope of keeping up with the pace of the game. Voice is also considered mandatory to do well since you'll have to keep in communication with your team's players. And even then, they may not listen to you so you'll have to work around that at times. Each side has a couple support units you can build and control...but the pathfinding is rather bad so be prepared to micro them.
Overall a great game once you get past the beginner/learning stage. 8/10

Alan Wake is a truly underrated and sadly ignored game which did not receive the kind of attention it deserves. This game is not perfect, but it still does most everything right to the smallest detail, in the most original and creative of ways.
First off, the atmosphere is absurdly engaging, realistic, absorbing, and scary. The lighting engine especially in this game is better than any game I've seen so far. Which makes sense, considering how essential the lighting mechanics are for this game.
What people say is correct - it is literally like playing through/experiencing a Stephen King novel. It is wonderfully cinematographic, during gameplay and in the cutscenes. Plus the voice acting is top notch, perfect attention was given to sound details and animations, and the story is really well paced. The story and the game's atmosphere keeps you on your toes the entire time, with unpredictable plot progression and developments, and a twisting, deep, surprise-filled story.
Speaking of tension, this is one of the few games that actually makes you address each battle scenario strategically (A few others being Bioshock, Borderlands, etc.). You are so scarce on ammo and flashlight batteries throughout most of the game, that you start to bug out when you are running out of ammo, and the enemies keep spawning anyway, as if they thought you were Rambo or something. You scour every area of the map looking for any bits of ammo you can find. Each enemy takes so much work to kill that it can easily get overwhelming and you can quickly use up your ammo.
The game implements some pretty crafty platforming and environmental puzzles, particularly in the The Writer DLC. Albeit short, I greatly enjoyed that DLC  because it was just pure creativity, from beginning to end. I did not enjoy the The Signal DLC as much, but it was still good. That one felt too repetitive and eventually got quite frustrating, but it still had creative content and impressive technical feats.
You get plenty of gametime out of this game - 11-14 hours for the main story alone. And then 1.5 hours for each of the DLC, and also however much time goes into finding all the hidden objects spread throughout the levels, if you are into that kind of thing.
So in summary, with a fantastic, original, well-paced, complex, non-cliche and creative story, a very impressive game engine that looks absolutely gorgeous a LOT of the time (I took 175 screenshots in my single playthrough. :D), solid shooting mechanics, nice attention to detail, a consistently frightening and tense environment, and excellent level design, this is a game I would HIGHLY recommend, to anyone who feels they can handle a psychological horror game of this degree.

One side of my fully laden truck is bogged down badly after trying to take a shortcut [no such thing in spintires], and the truck starts to lean. Tetering on the brink, neither way I steer the wheels has any positive effect, and both forwards and backwards torque sink the lower wheels deeper and edge the truck further towards tipping point. There are no practical winch points anywhere. At last, some forward forward momentum. I might make it out of this after all, and deliver this last load to the lumber yard. The truck falls over, and the engine stalls, but All is not lost - The logs are still in the cart. I try restarting the engine. It stalls again.
I walk back to the garage and get in my truck with a crane attatchment. If I can get the crane truck close enough, a combination of winch and crane might just do the trick. I traverse the boggy and hazardous road between the garage and the tipped log truck as night begins to fall. Upon reaching it, I realise that I'm going to have to get the crane truck into a narrow gap between the log truck and the edge of the nearby forest. And to get there I'm going to have to get through the same bog that I got the first truck stuck in, and move the truck most of the way into the forest. Here goes.
10 minutes later, The rescue mission is a failure. The rescue truck was able to get into position into the forest after many turns and wheel revolutions, but now is stuck between two trees with no hope of getting out. The load of logs was spilt after the first attempt to winch the truck back to vertical failed, and now it's out of range of the rescue truck's winch and crane.
I walk back to the garage, where my emergency fuel tanker lies waiting, and get the mechanics there to remove the fuel tank and install another crane. While they do this, I have a cup of tea and a vodka or two, while deliberating what to do with the stuck vehicles. Remembering that one of the local towing companies owns an eight wheeler missile truck that they picked up for cheap from a corrupt government official, I decide to just pick up the logs and carry them to the destination, leaving the two trucks stuck in the meantime. The money I get from this job will be able to pay for the towing and repairs for the other two trucks. I go back over to the mechanics and get them to put a log trailer on as well.
I arrive at the aparrent scrapyard and assess the situation. It's not as bad as it seems as the logs have fallen and rolled near some fairly stable piece of ground. The loading process goes without a hitch and I set off towards the lumber yard. Everything goes smoothly right until the entrance to the lumber yard. Here, the road is narrow, and I find the exact same thing that happened to the first truck happening again. No problems, I've been through this before, I know how to fix it. Winch onto the nearest tree, and use the extra pulling force to get at least my front wheel out. The truck starts to tip. I detach the winch. I try driving forward. Truck starts tipping further. Into reverse. Ah, some movement, but due to the direction I have to steer in, the trailer starts to jacknife horribly. Still, I push it as far as I can, and realign my front wheels after surveying the ground again. There's a way to the left, but it's between two trees that are in close proximity. The trees do damage to my trailer, but no considerably, and in return they stop my trailer from tipping again. I get through, park in the lumber yard, unload the lumber, then take another swig of vodka. Time to find the number of that towing guy.

Alan Wake is an exceptional game, but not without flaws. (Yes, that's possible!)
While the gameplay lacks certain fluidity when you use Keyboard+Mouse controls (camera sometimes flies away, mouse settings need adjustment), which probably has something to do with this game coming to Xbox360 first, it makes up with its brilliant use of darkness and light. Entire game's eerie atmosphere comes from the neverending waves of shadows that hide the enemies and take away the certainty in where the path is leading. Combined with fog and other atmospheric and sound effects, particularly in the forests, you will have to be on your toes. Jump scares are there, but followed with a cinematic slow-motion that informs you of the number of enemies you are facing, adding a visually interesting and life saving detail - if you can dodge the axe in time. That said, enemies are filled with darkness, it makes them stronger, so your flashlight is your friend, light keeps them away and gives you a fighting chance. You will need your flashlight, flares and similar gadgets more often than your revolver. There are also some puzzle elements, but nothing too difficult. If anything it gives you time to cool off after fights.
Scenery is amazing for this game, it really keeps up even with some newer titles, maybe even surpassing them. One problem though is that different locations sometimes keep the same looks with little changes made to them - forest is a different location further down the storyline, but still little is different in looks from the one at the start. Same goes for logging sites, farms, and parts of the city. But the lightning that will appear while you follow a mountain trail, constelations of stars, and many other intricate details keep it fresh.
Now the story is a thing that really is medal worthy. You play as Alan Wake, a bestseller author that has a writer's block and hasn't written anything in some time. In order to relax and maybe find some sort of inspiration, Alan and his wife go to a small american town. But wife has plans to help Alan's problem with writing, thus making an argument, and the entire story follows from this point never stopping with it's twists and turns, horrors and comedy parts, lovable characters and exceptional villains. Sci-fi/Fantasy elements are the core part, definetely inspired by Stephen King's novels. Other than what the game explains in it's own pace, finding pages of a manuscript (written by who is for you to discover) tells you more about characters, things happening parallely to Alan's own story and what will happen in mere minutes, just around the corner, rising the tensions even further. Then there are TV shows, radio shows, and many other ways that immerse you in the story and never let you go.
To conclude, great graphics, interesting gameplay elements, phenomenal storyline, and yes - amazing soundtrack, add up to a definite recommendation to anyone who is a fan of story-rich games and horror ones to boot.

One of the best games i played so far.
Kerbal Space Program is what i call a real "Sandbox Game", even in the campaign mode you got make the content by yourself deciding what you do and where you go next. For example i normally like to start a fresh campaign, do some missions, unlock a little techology to just spend 20hrs or more on developing a plane to do science research at the home-planet.
The game supports different 3 modes:
1. Campaign mode where you got to manage things like earn money, gain reputation, unlock a tech-tree by doing science, hire crew-members.... . There are plenty of different missions you can do but there is no story line that forces you to do certain things or go to special places.
2. Scientific mode which is more focused on developing vehicles to fly with and unlock the tech-tree.
3. Sandbox mode where you basicly just build whatever you want and fly around with it without having to worry about any tech-tree or rescources .
There is a number of feartures that i really love in this game as it is possible to setup the difficulty for the campaign and science-mode pretty free. There are multiplyers to increase or decrease rewards, fuel consumption and things like that. Another great thing is the flight-phyiscs of KSP. Flying is really easy you actually dont even need hardware like a joystick or pedals. I always played just with my keyboard and mouse while the flight itself always feels kind of great. The first steps of new pilots/astronauts may be a little pain though. When i remember of my first attempts to build vessels, it was a hard and confusing time. But this another thing i love about it: it feels like there is so many things to learn about how to build a rocket or plane or space-staton or crazy cars (or whatever). The whole thing is even fun when things do not work out like you want them to. The result is often a number disasterous accidents. As many things gone wrong with stuff i tried build, it was great fun to find out what exactly was the problem and how to fix stuff. There is no need to know alot about planes and rockets, the less you know the more there is to discover. In case there is something a player really is having real trouble with, there are many many guides on the internet. I should also mention that there is a number of mods available for this game, just check it out.
This is without a doubt the most fun ad amazing game of this style I have yet to play.

Absolutely fantastic game, cannot recommend it enough.
Basically, it's just building rockets to go to space. Sounds simple enough, but there are so many different aspects to take into account, from fuel management to delta-v to launch trajectories... the list goes on and on. There's a lot of depth to KSP, but it's also fun and goofy at the same time. It's also very humorous, like when Jebediah Kerman is having the time of his life while his spaceship is blowing up.
And if that isn't enough, there's extensive mod support for the game, from part mods to visual mods to sound mods to even mods that add guns and missiles that you can use for fighter aircraft.
Not only that, but the community is absolutely fantastic. Community generally isn't as important for singleplayer games as it is for multiplayer games, but it's still great nonetheless.
If you're on the fence about it, there's the demo (which admittedly is pretty bad compared to the paid version) and Steam refunds. Overall, it's definitely worth the purchase.
(I have much more time in KSP than Steam suggests, as I usually run modded instances that Steam doesn't record playtime for.)

I still have the original FSX Gold Edition disc, but I couldn't pass up the offer to buy the Steam Edition during a winter sale.
I don't regret it. The original version of FSX is 10 years old now, but the Steam version loads faster and plays out a lot more smoothly. And best of all, your favourite mods (payware and freeware alike) still work with it!
This game has such a strong community, as well. Most planes that exist in the real world have probably been made for FSX. Versions of all the Spitfires? Check. The F-19 fighter that may or may not be real? Check.
Even an X-Wing starfighter? (unfortunately, that's not real) Yeah, there's one of those, too. (Take that, X-Plane!)
I even make my own skins for the aircraft, quite often.
There are also tons of well-made, realistic payware choices available as DLC, just for FSX Steam Edition, and the list of them doesn't seem to be ending for a long time.
Overall, I believe that you should get the FSX Steam Edition, whether you're new to simulators as a whole or you just have an older, slower disc version (like I did.) It's just like the original, but it's actually better. You really can fly whatever you want, wherever you want.
It's certainly a 9/10 on its own, but all of the addons out there on websites like Simviation definitely bring it to a 10 for me.
Thank you, Dovetail, for bringing a legend back to life, and the community itself for keeping it that way.

I started this game on Steam and then purchased and completed the game on iOS (rationale for my low play time).
I am also a (slacker) backer for the game, and have been following the production documentary throughout the development.
The first half of this game was great. Having played LucasArts point-and-click adventure games in my youth, getting into Broken Age felt easy and familiar, but also fresh. The story, character, and settings have a level of polish and consideration that are hard to find in many games. The hand-painted art style is also quite captivating - I found myself pausing play to examine the minute details worked into every location. I have heard criticism that the puzzles could be considered too easy, and I will admit that I didn't run into some of the "try everything in the inventory" methods that I had to resort to in older point-and-click games (albeit with interesting dialogue in the case of the old LucasArts games). I wasn't bothered by the simplified puzzles — to me they felt seamlessly integrated with the story playthrough, and I also found that they made sharing this game with others (especially those without past experience with adventure games) especially easy.
I can't wait for the second half of the game to come out in 2015.

Hands down my favourite game.
It is always more and more challenging, and makes you want to always beat your previous best.
I am still learning new things and encountering new obstacles after 100 hours played.

First the positives:
The art style is beautifully done. The game is just a joy to look at the entire time. The soundtrack is just as uplifting as the visuals and really contributes to the unique world created by Tim Schafer. Honestly, the Broken Age universe is the best thing about this game. It manages to be a bright and whimsical world filled with interesting characters and funny dialogue whilst simultaneously sustaining really dark undercurrant themes such as human sacrifice, cults, extreme vanity, and imprisonment to name a few. This dichotomy makes Broken Age a really intrigueing game at first glance, but a few major flaws in the game prevent me from recomending it.
Not so positives:
Simply put, there really isn't enough 'game' here. The story is extremely linear and player choice doesn't seem to have any affect at all on outcomes or relations with NPCs. It feels like you are constantly playing with bumpers that carefully guide you to the next objective. Even the puzzle solving elements of the game are so simple and informed by hint-filled dialogue that any sense of achievement that could have been achieved through them is missing. If Broken Age didn't require an occasional click to keep the story rolling, it would be a great short-film. In fact, a very short film as Broken Age simply lacks enough content to warrent the current $25 (US) price tag. As I mentioned, there isn't a whole lot in terms gameplay, so it doesn't do much to increase the value.
I will be interested to see if the second act will do much to address these shortcomings, but as it stands I fear that the unique, beautiful world of Broken Age isn't quite enough to make it worth your time and money when gaming is filled with so many other beautiful worlds that have more to offer in terms of gameplay and content.

I think that it is kind of holarious when people get really mad about bad game launches and post things like "I'm going to tell all the big Youtubers about this! Everyone is going to know and they're not going to buy your game! I'll never buy your games again". For one, no one cares. Two, yes, you probably will buy more of their games. You hopefully won't be naive and preorder with expectations of a perfect game, but you will buy more 2K games. Three, most games aren't perfect on launch, especially console games that are ported to PC, which this obviously is. It should have been delayed, but games aren't made for you to enjoy, they are made to sell. Enjoyment is an extra, sadly. If they can convince you that you will have fun, they have acheived their goal. That's not to say that they just made crap on purpose, though. I truly believe the devs tried to make a great game, and in a lot of ways it truly shows. So lets try to take an objective look at what is really here to judge it fairly.
The Good:
Graphics are actually decent. They are not perfect. They are actually REALLY glitchy. But what is working actually looks really nice.
Gun play is pretty solid.
Vehicle handling on "simulation" mode is awesome. Seriously, they could make an awesome driving game.
The world feels incredibly expansive. This is because the game is so rich with detail. It may be a smaller map, but you really cannot tell with how detailed and alive it feels.
The characters are incredibly interesting. You find yourself really wanting to get to know them.
The sounds are outstanding. The devs went out of their way for not only the best music, but awesome sounds like the reving of engines, the way tires sound on different materials like asphalt and gravel, and even the voice-over work is superb here.
The story is gripping.
The game has a fashion-forward, modern UI that fits well with the aesthetic of the game, though it shouldn't.
There are a lot more good things, but lets move on to the bad ones.
The Bad:
This game is a glitch fest.
A lot of people can't even get this game to launch.
It was locked at 30 FPS at launch, which is RIDICULOUS AND SHOULD HAVE NEVER HAPPENED. (Was patched within 48 hours to include framerate caps of 30, 60 and unlimited.)
There are TONS of texture glitches, including decently sized blurry boxes that hover around, oddly.
Game crashes at least once per two hours, if not more.
vehicles apear out of nowhere, which can be distracting, and feels cheap.
PC controls were not considered at all, as default keyboard controls are the worst I might have ever seen.
UI bugs that make it not apear correctly. (Like button promps not popping up when you are asked to either kill or recruit a racket boss, meaning the process times out and you accidentally kill the boss because if you do nothing for too long, because you can't see the UI, the character just kills the boss anyways.)
Tons more overlooked bugs and things simply ignored and not cared about at all.
Overall, this is a great game with an abyssmal launch. I don't know if patches can save this one, but I'm glad I got the game anyways. It actually is a really good game. I don't know if I should be giving this a positive review, but I'm going to look at it this way... It is a good game. It could be near perfect with some patches. If it is patched, then the game will be amazing. Maybe even GoTY. All it needs is patches, a lot of them. The game is already great, it just runs and looks like crap do to (what I assume is) greedy publishers who wanted this game to be the first huge release in Gametober. Lets be honest... 2K knows this game isn't going to compete with BF One, so it released before it even though the game isn't ready.
So lets call this what it is..
Mafia 3 is a really good game. It was pushed out WAYYY too ealy by a publisher who was afraid to compete with the bigger dogs releasing later in the month. The game could be patched to perfection, but as it stands, it's a pretty BS experiance.

If I'm being fair (and I'm certainly trying to), then I can't fault Broken Age for going over budget. Voice acting alone must have cost quite a bit as they got some of the bigger names in the game VO biz including Jennifer Hale and Wil Wheaton. I can fault them for taking so long to put the first act out and taking just as long (still waiting) to get the second act out. This is not an article about what I perceive to be the shortcomings of Double Fine's production process however.
Act one of Broken Age easily belongs up there with Telltale's more recent offerings as a perfect example of how to bring the oft-considered antiquated adventure game style into the modern age. While relying more heavily on point-and-click gameplay than The Wolf Among Us or The Walking Dead, and treating its dialogue in a more traditional manner, Broken Age updates the classic adventure game through artful, top-quality presentation and production.
Putting the player in the shoes of two different characters, Broken Age's puzzles and interactions are simpler than some, but nonetheless interesting. What the game lacks in challenge it makes up on charm as it's filled with lovingly drawn landscapes and characters, and bolstered by Double Fine's signature off-kilter writing.
At full price I think the game (especially in this half finished state) is not quite worth the investment, but on sale I'd definitely pick it up.

First what I liked:
Pros:
-A lot like fallout 2, which was really great I haven't played a game from start to finish like this since I can't even remember. Probably fallout.
-Combat was really fun, weapons were enjoyable, deaths reminded me of fallout in a good way.
-I enjoyed the vast world, and exploring.
Really a great game, but
Cons (in my opinion)
Spoiler alert.
-First I have to mention the crashing, there was so much of that. I've never played a game with quite so much crashing and errors.
-Where are all the secrets? I found a lot of hidden boxes and stuff like that, but truely awesome secret stuff I found myself constantly looking for and not finding.
-No vaults? That was my favorite part of fallout, and yet no vaults to be found.
-No mystery. You pretty much always know your objective, what is going on, with no twists to be had for the most part.
Again I found myself wishing I would stumble across something epic, something amazing that changed the way I thought about the game. But no, just more of the same, kill move on, kill move on. I would definitely like to see mystery like the classic fallout games. You never knew what you were going to find at the depths of a random cave in the middle of no where.
-No special encounters. Sure you would encounter a passing trader, no fun, or a shrine that gives you a quote and a skill point, but I long for something more, don't you guys remember how amazing it was to see that lightning bolt in fallout 2 and discover something completely random, and truely amazing? I kept waiting for those to appear because they are so interesting and again, are full of mystery.
-Really cool followers. You guys remember the deathclaw/super mutant followers, as well as ghouls and various other creatures.  I didn't see anything remotely that cool, just a bunch of humans and of course there is the animal caller perk, but that wasn't really that cool either, the extent of the creatures you could control was so limited.
-More weapons, and make them more difficult to come by, I remember in fallout 2 you were SO stoked to get your first weapon, finally a shotgun, or pistol with just a few rounds of ammo. It was incredibly more difficult then wasteland in that way. And that made it so satifying to finally start picking up some of those high end energy weapons near the end of the game. Gatlin laser mini gun, damn that thing was sweet.
-No end game content, once you beat the game that's it. I would have loved if you had followed the fallout style and let you keep playing, maybe even adding in new locations and changing the areas based on what you found during the story line.
So in conclusion, I hate to compare you guys to fallout so much, because the game was really nice, and fun. But you yourselves set the bar by comparing yourselves to fallout. I was expecting so much more from this honestly, and I finish the game a little dissapointed. I would still recommend the game, but I hope you guys read this, and step up the bar with wasteland 3, which I will buy, but again I really hope you raise the mystery factor, remember a really good story line leaves you with a few questions unanswered even by the end, always guessing and wondering what could happen next. It's that mystery that is the driving force, and without it, it feels like just point and shoot, continue. Most of the time I found myself skipping a lot of text because it was just so plain, and didn't really have to do with anything interesting, or "out of the box" type of thinking. Also the voice acting was not my favorite, I found myself turning down the volumn often, because it came off kind of cheesy honestly, and I understand it's a indie game but with the money you guys had, I want to see some serious skilled voice actors nail their rolls and really make you feel emotion.
Sorry for all the negative feedback I hope you take it from a constructive perspective, I'm not trying to bash you guys I just want to see this game further embody the fallout genre.

Civilization III (or Civ III for short) is an argricultural war simulator, in which you build wheat, farm iron, and thresh people in a significant battle over land and cities.
Should you take too long to murder your foes, the game may decide to just let you win by saying you're so cultural that there's no way they can challenge you, and they automatically forefeit. This is a long review so let me give a tldr: I personally do not understand the plethora of positive reviews this game has garnered. If don't know about this game, save yourself some time and money and just boot up Fallout Tactics. For me, this game doesn't live up to it's reputation. It struck me as an unpolished and uninteresting product.
I kickstarted this game, and was excited to play it partly because of its purportedly stellar writing. Unfortunately, the basic format of tactics rpgs colludes with the lack of mechanical depth to severely limit the relevance of the writing. So while descriptions of areas that appear in a small text box are indeed well-executed and occasionally evocative, the lack of any meaningful interaction between your party members (or, indeed, any character or NPC) means that whatever that shows up in that little text box feels like window dressing. The lack of complexity in the gameplay means that what's contained in the textbox is also largely irrelevant to the experience of playing. The end result is pretty hollow. I suspect you could complete the entire game without ever glancing at the writing. This feeds into a more insidious problem, where the game's overall and immediate plots start to feel like a procession of meaningless skirmishes connected by an ephemeral charade of narrative, the kind you see in any MMO questline.
"But hey, this is a tactics RPG! Who cares about characters or writing or any of that crap?" Valid point. But unfortunately the game's shortfalls here are many, and worse. Where the writing was well-executed but irrelevant, the gameplay is unpolished and shallow. A problem for a game who's central focus is something like tactical combat. Combat in WL2 is a linear shootout, a numbers game where there are no meaningful tactical decision to be made once you're outside of a merchant's screen. I could make a really long list of gripes here, and cite the basically equidistant ranges of weapons, how gear is the single most important character element, aggressively incorrect "Hit %" in the UI, lack of any enemy AI outside of "rush up to face and use gun/crowbar", zero terrain relevance, and a hundred others. But the takeaway is that lack of polish I mentioned. The combat dies from a thousand of these tiny cuts, each of them trivial by themselves but fatally boring taken together.
And honestly, it could maybe have survived all those problems if the game had interesting choices to make. But. Remember that lack of mechanical depth I mentioned? In WL2, your only meaningful interaction with the world happens through skills. Skills have basically two purposes in the game: Opening Boxes and Murder. Social skills are a member of the former category. Maybe that doesn't seem like a problem, as hey, Fallout 1 and 2 come dreadfully close to doing the same thing. But compare this tactical rpg-elements game to other tactics classics like XCOM, Icewind Dale or Final Fantasy Tactics. Different Classes or Abilities on the battlefield dramatically change the landscape of any individual battle. "Should I Suppress or Flush?" is a question you have in XCOM only after you've acquired those abilities. Should I tank that group or kite them? Lightning Bolt or Fireball? No skill or weapon or indeed, any element in WL2 is going to approach altering your game choices, because all skills do is open boxes and give slight bonuses to hit chance.
Wasteland 2 relies on ancient game ideas with no new spin on them, and worse, seems to forget many lessons that've been learned about these systems in the last fifteen years. Which alone, would be acceptable, even enjoyably "retro". But the lack of polish or depth to these systems made playing the game aggressively monotonous. If this game had come out in 1999 it would have been a reasonable but ultimately forgettable companion to the then-game-market. But honestly, there are better places for your time and money, and if you're expecting a post-apocalyptic XCOM or Fallout experience then you're looking in the wrong place.

Basically, get this game.
Negatives: Writing and pacing, mainly. The story can bludgeon you over the head with grimdark sometimes. While I get the    "there are no good solutions to some situations" vibe they're going for, it can be annoying and tiresome at times. There's a shift in setting about twenty hours in and the second setting feels rushed as hell. Upon release, major quests in the region were completely broken, though inXile has fixed them at the time of this review. Furthermore, that portion of the game lacked the same sense of pacing the first half of the game had. Plus, you have puzzling gameplay/worlbuilding dissonance with things like wasteland traders dressed in rags selling power armor and military grade explosives.
Positives: Virtually everything else. Before getting to the second world map, Wasteland 2 is masterfully paced and intelligently constructed, with a real sense of progression as you complete quests. The supporting cast of rangers is well written, especially Snake Vargas, who feels like one of the only altruistic characters in the game. Upgrading your equipment is very satisfying and the "requisition" mechanic where NPCs will reward you with free equipment for finding unique items is fun-- too bad that goes away half way through. The combat is well designed and unforgiving-- exactly how it should be. Mark Morgan's score is good ambient, even if it's not as memorable or moody as the Fallout soundtrack. Being able to divvy up skills between four player characters is also a refreshing change from single-protagonist RPGs.
Side Note: I'd recommend a purchase on the sole basis that inXile releases spectacularly huge patches pretty consistently and these patches don't just fix bugs, but also add features and content based on player feedback. Despite Wasteland 2's flaws, the dev team's devotion to the project is commendable and, I think, something that should be rewarded.
Side Note 2: Unlike Shadowrun Returns, Wasteland 2 makes it very easy to import custom portraits for your characters, which is nice for RPers like me,

I'm new to Civilization games, and pretty new to turn based strategy games in general. However, I still enjoyed this game a lot. I'm awful, I lose pretty much every time, and I still have fun. This game has you building a civilization from scratch, trying to expand city by city to become the best civilization possible. At the start, you are given TONS of options. Picking what civilization you want to be to determine your starting perks, climate, weather, the age of the world, difficulty, barbarian options, AI agreesiveness, the ratio of water to land, and a whole bunch of customizable options for the rules and game limits. It's a lot to take in. And once you start, you can work towards whatever kind of civilization you want, from city structures to your units to your research... there's just a lot of options. But, what makes this game so cool is that there are not only a lot of options for starting and working your way through the game, there are also multiple ways to win the game as well. So you can replay lots of times trying to win in all the different ways available. If you are being severely outmatched in one area by another civilization, perhaps you can salvage your game by switching to another goal for victory. It's really very clever.
However, there ARE some issues with this game. It can be a lot to take in at first, especially since the tutorial mode is defaulted to off. I learned everything by winging it but not everyone will have the patience or luck for it. It'll take a while just to get used to what everything does and understanding how to navigate the game. Also, games tend to take hours to complete, which can also be rough if you don't have much time to play. It'll take A LOT of time to get acquainted with the game and to play in general so it's a HUGE time suck. I just wanted to get that point clearly across. Also... it's really hard... or I just suck... or both. Also... the online has been shut down, making this single player only. There ARE some complicated and iffy ways of working around it to play online, but they aren't worth the risk or hassle. The online is supposedly coming to Steamworks in the future, but until it comes, online is not a viable options, which is the whole reason I got it in the first place and that's diappointing, but it's my own fault for not looking into it more I guess.
Despite the issues, this game is VERY cheap. Five bucks for hours and hours of gameplay, including the two expansions to the game. Easily worth it, especially if you're looking to get into the Civilization series or TBS game in general. Just be aware of the time it will take to enjoy the game.

Ian McEwan once said that very few really long novels earn their length. I feel the same way about computer roleplaying games - especially the kind calling itself Final Fantasy.
Wasteland 2 is a game that requires a ♥♥♥♥ing huge commitment - beating it took me 100 hours (more or less, I tend to be a slowbie). And that was just one playthrough where I played the game as a stereotypical do-gooder hero, exploring everything and being a helpful do-gooder with a ♥♥♥♥ed up set of character skills and a tendency to reload and find the best outcome to satisfy my sad, sad do-gooder neediness.
But god damn it, this game is worth it if you're into these kinds of timesinks. It's a mix between the old gameplay styles of Wasteland and more recently released computer roleplaying games - a lot of the mechanics of the original Wasteland are at play here, re-tooled for an experience more suited for modern gaming. What I liked the most about it was the ability to solve problems through different means without hinting too deeply at what a solution could be, letting me get creative whenever I could. Locked safe? Hit it with a grenade. Locked door? Get that sledgehammer and ♥♥♥♥ it apart. Terrified settler due to gigantic robot scorpion? Hack the mini-scorpions that it produces to distract the big scorpion while drilling .50 caliber rounds into its face. A guy begging for a CD-i? Shoot him in the face and take his video game rocket launcher to sell for Snake Squeezins. This is such a refreshing breath of fresh air in a roleplaying game, this ability to solve problems!
And yes, it looks like something from 2003. Yes, you shouldn't need to read a little text box to figure out what's going on in the game, but what are you, scared of reading? Are you yeller about words? If I had any complaints beyond those two, I'd say the combat gets a wee bit much at times, the atmosphere and story are good but a bit flat in some places, and the thought of playing it AGAIN over another fifty hours or so is not something I'm interested at all in doing right now (but then again, I don't typically re-play video games I beat, mainly because I'm out chasing after a new experience or doing something equally wasteful with my time, like moving my eyes to read a page of things in a collection of pages bound by a spine that also is host to two covers HAVE YOU FIGURED IT OUT YET, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥S?)
So yes. I wholeheartedly recommend Wasteland 2. It's a goddamn joy to play, experience, and mess with.

I'll start this off by saying I really liked this game, I've always loved Lotr and everything about it /although I can say they mess with the lore quite a bit here, without spoilers, lol).  I also loved Shadow of Mordor. So a middle earth game centered around killing orcs for 40+ hours is something I'll be a bit biased about. I just love killing orcs as some kind of overpowered wraith/human thing, it's fun (really overpowered, I mean, even the highest difficulty is easy). But the game does have negatives too..
POSITIVES
-  Overpowered orc killing makes you feel like a god
.  Nice crafting/item system imo, albeit very simple
-  Creating your own army to become even more OP is really fun
- A lot of playing
- Even though lorewise it makes no sense, the story isn't TOO bad to play through.
- You get the "OP" and fun skills quite early on so you can be a god quickly
NEGATIVES
- Loot boxes
- Loot boxes...
- Why loot boxes in a full priced single player game Jesus Christ..
- The last act of the game (took me roughly 10 hours) is very repetitive and should honestly be significantly reduced gameplay wise or removed entirely. After completion, you see a "different ending" in a 3 minute cutscene that you could have easily googled and seen on youtube. From what I gather, the only reason they put this last act in the game is to make people frustrated with the difficulty/farming aspect and be forced to buy loot boxes. I died 2-3 times and difficulty wasn't really a problem for me neither was farming as I enjoy killing orcs for hours, but tbh I wouldn't even have bought loot boxes if I died 100 times.
- The last act was so repetitve that even though I love killing orcs and being this OP godlike character, I was getting sick of doing the same thing over and over. The last 2 hours I just wanted it to be over already, but I played through it because I love getting 100% game completion. So if you aren't so into 100% completion, and not so into killing orcs over and over, you're gonna hate this last act with a glowing passion.
OVERALL
I loved the game, I had so much fun with it, despite the flaws of the last act. That said I'm quite a biased lotr/orc killing fan. And the people who though loot boxes was a good idea should go and f**k themselves :)

Go Home Dinosaurs is an action/tower defense game with puzzle and card game elements. You unlock various towers as you progress through the levels in the form of cards, and before every new level, must choose a set of cards from your collection for use within the level.
Each card (tower) requires resources, which are coconuts and they spawn at random times throughout the level, meaning that you are constantly watching for the next coconut tree in order to gather resources so you can place your towers.
The "action" element comes from not only having to click coconuts, but clearing boulders and knocking down snowmen on some levels to make room for towers, and all while trying to get your squirrel into position to do damage when it's not collecting resources/clearing terrain as your main character also functions as a mobile tower.
It's not a traditional tower defense game, it requires much more hands on and faster reactions than most. There's no planning in advance, the dinosaurs travel along predetermined paths, so there's also a puzzle element regarding which tower cards to choose to be most effective on any particular level. It's well presented cartoon graphic style and sound effects are enjoyable.
The only negative I have is that even though I love tower defense games, this was a little too much action and not enough strategy. If you like TD games, I advise watching some gameplay videos on youtube before you make a purchase as it might not be what you are expecting.

Overall I'd say that game was pretty good, but given the current state of the game the base price point (59.99) is high for what you get.
Story seemed ok at the beginning but quickly devolves as the game progresses.
The story is broken up into individual quests spread in roughly 4 main quest chains.  You have the "main" questline that actually progresses the storyline, the Carnan questline, Bruz questline, and Eltariel questline.  There were some interesting moments in the main questline, but honestly most of the story in this game is disappointing.  There were some high impact moments early in the game, and then it transitions into almost generic kill/fetch type quests with some window dressing for story.  Honestly the Carnan questline, which is completely optional, was arguably the best part of the story since it seemed to have the most unique parts of the entire game.  It really just feels like the optional "collectible" questlines were just shoehorned in to accomodate the lack of story in the game.  However, at least there were things to work towards in this part of the game compared to the rest.
The biggest crime is the latter half of the story once you head into the "Shadow Wars".  I say latter half, but in actuality it may as well be 90% filler for virtually no reason.  All you do is defend/retake forts around 20 times. There were so many ways they could've made this Act IV more engaging.  There were zero unique boss fights, zero story cutscenes aside from the throwaway "this is what happened in the end" after the shadow wars, zero interaction between any of the characters introduced into the game, virtually zero dialogue by the main protagonist Talion.  I almost feel robbed and insulted by the lack of actual anything in Act IV.
If you enjoyed the gameplay of Shadow of Mordor then you'll likely enjoy what's on offer.
Traveling feels good and fast, although getting to a specific spot on and off walls is really finicky.  After unlocking all of the fast travel points on the map it usually takes you less than a minute to get to most places on every map.  For the most part it takes very little effort to get to anywhere on the map or on a battlefield.
Combat is engaging enough.  You have a number of combat options throughout the game, many of which will be required to be used given that many of the orcs will either have immunities to those options or develop them if you fail to dispatch them quick enough.  All the challenge in the game really just depends on what orcs you run into and how badly they screw with your established gameplan.  If you like vaulting and they're immune to vaulting, then you're just going to have to find something else.
Leveling lets you dominate high level orcs and gives you skill points to unlock various skills/abilities and variabilities on said skills/abilities.  However, by level 30/60 or so you will have unlocked virtually every skill and extention to each skill that you plan on using.  Every level and extra skill point after this can feel completely useless and leaves you with just unlocking skills just to use the skill points.  Once you get to this point all levels just let you dominate higher level orcs and use equipment.
As for equipment it feels somewhat shallow, but enough variation exists that people will definitely have their own favorites.  Depending on the rarity each equipment will have 0-3 different mods that are usually each part of their own set that will have values scaled to the item level.  Some of these mods can be quite useful like % chance to set enemies on fire, but honestly once you find something that works for you it really doesn't matter what level the item is because the modded values don't change very much aside from the main mods given by the items like damage and armor.  Even though numbers are given for virtually every stat mod, there is very little transparency in regards to what these numbers even mean.  200 armor compared to 500 armor?  How does that even change how much damage I take?  How much health do I really have? How much focus do my skills take?  The only other modifiers to equipment are the gems in which you can slot 1 gem for each type of equipment.  The gems are nice and all, but again very little transparency in regards to what these numbers do for you since they're just percentages added to vague numbers.
The main meat of the gameplay is the so called Nemesis system.  I have to say, that it is quite enjoyable.  There is enough variability and uniqueness to each orc that I can almost honestly say that no two orcs were ever the same.  Sadly, some doubles have definitely popped up not including the orcs that have unique names like "The Tower".  There are different archtypes, individual modifiers, and looks/personalities available to each orc.  Some orcs are more unique than others such as the bards, flame cannon ologs, spider orcs, necromancers.  I've found that these archetypes are a little too rare as I've only seen 1-2 of each of these types of orcs after seeing at least 100 individual ones.  One thing I've noticed is that although most orcs will not look the same you'll often see the same names pop up which can get annoying when you end up with 4 orcs with the same base name in a single army page.
There are a lot of neat little interactions in regards to the nemesis system.  You can have orcs randomly follow you between maps, ambush you, save you, humiliate you, betray you, return from the grave, etc.  Many of these seem to have small prerequisites to happening such as demoting orcs from warchief positions who will potentially betray you because of it.  Most orcs will have weaknesses or lack of immunities that will enable you to easily take care of them, but occasionally you'll run into an orc that may take you forever to deal with.  I've found that the dual wielding & shield orcs with sufficient immunities can provide the most challenge.  Otherwise, most orcs are easily dealt with with a combination of skills even up to levels 65.
The sound is ok.  Nothing bad, but nothing to particularly be excited about.  Explosions, weapon hits, grunts, etc all sound like what you would typically expect.  The music is forgettable.  Not much else to say.
There seems to be a lot of complaining about the loot system, but after playing through the game on Nemesis difficulty I can honestly say that it's completely redundant.  Unless your trying to get a fortress full of legendary orcs, which you can still do normally, I see no reason to buy anything from the market.  I hit level 60 around stage 8 of the shadow wars so if anything the XP boosters might be useful starting around Act IV to hit that level cap or at the very least level 55 as soon as possible.  I say level 55, because most of the orcs you run into will be at or under that level for most of the shadow war.  By the time I got to the Act IV I had around 40,000 natural Mirin so I was able to upgrade virtually everything, be it attacking or defending forces.  I only opened some free crates and just broke down every orc I got for more equipment since they were only decent in quality at best despite being epics/legendaries.
Defending a fort can either be significantly harder or take way more time than if you're attacking a fort.  This is because unless you have fully upgraded metal walls/door/spiked walls the attacking enemy force will usually make a breach and you'll often end up with 4 control points that you have to juggle because you'll have allied orcs going down every so often.  I found that unless I kept everyone outside it was very easy to have allied orcs bleed out.  I would suggest you lose the fort and retake it.  Plus you get significantly more XP just retaking the fort.
