I've updated the review after finally beated the game. Just in case, I'll say it. This is my review and nothing but my opinion. Feel free to agree or disagree as long as you respect it.
Tech-wise this game is a disaster. It's not polished at all. Plenty of bugs, blurry textures, upscaled from 720p, capped to 30fps at release (yet even with the unlock, the game is so poorly optimized, it's quite hard to maintain 60fps on high). Extreme popping and poor lod. I've seen a few times traffic spawn right in front of me. There's this time when the cops chased me just because some random car spawned right in front of me while I was at 120mph and, as you can guess, had no time to react and avoid the crash. And let's not talk about the lighting issues this game has...
Most of the models and textures seem taken from 2010, animations are clunky (Except during cutscenes), physics are completely broken (making your car do a barrel roll for hiting a pole). I can't understand what kind of QA they did to the game and also, where did all this extra time to polish the game go. Let me remind you that this game is sold as AAA for 60 bucks on release. That means, the game must have AAA quality in every aspect.
Credits to CrowbCat.
But ofc, as always, who cares about graphics, optimization and animations and all that bs, right? Well, content wise the game is a chore. Main missions are interesting, sure, but there are few and far between filled with repetitive side content in between that you have to do in order to unlock them. You will spend more time driving and doing the same tiresome tasks over and over rather than enjoying the story or the unique main missions. Even some "Favours" that your Capos ask you to do are the same thing over and over and those missions are considered "unique".
The territory system isn't anything new in the genre, you can select who takes the territory but in the end, it doesn't matter. Yes, you get certain bonuses depending on who gets the territory but that's about it. You can't decide what to build, how to expand, how many men you want to assign to certain districts, there's no gang wars (They just don't have any problem giving up their territory to you), it all feels so cheap and simple. A wasted opportunity.
Now moving on to the AI, it is dead on arrival. Simple as that. They are utterly blind, they sometimes try to flank you or use nades/molotovs to force you out of cover but most of the time are just dumber than a sack of bricks waiting for you to shoot them in the head. You kill one of their comrades a few meters right in front of them, and they don't even notice. Cops are also a joke, they can see you carrying a dead corpse and not even bat an eye. Pass next to them at 120MPH? Fine. Shoot some explosives? Like I care, Steal money from a shop? Go ahead!, but boy oh boy if you scratch their cars...
Credits to ASDF.
Many open worlds also have this problem, however, the devs clearly mentioned that they wanted to preserve certain "realism" the franchise is known for, like having to respect the speed limit, traffic lights and such. I guess in the end, they have decided to pull out a Saint's row/GTA.
The story is kinda simple and straight forward, and sometimes, cheesy. There's not a single plot twist. It's as simple as they can get.
It has some interesting dialogues but sadly, except a CIA agent, a friend priest who helps you, and sometimes the "nemesis" of this game; the rest of main characters are completely forgettable, including Lincoln. The game doesn't develope them during the game enough to even feel anything for them. I could include Vitto to the list of memorable characters, but only because we know his past thanks to Mafia II and that helps to understand his character. The rest, well, you will see them in a few scenes during the whole game and that's about it. You will get more info by reading their bios than conversing with them.
Lincoln through the game till the end is, by far, the worst main character in this franchise. Lacks depth or complexity. His character seems so disconnected from his actions that even a rock, is more complex than him. Imagine a grunt that is most of the time in a state of anger, not giving a fudge what others say to him, and only cares about revenge with 0 moral or any kind of thoughts or personal reflections. That's Lincoln. At the latter "stage/level" of the game, even the nemesis of this game is WAY more interesting and has a more interesting dialogues than Lincoln.
And the ending, is abrupt and unsatisfying. After spending almost 30 hours, I was expecting at least something more elaborated. The only enjoyable part is a scene that happens after the credits, and it's not even about Lincoln! Proving again that the strenght in franchise in terms of story telling, situations and characters is completely (except for a few characters and certain moments) and utterly gone.
Not everything is bad, the city and environments are recreated with great detail (The few details one can distinguish in that blurry mess). Great 60's vibe, awesome soundtrack (So many great classics are in the game) all this mixed with the racial tension suffered in the south. And like I've mentioned before, surprisingly the cutscenes are well done with superb facial animations.
Gunplay is on point, with many different weapons. There's also good ammount of vehicles, fictional though, but perfectly keeping that 60's style. Cover system works as it should, so no complains about it. You can also use a stealth approach, but only works because of the stupid AI. It's very lite, so don't get your hopes high on that regard.
To wrap things up, the game could have been better if the devs had more ambition. This feels like a cheap game from last gen. Like one of those "poor quality/GTA clones" we got a few years back (Like godfather or scarface). In certain aspects, the game does a good job, but not enough for a game that asks 60 bucks, let alone a AAA game in 2016. Neither brings anything new to the table, everything Mafia III has to offer has been done before in other games, bigger or better. I have forced myself to finish the game (Because after paying for this, I felt like I had to squeeze as much entertainment as possible) but I clearly not see myself coming back to this game to replay it.
Where the game shines is at the beginning and certain parts of the latter stages (except for the closure to Lincoln's adventure). I guess that's why many, who haven't played the game that much, praise it. But once you spend enough hours into this, you start to notice that this game is far from perfect or being that good.
Would I recommend its purchase? Only on sales (75% off) and after some patching. At 60 bucks? Hell no.
Another game to add to the long list of dissappointments of 2016. I can't wait for this year to be over...

Now this game doesn't feature a super-fancy graphics engine like crysis 7 will, but I think it's quite all right. What's more important for me, it runs perfectly on my medium-strength 2010 rig. The controls? They are exactly like in every other FPS game out there.

I still remember the first time I landed on Mun—planet Kerbin's closest moon. It was on the back of many failures; of countless times where my design, planning or ability fell short. One rocket would be too heavy, another too inefficient, another too explosive. I'd mess up my landing, splattering my little green astronauts all over the moon's jagged craters; or I'd fail to break out of Kerbin's atmosphere entirely, spinning them out into a watery grave. One time I ran out of fuel 5,000 meters above Mun's surface, and, unable to slow my descent, watched helplessly as they exploded on impact. It was heartbreaking.
Out of the countless defeats and sacrifices eventually came the answer. The successful rocket was ramshackle and ugly. It was the result of a hundred inelegant solutions to unforeseen problems. Nevertheless, it held steady through the launch ritual: keeping straight through the initial 10,000 meter ascent, the smooth transition to a suborbital arc and the controlled burn at the 70,000 meter apoapsis, first to orbit, then out of Kerbin's influence and into an encounter with Mun. Before descent, I transferred my Kerbal to a lander bolted on top of the launch payload (an over-engineered solution to my earlier fuel shortage.) Then I landed, and took one small step onto the surface.
I tell this story because it remains one of my greatest achievements in a game. It was a proper achievement, too. Not a pat-on-the-back trophy, created to convey incremental progress, but the successful completion of a challenging, self-made goal. The entire process—from failure, to revision, to hope, to euphoric completion—cemented for me why Kerbal Space Program is one of the best games on PC. That this all happened two years ago is why it feels strange to be reviewing the game now.
Kerbal Space Program is about building and flying rockets into space. Chances are you already knew that, because it was first released, in alpha, back in 2011. Thanks to the strength of the core sandbox concept, its potential was evident from the start. The added tools and features of subsequent patches have only strengthened the game's ability to deliver on that initial promise of full space program management and execution. Kerbal Space Program was one of the few Early Access games that I felt comfortable giving an unreserved recommendation. It was brilliant then, and it remains brilliant now that it's updated to version 1.0 for an official release.
The latest update brings some significant improvements, but none of its individual additions dramatically change the game. KSP's major pillars have been in place for a while now. Updates were designed to extend these pillars, and over the course of years have shaped the game into what it is now. To an extent, version 1.0 is the ornamental entablature that completes the construction. It overhauls the flight model, aerodynamics and heat simulation, bringing them closer in line with real-world physics. This simulation is the key to what makes KSP so compelling, and so it's fitting that its completion corresponds with the proper release.
The other additions make for nice extras. There are new missions types, more ship parts, female Kerbal astronauts, revised graphical effects, and a new 'Engineer Report' panel that advises about obvious errors in a ship's construction. The tutorial has been expanded too, and—although it's unlikely to diminish how overwhelming KSP's first hours can be—it does a better job of teaching the fundamentals, and so arms you with the base knowledge necessary to learn from your own experiences and failings. In all, it's a solid update, but it doesn't really convey any sense of what it is that makes the game so good. To do that, you have to dive into the heart of Kerbal Space Program.
Sandbox mode is the purest distillation of KSP's essence. In it, you have an unlimited budget and full access to the game's many ship parts. Step into the Vehicle Assembly Building and you're given a list of components. What do you want to do? Well, go into space, probably. How? Er, rockets. Oh, and an engine. There are multiple different parts in multiple different categories, but you can make a functional rocket with just a few basic bits. The Vehicle Assembly Building is a WYSIWYG modular editor that lets you easily add parts until they resemble something vaguely approximating a ship's shape. Click on a component and it appears as a ghostly outline that follows your mouse. Move it towards a previously placed part and it will snap into place. If you want to get really fancy, you can rotate and offset parts, or place multiple of the same piece symmetrically around the existing build.
All done? OK, click on the launch button and your construction is moved to the launchpad. Now you're no longer the engineer, but the pilot. Your creation will wobble and shake, but, as long as you've adhered to basic symmetry, will usually stay standing. You gingerly press the spacebar to activate the launch sequence. What happens next will define which of a constantly expanding set of branching possibilities you'll be sent tumbling down. Did you accidentally activate your engine and parachute at the same time, causing your ship to spin wildly a few feet off the ground? Did you attach an engine with too little thrust, thus preventing your ship from making it even a few inches into the air? Did you forget to even fit a parachute, forcing you to watch helplessly as your astronaut suffers the inevitability of gravity? Did you successfully break out of the atmosphere?
Whether it's success or failure, what happens during the launch arms you with new information about how to proceed. Fix the launch staging; add a bigger engine; add a parachute; add more fuel tanks in the hope of achieving stable orbit. With each launch, and each subsequent mistake, you're forced to re-evaluate and respond. You'll learn to add fairings to smooth the airflow, to use stability assists to dampen roll, to more effectively pilot through the first 70,000 meters in order to maximise fuel efficiency. Slowly, as you find pieces vital to solving whatever problem that you face, that overwhelming list of components starts to make sense.
From there, the solar system is yours for the taking. Sandbox games are, by definition, without structure. Minecraft, for example, is ostensibly a survival game, but, beyond having to satisfy a few basic needs, offers no real progression in terms of mid-term goals. For some, that's the key draw; for others, a major weakness. Kerbal Space Program is—in sandbox mode, at least—similarly structureless. At the same time, it has a natural progression you can choose to follow. There's a moon, and then planets—each far enough away that visiting the next is a significant step up in difficulty. These are logical goals, but you aren't forced to pursue them. You could instead decide to become good at making space planes, for no other reason than that space planes are really hard to build.
Persistence is a crucial part of KSP, and additional goals form out of past launches. Take my Mun landing as an example. Yes, it was a great achievement, but no, it wasn't wholly successful. Most would probably agree that one of the key steps in sending an astronaut to the moon is bringing him back home again. I didn't do that. He's still up there, waiting for me to launch a rescue mission. And if you think he has it bad, at least he's more comfortable than the astronaut of a previous mission. He's stuck in orbit around the moon. It was that or crash into the surface. If something goes wrong on a flight, you can always revert back to the moment of launch. Often, it's more fun to accept the mistake and deal with the consequences.
Edit: I had a lot more to say, but ran out of room. Quick summary, there is also a 'campaign' where you start with small facilities and parts and gain progress through research, and take contracts to do missions. This is an awesom game if you love space.

Oh boy, where do I start with this one;
is a top-down roguelike shooter which features twelve unlockable characters (currently) and a wide array of weapons and enemies.
The game also features many unlockables, such as golden weapons, different crowns and even different skins for characters.
Onto the actual review; this game is a great one, a game in which you will love whole-heartedly but also have a deep hatred for simultaneously. Sometimes games can't land this right in the middle; leading to a rage-inducing game which isn't fun to play; but Nuclear Throne does it well. The somewhat difficult levels and multiple areas keep you coming back to complete more and more runs, not to mention the achievements too..
Most of the characters have different abilites, such as Fish's rolling ability or Crystal's shielding; all character abilities are, by default, activated with the RMB. These become crucial in a run, some character's have pros and cons, some substitute ammo/HP for other buffs used during the game.
The upgrades during this game impact the style, success and the difficulty of your run, with the upgrades coming everytime you "level up" in-game. This is achieved by finding and consuming "rads", obtained by killing enemies and/or finding rad capsules (little green bottles) throughout the level.
The Daily and Weekly runs are also good for players who have completed the game fully (although this is very hard and is only achieved by a small percentage of players). The Daily is just a normal run, but you only get a single try, compete against others to get as many kills as possible (keep this is mind, the leaderboard is organised in kills, NOT distance of run). However the Weekly run is more specific, you get unlimited lives with the same leaderboard system (and a week to complete it, obviously) but only one character is playable and you sometimes even have weapon restrictions.
Saying anymore would ruin the random surprises this game has to offer, so I'll leave it up to you, the reader, to discover these for yourself.
Overall this game is very well made, a nice balance of rage-inducing gameplay and satisfaction all put into one. I would easily recommend this game to anyone who is interested.

Life is Strange sat in my Steam library for a long time. Despite the recommendations from people with gaming opinions I trust, I was nervous that the game's teenage high school setting would be hard to relate to as an old fart and that I would find the game to be little more than a Dawson's Crack-esque 'I'll stare at a lake to solve all my problems' affair.
How wrong I was I was.
As soon as the calming and emotive main menu theme started I instantly relaxed and within a minute or two of  the main protagonist Max's company at the start of the game I knew I my fears were unwarranted. What followed was a beautifully paced story, told with real heart. Characters are introduced that initially appear to be one dimensional caricatures, but soon reveal themselves to be much deeper and rounded, making early decisions taken in the game much more complex than they initially seemed. I frequently found myself overthinking things as critical choices came up, second guessing the potential motives of nearly every character.
The soundtrack and visuals massively contribute to the atmosphere and several times I wished I could just wander around the town of Arcadia Bay soaking up the Autumnal Oregon setting. Coupled with the many references to films such as The Breakfast Club & Bladerunner, not to mention games like The Longest Journey series and Bioshock Infinite, I felt that this game was really pitched at me as an adult and not the younger audience that I thought it was aimed at.
There is no doubt that some people will bounce off the game, the character Chloe can be very diffiult to relate to initially and I can see that some people would dismiss the game very quickly as a result. For me however, the game got under my skin and after the inevitably tough climax I found myself thinking about the game for days afterwards, about  the story,  about the characters and the effect my choices had on them. The start of chapter four will stay with me forever as a powerful piece of storytelling I think, something that very few games I've enjoyed in the last thirty odd years have been able to achieve.
A beautiful example of intelligent interactive fiction, hella recommended.

Whoa. Alright, so there is a lot about this CYOA novel/game. Both good and bad. I would recommend getting it on sale, though if you have $7 to spend with no cares, it's a good way to spend your time. I would recommend reading through it at least twice, which I've done at the writing of this review. And I still want to get a better understanding of what I can do and little bits of story I haven't gotten. There is a lot to say about and take notice from this CYOA novel, but I wouldn't say that there is much to keep anyone away from it, even if many flaws are showing (both a very flawed and very beautiful gem). I will try not to write anything that is too spoilerly or geared too much for assuaging opinions. Just a review on what I noticed to try to provide information for anyone interested in getting it.
Character Development is usually my main point of interest in a story. And it is the main reason why I think this CYOA novel should be read at least twice. I found the character development to be weak and slow throughout most of the novel. I only started to really feel like I cared about the characters later in. And when I say later in, I mean the Epilogue. The Venusian and Martian teammates were those who I actually started feeling invested in about halfway through and the Epilogue sealed the deal with them, though I wish I could have learned even more about their respective peoples and them as people. The romance choices are great, though few. There are three of them, but they are some of the most interesting characters. The two romance options I tried on my two playthroughs, also only really started to feel more fleshed out by the Epilogue. There was the smart research associate and the tragic Superlative. There is also a nice guy widower who I haven't romanced yet, nor have I tried an aromantic playthrough yet. These little descriptions are oversimplifications of these characters, but, quite sadly, not by much. I like feeling invested in characters and to start caring for them in a way. The romance options have you somewhat caring for them, especially by the end, but they still don't feel very fleshed out. Mostly some kind words and gestures, along with certain character traits. I really feel like giving more backstory to them would have helped a great deal, knowing more about them and their lives. There has been one character that I will try to interact more with a subsequent read, but I have still not seen much character building and wonder if they even have much written into the story. I think that the backstory and more thorough interactions during some time off from the main quest would have done wonders from fairly interesting stereotypes to full blown characters living in a big breathing world.
My biggest gripe with the novel is also tied with what I like most about it. The game has a lot of interesting themes, settings, and lore. This unfortunately accents how much potential that wasn't realized. Fairly concetrated amounts of aether found throughout the world (not just Earth, but at least the solar system?) that both has certain people with superpowers, as well as running many mechanisms, even seeming to provide something for vehicles to pass between plants. It sounds as to be something to shape a fascinating world, and yet not much seems to be told outside of the little world that your character occupies. Your character seems that they would know more, but that's not knowledge that seems to be thought of during the course of this novel. And creates an odd sort of disconnect with your character, you aren't given much of a world that your character was born and raised in. There even seemed to be hinting of further explanations of certain lore that did not occur. Some of these hints also seem to not be available for every play through. There are other situations where you aren't sure if something is being hinted at or it's actually just an analogy of something that is happening or is going to happen (such as with a near death experience that occurs). There is some explanation of how Class A automata come to be, though there also seems to be some contradiction. It seemed to be extrapolation to the point of alluding to something further and how it could occur, but a bit of information about Class A automata given earlier combined with the later explanation and contradiction makes it feel like what was being built was left back to where it started. It's a little example of what seems to happen a few times. In one thing told during my first plathrough's Epilogue, there was a telling of a certain scene that seemed to tell of something far greater that could explain a lot of things that happened, including what happened during your near death experience. That scene was one of my favorite parts of the game, it sounded awesome and helped tie a lot of things togehter into a package of great lore behind certain happenings. I even started my second playthrough in the hopes of learning more about it. I did learn a little more, but there doesn't seem to be much in-depth information regarding it. It one of the main reasons why I would probably get a sequal, or something by this author based in the same "world." There really does feel like there needs to be a sequal, though I'm not sure how all choices would be reflected well in it.
There appears to be at least one bug that people have mentioned involving Gatsby and Dusk. Which seems to just be something that slipped through, and is worth notice, if not quite wariness, on the prospective buyers part. What's odd is that there are mechanics that can be kind of interesting, but give the feeling that they were meant for a far larger game. You can do some base building, though I'm not sure if certain things even have much of a function, such as expanding the study into a library and salon. Perhaps I didn't build them at the right times or go down paths that would have elicited at least a little something from them. You can make the base safer, but unless there are some drastically different paths that weigh in on it, it really seems to have no call for it. Certain stats don't seem to have much opportunity to be utilized, though maybe doing some Derring-do leads to a good bit more Derring-do paths. You also seem to be able to possess more aetheric capacity than you would ever need. Feeling like there might have been more protracted/epic fights that never occurred.
This CYOA novel could use more fleshed out scenes, characters, and writing in general. But it has the wonderful synthesis of tying lore with characters. That the way the world is, the way Superlatives and aether works is so much of a part of who the characters are. That they are so a part of their world. More in-depth writing would help support the story immensely, and would help it put it up there as one of the best CYOA games in my book. I am admittedly a sucker for lore and character development, and the hints of aspects of the lore entices me to this story. It gives an interesting ride that really should be done at least twice in order to get a better feel. But it is also something that has a sense of being incomplete, the Epilogue tried to resolve some things, but it even seemed to say that there is more to know and it's not over yet. And I probably will go through it more to find them and might even come back to edit this review. The way the title is structured with the separation by the ":" also seems to hint at it being part of a series. It has a strucute as a single story that is rushed and hints at further developments. I hope to find more of what I'm looking for in a sequal, but what it has now is something that you can have fun with and can grow attached to certain characters. There is also some opportunity to sniff out lore if you find that interesting (which I do :)

Middle Earth : Shadow of War takes what's in the first game and expands on every aspect. The nemesis system has been greatly expanded on. Orcs can betray you, ally with each other and become blood-brothers, you can assign one to be your body guard and summon him out in the world, and then there's the fort assault and defense feature. The game has 5 regions, compared to the first game's 2. In 4 of them there are forts controlled by an orc overlord and his warchiefs. The goal is to assault the fort, conquer it, and place your own orcs in its overlord and warchief spaces. In act 4 you have to defend the forts multiple times if you want the ending cutscene. Alternatively you can watch the ending cutscene on youtube and then do the fort defenses at your leisure if you want to. The nemesis system is almost like an interactive Shakespearian play.
People say it's a grind. The grind is that there are 20 fort defenses in a row. However you can dominate the orcs attacking your fort to replace any losses and just power through them if you want.
Now the lootcrates aren't required in any way shape or form. The orcs you get from them are inferior to the normal orcs with their traits, and often they'll betray you right when you deploy them. So they're actually pay to lose rather than pay to win. Still, if you really want to open them, there are some that require an in game currency called mirian which is free and plentiful and they can be used to open silver boxes. The gold boxes that cost real money give orcs that are legendary, but I have multiple legendary orcs from them that would die in 1 hit if hit by fire if I were to deploy them. Don't open boxes for orcs. The silver boxes and gold boxes give training orders which can be used to teach your orcs an ability, with the difference that gold boxes give 2 at a time while silver boxes give 1. They're random but they're all from the same pool of orders so again you shouldn't spend money on the gold boxes. Just farm mirian and open the silver ones for free. Or skip them entirely.
If you liked the first game, you would like this game because it's like the first game but more.

A Steampunk/superhero mix, with a dab of Sci-fi; in fact, it's style resembles the Mass Effect series in that the presence of aliens and interplanetary politics is a common point of the game. The mixture is fairly seamless and organic and it works well enough.
The writing itself, in my opinion, could be improved, since the narrative sometimes can feel rushed by the lack of description or attempts to set the reader in the current scenario, but judging by other reviews praising the story's pacing, it might be a personal preference. Sometimes I felt things just happened for the sake of continuing the plot, even though I believe it wouldn't be so simple like that, and would appreciate some more interference from other characters in scenes that aren't explicitly scripted for them - they have a hard time shining and feeling alive when the writer doesn't turn the focus on them. To balance that, there is a fairly good ammount of different scenarios to be played out, and judging by the ammount of choices, even more results; so even if the characters and immersion feel cast aside sometimes, the variety of approaches you can take (sometimes with a specific character, further increasing their screetime) sort of makes up for it. Like, really, even though I feel the writing lacks some detail, I get the impression the author spent A LOT of time writing different individual scenarios, and honestly, I think they deserve some praise for that. COG games sometimes get a reputation for being rail-roaded and I feel the author put some effort in minimizing that effect.
The plot is interesting and compelling, and succeeds in delivering a good story. It finishes well with few loose ends, but teases the possibility of a sequel. The characters are well fleshed out, especially the romance options and the main group (albeit with one or two too-superficial exceptions) and the game will have you slowly building your relationships with them, very much like, again, the Mass Effect series. In fact, the pacing in the building of your friendship (or romance) is superb, in that it takes time for it to happen and lets you throughly enjoy their personalities and their dynamics with your protagonist. The romancing part is well done, especially for me, who appreciates slow-burning romances and has a hard time enjoying other games that are more... concise on that aspect. Different from this one, a lot of COG games downplay the participation of your Significant Other to a couple of scenes during the story and one at the epilogue. I'm glad The Superlatives: Aetherfall is more succesful in weaving the romance options into the plot and making them real characters in the story world.
Gameplay-wise, the stat-building portion seemed both overly complicated and forgiving; complicated because there are a lot of them (and some are not instantly clear on their purpose) and the chances to improve certain ones are rare and ambiguous. But also forgiving because the requirements of percentage in tests doesn't seem to be high and there's a lot of choices to pick from. They can range from 3 to 10 (a rather big number for a prompt that is only shown once), and you definitely will be able to pick the higher stat you currently have.
All in all, I really enjoyed the dynamics between the characters, the difficulty of the tests, the variety of directions you can take and the plot in general. I believe the narrative could benefit from a bigger effort in detailing the scenarios, characters actions, settings and scenes. I will keep an eye out for more stuff from the same author, and hope they are as enjoyable as this one was :)

Whether or not you like text-based games like these tends to come down to a combination of interest in the subject matter and themes and the writing style of the author.  (Even for as well-written as Neighbourhood Necromancer is, I just can't stomach the zombie genre any more....) Since this can be highly subjective, the best advice I can give is to just download the demo, which holds a decent chunk of the game, so you can see if it rings any of your bells for yourself.
So far as writing style goes, this one lacks some of the wittiness and flair of others, but if you enjoy the themes and want to immerse yourself in the fantasy it portrays, it's solid writing that won't distract from those themes and takes itself relatively seriously outside of some notable elements of its setting, like the alien races and some of the more roguish team member's witty rejoinders, so this is a game where your enjoyment will likely hinge upon whether you like the fantasy it portrays.
The theme, then, can basically be boiled down as a "Jules Verne meets Mass Effect".  All the planets of the solar system have fanciful but generally rubber forehead-style alien races, such as dryad-like Venutians that hate martial reptilian Martians (Turians), but in spite of making a point of having 5-gendered lizard people (which is used as an excuse for allowing women who are open lesbians to hold positions of power in Victorian London), everything is humanoid, breathes Nitrogen-Oxygen mixtures, and speaks English. The Mass Effect comparison can also extend into your powers, as you can choose to have Engineer-style Steampunk tech-based powers, or Adept-style natural "Aether" (Eezo) powers as a result of an unusual heritage.  There's even a "are automatons (synthetics) property or people?" theme in the game.
Unlike Mass Effect, though, your romantic partners and party members aren't one and the same, so you can't screw a genderless plant person or figure out how a "secondary male gender" works (or more importantly, how a secondary
gender works...).  (Darn.)
Choosing the source of your powers, between supernatural heritage or technological gadgets, but this seems to be more "cosmetic" choice than anything, and it changes the text descriptions of how you do something, but not their effect.  (I.E. you throw electricution grenades rather than shoot lighting from your hands.) Still, cosmetic changes strike a nice balance between giving player agency in their character customization and bogging the player down in certain choices being less viable than others.
The main deciding factors of success are those % bars in every one of these choice of games, and like a lot of superhero-themed choice of games, you basically want to max out a few stats and once you give yourself a big hammer, try to find ways to make all your problems nails.  Invest in Agility, then always try to outspeed your enemy, or pick Insight choices and use it to predict where your enemy will be first, or just take Vigor and trade blows like a heavy.
Compared to other Choice of Games, this is one of the more "RPG-like" games, with constant choices regarding things like building a base or powering up one stat in a direct "pick what you want to buff" style of choice.  This can be problematic for your first playthrough, because you're asked to decide what part of your base to build (and what buffs you will therefore get) before having any good grasp on the ramifications your choice will have.  (Choose between getting morale bonuses for the party members you haven't met yet, and therefore don't know whether you'll need help keeping in line or not, bonuses to combat powers before having any combat, bonuses to your aether reserves before having a good sense of how much you really have to start with, diplomacy with outside factions before you have any idea who they are or why you might need them,  or simple "base repair", whose impact is nebulous even well into the game.)
Also similar to Mass Effect, between missions, you get a chance to advance dialogue with the whole team before moving on for loyalty bonuses.  You basically need to keep team members in the party with loyalty bonuses and picking dialogue options that diffuse tensions between differing ideologies or backgrounds while keeping your stats high to pass skill checks for different situations, like combat.  This also means, however, that you want to just tell them what they want to hear (even when it's something different for every character) rather than get to actually express your own take on the issue.
There are then the "personality" bars that seem to make up the more informal parts of the game, but several seem "set in stone" fairly early, like Manners versus Pugnacious or Calculating versus Opportunistic, which only seemed to have a few choices that actually changed them in the whole game, seemingly being checked for success but never changed after you first make choices that give you one or the other.  (But I've not played a Pugnacious playthrough yet, so maybe you can be super-blunt, but not Little Miss Manners?)
In all, my largest complaints are that it seems a bit on the short side (which is inevitable considering the decently branching choices that give you the sense that your choices matter tend to come at the cost of overall game length), and that it feels a little too much on the "formal rules" side. It's one of those Choice of games that demands min-maxing your particular best skills, and then hoping you always get a choice to use your super-stat, and pick answers to max out relations scores rather than pick the things that actually express your point of view on a topic.

I don't like reading super long reviews, but I believe a detailed review will be more helpful than a super short one, in this case. So sorry in advance for the length.
Let me first off say that my opinion is heavily biased. I have been following this game since day 1, and I was super hyped for it. Shadow of Mordor was also my favorite game up until recently. So I came into this, expecting and hoping for the best. It did not disappoint.
+The gameplay, story and graphics: Fantastic. Gameplay is essentially the same as Mordor, with added skills and traits that change it up. Graphics are a huge improvement from Mordor, and there are some stunning enviroments that are cool to walk through. Story, see the note at the bottom of review.
+Voice acting: Excellent. I was happy with all the voices of the characters.
=Microtransactions: I am afraid to even approach this subject, but I must say something on it. I don't agree with microtransactions, and I certainly don't like to see them in games. But I made an exception with this game, since it was a singleplayer. It wasn't nearly as bad as it was made out to be by the community. Yes, they are ever present and they do have ads for them in the game menu, but it isn't a game changer. You can complete the entire game with out spending one extra dollar. You don't even have to open any free loot crates to win either. They are completely optional. But if you do feel like you need to progress further, faster, you can get the Gold Mirian in-game by completing community quests.
You don't have to pay a cent for it. I can totally understand people boycotting the game due to this, but by all means, the game is entirely possible and incredibly fun without the microtransactions.
-Glitches: There are a lot of bugs and glitches; some can be super frustrating and even cause you to die when they occur in a situation when you are low on health and trying to run away from or dominate an orc. It's painful to watch Talion stuck rolling into a wall, instead of climbing it. :'(
-Story accuracy: If you are a die-hard Tolkien fan and can't stand to see things that are totally inaccurate to the story of Middle-Earth, just don't even play the game. There is so much that I picked apart, and it kind of ruined the amazingness of the last few story missions. So, if it will kill you to watch such a story-changer, then stay away.
[Conclusion] I thoroughly enjoyed this game, and, despite the cons, I think it is one of my new favorites. I can't make your decision for you, but I have tried my best to give you a look at what the game holds, and hopefully this will help your decision. I would rate this 9/10.
Note concerning the Story: I mentioned both that the story was good, but also bad. I meant that the overall story is entertaining, and to someone who knows little, or cares little of Tolkien lore, it is a intriguing story. But for those who love Tolkien lore, don't expect a perfect puzzle piece to fit into the story of LOTR.

Edit 2: To be blunt, this "game" aka tech demo still is crap with little content, and now the publisher isn't paying the guy who made this game, so now more than ever:
Yes the physics are fantastic. Yes the terrain deformation is fantastic, until you realize all you'll be doing in this game is getting stuck in this OP mud as soon as you carry any load. This isn't an off-road simulator, its a winching simulator because all you do is get stuck in mud. There is no rock crawling or technical off-roading where you have to worry about articulation or angles, just mud. The devs found how to make cool mud in video games and just put it everywhere. I remember during a YouTube live stream the devs admitted they never actually had any off-roading experience. This should have been a red flag for me and IT SHOULD BE A RED FLAG FOR YOU, because it definitely shows in the game.
Furthermore, this is still nothing more than a glorified tech demo at its current stage. There is VERY little to do in it. Maybe if they continue to update this with more things to actually do it will be worth the price, but in its current form I feel like I wasted $26 (I got it on sale) on the same game that was a free demo a few months ago, with the addition of moving logs... Don't care about thumbs ups OR downs reall; gonna be honest, it's mixed feelings anyway. Alan Wake is a writer battling off surreal forces with light. It's an interesting concept, with good technical performance, a good port overall, and some moderately interesting things about it.
One is the story; it focuses heavily on narration and while unique, it moved too quickly, shoved too much dialogue into your face, in my opinion. Some levels are fun to run through and explore, but I quicky got tired of running through woods and similar looking locations. For some reason the game felt much longer than it was. Well, it was rather long to begin with. A LOOOT of "you need to go here! now here! now here!" around the town, and often times "it's right over there! there's just something blocking your way so you have to go around!" . Like, a lot. It became old fast. You also lose your weapons a lot, recurring trope. There are plenty of characters but... almost all of them are annoying and I didn't care for any of them. While Alan isn't a bad protagonist, if I have to hear him yell "ALICE!" one more time I'm gonna flip.
The difficulty is weird too, i found myself dying constantly even on Normal, but i perservered. It's hard to dodge when enemies all have endless throwing axes and run up to, often surround you, from behind and all other angles. Controls themselves were okay, but the silliness of just how short the battery life is in this world made me wish they had them last longer, and you just found fewer batteries. Personal preference though.
Ultimately...while the story is unique and it's not terrible, I'd really only recommend it for fans of psychological thrillers or decent 3rd person survival shooter types that aren't purely action. The story is unique, yes, but I mean that in a sense of "it doesn't sound like any other story i've heard of" not "it's really good". It was okay. Not my flavour of narrative, the speed at which Alan sputters out his lines, and the constant jerking around with the player making me constantly confused as to what was even happening til near the very end. Plot points were flying by left and right, and well, if you miss something, they probably won't go over it much again.
It's not a bad game, I just don't think it was for me. The frustration with difficulty and combat mixed with the meh characters and only decent plot idea yet in-your-face way of telling it jus wasn't my style, so I really couldn't think of enough good reasons to recommend it, that's all.

If you played the original Half-Life mod that was Natural Selection 1, NS2 is going to feel very familiar. There are quite a few small changes that improve the game in quite a few ways, but all the elements that made the original fun are still there.
For those unfamiliar with the title, NS2 can easily be summed up as a "Starcraft / Counter-Strike hybrid," with the theme basically being Terran vs Zerg (though they're called "Marines" and "Kharaa" respectively). It mirrors RTS titles like StarCraft when one plays as the a team's Commander, being responsible for expanding the base and upgrading tech for the entire team. Instead of ordering around idiotic NPC units, though, your 'units' are controlled by the rest of your team. Teammates build up their own resource pool by getting kills and completing tasks, which they in turn use to buy weapons and tech (marines) or evolve into more powerful lifeforms (Kharaa).
The teams play very differently but are very well balanced (in my opinion). If you liked the original, there are plenty of good reasons to check this out, and if you never played the original NS then there are still plenty of good reasons to check it out.

Oh the horror! And I meant the state of the game. Alan Wake is a third person horror adventure game that focus heavily on the story rather than gameplay. However, I personally find it hard to digest the story as the plots are not interesting or anything near spectacular. I do admit it gets to me at first but halfway through the second chapter you have literally seen or have a taste of what the game has to offer 'cept for more dull plots.
The gameplay is linear. There are no decisions to make, consequences to face, brain cramping puzzles or even quick time event (yes I am getting desperate here) to give me the jolt of excitement. You traverse through the game via planned and crampped route with enemies to fight from places to places. The weapons are limited with some additional supporting side gears which makes all combat pretty straight forward once you get your strategy right for the first time!
Conversations are dull and while it seems the protagonist is in a dire situation he sure doesn't sound like one. The combinations of the above points only makes this game good for a single playthrough but you will need to play it at least twice to unlock all the achievements.
However the developers did do a couple of goods to the game such as unannoying soundtrack and effects. Plus they did throw in two additional episodes for free!
But all in, Alan Wake is still a decent game that does not deserve a NO. If you are in a mood for a softcore horror game, you can give this a try.

Game trailer had so much promise, an old style point and click adventure, finished chapter 1 ages ago now and was not overly impressed. That being said I had thought that the target audience would have been older, the trailer let me to that conclusion as well, and even the game appears to have a more adult over-arching plot.
The puzzles all seem ridiculously childish and you don't get that feel that something is amiss, which it is. To be honest, I expected more from the mind of Tim Schafer, the man who brought us Grim Fandango, still my favorite adventure game of all time!
On the positive, the artwork is beautiful, and the interface of the game was pretty standard, but that is by no means a bad thing.
This review could so easily be turned around by a more adult part 2 of the game. Its missing that dark theme that something like Grim Fandango had, and more smart puzzles, not the terrible ones the majority of puzzle adventure seem to be having today.
My recommendation...when part 2 of the game comes out (if it ever does) and you read that those problems have been fixed. BUY IT, Tim Schafer is a really talented man who I think just needs a reminder of what people really want. Not the childish puzzles of his Psychonauts, but the engaging and heartfelt story of his masterpiece, Grim Fandango

Review as of 10/21/14 (and you'll understand why I included the date shortly)
In brief, Wasteland 2 is a mostly-awesome Kickstarter (TM) funded game tainted by some very bad decision making.
The game picks up where its predecessor left off, you are recruits for the Desert Rangers, a peace-keeping force in a post apocalyptic Arizona.  Your peace-keeping activities involve what you, the seasoned gamer, might have come to expect of the genre:  mutants, barbarians, and insane robots.  Where this game shines is in how it utilizes these very typical post-apocalyptic tropes to portray some very realistic and human settings as well as very real consequences for your actions.
This is the most interesting development of this game.  Typically role-playing type games cater to the completionist crowd by making most every quest available and completable.  Wasteland 2 rejects this model forcing the player into branches of decisions and consequences which make other outcomes and objectives inaccessible.  Complicating this new quest model is that these decisions are never simple.  It is not a matter of choosing to save one good guy or one bad guy.  Instead the game asks you to decided from among two terrible choices.  Save this murderer or save this♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  The game gives you the option to sit on the fence for most of the quests, however, this comes with its own (often terrible) perils.
Where this game also shines is in the little details.  Specifically the writing and music, both of which are excellent.  Even the voice-acting is mostly well done.  The game also plays like a sort of love-letter to the video game communmity.  This makes perfect sense as this game would not have been possible without the financial support of the fans of this community.
The little details is also where the game falls apart.  The GUI, graphics (the world map), and combat mechanics all leave something to be desired.  Where the game falls apart is the entire last 25% of the game.  Although the game was delayed by nearly one year from its original date, and although it enjoyed a great deal of free beta testing from the Steam Early Access Program, this game was rushed to market before it was polished and complete.  The game literally falls apart at the seams in the last 25%.  This lack of polish creates nonsensical dialogue choices which makes the quests  broken.  Even worse is that the final encounters (those which shoudl be the most emotionally impactful) are broken.  In one I had to manually attack the boss to force a battle.  The final encounter is a simple matter of hacking and slashing your way to victory.  I wasted one attempt looking around for a secret way to complete the encounter and eventually realized you are simply supposed to blow everything up.  This unfortunate final encounter is partially a result of the boring combat system, partially a lack of imagination, but primarily the result of a game which should have been delayed by another year.
It is easy to say this from the arm chair of course.  In another year the game probably would have run out of funding or the audience would have moved on.  InExile has been releasing rather huge patches every week since the game came out, however, one wonders how much a skeleton crew of developers on bug-fixing duty can really accomplish.  Each patch has thus far read like a bible but this game needs a church full of bibles to make the last quarter not suck.  I included the date because perhaps a year from now, if churches full of bibles, materialize, I coule recommend this game.  As it stands I only recommend the first 75%.

Alright i'll get right to the point,  this game has numerous technical issues and often requires outside help as there is very little explanation for most missions. My only wish for this game was that the world was 'more open' and that the last 10-15% of the game felt rushed. Now that the criticism is out of the way heres what you will like.
The meat of the gameplay is the RTS [duh] which is slick, and relatively smooth but often forces the player to watch all enemy moves [forces the camera to lock onto each hostile unit] but that is a small setback. The weapons and wearable cloths look great, with a fair amount of customization [not great but decent]. The combat is fun, and challenging and for loot hoarders such as myself there is ALWAYS something to loot, scavenge, and steal. The diologue system is great, but requires characters to upgrade non combat skills which can be frusterating for some, but offer rewarding new story archs for the player to follow which are otherwise impossible. I highly recommend creating you're own ranger or two [remember to specialize them in something] and create a backstory for them - makes you feel invested in the game and makes the player care who lives and who dies.
However anyone with a heart can tell this game is a love letter to the fans who have been waiting for decades to indulge themselves within the wasteland universe. As with most love letters they at times try to hard, and on occassion written in haste. This is evident in some parts of the game [specifically late game]; despite this the effort and excruciating detail that went it to this game shows how much InXile wanted to make this game for others and for themselves. Very enjoyable. A bit in the vein of Hero's Rise, or Community College Hero, though I certainly enjoyed it more than the former. It lacks the fake-out beginning of many Choice of Games... games, and does put one right into the thick of things.
The setting is engaging, definitely reminiscent of the works of Jules Verne, (though it also reminds me a bit of the works of Edgar Rice Burroghs) the technology interesting, and the game lacks the obnoxious gender restrictions of other choose-your-own-adventure games set in the time period.  One also has some choice as to one's ancestry in this, which I appreciate, as well, and there seem to be a fair number of romantic options, though I personally went for the mysterious stranger.
I will warn that, at times, it is a bit unclear what one could do better, or how to strengthen one's various abilities, though I'd not say the game is difficult. Further, the ending is rather weird. All in all, however, the game is good, with engaging characters, an interesting pulp-victorian world, and a plot in which one at least feels one's choices matter.

The story is really simple; you're a mute dude, "Jacket", who's getting strange phonecalls that tells you where to go and kill people. Judging my my 280 hours of play time, I think you can tell how much I like Nuclear Throne.
Out of the hundreds of games I've played in my life, few have the same level of polish and fun that this game has.
Everything on offer here is amazing, the character designs are colorful and creative, the guns are diverse and all of them are useful in some way (minus the flamethrower, that gun is completely worthless.) and the gunplay is above and beyond anything I could have expected, it's so good that you can dodge hundreds of fast projectiles while gunning down dozens of enemies if your skilled enough, and most deaths feel like they're your fault. Movement is spectacular, I never feel like I'm too clunky or too fast. Characters offer surprisingly diverse playstyles, each one has a unique personality and feel. The music, while not anything I would listen too outside of the game, is still serviceable, and fits right into the post-apocalyptic universe.
This honestly applies to just me and possibly a few others, but the ability to, "Loop" makes this game for me. Being able to never really beat the game is great, and I always manage to make it a little farther each time I play, which elevates replay value through the roof.
My only problems with this game has to be with how squishy your character is, and while not a problem at all in the normal game, by Loop 2 it boils down to dumb luck as to whether or not you get hit by one of the one hit kill enemies, or whether or not you run into a bad spawn. The insta-kill enemies in loop really make some deaths not your fault, since you can spawn right on yop of them from time to time. The 30fps frame lock is annoying, but the engine that Vlambeer used doesnt't allow 60fps anyway, so I can't really complain.
Overall, an amazing game, provided me with over 200 hours of fun. Worthy of it's 12 dollar price tag, I don't think you need to wait for a sale.

Short version: this is not a great game. It will not be remembered for years to come as a high point of the genre. It will not spawn remakes and imitators. But it's still good enough, and frankly, if you like your combat turn-based and your texts long and well-enough written, you have no choice this Autiman, but to spend some time playing Wasteland 2.
Now, let's dig in to see what went wrong.
At first, character development looks good enough. For the first half of the game, you will value every Skill Point you get. Unfortunately, after that it becomes evident that character development is quite limited in Wasteland 2. You can spend Skill Points to get slightly better at hitting enemies. Or opening locks. Or disarming traps. Et cetera. But if you try to make two characters with the same specialization (say, Sniper Rifles), you will develop them in pretty much the same way. There are no ways to make a character unique: no Perks, no Feats, nothing of that sort. Why didn't the developers add such feature to the game, I can't imagine. It's not like it would require expensive voice-acting or even additional 3d models...
At the very least, they could have borrowed a page from Shadowrun's rulebook, and give special abilities or bonuses at certain levels of skill. I don't really see a need to give my Sniper 10 in sniper rifles, when all it gets me is a few more percents of To Hit chance!
Combat here is turn-based and slightly more varied, that in Fallout 2. This is all good that could be said about it. Lacking abilities, this game offers little in a way of infulening the outcome of combat in dramatic way. This is especially dissapointing after GREAT combat in Divinity: Original Sin.
In terms of combat, Wasteland 2 is far behind not only D:OS, but also both Shadowrun and X-Com. This is made worse by strange balance, which allows enemies to mostly negate all your careful placement of characters by running a very long distance in a single turn (this is not a bug: with bug, they had pretty much unlimited running range, now it's just too big).
Should you expect a great, thoughtfull story from a game that has Toaster Repair in its list of skills? I guess you shouldn't. But I still was disappointed by a pretty cliche main quest.
Another bad mark here is tired trope where heroes take about 15 minutes to solve problems which locals could not solve for years. Negotiate a peace between two warring tribes? A bit of shooting and one dialog. Convince a community to stop ritual cannibalism? Two dialogs! Now, you shouldn't probably make the player feel like they are negotiating for peace in Middle East, but this is borderline insulting.
Dialogues here are all right. Text are well-enough written and I had no wish to skip them.
Still, there are to little Skill Checks, and lack of complex trees lead to shallow experience. Compare this to Arcanum's dialogues with Persuasion...
Post-apocalyptic games, books and movies are not known for a well-tought-out worlds. They are often seem more like a zoo. "See here, children, this farmers worship an unexploded nuke; and those town took their god from an old folk song!"
Wasteland 2 did nothing to change it. Still, some are turned off by what they consider over-the-top sillines, especially in the very beginning of the game, in Ag Center. I, for one, found acceptable, but no engaging, and the rest of the game is the same. This world does not seem alive, I can't feel anything for it, it's just a backdrop for some fighting, questing, looting and trading.
RiotPixels, gave the game 78% out of 100. I think this is exactly the right score for such a game. inXile failed to make a masterpiece, but, well, it's still a good, playable game. You can spend some fine time with it. Just don't place too much hopes in it, so as not to be disappointed. I, for example, do not regret backing it on Kickstarter, and will back other inXile projects in future. I mean, what's the alternative? How much turn-based RPGs are there every year? Two? Three? Another one is good, even if it's not a great one.

I really wanted to like this game. But i can't. I love isometric RPGs and i played them all. I even replay both the original Fallouts once every three years or so. Sadly, the Wasteland 2 fails on so many levels that the few that are actually good won't save it. And the fact that Divinity: Original Sin and Shadowrun: Dragonfall came out recently and are superior on almost every level makes this game look even worse.
Combat:
Total letdown. Almost no tactial options. While in Divinity i would use my rogue to sneak behind enemy lines and start with an ability that costs a lot of AP and is therefore only useful as an opening getting bonuses from backstab as well as from attack from stealth. After that i will use the artifact and teleport my tank to the rogue and make him knock down the most dangerous foe while my mage will teleport oil barrel near the enemies and ignite it. While my tank has fire resist over 100% so the flames actually heal him.
And in Wasteland? I open with a shot. After that all my other characters shoot. Some use the weapon ability to shoot multiple rounds as it has the best dmg/Ap. Then all the enemies shoot, now all my characters shoot. When you are skilled you can try for a headshots (And that just causes more dmg, no penalties to the enemy or anything and you can't aim for any other bodypart) Sometimes you can use verticality or cover (that has been clearly added to the game as an afterthought as it is not possible in most of the fighths) And THAT IS ALL! No abilities, no gadgets, no skills, no perks. NOTHING!!!
Character progression:
There is none! You have attributes and skills. Attributes can be minmaxed as some are clearly better than the others. Skills are just your percentual chance to do stuff. You will NEVER gain new ability or perk or anything. Nothing that will change the gameplay. You will just know how to open a box better. Mainly because boxes near the end of the game are harder to open than the boxes at the beginning of the game. Yes, the same boxes...
Quickloading:
As the game desing is bad you will load very often. In fact you will memorize the loading screen very well. You see, everything is percentual and dependant on your skill. Luck based. You see a locked box with a trap and an alarm. You have 50% to disarm the alarm, 40% to disarm the bomb and 70% to pick the lock. So disarm - fail - disarm - fail - disarm success - alarm - fail - alarm - fail - alarm - success - pick - fail - pick - critical fail - LOAD and repeat.
Graphics:
Amazingly bad. I mean really bad. Much worse than Fallout 1 or 2. It is technically bad (low res textures, low poly models) and aesthetically bad (repeating of assets, assests with different textures next to each other, the same mood everywhere, the same models everywhere). You don't even have much of an avatar picture choice when creating your characters. And some of that pictures are later used in the game on other characters! The graphics are much worse than in The Fall: Last days of Gaia which is old, low budget german post-apo game from noname developer.
Story
Here it isn't bad. The story is quite good. Sadly it is told via big chunks of texts. I like to read in games. Planescape Torment is one of my most beloved games and it has much more text. But the text in that game is exciting and relevant. Here most of the things that people will tell you are things that you have already heard milion times from others. But you have to read it all because sometimes in this ocean of text there is useful information.
Choices
The choices are a mixed bag. You are often presented with multiple choices and you actually feel the consequences. That is very good. But sometimes the choices themselves seem illogical. At the beginning of the game you have to choose to save one of two settlements. Either the superimportant one that feeds all the surrounding settlements (including your ranger base), or the other superimportant one that provides water to everyone. You as a new recruit. One ranger of many. And after you do that you suddenly hear the other rangers chat on radio. How they helped to save some merchants or how they saved some cows. Yea, but they couldn't save the superimportant settlement...
Conclusion:
This review might seem too harsh but if someone asked me what game to play - Wasteland 2 or Fallout 1, the game that came out 17 years ago, i would recomment F1 without hesitation. And that tells you something about this game...
If you want to play good modern isometric RPG, play Shadowrun: Dragonfall or Divinity: Original Sin.

Baby's first tower defense. Not bad, mind you, but rather underwhelming.
The game has a couple of clever ideas and mechanics, but in the end it's laughably easy and has little to no replay value whatsoever, aside from perhaps getting all the achievements (which are mostly focused on grind, rather than skill).
The overall artstyle is cutesy and child-friendly, full of obscure references, clearly made with both kids and adults in mind. But the latter will get annoyed by it rather quickly, mostly due to repetitive sound assets. Same goes for the music, which is so terribly bland that you'll most likely end up muting it.
As for the gameplay, the puzzle-like "tower" placing seems like a decent idea at first, but sadly most of them are essentially worthless, while others are used reguarly throughout the game, making most of the levels rather tedious and boring.
It's a game you can safely give your kid to play. Other than that it can be relaxing, but you'd better get it either at a high discount or for a mobile device.

Go Home Dinosaurs! is a cartoonish tower defense game similar to Plants vs. Zombies.  Dinosaurs walk a linear, unalterable path towards their goal.  Before the start of each level, the player have to choose a set amount of cards, which will represent what the player will be able to purchase during the duration of the level.  The player uses cocounts (currency) to purchase permanent installations (gunners, traps), power-ups, and bombs (as represented by cards).  The player is mobile across the board, collects coconuts from trees, and can fire upon the dinosaurs freeley within range.  The foundations of the installations have tetris-esque shapes, which you need to fit around the shape of the path.  There are a good amount of variation of dinosaurs the players will face, all with variations of speed and armor (no attacks).  Controls are very simple, only using a mouse and a spacebar.
That being said, the game is very cartoonish, making a strong appeal towards a younger audience.  Don't be fooled though.  The later levels are very puzzling and require a good amount of finess (I stress finess more than puzzle detail).  The overall difficulty is definitely harder than Plants vs. Zombies (coming from a guy who broke level 100 in PvZ survival).  For those who really love the challenge, there are Steam achievements for completing certain levels using only specific cards.  Even with the high difficulty factor, I still encourage anyone (seriously, anyone) who loves tower defense games (or just PvZ) to play it.  It really is a fun casual game.

Does FPS finally meet RTS in a balanced amazing mix?
This game is really interesting to me for two reasons:
First of all it's a really solid FPS with tight and responsive controls.
Secondly it's a really solid RTS with interesting upgrades and fun base building.
Now that the meld of the two genres is out of the way, let's talk about how it works.
The game is centred around two asymmetric teams; the aliens and the marines. Each team has a commander who will be playing the RTS game while the rest will be the "grunts" on the battlefield and play the FPS game. As you can probably imagine this requires a lot of teamwork and communication to work properly and give an interesting, fun match. The commander definitely has the most crucial and stressful job here, where the "units" won't necessarily follow orders. That certainly never happened in traditional RTS's.
The asymmetric teams are really well balanced and the whole outset of the game just works flawlessly. The aliens are creepy and surprisingly varied in their different evolutions/classes, able to give the marines some great jump-scares by jumping out of nowhere as the invisible Fade or the many airducts scattered throughout the level.
The marines are much more homogeneous, changing weapons and armour but of course staying in the same humanoid bodies.
If you have fond memories of the Alien vs Predator franchise this might just be an amazing experience for you. The alien team can of course crawl on walls and ceilings as any proper alien creature needs to do, and the marines have large and loud weapons... by my descriptions you can probably tell which I enjoy playing more.
The first couple of games are going to be incredibly confusing, so I'd definitely recommend watching some gameplay videos beforehand.

Alan Wake is a weird game for me to recommend.  The gameplay gets stale, the voice acting can be bad at times, and the narration style initially got on my nerves.  But yet I felt drawn to finish the story the farther into the game I got.
The game makes references and commonly borrows other horror archetypes, openly stating influences like Stephen King and The Twilight Zone.  Alan Wake is himself a horror writer, but is introduced as a sort of troubled character (again, borrowing the troubled writer archetype) and is likeable enough.  The game also uses a television show structure where everything is split into chapters, each starting with a “Previously on Alan Wake” and ending with a cliffhanger.  I think this mostly works, and perhaps hints you to take a break and maybe revisit the game every few days.  Most of the supporting cast is OK, although I really ended up liking Alan Wake’s agent/friend Barry.  He’s is introduced as a scared, money hungry guy but is actually developed into a cool character.  The actual plot revolves around Alan and his wife taking a vacation after his book tour, but of course not everything goes according to plan.  The plot starts off a bit slow, and the opening tutorial section was a bit too on the nose for me, but it actually does build up some steam and by the second half of the game I really wanted to see what happened next.  It’s a pretty tight story, although I do have some gripes (mostly with the introduction of a brand new character literally 30 minutes before the game ends, and with the ending of both the main game and the two DLC “Special Features”).  If you are not a big fan of monologues, Alan could get on your nerves as he constantly talks in his head while you are walking around in game.  Initially I thought this was annoying but I grew to enjoy it somewhat.
The actual gameplay is a third person shooter with light-based mechanics.  Enemies are shrouded in darkness and first have to be weakened by your flashlight (which you can boost at the expense of battery power) and other light sources.  Once they have been weakened enough Alan can dispatch them with bullets.  The game slowly introduces new enemies, weapons, and utility items (road flares, ect) until about half way through the game.  The gameplay does get pretty tedious, even on normal difficulty, where some bigger enemies take longer to weaken and take down.  Instead of being a challenge, it just ends up feeling like each enemy is a bullet sponge.  It’s also not much of a survival horror game; there were few instances where I felt like I had to run or was low on supplies, but I’m sure on the hardest difficulty level that this will be much more common.   In terms of the spookyness factor, the claustrophobic nature of the forests of the American Northwest work their magic until about half way through the game where you start to realize you’ve seen it all and develop a good way to fight enemies. Graphically the game looks pretty good, with particle and light effects really enhancing the mood of the game.  Something I initially found odd is that real actors are used for clips found on televisions you can find.  At first I found this a bit cheesy, but as I played through the game I realized having actual actors helped sell the fiction of this universe (seeing real people’s emotions also helps us to connect to the characters, and is used in great effect in the two DLC chapters).  Actual in-game models are used for cutscenes.  The first third of the initial DLC chapter had me worried because it’s a retread of an entire section of the main game, but luckily the level design becomes varied after this starting section.  Besides the difficulty of the first DLC, I felt both chapters had great pace and a pretty decent story that continues on from the events of the main game.  They even expand on a mechanic that is introduced in the last chapter of the main game.
Overall, the gameplay of Alan Wake can get repetitive after the first half of the game, but for me the story was enough to keep me going until the end.  It’s a game that wears its influences on its sleeves, so if you are a fan of horror films or books you will probably like it.  If you are worried about the gameplay becoming boring, just turn the difficulty down to Easy or take breaks in between chapters to help break up what can become tedious.

Alan Wake and Barry Wheeler = Children of the Elder Gods!
Triple A quality third person/mystery/thriller/slight horror/ of the highest order, Alan Wake is a game that oozes confidence and quality that is rarely matched in the suspense/horror genre(this isn't so much a horror game, as it more so just included horror elements). For a game that is now 5 years old, it holds up extremely well in every way, giving newer big budget games of this genre a run for their money. The game isn't perfect, but it sure acts like it.
The Pros:
Presentation: Flawless presentation. The game presents itself in an episodic manner much like a high quality production of a television miniseries. Each episode can run up to 1 1/2 hours, sometimes longer.
Story: its fantastic.  Superb supernatural Thriller that will keep you guessing around every corner, while still managing to be light hearted and funny. the story manages to not take itself to seriously at times which was a good move by the writers of this game . I wish more games had this aspect.
Characters: Very well done, interesting characters. Each with their own personalities and slight backgrounds. Alan himself is a human person with many flaws, at times he isnt the most likable person, but this contributes well to the story. Not every protagonist you play in a videogame needs to be the most popular kid in town with an infallable personality. Alan's manager is a riot, he's straight out of a 90's movie. The townsfolk were very interesting with there own unique personalities and backgrounds, which were further explained in manuscripts you found throughout the game.
Graphics: This game is freakin beautiful. Rocky Mountain scenery and towns . Amazing set pieces. I dont think they could have done a better job with this in 2010.
Voice acting: Top notch professional quality, during cutscenes you feel like your watching a movie.
Sounds: Great diverse soundtrack that fits in with the personality of the game, again it felt like a movie/miniseries. Ambient effects really set the mood when truckin along through forests and dark areas.
Entertainment value: This game is incredibly entertainment all the way through
The Cons:
slight texture pop ins when playing on high setting.(it was minimal and only happened for objects far away)
MINOR SPOILER: A cupple very minor small things that happened story wise in the game seemed really really stupid and uneccessary, like when alan pulled the gun on sara in the well lit room , telling her he wanted to go to the lake alone. That seemed like the biggest dooch bag move in the world. she totally went out of her way to help him more than anyone in the game besides barry. I know it was to prevent her from going but it seemed so awkward and out of place. I know It was very suttle and didnt effect the story at all, but it seemed so pointless. he should have atleast tried to explain before pointing his gun at somebody like an♥♥♥♥♥hole. you dont point a gun at somebody unless you intent to use it, and im pretty sure 100% of people that played this wouldnt think for a second that alan would have shot sara.
Alan can make stupid faces sometimes.
Not much variety for enemies.
In conclusion: This game should be played be all people that enjoy third person action/adventure games with a fantastic story. I cant stress enough how much the presentation impressed me, it was perfect. this game rocks
