As of writing this, I have played 17.5 hours in to Flight Simulator X. So in my experience playing this, I will give my review. (I highly recommend getting this with a joystick, I use a Logitech extreme 3d pro, it's cheap, and it works great.)
What I like: There is no boundries to where you can go, from what I know, the whole world is your map. Each plane is almost spot on with the cockpit, whether it be gauges and where they're placed, to COMMS and Autopilot. Another thing I like is the amount of airports there are, there are about 24,000 airports, heck, it even has the very airports/airstrips in my home town, which surprised me because I don't live in a very big city at all. I've never flown a real plane before, let alone much experience in simulators, and I was able to pick up on this fairly quickly, the tutorials are easy, and not to complex, they explain a lot of what you need to know, so don't worry if you think you won't be able to to get a plane off the ground. The standard game itself has a large variety of missions, some for beginners, and some for pros. You can be very specific in free-flight, you can change time of day, weather, month, day, whatever, so if you like flying on clear days or in stormy nights, this game has it.
I could explain a lot more that I like, but I don't want to make this review as long as a novel, so let's move on.
Mixed opinions/dislikes: There isn't much negativity I can say about this game in my experience of playing, but there are some mixed opinions I still have for the game. There isn't a whole lot of planes, maybe it's because I bought the standard $25 edition, however there are some DLCs for the game that do add more planes, but they my cost you. The game isn't very fun nor immersive with just a keyboard, so it's recomended you get a joystick, it's not needed, but it will make this game a whole lot more fun and realistic.
So there you have it, it's not as detailed as some of the other reviews I've seen for this game, but it's my best. Over all, if you like flying planes and helicopters, in a pretty realistic flying simulator, this is for you. To rate this, I would give this a fair 8.5/10, There isn't a huge amount of planes to choose from, but it should be enough. I haven't played multi-player yet, so I can't really say anything about that. Anyways, thank you all so much for taking the time to read my review!
Also, I have a question you could answer in the comments, would this be good practice while taking real life flight school? Because my dad is starting to take flight school, so I want to know if this could help him learn to fly, so if any of you can say yes or no, please put it down in the comments, thanks!

Really good, unforgiving game. Would have been a great couch game but it has horrible controller support. Only one negative but its a big one.

Act 1:
The first hour of the game is pretty terrible, as there are no puzzles and hardly any user interaction, you are basically clicking your way through a cartoon and not a good one, as there is a ton of repetition. It does get better later on as the game opens up and you are allowed to run around on your own, but it still never quite captures what made the classical LucasArts adventure great.
In terms of interface it feels disappointing and like a step backward for the genre. You don't have a dialogue-skip button and can only skip full cutscenes, that makes it far to easy to skip over important content. And the lack of a dedicated view-action means you aren't allowed to inspect the environment properly. There isn't a hotspot-highlight button either. All of that have been standard parts of most modern point&click games.
Graphically the game is ok, but just barely so. The sprites all look really flat and cheaply animated (i.e. what you expect from Flash animation) and the backgrounds show some ugly pixelation when the camera zooms in. On the plus side the game does a lot of camera motion to keep things interesting and it has quite a few custom animation.
All that said, I did start having fun with the game before the end. As once the game opens up and you get a little more familiar with the characters and the overall situation it starts to feel more like a proper point&click game. If they can improve a little on that this might turn on into a really good adventure game. But compared to all the stuff Daedalic has put out this just doesn't really look all that impressive and as a callback to the classic days it kind of fails, as it feels to watered down and artsy for it's own good. It's still good enough to recommend it, just don't expect a worthy successor to the LucasArts adventures.
Act 2:
Continues exactly where the first one left off. There are no updates to the interface, graphics or anything. Puzzles are this time a little harder then before, but not in a good way. There is a lot of walking forward and backward through scenes and it can be easy to miss a critical clue. The game is also filled with time based puzzles and puzzles that require correct setup or else they reset, this leads to a lot of repetition and frustration due to the lack of proper dialogue skip. Good inventory based puzzles don't really exist and the game doesn't really do much with the character switching either. You can play each character almost completely separate from the other and outside the very last sequence they never interact.
As far as setting is concerned, act 2 reuses most locations from act 1 with some small changes. There is very little new happening here and the story reveal feels pretty "meh", as it doesn't really open up any new areas or anything. The whole mythology of that world feels pretty underdeveloped and not really explained enough. The ending feels like there would be an Act 3 to follow that plugs those holes, but there isn't one.
Overall this isn't a horrible adventure by any means and it has it's moments, but it's pretty mediocre and certainly not up to classical LucasArts quality and with all the simplification going on in the interface it feels like they weren't even trying to get there.
On the positive side: The game runs flawlessly on Linux with Open Source ATI drivers.

You can outflank and stealth and whatnot, but in the end focus fire is the main thing.

Skills and characters are bland. Just dump all points into two or three skills per teammember and over-specialise. NPC's are cardboard boring figures with no depth. Your actions do not have real consequences, it may seem like it, but nuh-uh.

In the second Act there's some reveals you might have a problem with, but for me it was the repetition of the same areas from the first game, over and over again, plus puzzles that were just kind of dull.
One complaint many have is the need to swap between characters to solve puzzles, something that didn't come up in the first Act. This is an incredibly addictive, creative, hypnotic, frustrating, annoying, challenging, surprising, way too difficult, fantastic gem of a game. It's everything that I love about video games: tons of action, lots of style, weird and creepy and funny and epic all at once. There’s an incredible amount of re-playability, with a bunch of weapons, character classes, and mutations to mix, match, and experiment with. All of the characters are cool and viable options for working your way through the wasteland, with their own unique powers and passive abilities.
Overall, this is simply one of the best examples I've ever played of the "just one more" design philosophy - the game locks you into its twisted little world and won't let go. Before you know it, you're lost in a brutal cycle of radioactive rats,  machine guns, and interdimensional police officers. Nuclear Throne still continues to surprise me, round after round. I haven't gotten even remotely close to reaching the final level, but that's okay. I've played NetHack for almost 15 years, and I've never ascended. I'm used to this sort of thing.
Now, are there any drawbacks? Sure. It's the same sort of stuff that makes any rogue-like game into a rough, sometimes alienating experience. It's really hard and it's often unfair. Be prepared to spawn right into a nest of energy-spewing scorpions. Be prepared for a very bad dude named Big Bandit to show up at the worst possible time. Be prepared to run out of ammo right when you’ll need your weapons the most. Be prepared to grind your way through a bunch of levels and narrowly survive huge battles, only to unceremoniously blow up because you accidentally shot a grenade at the wrong wall.
Yes, if you die, you lose everything and need to start all over. It’s definitely a pain and it can make you grind your teeth when you get so dang far and then lose it all. Some people may not be into this sort of experience, and I understand that. I can only encourage you to give it a try, because Nuclear Throne will really knock your socks off if you approach it with the right attitude. If you've never played a game like this before, it might be a good idea to get your feet wet with a cheaper or free rogue-like, so that you can see how you feel about some of these design decisions.

Life is Strange sat in my Steam library for a long time. Despite the recommendations from people with gaming opinions I trust, I was nervous that the game's teenage high school setting would be hard to relate to as an old fart and that I would find the game to be little more than a Dawson's Crack-esque 'I'll stare at a lake to solve all my problems' affair.
How wrong I was I was.
As soon as the calming and emotive main menu theme started I instantly relaxed and within a minute or two of  the main protagonist Max's company at the start of the game I knew I my fears were unwarranted. What followed was a beautifully paced story, told with real heart. Characters are introduced that initially appear to be one dimensional caricatures, but soon reveal themselves to be much deeper and rounded, making early decisions taken in the game much more complex than they initially seemed. I frequently found myself overthinking things as critical choices came up, second guessing the potential motives of nearly every character.
The soundtrack and visuals massively contribute to the atmosphere and several times I wished I could just wander around the town of Arcadia Bay soaking up the Autumnal Oregon setting. Coupled with the many references to films such as The Breakfast Club & Bladerunner, not to mention games like The Longest Journey series and Bioshock Infinite, I felt that this game was really pitched at me as an adult and not the younger audience that I thought it was aimed at.
There is no doubt that some people will bounce off the game, the character Chloe can be very diffiult to relate to initially and I can see that some people would dismiss the game very quickly as a result. For me however, the game got under my skin and after the inevitably tough climax I found myself thinking about the game for days afterwards, about  the story,  about the characters and the effect my choices had on them. The start of chapter four will stay with me forever as a powerful piece of storytelling I think, something that very few games I've enjoyed in the last thirty odd years have been able to achieve.
A beautiful example of intelligent interactive fiction, hella recommended.

Lootboxes don't hinder the gameplay like people think, but it's still a crappy system, and does take the game down a notch.  But that's not really what this review is about.
Instead, I can't recommend this game because of the sorry state of Act 4.
.  It feels like an early access game: unfinished.  There is literally no dialog in Act 4, and no exposition at all, until several hours later at the very end.  You don't even talk to orcs anymore when you dominate/shame them.  All they had to do was play the 'real' ending after Act 3 and have Act 4 be an epilogue open world mode, and it would have felt complete.  Instead they have you run 20 missions with no dialog or story behind it at all.
The actual gameplay is mostly improved upon from Shadow of Mordor.  They added depth to the skill system, and the gear system.  They did not, however, do anything to improve the targeting system, which has led to the most frustration I've ever experienced in the series, because now there are even more skills to use that can target the wrong thing.  I've even had multiple instances of Talion attacking in literally 180 degrees opposite of the direction I'm holding.
Unless they patch in some story to Act 4, get it on sale for $20 or less.  All the way up until Act 4 I thought this was superior to Shadow of Mordor in every way, but after the steep drop that is Act 4 I think the sequel is now merely on par with the original.  Monolith seems to always drop the ball at the finish line.

**UPDATE 11/14/17**
I'm changing my review to negative and here's why. I'm in act IV, which has just become god awful now that I've played it more, and I'm trying to defend one of my fortresses. The final warchief I have to kill to end the siege will not die. He's just some berseker captain, but his health regens almost immediately after I take any of it away. He gains health back faster than I can take it away. I must have tried hacking away at him for 20 minutes before I gave up and quit without saving so the siege would start over and I could try again, hopefully with a different result. Well, I just finished my second try, and had the same result, except this time he killed me and was promoted to overlord. So now an orc that is impossible to kill is overlord of the fort I have to take back, and basically I can't progress anymore. I pour almost 40 hours into the game before it just breaks on me right before the end. I have not found any solution, so as it stands right now, my game is broken and unprogressable, and as long as it stays like that, my review will stay negative.
*TLDR at bottom*
First, let me address the microtransaction marketplace that so many people are leaving negative reviews for. Just ignore it. Do not buy anything from it. Do not boycott the game itself, boycott the shady practice of having microtransactions in a single player game. Buy the game, support the game, but do not buy those loot boxes.
Now for the actual game.
This game is absolutely MASSIVE. In fact, I'm enjoying this game more than I enjoyed the first one. I'm writing this review the day after I stayed up until 4:30 in the morning without realizing it; there's just so much to do and I've been addicted.
Building my orc army has never been more fun. The countless and unique interactions you have with each orc makes for some hilarious, or sometimes infuriating encounters. Some orcs will serenade you before you attempt to slice them into bits, others will taunt you as you come back for another attempt to kill them after they killed you once (or twice, or three times).  The nemesis system has returned and it is bigger and better than ever. Each orc captain has their own strengths and weaknesses that you sometimes must exploit if you are having trouble killing them. If you play your cards right, fights with orc captains can be ended in just seconds. Once you start building your army and getting more followers, you'll get ambushed, betrayed, and sought out by the blood brothers of the orcs you have slain. There's nothing like getting betrayed, getting betrayed again, getting ambushed, then having a blood brother come for you all at the same time. And yes, things like that actually happen. Another addition to this game are the siege battles. You must build your army and take over the fortress controlling each of the areas in the game. Each fort has multiple warchief and one overlord that you must defeat before taking over the fort. There's nothing more satisfying than having the warchiefs' entire bodyguard force betray them and kill them so you can breeze through the fort easily. Alternitavely, you can hunt down each warchief before the siege and either kill them or make them your spy, which in turn decreases the fort's level and defenses to nothing. This being pretty much the game's main focus, it needed to be good, and they nailed it.
Combat feels great, seamlessly countering and slashing through a mob of orcs is as smooth as ever. The new skill tree allows for a slew of different combinations you can create and TONS of skills you can choose from that keeps combat interesting and always badass. Shadow of War feels much more like an RPG, with its skill tree and new gear system. You can pick up gear of various rarities from killing captains. Each piece of gear changes the appearance of Talion in game, which is great, however his appearance in the cutscenes always remains the same. Climbing is still present, and traversing Mordor Assassins Creed style, swiftly running and climbing up and across buildings is fun and feels good.
Shadow of War picks up where Shadow of Mordor left off, so I would recommend you play that before playing this, or else you'll have no idea what is happening and why. With the forging of a new ring, Talion and Celebrimbor must grow their orc army to bring Mordor into the light, and defeat Sauron. With the help of Shelob's visions, Talion must stop the Dark Lord's forces from taking over Minas Ithil. However, with a traitor in the midst of Gondor's forces, Minas Ithil falls, and so becomes Minas Morgul. This is where the game really starts. Now, Talion must use the ring to dominate orc captains and build his army to take over the lands of Morder and put an end to the evil. Thats really as far as I can go without giving away too much, but I will say there is quite the twist somewhere in there, and I am really enjoying the story.
Act IV kinda sucks. Basically, you have to defend every one of your forts from a very high level attacking army. This means grinding to upgrade your fort and to increase the levels of your followers. The inclusion of this into the game is just obnoxious.
I have been running on the highest graphical setting with a solid ~60 FPS. I have had no crashes and no bugs or other problems minus the one time I fell through the map and died and some stuttering here and there. The game looks and runs great
I love this game even more than the first one. There is TONS of content in this absolutely massive game. The nemesis system is spot on, the combat is great, the RPG elements are a very nice addition, and the story is interesting. Act IV holds it back a little bit, but not so bad that it completely ruined my experience. ABSOLUTELY buy this game, especially if you enjoyed the first one. 8/10

This game is simply amazing.  The graphics are top notch--assuming you have a decent rig--and the intricately woven plot compels the player to advance the story.  Aside from visuals, The Witcher 2 is also aurally pleasing: well-composed and orchestrated music, exvellent implementation of ambiance, and truely astounding voice work comprise the game's sound.  There are, however, little short-commings that may turn the casual gamer away.  For one, combat can be downright brutal in its difficulty--much akin to PS3's Demon's Souls.  You have to earn your kills, and you have to utilize patience and cunning to succeed.  Also, enemy targetting can be a bit cumbersome at times.  As a result, commands often fail to execute when precision timing is required, such as casting a spell upon retreating from an enemy, because running away can often deselect the targeted foe.  However, avid RPG fans will easily overlook these short-commings and find themselves a truely rewarding play experience.

If you love kinds of mystery, you should find this interesting.
::: Story :::
The story is a bit hard to get a hang of, I was confused until I was in the middle of the story, where everything started to reveal themselves. Nice story with twists here and there, and keep me wanting to see more till the end. However, I personally think that it shouldn't end where it is, just a little bit further would be nice !
::: Visual and FX :::
The game looks nice indeed, you can play as vanilla or enhance it with tool of your choice, sweetfx for example. One thing to look for is that the game use a lot of light FX, i mean, tons of them. (as the game concept is based around the light and the dark) If you have problem with dynamic lighting fx, feeling dizzy from looking at them, you might not enjoy the game much.
::: Gameplay :::
The overall gameplay is okay, the unique combat system, light the darkness then blow it away, is fresh enough to be enjoyable. however, I was expecting that it would be more of the adventure, but instead, it is more action-oriented game. I don't mean that it is bad, but the game will throw enemies at you along your journey to the level that it losts its charm as mystery-themed game.
Most encounters give you choices, to fight or to run. You can blast everything in your path with whatever at your disposal (tools, weapons, or even world's interactive objects), or avoid the encounter (if it isn't forced you to fight in the story), you can perform a timed-dodge, or even knock enemies off balance to get away from harms. The game utilized checkpoint system, when you reach it, the pursuers will be disappeared, and believe me, you will strive to get to it than stay and fight (especially in nightmare difficulty on your 2nd playthrough).
Encounters are well-designed, though they lack of visual variations (you will see them again and again). Almost all of them can be staggered, which will give you some breathing room for whatever reason. They will surprise you from time to time (on your first playthrough).
Your first playthrough will be a good experience, but on your 2nd or 3rd one on Nightmare difficulty, which you will be forced to play if you are intended to 100% the game, will become quite a task to finish, if you are the go-loud type. The achievements can be annoying (collect 100 of easily missed bottles), refering to the guide can help, a lot. It is fortunate that the game is in episodes, and can be replayed later.
The control is responsive and is good enough to allow you to face multiple enemies at once without too much troubles, although sometimes it is too fast XD.
::: Overall :::
The game is good. The designs match the concepts, however, they seems to think that more actions are better for this kind of games, but really, they are too much. It play nicely from the beginning to the end. I recommend this for a single playthough, as it lacks of dynamic elements, making the game predictable. 2nd or 3rd playthough will be more like archievement runs.

TL;DR - Is this the best game ever? No. - Should you still play it? Yes!
Review for Act I
------------------------
I first played Broken Age on iPad before playing it a second time on Steam. It is a wonderful point-and-click adventure, exuding the old-school charms of games like "Day of the Tentacle", with which it shares its creator, Tim Schafer. The compelling story and artwork make it one of my current favourites. Can't wait to see what's in store for Act II, the sequel announced for 2015.
Review for Act II
-------------------------
Finally, the 2nd act of Broken Age came out and I had time to play it. This time on iPad instead of Steam. I started from the beginning of Act 1 and in hindsight, it was the best decision I could have made. Many puzzles and concepts of Act 1 carry over into Act 2 and make a replay necessary, unless you remember what you did in Act 1. A waste of time, some might say, but I think it was worth it.
The 2nd Act picks up directly where the first left off and is really just that, the second act of one whole game, and not its sequel. Frankly, I was surprised to see relatively many negative reviews, and I think this was exactly one of the reasons why it came to them.
You can play the second act as if it were a separate game, or a sequel, but be prepared to get frustrated with overly tough puzzles and disappointed by the plotholes. Some of the latter make the second act feel quite rushed. We get a glimpse of a potentially very interesting backstory that sadly remains very vague and leaves you with many open questions. However, the little snippets you get while playing are enough to fire up your imagination (and spawn a torrent of fanfiction if you're so inclined).
Without spoiling too much, let's just say that yes, the puzzles are harder than in the first act and yes, the story might be a bumpy ride sometimes, but Broken Age has nevertheless managed to become one of my favourite games and one I would gladly recommend to anyone who loves a classic adventure... Just remember to start from the beginning ;-)

10/19/2014. At least 100 hours of actual play time clocked as of this review.
Might not be for everyone, but it's a good solid game. Requires a decent amount of time investment. 8/10
YOU MIGHT LIKE THIS GAME IF
- You like creating custom teams
- You like long rpg games
- You like tactics games
- You like post-apocalyptic themes
WHAT I LIKED ABOUT THE GAME
- Character creator is in-depth enough.
- Combat is decent enough.
- Decent difficulty level. You don't get to just breeze through everything. You need the right stats and the right items to accomplish certain parts of the game. Really makes you be observant of your environment.
- Your characters don't become overwhelmingly powerful. You always have to be careful and employ some degree of strategizing (e.g. unit placement, wepon equipment, team composition).

- Story is generic, but engaging enough.
- Your characters stats and skills are actually useful. There's a skill called "Fix Toasters"... and it's actually useful for something.
- Gives you the option to add notes to your quests (which already have a decent description). These can be helpful to remind yourself about what you need to do or what course of action you may want to take when tackling a quest.
WHAT I DIDN'T LIKE ABOUT THE GAME
- Mainly UI issues.
- Item management could be better, but it's nowhere near game-breaking.
- Some rare glitches with the screen scrolling. When in combat, sometimes you can't scroll the screen. This can sometimes prevent you from clicking on your target. You have to wait for an enemy to attack you before the scrolling kicks in again. I'm sure it can be fixed with an update.
- Sometimes, I felt like some of the missions/quests/storyline dragged. But, it was rare and may be expected of long rpgs.

It’s a slow, slow game.
Yet, Wasteland 2 has so much to offer. The second half of the game is an immediate improvement in quest and map design and features interesting factions and story choices. The second half opens up a lot more, giving you less directed main quests and giving you a good amount of freedom to solve your way through side quests at your own pace.
The roleplaying aspect of Wasteland 2 is great. Designing your specialized characters and seeing how they make their way through a story with real consequences offers a good deal of replay value.
If you are patient and give Wasteland 2 the time it needs to show its potential, it will be a tremendously enjoyable experience. Time definitely worth investing.

Wasteland 2 was one of those games that really speaks to older generations of games. There are many good as well as bad design features, but overall it's an enjoyable experience if you're willing to put yourself through it.
Upon starting up your first game you create a party of four Rangers and can choose their stats and skills, select character appearance options, and write a quick bio should you so desire. Of course, one of the things that is limited by the standards of old crpgs is that you can't play your character too far off the path of the desert rangers, but still the story is interesting and features a lot of unique ideas that might just get you to crack a smile.
Now there is a ton of dialogue and text in this game, but of course that means a lot of conversation options come up time after time. You'll find your self clicking things to get them out of the way, and of course sometimes this can get you into confrontations without any clear indications. Since I like to schmooze my way through many of these it was kind of annoying that there werent more options to use the skills associated with conversation, but at least they were there.
The combat mechanics were probably the most fun. I played this game at the second highest difficulty on my first try and didn't have too much trouble. There are some frustrating things, like enemies walking 150 tiles across the map straight up to your characters on the first turn and punching them in the face, but so long as you're prepared you can usually deal with this by lobbing out grenades and rockets. That being said, there are plenty of different weapons to take advantage of and they are all useful and unique in different ways. Some character stats are more useful to combat than others, so it helps a ton to diversify your party because the situations that arise require different skills and weapons. Some enemies are tough to take out with light weapons, but easy targets with energy guns, and vice versa.
As a piece of advice you will be binding quick save to the key closest to your keyboard hand, and pressing it often. There are times where it is not always clear what you have to do, and if you do them in the wrong order you can get into situations like endless combat for HOURS before you give up and reload. It's truly unfortunate that unorthodox situations do this to the player, as it feels restricting at times. I remember early in the game trying to expedite a mayoral race, and did as many helpful tasks as I could save for one that I could not find. Turns out the doctor, who said he didn't need any help, actually needec you to use your surgeon skill on his patients... seriously? I spent hours trying to figure this out before looking it up.
Another gripe is that you will spend hours just walking across maps, for no purpouse other than you're going back and fourth for quests. There are sometimes ways around this that open up after having done enough to open up a quicker passage, but usually by this point it doesn't even matter anymore. You'll experience this enough to come to hate the experience. You'll be getting out your chair to find something to distract you for three minutes while your party walks around, and sometimes you have no idea if where you're going is going to help your quest. Truly this was the most frustrating aspect of the game.
Yet another thing, many characters have the same portraits, even important ones at times. I really wish that they had taken the Baldurs Gate appreach and only gave important characters unique portraits. And the portraits, they look like they were painted by a college student. They werent bad, but felt lacking. Sometimes it made the characters you meet less unique, as they just sort of blend into each other.
Now it might seem i'm going off on the negative aspects of the game, but these are things you should know before you start playing. It's by no means perfect, but hightly enjoyable. Comparable to Shadowrun Returns, where as shadowrun had a really focused story and an enjoyable simplicity, Wasteland 2 has a very big and diluted feel with explosive chests falling out of the sky and arguably more interesting combat mechanics and a big world.

FSX + All DLC = $2,530.63 USD. Did you know the most expansive and beautifully detailed flight simulator is free? It displays actual images of the earth taken within the last few years. Yeah. Google Earth. Didn't know Google Earth had a flight simulator? Just load Google Earth and press Ctrl + Alt + A. It's fun to just fly around with amazing detail. If you are looking for a much immersive experience, sure FSX can help you there just don't expect graphics of a current generation triple A game. Another thing, this isn't a game. This is a simulator. Moving forward.
FSX doesn't sport the glamor that Google Earth can muster, not even close. To be exact in a detailed way, FSX is largely outdated. It makes up for the sounds, details to physics, weather, AI, multiplayer and the single player missions are well rounded, fun and interesting for plenty of hours of fun. But....but I've always just loved flying for the scenery. All of the current 137 DLC items available on Steam equals a total cost of $2,530.63 USD. Majority of items are single aircraft downloads that cost an average of $20 USD while larger city packs or even single planes can cost you over $39 USD.  Is Steam overcharging for all the available DLC? Eh, you decide. I've flown with plenty of people where the hub is a particualr city, which, then we just downloaded a mod that we all had in that particular server but I don't know how things are done this day. Everyone must be paying crazy amounts for just one city. Eh.
Having DLC of one city at the cost of $25 USD is a bit greedy, and besides, the game is about flying and if anyone in charge of the Steam FSX DLC prices has ever flown in a plane, you're not over a city that long. Sure I'd pay for the DLC that make the game look more detailed and photorealistic but FSX is a massive world and as for DLC scenery, it only affects one location (on that massive 1:1 scale world known as Earth) because, well, it's the entire world. And is $25 USD really worth a change in a single tiny location? Why not just download all the DLC for $2,530.63?!? (Please, don't take my money).
I just can't seem to stomach the price tags of any FSX-SE DLC to be honest, cause even a tree pack is $12 USD. (cough*mods*cough) Maybe it's just the way I fly because I prefer to "hop" my flights VFR from field to field spanning wilderness and mountains, over rivers and canyons Let me continue.... 137 items at $2,530.63. SMH.
Moving on. FSX isn't your average "game" because it is actually a "simulator." Multiplayer? For anyone who has been with FSX since the end of GameSpy we all went to dedicated servers or hosting/connecting. So I'm only sure FSX-SE multiplayer connectivity will be swarms of F-18's flying fast as possible thru any controlled airspace from the grass blades to the heavens edge.  Or the frequencies will be jammed with "maydays" every twenty minutes clogging ATC landing/take-off priorities... I don't miss that, that's right.
FSX was not a "game" to me as I had binders of printed pages all printed off
or my personal VFR map

(or something)....
This is a simulator, it is the "steam edition" and this truely is all about "flight." Maybe even some over priced DLC. So yeah. Microsoft Flight Simulator X: Steam Edition: Over-priced Downloadable Content Option. Enjoy! (cough*mods*cough)

Life is Strange sat in my Steam library for a long time. Despite the recommendations from people with gaming opinions I trust, I was nervous that the game's teenage high school setting would be hard to relate to as an old fart and that I would find the game to be little more than a Dawson's Crack-esque 'I'll stare at a lake to solve all my problems' affair.
How wrong I was I was.
As soon as the calming and emotive main menu theme started I instantly relaxed and within a minute or two of  the main protagonist Max's company at the start of the game I knew I my fears were unwarranted. What followed was a beautifully paced story, told with real heart. Characters are introduced that initially appear to be one dimensional caricatures, but soon reveal themselves to be much deeper and rounded, making early decisions taken in the game much more complex than they initially seemed. I frequently found myself overthinking things as critical choices came up, second guessing the potential motives of nearly every character.
The soundtrack and visuals massively contribute to the atmosphere and several times I wished I could just wander around the town of Arcadia Bay soaking up the Autumnal Oregon setting. Coupled with the many references to films such as The Breakfast Club & Bladerunner, not to mention games like The Longest Journey series and Bioshock Infinite, I felt that this game was really pitched at me as an adult and not the younger audience that I thought it was aimed at.
There is no doubt that some people will bounce off the game, the character Chloe can be very diffiult to relate to initially and I can see that some people would dismiss the game very quickly as a result. For me however, the game got under my skin and after the inevitably tough climax I found myself thinking about the game for days afterwards, about  the story,  about the characters and the effect my choices had on them. The start of chapter four will stay with me forever as a powerful piece of storytelling I think, something that very few games I've enjoyed in the last thirty odd years have been able to achieve.
A beautiful example of intelligent interactive fiction, hella recommended.

I have about 72hrs logged in SOM and I love that game. I have really been looking forward to SOW with many new features. I have to note that I have not completely finished the game because the ending cinematic is hidden behind a grind that is just not worth it for me. The last stage is fortress sieges over and over and over again... I would have understood defending each of your fortresses once, but the way it's designed is very grindy and boring. I quit after finishing stage 6 of the Shadow Wars. This just seems like a way to push you towards the micro-transactions, which I hate in a single player game. I have not accepted the EULA for the marketplace during my entire play-through and the game really tried to push me into it with many warnings and notifications.
PROS
+ Better loot system
+ Armor customization and looks
+ Skill system
+ New enemy type (olog-hai)
+ New captain types and encounters (singers, ambushers, blood brothers...)
+ I have not experienced any crashes (opposed to what other players are experiencing)
CONS
- Controls are sometimes inconsistent (especially the double jump distance seems to be very varied)
- The armor and weapons you wear does not appear in the cut scenes (it always reverts to the default armor)
- There are very little new animations and models (gets repetitive very soon)
- The micro-transactions / loot boxes
- The same dialogues from orcs (which can fortunately be disabled)
- The Shadow Wars stage grind for the ending cinematic is way too long and in my opinion not worth it
In conclusion SOW is not a bad game, it just doesn't bring enough new features like SOM did. I will not even be finishing the Shadow Wars stage and rather watch the ending cinematic on youtube. The Shadow Wars stage seems like a wall put in the game just to force you to use micros-transactions.
I can not recommend it for the full price, just wait for some sale or until it gets to the price of SOM (GOTY edition can be had for ~5€).

But all the storyline in between where you need to fight really made me butthurt; here are the issues:
1: Glass windows.
This feature always makes me want to break my PC not only because it allows your enemies to see and shoot you clearly, it also alters their attitude. One second you could be looking at them - nothing happens - the next second you have been shot down and everyone on the map is hurdling towards you.
2: Enemy accuracy and collision detection.
I have had moments where enemies sometimes shoot or swing in the opposite direction and guess what? My brains are all over the floor. Or the inpenetrable walls sometimes become paper mâché and all bullets shot come right at me. Nothing more to say.
3: Enemy spray paterns and accuracy.
While it is significantly easy to kill your opponents, some of them pull a 6th sense and know where you are. Another thing is that you either have to have Graham equiped or have a lot of walls seperating you in order to dodge the enemies' aimbot/triggerbot. I know they are CPUs but they should not have instant snap-to-point reaction time.
4: Cross-Map deaths
This is fairly uncommon but it still happens, your screen can't see your enemies but they can see you. Like when walking up a long hallway and shift can't go far enough, which results in you getting a surprise heart attack when your enemies jump you.
Overall I would give this game a nice 5 stars out of 5, great plot, great gameplay only a couple bugs.

Maybe from that you can already tell I will not just be talking about the base-game of Shadow of War for the whole review. Most reviewers policy is to separate industry practices from the game to judge the game "on its own merits". Well, here's my issues with that. If you are compromising the product on purpose, in order to drag the game out, or purposely tear the game apart in order for you sell us content later down the line, that is most definitely an already compromised (ethically and mechanically) product.
If WB had kept their grubby mitts of this game, I would most definitely have given this a positive review. However, since that is not what they have done, this review will remain negative.
Some in-depth analysis here. Firstly, the infamous loot box situation. You can buy orks from loots boxes, not just getting them out in the in-game world. This completely breaks in-game immersion and the economy of the game. You can either choose to ignore the loot boxes and go at it vanilla, where you're missing out on possible high-level minions, as the game was obviously intended, as the level of orks you find are introduced on a gradient; the higher level you are, the better orks you will find. Additionally, what are essentially ads for the lootboxes keep popping up in game, where you are prompted to go and buy them. Also, if you want any hope of being 'competitive' in the online game mode Shadow Wars, you'll need some super powerful orks, something the lootboxes have the slight possibility to help with.
Consequently, you will notice every dynamic in the game becomes centered around these things in some form of another:
You want an high level ork? Cough up!
You want to upgrade your weapons and armor? You'll need additional gems to do that, cough up!
You want to play multiplayer? Better have some good orks, so cough up!!
Whether the game would have been constructed like this without the cancer that is WarnerBrothers getting their claws into the mechanics of the game is completely moot.
Now, with that out of the way, let's talk about the game.
You a lord of the rings lore fan? This is going to be a rough ride.
The game, for better or for worse, plays fast and lose with the canon to such an extent you wonder why not just set this in the time of the silmerilian and call it a day. However, if you can get past the desecration of established law (which I can), the story is actually quite compelling.
Following on the last game, Ranger Talion and his ancient dead elf-friendo Calimbrimbor have made a new ring of power, just like Saurons. Great! What could go wrong. Turns out quite a lot actually. What follows is an epic, continent spanning war between the 'Bright Lord' and Sauron. All sorts of shenanigans ensue! Just don't get too disappointed if you were expecting high-brow Shakespeare.
Like Shadows of Mordor but better. Everything is back from the last game, but with added upppf. Movement is buttery smooth, and really the game plays just like every other third-person openworld, Arkyum style game. Speaking of which, the combat system is straight outta Batman, which isn't a bad thing.
Combat is fun and Talion's wraith powers are suitably beefed up from the last game.
I was going to add this to the last section however, it more or less is one of the most original ideas in the last decade in gaming. Essentially, the Nemesis system allows every individual ork to remember you, and everything you've done to them. Burn that ork captain in a fire, he might come for you later on. This is extended to the 'meta game' aspect for creating armies. Your generals might betray you, or save your life. This creates some of the best dynamic stories in gaming really. However, sometimes the betrayals get a little too common, and you'll find yourself trying to game the system in order to keep your orks on your side.
I won't say anything more, it really is something better to experience for yourself.
Not the best, not the worst. Voice acting is passable, with a few exceptions. Talion seems mostly asleep during his cutscenes, the voice actor is clearly phoning it in for his paycheck at this point. On the other hand, Calimbrimbor is the star of the show. His gravely tones are both charismatic and slightly scary, especially when he gets all shouty.
Combat noises are also quite good. Swords ring and the screams of orks will pervade your ears constantly. In this universe, all orks seem to have a slightly comical British cocny accent. You'll either love it or hate it.
Not concentrating on the poor industry behavior, this is a great game. However, I will not simply segregate them out of the review, because this stuff definitely effects the end product. Great game! But make a statement and wait for this to get to a low price. And DON'T, DON'T, DON'T buy those damn lootboxes!!

The Mountain is constantly changing and metamorphosing. When you
, it blossoms into its own experience.  And what it is, is more virtual plant, than anything else; is that a bad thing? Read on!
If you let it, the Mountain can be a soothing and relaxing experience if you need 5-10 minutes (taken) away from your life.  It's a slowly spinning Mountain in Space.  You can zoom out to see nearby galaxies and star clusters, or zoom in to fill your view with the mountain and the surrounding atmosphere.  There are so many variables that change and the changes/additions appear every 30 seconds or so, it has enough to keep your eyes trained and your mind engaged in thought.
In a nutshell: if you enjoy sitting on a bench watching nature around you (e.g., the ocean, a coast, a forest, a vista), then you will enjoy this experience.  But understand that virtual-mountain-in-space-watching is the only experience it can innately provide you.  Anything else you experience, is a result of where your thoughts and your psyche take you.  And that's Zen. :)
The Mountain does nothing in particular, but does it very well.
+Beautiful scenery/lighting effects
+Soothing audio effects
+Striking day/night cycle
+Well-done weather and season cycles
+Occasional random or pseudo-inspirational captions
+Occasional random object collisions (some can be quite funny)
+Some interactivity (POV, musical keys)
-You have to pay for it
-Surprisingly resource intensive

If you love kinds of mystery, you should find this interesting.
::: Story :::
The story is a bit hard to get a hang of, I was confused until I was in the middle of the story, where everything started to reveal themselves. Nice story with twists here and there, and keep me wanting to see more till the end. However, I personally think that it shouldn't end where it is, just a little bit further would be nice !
::: Visual and FX :::
The game looks nice indeed, you can play as vanilla or enhance it with tool of your choice, sweetfx for example. One thing to look for is that the game use a lot of light FX, i mean, tons of them. (as the game concept is based around the light and the dark) If you have problem with dynamic lighting fx, feeling dizzy from looking at them, you might not enjoy the game much.
::: Gameplay :::
The overall gameplay is okay, the unique combat system, light the darkness then blow it away, is fresh enough to be enjoyable. however, I was expecting that it would be more of the adventure, but instead, it is more action-oriented game. I don't mean that it is bad, but the game will throw enemies at you along your journey to the level that it losts its charm as mystery-themed game.
Most encounters give you choices, to fight or to run. You can blast everything in your path with whatever at your disposal (tools, weapons, or even world's interactive objects), or avoid the encounter (if it isn't forced you to fight in the story), you can perform a timed-dodge, or even knock enemies off balance to get away from harms. The game utilized checkpoint system, when you reach it, the pursuers will be disappeared, and believe me, you will strive to get to it than stay and fight (especially in nightmare difficulty on your 2nd playthrough).
Encounters are well-designed, though they lack of visual variations (you will see them again and again). Almost all of them can be staggered, which will give you some breathing room for whatever reason. They will surprise you from time to time (on your first playthrough).
Your first playthrough will be a good experience, but on your 2nd or 3rd one on Nightmare difficulty, which you will be forced to play if you are intended to 100% the game, will become quite a task to finish, if you are the go-loud type. The achievements can be annoying (collect 100 of easily missed bottles), refering to the guide can help, a lot. It is fortunate that the game is in episodes, and can be replayed later.
The control is responsive and is good enough to allow you to face multiple enemies at once without too much troubles, although sometimes it is too fast XD.
::: Overall :::
The game is good. The designs match the concepts, however, they seems to think that more actions are better for this kind of games, but really, they are too much. It play nicely from the beginning to the end. I recommend this for a single playthough, as it lacks of dynamic elements, making the game predictable. 2nd or 3rd playthough will be more like archievement runs.

All jokes, existentialism, and overly cute rhetoric aside Mountain not worth the hype surrounding it.
Mountain reminds me more of "The Fountain (2006)", an endlessly spinning self contained biome floating through space. Clouds appear from nowhere and obstruct your view of the mountain, rain or snow falls (with some Zelda-esque playing you can call down blood, hearts, coins, fire, frogs and more), Seasons change and days pass, the mountain has a an internal monoloque that displays every so often. You can spin the mountain, watch the mountain, play music to the mountain or kill the mountain. Other than that you just watch or check back into the mountain every so often to see what random items have impacted it. I say impacted but I've never actually witnessed the collision of space object and mountain. That's your entire spoiled playthrough.
I bought the game knowing what I was getting, A screen saver, a diversion,  a pretentious art piece by a student waxing long about the deeper meaning of his or her half hearted art project, thrown together at the last minute in-between beer, pizza, weed and a dead end part time job at a fast food drive through.
I wanted to like this game. I wanted to feel the zen of the universe. But I felt nothing. I ended up getting stuck on the artificiality surrounding it to the point where I wasn't able to enjoy the experience myself. Some art evokes deep emotion and memory in me. But the stories and reviews from writers so exhausted of novel subjects that they jump on this like a pack of starving wolves, bleeding each insignificant detail completely dry is just sad. I read a dozen 'reviews' by amateur story writers who were obviously tickled pink reading and re-reading their own pithy one liners and cute contrived conversations. This mountain has brought in a certain crowd of people that I mocked in art school, bested in critiques, left behind in the art industry, and finally once they came to their senses - hired to work for me.
I expected more depth to the mountain, more detail, leaves on trees, exposed jagged rocks, particle physics rather than textures, better clouds, flowing water, rainbows, wildlife, more easter eggs, just more.
For most people I can't recommend it. For those who I have described in my review, get it in spite of me.

This game is everything I want out of the Civilization series, even if a bit dated. The graphics have aged fairly well in my opinion, especially for a game from the very early 2000s. The old map-like aesthetic of the game's empire view is very nice, and the unit sprites are done very well for a game from a time with extremely limited graphical capabilities. One feature I especially love that I think shouldn't have been done away with in future Civilization games is the 'aerial view', which allows you to get an extremely detailed view of your cities.
However, even if the graphics are considered lackluster by some in this time, the soundtrack still holds up extremely well and is possibly the best soundtrack out of the entire Civilization series. From the piano-based melodies of the Medieval era to the jazzy guitar riffs of the Modern era, the soundtrack is extremely immersive and well-produced. Even some DLC scenarios have custom soundtracks, which are just as well-made as the soundtracks of the main game.
The gameplay is also well-done and it isn't too easy, nor is it too hard. The difficulty scaling in this game works well enough, and you are able to even change specifics such as AI aggressiveness, something that appears to be absent from later entries in the series. The advisors in this game are actually quite helpful and their associated menu screens allow you to easily get a detailed overview of your empire in order to best manage it. My only criticism of the more domestic side of gameplay is the way corruption works in this game; it tends to be quite rampant (especially on larger maps, and ESPECIALLY in the later stages of the game) although it can be reduced with wonders such as the Forbidden Palace and buildings such as courthouses.
Combat in this game is based off of an RNG system that works fairly well, although there is the occasional absolutely ludicrous outcome where a spearman will manage to defeat a tank. Unit promotions in this game work on four levels: conscript (the starting level for conscripted units as well as units gifted by villages), regular (the starting level for built units), veteran, and elite. Each promotion grants an extra bar of health. While much more simple than the extensive promotions in games such as Civilization 5, this system still works quite well as Civilization 3 tends to focus much more on wider-scale combat and empire management than single-unit powerhouses.
Overall, Civilization 3 is an excellent -- albeit, somewhat dated -- entry into the Civilization series. I'd probably give up both of my legs to see a remastering of this game.

Alan Wake is a story-driven, survival horror thriller. Alan Wake is a writer who comes to the town of Bright Falls for inspiration, to work on his next novel and hopefully get over his writer's block. Bright Falls is a seemingly simple town until things start to happen that only Alan Wake can explain. He wrote those things in his upcoming novel, the same one he is working on. The story is well thought, perhaps one of the finest in a long time.
The game puts you up against the Darkeness and its minions the 'taken' who can only be killed after their shadow 'armor' has been shattered. To do so, they have to be damaged by light before they can be killed. Although the game puts you up against the same enemies for majority of the game, they do tend to ramp up the difficulty and situations to make it seem fresh enough. There are few weapons to choose from and most will be using the revolver and shotgun for the most part, you can forgive that point considering the premise. Its a small town, you won't expect to find M16s or grenade launchers after all.
I recommend this game for anyone who likes survival horror and a good story.

Fallout Shelter is a spin-off 'Fallout' game that delves into the 'mobile gaming' genre. Usually these mobile games communicate whether you should be playing a lot online or leaving it to run offline, and this one can't really decide.
For a Steam port, I expected a graphical upgrade since you can really see these textures up-close, and they are pretty reminiscent of N64 games. The UI overall is actually pretty poor, I find myself struggling to put people in the right places and to pick up things on quests because the spaces are so tight and crowded. There isn't a lot of organization either, there should be some sort of family tree categorization as well as organization by chronological appearance. To use every single 'dweller' to the perfect advantage would actually require studying because of the annoying options here. There should be an option to see every weapon and outfit even if it is held by the characters.
Quests are actually fun enough despite the idea being so bland. Combat does feel slow though, and like there should be more interaction. I feel like this game would be very fitting for some strategic combat.
There is a pretty good variety of outfits and weapons wielding different stats as well as different rooms to use and some good humor as well. For a free game I can't complain, but for a free game that has been out for a while and obviously still containing issues like these I'm not really impressed. I look forward to future updates if there are any, in hopes of these small issues being fixed.

Interesting, fun game, much in the spirit of the Baldur's Gate games and the original Wasteland. Old-school, pretty long and reasonably hard, with focus more on gameplay than on graphics. Plenty of choices, lots of possible ways to outfit your party, no "right choice". You can play as you like, and are actually encouraged to do so. You may very well be locked out from several parts of the game through your choices, but that tends to happen anyway, whichever choice you make. If you really want to see everything the game has to offer, you have to play multiple times, and fortunately the game makes that a viable option as different playthroughs will feel differently.
So I recommend this game on its gameplay merits, but I have to warn new players for the fact that the game, at the moment of this writing, still seems to be in the beta phase. While it has officially been released a month ago, there are plenty of quests in the late game that may still get into an unresolvable state -- this is a consequence of the fact that the player may go anywhere he likes, and thus may get into areas that are quest-related without having got the quest in the first place. There are also quite a few bugs left which may cause a forced reload.
So my recommendation is: if the style of game appeals to you, get it (preferably in some kind of sale), but wait with playing until the bugs are ironed out. It looks like the game will get a major update soon, considering that Steam has made it clear that achievements will be added.

Enforcer is the game that X-COM fans love to hate. It breaks from tradition by being a 3rd-person shooter in an era where the game type was not popular and by changing up the way lots of the classic aliens are handled. For all the complaints about it though, it actually is a fairly fun game, if you approach it less as an X-Com styled game where tactics reign supreme, and treat it more like an arcade style run and gun game. In that respect, this is a highly entertaining game where you're granted a wide variety of weapons, upgrades, and equipment to slaughter hordes of aliens that oppose you. The nature of this game simply demands that you do not take it too seriously, which is admittedly out of place for an X-COM game. Given that you start off with a simple laser rifle and work your way up to nastier toys like rocket launchers, plasma cannons, and an entire turboprop fan grafted to your arm, you can imagine the kind of carnage you end up wading through to accomplish your missions.

What can be said about this game. I never played the first game, and never really got into it when i tried. But that does not mean i do not know of it. I watched full walkthroughs to understand the first game years before Wasteland 2 was a recent concept. Because i am a fan of the Post-Apocolyptic genre, i knew Wasteland 2 would apeal to me as Fallout's 1, 2, 3, and New Vegas has done for me in the past. This game, from what i know of as one of the bigger kickstarter projects of its time, is well worth it.
This game is not only a "True" sequal to the first game, but it also is NOT half-asses like some other abondoned Early Release titles that never were finished. Not only was thsi game finished, but the story is compelling, the charactors are likable, the voice acting is incredible, and the overall gameplay is rock solid with very minute bugs every now and again (enemy i was fighting once fell through the ground and got stuck in part of the map, kept shooting me but i couldnt shoot him, but i eventually used a grenade and got him).
The map design is great, it does get repetative having to backtrack, but at least you have a feeling of accomplishment when you get further into the story. The weapons are great, as well as the skills and leveling aspect (I can have a trained SMG guy be able to mow down enemies with a trained sniper or 2 backing him up).
To conclude, this game is great and worth the money for both a great game and a great time waster, because once you start playing, you wont want to put it down any time soon.

This game is simply amazing.  The graphics are top notch--assuming you have a decent rig--and the intricately woven plot compels the player to advance the story.  Aside from visuals, The Witcher 2 is also aurally pleasing: well-composed and orchestrated music, exvellent implementation of ambiance, and truely astounding voice work comprise the game's sound.  There are, however, little short-commings that may turn the casual gamer away.  For one, combat can be downright brutal in its difficulty--much akin to PS3's Demon's Souls.  You have to earn your kills, and you have to utilize patience and cunning to succeed.  Also, enemy targetting can be a bit cumbersome at times.  As a result, commands often fail to execute when precision timing is required, such as casting a spell upon retreating from an enemy, because running away can often deselect the targeted foe.  However, avid RPG fans will easily overlook these short-commings and find themselves a truely rewarding play experience.

----ORIGINAL REVIEW BELOW---
When I first heard about this game, I read a lot of reviews saying that this game is both challenging, fun and relaxing.
What a combination I thought, for a game with such a simple premise. Drive big russian trucks through hazardous environments to collect lumber, and deliver it to locations on the map. The game looks gorgeous, but I had to try it before I considered buying it. I went to the Spintires website and downloaded the tech demo.
I can easily say that I played the demo for more than 10 hours play time. And there weren't even any objectives in the demo. JUST DRIVING. The act of driving a large vehicle through mud, water and any other terrain the game had was fun enough. The terrain deforms in real time as the tires cut through it, this is a simulation game like no other. EVERY FACTOR MATTERS, the weight, which tires are spinning and making contact, are the tires wet? How heavy is the vehicle itself? How much is the force of the river pushing you off the road? How big is the tree you're making contact with and can you knock it over?
Seriously, this game is just an early access game and already it has so much going for it.
I bought the game and already after the amount of hours I've played it (at the time of this review (6 hours) I have yet to see the entire first map I've played and I haven't completed one objective yet (because I'm still enduring all that nature and it's mud can throw at me and my trucks).
This game is zen, it is a challenging and VERY rewarding experience for those who persist and overcome the obstacles in it. For those who look at this game and wonder, "But it's just driving through mud and getting stuck in it." No, it's about getting out of the mud. Just go download the tech demo now to see if it's for you.
UPDATE: So I finally played multiplayer.
It's great! It was fun enough to just play with one other person, so I'm sure it's great with more. I cleared all cloaks and assisted the other player while they hauled loads of lumber. It's a great co op experience. But you know what this needs? Team VS matches. Also, time trials. That would up the ante.
Got disconnected at one point when I FINALLY got to the other player to unflip their vehicle. haha

The blend of strategy, stealth, and extraordinary violence surprisingly ties together nicely and makes for a short, but quite enjoyable videogame. The story is compelling enough, but the gruesome, gorey combat is what carries it above and beyond other independent games of the sort. It's not a game for everyone, that's for sure, but if you can find it on sale (I believe I bought it for $7), I recommend trying it. Looking forward to playing the sequel.

A pretty good squad-based RTS and shooter.  One player assumes the role as a commander and deploys base assets, while the other players attack/defend control points where resource collectors are deployed, in an effort to ultimately destroy all of the opposing team's command stations.  The beauty of this game is that there are a variety of strategies.  Rounds can be dragged out so a team can develop their highest technology tree and hit harder to end the game, or you can choose to coordinately blitzkrieg the opposing team before they have a chance to expand their base or research any technologies.  The tactics are entirely dependent on your skill as a player as well as the organization of your team.  NS2 is very fast-paced, so you might find yourself dying a lot and cursing at your screen, but once you find your niche, whether it's a commander or a grunt, and learn to work as a part of a functional team, NS2 can be one of the most entertaining team-based shooters that money can buy.  It's relatively inexpensive at $25 MSRP, too.

A little undercooked but still tasty and filling.

Having played the original Wasteland and every Fallout game released, (Yes, even that one for the X-Box. You know the one I'm talking about), I was pretty much expecting a better version of Fallout Tactics with a deeper, richer story line. The result? I little underwhelming, but overall a good experience.
Tight, turn-based tactical combat with a rotatable isometric view mean that other than a few oddities that occur with objects that are "between the camera and the view," the control is pretty solid. The game rewards you for good tactics and positioning with every weapon skill having it's pro's and it's cons. You're not penalized for having a diverse team and the biggest problem of simply having a team of grunts with no real other skills is simply that a lot of side missions will be more difficult, if not impossible.
The downside... the story feels a little "been there, bought the t-shirt." And not just for a player of wasteland. There really isn't anything in this world that the game presents that genuinely feels original in any way, with the unfortunate majority of the various groups you come across feeling like someone blew the dust off and gave it a new coat of paint. Not a slapdash job though, but a loving restoration with a few embellishments here-and-there. The big disappointment was the final mission/ending. If any part felt like you'd played it before, it was this one. *sigh*
Still, an enjoyable game for Hardcore fans of the Post Apocalyptic genre, or relative newcomers. But anyone else may want to give it a miss if retreading familiar ground doesn't catch their fancy.

Crashlands is pretty fun, and I plan on playing it quite a bit more, but this game is way too grindy. It feels like I'm playing an mmo alone. Enemies can one-shot you easily, even with up to date gear. This wouldn't be so bad if they didn't also have crazy amounts of hp. It takes minutes to kill a single monster. That's a long time when you consder that you need at least 150 of every item a species drops. I'm not even considering the cost of decorating your home.
I wanted to play a harder difficulty, but i realized right from the start that the hp pools are insane, so I swapped to adventure. Starting to think I should have just gone to the easiest one. It's not that I don't like a challenge, but the time it takes to kill the monsters is just absurd.
Something else I found bizarre was the crafting timers. I'm at the level 5 set of gear, and items take over a minute to craft. What is even the point of timers like that in a single player game? I spent two hours farming materials, now I need to alt tab for 10 minutes? Silly.
It's a fun game, and I like the combat, but I don't recommend purchasing it.

In combat your options range from: Shooting, Crouching to Shoot, and Reloading. You can also hide behind arbitarily designated cover positions. If you've played XCom or Divinity: Original Sin you know this style of Turn-Based combat, and what you'll find here pales in comparison.
The AI of the enemies is basically nonexistent. They will run at you and shoot you or they will run at you and stab/bludgeon you. Upping the difficulty seems to only increase the Bullet Sponginess of your foes.  Since you have extremely limited tactical options there's basically no point in playing on anything beyond normal unless you enjoy reloading quicksaves.
Combat initiation is wonky. You can attempt to arrange your characters behind cover beforehand, but this process is extremely janky and you'll probably inadvertently trigger combat before you intended to.
There are no real characters. There's a Native American companion who has a bow and is really good at sharpshooting. She talks a lot in ham-fisted stereotypical fashion. Oh and she also has a skill that allows her to Tame Wild Animals.  There's a gruff commander. He is gruff and old. There is a ranger who is sad that another ranger died.
The entire thing feels completely perfunctory.  I got about four hours into the game and had yet to decipher what the game was supposed to be about beyond meandering from fetch quest to fetch quest.
One storyline involves doing a bunch of quests for some townsfolk. One guy's house is on fire. One guy's dog is missing. The waterpumps aren't working.  If you help the people in these quests, the townsfolk will elect a good mayor. You know she's good because she's nice to you. If you don't do the quests the townsfolk elect a bad mayor. You know he's bad because he's mean to you. There are virtually no consequences in either result. If you enjoy this kind of compelling, interactive storytelling this game is for you.

I'm a big fan of Fallout 2 and I`m very disappointed with this one. After playing Divinity:Original SIn, that was developed from the same amount of money, this game feels like a pile of junk from the hand of total amateurs.
It is amazing that you can have such a huge difference between the quality of two games that were devloped from a fairly low budged, and both were a kind of a passion/fun project. It clearly shows that Brian Fargo might had the passion but the team lacked the knowledge.
I don`t want to go into detail with my analysis, I`ll highlight only the key moments that made me turn away from this game:
- Graphics are BAD. Insanely bad. From the character creation to the envirionment, it just radiates the lack of talent on the art team. Unfortuantely for me it`s very inportant.
- Animations are BAD. Also very important for me, especially in 3d isometric style games. Fallout had great and fun animations. Jagged Alliance too. Wasteland 2 delivers just boring animations with a lot of glitches.
- Lack of tactical and strategical elements in combat. Lack of use of the environment in combat.
- Weird skill/attribute system. Well maybe this was good, or can be solved easily but for me it was unclear how the main attributes affect the skills. In Fallout 2 it was better. No special skills/perks.
- Unpolished feel of the levels and the game overall.
These are the most memorable annoyances that made me stop playing the game after about 50hours. Playing started to feel like a waste of time, there was no fun in it for me. Even though the story was quite interesting.
I`ll check back after a while, if there will be any improvements for the game, maybe it can be worked out somehow. But looking at what the competition (Larian) has to offer... I doubt that this game can be interesting any more.
If you are a fan of the genre, buy it on a sale. Definitely doesn`t worth 40EUR.

Lemme start off right now by saying that Garry's Mod is NOT a traditional game. If you want to experience Garry's Mod, you will need to download some other games as well: Mostly Valve titles. With just the base game, 90% of the content will be displayed with Purple and Black Checkerboard textures, indicating a missing or invalid texture: You will need the following games to make GMod playable:
- TF2 (Free, offers you TF2 content and a lot of mods use it)
- HL2: Episodes 1 and 2 (Garry's Mod comes with the Default HL2 content, but Episode 2 is commonly used for mod content)
- Counter Strike: Source (EXTREMELY RECOMMENDED: Most content creators use CS:S to make mods. Without this, you'll miss out on a lot of content).
In the main menu, there is a checklist of games you can load (Most are optional: But the ones I recommend will get you the least amount of missing textures).
Anyway, with that out of the way: Garry's Mod is not a traditional Video Game. It gives you the Engine of HL2, and basically lets you do whatever you want. It's a sandbox with no rules; and the modding community has created a TON of content for it, including ragdolls for posing, weapons, maps, game mods, playermodels and more.
You can play solo or with friends. You can make pictures or movies. You can play make up your own games, or play things like Trouble in Terrorist Town, Stop it Slendy, Prophunt, etc. Garry's Mod is open for a lot of fun, but it does require some devotion to get functional. The game also has a tendency to become unstable after updates, but they are fixed quickly. I can recommend GMod, but I mostly recommend it to the creative, willing to experiment types. It's not a game built for people who just follow orders; there's no main objective to complete; it's all free creativity.

Oik is a wonderful little puzzle game and is very much like the half-brother to the widely known and popular Zup! games. Despite its 'Mostly Positive' rating along with moans about it being nothing more than a clone; this game is very good on its own merit.
The only significant difference being, instead of exploding blocks to instigate the physics; you click to remove them one by one to land the blue cube in the zone. The puzzles here are far more interactive and responsive when compared to Zup! and may require you to perform several moves to complete the level which includes timing and complete precision.
The game isn't a huge challenge but there are some great puzzles within the 60-odd levels that will take roughtly 45 minutes to finish. With 201 achievements and trading cards; it's a great little purchase and a sequel would be more than welcome.

I figured it's a good idea to revamp my previous "5 word review", as it didn't quite do this game justice and wanted to add more details this time around.
Hotline Miami, the first instalment of the Hotline Miami games, is a 2D top down shooter of which the plot takes place in the late 80s, surrounding many strange incidents in areas around Miami. Based on the many movies and tv shows surrounding the drug trafficking scene in Miami of the 80s, flashy neon lights, and vivid tunes of neo 80s soundtracks set the mood as our hero, "Jacket", enters the nights out for blood as he continues his massacres, slaughtering all types of bad guys, of which most are being members of the russian mob.
On a quest for answers, Jacket finds himself with more questions, desperately inching towards the truth that could offer clarity, as he continues his illdoings for a faceless employer, who is only known to him through mysterious phone calls.
While the environments in this game generates a adrenaline-filled and retro ambience, the gameplay does not in any way fall short. Maps structured to give an oversight of what awaits in the next room leave the player assured to press for more and more reckless approaches for combo takedowns and varieties, more efficiently satisfying the thirst for blood (heh) and rewarding the player with a higher score as well.
The wide variety of weapons available to get the job done are many and are unlocked as the player advances in the game. Furthermore the player can unlock characters, which can either be achieved through completing stages or finding the masks in the stages, making the found character available for the next stages. As with each character, they have their own special ability. Some can kill people with one punch while others can blend into the background, making themselves unnoticable to enemies which pass by and many, many more skills that can come in handy in more effectively taking out targets.
But where there's the feeling of invincibility in each approach, as the player ever so often dives into rooms filled with baddies, there's also the fairly high frequency of deaths, over and over and over again. While the opponents' random and glitchy reactions might be frustrating at first, it rarely ever reached the point of straight away rage quitting the video game but rather pushes the player to give it yet another go, yet another shot, to go even more recklessly into the stages and annihilating every brute that stands in the way and coming out on top.
All in all, I think this title hit the nail when it comes to being a challenging yet fair video game, where the gameplay, the general ambience and plot works together to turn this game into an addictive and satisfying experience.

Having just finished the main campaign for Alan Wake, I'm struck by two things. One, I need closure! And two, what a damned well made experience of a game.
It's simple, the story is well written, the graphics are nice, the settings are well realised, the gameplay is straight forward. the characters are good and the town is a great backdrop for the story to unfold. The tone of this game is pretty spot-on. You can have scary jump scares one second and then feel totally empowered the next as, you fight the "Taken." The mystery of what's happened to poor ol' Wake's wife at the beginning of the game had me gripped. And of course, what the heck is happening in the darkness?!
I'll try and keep this brief. It's a thumbs-up! There may be some moments of repetition in the gameplay, but, if you pace yourself, you'll enjoy this game like a good book. I haven't played "The Signal" or "The Writer" DLC episodes, yet. So, I may update this review when I do.
However, there is one glaring issue that definitely annoyed me. Framerate issues. When running the game full-screen, it could sit around 135fps or so. However, there were times when the framerate took a nosedive to 18fps...frequently. It was pretty horrible and it's also sad to see this flaw in the game, 3 years after it came out on PC. And, it definitely took away from my experience at times.
But, while this problem occurred a number of times, strangely, it didn't happen everytime I loaded the game up. I can't explain why it only happened on some occasions, but, I just know that it did. Go figure.
Other than that, it's a classic. Can't wait to jump back into the DLC episodes (free with the PC version) and see what happens next. Again, a BIG thumbs-up!
