Yes, as I post this I only have 3.7 hours on record. That does not exempt me from understanding the vast improvements from Mafia II to this game. The cinematic sequences alone are worthy of their own movie. Almost 4 hours in and I feel as though I'm only scraping the top of the barrel. Without further adue I shall do my pros and cons (apparently that's standard now)
Pros:
-Storyline is excellent
-Action so far is great
-Graphics (even with the 30fps lock) are pretty decent
-Using a logitech gamepad is easy and makes the game much more enjoyable
-Did I mention the storyline?
-Cinematic sequences are amazing. Maybe I'm post patch, but my fps counter goes well above 30 for the cinematic sepuences and they look amazing.
Cons:
-There were times when the dialogue seemed forced. As in they created lines of dialogue to push into the next chapter. Wasn't as smooth a transition as I would have liked.
-The frame rate is locked in at 30fps, which to me isn't a huge deal (I'm running an R9-380) but never-the-less I would still like that uncapped.
-The default controller setup is for an XBOX One controller which I do not have. Wish they would build in some software to recognize what kind of gamepad the user is using.
-Lincoln Clay's hair totally white dudes hair. Which is kinda funny because at the beginning they mentioned Lincoln's dad is probably white. I feel like they inserted that dialogue because they are inable to recreate a brother's hair-do in their engine.
Overall, I think this is an awesome game. I saw alot of reviews comparing this game to GTA V. This is not a Rockstar game. I don't understand how people could even compare the Mafia series to GTA. They have completely different dynamics and are in completely different time zones. If you want to play this game thinking its a GTA based in the 60's don't buy it. This is a continuation of the Mafia series and it is very well done. I'm thoroughly enjoying it so far and I feel like I will continue enjoying it for weeks/months to come.

This is definitely an old style game, meant mostly for people who loved the first Wasteland, the first two Fallout games, and  generally people that played computer videogames in the 90s. It does seem to try and trade off aesthetic quality for some kind of nostalgia feeling that in a way condones how the game looks and moves on the screen, and how some aspects not only seem rough and unpolished but even not finished.
Those that think they're gonna buy an RPG with this game might be let down to find out that this game feels and plays more like a Desperados game than an actual RPG, except the tactical aspect is shallow waters, and moves like crouch and headshot are practically never used: you end up doing a little more than spamming attack on the enemies. There are stats(which, oddly enough, do not affect your skills, so how much charisma you have counts nothing on how good a barter you are or how well you can persuade, and so on), dialogues and choices but the game ends up boiling down to a turn-based shooter, where non combat skills and attributes don't count as much as how many points you have put in your shooting skills.
Too many times i felt that a certain situation should have hadthe possibility of being dealt with with wits and a good dialogue, since dialogue based skills are there for the characters, and not just circumstantial fights. You can SOME times select a Hard♥♥♥♥♥Kiss♥♥♥♥♥Smart♥♥♥♥♥answer that will gain you some advantage, but it simply isn't worth spending skill points on three separate things you will be using so rarely along the game. It often feels like those alternative options were not YET implemented, because of time and resources, and not just not meant to be there at all, but that is just a feeling. Which makes some situations kinda awkward to play..
It also needs to be stated that the game needs 21GB of free space on the hard disk, and patches come at sizes of more than 1 GB, which is kinda hard to explain for a game of this nature, since there aren't many cinematics at all and a lot of the dialogues are text-only.
In the end, though, the game is ok and even fun to play, especially for those that are feeling nostalgic. It just seems to rely on the nostalgia a bit too relentlessly.

Ultimately, Wasteland 2 is an average game that scratches a particular nostalgia itch for many gamers and is receiving praise beyond its merits.  Quite frankly, the Turn-based strategy genre has been in a drought for nearly a decade and fans are dying of thirst to the extent they'll lap up contaminated water riddled with disease and ask for seconds.  They're so enamored with a sub-standard product they don't recognize they're dying a most dishonorable death from dysentery.
Combat - The combat is lackluster and is not tactical nor strategic in any sense of the fashion.  OK Corral gun duels might be more appropriate, except slow and with none of the skill involved.  If you want a game with good combat, just replay XCOM2012 or Xenonauts.
Character building - No skill tree, no perks, nothing to be found except redundant skills to simply dump your stat points into every time you level up.  If you're looking for the complexity and fun of a D&D style character sheet, keep looking.  If you're looking for a Fallout perk system... keep looking.  Even Diablo 3, which the avid fans of W2 seem keen to mock, has a far more indepth character building system.
Story -  Glaring plot hole at the beginning of the game that most people seem to overlook or simply not notice.  Even if you look past that, the only clever aspect of the entire game is the little Easter Eggs you'll occasionally find.  However, finding kitty litter, a condom, or big black didlo for the 15th time is just sad.  It's funny the first time, but like any good joke, you have to know when to quit effing telling it.  If you want a game with a good story, reboot Mass Effect, BG, Fallout... pretty much any other CRPG.
Characters - Easily forgettable and none that will be remembered.  No Minsc & Boo, HK-47, Commander Shepards, Irenicus (best villain ever), Tomi Grin Undergallows etc.  No Delita or Ramza to be found here.  For the most part, they're as bland and lifeless as the Arizona wastes you'll wander around for the first half of the game.
Exploration - Some of the environments are interesting, but with the terrible combat and random loot, much of the fun is taken out of it.
Graphics - The game wasn't trying to inspire us with graphical prowess or eye porn, but what it delivered is unpolished and ugly.  Some will argue it's stylistic or gritty, but to each their own.
Sound - Ok, but no gripping musical scores to be found here.
At the end of the day, everything W2 set out to do has been done before (obviously), but done far better.

Lets cut to the chase shall we? Youre here looking to see if this game is ball or if its worth you hard earned steam munnies. I wont sugar coat it honey, these are simple facts.
When it comes to survival, it is a little lacking unless played on harder difficulties. The fact that you get 4 team mates to help out means you can distribute the skills accordingly so no skill-based action will be difficult. You've got your basics skills: your doctor, your blowey-uppey guy, you smooth talker, and your hackey-stealy guy. Basically if you could make four Fallout characters at once. Not to mention the game hands you extra characters that have the skills you thought were useless (get to the native american girl, you'll see) and there ya go. Free pass. In fact the only reason you may lose a fight is if you sold all yer loot for a badass pistol so you can kill even MORE people in 1-2 shots. Food is nothing, and water is not hard to find. literally. its the easiest thing if you allocate more than 3 points to your outdoorsey character.
Next the fighting. Like i said before, 1-2 shots if you dont miss. This is changed alot by the difficulty, and reloading, but in all honesty those of you actually using this review to see if you want to buy the game will not be starting on sooper-gawdmode-h4x level. The fighting is simple and repetitive. the only changes are a cycle between four-five level schemes per fighting area and the enemies fought. oh theres some big toads that steal yer guns beeteedubs. so theres that. But when it comes to this game, do not buy it for the fighting.
On to gameplay. This game is a good immerser, regardless of the simplicity of it all i felt actually effected by decisions i made in game, and you do not get long before you start getting those decisions. The story thus far is decent, but i havent beaten the game quite yet. ill get back to ye on tha one m8.
Graphics, dont even. they are okay but you know.... just okay.
Lets Recap:
Survival: 3/10
While you may have to skip things because you dont have the skill, you could come back later. Water is abundant, food is unneccesary, and health packs are literally everywhere. Unless on a harder difficulty that is.
Fighting: 4/10
While sometimes fun, it gets quite dull and repetitive. Dont be surprised when you inwardly/outwardly groan when some foamy mouthed bandits decide to try and jump you with STICKS without taking into account that you are all wearing armor made of super-metal. Just keep that mouse hovered over "Sneak past em m8"
Story/immersion: 8/10
The story is well written, the choices are set in stone and there is normally no wrong answer. with side quests everywhere you can always expect to have one or two things to do at one time.
All in all, if you're looking for a good action story in which you shoot da baddies, then go right ahead and click that buy button. The story is quite literally the only reason im rating this up, but by no means is it a bad game.

I have a love hate relationship with this Shadow of War game.  I want to like this game and there are moments where I find myself enjoying it but the sad truth is I secretly despise it.
I think the Nemesis system is a great concept and adds a sort of spice that you don't get from other games.  Most orcs you meet are different in some way shape or form but I started finding them recycling content earlier than I expected.  I thought their concept of attack and defend fortresses was great but was lacking in design.
You pretty much only do three things the whole game.  You go through the prologue, you raise an army, you defend your forts.  THATS IT!  Thats all this game has to offer.  And its all not mixed together its all just different parts of the game.  You can siege other players forts but it becomes repetitive.  The ending of this game is a joke it straight infuriated me.  I felt I breezed through story missions in less than five minutes, which added even more of a grindy feel to the game.
The combat and the controls were straight garbage imo.  It all felt extremely clunky.  The "A" button is like your bread and butter for most movement in the game but will not recognize the way I wish to go or will straight take me in another direction.  It feels like they took the combat straight out of a Batman game but decided not to refine it.
If you can ignore the clunky controls and the grindy repetition then perhaps you will enjoy this.  The game has character I will give it that.  Lets face it nothing is more satisfying than beheading or cleaving an orc in half.  But I don't think that character is worth investing $60.00 to deal with. Wait for a hell of a price drop. For those worried about in-game purchases they really don't matter at all.  You get silver at a really stupid rate in the game.  I finished the game with over 70k in silver and only used the silver to upgrade my forts and replace orcs I had lost.
P.S.  Why do you give skill points after level 53 when there are no more skill points to gain?  Its really annoying to see that I have 9 unspent skill points but nothing to invest them in.  And that you keep reminding me that I have unspent skill points -_-

I really thought I was going to play this game and love it, but it's disappointingly bad. Especially after looking at all the high ratings it has pretty much everywhere. I'm not even done with "Episode 2" and I'm thinking about putting it down for good.
First of all the combat feels awful. If you need to create distance between you and some shadow things, you can't outrun them even at a full ♥♥♥♥ing sprint, so I have to wonder why there's an option to sprint at all, because you'll turn around and they'll be right on your♥♥♥♥♥waiting to take a swing. This makes fighting more than one mob a headache-inducing experience because the only way to make distance is to backpedal and shine your light, hoping nothing comes up from behind or you don't have your back to a cliff. Alan can't seem to load his weapon and run at the same time even in life threatening situations, which adds to the clunky feel of combat all the more.
Doing something as simple as exploring is tedious because every time you think about looking for some scraps of paper or coffee you're thinking how annoying it will be to deal with those shadow people that will undoubtedly ambush you 10 times while you're searching. Part of the fun I have with games like this is the exploration and getting a chance to look at the atmosphere, but maybe that's just me. But no huge loss, I wasn't really reading those papers anyway, because some of them are only available on nightmare difficulty, so it feels ultimately pointless because you're not going to collect them all the first time through anyway.
"Boss" fights are a cake walk, especially after having to deal with being swarmed every time you take 2 steps in the woods. The boss doesn't really make you feel threatened or limited because there always seems to be a huge crate full of seemingly endless ammo refills sitting around, which you can pretty much stand next to and take a breather because the bosses don't do anything special other than teleport around and make themselves easy targets.
The game feels the need to start a new chapter(or "Episode") with "PREVIOUSLY ON ALAN WAKE..." as if you were watching the new episode of a TV series, even if you just finished the last chapter and started the new one without delay. Oh yes, I really needed a refresher on that thing I spent the past 30 minutes doing. Thank you, that was necessary. Couple that with ridiculously bad typos I've found while bothering to read all of the signs I come across and I feel like I would be embarrased to have to admit I was a writer for this game.
Finally, you can't at all identify with dear Alan. He's just kind of an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ "celebrity" special snowflake who acts like everyone around him is a nuisance, including his wife, so it's really hard to care what happens to either of them. I genuinely have no drive to finish this game.

SoW is a wonderful sequel to Shadow of Mordor in everyway imaginable. Better combat, better perks, better gear, better story, more content, etc. But as much as I really enjoyed playing it for ~30 hours before i got to the end game, the end game was so unbelievable frustrating and awful that I couldn't even finish it. As a completionist, this really hurts.
One of the main points of this game's story and gameplay is fortress assaults and sieges. They scatter them throughout the game, but sparingly as they get quite dull if you do them too many times in a row. This was really well done as they are scattered. But then you get to Act 4 and everything takes a turn for the worst. This is the end game, the epic conclusion to the story and thats where the game hits you hard and punishes you for all your time and dedication. At this point, theres literally nothing else to do except for the fortress sieges unless you somehow never did any of the side quests (most of which unlock useful perks and are fairly interesting in their own right). I only got to Stage 8 of the Shadow Wars, but at this point, you've done 10 sieges back to back and have 3 more to go before you can progress further. What makes this even worse than the fact that you have to grind so many sieges in a row (which get incredibly boring and frustrating) is that if you lose any of them, the fortress gets taken from you and you have to assault it again to get control just to continue the story which will, of course, involve redoing the siege you lost.
Now, i'm not usually one to quit when things get long or hard, but this was just a horrible slap in the face after spending 30+ hours playing and loving the game in every way. All of this, just to try and finish the game which did not need such a drawn out ending. If you want the get this game, then please come in with the expectation of not completing the story unelss you want to do the very long grind of Act 4 just to see the story come to an end. If you come in for everything else, then you will really enjoy this wonderful sequel that I wish I could praise.

Well, it's playable, bug free, and a neat concept. I can give it that. For the first two chapters the atmosphere is really nice and the game is fun for awhile longer. But that atmosphere fades into monotony. And what you see gameplay wise is what you get. For the whole rest of the 9 hour game...
So... early on in the game it talks about horror stories and horror novels and one of the quotes in particular it holds up is about the allure of horror stories lies behind mystery and the unknown. It's actually kind of funny, because about halfway through the second episode it basically tells you exactly what's happening. The unknowns become knowns and you're no longer trying to escape a  horrible mysterious death... You're just trying to save the damsel in distress. Alan Wake must be a pretty terrible author because all the characters he wrote are flat and all the plot twists are arbitrary and uninteresting. Without spoiling it the whole crux of the plot is something that would be best used as a final twist rather than revealed early on OR it should have been expanded and executed better. It feels as if the choice of setting was to give the writers maximum freedom in cramming every cliche hook in horror stories possible. A good example of this  is
It's really disappointing because Remedy has proven they're capable of better with Max Payne 2. They had five years to make this game so there's really no excuse.
The gameplay again is decent... for the first two hours. It gets repetitive, fast. You shine flashlights on thing to break away the darkness, then shoot them. Okay neat. Now enjoy that for the entire game. There are a total of 4 weapons (5 if you count both shotguns), 2 items, and 6 enemies. You're introduced to all of them right quite early save for the flying objects. Have fun and follow the yellow dot on the radar. Oh and get the collectibles too if you want. There is very little besides cutscenes to break up the monotony of the combat. What few "puzzles" the game has are pretty much all Skyrim level easy and take about a minute to solve. On the plus side you never really have to worry about getting stuck, I guess. But even playing the game 2 hours a day for a week it got monotonous. God forbid you marathon it.
Overall, the game is a playable, passable, and acceptable third-person shooter. But that is all it is. Alan Wake is the definition of mediocre. Just another game with a good concept and hype that simply didn't have the execution to live up to it.

Shadow of War is a bad game. That's not to say there aren't elements to be enjoyed, but this is not a game I would recommend to anyone. The open world structure cribs from a well known formula blending together elements of Assassin's Creed and Batman combat. There are hidden collectibles, side missions, plenty of diversions to keep the 100% gamer occupied. The nemesis system feels novel and well motion captured. The story is even interesting at times but again,
The reasons I loathe the game are many, but largely stem from what the game refers to as "Act 4". The game enters pure filler mode, forcing you to repeat tedious after tedious defense missions of which you have already done 10+ times. All the while the game is ramping up the difficultly to starve you towards purchasing their in game loot boxes in hopes of getting better gear or followers. It feels shady, slimy, and shameless in the game's attempt to force the player toward a pay to win strategy in the second half of a game that players are likely 15+ hours invested in. The worst part is that the story feels like it has no payoff, making that 2nd half grind feel meaningless. It is a disturbing trend of making the player feel gimped and marginally getting better equipment, the value treadmill is in full view. Much like the NBA 2k games, the difficultly seems less due to player skill than the game arbitrarily gating the player to make them spend more money.
A minor issue that might disturb some players is the game's almost fetishistic approach towards violence. Often the game has extreme close ups on enemy faces right before monster is savagely executed. As in, the on screen character is on their knees, the enemy's eyes will swivel directly toward the camera and deliver some parting words directly before their head explodes. The game humanizes these fantasy races while utterly destroying them in an inhuman fashion. It is a video game but the lingering extremely zoomed in views of the gore is a little sickening at times.
All these things aside, I had fun playing Shadow of War. Mindlessly repeating certain actions, stealth sequences, gathering collectibles is a fun diversion. The game just holds on a little too long. It is very obviously padded out with no real content in the second half. The game just feels unfinished, the story heads towards a climax and suddenly disappears never to be seen again.
If you still want to enjoy the blend of Batman Arkham style combat with an Assassin's Creed style climbing/stealth, at least wait for the game to go on sale. If you buy the game let me forwarn you,

If anything, Alan wake is a brilliant instance of storytelling. The plot is dark and obscure and you go through the motions with a permanent sense of dread that keeps you on edge without overwhelming you in typical survival horror fashion. The atmosphere inspires true fear of the dark and you find yourself drawn to lights that shatter upon your arrival. Puzzle-solving is satisfying and punctuated by fight-or-flight situations that require you to have your wits about you. More importantly, the thrill lasts throughout the whole game and you find yourself as invested as you would be in a good mystery novel.

The cinematic sequences alone are worthy of their own movie. Almost 4 hours in and I feel as though I'm only scraping the top of the barrel. Without further adue I shall do my pros and cons (apparently that's standard now)
Pros:
-Storyline is excellent
-Action so far is great
-Graphics (even with the 30fps lock) are pretty decent
-Using a logitech gamepad is easy and makes the game much more enjoyable
-Did I mention the storyline?
-Cinematic sequences are amazing. Maybe I'm post patch, but my fps counter goes well above 30 for the cinematic sepuences and they look amazing.
Cons:
-There were times when the dialogue seemed forced. As in they created lines of dialogue to push into the next chapter. Wasn't as smooth a transition as I would have liked.
-The frame rate is locked in at 30fps, which to me isn't a huge deal (I'm running an R9-380) but never-the-less I would still like that uncapped.
-The default controller setup is for an XBOX One controller which I do not have. Wish they would build in some software to recognize what kind of gamepad the user is using.
-Lincoln Clay's hair totally white dudes hair. Which is kinda funny because at the beginning they mentioned Lincoln's dad is probably white. I feel like they inserted that dialogue because they are inable to recreate a brother's hair-do in their engine.
Overall, I think this is an awesome game. I saw alot of reviews comparing this game to GTA V. This is not a Rockstar game. I don't understand how people could even compare the Mafia series to GTA. They have completely different dynamics and are in completely different time zones. If you want to play this game thinking its a GTA based in the 60's don't buy it. This is a continuation of the Mafia series and it is very well done. I'm thoroughly enjoying it so far and I feel like I will continue enjoying it for weeks/months to come.

I figured it's a good idea to revamp my previous "5 word review", as it didn't quite do this game justice and wanted to add more details this time around.
Hotline Miami, the first instalment of the Hotline Miami games, is a 2D top down shooter of which the plot takes place in the late 80s, surrounding many strange incidents in areas around Miami. Based on the many movies and tv shows surrounding the drug trafficking scene in Miami of the 80s, flashy neon lights, and vivid tunes of neo 80s soundtracks set the mood as our hero, "Jacket", enters the nights out for blood as he continues his massacres, slaughtering all types of bad guys, of which most are being members of the russian mob.
On a quest for answers, Jacket finds himself with more questions, desperately inching towards the truth that could offer clarity, as he continues his illdoings for a faceless employer, who is only known to him through mysterious phone calls.
While the environments in this game generates a adrenaline-filled and retro ambience, the gameplay does not in any way fall short. Maps structured to give an oversight of what awaits in the next room leave the player assured to press for more and more reckless approaches for combo takedowns and varieties, more efficiently satisfying the thirst for blood (heh) and rewarding the player with a higher score as well.
The wide variety of weapons available to get the job done are many and are unlocked as the player advances in the game. Furthermore the player can unlock characters, which can either be achieved through completing stages or finding the masks in the stages, making the found character available for the next stages. As with each character, they have their own special ability. Some can kill people with one punch while others can blend into the background, making themselves unnoticable to enemies which pass by and many, many more skills that can come in handy in more effectively taking out targets.
But where there's the feeling of invincibility in each approach, as the player ever so often dives into rooms filled with baddies, there's also the fairly high frequency of deaths, over and over and over again. While the opponents' random and glitchy reactions might be frustrating at first, it rarely ever reached the point of straight away rage quitting the video game but rather pushes the player to give it yet another go, yet another shot, to go even more recklessly into the stages and annihilating every brute that stands in the way and coming out on top.
All in all, I think this title hit the nail when it comes to being a challenging yet fair video game, where the gameplay, the general ambience and plot works together to turn this game into an addictive and satisfying experience.

This is a game I would say is 'well directed' as opposed to 'well designed'. For example, the opening cut scene and extended tutorial sequence are exceptional. The person who designed the first two hours of the game is an individual possessive of extensive knowledge with regards to narrative composition, intertextuality and era-feature modal delivery. The gameplay itself, from visual direction point of view, is also sublime. Shooting someone feels real; your victims squirm and writhe and even taunt you as they die or suffer. This is exceptional as it makes the player shocked at both what they have done and what their character is doing. Blood, lighting, city design - all amazing. (The sky-box is perhaps the only exception as it is 1990s bad for some reason).
However, while exceptionally directed, gameplay has not been designed as well. There are many examples but perhaps the most significant one is when you start a mission on a boat, surrounded by gunmen being shot at. There is no way to take cover (you're in a boat) and the boat itself is slow to accelerate away. The game is flush with design-flaws like this, everything from your character changing position in a room following a cut-scene to mysteriously coming into the possession of a lantern when you did not have one in the previous second. Basically, the game looks, sounds, and feels exceptional - the hard parts were done extremely well. The easy parts however, like where to put bad-guys at the beginning of a mission, were sometimes (not always but often enough to warrant mention) elementary-school bad.
Never-the-less, context-specific disappointment aside, this game is a good game and definitely worth the price compared to other games of a similar price. Also, the game has recently unlocked 60fps. I personally did not mind it at 30, but that does not mean others weren't annoyed by the low frames so I'm glad that this oversight has been fixed.

For my money this is still the best Civilization game in the franchise (I have played every one extensively, with the exception of Civ V brave new world). After this entry the focus became less on society building simulation and more on micromanging increasingly Byzantine (pun intended) resources and minmaxing to hit various win conditions. Civ III is the last one you can really just chill and play however you like without regards to whether you win or lose and still have fun with. Complete is required, the vanilla Civ III had tons of balance issues.
I also like how in III the civilizations have a hint of individual flavor without being locked into an identity. After this game the wrong combination of civilization and starting position could be really killer, in this game it just means you don't have as much of an edge. There are some unique units that can be really game changing depending on the situation you are in when you hit them, but ultimately it's still very situational. I recommend playing around Monarch level for a good mix of challenge and relaxation, below this level enemy civs don't develop enough to make decent trading partners, above it they start with such an advantage you're scrambling to play catch up until late in the game.
For fans of old school civ, this is the game you want.
(Note I probably have played several hundred hours of this game, but mostly before Steam even existed).

Shadow of War takes its predecessor and improves almost every aspect of it. Though it was a short experience, I was a huge fan of Shadow of Mordor. So how could I possibly give Shadow of War, admittedly an overall better game with an even longer experience, a bad review?
A lot of people have had issues with performance and bugs, but in my time I haven't had a single crash and every bug has been very minor.
The key bindings for this game are a bit ridiculous simply due to how many there are, and the controls can be fairly annoying at times (executing the wrong orc, jumping on the wrong thing, etc)
But the main reason I gave this game a negative review is simply the microtransactions. Yes, I am completely aware that you do not have to purchase a single microtransaction in order to beat the game, but the game is intentionally designed to be a painful grind in its later stage so that you are encouraged to spend money in order to speed it up. Imagine if a game like Skyrim or The Witcher, instead of providing unique quests and opportunities to gain xp and better gear, forced you to complete the same task over and over, while also constantly hovering purchasable xp boosts and loot chests over your head. Instead of ending the game, Shadow of War forces you to grind for hours in order to unlock the "true" ending, so every task becomes a chore you must repeat over and over in order to get enough experience. Online modes such as vendetta and fortress assault are fun for the first few times but also become a chore later on, making it so if you aren't willing to spend money, unlocking the end isn't even worth it.

I have beaten Alan Wake multiple times on Consoles, so i think this review should suffice since there are practically no differences. The Port is great.
Alan Wake is a game that nails Atmosphere, Gameplay and Story. (most of the time) What else do you expect from Remedy? They are known for polishing their products to absolute perfection, even though Alan Wake sounds like it was in development hell for awhile and people thought it wouldn't even be released.
You play as Alan Wake a famous writer on vacation at a place called Bright Falls, Alan with his Wife, Alice stay in a Cabin on the lake and then that is how it all begins. Literally saying anymore than that is enough, there is so much to enjoy with the narrative that it is absolutely astounding. Each "Episode" of Alan Wake works exactly like a TV Episode, with a clear goal for the episode, a journey to resolution, trying to survive the events of the episode, or hell Alan trying to explain what is going on. The writing for the most part is top notch, and the greatest thing about it is that it never breaks suspension of disbelief like others have done. For example, the Alone in the Dark remake. The best part of it for me is a short pause between episodes basically saying "Take a break, get a coffee, kick back and relax to some music before you play the rest", basically letting the episode mentally settle in your mind instead of grate as section after section feels more arduous than the rest like other games.  It does this better than any other video game i have ever played.
The Atmosphere is really nailed by the Twin Peakseque scenery and it cements the bright falls setting into your memory, you'll remember the coffee shop, the police station and all of the old timey american establishments. You can tell that whoever was the designer for the Environments actually went to the god damned coffee shop and said to himself, how would i portray this or this or this ingame? The same with the forest environments, although it does get a bit iffy particularly during the 3rd Episode and can seem a bit like too much woodland with nothing inbetween because your practically in the wilderness.
The Gameplay is Fun, but its nothing mindblowing. Personally i think American Nightmare handles it a little better as well as adopting a new style for the game, but i'll talk about American Nightmare once ive replayed it again. The game works on a basic life system, regenerating when your in the light and slowly regenerating in the dark. The battery system is a bit more interesting, forcing you to use a Flashlight and Gun in combination to defeat the enemies, or using a flare gun to flatout do both with an explosive effect. (Never neglect to use a flare gun, they can save you when your being attacked by birds, bigger enemies and poltergeists.) There is a nice variety to the weapons and your given variety often enough so that combat doesn't get boring. (Which personally i think American Nightmare really excells at exciting weaponry.)
Great soundtrack, often minimal at times it settles in when it needs to hold up the episode and is especially prevelent at the Beginning of the Game and at the end of the game. The third party tracks are pretty solid and i like to go back to listen to them from time to time. Poets of the Fall do most of it but even all of the music played inbetween the episodes is great.
All in all, considering how cheap the game is you might want to pick up Alan Wake first and if you enjoyed the game like i did finish it on Nightmare and consider American Nightmare.

When I first started playing Crashlands I didn't think I'd like it much truthfully. Still it was sent to me as a gift from a friend so I chose to give it a fair amount of time before deciding if I would continue playing.
This decision became sort of a non issue the more I played. This game is a time vacuum. If you enjoy grinding this game has it in spades. I'm usually not a huge fan of an over abundance of crafting in games but this game seems to pull that off quite naturally.
The game gives you the ability to track the progress of the next item you want to craft in the main UI. Speaking of the UI, you can also disable\enable the HUD with a single key.
I appreciate a game in which everything or at least many things can be done with only the mouse. You can harvest lots of materials using only the mouse here and do decent in early enemy encounters. It may be a good idea to grab the keyboard for hotkey button use if you need to employ more bombs\stuns etc though.
The gameplay loop & mechanics are something I'm a fan of as you've surely gathered by now. There is an odd sense of humor present throughout the story of the game that feels quite charming at times.
The crux of the plot is quite simple: repair your ship to make deliveries on time. Things just seem to spiral out of control as you attempt to do this the simplest of tasks. That's okay though, how else would adventure find us?
In addition to the entertaining story you craft hunting trophies, fish, plant crops, & raise domesticated monsters.
One of my main issues with Crashlands is that you can only assign 4 items at a time to the hotbar.
In a game with lots of bombs, buff potions, stun items, & more this isn't near enough space to assign keys to items you may wish to often utilize.
Fantastic game.

I've been playing Wasteland 2 and feeling a little disappointed. It's too retro.
The pacing is on the slow side, and it's not the best-looking game.
OK, it's set in a post-apocalyptic wasteland, but character designs and backgrounds can still look good. Like, the environments of Bethesda's Fallout 3 were dramatic and beautiful even if they were all drab gray ruins. My performance should not be this poor for a game that looks like this.
And the skill use is just a touch too slow. If one needs to save-load-spam to get past a lock, or if there are a lot of mines to disarm, it's tedious.
And the combat does not feel as dynamic and tactical as, say, the X-Com remake's. There's really only 2 options: headshot and burst, otherwise one crouches the team and shoots and that's it for tactics. X-Com's system encouraged much more movement and flanking, as well as having special abilities by class that affect tactics. And of course, Divinity: Original Sin introduces a lot of tricks with spell interactions that can control the battlefield, or that rapidly move characters around the battlefield. Compared to X-Com and D:OS, the combat in W2 feels primitive.
Also, it REALLY needs formation options. It's damn tedious having to individually click on the characters to spread them out before triggering combat. Most of the time I just have them clustered up non-optimally because I can get away with it, but it would have been nice if there were Baldur's Gate style formations. If there is an option for this and I'm just too slack to find it in the interface, please, tell me.
If I hadn't played Divinity: Original Sin or X-Com, I would probably really enjoy Wasteland 2. It's still a decent game, but it feels like D:OS just does it better. It's prettier, the combat is more fun, the pacing is better....
Wasteland 2 feels like there was a little too much old-school thinking limiting their design decisions.
And some of the mechanics just plain feel WEIRD. Like how disconnected attributes are from skill use. Or the way energy weapons work with armor. There should NEVER be a situation where it's better to have lower armor, that's just dumb.
Plus there are too many skills that cover similar things like lockpick + safecracaking, 3 skills all covering dialogue, etc. Do shotguns, rifles, sniper rifles, smgs really all need separate skills? It ought to just be small arms, long arms, energy weapons and heavy. It seems COMPLETELY random that toaster repair requires its own skill.
Normally, I'd still recommend this game as it's still above average, but there are SO many great games out or soon to be out; I would hold this purchase until it's on sale.
I'm frankly astonished at how many people seem to love it. I mean, it's okay, and I'm still going to finish it, but they write like they love it. Did they not also play Divinity: Original Sin, an also crowdfunded game that is superior in nearly every way? I loved the old school rpgs too (the Fallout games, the Infinity Engine games, the gold box games), but a great deal of the good feelings around this game seem to be driven by nostalgia more than what it actually delivers.

Combat in Alan Wake was nice and refreshing. It was a nice touch that you simply can't shoot your enemies, but have to decide how to take on a pack. While the selections of weapons in the game was modest, you could use them to great effect. I fell in love with the way dodging works in this game, and it made defensive evasion - something that people often overlook in favor of brute force - a pleasant skill to practice.
This game was long, and it was good. It is definitely one of the most enjoyable experiences I've had in a long time (9/10).

Before I knew it five hours had passed is I think all I need to say about this game.
To be more specific though... it kind of feels like it reinvents the wheel when it comes to crafting/building RPG games. In a good way. There's very little in the way of tedious wait times when things are crafting and the recipes are usually simple enough not to have a whole ton of things you need to build to build things you need to build things with. If that makes sense. It's fast in other words so you can get back to smashing things.
Combat is slightly more complicated than it seems with each enemy having unique attack patterns that you need to learn to avoid. However realistically I found that since most of the big enemies could kill me outright in one or two hits dancing around them trying to get hits in is just too risky most of the time. Even a small enemy attacks so fast they can catch you off guard or between healing item cooldowns and wipe you out.
The best option seems to be to just aggro as much stuff as possible with ranged attacks and let your trusty one legged rhino-cow-thing AOE stomp everything into oblivion whilst you carry on mining stuff or chopping wood whilst dodging attacks. This is pretty hilarious to watch and somehow never really gets old. The only problem is said trusty rhino-cow isn't so trusty as to continue attacking the swarm of cosmic monstrosities following you unless you keep throwing in the odd ranged attack to keep his interest. If he kills his target he'll just run back to you and ignore the other dozen critters until you attack something too. I feel this was done deliberately to stop easy farming by just letting the pet do all the work but it can make things awkward as it is often near impossible to actually get an attack in whilst giant land-squids, butterflys and rhinos are doing their best to separate your brains from your skull.
One big issue I continually had is the pathfinding. Click to move games are never my favourite but after a few minutes of instinctively trying to WASD my way around the place I had become quite comfortable with it. Until I clicked inside the house only for my character to run headfirst into a wall for ten seconds. Try to cross any land dotted with water and it's even worse requiring constant clicks right in front of you just to keep him from trying to drown himself. This can be even more awkward in combat when you try to use a ranged attack only for him to run directly into melee range because there just happened to be a small bush blocking the shot. In a game with mouse only control the pathfinding really could do with being a bit better than this.
Having WASD as the item bar seems like a clever middle finger to traditional keyboard controls however having access to just four items can be a little limited and detrimental to the game. Two of those slots have to be taken by the wrench and blowpipe ranged weapons for practicality and the other two have to be taken by the basic food items at the moment since the cooldown is so high on them and the amount they heal so low. All the nice bomb recipes I've found are too dangerous to use until I get better healing items. I found a recipe for a HP potion but it is quite costly and currently heals more health than I actually have... and presumably will also be on a 30 second cooldown.
That said there isn't really any penalty to dying, true to the quick paced nature of the game. You can just teleport immediately after respawning to a nearby portal and are rarely more than 30 seconds away from recovering all your stuff. Whilst it may seem a little weird to totally remove any fear of death like this it really just serves to make the game more enjoyable. I can't count the amount of times in Terraria, Minecraft or similar that I've spent an hour grinding resources only to get killed by something stupid and rush back as quickly as possible to get my gear only to find it gone. In at least half of those innumerous situations I've just quit the game and got bored of it for the day.
The infinite inventory and lack of hours spent sorting through chests and juggling resources around also serves well to focus this game on actual gameplay and not a shelf stacking simulator. All of these things make it feel like a far more casual and basic game but they also make it more about action. The game is also pretty funny with great dialogue however it does concern me that it is very linear so far so I don't know that it will have anywhere near as much replay value as similar games. That said, after five hours I don't appear to have even glimpsed the end so all in all it is well worth the £10.

Serious review:
I honestly love this game! I'm a huge fan of Mafia 2, so naturally, I preordered Mafia 3.
Pros
+Map size. Not nearly as big as GTA V but at least twice the size of Mafia 2's map.
+Nice visuals. The lighting during sunsets is really nice. Some people say the graphics look blurry but I'm honestly not seeing it. I'm using a 1080p monitor, maybe they're using 4k or something. Some low quality textures here and there, but nothing too bad.
+Driving physics. In my opinion, the driving physics are excellent. This is entirely subjective, but I think the cars have a perfect weight to them. They're a bit lighter than in Mafia 2, but much heavier than in GTA. On a side note, I completely fail to see how this game and GTA V have terrible driving as i've seen people say, but I guess there's no accounting for taste.
+Gunplay. Also subjective. The biggest thing for me that makes gunplay feel nice are the sound effects and the visual feedback you get from shooting an enemy. The animations on characters when they get shot are stellar in my opinion and a good amount of blood sprays everywhere so this is pretty fun.
+Vito.
+1960s. Segregation and the civil rights movement is a theme I've always had an interest in, so again this is subjective.
+Getting cars and guns delivered to you. I just think this is a neat feature that's really handy. In GTA or Mafia 2, if you go to a mission but realize you forgot to stock up on ammo, you don't need to drive all the way to gun store. You can have the gun store delivered to you!
Cons:
-Poor PC port. The optimization isn't that great. I'm experiencing framerates between 45 and 60 and occasional hitching (mainly when entering a different district of the city)
The game has crashed twice in only 24 hours of play. Not enough to really complain about for me, but it's important to know.
My specs:
GTX 970
AMD FX 6300 Six core
8gb RAM
Windows 10
-Repetitive missions. Be careful when you buy this, because most of the missions are basically the same thing. Drive to a location, shoot a bunch of guys. This isn't a big problem for me because I love the gunplay so much, but I know it will be problematic for other people. If you decide to try this game, you may want to refund it if you think you'll get bored in after the first few missions.
-Wanted system. Mafia 2 had one of the best wanted systems. Cops would pull you over for speeding and hitting other cars. When they catch you they would write you a ticket and you could either pay the fine or run away, which would result in them chasing you down. They would also remember what you looked like and what car you were driving, so if they saw you in the same clothes or driving the same car, they would come after you. Mafia 3 does not have these features. Instead, when you are wanted by the police, you only need to escape a circle where the police look for you. They also will not stop you for breaking traffic laws unless you smash into a police car, and they will always shoot to kill, never try to fine you. I don't think Mafia 3's system is particularly bad, but Mafia 2's was waaaay better.
-Can't change clothes. Mafia 2 had clothing stores. Basically every open world crime game has clothing stores. wtf? (I beleive this is coming in a free update)
-No real vehicle customization. Mafia 2 had body shops to customize vehicles. Basically every open world crime game has vehicle customization. wtf?
The extent of vehicle customization are statistical upgrades, but they only apply to 9 preset cars you can have delivered to you. (I belive better customization is coming in a free update)
The missions in this game kind of make you feel like you're doing all the dirty work. Mafia 2's missions always have some major story element. These missions usually involve going to a waypoint and killing a bunch of guys. It's also possible to run into a group of baddies before you get the mission and kill them so you don't have to later.

Summary at bottom for those of you in a hurry.
I approached this game as a newcomer to the series. I had never played the original. So, I have no fan boy bias at all. I will probably end up comparing it to Fallout at times, but I WAS NOT expecting it to be a clone of Fallout. I will repeat that to make sure everyone understands that. I WAS NOT expecting this game to be exactly like Fallout. That being said, nobody can deny the two are similar. They’re both apocalypse’ish games that are centered on RPG mechanics.
The Good: I actually liked the looks of the game. They’re aren’t the most high definition graphics, but they do look right. The game mechanics work well when it comes to combat. I liked that you got to customize up to four characters to play as. That’s something you don’t get to see very often. The last time I remember getting to customize more than one character in a game like this is Jagged Alliance 2. The combat was pretty solid. It has some issues, but nothing that can’t be fixed with some tweaking. The sound effects were good and so was the music. Sadly that’s about where my praise for the game ends.
The Bad: The characters. I didn’t really find any to get attached to. The only character I liked was one of the random NPC characters you can pick up. Any game like this has to have characters with personality. You have to either love or hate at least some of the characters for anything to matter. Fallout 2, which is the closest game to compare this to, had great NPC characters. I just would have liked more connection with the characters. I remember going around with Cassidy (and his daughter in New Vegas) and enjoying their company. Next, there are the bugs. This game has acres of them, but I’m willing to give that a pass right now since it’s new and this is an indie developer. They seem determined to fix them, so good on them.
The Ugly: The story. I found it boring. There was no hook to it. The story starts off with you attending Ace’s funeral. Ace was a ranger and so is your party. You are tasked with the mission he was trying to complete of attaching devices to some nearby towers to track a transmission. This transmission has been transmitting some very worrisome messages. The problem with this whole plot is there’s no attachment to it. I didn’t know Ace before he was dead, so there’s no attachment to him. I don’t know the Rangers, so I can’t feel attached to them. This comes especially so when the General doesn’t let you in the main fort to get supplies. He even lampshades this saying something about it being a real dangerous mission when you ask to go inside to get supplies. You can very minimal supplies outside at a trader, but still. You don’t feel like you’re being treated like one of the group, so why should you care about them? Without spoiling anything, you get to a point in the story where some bandits are harassing the area, so you have to deal with them. Now, their camp is guarded by these huge invincible turrets. I was gratuitously over leveled at this point because I had explored every square inch of the game so far, but they slaughtered me. I was frustrated with this, but accepted it at the moment. But, on a whim, I decided to see if I could take on Ranger Citadel (the Ranger HQ). I wanted to do it just for fun, not to actually keep as part of my save. I slaughtered everyone with ease in there and the only one who posed a threat was the General. The four turrets in Ranger Citadel went down it 2-3 hits each. It made no sense that the highly militarized and organized group had worse equipment than some bandits. To be fair though, I did like the second half of the story a lot more. The second half of the game could have been the start and I would have liked it a lot more. There was more personalization with the characters and therefore the events happening in the story mattered.
Long story short: I do not recommend this game. The story was lackluster. It lacked any sort of immediate trouble in the game. There weren’t any memorable characters for me. I had the same problem with Skyrim (I know they’re very different games). They both had good gameplay, but lacked anything that could remotely be called a good story or characters. Good story and characters is pretty much 75% of an RPG.

All those negative reviews ♥♥♥♥♥ing about these various non-sensical issues are just trash.

Life is Strange is poorly animated, has childishly simple and yet still unintuitive controls, and the gameplay is almost nonexistent. And yet, through all these faults I loved the game all the way through the first four chapters.
Unfortunately, the game suffers from the awful Mass Effect 3 Syndrome, in which a game that purports to be about small individual choices comes down to one big choice in the end that completely wipes out any other choices you may have made. In a short game, this is a fatal flaw.
And it's not just the ending - the entire last chapter is a complete departure from the earlier chapters. Chapter 1 and 2 are about high school drama, Chapter 3 and 4 are an investigation into a mystery disappearance. Those are great. Chapter 5 is a psychological/supernatural head trip in which nothing is explained or investigated and must be taken on face value (the opposite of what the other 4 chapters tried to teach you).
This would have been a great game if they'd completely gotten rid of the tornado sub-plot, taken out the nightmare scene at the end, and tied things up neatly with an ending that shows you all the consequences of your other actions, and maybe has some small choices in the beginning turn out to be very important in the end.
I wish I could recommend getting invested in this game, but I felt so betrayed by the final chapter that I cannot.

For my money this is still the best Civilization game in the franchise (I have played every one extensively, with the exception of Civ V brave new world). After this entry the focus became less on society building simulation and more on micromanging increasingly Byzantine (pun intended) resources and minmaxing to hit various win conditions. Civ III is the last one you can really just chill and play however you like without regards to whether you win or lose and still have fun with. Complete is required, the vanilla Civ III had tons of balance issues.
I also like how in III the civilizations have a hint of individual flavor without being locked into an identity. After this game the wrong combination of civilization and starting position could be really killer, in this game it just means you don't have as much of an edge. There are some unique units that can be really game changing depending on the situation you are in when you hit them, but ultimately it's still very situational. I recommend playing around Monarch level for a good mix of challenge and relaxation, below this level enemy civs don't develop enough to make decent trading partners, above it they start with such an advantage you're scrambling to play catch up until late in the game.
For fans of old school civ, this is the game you want.
(Note I probably have played several hundred hours of this game, but mostly before Steam even existed).

Middle-Earth: Shadow of War is the sequel to 2014's critically acclaimed shadow of mordor, and continues the story of Talion. I will start my review by saying this, DONT BUY THE MICROTRANSACTIONS! They are a waste of money and serve little to no purpose to the gameplay. Now with that out of the way lets talk about the game.
Middle-Earth: Shadow of War is a good game with alot of improvements and also brings new problems. First, lets talk about the good things.
1. First the skill system has been overhauled, while at first it might be a bit confusing but after you get used to it, it is pretty good.
2. One of the biggest improvements from the last game is the map, there are now 5 regions instead of two and all of them are as big as the 2 regions from shadow of mordor.
3. The nemesis system has also been really improved with new mechanics.
4. The story is not the best, but its an improvement from the last game.
5. While it can be repetive, i really enjoy the combat and in my opinion its better than the last game, because enemies are now much harder and can't be exploited with one move.
6. Rewarding collectibles, unlike most Open-World games these days.
7. The introduction of fortresses and siege battles.
There are more that i certainly haven't mentioned but those are the pros in my review, now lets get to the bad stuff...
1. Micro-♥♥♥♥in'-Transactions. This♥♥♥♥♥♥has no place to be in a 60$ Open-World single-player game, not only that they have little to no use to the ♥♥♥♥ing game, except if you want to have less fun.
2. Unskippable orc cutscenes. enjoyable at first, gets old after the 50th time.
3. Breaking the lore of Lord of The Rings. While the devs has said that the story connects, its still abit weird, i wont spoil things in this review but if you've played the game then you should know what i'm talking about.
4. Act 4. In my opinion the worst thing about this game other than the microtransactions. Why? well not only its ♥♥♥♥ing grindy, it took me about 8-10 hours just finishing the final act, there's no story or side missions just non-stop siege battles.
5. The "True/secret ending". The ending is not really secret, but it is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to get it, which is by completing act 4, but the thing is the ending was not that satisfying in my opinion. It makes no sense.
In the end Shadow of War did things right and also did things really wrong, If you want to waste your time then go ahead. Its a really fun game and you can spend a ton of hours sinking your experience to the game, And yes in my opinion its worth your money (maybe not at full price and btw i got this game for around 30$ as that is how much it is price in my country), just dont buy the microtransactions. If you like the last game then you'll probably like this one.

Unfortunately, in the state it is currently in I would advise on waiting. Waiting for the numerous bugs, glitches, and balancing issues to hopefully be ironed out to justify the purchase.
Many single-player missions later in the game  are simply poorly balanced and make for a frustrating experience. This may or may not get fixed and isnt in itself game-breaking as you can lower the difficiulty knowing you are just compensating for a poorly designed experience. In terms of the core gameplay though, you will experience numerous frustrating bugs and glitches. Such as points where the controls just give out. Buttons stop functioning as they should. For instance, I was raiding a camp and trying to dominate a captain(more than one in fact) spending a good half hour breaking them down on Nemesis difficulty, only for the dominate button to suddenly stop working.  Making all the work I put in in vain.
Or as another example, getting deep into a mission only for the game to stop registering hits on one of the story captains. So I reset the level and the same thing happened. Reset it again and same problem. It took almost half a dozen tries to finally get it to work. For the story captain to start registering hits so I could progress the mission.
A third example will be that many times the creatures you summon will just randomly fail o inflict any damage on captains. A Graug summon(or Graug trap) for example regularly(but randomly) failed to inflict any damage on captains.
A final critique is that the game just feels like certain sections of the game were rushed. You will notice a stark difference with a couple of the locations compared to others. As if some of the locations were never fully finished. For instance two of the locations will incorporate orcs with more unique personalities and random missions that reflect the change in the main characters influence while other areas will be completely devoid of that influence. Your allies will in some areas seem more intuitive than in others. Following you where you lead while in the other sections seemingly staying stuck in their location as if the AI wasnt properly incorporated. Its hard to describe but as you progress you notice the way certain areas just feel under developed.
In its current state the game is not worth it to me. Maybe after patches or if the price comes down considerably. I regret my purchase at full price after having high expectations based on the core gameplay of the first one.
EDIT: Finishing up the last mission I am actually going to go a step further, this game is broken in it's current state, it is barely playable and has core gameplay issues I don't think can be fixed. The AI just seems flat out broken. Stay away, this game has gone from solid, to frustrating but alright to downright trash. I am incredibly disappointed that one of my favorite hidden gems of this generation has turned into complete garbage. Maybe at a 75% on sale the frustration can be justified but until then, or until it is drastically fixed, I recommend against the game.
EDIT 2: If you have a disagreement with the review, please express it in the comments.

This isn't a game for everyone, but it will suit you if you like something a bit quirky and enjoy simulations. The game is mainly about driving, but you usually don't drive for very long. Often you are only trying to travel a kilometre or so, and will get stuck  about three times in the process. Getting lost is also surprisingly easy over such short distances unless you use the map marker to help you. The water looks right, and the physics of the trucks feels pretty good, too.
It's the mud that really makes the game - it deforms realistically and mostly looks great. You get used to recognising the different types of mud pretty quickly, since that's what the game is often about - picking your way over stretches of mud or rivers with the aid of winches, rescue vehicles and really big tyres. There is a puzzle/planning element to this as you are trying to complete your tasks efficiently. You have to move fuel and repair equipment around as well as cargo and trucks. Some puzzles are deliberately worked into the level design, but quite often you just create them for yourself simply by getting stuck and having to mount a rescue operation.
There are a few downsides to be aware of. Some people seem to be finding the hardcore mode frustrating, as you can get yourself into a no-win situation without much warning. Picking up tactics on the casual mode seems to help, though. There are some things the developers could work on -  sand that's as good as the mud, clanky sound effects, better-looking winches.

This is a great engine. The reason I say engine instead of game is because there's actually very little to do once you start playing. You can uncloak hidden areas of each map, unlock vehicles by getting close to them, deliver resources to unlock garages, and finally deliver logs to finish the map objectives, but basically you drive from A to B. I say this not to imply that Spintires isn't worthy of our praise, or your support, but to make it clear that Spintires is not about the destination, so much as the journey there.
As other games have similarly done before, Spintires gives us an engine to create our own personalized experiences based on our direct interaction with this games biggest foe, the terrain.  Where Arma 3 has you perform recon and select the most tactical positions for your squad before a firefight, Spintires has you controlling gearboxes and determining the best tire placement over the most unforgiving, and detailed terrain I've ever encountered in a game.  While some people may find Spintires boring, other games have proven over and over that even some of the most tedious tasks supported on a solid foundation can find a strong following.  Those who may find navigating European roads, piloting an aircraft, or managing resources enjoyable may also find some fun and often exhilarating moments in lining up the perfect path between trees, struggling through mud holes with a large log trailer, or winching your friend out of an impossible situation so you can both continue exploring.
With the praise I'm giving the game I will point out some flaws. First, the camera isn't the easiest to work with, but this is being remedied. Second, you currently cannot see the terrain deformation caused by fellow players in multiplayer, also planned to be fixed I believe. Third, other small glitches occur(sometimes resources wont be counted as delivered, chat box closes randomly, winch can cause problems occasionally in multiplayer, and other small things that will be addressed).  I would have suggested releasing this title in it's current state under Early Access, because even though I love the game and trust they will fix everything, it doesn't help your credibility to release a title in this state. I would have purchased it at the same price in Early Access, and would not have batted an eye at any bugs or flaws currently occuring, in fact I probably would have been impressed at how completed the title already was. I know this makes no actual difference, but from a consumer standpoint I can see how the developers might have benefitted from the Early Access program, giving them more time to run public beta, and also more funding to allow for the extended beta development stage.
This game scratches the itch that I have never been able to reach. It started with 4x4 Evolution and Test Drive: Offroad on PS2, continued with MotorM4x and Offroad Drive on PC, and finally Spintires gets it right.  As it stands I highly recommend this game to anyone interested in any of the titles I just mentioned, I also want to press that this is a much more realistic offroad representation, you will very rarely break the 30mph mark, and you will get stuck often, the game is called Spintires, and it ain't cause your doing burnouts.  If this game receives the mod support it deserves I would bet we will be seeing this game for a long time to come.

I'm mainly writing this for my friends because I recommended this game to them before I spent enough time with it. I had really high expectations for this game but I really can't recommend it.  I wanted to love this game, I mean really LOVE it like I loved Fallout 2 or Jagged Alliance 2 or Morrowind. And I tried so hard to overlook the flaws I saw because damn it, I was waiting for this game over 20 years and I wasn't going to let some nittpicky BS stop me. But unfortunately all the problems I kept encountering just kept building up on each other until I pretty much gave up. Some of these problems are as follows:
The combat is shallow and lacks any sort of tactical feel despite being turn based; You rarely have a need to move your characters and most battles can be won by standing still and spaming attack or maybe toss a grenade. You can crouch or use a headshot but there's no real advantage that I notice to even bother with these moves.

The missions all seem half finished; apparently it's "hand holding" to ask for any sort of clue as to what you need to do or even why you need to do it. And all of the quests have multiple ways to "complete" them but if you're looking for multiple ways to complete them in a manner that the devs wanted you to in order to "win" the game then you'll need to rely on online guides because those solutions require an extremely linear path to be followed. And by "win" the game I mean by having the optimal completion where everyone you encounter was happy with what you did. Those endings are there but as I said they're not very easy to figure out.
"Conversations" with NPC's are nothing more than triggering the next bit of dialog by clicking on the keyword; there's no branching at all and you're really not interacting with NPC's in any meaningful way.
Character creation is also an oddity since it breaks the norm in most RPG's by having skills act completely independant of  attributes; ie charisma has no effect on your characters conversation skills or barter.
And lastly there are some really bad bugs that have caused me to lose a lot of game play time; there's 3 quick save slots for a reason and you should be sure to use them.
There's a lot to like here but I'm not going to sit here with a "pros and cons" list because I figure a lot of people are like me: if I'm thinking about buying a game I'm pretty much sold on it already and what I need to know is the bad stuff. Now none of the stuff I said above is so much that it's caused me to hate the game but it is enough to make me wish I had held off and waited for more reviews instead of buying it day one. $14.99-$19.99 is probably a good price point for this game but $40 is too much for what you get.

Played through in 30+ hours.
The technical problems are overrated, i really didn't encounter any major bugs. Maybe I was just lucky. After the day one patch I am also fully satisfied with the keybindings.
The game actually has decent graphics and the overall vibe of "Miami Vice". It may not be the most advanced title in the world, but the cutscenes are nice to look at (especially the smoke), lipsync is very well done and the audio is somewhere at 9/10 for me. And don't forget the soundtrack - it actually makes you stay in the car for one more song instead of doing the mission.
The screenplay in this game was a cliché story (guess what, it's all about revenge) with lots of cliché characters, but surprisingly it doesn't really feel like a bad thing. It rather feels like one of those action movies - there is a decent plot, but it's not one that has many unexpected twists or is hard to follow. There is a decent amount of humor, some of it rather dark. And the ending is perfect!
Shooting feels really good in the game and it's a good thing since you get to shoot A LOT.
Now to the points that are a bit disapponting:
they tried hard making this an open world game and they somewhat succeeded. But, what I would expect from an open world game and where this game falls short is the ability to stray off a preset course and not break the gameplay. The dumb AI make this hard - it acts OK is you play the game as the developers intended, but acts very stupid if you start to improvise.
Driving feels pretty good, but again - in an open world game I would expect better collisions (solid bushes in 2016, really?) and a better damage model (crashing may or may not destroy a couple of lights, that's it).
Missions are a bit repetitive, but so are they in pretty much all open world games. So no real difference there.
Overall it's a pretty solid experience and i would recommend this game to people who are into story driven narratives.

Charming, sweet and stylistically stunning, this point-and-click adventure game from Double Fine is highly recommended to newcomers to the genre, although seasoned vets will still find quite a lot to appreciate.
It should be stated that there is very little that Double Fine has offered that I was not a fan of immediately. Broken Age marks the developer’s first journey into a new genre, and although the game mainly plays it “safe,” it’s definitely worth playing.
Broken Age allows the player to choose to experience two parallel storylines at your own leisure, though nothing is lost by completing each of the (short) tales one after the other. It isn’t completely obvious through the game as to how the two main characters are linked to each other, though the groundwork is set for greater adventures in future installments. This episode mainly serves as the token introductory tale - Vella lives in a rustic village by the sea, and is to be sacrificed to the local monster as part of an ancient ritual. Shay, meanwhile, is a teenager living alone on a spaceship with an advanced AI taking care of him, although it’s obvious that the computer may have some outdated principles in relation to how to treat a grown boy.
Something I greatly appreciated about this game was the art direction - the UI is minimalistic, allowing you a full view of the storybook paintings that serve as the world of Broken Age. Honestly, I haven’t seen anything that (stylistically) has looked this good in a long time, but it’s a taste that won’t be favored by all, for sure. The dialogue is lighthearted and well-delivered, including voice acting by Jack Black and Elijah Wood, and the soundtrack is appropriately orchestrated like a cartoon movie. In all, I believe this game will never look outdated because of the design choices made.
The gameplay isn’t very difficult - I’m used to old-school point-and-clicks that required some strange leaps of logic in order to solve multi-step puzzles, but Broken Age is significantly straightforward. If a person says they need an object to cut a string, you will find them a knife, simple as that. Because of this, I did feel that I spent less time exploring the world, looking for clues in comparison to clicking through dialogue trees. Although the writing isn’t bad, I found that I basically would meet a new NPC, and then work from top to bottom through the conversation options before getting a new item. Hopefully, future episodes will instead offer more gameplay via item hunting and puzzle solving.
Still, I had a good experience with the game, and a single playthrough will probably take around six hours (with no additional goals or secrets to be unearthed afterwards). I’m looking forward to the next installment, whenever that may be.

You follow two separate storylines of a yound girl and a boy set in completely different environments trying to find solutions for the problems that arise. Most of the time spent in the game is listening to well written dialogue and experiencing neatly animated cut-scenes.

There are also missions to take on, such as Search and Rescue and Red Bull Air Races. These give the game attitude and some neat ways to experiment with different vehicles. But you’ll probably have the most fun creating your own flight paths, weather conditions, time of day, and where to take off and land at. The game is a true sandbox allowing you to be your own pilot on many types of aircraft.
The terms of the partnership deal do not allow for any graphical updates. So you should go into this knowing that it isn’t an HD remake, but rather just an update so that modern machines and operating systems can run the game. And with that, using Steamworks, allows for the game’s multiplayer to be updated and enhanced to talk to each other over modern connections. It is still the same great game from 8 years ago. But for anyone who has never played the game before, might be a little disappointed.
There are over 24,000 of the world’s airports to take off and land on. All of it can take place in real-time, or a time of your choosing. Airports look busier, as AI now fills the runways with fuel trucks, baggage carts that make things feel less empty. It’s a small, but meaningful change to the game that makes things seem more lively.
If Microsoft Flight Simulator X: Steam Edition seems too outdated for you, then a new Flight Simulator from Deovetail will probably resemble what you’re looking for, and be worth waiting for. This game is approaching a decade after it’s original release, and the game’s graphical fidelity is not holding up. For everyone else, this is an easy repurchase for an impeccable and realistic tool on learning how to fly with some great gameplay, alongside some challenging fun to be had with the missions.

OKay, First off, this may be a little biased as Civ 3 was the game that introduced me to the franchise. That said, It' s a solid 4X title, Graphically, it's obviously not going to be State of the Art, but I've never found that to matter with this genre; and apparently neither have most people given that one of the most popular 4X games around is Alpha Centari, which came out in 1999.
Sorry, got a bit off topic.
Like all the Civ games, Civilization 3 puts you in control of a settler and warrior, kicks you into the oceon that is its game play and tells you to swim. The tutorial is there, but it's basically a series of tips that pop up when you start doing things. well written and concise, but they don't force your hand. Also like the other Civ games, there is a large tech tree and ages to advance through as your empire grows. The main appeal of the game is that no two playthroughs [which can take weeks to months if you play casually] are ever going to be the same. One game History may play out as you destroy the Aztecs as the Spanish... but in the next game, Gahndi might nuke your American♥♥♥♥♥into oblivion.
Ultimately, 4X games aren't for everyone, but everyone should give the genre a try and at the price they're asking for it, Civ 3 is an affordable, still good looking, and complete introduction to the genre as well as a game that experienced players will enjoy for years to come.
[[A note on the CIv Franchise: those of you who started civ with 4 or 5 should also give 3 a try, the three titles are honestly different enough that they could be said to be equally good in their own right, assuming of course that you have the DLC for Civ 5, otherwise.... *shudders*]]
