Playing Shadow of Mordor was amazing, it introduced something no other game had done before, and in this installment of the franchise, they have IMPROVED it beyond comprehension! so without futher ado, let us begin with our adventure of Talion and Celebrimbor, and their army
the game starts off with JAW-DROPPING visuals, if you saw the trailer, then you know what im talking about, and all of the mechanics from the first game is still there! you visit Shelob, and she holds Celebrimbor hostage, and will let him go, on one condition, the ring that they made, Talion gives it to her, and thus we go to Minas Ithil!
i will admit that at this point, the game does get very invested in the story, and goes slow, and because of the RIng, you can't dominate people, which is kinda stupid IMO and the combat does take some getting used to, as you can't execute your insta-kill move from building up your hitstreak, also you don't get to stun people and do that cool super fast attack until you purchase it with your skill point
i won't be spoiling much of the story (only bits and pieces) so i will be talking about some of the other things thats in the game
in Act 2, you finally have the ability to dominate Uruks again, and the game for some reason, explains stuff that the last game did, its as if we didn't play Shadow of Mordor so it reintroduces stuff you already know about (or for people who didn't play the first one)
you then meet some Uruks, and if you're lucky like me, you get some of the interesting and funny Uruks! these guys are a blast to listen to! there is even an Uruk that SINGS! and some that scream and moan! they really stepped it up with the Uruks in this game!
dominating and managing your Guys is so much more fun! you can banish them from your Army, and they can't be dominated again because they hate you for banishing them! there are some who can betray you and leave your army willingly if you hit them too much or when they become a higher level than you! it shows that you really have to take care of your army, otherwise the odds turn in their favor..
there is now an RPG Loot system involved, so you can customize Talion with different armor pieces and swords, also Daggers and bows! hammers too! it also applies to Uruks as well, and here comes the thing everyone canceled their pre-orders for.... Microtransactions, in a SINGLEPLAYER GAME! the funny thing is, you don't EVER need to buy them because people have found ways to get higher level Uruks anyway, so it was totally pointless! i never spent ONE PENNY on it and i never will! Seriously, how many times do we, as GAMERS have to shout to other game companies, that we DON'T NEED THIS SHADY PRACTICE IN SINGLE PLAYER GAMES! its disgusting how greed has infested our favorite game companies and shove it down our throats every time we boot up the game! STOP IT!!
ahem... sorry for that outburst, but before i continue, let me do something, (sliently chokes out someone and stomps while each and every finger gets snapped) i am back, now lets continue!
you also get to do sieges! they are basically taking over a fortress, and the first time that you do it with your Uruks right beside you, its such an amazing experience! especially with hundreds of Uruks on screen, (if your PC can handle it)
there is also a tribute to Mike “Forthog” Forger, at Monolith who passed away last year, and they made a character for him, to honor his death, rest in peace.. you always protect in Shadow of War
and finally, at the very last Act in the Game which people call the "True Ending" it isnt, there are no alternate endings, so stop misleading, Talion becomes a Ringwraith and you have to partake in the Shadow Wars, where your Conquered fortresses have to be defended, and you have to do 10 stages of this, now after doing this for a couple hours it got, very tedious and sometimes, they are way too tough, so your best bet is to just let them take it, kill the Warchiefs and retake it, takes longer, but you get the job done easier that way
overall, what do i think of this game? i love it, i invested alot of hours into it, and i enjoyed every second of it, but the Shadow Wars was tedious and annoying, so i would recommend this, i will give a 8.5/10, i would give it a 9 or maybe a 10, but had the Shadow Wars been something different, i would have enjoyed this a whole lot more! thanks for reading, and give this game a try if you want to control an army!

It also has a different system of killing enemy which eliminates just spraying at them and involves constantly dodging unpredicted melee attacks. Middle-earth: Shadow of War is a game that gives each player a unique story through the nemesis system by having orcs with different characteristics fight you and taunt you in their own way making them a character you remember through the whole game. these unique characters aren't even a part of the main narrative, but they are a part of you own narrative as you play through the game. The nemesis system is by far the best part of this game and it's the main reason why i'm recommending this game.
Here are some Pros and Cons for Middle-earth: Shadow of War:
Pros:
- The nemesis system; As you get these unique characters that can taunt you, betray you and even cheat death once you think you have finally killed an orc that keeps ambushing or killing you.
- Domination over the orcs; You can turn an orc form trying to kill you to instead serve you and then send them to hunt down other orcs, become a backstabbing bodyguard for the current warchiefs by sending them to the fight pits to fight against your other orcs.
- Capturing and defending the fortresses; Each zone in the game has a fort that you must capture by staging an assault, this can be done by assigning the orcs you have dominated as assault leaders who will command a small force when the siege begins. You can also kill the current war-chief to remove the forts defences and then if you want to go further you send your orcs as spy war-chiefs to sabotage the forts wall and gates.
- The Fight Pits; Once the fort has been capture you can you can train up your orcs by sending them to fight a random orc or one of your own, however you cannot interfere, if your or wins then they will level up to a maximum of the players current level, however if they lose then they will be killed and that specific orc may be lost forever.
- The events the orcs create; Each and every orc in the game can bring different events for the player, most will be a one time orc that you kill or dominate and don't have any real connection with but some will give you an experience not found in many other games. As an example i'll tell you one of my experiences. I found a random orc captain named Zugor and decided to dominate him, I then sent him to be the bodyguard to one of the war-chiefs and he had to fight a guy in the fight pits; he was killed by fire. I thought it's not that bad I didn't really like him but later on he turned up with a burns all over him and betrayed me because I left him to die in the fight pits. We had a couple of fights I killed him a few times and he kept coming back until one time I cut him in half and thought well he's finally dead, but no he became Zugor the Machine and becoming way more interesting than before so I dominated him after a couple of attempt and now he is the overlord of the local fort.
- Shaming and Cheating death: If an orc is too high level for you to recruit (higher than the players current level) then you can shame them by branding a hand-print into their face this can have all sorts of effects on their character such as, them flaunting it and becoming 'The Unashamed', them telling you that no one takes them seriously anymore, to them becoming mad or deranged. a similar thing also happens when you kill a character and they 'Cheat Death' they will usually gain a characteristic based on the way that you killed them, for example, if you throw a knife at them they will have a knife sticking out of their head when they return, a metal arm if you cut their arm off a bag over their head if you burn them and many others.
Cons:
- The story: The story for this game is not very good the characters seem underdeveloped and poorly written other than Talion and Celebrimbor in the early parts of the game and they seem to completely forget about the one ring and only focus on the new one, which didn't make much sense to me.
- The Movement and Combat: The movement of this game is clunky you will run in one direction and start climbing on something in your path that you didn't want to climb. The combat in the early part of the game isn't as bad as the late part as in the early part you are usually only fighting one orc captain and a handful of orcs which is fairly easy to manage. However in the late stages of the game you could be fighting 3 to 4 orc captains and a bunch of different types of the orc grunts. when this happens the targeting system doesn't seem to know what to do and will pick seemingly random targets, for example trying to drain orcs for health and it drains a troll which cannot be drained or trying to use a finisher on a orc captain and it decides to use it on the orc grunt next to the captain. This becomes extremely frustrating in the late game because it happens so often and it's incredibly irritating.
- The Shadow Wars: This is thrown in at the last part of the game to have you defend the forts that you have captured rather than attacking them, which was fun for doing it in each of the zones that you capture but then it began to drag on as it kept going after you defend the forts you have to do it again and again and again just to get a conclusion to the game. It feels like they just added extend that part of the game to convince people to buy the loot boxes so they can get good orcs to defend the fort with.
- Loot Boxes: I don't even know why they put loot boxes in this game (apart from making money) they seem completely irrelevant   as you can earn just good, if not better orcs from just playing the game, plus you get to have the experiences with their characteristics as you would if you just found them in the game yourself rather than buying a loot box and getting them.
Overall I recommend this game due to the interactions with the nemesis system and unique interactions it can bring, however the story and movement are not great. I recommend getting this when it's on sale or wait for the GOTY edition for the full experience.

As a huge fan of the first game, the fact that it doesn't revolve around the italian mafia kind of dissappointed me, but I knew that before buying it, so it's not much of a point. Besides, Mafia 1 handled the mystique surrounding the italian mob and cosa nostra a hell of a lot better than Mafia 2 anyways, so I didn't mind the new approach that much. What I do mind though, is how the new characters, and especially the enemies, are portrayed as charicatures. They are tasteless, horrible and unrealisticly unlikable characters without any credibility what so ever. It's like Batman villains, except these are cast in a universe that expects us to take them seriously. It simply just doesn't do it for me, and it doesn't make sense at all.
Now, lastly on to the gameplay. It mostly consists of driving from place to place, breaking up doors with a stupid and simple mini game, hiding behind a crate and whissleing. One enemy will approach you at a time, allowing you to simply knock him down. Once he is down, whissle for the next guy, rinse and repeat. If you are discovered, a very simple gun fight emerges, and you'll only be in real trouble if you are facing a lot of enemies surrounding you. The AI is stupid as ♥♥♥♥.
Furthermore... gone are the ticket system of the former games. The police is even more stupid than the regular enemies, you'll have to put some real effort in in order to get noticed.
And lastly, the support system is ridiculous. You have xray vision, you can order allies to bring you cars, weapons or to stash money for you with a menu, having your request fulfilled within seconds. How Lincoln is pulling this off, I don't know, since you know... Mobile phones wouldn't be a thing before 20 years after the period this game takes place in.
I really, really wanted this to be good. I did. But it isn't. Objectively, this must be the worst tripple A release this year by a long shot. It has very few redeeming qualities. The only thing I like about it is the opening of it.
And I just don't get it, as these are the same people that made Mafia I, one of the best games ever made. Don't buy this... Just don't.

If you're looking for an empire building game, don't buy Mafia 3. Your wannabe crime syndicate consists of "partners", which will provide you with some kickback and favors - that's it. No big mansion. No goons. Nothing. Your partners even send you around to do the dirty work for them. Dirty work includes getting trucks, ships, and cars to a racket. Rinse and repeat. Repetition is an enormous flaw of this game. Although the world is pretty big, you'll be visiting the same locations repeatedly. It's just terribly boring.
You don't seem to be able to have a personal car, upgrade your accomodations, change your appearance, etc. Hell, you don't even have a garage.
The cops seem to be blind. You can pass red lights, cause a massive car crash 20 meters infront of them, overtake them with full speed: nothing. Zero ♥♥♥♥s given. But stand next to them for too long, not even looking at them, they'll come crashing down on you.
Stealth/Melee Kills is a joke. You can simply walk around and kill everyone in a single room without getting any heat.
And then there's the collectibles. If you're a completionist like me, you will hate this game so, so much. The collectibles are scattered all over the place - and there are so many. In order to get them, most of the times you'll have to break into buildings, which are totally empty and seem only to exist to make the collectible less accessible. PRO TIP: You can kick down doors. I found out only after half way into the game.
You'll be spending most of your time driving around. Driving is super easy as compared to Mafia 2. I've been driving on simulation mode since the very beginning. What makes driving hard are immovable objects like bushes. Bushes will wreck your car and health bar, it's ridiculous.
Despite all the hate, there are a few good things. Story is great, although I have trouble keeping up with all the different characters. The setting is awesome and it seems that the designers have put alot of effort into building an authentic world. The character animations in the cut scenes are fantastic. The animations are so good, you could actually read their lips and know what they're saying and in what mood. Oh, the soundtrack is great too. But you know what? Just buy the OST, and you'll probably have the best part of the game.
I've been expecting way more from a game with such a considerable price tag. I'll finish the story, but after that it's going straight to the shelf.
Update: Finished the game. Ending was - as the whole game - disappointing. There are three possible endings, which all result from the final choice you get to make. Are you the person who likes to explore all different endings in a game? So am I. But I was so fed up with this game, I didn't even bother making different choices. So, so sad.

Overall, Wasteland 2 is a game defined by its deep storytelling, difficult decision making and engaging problem solving. I am having a great time with this title and am completely invested in the characters I have created and the story I am uncovering. The clunky menus are a small blemish on what is a remarkable game, and while I am still getting used to the combat style, the depth it offers is truly amazing. Wasteland 2 is an incredible achievement for a crowd funded title and has earned 9.5 out of 10 from me.
GAMEPLAY
Wasteland 2 impressed me from the starting screen, with its deep character customisation, allowing players to build their four person team from the ground up. Being able to make your team look how you want, fight how you want, talk how you want and be as technically trained as you want, is an amazing feat and makes the player instantly more attached to the characters that they have created.
All of the standard RPG experience gaining, levelling up, looting and questing are here in Wasteland 2, and all feel realistic and tie in well with the main storyline. My only minor gripe with the character development and management is that some of the menus are a tad clunky, but with the correct use of hotkeys, the time spent navigating the menus can be minimised.
Problem solving and story unravelling in Wasteland 2, is a return to old school gaming styles and is perfectly delivered. Players can choose specific discussion points in conversations that reveal interesting background information and new missions, but can also completely avoid them if they wish. Skills like smart♥♥♥♥♥♥and hard♥♥♥♥♥♥offer another layer of conversation options for players, and keep things fresh in the more slow paced conversation sections.
Wasteland 2 also offers a less, "hand-holdy" approach to problem solving, with the player required to truly understand and think about what they do, before they do it. Unlocking a safe found when questing is not as easy a clicking on it and moving on. Players must assess the type of lock, whether the safe is alarmed or trapped, and their likelihood of overcoming its specific challenges before they choose to give it a crack.
COMBAT
This less, "hand-holdy" approach carries through into the combat of Wasteland 2. Combat is turn based and strategic in nature, with players required to know the strengths and weaknesses of each party member, to win combat. A standard battle involves the player manoeuvring their team into various forms of cover to give them the best probability to hit their enemies while not leaving them open to attack. Consequences of combat make battles extremely exciting, with players really having to plan their assaults or risk the death of one of their characters.
VISUALS & MUSIC
The visuals of Wasteland 2 are great, and complement the old school style well, while paying homage to the original Wasteland. The top down view with a rotatable camera is a kick back to the original Fallout series and plays in well with the strategic combat. The music and sounds fit perfectly with Wasteland 2 and every radio transmission and voice acted conversation are a pleasure to listen to.

Ok so I was rather doubtful, but this game is actually really good.
Its a nice combination of RPG with crafting, housing, having your pet and resource gathering.
-- Biggst pros --
- Humor (some might not like it, Im having lots of fun)
- Graphics are actually very nice after you get used to it
- Gameplay is altogether fun, although I really miss being able to control my character with WSAD (you have to use the mouse)
-- Cons --
- You can really tell its a multiplatform (you can play it on your tablet too). The UI is simply not ideal for a PC game, and I miss some features of the UI (like being able to track any recipe at any time, now you can switch tracked recipe only at a craft station)
- Quests are often a bit vague, and you need to hope you get it right.
- Random crafting. Whenever you craft a weapon or a piece of armor, you randomly get one of 4 qualities (normal, acceptable, satysfying, excellent). Since you really need Excellent quality items (they have much better stats), sometimes you end up on a bad streak, creating 20 pieces of a single armor/weapon that you simply cant get an Excellent version of, which leads to mats grinding, which can be very frustrating.
- Many elements of the housing seems absolutely pointless. There is a ton of "furniture/decorative" items that are simple useless, providing 0 benefits while often costing much of your precious resources. Also, since there is literally no reason to build a better quality walls/floors, I have no idea why should I spend more time and resources to get a "better base", since the only purpose for your base is to shelter your pets and your crafting stations. This could DEFINITELY be improved.
All and all Im having a good time, definitely worth the money I got it for.

Alan Wake, from the creators of Max Payne, is a rare instance where storytelling and game design mix properly to present a horror game that is both fun to play, intense, and actually tells a story that will stick with you. It takes elements from popular survival horror titles, third person shooters, Stephen King, and many other sources to produce a well written story in an atmosphere with character, as well as a knack for keeping you off balance,
Many have occused the story of making no sense and/or being poorly written by hacks, but this is basically a Stephen King novel. Yea, he isn't amazing, but he still gets the job done and  keeps selling. Unless you absolutely hate games with stories and scripted events, within about 20 minutes you should be hooked, and you won't be leaving until it's over.
It simply cannot be overstated how excellent of a game this is. Remedy put the utmost detail into creating an authentic world, and character's that you can actually find interesting, not to mention care about. Frankly I always have preferred Noah Wyle be cast as the live actor for Alan, but the person who is does a fine job. As long as it's not Nolan North or Troy Baker for the 900th time, there's no issue.
I own both AW games on 360 and PC and most definitely recommend buying it, as it can frequently be found in a bundle for less than 5 dollars for both games and all DLC. Survival horror, horror, if you like either, get this.

First of all, the first game was great. The combat the nemesis system all of that. The story lacked, however. It was just "there." I couldn't feel anger towards the people I was supposed to. However, this series is definatley one that learns from it's mistakes.

The gameplay is great, minus a few glitches, and world obstacles that for some reason are impassable. For instance, you can get stuck on a ledge that you would otherwise be able to just run over. There are also times where Talion will not do a thing that you ask of him.
The game is quite easy, so I do reccomend that you play on Nemesis difficulty. No matter how♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥you get. I have spent easily 15+ hours dedicating specific captains and warchiefs to my time. I never would have thought that a game based on delivery and exploration off road could be so fun and challenging.  I have never been so driven to bring a load of wood from one area to another.  There is much more to this game than when you initially start.  You think, "I drove all the way here to pick up the load, big deal."  Well then comes the challenge of delivering the load with the extra weight.  With mud pits, streams, river, fallen trees, boulders and occasionally unconecting roads you will find our how difficult.  This is all based off the first level which I have yet to complete.
Graphcs are very nice and sounds put you in the moment.  The terrain deformation is amazing.  I was really impressed that it seems to stay that way.  I can tell when I have already driven a trail as opposed to one I have yet to explorer.
A small group of vehicles allows you to explore in different ways.  You'll settle in on a favorite, but I like to try routes with different abilities just to see what is possible.
I have gotten myself out of a sticky situation using the crane to "dig" boulders out of the way.  I even found I could push them with the crane as well.  I even pushed the truck up to a more level area and was able to drive away afterwards.  It really is pretty realistic.
My only real issue is occasionally the camera gets outs of whack and it becomes difficult to see what you want, but I have managed to work around it but would like to see a bit better control.  This is an issue when you are stuck and rying to figure the best way to free yourself.
I have been using the 360 controller and it works pretty well.  Once they resolve the brake being 100% or nothing it should give a bit better controll when descending.  This is not an isssue with the accelerator though.
Overall a really fun and satisfying game.

Playing Shadow of Mordor was amazing, it introduced something no other game had done before, and in this installment of the franchise, they have IMPROVED it beyond comprehension! so without futher ado, let us begin with our adventure of Talion and Celebrimbor, and their army
the game starts off with JAW-DROPPING visuals, if you saw the trailer, then you know what im talking about, and all of the mechanics from the first game is still there! you visit Shelob, and she holds Celebrimbor hostage, and will let him go, on one condition, the ring that they made, Talion gives it to her, and thus we go to Minas Ithil!
i will admit that at this point, the game does get very invested in the story, and goes slow, and because of the RIng, you can't dominate people, which is kinda stupid IMO and the combat does take some getting used to, as you can't execute your insta-kill move from building up your hitstreak, also you don't get to stun people and do that cool super fast attack until you purchase it with your skill point
i won't be spoiling much of the story (only bits and pieces) so i will be talking about some of the other things thats in the game
in Act 2, you finally have the ability to dominate Uruks again, and the game for some reason, explains stuff that the last game did, its as if we didn't play Shadow of Mordor so it reintroduces stuff you already know about (or for people who didn't play the first one)
you then meet some Uruks, and if you're lucky like me, you get some of the interesting and funny Uruks! these guys are a blast to listen to! there is even an Uruk that SINGS! and some that scream and moan! they really stepped it up with the Uruks in this game!
dominating and managing your Guys is so much more fun! you can banish them from your Army, and they can't be dominated again because they hate you for banishing them! there are some who can betray you and leave your army willingly if you hit them too much or when they become a higher level than you! it shows that you really have to take care of your army, otherwise the odds turn in their favor..
there is now an RPG Loot system involved, so you can customize Talion with different armor pieces and swords, also Daggers and bows! hammers too! it also applies to Uruks as well, and here comes the thing everyone canceled their pre-orders for.... Microtransactions, in a SINGLEPLAYER GAME! the funny thing is, you don't EVER need to buy them because people have found ways to get higher level Uruks anyway, so it was totally pointless! i never spent ONE PENNY on it and i never will! Seriously, how many times do we, as GAMERS have to shout to other game companies, that we DON'T NEED THIS SHADY PRACTICE IN SINGLE PLAYER GAMES! its disgusting how greed has infested our favorite game companies and shove it down our throats every time we boot up the game! STOP IT!!
ahem... sorry for that outburst, but before i continue, let me do something, (sliently chokes out someone and stomps while each and every finger gets snapped) i am back, now lets continue!
you also get to do sieges! they are basically taking over a fortress, and the first time that you do it with your Uruks right beside you, its such an amazing experience! especially with hundreds of Uruks on screen, (if your PC can handle it)
there is also a tribute to Mike “Forthog” Forger, at Monolith who passed away last year, and they made a character for him, to honor his death, rest in peace.. you always protect in Shadow of War
and finally, at the very last Act in the Game which people call the "True Ending" it isnt, there are no alternate endings, so stop misleading, Talion becomes a Ringwraith and you have to partake in the Shadow Wars, where your Conquered fortresses have to be defended, and you have to do 10 stages of this, now after doing this for a couple hours it got, very tedious and sometimes, they are way too tough, so your best bet is to just let them take it, kill the Warchiefs and retake it, takes longer, but you get the job done easier that way
overall, what do i think of this game? i love it, i invested alot of hours into it, and i enjoyed every second of it, but the Shadow Wars was tedious and annoying, so i would recommend this, i will give a 8.5/10, i would give it a 9 or maybe a 10, but had the Shadow Wars been something different, i would have enjoyed this a whole lot more! thanks for reading, and give this game a try if you want to control an army!

Although the game is over a decade old, its gameplay, mechanics, and tactical strategies manage to please and challenge strategy gamers, especially within the harder difficulty levels.
The highlights within the game include a wide array of civilizations to choose from around the world and throughout history, a refined isometric perspective from its precedessor, unique qualities to match your gameplay style, and challenging gameplay tactics as you progress through its difficulty. The Complete Edition also features a Conquests version for increased replayability that focuses on your tactical thinking without rapid reactions.
Within the negative aspects of the game, the AI seems a bit limited on handling some of its positive attributes or buffs (normally happens with harder difficulty levels), meaning that it has no idea how to handle its resources efficiently, thus limiting gameplay challenge compared to later Civilization games.  Furthermore, it is difficult to establish friendships and allies within the game, as every opponent seems to collide against you (in the World War II map, even England is your enemy if you select the United States as your civilization), also limiting attaining diplomatic victories.
Overall, the game remains strong based on its design and gameplay, and at an inexpensive price, you really cannot go wrong, especially when there is a discount lurking from time to time.

Middle-earth: Shadow of War is a game that gives each player a unique story through the nemesis system by having orcs with different characteristics fight you and taunt you in their own way making them a character you remember through the whole game. these unique characters aren't even a part of the main narrative, but they are a part of you own narrative as you play through the game. The nemesis system is by far the best part of this game and it's the main reason why i'm recommending this game.
Here are some Pros and Cons for Middle-earth: Shadow of War:
Pros:
- The nemesis system; As you get these unique characters that can taunt you, betray you and even cheat death once you think you have finally killed an orc that keeps ambushing or killing you.
- Domination over the orcs; You can turn an orc form trying to kill you to instead serve you and then send them to hunt down other orcs, become a backstabbing bodyguard for the current warchiefs by sending them to the fight pits to fight against your other orcs.
- Capturing and defending the fortresses; Each zone in the game has a fort that you must capture by staging an assault, this can be done by assigning the orcs you have dominated as assault leaders who will command a small force when the siege begins. You can also kill the current war-chief to remove the forts defences and then if you want to go further you send your orcs as spy war-chiefs to sabotage the forts wall and gates.
- The Fight Pits; Once the fort has been capture you can you can train up your orcs by sending them to fight a random orc or one of your own, however you cannot interfere, if your or wins then they will level up to a maximum of the players current level, however if they lose then they will be killed and that specific orc may be lost forever.
- The events the orcs create; Each and every orc in the game can bring different events for the player, most will be a one time orc that you kill or dominate and don't have any real connection with but some will give you an experience not found in many other games. As an example i'll tell you one of my experiences. I found a random orc captain named Zugor and decided to dominate him, I then sent him to be the bodyguard to one of the war-chiefs and he had to fight a guy in the fight pits; he was killed by fire. I thought it's not that bad I didn't really like him but later on he turned up with a burns all over him and betrayed me because I left him to die in the fight pits. We had a couple of fights I killed him a few times and he kept coming back until one time I cut him in half and thought well he's finally dead, but no he became Zugor the Machine and becoming way more interesting than before so I dominated him after a couple of attempt and now he is the overlord of the local fort.
- Shaming and Cheating death: If an orc is too high level for you to recruit (higher than the players current level) then you can shame them by branding a hand-print into their face this can have all sorts of effects on their character such as, them flaunting it and becoming 'The Unashamed', them telling you that no one takes them seriously anymore, to them becoming mad or deranged. a similar thing also happens when you kill a character and they 'Cheat Death' they will usually gain a characteristic based on the way that you killed them, for example, if you throw a knife at them they will have a knife sticking out of their head when they return, a metal arm if you cut their arm off a bag over their head if you burn them and many others.
Cons:
- The story: The story for this game is not very good the characters seem underdeveloped and poorly written other than Talion and Celebrimbor in the early parts of the game and they seem to completely forget about the one ring and only focus on the new one, which didn't make much sense to me.
- The Movement and Combat: The movement of this game is clunky you will run in one direction and start climbing on something in your path that you didn't want to climb. The combat in the early part of the game isn't as bad as the late part as in the early part you are usually only fighting one orc captain and a handful of orcs which is fairly easy to manage. However in the late stages of the game you could be fighting 3 to 4 orc captains and a bunch of different types of the orc grunts. when this happens the targeting system doesn't seem to know what to do and will pick seemingly random targets, for example trying to drain orcs for health and it drains a troll which cannot be drained or trying to use a finisher on a orc captain and it decides to use it on the orc grunt next to the captain. This becomes extremely frustrating in the late game because it happens so often and it's incredibly irritating.
- The Shadow Wars: This is thrown in at the last part of the game to have you defend the forts that you have captured rather than attacking them, which was fun for doing it in each of the zones that you capture but then it began to drag on as it kept going after you defend the forts you have to do it again and again and again just to get a conclusion to the game. It feels like they just added extend that part of the game to convince people to buy the loot boxes so they can get good orcs to defend the fort with.
- Loot Boxes: I don't even know why they put loot boxes in this game (apart from making money) they seem completely irrelevant   as you can earn just good, if not better orcs from just playing the game, plus you get to have the experiences with their characteristics as you would if you just found them in the game yourself rather than buying a loot box and getting them.
Overall I recommend this game due to the interactions with the nemesis system and unique interactions it can bring, however the story and movement are not great. I recommend getting this when it's on sale or wait for the GOTY edition for the full experience.

I thought this game would be fun, but it is AMAZING. It is one of my favourite games because everything in it is excellent. With other games I tend to get bored if I play it for too long, or I can't just play them for 20 minuted and then do something else, but with this game, it I have 10 minutes of time free, this game would be perfect, and I can play it for 4 hours straight without getting bored.
-----Game Progression-----
You gradually progress through different levels of armour, weapons, and decorative items, each which come from a different workstation. Each workstation has a set of materials that you need to build pretty much any item for it, meaning that when you unlock that workstation, those items are super valuable, and you need as much of them as you can get. A while afterwards, you unlock the next workstation, and then you don't care about those items anymore. To craft some better items you need to do a bit of hunting, sometimes for a little while, but it doesn't reach the point that it gets tedious.
The crafting and inventory system are quite useful, as you don't have to try and drag items around and sort them and try to find the items that you need in your inventory. (Just read any of the promotional material for this game, they do a better job of explaining it)
-----Pets-----
After a while of fighting a specific enemy you will eventually get an egg, which you can then hatch, name, and then it will aid you in fights. You can also craft items that make the pet become more powerful. Pets are really useful in taking out difficult enemies, because you dodge their attacks whilst your pet kills them.
-----Enemies-----
Every enemy has a unique look, sound, and attack. meaning that fighting them never gets repetitive. with each enemy, there is also a specific technique that you need to use to kill it without getting rekt.
-----The World-----
The whole map of the game is quite large, and as you explore it, it is added to your map, with specific goals for missions marked on your maps, making it easy to find where to go next. There are teleporters scattered around the map, which you can teleport to from any location, whenever you are not in battle.
-----Building-----
You can create your home using a paintbrush tool, which you can use to put items down anywhere in your vision. The items you can put down are also grouped by categories, meaning that you can easily find what you need.
-----Audio-----
The music is gr8, as each area has different music used, and the biomes also have different music that is played at night. The sounds for enemies are unique, meaning that with each new enemy you can enjoy some new weird sounds. The sounds for other things are also good. (esp when "embiggening" a creature).
-----Visuals-----
The graphics are just amazing, and it never looks plain or boring, due to how detailed everything looks.
-----Performance-----
I play this game (along with all my other games) on a surface pro 3 i5 with an integrated gpu (no dedicated graphics). It can easily run this game, at 2140x1440 at 60 fps, which is very good (I'm not sure about the performace with other 2D games, but with fps games I am used to 20 fps when playing at a much lower resolution)
Two thing that I would like would to be able to see a list of all your items and recipies, and being able to track multiple recipies at once would be useful.
I bought this game when it was on sale, but it is definitely worth the full price

Quick and dirty review:
I approve of Inxile, their roots and what they stand for, but I was discouraged from what I heard about early access "missteps." That said, after playing very little of Wasteland 2 I realized that it combines some of the best aspects of many of my favorite games of ALL TIME. Actually, probably most of them. Let that sink in.
- Area exploration reminds me of Baldur's Gate series, including finding loot, unlocking/disabling traps.
- Combat reminds me of XCOM, minus the focus on cover and more focus on consumables and abilities.
- Narrative text reminds me of... nothing. Nothing has the same amount of flavour. Planescape: Torment, maybe.
- Over-world exploration reminds me of the NWN2 Expansion, Storm of Zehir (only far better).
- Creating all your characters from scratch gives me a bit of an XCOM or Final Fantasy Tactics vibe, only with the stat detail of a D&D game.
- Obviously, atmosphere is very Fallout, only more fleshed out and in my opinion, better.
This is just meant to be a quick run-down, but Wasteland inspired many of these games, or inspired the games that inspired them, and considering the past pedigree of Inxile's devs these influences are both understandable, and awesome.
Small disclaimer: my taste in games seems almost custom tailored to Wasteland 2 so if you know not of what I speak, look elsewhere. If you found yourself nodding at these references, stop reading reviews and buy this game. Actually, do that anyway. I'm pretty sure it's going to go down as one of my next All-Time Favorites, maybe it'll be one of yours too.

Updated Review for Act 2 (Original  review is below. Some things will be repeated. No spoilers for either Act 1 or 2):
TLDR: It's not bad, but it's disappointing. The story loses it's attraction as the game goes on, and the puzzles get more tedious to solve. The writing, the art, and the world are good enough that I wouldn't want to prevent anyone from experiencing them, but the story and the puzzles just don't come together well enough for this game to be worth recommending. It's almost good enough, but the bottom line is that even if you go in with no expectations, you'll be disappointed by the time you finish.
Story: The flaw in the story is how discordant it is. The strength of the first act was the discovery of the world these characters live in, and the troubling mystery behind it. But the second part, instead of continuing down that path, abandons those mysteries in favor of new, less interesting mysteries, that don't get the time to go through a fulfilling arc. You just get talked at about them, and don't get to explore any of it. And there are many, many points where the only reasonable thing for characters to do is have a thorough conversation about what they know, but it just isn't an option, for no narrative reason. In fact, there are many points where everything we know about the characters indicates that they should be reacting completely differently than they do. Worst of all, there are "revelations" that are so jarring that they can only be considered mid-story retcons, that just kind of slide by without comment.
Puzzles: Very few puzzles made me feel clever or accomplished. Very few puzzles were seriously illogical (as far as adventure games go). Quite a few more puzzles, while not totally illogical, required experimentation that was tedious to execute (like traversing many screens just to test out a theory that might eventually lead you to the solution). The game frequently presents you with clear lists of goals you can work to achieve in parallel (which is a good thing in adventure games, IMO). But just as frequently, it turns out that one of those goals is completely unachievable until you've completed one of the other tasks (with no indiciation that that might be the case), which means that they're not at all parellel, and all the time you spent trying to progress down one path was a complete waste. This is a huge adventure game design sin, and it's employed here as a standard recurring design element.
There's something else that deserves special mention, for being a sin in both the narrative and the game design. There are multiple puzzles in the game that require the player to exploit their omniscience of boths sides of the story. Information that *cannot* be known by the characters is necessary to solve certain puzzles, and the game is designed around this. You'd be forgiven for hoping that this might lead to some interesting twist that makes it make narrative sense, but it's a stunt that is pulled straight-faced and without apology.
Humor: There are some funny bits, but this isn't a comedy game. If you're seeking calssic Tim Schafer humor, you'll be mostly disappointed. Humorous dialog keeps the tone light, but the subject matter and the characters aren't really comic in nature, so the game can't avoid being generally mellow with a few laughs. There was only one moment that stood out to me as truly hilarious.
Visual / Audio Design: Top notch. The characters, environments, animations and virtually all the voices are amazingly well done, with their own unique style.
Overall: I know I'm sounding hard on it, but it isn't a bad game. I was actually on the fence of giving it a positive recommendation. But it just doesn't hold together well enough. The flaws that hurt the game the most are all clearly deliberate (rather than being a failure to achieve goals), and that's frankly inexcusable for a game with this pedigree.
Original Review of Act 1 Alone (Not Recommended):
I recommend the game if you're either totally in it for the story, OR if you're academically interested in the genre. It will be interesting to see where Broken Age lies in the history of adventure games and interactive storytelling.
But overall, the game itself is actually kind of hit and miss. I'd have to wait to see if the second half really ties it together before giving it a solid general recommendation.
The puzzles are...whatever. Nothing stood out as particularly clever or interesting. I think part of the problem was that problem space to work with was always so small that matching puzzles to their solutions was straightforward. It was very linear for an adventure game. The dual-story thing was an interesting idea, mechanically, because it lets the player progress along different lines if they're feeling stuck on something. However, that idea was kind of wasted on a game as "narrow" as this.
Speaking of the story, thumbs up. It's interesting and pretty unique, and maintains a feel of wonder and mystery, as you try to piece everything together. The dual-story contributed to that a lot. The world was filled with neat characters; by that I mean they weren't particularly likeable or memorable, but they were distinct and well conveyed. There's a lot in the world that I'm still curious about, but I feel like this is one of those things where if the payoff in the conclusion isn't good, it'll just spoil everything up to that point.
The game isn't funny. It's humorous, sure. The characters have a sense of humor, and there are jokes, and it doesn't take itself too seriously, but it's not a comedy, which is disappointing for a project funded on the dream of classic Tim Schafer adventure games.
The art is downright stunning. It's amazing how well the visuals, the animation, and the sound blend seamlessly into such a cohesive style.

This is the best survival horror game you never heard of.  Unlike the cliche of most horror games, you are certainly not defenseless.  At the same time though, your character definitely feels like the everyman who is fighting for his life against the supernatural.  A great story, plenty of action, and excellent controls (bonus points for being in a genre filled with games that have poor controls) make this an experience you may not have heard of, but you MUST try.

Although the game is over a decade old, its gameplay, mechanics, and tactical strategies manage to please and challenge strategy gamers, especially within the harder difficulty levels.
The highlights within the game include a wide array of civilizations to choose from around the world and throughout history, a refined isometric perspective from its precedessor, unique qualities to match your gameplay style, and challenging gameplay tactics as you progress through its difficulty. The Complete Edition also features a Conquests version for increased replayability that focuses on your tactical thinking without rapid reactions.
Within the negative aspects of the game, the AI seems a bit limited on handling some of its positive attributes or buffs (normally happens with harder difficulty levels), meaning that it has no idea how to handle its resources efficiently, thus limiting gameplay challenge compared to later Civilization games.  Furthermore, it is difficult to establish friendships and allies within the game, as every opponent seems to collide against you (in the World War II map, even England is your enemy if you select the United States as your civilization), also limiting attaining diplomatic victories.
Overall, the game remains strong based on its design and gameplay, and at an inexpensive price, you really cannot go wrong, especially when there is a discount lurking from time to time.

Let me say that this was my first Civilization game, and for being on sale for $5, I am sure I would buy the game again.
If you're new or interested in Civilization games, I HIGHLY recommend reading further and/or watching videos to understand what you are getting into:
Pros-
This game is highly detailed and allows for a significant amount of strategy-management decisions. Learning the system and "how to beat it" itself was an enjoyable that I still can't fully claim to have achieved.
Cons-
There is no help in-game in actually learning the game. This will either add hours of patience in learning the game, or frustration.
The computer AI is abhorrent for trading.
Fair Warning: This game is SLOW. I am okay about slow games, when I am mentally prepared for it. This game is so slow, whether due to micromanagement, organizing your thoughts, or constant unit/city decisions. In my opinion, the pacing of this game is not evidence of a detailed well thought out game (which yes, it is), but of a poorly designed game. Even in "speed-mode"...just ugh, it's still slow.
I suggest that if you are interested in a strategic, decision-making game, and ok with long games, the Civilization games will suit your needs. Furthermore, I suggest looking into Galactic Civilizations, at the least for the sake of a real tutorial.
Again, if you're new to these games, do your research and check out other people's opinions before diving into the Civilization world.

I feel there's been a lot of undeserved attention towards loot boxes and micro transactions in this game.  I feel compelled to write this review to counter act it.  While I do agree there is a "supposed" grind wall that prevents you from seeing the game's true ending that bridges The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings (maybe even past that), there's absolutely no need to get those paid loot boxes and I will explain why.
Legendary Orcs (Legendary Gear) appear within reasonable frequency and are not that difficult to kill.  If you decide to kill them (which you should if you have no legendary gear), you will get legendary equipment which can be upgraded all the way to 60.  Each fortress should have a Legendary Orc as an overlord, just kill him for loot.  The set bonuses form the Legendary Gear will aid you in any missions you need to do.  By the end of the end of the game (True ending), I've amassed over 30 pieces of legendary gear just to give you an idea of how easy it is to obtain loot.  I do not recommend trying to keep a Legendary Orc unless they have really nice strengths with very few or no weaknesses.  It doesn't make sense to keep a Legendary Orc who is terrified of fire or mortally wounded by poison so just kill them for loot.
The Grind Wall to the True Ending isn't too bad, I viewed it as an opportunity to get loot each fort defense (which by the way is incredibly easy to win if you level your warchiefs and assign 2 body guards via fight pits maggots each before starting the mission).  The final wave always has a guaranteed legendary orc (should be the guy with the highest level of the pack), kill or dominate for loot/orc.  My only gripe is that the Ending wasn't as detailed or long as I would have liked for the time investment but I don't think it promotes loot chest buying as some others have indicated.  Use Orc weakenesses to your advantage, there are only very few instances where an orc is really hard to defeat, there is no percieved "paywall" to win this game.
Bottom LIne, the game is entertaining.  I like the story they tried to tell and there is absolutely no "PAYWALL" that people might lead you to believe, if they do insist there is, this is a L2P moment for them.  YES, I do believe it's bad for PC games to institute loot boxes and microtransations especially a SINGLE PLAYER game.  YES, I do think it's a bad decision on Monolith's part for doing this because of the negativity it adds to their game for proabably a meagre return (not needed + a lot of people resent it).  Do I think you will require it to progress?  No, so stop whining and L2P.

This is a great game, but not perfect. It ticks a lot of the boxes right while leaving some boxes blank instead.
THE STORY
The story is nothing special. If you're expecting a masterpiece of a story, you're going to be dissapointed. More so if you're one of the so-called Tolkien-purists. This game is going to grind the hell out of your gears if that's the case. Despite of it, it's still a good story. Pretty much what you'd expect if you've played the first game.
To be honest, some side quests like the Bruz questline is much more engaging than the main story itself. A damn shame, to be honest, but it's not something I particularly mind. The personal stories with the orcs are, after all, what most of you are buying this game for.
THE GAMEPLAY
It's Shadow of Mordor's gameplay refined to a T. Sure, there are some frustrating bits where Talion runs up a wall you don't want to, but nowadays, that's kind of expected from AC's brand of freerunning. You have soo much more freedom in combat, and the enemies are much more varied in terms of ability as well. Orcs will adapt to your playstyle, forcing you to change your tactics on the fly if you want to be the one left standing.
Nemesis Difficulty is also the way to go for this game. IMO, it's the way the game is intended to be played. Orcs use their abilities much more often. Orc captains don't stand around, getting in your face and bringing the battle up close most of the time.
Side missions are always a thing with this game in the form of power struggles between orcs, but some of the collectibles are fine on their own, if you care about the game's lore-building at all. Gondorian artifacts gives insight into the lore of LotR for the uninitiated, as well as providing some amusing back and forth banter between Talion and Celebrimbor. Unfortunately, if you're not interested in any personal stories with the orcs, there isn't much to this game's side-content. The orcs are the main and side attractions, love them or hate them.
This game is also really generous in giving you skill points and Mirians (the in-game money). Perhaps too generous. By the end of the game, at level 60, I have 50k unspent Mirians that I have no idea what to do with, as well as 29 unspent skill points.
The UI is also a bit cluttered, but thankfully, you can turn some elements of the HUD off if you want.
The introduction of loot system and gear management is also a nice change. Unfortunately, they don't show up in cutscenes, since most of the cutscenes are pre-rendered. Other than that, gears are a useful way to spice up your playstyle, with legendary gears giving you some game-changing quirks. Make no mistake, though. This is still a very skill-dependent game. All the legendary gear sets in the game won't matter if you're playing it like a certain game journalist plays Cuphead's tutorial level.
And then there's the Photo Mode. You can blame some of my hours in this game solely on the Photo Mode. That pretty much sums up the Photo Mode.
THE NEMESIS SYSTEM
The Nemesis System from the previous game have been refined into a much better version of it, allowing you to craft your story with various orcs from many different tribes and classes. Orcs are much more varied now, with even a few eyebrow-raising and jaw-dropping orcs to greet you. Scars are much better now, and ambushes are also integrated dynamically. Attacking a captain's blood brother? You may find yourself ambushed while fighting said captain, or even after killing said captain. Attacking a warchief's bodyguard? Said warchief may not be pleased and might just decide to take matters into his own hands to save his bodyguard from you.
Some orcs may hold so much grudge against you that they chase you from region to region to ambush you during the least expected moments. Your allied captains can betray you, and captains can come back from pretty much anything, even decapitation, giving a sense of tension on whether or not that captain will come back to haunt you.
PERFORMANCE
This game runs really well for my admittedly, outdated laptop. I would imagine that more recent computers would be able to handle this game fairly easily. There are also some really detailed settings for the graphics, allowing you to see which setting impacts your hardware the most.
ONLINE
Shadow of Mordor had online vendettas, and so does this game. The online vendetta has been tweaked a bit, allowing you to hunt down other players' nemesis. The difference being, you're not only hunting down said orc, but you're loaded into the other players' game world. You may just get ambushed by other orcs from the other players' game world during an online vendetta mission.
Online conquests are divided into two. Friendly and Ranked. In friendly, you test yourself against your friends' fortresses, and you will not lose your orcs in this game mode. Ranked is a different story. If the assaulting force had one of its orcs die during an assault, that orc will be dead permanently, unless he cheated death later on. Winning in ranked conquest gives you spoils of war to get a Spoils of War chest, as well as an extra reward, depending on your performance during said assault.
MICROTRANSACTIONS AND ENDGAME
The elephant in the room, and one I'm saving for last. After the amount of hours I've put in, I can safely say that the microtransactions are not needed to complete the game. Nor does the game need unreasonable amount of hours to get the final ending.
The tiers for items are divided into Silver, Gold, and Mithril, with Gold and Mithril only able to be purchased with the Premium currency. If you're like me, and have ungodly amount of unused Mirians, just use some of them to buy silver boxes for the heck of it.
How do you earn premium currency? By cashing out some money, or by doing community challenges. These challenges pop up daily, with most of them rewarding you with Mirians, or small amount of Gold. They usually reward you with 50 Gold, but some challenges can be rather generous, and don't be surprised to see higher amount of Gold rewards. There are also weekly challenges, and these challenges either reward you with very generous amount of Gold (say, like, 500), or just straight up give you a Gold War Chest, or even a special chest with more value. The Challenges aren't a bad way to prolong the game's life, if I'm being honest. I would've liked for more variety on the challenges, though.
How is the endgame grind? As you may know, some have reported that it borders on being unreasonable. On the contrary, the endgame portion is where XP drops like candies, to the point of being a tad bit ridiculous, if you know what you're doing. The game doesn't hold your hand, but don't let the lack of hand-holding discourage you. It's very easy to advance two levels in a heartbeat without the use of XP boosts, and you get even more if you do, even advancing four levels at once.
Besides, the MTs are kind of Pay-to-Lose. It's like Monolith deliberately sabotaged it to drive people away and as a silent protest towards WB, lol.
VERDICT
A great game that unfortunately, caters to quite a specific audience. If you're like me, and like the thought of just running around in a game and fooling around with the game's system, then definitely get this game. If you don't like spending hours on a game and want a quick, but satisfying experience, this is anything but that. This isn't a game you finish in a day or two. It's a game that takes time and an appreciation for what it is. This game knows what it wants to be, and it succeeded for the most part.
I would also applaud the devs on being very responsive with the community on Discord, Reddit, Twitch, etc.

I'm recommending this because the art is cute, the writing is funny, the story is silly, and it's pretty cheap. I paid $10 and got about three hours of entertainment out of it, which is a pretty good return on investment.
Having said that, it's boring.
All you do is left click. Left click to walk somewhere. Click to attack, and click to move away from the red danger zone of a counter attack. Click to harvest. Click to craft. Click here. Click there. That's it. Monsters are moving blobs you click to attack. Resources are stationary blobs you click to harvest. Crafting is a window you click to craft.
And that's totally ok, especially for a mobile game. If you enjoy clicking, and silly stories, and colorful artwork, then you too will probably get a few hours of fun out of this game. And that's cool.
Just please, don't get into this expecting depth or strategy or sandboxing. It isn't that sort of game. It's the kind of game you play while you poop, or while you're killing time on your lunch break, or when you only have one functional finger because of a tragic ninja injury. Expect anything else and you'll be upset.

TL;DR
I really want to like this game. It's got a quirky vibe (Baconweed, the Skinnery, Tar monsters), the writing is funny if a bit dad-humorish sometimes, and unlike a lot of games that lean of a crafting mechanic, it actually has a goal. Unfortunately I found the gameplay moderately tedious and both the control scheme and the interface for inventory & crafting really lacking.
Gameplay:
You progress through the game by quests, most of which involve crafting an item you will just receive the recipe for. This involves either harvesting plant/mineral resources or killing creatures. In either case, the drops are random enough that if you're looking for a somewhat rare drop, you can spend a lot of time grinding until you get enough of the drop you need.
Sometimes items from one quest depend on a recipe you'd get from another quest. For example, I needed to upgrade my saw, but hadn't yet gone out to start the quest which gave me the recipe for the water pump I needed so I could make water balloons which I needed for the upgraded saw (yes, you read that right). If the game's writing were consistent, your sidekick would have said "oh, you need water balloons, huh? well let me give you a recipe for a WATER PUMP", but instead I spent some time trying (and occasionally succeeding) in killing enemies I had previously had a very hard time with (for reasons described below), thinking maybe they dropped a water balloon. Nope. They did drop the necessary components.
I would have loved to see more building involved in the actual gameplay – mostly it consists of having enough floors on hand to build a bridge to an island with a rare resource you want, or across a river you don't want to around.
The environments are a bit homogeneous as well. Perhaps to be expected from a sandbox game, but it was a few hours before I got far enough out from the starting point to see the tarpit areas.
Combat:
The combat controls somewhat like Diablo or Torchlight – you click an enemy to attack it with your melee weapon. Unfortunately this also involves dogding a lot of area-of-effect attacks, for which you get a short preview of the area just before they strike, which means clicking to dodge, then trying to click the enemy again to attack between their strikes. I don't own a mouse (and I'm not going to buy one for this game) – I prefer playing with a controller, or barring that, games controlled primarily by the keyboard with some light mousing done on my laptop's trackpad. I've logged a lot of time on Minecraft and Terrarria that way.
While you do have some ranged weapons available, I found them problematic to use precisely in combat. You have to have them in your very limited hotbar, hit they key and then click the enemy, and then wait out a recharge time. In the middle of combat, I found this required more precision than I was able to give while dodging attacks from the gangs of enemies that would accrue while I was running around trying to dodge the thing I was trying to kill in the first place.
Healing items also have a recharge time, in my experience a longer one. While you can use a different healing item while the one you just used is recharging, they take up limited space in your hotbar menu, and you can't change hotbar items in combat.
Finally, while there are varying difficulty modes available, you have to choose at the start of your game. I might have kept playing had I been able to lower the difficulty once I got six hours in, but I can't, so I won't.
Inventory and Crafting:
For as much ballyhoo as the unlimited inventory and guided crafting got, I found it problematic for a few reaons.
First off, there's no actual inventory screen. If you want to know how much of something you have, you have to look at a crafting recipe that contains it. Second, you can only see your progress on one recipe ("track") at a time while away from your crafting stations. So basically you're tracking what you need to upgrade your weapon or armor, or the current quest item. For anything else you need to make notes or go from memory. Remember, there's no inventory screen to open up and ask, "Do I have enough of Item B to make Item E that I'm not tracking?" you have rely on the count of those you get when you pick up a drop of them.
You also need to keep track of what you can build at which stations. You want to build item X at station A, but it requires item Y and it kinda looks familiar but you're not sure so you have to go to each of your other stations to remember you can build it at station C.
These two gripes with the inventory and  Par for the course on crafting games, sure, but when you claim you've improved on them quite a bit I would expect more significant improvements than what was delivered.
Final thoughts:
Like I said, I really want to like this game. The vibe and humor had me sticking through it for longer than I would have otherwise. But I wouldn't consider playing again until it got controller support and improvements to inventory & crafting interfaces.

I do recognize however that not everyone is into this style of gaming, but this game might make you change your mind.

Alan Wake is a gem, just like any other gem produced by Sam Lake and his Finnish comrades. If you're a fan of the horror genre, you ought to play this game. It's a class act on its own with the superb storyline. It's basically about a writer who got entangled in the battle between dark and light. The atmosphere, the art direction, the sound design, the soundtrack are all AAA.
The sense of vulnerability is ever present in this game, and you ain't going to be blessed with superhuman reflexes like that of F.E.A.R or BFGs in Doom 3. Mind you, this is also nothing like Resident Evil where you got powerful weapons to help you get through the gritty parts. As one would most of the time be outnumbered in Alan Wake. Should I mention that it involves the woods or forest during the night for most of the time? Think Slenderman getting mixed up with Silent Hill.
The gameplay mechanics, is what survival horror supposed to be. There's a compulsory two step mechanics to kill the enemies: First the player must shine the light towards the enemies to "unbuff" them, only then he can actually shoot and kill them.  It's a nerve-wrecking-at-the-edge-of-the-sit kind of experience.

Some very nice additions, especially if you're into dodge because all of the weapons boast very good base concealment in their respective classes.
- The Desert Fox sniper rifle: R93-ish damage, pretty bad base accuracy, very good concealment (for a sniper rifle). Perfect if you want a strong sniper for dodge, as long as you pick up some skills to improve its subpar accuracy.
- The Contractor pistol: Nothing particularly special about this one, the stats are vaguely Crosskill-like and the overall performance is no different from pistols of that variety. There's also an akimbo variant if you're into spamming.
- UMP45 (or the Jackal SMG): I like this one, it has that high damage shared with guns like Krinkov, CR805B and Swedish K but it can have really good concealment without you having to go TOO far out of your way to achieve it. It can also be modded as a solid backup weapon for armour builds. The base accuracy is pretty bad (60) for a hard hitting low ammo SMG so it's a good idea to help that with some skills.
- Throwing knives can be decent in the right hands I guess, personally I can't get a whole lot of use out of them.
EDIT: They're actually pretty good once you get used to what their flight trajectory is like, great with crits.
Definitely get this if you want to expand your arsenal for low visibility builds. It doesn't offer anything HUGELY gamechanging for loud non-dodge gameplay although all of the weapons can be made better by sacrificing concealment, as per usual.

Alan Wake is probably one of the most tedious horror games you will play. You actually feel like you're grinding in pokemon to accomplish a level up that never happens. Now this enemy is unlike any enemy you have ever faced before. It is called the household appliance. This game decided that the shadows that you fight are going to make the refrigerator lift off and launch itself in your general. 9/10 times this will insta kill you and you will be set back to a checkpoint pretty damn far away, where you will have to repeat all your lumberjack killings all over again.
Now don't get me wrong the story is phenomenal and as stated before the atmoshpere is goddamn perfect, and the lack of ammo involved is the only real challenge. I do recommend this game if you aren't here for the gameplay though. otherwise meh get it during a sale.

This one surprised me.  I wasn't expecting much from it, but the Stephen King like plot kept me attached.  I definitely found myself repeatedly telling myself "just five more minutes"
That being said, the focus on action did a bit to take me out of the plot.  The mechanics in the game are good, but not great.  Dodging, in many video games, makes you "invulnerable" to damage while doing so.  In here, its possible to dodge and still take damage.  And it doesn't take a ton of hits to kill Wake.
There are some minor platforming elements as well.  This is definitely not a platforming game, but I always feel at a loss with these types of puzzles in this type of game.  Could've done without.  Especially considering how long Alan Wake's over-the-shoulder camera took me to adapt to.  I've played plenty of games with this style, but in Alan Wake it took some adjusting.
The reason to play this game is the episode-style plot.  It can be a bit cliche at times, but if this game is available for $5-$10 then I would definitely go for it,  You won't regret it.

Alright so I'm gonna list things I've noticed so far in the game from graphics to everything else.
Graphics:  (7/10)
This game has very good motion capture, therefore the actors and the voice acting with facial detail is some of the best I've seen in games, if I had to give an example its between GTA V and Uncharted 4, which imo is still very good. The games lighting effects at day time as of now is lackluster and the shadows look like pixelated crayons for most of the environment and objects, but character shadows are decent. The night time lighting looks decent but when you're in the swamp areas it gets really dark so you might want to crank up the brightness a bit. The cars along with the car damage look good for the most part but the reflections are a mess and they need to fix the skybox as well. Overall its a mixed bag where it can look really good in some indoor areas and then really washed out during daytime outside, they can patch some lighting fixes and add better textures so I'm not too worried about that.
Sound: (9/10)
As I mentioned before the acting and voice acting is top notch so this is gonna be some of the best work you're gonna see in recent video games. All the characters have the right emotion and tone that bring them to immerse you into believing they're real, and for the most part they are since they used real actors lol. Now for the music, this is also again some of the best in any video game. Using classic music from the 60s and 70s it brings out feel of New Bordeux and really fits the era. The game also has a lot of weapons, and so far from all the ones I used they all have a nice sound and kick to them, which is very satisfying and important in a game like this. Overall it has very good sound, except for the cars. Yeah so the cars sound off, I can't exactly explain but I'm sure the cars from that time were louder but meh its not really that bothersome to a lot of people but it's just something I wanted to point out.
Gameplay: (8/10)
Alright so the gameplay is the basic open world third person shooter type that we've seen in many games before, like the prequel Mafia Games, GTA series, Sleeping Dogs, Watch Dogs, etc. Compared to the last Mafia game this one feels may more open if that makes sense and is just an overall improvement to Mafia II. The gunplay feels very satisfying and the melee attacks pack a punch. The execution animations are brutal and always fun to use as well. Now for the driving, it feels decent, the cars aren't super slippery and depending on the vehicles it has some weight to them so that always good for added realism, and they give you the option for simulated driving so if you're into that you're in luck. The missions are all tied together properly with the story so far so I really can't complain, because this is the first time I feel like I have an excuse to actually murder people, unlike other games that just give you a gun and the freedom to kill random people. So again overall its everything that Mafia II did but bigger and better so if you liked that game you will like this one. This is not GTA, so don't buy it expecting GTA and then talk♥♥♥♥♥♥about it.
Overall: (8/10)
Too keep this short I think this is a good game. It's not better than Mafia 1, but it does have potential to be better than Mafia II and that itself is a good feat. The game immerses you with a good story, with spetacular acting from all the characters and the gameplay is good old fashion ♥♥♥♥ em up fun. If you're looking for a brutal action game with a good revenge story this is it, again don't expect this to be a GTA style game because there's not much to do aside from the story missions and side missions and it has no multiplayer. This is strictly a story based game and a damn good at that so if you understood every I wrote here then you know what to do.

So far have mixed opinions about the product.
Pro's
-Great story line gameplay
-The setting and the time zone era is really immersive, you really feel like your in the heart of the change in america, fighting within the race war before equality hits.
-The UI it's self I find pretty neet, slightly to scaled up in my opinion but I love the feel and look of it.

Con's
-Some of the texture's also swing the other way, you get a grainy feel to the sky/people around you.
- During Cut scenes, clothes like to sometimes come alive, causing them to jump around in a rag doll like affect, this is really off putting when your in the middle of a dramatic scene with the clothes moving all other the show.
- Sometimes it can get a bit repetitive, you end up doing the same things over and over again, luckily the cut scenes and the story line in the back make these still feel intresting, there are also many ways in which you can launch your assault, you're just forced to vary them up a bit for entertainment value.

After reading many reviews, and watching many videos, I decided to buy, Spin Tires. I was excited, it was one of a kind game. So, I bought the game, and began my adventure. As soon as I began, I was at awe.  In the videos the game looked great, but this was even better. After putting several hours((Somewhere around 4-6 I just got it xD)) I loved the game. There were a couple problems that I will point out.
1: Camera Angles; I understand they tried, and I like what they were doing with it. But, they just didn't do a amazing job at it. The camera is never where I want, or need it. Please add a dash cam as well.
2: The Chat; The chat was different. You push Y. Why y? Why not enter? Why Y? I understand they wanted to be different, and that doesn't bother me. What bothers me is the chat itself. There is no really canceling a message except for clicking somewhere outside the box. I found that stupid. If you put it enter, it'd be fine. It also randomly disappears.
3: A few glitchs; I was playing multiplayer when I flipped myself. So, two of my buddies came to help. One of them tried winching me, but it didn't work. He backed up, and the other guy pulled up. I switched winchs, and my truck shot for the moon. I left. I felt like I was Neil Armstrong. But, I came back. I landed almost in the same spot, still flipped. At this point, my truck was destroyed. So, we tried the same thing, and I shot for the moon again. It was crazy! Again, I came back down, and this time, I landed in trees. Luckily, I was able to repair myself, and my friends could knock down trees to get to me. I was finally able to get the last two garage points.
All in all, the game is great. Of course it's going to have bugs, all games will. I'm sure the Dev's will fix them, and make the game better to come.

I just completed the game, 100% in game and 100% achievements.
I had an absolute blast playing this. The game is wonderful.
If you're enjoyed the original this one is better on all fronts.
So many small improvements and big additions make this experience much more satisfying than the fun first game.
Building armies, conquests, managing orcs, you have to use strategy and skills, to slaughter everything in sight.
The only negative is the last ACT that seemed a bit long and artificial, it consists of 20 conquest missions. Half of that would've been enough, but I was having so much fun I didnt mind it so much.
Regarding Lootboxes:
First off, you can buy them with in-game money, secondly you get gold coins for completing daily missions and can use those as well, and lastly many gold lootboxes drop in game for completing missions, vendettas and conquests.
So you have tons of lootboxes without paying a dollar for them.
The other thing is, you dont need them AT ALL. I got far better loot just playing the game than the loot you can find in gold lootboxes. I actually finished the game with over 60 or 70 lootboxes and I only opened 5 of them!
You simply dont need any of it.
There is too much drama surrounding them, sure microtransactions suck, but in this game you can totally ignore them, they bring nothing extra, you dont need them at all, and you get a ton of them for free anyway.
It's a shame that it has hurt an otherwise awesome game. I had the best time playing this.
