After Divinity: Original Sin blew my socks off, I was expecting big things from one of my other kickstarted projects, Wasteland 2. Unfortunately Wasteland 2 has left me a little cold. It's not a bad game, certainly, as there's a lot to like about the depth of RPG mechanics one display here, but the game's first act is an absolute slog and a half. It takes far too long for anything interesting to happen, and it never quite reaches the heights of Fallout 2, the game it's clearly emulating. Like Divinity, the UI sucks, and the general user experience is clunky at best. It's still a good game if you can look past those shortcomings, but it's unfortunately stuck in the past in both the good ways...and the bad ways.

I have spent many pleasurable hours in Crashlands, so I figured I should write a bit about it ;-)
Crashlands is a game about learning your enemy... each mob has a different attack pattern, and a very handy thing to notice, since you can collect each mob as an attack pet that will help you defeat the rest of the mobs in the world.
The immense variety of monsters is a joy to behold... especially if you aggro a bunch of them and they end up chasing you down! haha
Learning to dodge is a skill you will need, but as long as you pay attention, you will succeed.
Crafting is easy, with ingredients specified at each station... and inventory is infinite, (yay!)  Crafting progresses through each biome at a natural pace, and though at times it can get a bit grindy, you are always challenged by the next new or upgraded mob that appears as you venture further and further from your base.
The three original biomes provide plenty of variety in terms of materials, mobs, and setting, and are a nice change of pace after you've farmed the previous ones.
The story is one of the best features of the game!  I thoroughly enjoyed the humor, and I still remember  the amusing and unique characters, and the entertaining quests they send you on.
Each biome also has its own share of bosses, each with different mechanics.  Craftable potions & gadgets allow you to customize your build to suit your playstyle.
Tl;DR
I thoroughly enjoyed playing Crashlands – every new recipe created a desire to hunt down new ingredients without it feeling like a chore.  The humor-driven story was hilarious, and well worth the price of admission!  I admit: I came into this game thinking it was something very casual, but it has a surprising amount of depth – a rare commodity these days!

Perhaps all the glowing reviews raised my expectation too far, I did not find the story compelling or well written; wasn’t even original. Just your typical "what’s going on?" puzzle story. The main character is also unlikable and simplistic (doesn’t seem to be that good writer either by what I read of his manuscripts).
There are a few cut scenes with his wife and I honestly don’t even know why he (or I) should be trying to save her; there was literally zero emotion shown between them, and all the time Alan was bitter and rather annoying.
The combat seemed new and refreshing at first glance- I had fun with the first chapter and wondered what sort of new weapons, combat abilities, and enemies, there might be later on. But there are none. The combat and environment varied very little throughout the game with enemies and weapons getting only “bigger” and “stronger.”  By the end of the third chapter I was hoping for a “skip combat” button just to get to the next cut scene (hate leaving game unfinished).
*”spoilers” regarding the end of the story ahead*
The ending was so generic I feel that the spoiler warning was almost unneeded. It did what every movie/book that is trying to be “different” does. It leaves you “wondering” if the final act was real or if it was a dream. The extra endings do basically the same thing again.
but take my review with a grain of salt as I am clearly in the minority here. maybe the story went over my head, or I wasnt using the simple 3 basic weapon (flashlight, grenade, firearm) system correctly.
not sure what happened.

Nuclear Throne is a over-the-top top-down roguelike bullet hell shooter. And I still get confused by music genres. Nice.
Nuclear Throne is a very action packed, almost 90s-style game with explosions every picosecond and a constant tinnitus of gunfire in your ear, not unlike DOOM. A "testosteronefest," if you will. Nuclear Throne pulls this off very well with a great blend of fast-paced gameplay, gritty retro aesthetics, satisfying gun sounds, and an enormous arsenal of ridiculous and barbaric weapons.
The game features a cast of interesting characters to fit different play styles. If you want to be super aggressive, you can play as "Steroids,"  who can wield 2 weapons at once and go full-auto with any weapons. If you're a ♥♥♥♥♥ like myself, you can play crystal, who can surround themself in a crystal shield and ignore any outside dangers. Kind of like how I deal with responsibilities in real life, only it actually works.
Being a roguelike, there is a lot of RNG in Nuclear Throne. Unlike some games, though, RNG doesn't really dictate how well your run goes, apart from an awkward spawn location every once in a while. Basically, if you want to get it up the♥♥♥♥♥from RNGsus, there's a game called Binding Of Isaac which you would probably enjoy.
Though RNG isn't going to kill your dreams, it's not going to hand them over to you, either. There are no absurdly game-breaking combos that will basically win the game for you.
That brings me to my next point: the difficulty. This game doesn't mess around. You usually take between 3-5 damage per shot, and health pickups only restore 2. Since you only have a max health of 8, there's little room for error.
To conclude, Nuclear Throne is a very solid game if you want a repeatable and exciting roguelike.

Spintires is a pretty unique simulation compared to other franchises on Steam. The goal for the game is simple; get the logs to the objective. The larger the logs the more points you will earn. However, don't let that simple concept fool you. In order to get  to the logging site and offloading site you must first traverse through very unforgiving landscape from rushing rivers, thick forests, and miles of thick mud with only a compass, a map, and your rugged soviet strong vehicles.
This is game is more about slow and steady rather than going fast. you must plan out your routes as not all vehicles will make it through certain terrain as well as making sure you do not total your vehicle as well as having enough fuel to make it to your destination. You are able to unlock vehicles, garages, fuel depots and uncover cloaked parts of the map to make your journey somewhat easier in the 5 maps that are currently in the game. The vehicles also come with a myriad of different modifications such as fuel tanks and utility trailers for remote repairs and refueling.
The terrain is completely moldable to the situation with muddy areas shaping differently when you pass it as well as your vehicle sinking in softer ground if it is heavy enough. Along with the unique type of terrain comes with a realistic sense of physics. Meaning you have to make use of the breaks and winch in order to get out of tough binds or avoid slamming your vehicle into the thick forests that encompass the landscape. Do not expect the physics to be in your favor either, expect to get stuck, slip, sink and damage your vehicle at even the slightest bump or error. This combined with a very well done day and night sequence and the ability to switch to a hardcore mode removing some of the crutches will be quite the challenge.
The UI for the game is a little confusing at first. It is strongly recommended reading the help guide as the game pretty much throws you in without telling you whats going on. The camera as well is very finnicky and is very challenge to find that perfect spot for it since it will move on you as well as hide areas of the terrain that could make or break your route. However there is a multiplayer feature that can help allievate the pain of getting stuck or lost.
Overall Spintires is a game that may not be for everyone. It is a different approach to the simulation and offroad genres that may leave a much to be desired taste to many. However, if you are looking for a unique type of gameplay with interesting terrain physics and rugged looking vehicles than this game may be a decent buy if not full price than at least on a sale.

Great universe, humor, exploration, automatic farming.
I've been playing since the beta; around 55 hours on mobile in addition to the time logged here. The universe and humor is a lot of fun. It's a good introduction if this is your first bscotch game, but there's a lot of smiles and crossovers if you've played their other games.
A big part of the appeal is exploration, building out your base, and the story.
The game goes out of its way to avoid grinding. Mark the map when you find a dense area for certain crafting mats, set up farms near your base, and you'll have a constant income for crafting. The only grinding in the game is when looking for rare mats -- best done as part of normal exploration. There isn't much variety for weapons/armor/equipment, so much of the crafting is around making your base look awesome.
The story and encounters are simple but fun and humorous, with a hint of dark since you're fighting against oppression and for survival.
Combat is tight and requires precise control. You're always on the edge of not quite being powerful enough. There's a good variety of enemies each with their own attack patterns that require constant attention. It's not a major focus of the game and battles are generally quick. It's fun to min/max your pets for attack type and supporting damage.
It's one of the best games available on mobile and jumping between mobile and the bigger screen of a PC is seamless. It really lends itself to spells of gameplay throughout the day. A little exploration in the morning on the phone while eating breakfast, base building at lunch at work, questing and boss fights on the bigger PC screen in the evening.
Well worth grabbing both the PC and mobile clients for a great deal of solid gameplay.

I feel there's been a lot of undeserved attention towards loot boxes and micro transactions in this game.  I feel compelled to write this review to counter act it.  While I do agree there is a "supposed" grind wall that prevents you from seeing the game's true ending that bridges The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings (maybe even past that), there's absolutely no need to get those paid loot boxes and I will explain why.
Legendary Orcs (Legendary Gear) appear within reasonable frequency and are not that difficult to kill.  If you decide to kill them (which you should if you have no legendary gear), you will get legendary equipment which can be upgraded all the way to 60.  Each fortress should have a Legendary Orc as an overlord, just kill him for loot.  The set bonuses form the Legendary Gear will aid you in any missions you need to do.  By the end of the end of the game (True ending), I've amassed over 30 pieces of legendary gear just to give you an idea of how easy it is to obtain loot.  I do not recommend trying to keep a Legendary Orc unless they have really nice strengths with very few or no weaknesses.  It doesn't make sense to keep a Legendary Orc who is terrified of fire or mortally wounded by poison so just kill them for loot.
The Grind Wall to the True Ending isn't too bad, I viewed it as an opportunity to get loot each fort defense (which by the way is incredibly easy to win if you level your warchiefs and assign 2 body guards via fight pits maggots each before starting the mission).  The final wave always has a guaranteed legendary orc (should be the guy with the highest level of the pack), kill or dominate for loot/orc.  My only gripe is that the Ending wasn't as detailed or long as I would have liked for the time investment but I don't think it promotes loot chest buying as some others have indicated.  Use Orc weakenesses to your advantage, there are only very few instances where an orc is really hard to defeat, there is no percieved "paywall" to win this game.
Bottom LIne, the game is entertaining.  I like the story they tried to tell and there is absolutely no "PAYWALL" that people might lead you to believe, if they do insist there is, this is a L2P moment for them.  YES, I do believe it's bad for PC games to institute loot boxes and microtransations especially a SINGLE PLAYER game.  YES, I do think it's a bad decision on Monolith's part for doing this because of the negativity it adds to their game for proabably a meagre return (not needed + a lot of people resent it).  Do I think you will require it to progress?  No, so stop whining and L2P.

I highly recommend this game if you have any interest in RPGs. It seems to be patched to a high degree now, no gamestoppers left.
The plot and quests are highly engaging and the atmosphere and style are relentless. Playing is fun at every turn - once you settle in - with plenty to explore. Wasteland 2 is rougher and meaner than Fallouts with no punches pulled, simply an amazing experience; the world can be unfair, it certainly is cruel, and it is very easy to not have a happy ending.
Here there was challenge and variety I have not found in singleplayer games for a long time.
The Unity engine does not offer the most varied tactics and environments (and gets in the player's way constantly), and parts of the resource pallette get recycled, but inXile pulled off a brilliant and rewarding world regardless. The game keeps you playing for hours and hours if you let it. I sunk in 4, 6, 8, 12 hours at a time; parts of the game were just too good to quit on. A total of 99 hours just to finish the first playthrough (I like to be thorough, plus the foreign character system led to some rerolls). That is a lot of quality playtime for your money. If you want to hurry and/or know what you're doing, I'm sure that time could be cut in half - it's still a lot, but the undertaking won't be nearly as daunting.
Full price or sale, this is absolutely worth your money. If you have tried Shadowrun Returns - another Kickstarter squad-RPG on Unity - and have your doubts, don't worry, Wasteland 2 is a different animal and a much, much better show. SRR is short, bland and repetitive by comparison (although I would still recommend the core game of that if you get it on sale).

This is a great game, but not perfect. It ticks a lot of the boxes right while leaving some boxes blank instead.
THE STORY
The story is nothing special. If you're expecting a masterpiece of a story, you're going to be dissapointed. More so if you're one of the so-called Tolkien-purists. This game is going to grind the hell out of your gears if that's the case. Despite of it, it's still a good story. Pretty much what you'd expect if you've played the first game.
To be honest, some side quests like the Bruz questline is much more engaging than the main story itself. A damn shame, to be honest, but it's not something I particularly mind. The personal stories with the orcs are, after all, what most of you are buying this game for.
THE GAMEPLAY
It's Shadow of Mordor's gameplay refined to a T. Sure, there are some frustrating bits where Talion runs up a wall you don't want to, but nowadays, that's kind of expected from AC's brand of freerunning. You have soo much more freedom in combat, and the enemies are much more varied in terms of ability as well. Orcs will adapt to your playstyle, forcing you to change your tactics on the fly if you want to be the one left standing.
Nemesis Difficulty is also the way to go for this game. IMO, it's the way the game is intended to be played. Orcs use their abilities much more often. Orc captains don't stand around, getting in your face and bringing the battle up close most of the time.
Side missions are always a thing with this game in the form of power struggles between orcs, but some of the collectibles are fine on their own, if you care about the game's lore-building at all. Gondorian artifacts gives insight into the lore of LotR for the uninitiated, as well as providing some amusing back and forth banter between Talion and Celebrimbor. Unfortunately, if you're not interested in any personal stories with the orcs, there isn't much to this game's side-content. The orcs are the main and side attractions, love them or hate them.
This game is also really generous in giving you skill points and Mirians (the in-game money). Perhaps too generous. By the end of the game, at level 60, I have 50k unspent Mirians that I have no idea what to do with, as well as 29 unspent skill points.
The UI is also a bit cluttered, but thankfully, you can turn some elements of the HUD off if you want.
The introduction of loot system and gear management is also a nice change. Unfortunately, they don't show up in cutscenes, since most of the cutscenes are pre-rendered. Other than that, gears are a useful way to spice up your playstyle, with legendary gears giving you some game-changing quirks. Make no mistake, though. This is still a very skill-dependent game. All the legendary gear sets in the game won't matter if you're playing it like a certain game journalist plays Cuphead's tutorial level.
And then there's the Photo Mode. You can blame some of my hours in this game solely on the Photo Mode. That pretty much sums up the Photo Mode.
THE NEMESIS SYSTEM
The Nemesis System from the previous game have been refined into a much better version of it, allowing you to craft your story with various orcs from many different tribes and classes. Orcs are much more varied now, with even a few eyebrow-raising and jaw-dropping orcs to greet you. Scars are much better now, and ambushes are also integrated dynamically. Attacking a captain's blood brother? You may find yourself ambushed while fighting said captain, or even after killing said captain. Attacking a warchief's bodyguard? Said warchief may not be pleased and might just decide to take matters into his own hands to save his bodyguard from you.
Some orcs may hold so much grudge against you that they chase you from region to region to ambush you during the least expected moments. Your allied captains can betray you, and captains can come back from pretty much anything, even decapitation, giving a sense of tension on whether or not that captain will come back to haunt you.
PERFORMANCE
This game runs really well for my admittedly, outdated laptop. I would imagine that more recent computers would be able to handle this game fairly easily. There are also some really detailed settings for the graphics, allowing you to see which setting impacts your hardware the most.
ONLINE
Shadow of Mordor had online vendettas, and so does this game. The online vendetta has been tweaked a bit, allowing you to hunt down other players' nemesis. The difference being, you're not only hunting down said orc, but you're loaded into the other players' game world. You may just get ambushed by other orcs from the other players' game world during an online vendetta mission.
Online conquests are divided into two. Friendly and Ranked. In friendly, you test yourself against your friends' fortresses, and you will not lose your orcs in this game mode. Ranked is a different story. If the assaulting force had one of its orcs die during an assault, that orc will be dead permanently, unless he cheated death later on. Winning in ranked conquest gives you spoils of war to get a Spoils of War chest, as well as an extra reward, depending on your performance during said assault.
MICROTRANSACTIONS AND ENDGAME
The elephant in the room, and one I'm saving for last. After the amount of hours I've put in, I can safely say that the microtransactions are not needed to complete the game. Nor does the game need unreasonable amount of hours to get the final ending.
The tiers for items are divided into Silver, Gold, and Mithril, with Gold and Mithril only able to be purchased with the Premium currency. If you're like me, and have ungodly amount of unused Mirians, just use some of them to buy silver boxes for the heck of it.
How do you earn premium currency? By cashing out some money, or by doing community challenges. These challenges pop up daily, with most of them rewarding you with Mirians, or small amount of Gold. They usually reward you with 50 Gold, but some challenges can be rather generous, and don't be surprised to see higher amount of Gold rewards. There are also weekly challenges, and these challenges either reward you with very generous amount of Gold (say, like, 500), or just straight up give you a Gold War Chest, or even a special chest with more value. The Challenges aren't a bad way to prolong the game's life, if I'm being honest. I would've liked for more variety on the challenges, though.
How is the endgame grind? As you may know, some have reported that it borders on being unreasonable. On the contrary, the endgame portion is where XP drops like candies, to the point of being a tad bit ridiculous, if you know what you're doing. The game doesn't hold your hand, but don't let the lack of hand-holding discourage you. It's very easy to advance two levels in a heartbeat without the use of XP boosts, and you get even more if you do, even advancing four levels at once.
Besides, the MTs are kind of Pay-to-Lose. It's like Monolith deliberately sabotaged it to drive people away and as a silent protest towards WB, lol.
VERDICT
A great game that unfortunately, caters to quite a specific audience. If you're like me, and like the thought of just running around in a game and fooling around with the game's system, then definitely get this game. If you don't like spending hours on a game and want a quick, but satisfying experience, this is anything but that. This isn't a game you finish in a day or two. It's a game that takes time and an appreciation for what it is. This game knows what it wants to be, and it succeeded for the most part.
I would also applaud the devs on being very responsive with the community on Discord, Reddit, Twitch, etc.

Paladins: Champions of the Realm is a great game made by Hi-Rez Studios (the makers of SMITE and Tribes: Ascend).
Paladins is a team-based shooter similar to Team Fortress 2, but is much more MOBA-like with items that can be purchased with in-game credits, custom loadouts, unique characters and abilities, several different character roles, and unlimited ammo.
There are mainly three game modes: Siege, Payload, and Survival.
Siege is the most popular game mode, where the first team to reach 4 points wins. This is done by capturing the objective and pushing a payload after. If the other team captures the objective, you must keep them from pushing the payload until the time expires.
Payload is the second game mode, where each team starts on either the attacking or defending side. The attacking team has limited time to escort the payload as far as they can, while the defending team has to keep them from pushing so until the time runs out. After the first round ends, both teams switch places. The team that pushes the payload the farthest wins.
Survival is the newest game mode, where teams have to battle until only one team remains while a deadly fog envelops the map and forces both teams to the center.

Seriously, don't buy it unless you have nothing else to spend Steam dosh on because you will gain very little actual value from this DLC. Let's go over what it has:
-The UMP45 "Jackal:" a submachinegun almost identical to the AK-pattern "Krinkov" already ingame for free.
The '45 does have one advantage in that it can sacrifice performance for concealment. This lets you get more creative with your primary weapon when running concealment-sensitive dodge builds... However, the '45 has so much spread and recoil that you may as well bring a 70-80 damage pistol and land more shots with the higher performance they offer for the same concealment.
Its applications in high-concealment mag-dumping aren't enough to redeem this needless sidegrade weapon.
Useless.
-A .308 bolt-action with terrible accuracy and heavy recoil - a straight downgrade from the "platypus," R93, and Mosin-Nagant rifles already available. Its high concealment gives it limited applications for dodge, but you may as well bring an AP shotgun or just a hard-hitting pistol.
Useless.
-YET ANOTHER M1911 SIDEGRADE. GOSH.
It's a 1911 "Crosskill" reskin.
Not useless but no need to take it over any of the million other pistols with almost identical stats.
So the guns are a write-off.
However, there is just one item that gives a limited value to this pack, and that is the throwing knife.
I suck with throwing knives but I'm trying to get better because they are statistically brilliant. Unlimited use, one-shot-heads even on One Down Zealots. The throwing axes or javelins are perfectly acceptable sidegrades, but the knives have twice as many in reserve which makes them far more useful on 1D, because you may need to dispatch multiple enemies to recover your thrown knives and having more in reserve is a great way to do that.
Throwing knives deal so much damage, I've pushed my way out of failed 1D stealth jobs by abusing armour gates and wiping six Zealots at a time with well=placed knives to push my way to the van.
All in all, there is only one real reason to buy this DLC and if you already have the Biker or Medieval packs then that utility is greatly diminished, but if it comes on special for -75% you should take a look at least, to add these vital throwables to your arsenal.
Careful though - these knives could be in line for a heavy nerf at any time.

This DLC is pretty good, but not necessary if you just want to play the game. It doesn't really add anything new, but it's good to have options. The Desertfox is a solid mid-tier sniper that has fairly good concealment which makes it preferrable for crit/dodge builds if you wanna bring a sniper along. The Jackal is the long-awaited UMP45, complete with a rather small ammo pool (which leads me to usually choose more sustainable SMGs), but pretty high damage for an SMG at around 80. The Jackal also introduced the concept of attachments having integrated flashlights and lasers with its Twinkle Grip. The Contractor is a pretty solid choice for a pistol, with a forgiving ammo pool, good accuracy, and damage that makes it comparable to the Deagle, Baby Deagle, and White Streak pistols (two of those three being free). It also has an akimbo variant with all of the pros and cons that come with it. The Throwing Knife throwables appear to be around the same damage as the Combat Axes, but come with 6 instead of 3. This allows for more spammy use of them, leading to some fun kills when you're low on ammo. I may be wrong, the knives may be weaker, but I've never noticed it. All 4 masks are interesting, as well as the materials. Though only Daisy and the Mustang resemble anything from John Wick. (The Continental just looks like one of the White Gloves from Fallout: New Vegas) and the fourth mask (whose name escapes me) just looks like a fuller version of the Gage Blade.
TL;DR -  You won't feel like John Wick really. You'll have a bunch of guns instead of a dog keeping you company. Not that you needed company.

Each side has a commander in charge of building new structures, getting upgrades, and giving orders.  The commander plays very much like a standard RTS.  The rest of the players experience an FPS. Jolly good fun.
In all seriousness, this the most tactical FPS I've ever played -  the fact that it has its wonderful duality with RTS elements is only icing on the cake. The assymetry with the aliens (Kharaa) and marines (Frontiersman) plays out beautifully from beginning to end, with all the wild craziness between. Get this game, and then tell your friends about it.
My only warning would be this: there is a learning curve to the game, and it plays VERY differently from traditional FPS games. In Natural Selection 2, on the field, your duty is to work as a cohesive body with your team AND your commander to further your tech/evolutions (to be researched by the one in the 'chair' - hence RTS) with the goal of eliminating all of the enemy's hives/command centers... I must iterate, this is NOT a team deathmatch. (Though there are modded game lobbies which support that.)
All-in-all, super satisfying game with endless variability in combat. It has a high skillcap for those willing to learn its ins-and-outs, despite its steep learning curve.
Edit: Over four years later, and I'd still recommend this game

Where to start. The gameplay itself is fun. Kind of a clone of the first one with a bit of extras. No refinement at all just a little more stuff. The skills trees are an interesting idea where you get the base skill with one of three upgrades but generally speaking you need a higher level to unlock the second and third augment so theyre usually better. Despite all the "customization" in builds they have added I can't recall a single time where I actually stopped a fight and respeced to adapt to the fight, its just pretty unnecessary and most times I wish I could just have all three since theyre all only actually slightly useful.
The combat is still fun it hasnt actually changed at all except with one new enemy where you can counter with a different key to stun and then rodeo. Otherwise exactly the same.
There doesn't really seem to have been a point in adding a leveling gear system except for wanting to make premium chests with legendary gear... There doesnt really feel like theres any change at all when you upgrade your weapons. It literally just feels like a requirement so youre not hitting orcs with a wooden sword. Rare gear has unlockable perks you can obtain by completing a certain task but since its just based on a flat damage system even if you find a perk you really like (which is rare) its not long before the weapon is obsolete.
The nemesis system is pretty much the same with a few changes. The only real change that sticks out in my mind is the ability for
Its not super common but in my relatively short playthrough of the game it happened to me quite literally back to back seven times. It sort of made me feel like even though I have dominated the orcs its not really my army and stopped caring about them.
The game has a pretty high level cap at 60 (I believe). Which is fine but theres not really a point in making it that high except coercing players into buying new premium loot chests for legendary gear every 10 levels or so. I also makes it really annoying with the nemesis system because your followers cant be a higher level than you so you can only dominate orcs of an equal or lower level. Its not a big deal but since theres more than one region youre a very differnet level in each of them so once you reach the last act and youre in the 40+ level range the first and second areas you play are vastly underleveled. This presents a unique problem because you can either kill all your followers  and wait for new hopefully higher leveled orcs to take their place, which would effectively mean redomination the entire region, or leveling them up by fighting randomly generated captains in the arena. The arena isnt to bad because they level 3 or 4 levels at a time but you have to actually watch each individual fight and you cant skip them. They have a 3 minute timer but each fight only takes ~2 minutes. Again not a big deal but when you have to fight each follower 4 or 5 times and you have 20 followers it can literally take hours for each region if you go the arena route.
The story is fine. They took a wierd approach to the story missions where each person is a different totally disconnected questline. Overall theyre pretty short and very unimmersive but theyre not that bad. I could be wrong because i finished them but at one point I was given a disclaimer saying if I hadnt finished the quests I wouldnt be able to if I continued which leads me to believe that almost all of the questlines are completely skippable. Towards the end of the story
Last but not least the thing that has annoyed me the most above the microtransactions, crappy story, bugs and grindfest is the fact that you cant skip anything. You cant skip cutscenes you cant skip dialogue you cant skip arena fights you cant skip trials. You cant skip anything you have to watch it in its entirety. Every. Single. TIme. Its great where if on a mission you encounter a particually tough boss that takes a learning curve to beat but every time you reload you have to listen to the speech again. You cant skip arena fights where you arent even present. You dont even have a body you are literally a floating camera spectating but you cant skip. Also when you go on a mission to fight an outpost commander or warchief or overlord you have to listen to the whole speech when  they arrive and then a different speech when you make first contact.
Overall I loved the first one and recommended it to all of my friends. Having played this game I would honestly just recommend people to play the first one and skip this one. Unless ofcourse you really want to spend 60 bones a mediocre money grab sequal.

Alan Wake is probably best described by the darkness that opposes you when you play it: all-consuming, hard to get a grasp on, a little confusing, but real enough to accomplish what it sets out to do.
From the beginning Alan Wake is presented as a psychological horror in Alan's dreams before jumping into a mysterious thriller plot. What's obnoxious is that by the time you're finished with the first Episode you should have a good grasp about how the plot runs and yet Mr. Writer Alan seems to grasp at straws. Thankfully this doesn't last too long since by about the halfway point Alan begins going on the attack and the game's plot improves because of it. Not to say that the first half isn't good, it's very good in fact. It just focuses more on atmosphere before working on the characters before settling into the antagonistic force, so the plot kinda jumps around a bit for the genre savvy. It doesn't get too caught up with itself and there are certainly better plots, but it's a solid one which supplements the game.
As for gameplay, Alan Wake takes some interesting ideas. Enemies can only be harmed by exposing them to acute amounts of light before laying into them with the firearm of your choice. Alan's magical flashlight can be focused - which drains the battery quickly but exposes enemies much faster - or you can just let the beam sit on them until you break through the darkness. After killing them they drop nothing, meaning that you're only getting refills on ammunition between locations. I found both ammuntion and batteries for the flashlight to be plentiful, but I can imagine on Nightmare that the supplies will be much more limited as enemies can respawn indefinately if you stand around with your thumb up your♥♥♥♥♥ This helps with the atmosphere as well as you should be running for the end, not fight everything you see, though it certainly helps if you do. Just make sure you know how to dodge, dodging in this game is weirdly made, but essential, as well as learning the different types of enemies and how to fight them.
Alan Wake is about 6 hours long with each of the six episodes being about an hour each, though you could probably finish them faster if you don't fight anything. There's also a pair of DLC episodes that remix a few Episodes while adding new content along with completing the first part of the Alan Wake story, neither are essential but they're pleasant little games. If you're on the edge about this, Alan Wake often goes on sale for dirt cheap and even at its full price I can easily call it worth it. Though there is some repetition, it isn't enough to drag on and feel like they're not worth playing. Whenever Alan Wake exposes a moment of weakness, there's another part of the game to make up for it.

This game has had my attention the minute my eyes landed on it and then I saw it on early access, I just had to get my hands on it. It seemed to bring something quaint and unique to the table.. Turns out, that guess was right.
The sceneries being 2D hand-painted is an art in itself. Honestly, I found myself just staring at how beautiful the game was quite a few times, I mean, even the menu was quaint, as much of a redundant thing that may be to mention. Topped with a lovely and perfectly fitting soundtrack from Peter McConnel (Who also put together the soundtracks for; Brütal Legend and Grim Fandango). it's all the little things that just make the entirety of it so appealing.
The story-line giving you two different lives with different things to do on each side is already a concept I quite enjoy, it doesn't overwhelm you with too much to do or a need to switch between the two, it just melds in a whole, brilliantly.
The only thing that may throw it off for some is the movement system and no kind of hints for some puzzles can make for a bit of back and forthing looking for required pieces. That aside making a point and click so enjoyable is quite the achievement.
I'm glad they have gotten far more than their goal funding so there will be a chapter 2 soon released as I cannot wait to play the next adventure. Although I have seen a lot of complaints that it is far too short and too expensive for 3-4 hours of play time just in chapter 1, it is an early access game, you buy it to be part of the process of it growing and bettering itself through good and bad. It's always a given in early access. Now they have more than enough funding for a chapter 2 and most likely quite a few more chapters, I personally think it will end up being quite worth it even though for me it already is, just for the amount of work and detail poured into it, I mean, just the surroundings being hand-painted seems to be such a rare and beautiful thing to see.
Final summation, lovely game, awesome story-line, characters, voice-acting and all around charming game. Will be worth it to see it develop into a full game.
****REVIEW UPDATE!****
As chapter two has finally come out, I feel this is due for an update.
Now mind you, I still love this game, I however feel that the execution for most of the puzzles in this chapter were even more obtuse and just downright annoying. Now, I'll be dropping a few tiny spoilers to anyone who hasn't played this yet, just a forewarning.
The fact that the game has gone through hoops just to make these incredibly and punishingly difficult really bothered me. I mean, one example is where you need to figure out how to rewire Shay's robot.. After at least an hour of raging, going back and forth, trying every combination I could think of, I still turned out empty handed. It was only when I went and looked up a walkthrough to see what I was doing wrong, that I felt like putting my head through a wall even more. The answer to the rewire was in a picture that was found in Vella's side. This is using information you never would have known been on the other characters side and something I think barely anyone would ever pick up.
Being able to switch to find out information is an okay way to do things, but the characters would have no way to actually find this out from an in-game perspective.
That aside, the entire chapter was put together really nicely with a range of different mini events happening within the game as you unlock and solve puzzles.
All in all, it's still a more than worthwhile play. Offering a total of about 10 hours of play, give or take however much you rage. Word of advice, have a game guide handy for when you get stuck and close to rage quitting, you may already have all the pieces of what you need to continue.

Okay, I think it's time for me to review this game.
First off, it's fantastic: it's tight, responsive, and feels right. It's well optimized and should work on most modern PC's.
The champions are fun too use and have nice designs. Yes, there are some similarities to Overwatch in terms of character design, but I think that coincidental.
You can unlock cards for each champion which allow for different play styles, which is nice, but not entirely necessary in my opinion.
Now, to address the issue most people have a problem with: The Legendary Card System.
Is it a good system? No, I think not.
Is it game breaking? Maybe slightly, but not heavily.
Is it pay-to-win? Not really, each champion automatically recieves one for free (and it's the best one for a few champions).
Does it ruin the game? Hell no.
After having played several matches since the Open Beta 44 patch, and the Legendary cards have been only an annoyance, but not a huge one. Legendary cards require a new in-game currency called Essence to unlock, which I have plenty of because I bought the founders pack and I've played alot. However, I have not felt the need as of yet, to use any of my essance, because the cards you recieve for free are just about as the ones you need to purchase.
You earn Essence in the same way you unlock anything in the game: by playing the game. You don't need to pay with real money, even though I've been hearing claims that the system is pay-to-win. It's not. It may take a while to unlock enough essence to buy cards, but the cards aren't necessary to have fun in the game.
And with that, it's time to look at the basic principle which lays the true groundwork of the game: Teamwork.
Yeah, yeah, teamwork sounds old and cliché, but for this game, it's important. The ultimate game-changer here is how well your team cooperates with each other; if someone's not doing their job, you're likely going to lose, regardless of how good your cards are.
Communication is also important, but necessary as long as everyone knows what they are doing. If all the players are trying their hardest and pulling their weight, each match is incredibly fun and intense. If not, one team's going to mow the other down.
It's especially difficult when grouping, because you're set up against another grouped team, so you and your team need lots of practice.
Now, to have a good team, each player needs to know their role.
Frontlines should stay as close to the objective as possible at all times, while sheilding allies (particularly the Support).
Supports should also stay near the objective and focus most of their healing on the Frontline.
Damage champions need to keep moving, pushing enemies away from the Support and Frontline, and occasionally hold objectives when the Frontline is down or near death.
Flanks... flank. They do pretty much the same thing as damage, but due generally lower health and better mobility, they should take a little more stealthy approach.
On the whole, Paladins is an excellent game, though right now it doesn't have a whole lot of content, and I highly recommend it. No, I don't like the Legendary card system, but don't let it scare you away from a great game. Yes, there are still some balancing issues to iron out, but it's still very fun and very addicting, especially when you win.
I give Paladins an 8/10, and might give it a 9/10 when we get more maps and better PVE content. Go play it.

Absolutely incredible sandbox space simulator. The initial learning curve is quite steep, but if you stick with it, you’ll quickly come to understand the infinite number of ways to explore the solar system in your own custom-made rockets. The excitement hits you after you hit each personal goal… for me, it all started when I was finally able to build and launch a (non-exploding) rocket from the launch pad. The next goal was to get into orbit. Then the Mun. Then the outer reaches of the solar system. Each new goal was exponentially more complex than the last, and that much more fun. One of the most rewarding challenges was to build a rocket to get to low-Duna (“Mars”) orbit, do an EVA to collect science, and land safely back on Kerbin (“Earth”). This seemingly simple objective took me days of gameplay and an unmentionable number of Kerbal debris to achieve. But on the final (and successful) attempt, watching the entire mission unfold in a well-orchestrated symphony of coordinated machinery was truly awesome. At the time of writing, there are nearly 32,000 user reviews with an average rating of 97% on Steam. I’ll add my thumbs up to the pack. Kerbal Space Program is worth every penny.
Dec 2017: Attempted career mode. The wide variety of 'contracts'  opened up a whole new set of challenges, including testing experimental parts at various altitudes/speeds, launching satellites into specific orbits, rescuing stranded Kerbins, and much more. By far, my favourite contracts were the ones where you had to try and figure out how to shuttle tourists safely to various planetary destinations and land them (in one piece) back on Kerbin. Added a whole new degree of difficulty (and fun). With 78 in-game hours, it's now my 2nd most played game on Steam, yet I feel like I've only scratched the surface.

I wasn't keen with buying a game twice to enjoy games across multiple platforms but, being on sale for the first time I had to jump on it. Ok, so I wasn't waiting around for this game to be released and I really didnt follow it up to the release other than PC gamer reviews here an there.  Decided to pre-order a few hours before release.  GLAD I DID.  I am about 6 hours in and all I can say is wow!
As others have complained, the frame rate cap wasn't the best move but that was fixed today.  I have experienced a few crashes, actually just now before I wrote this, but that gets me up from my computer.  I am sure they will fix these soon enough.
The story is absolutly great.  It is compelling and actually makes me want to continue and learn more about Lincoln.  The way it's told and the cut scenes are terrific.
The driving reminds me of "Driver - You are the wheel Man" that I spent coutless hours playing on PS1.  The sounds of the vehicles are fantastic.  Its more arcade driving then true to life, but it doesn't take you out of the realisim (like watchdog driving, yuck).
The combat system is good but can get challenging depending on your key mapping.
The graphics are not GTA 5 or Forza but they have moments when little details shine through.  Cloudy day causes random shading as clouds block the sun, when it rains the streets have a glistning effect as well as puddles that react to vehicles driving through.
The audio is where this game has exceeded my expectations.  Vehicle engine sounds, tires skidding, burnouts with realistic sounding posi traction, bidirectional audio based on player position.  The city itself feels alive!
End of the day its $60.  If you play it for a 6 hours its like going to the movies 3 times.  If you complain about the cost you probably shouldnt be buying games in the first place.  :)

Unless you really want to take a sniper rifle into battle when you go with dodge, or if you cant live without the UMP, this pack is not worth it. I bought it at 50% off (should've waited some more) and I immediately regretted it.
The Contractor pistol is a Interceptor "reskin" which focuses more on accuracy. The Tritium Sights mod gives +4 accuracy, but can not be used with other guns (unlike the Marksman Sight which is in the base game and gives +4 acc and +4 sta, usable on Bernetti, Crosskill and Deagle (who all have the same concealment possibilites, except the Bernetti with +3 conc boost)). The Contractors Compensator is a Facepunch Compensator with a focus on accuracy. The akimbo variant works the same. It has a fancy mag-out reload animation, but thats it.
The Desertfox has a high base concealment and can not be modded further in that direction (except for the +1 conc boost). It comes also with a Long Barrel (increases acc, decreases conc) and the obvious supressor. This makes it a mediocre rifle that lacks other possibilities to use except for concealment.
The Jackal (UMP) is a long awaited SMG that fits into the "high dmg and low ammo" category with Swedish K, Krinkov and that Biker Heist SMG (CR something). It brings a Long Barrel, its own silencer, 2 mags (more ammo + less conc and less ammo + more conc), 2 stocks (more stability + less conc and more conc + less stability), and of course the obvious Barrel Ext, Gadget, Boost and Sight slots. Its main purpose is the concealment build, which brings you to around 29 (not including silencer skills); building it with less conc makes is inferior to Krinkov and the others.
Last but not least: the Throwing Knife. Its actually pretty cool, high damage (from what it feels like) and can be recovered for more throws. But thats about it. No crowd effect or something (obvious), which makes grenades still a better throwable to take care of large groups and shields.
All in all, the pack is ok. Not really bad, but definitely not great. Wait until it hits 75% off, probably in the next sale.

It's a good simulator, a tad dated but there is essentially infinite content to create a better world. Default is fun, interesting, and you can see parts of the world - however it's not entirely realistic. Some of the larger cities have more details but if you make a lot of road trips or spend out time in the country you'll quickly realize that there's not a lot of realism near ground level. I prefer to fly low following roads, rivers, streams, canyons and it always amazes me when I see a house in the middle of an interstate or houses lining runways at smaller airports next to terminal buildings and hangars. I'm not complaining too much because the game is dated but the fact that it's still in use by so many and new content is always appearing shows that there is a lot of love for this sim. You will probably spend days or weeks searching through free content and you could easily spend hundreds or thousands of dollars for paid content. Personally, I don't want to spend too much to make it better I would rather wait for a newer sim with better/modern coding and better graphics out-of-the-box. I think Dovetail is going to be delivering something soon or perhaps I would look into P3D or X-plane.
This is still a great sim though and is usually on sale throughout the year for a low price. If you fly high or do standard traffic routes you may not care about the up-close ground level details, but if you prefer to fly under 500ft you're going to notice a lot of goofs and glitches with the world. There are mods and DLC packs that can correct and modernize and make things more realistic, but again it's going to take or money or both and the game is around ten years old or so.
I love the amount of content though, sadly a lot of the freeware aircraft out there are still optimized only for DX9 and I don't like having to turn my graphics down to enjoy games or simulators so I've wasted many hours, probably days or maybe even a week or two downloading and trying to use aircraft only to delete them after being forced to cut my graphics and performance backwards. I recommend it, it's great for beginners or advanced flight sim fans but just like any other simulator or hobby it can become quite pricey depending on what you want to fly, where you want to go, what you want to see, and how much detail and realism you want to experience. There are plenty of stores that offer content and they have plenty of sales throughout the year as well. Be warned though, more realism you want the more you will spend - but even going baseline or buying one of the packages on a Steam sale you'll get plenty hours of this. After-all there have been sim pilots flying this for over ten years...
Even taking the age into account I would give it 7 or 8 out of ten, fly high and it looks good enough, fly low and you'll need to make it look better. I'm not talking about 4k textures or over-detailed roads or anything but I tried following a couple familiar interstates and highways and found very little realism - even some smaller cities and towns the layout just appears completely randomized. I found a spot on I10 where the interstate twisted around a random house - I've seen HP cars sitting in the medians before but never houses. So take that how you will, good simulator, good out of the box, great with pricey add-ons like ORBX.
*You can get a lot of free trial-ware add-ons for scenery but most of the trial aircraft are so limited it's not worth it. Yay I can throttle up and throttle down and look at it in chase plane but can't lift off or turn! If you go with add-ons I would suggest flying a specific path in stock version, load the add-on - I love the Pacific Northwest trial from ORBX - fly the exact same path to see the new level of detail. Stock version you may see power line towers, with a good add-on package you can actually follow the power lines visually, or follow actual roads.
I have not tried any of the "Photo-real" packages though but I'm tempted - however P3D and X-plane are also trying to tempt me these days. 64bit optimized versus adding onto 32bit...
FSX is good though, just make sure you have plenty of hard drive space and some extra spending money to make it better for you.

Long and short of it:  This is a prime example of a crowdfunding failure.
I backed this game on Indiegogo, for a lot of money (hundreds of dollars), when the idea was first floated back in 2012.  I was already a big fan of their pewter miniatures line for wargames, which basically took the place of Warhammer 40k "Epic"/"Space Marine"/"Adeptus Titanicus" for me after Games Workshop shut those down.  I was crazy excited and was happy to share my reward game keys with others and get them excited too.
Sadly it wasn't long before it became apparent the developer could not devote much time to the game at all, and you will see immediately the age of the engine.  It's almost no different than it was back then.  Some effort was put into some things, and very little in others.  The splash screen is sophomoric and unit models are unadorned, some not even fully solid.  There is no movement animation and the colors and textures are blurred and drab.  I was momentarily impressed with some intro scenes and the tutorial narration but the rest looks very much like a high school project.
The developer didn't get his full funding on Indiegogo and decided to accept the partial payout, and still never delivered much of what was promised.  The game is buggy and very shallow, with no multiplayer, despite showing good potential.  The original website,
is now just a parking site.  I don't recommend anyone actually purchase the game ever again, because it will never be finished.  Better to let it fade into obscurity.
Even so, I don't wish ill upon the developers, so long as they've learned their lesson.  They still appear to be an active development house and hopefully the next thing they put out will have more effort and thought behind it.  But they should not under any circumstances be trying to capitalize on this failure any longer.  Have some dignity and let it die.

While promising, Wasteland 2 is ultimately a shallow experience. The tactics used in combat never change--the enemies all rush the player or hide behind cover like their feet were nailed in place. The weapons never get particularly interesting. The skills are generic and essentially amount to "use X to open box." The dialogue is buggy and often opaque.
I put 55 hours into this game before giving up. Not because it was hard, but because it was dull. The story beats are the same you see in every post-apocalypse story. If you've played the Fallout games, everything here is distressingly familiar without ever improving on or deepening the experience.
The characters are all one note. The story has virtually no twists. It pretends to be an open map but is really a guided, railroaded experience. There are no random encounters bringing levity and humor, like in the Fallout games. And any emotional resonance the game has requires you to have played a 20-year-old game.

There are definitely more things I could touch upon in this review but I am going to focus instead on the two areas that makes this game a chore for me that I feel any prospective buyer should be made aware of. I could touch upon the story or combat but it is better left to others.
This was the game I was looking forward to the most this year. The original game had missteps but the devs didn't know what they had until the reviews came in. The true heroes, the real purpose of the original game, was the orcs themselves.
So the slate has been wiped clean and the developers know that the Orcs are the driving force of the game and the narrative. So this must be a better game right? Well unfortunately this is where they dropped the ball overall.
The Orcs in this game are far more expendable and as such they don't get too much time receiving character as they must be squeezed in with all the other orcs you will have. Since your orcs are set against an enemy they also don't receive as much time being orcs. This is where the game should have been improved with the orc activities being expanded instead of feeling compressed.
This isn't helped by the lootboxes. These hurt the orcs in two fundamental ways: One is that because you earn orcs lootboxes they have ceased to be living breathing entities in the meta-narrative in the game, they might as well be your sword for all the importance they have. The second is that the features created to influence you to purchase more lootboxes such as the Online mode, will cheaply kill off Orcs or require you to treat them as highly disposable units.
Now if Orcs losing their personality due to a shift in the game was the only issue I'd probably say this game errs on the good side of average. Yet this is where the other aspect of the game pops up which is the grinding.
I will admit that if you do not care about equipment, orcs, skill points, collectibles, or anything this game throws at you then this problem should be rather mild overall. I, and I am sure a lot of other people, are not the same way and this game presents you with many grinding opportunities many of which require large  investments of time.
For example the best way to receive equipment is to play online assassination missions or online conquests and these on their own only take about 2-6 minutes if you are particularly quick, but can last longer if you like to take your time. You will receive usable equipment about a quarter of the time and so if you get into the loop of trying to find equipment you can end up playing for over an hour for very little reward.
For brevity, this game presents a lot of busy work at the player but often doesn't make them feel like they are playing the game. When you do grinding in a game it should feel like a compliment, that you enjoy the game so much that you are willing to work at it to unearth further enjoyment. This game presents grinding as the other 80% of the game. Shutting down camps, taking down warchiefs, Assassination Missions, several story missions, and the like are all handled with the same busy work mission structure.
In the end I felt like this game beat me down. I hesitate to play it because I know I have another twenty of hours of grinding ahead of me. If you are someone who finds themselves grinding in games just as a matter of discourse, think before you pick up this game.

Ok so I am going to give my review of Shadow of War now that I have finally completed it.
Graphics - Of cource like most WB games it always has great graphics meaning if your a graphic freak this will be alright for you. I can't help but notice the fact that some of the faces look a bit blurred sometimes (mainly Talion). In terms of graphics everything is alright though.
Nemisis System - This is probably the best part of the game and capturing orcs and commanding them is really fun. Although it is nice it is a real grind to get orcs in the later game and pretty much makes it unplayable without Lootboxes so I think it will put many people off (note I did not buy ANY lootboxes apart from ones with silver coins). I like how all the orcs are somewhat different and it adds a lot of personality to them which at the start makes you want to actually protect some of them but that attitude fades away in the later game.
Combat/Climbing - This game takes from the Arkham games which is alright since I love the games (Arkham Knight is amazing) but it can be a bit clonky sometimes and increadibly hard and fustrating to kill some high level orcs as they bassicly adapt to your moves and are normally not affected by arrows. The same goes to climbing in this game which is A LOT WORSE! For some reason they made climbing such a fustrating system to use. Bassicly what happens is half the time you are either rolling into a wall you want to climb or leaping to something you don't want to leap to because it dosen't listen to your controller/keyboard inputs half the time. It is increadibly fustrating in difficult situations.
Lootboxes - OK lets discuss the elephant in the room here. Lootboxes are terrible and I don't think anyone can say other wise and the way they are implemented into this game is a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ They diliberatly made the later game such a grind so that people will pretty much be forced to buy orcs if they don't want to spend hours getting them normally. The worst part is that the grind showed up in the later game meaning more critics wouldn't experiance it and that is just sick. I also want to state that you shouldn't JUST hate on this game for the loot boxes as it does do a lot of things really well. The fact that lootboxes don't result in drops of sales is because the games are still good wheather they have lootboxes in them or not and the only true way to kill it is to NOT BUY THEM. If its not profitable they won't try it.
Story/Ending - This was the main reason I played Shadow of War and I have to say i'm pretty dissapointed. The whole story just seems broken as it ends obviously leading to the lord of the rings films which I am not personally much of a fan of even though I have liked these games so far. There isn't a final boss but a MASSIVE amount of defend missions which are all so painful to play through and such a grind. Although we find out Talions fate it just seems rushed and I would of liked to see something more than just a cutscene showing his fate. I also want to say how short the plot is and how I can bassicly just summerize it here. Make ring, loose ring, get ring, take over mordor, betrayal, dead people stuff, defend, ending. The amount of content just really comes from the grind of taking over and defending bases which is a real shame.
World - I really like what they did with the open world in this game. Making it so that there are individual open areas to explore instead of one massive area which unique features to all of them makes it so much more interesting and means your not just running around everywhere all the time. Sadly the generic open world stuff is there like collectables and ♥♥♥♥ING TOWERS to help find the items. Bassicly getting all the items and doing all the challenges is pretty much a waste  of your time unless you want to find out more about the spider (forgot her name already) or your some hardcore completionist like Jirard.
Conclusion - I would not buy this game at this price. Usually the price of WB games drop like crazy once all the content is out so if your that bothered I would buy it then. I think the main issue with this game is the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ plot and the massive grind for orcs since WB wants all your money by buying lootboxes. I'm sure if they didn't have lootboxes the massive grind wouldn't even exist. If you want a good WB game with great graphics and a great plot just play Arkham Knight since it is so damn cheap now.

Fallout Shelter is a nice little F2P micromanagement game where you build one of Fallout's infamous vaults from scratch. Every vault consists of many different rooms which all serve one specific purpose like generating energy or drinking water. Then there are your inhabitants or dwellers which are necessary to do the actual work. Every dweller has his/her own unique strenghts and weaknesses which makes some of them better suited to perform certain tasks (rooms) than others. When you click on a power generation room, for example, a new display will pop up, there you will notice a circle with a capital 'S' in it which stands for strenght. Now you wanna check your dwellers' stats and assign the ones with high strenght (S) to the power generation room. To prevent things from becoming too easy the game will randomly throw threats at you which threaten your inhabitants. Usually, however, are your dwellers quite capable of handling such situations on their own as long as you have enough of them assigned to the room where the threat will initially occur or spread to. Weapons, armor and pets can help to deal with threats inside your vault easier and are also recommended to increase the chances of survival in the wastes. When you drag a dweller outside of your shelter you can order them to go on exploration missions or build the Overseer's office to send your dwellers on quests for rewards.
That's more or less it. What I still should point out is that Fallout Shelter isn't a game you could play for hours on end! You wanna load it up in the morning and before you go sleep, for example, to get maximum enjoyment out of it. It WiLL definitely bore you out of your mind if you think you could get entire gaming sessions out of it! I have played the game for about 5 hours now and didn't run into any annoying F2P crap yet. Those loot boxes or Nuka Colas which you can buy for real money aren't exactly necessary in my opinion to enjoy or survive in the game (at least not yet?).
While I liked the first 10 hours I lost interest pretty quickly once those feral ghouls started to constantly attack my vault. Annoying, especially due to the fact that those suckers do not even drop any rewards except for contaminating my vault with radiation.. Constantly swapping weapons around where they are needed also became infuriating way too fast to ever even consider putting any real money into it..
Shelter is still alright but it can go and ♥♥♥♥ off as far as I am concerned ; P

Alan Wake is the sort of game only the people at Remedy could pull off. It has all the charm and meticulous world-building that made the Max Payne series great with the game universe having its own pop culture you're privvy to and yet managing to keep your nerves on edge.
It's not a terrifying game in the sense that Amnesia or Silent Hill are (though Silent Hill is the series I'd liken it to the most) but it does its job as a suspenseful and tense survival horror nonetheless. Using light as a weapon and having to conserve your resources makes every fight an exciting one and the pacing is very well executed, giving you the occasional downtime while the story advances.
The story is an interesting breed and pays homage to multiple works from HP Lovecraft and Stephen King to Twin Peaks and the Twilight Zone and does its job well to keep you playing. There are some over-arching themes that I found interesting, but that I won't spoil here. Suffice to say that as far as Survival Horror stories go, Alan Wake is at least moderately ambitious, thematically. The structure is an episodic one splitting the story in several manageable 2-3 hour long chapters giving you a clear cut between story arcs so that you can take a break for the day.
The graphics make for some beautiful, if perhaps a bit dated, sceneries even if most of the game takes place at night. There is attention to detail to spare in Alan Wake and it seems to be a labor of love. The sound and voice acting are subject to little criticism and I guarantee that at least one or two tracks from the score and soundtrack will wind up in your playlist.
It comes highly recommended.

I always thought that I started gaming while playing the platforming genre like Mario and Sonic the Hedgehog being one of my favorite series of all time. As I thought about it for a minute, I remember I used to play a certain type of game even earlier than that. It involved using the mouse to click on parts of the environment to move your character, interact with it and solve puzzles. I never knew the name of the genre until a few years later when it peaked my curiosity enough to Google it. The genre was appropriately called 'Point and Click adventure games'.
So why it was so hard for me to pinpoint the genre? Well, gaming between now and then exploded in a ton of different genres, which further splintered into a variety of subgenres. Between all this chaotic explosion of genres, one got caught in the crossfire and badly wounded to the point it almost got killed, yes you know what genre I am talking about.
After more than a decade after that incident, the folks at Double Fine used their powers of necromancy to
of the genre back to life. They had to tap into the power of hundreds and thousands of souls to make it happen. Ok, I am very dramatic here but it kinda works doesn't it! The crowd funded Kickstarter campaign was a huge success, not only they greatly exceeded the funds to make their original vision of the game possible, but they kept on breaking all kinds of Kickstarter records in the process. The additional capital went further into making the game we all deserved but never asked for...or something like that.
So how is the game? Double Fine crafted a beautiful imaginative world with colorful characters while some carrying surprisingly muted intentions. It tells a story about a boy and a girl from two entirely different environments, yet facing the exact same problem: being captive in one's fate, as they both try to defy the fate placed upon themselves.
The world looks hand-drawn and reminds me of the story books I used to gross over as a child with the smallest of details carrying the biggest impressions. What is brilliant is how Double Fine lays down such a mature tale through the light hearted visuals and very simplistic and pleasing audio cues.
As someone who played a lot of adventure games when he was a kid, but sadly gone out of touch with it - because of lack of such games out in the market. I got stuck in a couple of  puzzles, some of them took more than hour for me to figure it out!  I took about 6 hours or so to finish the first act. Your milage may vary depending on how good you are at solving the puzzles.
If I had a gripe with this game, it is how much you are limited in solving the puzzles: I wish the game was a bit more open to clever to players out there. At times I felt I had the tools to handle a situation in an alternate way, but the game never really responded to such ideas. I know the game is playing it to it's well documented traditions, but I wish the game explored a bit further out the boundaries of this genre like this without taking away it's heart.
For the asking price of 25$, it might put off a lot of people off considering the short ride they are getting. The ride may be short, but it is a much more memorable. They could have easily went the road most other games take by stretching the length with filler content, but they didn't. Not a single time in the game I felt it was wasted, it is even more true for games of this class as any sort of filler content will distract it further from it's puzzle solving elements. So what are you waiting for? Hop in the Double Fine express for a beautiful journey that you won't be forgetting anytime soon!

With Telltale leading the effort in evolving the point & click adventure genre, it can’t be easy for other aspiring developers to catch up. In Double Fine’s Broken Age the first act is a bit of a strange case. The sound design is solid, with the voice acting delivered by several big movie actors. The soundtrack is also fantastic. The art style is clearly thought out, feels unique and works well with the story. The gameplay and puzzles feel streamlined. And yet, it just doesn’t feel like fun. It’s half the time downright boring. Both the story and the gameplay refused to interest me throughout much of this first act.
The two seemingly unrelated stories of Shay and Vella both start off very slow and frankly feel a little dull. The current life that Shay wants to break out of is boring and meaningless to him. This is projected well on to the player, who will feel the exact same. But the player’s feeling doesn’t let go once Shay starts on his big adventure. In fact, it still feels unmotivated and dull all the way towards the last ten minutes of the campaign. Only then does it pick up some speed, right before it abruptly ends with a tedious cliffhanger. Vella’s story is better and at least feels more focused.
Broken Age’s first act isn’t a bad piece of work. There’s just too little of it. It’s a slow game, but a short one at the same time. Most of the puzzles feel devoid of any real cerebral challenge, and consistently remains on a level that a child can master. But more seasoned veterans of the adventure genre - which likely includes most of the people who backed the Kickstarter campaign - will be disappointed by what Double Fine are offering. The game isn’t bad by any means; it looks beautiful and the last few seconds of Vella’s story really makes me interested in what will happen next. But so far I can’t recommend Broken Age to any seasoned adventurers, with this two hour unoriginal and uninspired first act. Telltale has grown this genre so much. Why are you treading backwards, Double Fine?

: Butterscotch Shenanigans
: Butterscotch Shenanigans
==========
When I first started playing Crashlands, my initial impression was "Oh, it's like Don't Starve...". But after the first 15 or so minutes though, that initial impression was blown out the window. Crashlands is so much deeper than I originally thought. It's completely story-driven, and it goes along at a fair pace.
The player character, Flux, is a delivery specialist for the largest shipping company in the universe. During one delivery of three very important packages, your ship is yanked out of hyper-drive (impossible!!!) by a cosmic entity resembling a floating head in the outer atmosphere of a seemingly uncharted planet. After removing a crucial part from your ship (a Quantum Electrodongle), this entity shoots your ship down and you crash onto the planet's surface. With nothing left but a basic craftin station and your semi-sentient AI floating robot storage thing called Juicebox, it's your mission to use whatever resources you can get your hands on to get those packages delivered! Needless to say, you have your work cut out for you.
==========
Once on the planet, you start by gathering up whatever resources you can to craft into basic tools. Juicebox will teach you all the basics as you go along, so pay attention when he tells you something! Gathering resources is your primary focus, and using them to craft weapons, armor and tools will help you progress towards your goals. There are quests scattered here and there, with varying rewards. NPC dialogue (all dialogue, really) is very light-hearted, but genuinely funny. Possibly the best feature of this game is Flux's suit. It stores EVERYTHING you gather, and has an unlimited capacity. You do not need to worry about managing your inventory, just how much of a given resource you have to craft what you need. You can "track" an item and it's components, so you know when you have enough to make the item.
You start out using your ship's little crash site as a makeshift base, but as you gather materials you can set up a base anywhere you like. Build Mode is very simple and easy to use, and you are free to set things down pretty much wherever you want. You can pick them back up too, without losing the item or components. At some point, you will be able to hatch companion monsters that will follow you around and help you in combat. You can then "enlargen" them with a crafted item to make them more powerful.
Crashlands has a very nice flow, and plays out at a great pace. It's not annoyingly easy, nor is it ball-breakingly hard (unless you don't keep your gear up-to-date). As you craft one station and gather materials, you'll unlock another crafting station with more recipes, weapons, and armor to craft. As you gather materials, you'll come across new schematics that allow you to make new items. Each section more or less rolls right into the next, and it's up to you how fast you want things to go. The world map is vast, and there is plenty to kill and gather. Thankfully, you can freely warp to your home or telepads you discover while exploring to get around quickly.
There's just so much I can go on and on about with Crashlands, but let's leave some surprises, shall we? Suffice it to say, there is PLENTY to do.
==========
The game looks very nice for a game with this kind of artstyle. Animations for everything look great, and the environments look nice too. You'll see a lot of the same for awhile though, until you move on after a certain point in quests. After that, environments are a little more diverse. Day and night transitions work well, and different, more powerful monsters come out at night. The game's UI is very easy to read and get used to.
==========
One of the shortcomings of this game is the soundtrack. For a long time you'll only be hearing the same 2 or 3 tracks. Daytime, nighttime, and event tracks. They are pretty nice though, and are often pretty chill and soothing. Great for just running around and gathering materials to relax. Sounds effects are pretty well done, and I always laugh when I hear the sound a Wompit makes when it's jumps you. The *smack* sound when you talk to NPCs or gather materials is quite satisfying too.
==========
I haven't had any issues running Crashlands whatsoever. It seems like it would work on nearly any kind of rig. It's not a particularly demanding game. Best played with mouse/keyboard, as most games of this type are. I didn't even think to try my controller, though I imagine it *could* work. NP FPS issues, no lag, and no stuttering. No random crashes either.
==========
If you enjoy games from this genre, you -need- to pickup Crashlands. Its humor is enough to warrant a purchase, nevermind the hours and hours of content packed into it! As I said before, it's not too easy or too hard, so most players should find it quite enjoyable to play for a relaxing evening. A great game that's very easy to recommend.

I've played this game since January 2012 (according to the ksp store, though I'm sure I played it longer, looking through patch histories) and even back then, with the basic alpha of a game that existed at the time, I could see the amazing potential.
5 (or more) years later, and I'm still going. I've got 872 hours in the steam version of the game, and many more hours from before then.
As an engineer, the creative and design aspects of this game are very satisfying. It takes one of the most complex areas of engineering and design, and simplifies it just enough that anyone can have a go, and then figure out why their rocket is pointing the wrong way.
For those who like a challenge (or less of one), there's plenty of ability to customize things, both in game, or with the massive selection of community mods. You can add so many factors that you spend hours or days designing a rocket and mission, only to realise 300 days into the journey you forgot to include a parachute. Even then, things aren't over yet, because you can now try to do some crazy in-situ problem solving, and complete the mission regardless.
Thoroughly recommend this game to just about everyone. Worth every cent.
