Boring, uncreative game with nothing else to it than "grind for a better weapon" or "grind for some better armour" add a pinch of totally cringy, uncreative puns which you could see from a mile away and a little bit of "fetch" quests or "kill that guy" quests and you got yourself this.... game?
Let me explain.
The grinding in this game is repetitive and boring, and the only interesting part about it is the "combat" that you get into every once in a while while trying to get some resources to get some COMPLETELY RADICAL armour (a.k.a. beat some trees for ten minutes then craft some wooden armour which boosts your health by 1) Seriously, the combat in this game is atrocious and feels like a mobile game. OH WAIT... It's a port! Oh boy! You just know its gonna be a great game when its a port!.... Besides that, the combat is literally just dodge the red area and smack your enemy a couple of times, then run away like a ♥♥♥♥♥... repeat, repeat, blah blah blah. It's fun at first, but then it gets boring.
Building in this game is non-existant. You place down a couple of grass foundations and thats all you'll need for the rest of the game.... literally. No enemies attack your base, and the foundations just provide somewhere to put the ten trillion crafting tables that youll make throughout the game, so whats the point of actually making a house other than some foundations? Sure, maybe you'll get a couple of stray animals wondering into your house, but by the time your base is that big that animals start wandering into it by accident you'll already have a weapon that can one-shot them in that area that you built in. Building any more than a couple of foundations is just a waste of precious resources.
The UI is slick and clean, easy to get used to even in PC, nothing to complain about here.
The story is rather predictable. Your ship gets highjacked by some super powerful alien creature, you crash land on this planet, blah blah blah. Just bland and predictable.
The.... "jokes" and "dialogue" is, well, a joke! The "jokes" consist of, like I said, puns that you can see from miles away, even before the dialogue starts. And the dialogue is nonsensical. Unknown space aliens that speak a completely different language than you? Fluently speak english no problem! I know thats a little nitpicky, but I couldn't help but just notice that whenever I spoke with them. It just felt wierd.
There are overpowered creatures in noobie areas with essential resources. Its not bad to have a challenge in a game at all, heck, a nice overpowered enemy is great to have in games like these. But when thier widespread in the exact area as the place you need to be in, it's just stupid. I cannot tell you how many times I was killed by those stupid octopus ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s every single time I tried to grind some stone to progress a little in the game. Its just so stupid! Why would you have them in such a key area! Like I said, it's nice to have a challenge, it's just the fact that you have it in such an area that it's just stupid! Speaking of challanges...
There is no immenent threat! There is no reason to grind, build a house, find something to eat, nothing! You can win this game by standing completely still! They say they removed everything that made a survival-rpg bad, but in reality instead of keeping the core essence of a survival game (starvation, thirst and immenent threats) they just removed it all and they still called it a survival-rpg in the end. A survival game is not a grind simulator, it's a game where you need to eat and drink and build a shelter to survive, not slap some grass until you get a new weapon or piece of armour. This game is just, in reality, a grindy RPG that feels badly executed, trying to be something it isin't.
If you like ♥♥♥♥♥♥ puns, fetch quests and smacking♥♥♥♥♥♥with various objects for multiple hours on end then this is the game for you!

You think a Don't Starve / Terraria mash-up is a brilliant idea. Or if you've never heard of those games... You want to unashamedly wander the wilderness, beating things up.
They have Baconweed
THEY HAVE FREAKING BACONWEED
It's like a weed... but it's made of bacon
Ok, I appreciate that did very little in selling the game to you. But what it does tell you is how seriously Butterscotch Shenanigans takes their game...
Answer: Not very
What we have here is the aim to take out everthing tedious from world-sprawling RPG's... and just make them all about
. So the guys blasphemously ripped out many of staples we're sick of... Letting us focus on the important things: Beating up the local wildlife and collecting stuff to make bigger stuff to beat up bigger local wildlife. So we no longer have to manage an unweildy inventory and angrily raid about 50 chests for that 1 item we know we picked up somewhere, but likely left in an outpost in God-knows-where (yay). The map is littered with teleporters that let us hop around the place on a whim (yay). And if you die, you can just go back, pick up your stuff and carry on (yay)
On the surface, this might seem worrying. By removing all this, does it leave a rather shallow game? Not really. What it ultimately does is make it exceptionally approachable and give you the freedom to muck about and just... enjoy it. Seriously, I could just mill about the Savannah for ages - it was just so relaxing. That's not to say it's easy (you will die... a lot), but it's laid back and easy to dip into.
The only real weak point is the armour crafting. Basically, your kit will randomly have special effects when you craft them (poisoning, going berserk, resisting damage...) - but it cannot be carried over when you upgrade. This sucks big time, as you'll repeatedly end up with Excellent Level kit... then have to forge like 30 items of the next level in the hope that one of them will actually have bonuses worth upgrading to. And you're forced to upgrade A LOT (the enemies scale quite dramatically). It ironically adds a lot of tedium to a game hell-bent on removing it. It's frustrating and can detract from the enjoyment - but there is at least enough enjoyment to be had to mitigate it to a degree.
Other than that though, it's great fun! The combat is reminiscent of the old Mega Drive platformers: Studying the attack patterns and finding the sequences to best get a hit in. The pets are an inspired (and fun) addition and the writing is utterly wonderful. It's cheeky, playful and there are tons of laugh-out-loud moments to be had. The characters are brilliant and the item descriptions equally funny. The end is charmingly sweet and rounds it off perfectly.
All I can echo is the same thing I said to my partner smack-bang during my first boss fight: "Holy crap this game is so cool!" - (then buying her a copy immediately after)
Little tip... pay attention to the names (especially the Polari) - They snuck in a lot more jokes than meets the eye...

What is it?
Exodus Wars: Fractured empire is a turn based strategy game.  The ambitious result of taking an established tabletop and miniature ruleset and optimising it for electronic gameplay.  Tabletop players, of which I only identify as a casual player, tend to be a very rules focused bunch and it is clear that the Membraine team have exposed their tabletop gaming roots by their faithful implementation of the Exodus Wars rules and units.  This results in an easy to pick up, hard to master, strategy game with a few twists.
How does it play?
The game focuses on formations, rather than individual units, requiring you to activate an move them across the battlefield with reasonably tight constraints on movement and actions.  Victory is also primairly determined by controlling locations on the field, as opposed to destroying or defeating your opponent.  As a result this places a much greater emphasis on positioning and placement of your formations rather than straight out combat.
Games are also limited to four turns, and can be even shorter if you control the victory locations.  While I understand this is primarily a tabletop constraint, where each turn can take several minutes to measure and move all your formations.  As this is all handled automatically by EW:FE the battles are sometimes over just as I'm getting set up.  That being said, I've found it a great game to pick up for a quick battle when I have a few moments to spare.
The emphasis on victory positions vs straight out combat is another positive shift from the tactical gameplay of other computer strategy games to the deep strategic gameplay of the tabletop rules.  You're almost forced to consider formation placement and control of the victory points.  Spend too much time focusing on destroying enemy formations and they'll win by capturing the battlefield.
What about controls?
There is a simple mouse point and click interface for most formations and actions with mouse-overs for detailed formation stats.  Membraine have done a pretty good job of showing formation feedback and status and the overall victory status of the battlefield. It is accessible and simple to use, however I do miss some of the more advanced UI elements like radial command menus and right click context menus from other titles.
It looks a bit complex!
While initially intimidating, EW:FE does a good job of trying to bring you up to speed with the core rules the game is based on.  Most of the well established strategy precepts of infantry and armor and their relative effectiveness against different unit types is present in the detailed unit statistics, if not extensively explained.  Fortunately a few skirmish matches and experimentation during play sored out what did what pretty quickly.
How does it look and run.
I understand the game is based on Unity and so it runs and looks good on my platform.  The units, when zoomed in, are beautifully modelled and detailed but are an almost missed detail considering you spend most of your time zoomed out looking at the whole battlefileld.  The battlefields are well textured and detailed with cover and concealment, but I do find myself wishing for more diversity; a ruined cityscape, enemy fortification or capturing a starbase.  Hopefully Membraine will consider this for any expansions or updates in the future.
Any downsides?
One aspect I wasn't used to was that each formation has a chance of not "activating" or not following your orders. In most computer strategy games you click on a unit, give it orders and off it goes.  While initially surprising and frustrating, it is another tactical element of the tabletop game which a player needs to be aware of, that formations may be unable or unwilling to execute your orders. Once you understand it, the activation rule becomes another layer in the overall  strategic outcome.
Final thoughts.
Overall, Membraine have done a highly faithful and realistic conversion of the Exodus Wars tabletop game and ruleset, but they have also taken the opportunity to streamline the command system and interface for rapid gameplay.  This improves upon some of the slower tabletop elements like measuring, dice rolling and referring to manuals to compare unti stats and combat outcomes.  This, in my opinion, provdes the best of both worlds; solid rules and gameplay simplified and accessible gameplay interface.
I am interested in where the developers go from there.  Expansion campaings, additional units and battlefields, more sophisticated victory conditions, perhaps even online multiplayer.  Well done guys...

This game is fun, and if you enjoy offroading there are certainly some hairy moments that will keep you on the edge.  The reason for me not recommending is because this is not a finished product.  I would agree this is an alpha or pre-release, and were it marketed this way I would be fine with it, but I thought I was buying a finished product.  If you want to try a finished product, wait for about a year.
1.  There are no saves in multiplayer, if the host loses an internet connection, everyone, including the host, are kicked to the main menu and 100% of the progress is lost.  You cannot continue the game the next day.
2.  You only get a very crappy 3rd person view.  Its nice when you are trying to get out of a bind, but worthless if you are trying to drive through a trail or a straight line.
3.  There are 6 maps, but all of them are the same thing, with slightly different surroundings.  You take logs from point A to point B while trying not to get stuck in 5 foot deep mud pits every 20 yards.  Nothing else to this game.
4.  Exploring is not even fun, since there is too much mud.  "It is not drive for a bit, and oh, there's some mud."  Its "yeah, finally got out of the mud, oh wait there's more."  I spend 95% of my time in 1st gear, Differential locked, and all wheel  drive engaged.  Otherwise you get stuck every 20 feet.
5.  The developers have promised more content, such as fixing the bugs, views, and adding more content, but again, this is supposed be a finished product.
6.  There are mods out there, but you cannot  use any and play multiplayer.

An enjoyable, unique,  if somewhat incomplete turn based wargame.
Only clocked up 3 hours, but rushing through a review in case it helps fellow gamers make their minds up on whether to take advantage of the sale.
Pros:
* The non grid based free form movement has not been done before in this sort of PC  game AFAIK. Together with the games other unusual rules,  it feels like it's more faithful to the challenges a real battle field commander would face, and it gives you a unique wargaming experience.
* At least for the parts of the game that are well polished,  the production values seem outstandingly good for an indie developer.
*  No significant bugs at all  (At least not for me, Im on Win 8.1)
* Nice music and good ingame sounds (could do with more variation though)
Neutral:
* The UI is ok but far from excellent.  Took me about an hour to learn the controls, unlike say Armageddon 4000 where I was up and running in 3 mins.  Less than optimal use of small fonts, have to sit quite close to the screen to read the full unit info.
Cons:
* Not many units or scenarios
* Very little in the way of unit & weapon description. Some unit types stuck with bland generic names like "Conscript heave weapons".
* Poor story, both  plot wise and in delivery.   (In fairness I may be biased here, as am not the sort to like a story where the capitalists seem to be the good guys and the traditional / religious side seem to relatively oppressive)
In summary,  great value while on the half price launch sale, and even at full price it would be good value for wargamers wanting something different,  especially if they don't mind a lack of good story and a lack of unit / scenario variety.

Ok. Lets start with the elephant in the room. First of all, this game WAS framerate locked at 30FPS on launch. LAME. It took the developers about 30 hours (after an uproar from PC gamers) to patch the game. Now the framerate is unlocked. Additionally, the patch appears to have polished the game in a few other ways as well. If you were holding off because of this, now is the time to buy, as it has been resolved. I'm frankly annoyed that the issue was there to begin with, but I'm also extremely impressed at how quickly it was patched. This game is raw, and gritty. I like that! They don't attempt to hide any racial tension, swear words, gore, or anything else that might offend anyone. This is a raw gangster story, and thats what the Mafia games have always been about. It is slightly strange to be taking down the Italian Mob that we worked so hard on building in the last 2 games, but the new characters are voiced well, interesting, and well written. I'm ok with this too! This game goes out on a limb and takes risks. They are portraying content that some may not like, and making a huge change on a beloved series. As a MASSIVE Mafia 2 fan, I'm actually ok with this. I would like to see Mafia 4 return to the Italian mob, as that bunch has always been a fun one to explore, but I'm ok with this detour. This game explores the other side of the Italian Mob. What happens when they run over the wrong people. Ect. If you like open world games, this is certainly worth a purchase. Especially when I see that we have been given some wonderful options like disabling aim assitance and field of view. I do wish there were a few more graphical choices in the settings menu, but overall I am pleased with my purchase, and post-patch I've decided NOT to refund. Enjoy! -PR0XIDIAN

There are definitely more things I could touch upon in this review but I am going to focus instead on the two areas that makes this game a chore for me that I feel any prospective buyer should be made aware of. I could touch upon the story or combat but it is better left to others.
This was the game I was looking forward to the most this year. The original game had missteps but the devs didn't know what they had until the reviews came in. The true heroes, the real purpose of the original game, was the orcs themselves.
So the slate has been wiped clean and the developers know that the Orcs are the driving force of the game and the narrative. So this must be a better game right? Well unfortunately this is where they dropped the ball overall.
The Orcs in this game are far more expendable and as such they don't get too much time receiving character as they must be squeezed in with all the other orcs you will have. Since your orcs are set against an enemy they also don't receive as much time being orcs. This is where the game should have been improved with the orc activities being expanded instead of feeling compressed.
This isn't helped by the lootboxes. These hurt the orcs in two fundamental ways: One is that because you earn orcs lootboxes they have ceased to be living breathing entities in the meta-narrative in the game, they might as well be your sword for all the importance they have. The second is that the features created to influence you to purchase more lootboxes such as the Online mode, will cheaply kill off Orcs or require you to treat them as highly disposable units.
Now if Orcs losing their personality due to a shift in the game was the only issue I'd probably say this game errs on the good side of average. Yet this is where the other aspect of the game pops up which is the grinding.
I will admit that if you do not care about equipment, orcs, skill points, collectibles, or anything this game throws at you then this problem should be rather mild overall. I, and I am sure a lot of other people, are not the same way and this game presents you with many grinding opportunities many of which require large  investments of time.
For example the best way to receive equipment is to play online assassination missions or online conquests and these on their own only take about 2-6 minutes if you are particularly quick, but can last longer if you like to take your time. You will receive usable equipment about a quarter of the time and so if you get into the loop of trying to find equipment you can end up playing for over an hour for very little reward.
For brevity, this game presents a lot of busy work at the player but often doesn't make them feel like they are playing the game. When you do grinding in a game it should feel like a compliment, that you enjoy the game so much that you are willing to work at it to unearth further enjoyment. This game presents grinding as the other 80% of the game. Shutting down camps, taking down warchiefs, Assassination Missions, several story missions, and the like are all handled with the same busy work mission structure.
In the end I felt like this game beat me down. I hesitate to play it because I know I have another twenty of hours of grinding ahead of me. If you are someone who finds themselves grinding in games just as a matter of discourse, think before you pick up this game.
Buy it only on sale.

Alan Wake is the sort of game only the people at Remedy could pull off. It has all the charm and meticulous world-building that made the Max Payne series great with the game universe having its own pop culture you're privvy to and yet managing to keep your nerves on edge.
It's not a terrifying game in the sense that Amnesia or Silent Hill are (though Silent Hill is the series I'd liken it to the most) but it does its job as a suspenseful and tense survival horror nonetheless. Using light as a weapon and having to conserve your resources makes every fight an exciting one and the pacing is very well executed, giving you the occasional downtime while the story advances.
The story is an interesting breed and pays homage to multiple works from HP Lovecraft and Stephen King to Twin Peaks and the Twilight Zone and does its job well to keep you playing. There are some over-arching themes that I found interesting, but that I won't spoil here. Suffice to say that as far as Survival Horror stories go, Alan Wake is at least moderately ambitious, thematically. The structure is an episodic one splitting the story in several manageable 2-3 hour long chapters giving you a clear cut between story arcs so that you can take a break for the day.
The graphics make for some beautiful, if perhaps a bit dated, sceneries even if most of the game takes place at night. There is attention to detail to spare in Alan Wake and it seems to be a labor of love. The sound and voice acting are subject to little criticism and I guarantee that at least one or two tracks from the score and soundtrack will wind up in your playlist.
It comes highly recommended.

Ok so I am going to give my review of Shadow of War now that I have finally completed it.
Graphics - Of cource like most WB games it always has great graphics meaning if your a graphic freak this will be alright for you. I can't help but notice the fact that some of the faces look a bit blurred sometimes (mainly Talion). In terms of graphics everything is alright though.
Nemisis System - This is probably the best part of the game and capturing orcs and commanding them is really fun. Although it is nice it is a real grind to get orcs in the later game and pretty much makes it unplayable without Lootboxes so I think it will put many people off (note I did not buy ANY lootboxes apart from ones with silver coins). I like how all the orcs are somewhat different and it adds a lot of personality to them which at the start makes you want to actually protect some of them but that attitude fades away in the later game.
Combat/Climbing - This game takes from the Arkham games which is alright since I love the games (Arkham Knight is amazing) but it can be a bit clonky sometimes and increadibly hard and fustrating to kill some high level orcs as they bassicly adapt to your moves and are normally not affected by arrows. The same goes to climbing in this game which is A LOT WORSE! For some reason they made climbing such a fustrating system to use. Bassicly what happens is half the time you are either rolling into a wall you want to climb or leaping to something you don't want to leap to because it dosen't listen to your controller/keyboard inputs half the time. It is increadibly fustrating in difficult situations.
Lootboxes - OK lets discuss the elephant in the room here. Lootboxes are terrible and I don't think anyone can say other wise and the way they are implemented into this game is a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ They diliberatly made the later game such a grind so that people will pretty much be forced to buy orcs if they don't want to spend hours getting them normally. The worst part is that the grind showed up in the later game meaning more critics wouldn't experiance it and that is just sick. I also want to state that you shouldn't JUST hate on this game for the loot boxes as it does do a lot of things really well. The fact that lootboxes don't result in drops of sales is because the games are still good wheather they have lootboxes in them or not and the only true way to kill it is to NOT BUY THEM. If its not profitable they won't try it.
Story/Ending - This was the main reason I played Shadow of War and I have to say i'm pretty dissapointed. The whole story just seems broken as it ends obviously leading to the lord of the rings films which I am not personally much of a fan of even though I have liked these games so far. There isn't a final boss but a MASSIVE amount of defend missions which are all so painful to play through and such a grind. Although we find out Talions fate it just seems rushed and I would of liked to see something more than just a cutscene showing his fate. I also want to say how short the plot is and how I can bassicly just summerize it here. Make ring, loose ring, get ring, take over mordor, betrayal, dead people stuff, defend, ending. The amount of content just really comes from the grind of taking over and defending bases which is a real shame.
World - I really like what they did with the open world in this game. Making it so that there are individual open areas to explore instead of one massive area which unique features to all of them makes it so much more interesting and means your not just running around everywhere all the time. Sadly the generic open world stuff is there like collectables and ♥♥♥♥ING TOWERS to help find the items. Bassicly getting all the items and doing all the challenges is pretty much a waste  of your time unless you want to find out more about the spider (forgot her name already) or your some hardcore completionist like Jirard.
Conclusion - I would not buy this game at this price. Usually the price of WB games drop like crazy once all the content is out so if your that bothered I would buy it then. I think the main issue with this game is the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ plot and the massive grind for orcs since WB wants all your money by buying lootboxes. Broken Age is a game with two co-existing stories that are set in
seperate worlds.  One story follows Vella, a girl from the bakery town of Sugar Bunting who has been selected to be sacrificed to a monster known as Mog Chothra as part of the town's "maiden feast"- which is apparently a great honor- and ultimately chooses to escape the event in search of a way to kill the beast.  The other story centers on Shay, a boy who is alone on a sentient spaceship that takes care of him, and more importantly, keeps him safe.  Shay, however, is bored of the childish, mundane routine that the ship puts him through every day to keep him entertained, and discovers that the ship's AI has been lying to him, which sets him on a quest to take control of the ship himself.
Broken Age plays as a point-and-click adventure game; in most situations, you click areas you want to move to or investigate, ask questions from NPCs to figure out what to do or where to go, solve puzzles, collect items, use items to solve more puzzles, and most importantly, discover the world and immerse yourself in the story of the world.  The game allows you to transition from Vella's and Shay's stories at any time via. the Inventory Window, so if you get stuck on a puzzle in one world, you can switch to the other for a while so you can continue playing the game without getting super frustrated. There are many ways to use this system to fit your playing preferences; you can switch the stories regularly, you can switch the stories when you get stuck on a character, or you can just play through one character at a time as you wish.
Overall, the game feels pretty good- that is, the game flows for me.  If I click an area farther away, the characters will run to the target, whereas if I click an area closer to me, the characters will walk.  The camera-work feels right for the most part, however sometimes the inventory will pop up if I move the cursor too close to the bottom left of the screen, especially when a place I want to click is located near that location. Cutscenes are generally done through a close-up view of the characters as they speak, and the animations during the cutscenes are fun and captivating.  I'm never terribly confused as to what an item in my inventory does, as clicking on them without dragging them on anything gives me a decent description of the item. Sometimes, dragging certain items towards certain characters results in a fun(ny) interaction between the player character and the respective other characters.
Generally, anything that is clickable that is not a walkable path presents useful or amusing information / dialogue about the objects when clicked.  NPCs never feel totally boring to listen to, and if you are a faster reader than the voice acting (and happen to have subtitles on), you can skip any cutscenes by hitting space once or twice.
The illustration style is quirky, painterly, and well-done.  It's also sometimes surreal, but there's nothing remarkably too creepy or unsettling generally found in surrealist paintings; if that's kind of your thing, you'll probably disagree with me on its surreality. As mentioned early, the characters are animated in a way that is fun and captivating, and it's fun to watch the characters move, even with their idle animations.  The visual effects really make everything come together, from background objects rotating to in-game LED screens flashing words, to puffs of clouds kicking up as a chracter walks, they really help background elements feel more real and connected the characters that inhabbit the spaces.
The music is beautiful.  (If you grab the soundtrack, I highly suggest listening to Vella and Shay's theme songs all the way through.)  Overall, it really makes the atmosphere of the game come alive, especially with the cutscenes with songs that are scored into the game, or the ones that don't feature a lot (or any) interaction with the game itself, which sets up a nice cinematic feeling that, in my opinion, adds to the game rather than take away from it.
Some of the things I noted people complain about are the difficulty of the puzzles and the linearity of choices as you go through the game.  While I recognize that the difficulty of the puzzles is low, and generally not super-challenging, I feel that for the sake of being only the first half the game, it definitely is better for those gamers who are not common adventure game players to ease into the logic of the game puzzles.  Plus, I thought they were hard enough for most people to not realize immediately how to solve several of the puzzles, especially when the options are not immediately or obvious or sometimes overlooked for feeling they are a tad ridiculous.  (In my experience, the more difficult puzzles took me much longer to figure out in comparison to the ones that were intentionally much easier. Additionally, I have to mention that not a lot of people realize the solution to one of the first puzzles in one of the stories until it's almost directly stated in the dialogue.)
In response to the linearity of choices as you go through the game, I feel like if you weren't given some sort of goal to work towards as you get through the game, many of the players would spend a lot of time in the game getting next to nothing done.  I don't say this as if a game is meant to be beaten, but for a game heavily focused on the stories of two characters, it's not as if the fate of these characters are ultimately determined by what the player does in the game, but more by the story. To make my point clear; the reason some puzzles are presented to you at certain times if for the sake of story progression.  You would be totally stuck if you didn't know what to at times.  If the problem is less so linearity due to story progression and more the lack of extra things to do, well.... I don't think you realize this, but even this amount of content was super-expensive to make, and you wouldn't realize this if you hadn't been watching the Double Fine Adventure documentary (or, for that matter, have been interested in the games industry besides as a consumer in the first place).
It's not like I don't have any problems with the game at all; some important objects you need for puzzles blend into the background, or are looked over in the first few times you pass the area they're contained in.  Some jokes fall flat, which is fine for the most part I suppose, because otherwise the dialogue is amazing for all reasons.  As mentioned earlier, sometimes the camera placement results in clickable locations being located in the bottom-left corner of the screen, so the inventory likes to pop up and you'll wind up clicking an item instead of the intended location.
As mentioned earlier, this review doesn't take into account the amount of time you can play compared to it's price in it's current state.  Also as mentioned, the game plays for about four hours and 30 minutes total, with about 2 hours and 15 minutes per character for a more experienced adventure gamer.  If the rest of the game was canceled right now, I wouldn't suggest purchasing the game.
However, Act 2 is being added for free soon, so I think the money's worth it.
I'm running out of characters; all-in-all, 9.5 / 10 from me, can't wait for Act 2. :)

(As a disclaimer, my love for DoubleFine and Tim Schafer is limitless, and I was a backer, so don't expect any level of objectivity. This review is before the release of the second act too.)
With this sort of game, you need to know what you're getting in for. It's a point and click adventure game - not quite in the classic style with a dozen commands you can use on objects on the screen, but still of that heritage. If solving puzzles and clicking isn't your thing, then you're probably not going to enjoy this.
If you do however, Broken Age is simply marvelous. The patented Schafer writing and charm can be found all other this, with an interesting setting and an even more interesting twist. The characterisation for the two leads leaves something to be desired - but then again, it's only half way through, and the voice acting is enough to make up for what the writing might not have explicitly. The game is full of polish and small tidbits that may not even be noticed in a casual playthrough, so I'd highly recommend playing through multiple times. Look at the backgrounds, look at the foreground, click on everything, and you'll probably discover a lot that you wouldn't if you focussed solely on what the plot wanted you to do.
That's really the charm of these sort of games. It's a calm, relaxing walk in a different world with some plot and puzzles layed on top of that. The world is the most important part. On the subject of puzzles, Broken Age largely does not suffer from the same obscure or arcana logic that traditional adventure games do (indeed, a lot of people including myself consider it too easy) - I can only think of one puzzle that required a lot of backtracking to get the solution to, something many people wouldn't guess to do.
The music is great. The world is great. The voice acting is great. The writing is average, as is the puzzle design. However, the love and the attention to detail that has been put into this game is clear to see, and I love every bit of it. Is it worth £19? To me, yes, but perhaps not to you. I guess you should get it and then decide.

I talk mostly from the perspective of a support class player:
We all agree skill must count. But all "fixes" / "nerfs" / new aditions to the game i've seen recently are just making low dps champions obsolete, aim the only skill that apparently matters & accuracy + dps the main stats to look for in your champion of choice.
In a class based game healing has 4 essential requirements:
- Being aware who needs that heal the most
- Being in range & or sight
- Being on time
- And obviously not having your heals in cooldown.
Then the healer has to make a choice between all the candidates who meet those requirements.
(Meaning usually someone else will be left to die)
In a game where so many champions have close to instakill skills or ludicrously high overall dps, a game where some champions can kill anything but a tank in 2 hits or in less than 3 seconds... the class-based concept evaporates and it becomes a frag contest between hardcore aim gamers playing the "highest-dps & accuracy-champ available".
While obviously healing & tanking are still necessary, anyone can also see that those are the most undesirable choices for most people when matchmaking.
In balanced class based games every class or character has his/her counter.
In Paladins that's not necessarily true.

Nuclear Throne is a game with plenty of potential. Having many adrenaline pumping moments and unique characters that all have their own playstyles and personal unlockable content to enjoy, there are plenty of hours of gameplay waiting in a unique world for those willing to subject themselves to a community crafted hell.
Nuclear Throne is not a game for beginners or anyone that wants to enjoy a remotely casual experience, it is a game crafted to beat you into the ground and spit on your grave, but it plays in such a way that you might consider trying it again for those moments of immense satisfaction.
However, over the years of playing Nuclear Throne there have been rebalances that have changed the core concept from accessible but unforgiving, to an outright merciless sadistic disaster. If the game was only about reaching the throne, the difficulty spikes would be forgivable, but the goal is always to surpass the throne and head even further into an absolute mess that only the most hardened veterans could manage to overcome.
Nuclear Throne isn't made for anyone. It's a test for those willing to spend countless hours in frustratingly overbearing situations that will absolutely beat you back to square one again and again. Some may adapt better than I have with all the time I've invested in an evolving game, but unless you're able to play with friends or are willing to mod the game, I don't suggest trying it.

Wasteland 2 has hit that magical spot of being a nostalgia game that is much more than its heritage and requires no knowledge of his history for a new player to get into it.
First and foremost in its achievements is the story, something oft lacking in games (of any generation) and more importantly the story is coherent and makes sense within its own universe without falling into stupidity or badly contradicting itself *cough*masseffect*cough*.  You can properly immerse yourself into the lives and motivations of the people around you.
Gameplay is uncomplicated but solid, and even after you have mastered the art of making money and buying the best gear there will be combats which can challenge you.  Of course as in any good game, combat is always the side dish with the real challenge coming in surviving the wasteland and its problems.  A combat wombat specced team will be able to shoot their way through most of the game but will miss half the dialogue and die on a mine they didn't spot.  (Seriously spec  your main character to be good at demolitions.)
This is where the team mechanic shines, you are no ubermensch of Skyrim who can be the best at everything and solo Fus-Ro-Dah your way through any challange, your medic, your rogue and your sniper will all have their moment in the sun.  Even the stats matter more than in most games, Intelligence is clearly the best, but scrimp too much on strength and that sweet minigun you could have sold for top dollar in town is going to have to be left behind and even though skills can improve vastly over the course of the game, you will likely only get 3-4 single stat point increases from go to whoa.
In short, a definite thumbs up, go buy this game now and not out of some blind support of indi games but because this genuinely is a good quality, well considered, and entertaining game which while technically a sequel is so far beyond its predecessor as to stand entirely on its own.

This game had so much potential: it achieved so much, but its fault are blatant as well.  The artwork was great, but there needed to be more, especially character portraits; it becomes redundant when 5 different characters all share the same portrait and half the time their description doesn't match their portrait.  The other thing abou the game that could use significant improvement is the UI.  The UI was decent, but I use a mac and I've seen significant improvements in UI since the Window's era of the 90's.  I felt like the UI was designed on a 90's mentality.  Why are developers afraid of making UI easy to understand and simple to use? Does it make hardcore gamers feel less vested in a unique game that fits their demographic? The game tends to make you click a lot of buttons, redundantly.  I was plagued with graphics/memory issues during my 50+ hours of gameplay, so I had to save the game after each action, so I wouldn't have to continueally redo everything I had already accomplished.  I'll admit I wanted this game so badly I dreamed about it months before it was released.  I was huge Fallout 2 fan, and I thought this would finally be its successor, but I was a little let down.  The story was decent, but the hallmark was the ability to choose any action and not be limited to the proper plot line.  Graphics could have been better as well, there's a little note you find towards the end of the story that says something to the effect of, "I wished they'd used the unreal engine," which is rather true.  But I don't know the constraints that the developers had, all I know is what could have made it better.  I suppose it goes without saying that I played the entire game and tried to do all the mini mission, so it was a good enough game that I had to finish it.  Hopefully the bugs can be fixed and the next WL3 will have improved UI, artwork, and graphics.  I should say thank you to the InExile team for putting together a fun game.

The concept
For those who are familiar with table-top war games its basically Epic 40,000 translated to PC, so a modern day Final Liberation. The two factions available are effectively elite imperial guard troops plus their tank and super heavy tank support, vs Penal Legion imperial Guard with Titan Legions / Knight Titan support.
For those not familiar with Games Workshop games, its basically the Total War series battles, but turn based where each side takes it in turns to move one set of troops. One side has huge tanks and men in armour, one side has big robots and poorly armed conscripts.
The Good:
It’s a genuine recreation of table-top mechanics, with morale, % to hit, armour, turns, army deployment, objectives, overwatch, cover. No stupid ultra detailed rules that can plague tabletop rules and require extensive learning - things do what you expect them to..
Build your own army, based on their points costs (price to buy) etc.
Intuitive simple mechanics
Balanced factions and units.
Scale – this is war between armies and massive war machines, not squads.
Responsive dev team – they are active of the forums and have implemented feedback from the community in the alpha tests.
The maps and infantry look good.
Performs well on low-end pc
The Bad: (written when game in early access alphs testing phase)
Bugs. Mostly visual rather than game-breaking, e.g. unit facing the wrong way.
Limited number of unit types per side. - 4 different units on one side, 6 on the other.
Only two factions - both are human. i think there are aliens in the IP, dont know if they will make it into the game
No online multiplayer - but it is planned
No army painter (first world problems)
The vehicle models are presumably placeholders and need to be upgraded to the same level as the infantry models.

Overall
The core feel of table top warfare is clearly there, the graphics wont set the world alight but they are up to Total war standard and its a strategy game afterall. It just needs more units, multiplayer, and some bug crunching which we will hopefully get over the next few months, and then we’ve got a great game,

Announced to get fixed - 4/5 of the game are solid, id wager if you pick it up now it should be patched by the time you reach that part.

Everything good about this game is a copy/paste straight from 'Shadow of Mordor'.
Everything original in this game is a poorly written, buggy and (worst of all) boring mess.
I'm currently grinding through the end game 'Shadow Wars' and no 'real ending' is worth this - It is simply not fun.
I can't help but come away thinking that we're being charged full price for 'Shadow of Mordor 1.5' + a Fort minigame.
Personal big gripes for me are the following:
Boring Maps
All very samey with the exception of Minas Morgul, I couldn't even tell you the names of the others, even after 50 hours of playtime.
Broken Movement
Clearly the devs have tried to impliment a better/faster way of getting around, but the maps aren't designed to support it. I was frequently getting stuck in the terrain, wether it be inside walls (sometimes forcing a reload) or running up against a small mound and having to stop running in order to awkwardly walk around it :/
Broken Camera
No-where NEAR as reliable as the previous game, the camera gets stuck in corners & walls far too frequently for a mostly reaction-based combat system.
Constant interruptions
During combat, expect to be interrupted sometimes several times every few minutes depending on whats going on. Unskippable Orc dialogue made up way too much of my playtime. Whats worse, these mini cutscenes can actually CANCEL what you're doing, depending on how far through an animation you are.
About to finish off that annoying Orc just before an enemy hits you with an arrow you can't see coming because it's off camera? Too bad; 'Pushkrimp the Bingler' wants to let you know that he hates spiders. you get hit by an arrow because you can't move for half a second while control is handed back, and you have to wait for the next opportunity, or worse, you die.
Ruined Free-Flow Combat
This has got to be the worst thing about this game.
I love the free-flow combat system introduced by the Batman: Arkham games. They got it just right years ago, and managed to refine it over the years to almost perfection. With the FF combat system, you are given constant subtle but noticable cues as to whats going on: Controller rumble, slo-mo sequences and info on screen lets you know when you can pull off certain moves.
Much of that is done away with here and replaced with the god-awful 'Rage' meter. Rather than knowing when you'll be able to pull off a special move by hitting a certain combo amount, you've just got to keep your eye on a meter that fills at a different rate depending on dozens of factors. Less haptic and visual feedback make this feel like when Assassins Creed tried to copy the FF combat system without getting sued. Why ruin something that the previous game had NAILED!?
I could go on - I've intentionally not gone into the microtransactions, but suffice it to say that they are a joke.
All in all, this is a downgraded and messy expension to 'Shadow of Mordor', which was an amazing experience.
I recommend you play that instead :)

With two distinct factions, playing as either a soldier or alien feels very different, and somewhat similar to Aliens vs. Predator (2000) overall. A multiplayer FPS that distinguishes itself though one player on each side taking a 'commander' role. This plays like an RTS, where that player can give orders to other players, and build structures. Upgrades can be unlocked by the commander, using resources gained through capture-and-hold style locations, held by the players. Because of all this, each match tends to play out very differently from the last.
Commanding (marines or aliens) plays like a game of Starcraft: albeit with all the unpredictability and drama "intelligent" units bring to the battle (just be sure to bring a microphone if you intend to command!). When everything goes right, (no small feat) the game mechanics create a fairly unique atmosphere and a strong sense of teamwork. When things go wrong, prepare to lose.. horribly.
I like the idea of a commander, but I feel that too much responsibility and control lies with the one player (commander), for a game with ~6-10 players on each side.

My review is probably somewhat biased because I am one of the many die-hard fans of the LucasArts adventure games of yore. Point and click adventure games are my bread and butter, and I have enjoyed everything from the classic Monkey Island, LOOM, DOTT, and The Dig, to the newer TellTale adventure games and the indie Blackwell adventure series. So needless to say, I approached this game with the discerning eye of an afficianato. That said, I absolutely loved part one of Broken Age. I was one of those people who were hidden under a rock and did not really know about the game until last week. I played through the game in two three hour long sittings, devouring the incredible artwork, wonderful voice acting, and classic Tim Schaffer humor. Sure, the game was quick, leaving me with that strange empty feeling after finishing a great novel - but that feeling is one of the things I love about the genre. I think the only reason that it took me weeks to finish Day of the Tentacle back when I was 13 is that I was stuck trying to figure out what the heck to do with a frozen hamster. Playing through those games now is an incredibly quick process. It doesn't make the experience any less sweet. Admittedly there were no times that I had to pause for more than a few moments to figure out the puzzles in Broken Age, but that honestly matters little to me. What I found was a beautiful, quirky game that I cannot reccomend enough. I cannot wait for Part 2. Great job Double Fine!

Man, the game's simply awesome. I can't fully describe the imperession it had on me, though I completed only the first chapter.
It doesn't have any obvious disasvantages, and those which are not obvious are not actually cons.
Firstly, I should say about the visual component. The game is really beuatiful. Every detail is drawn exceptionally good and stylish. You are walking in the Blackwell Academy and you feel like you're in the real high school.
You're lying on a bed in Max' room and the whole room feels like a real hipster-geek girl room. Speaking about room, it concerns every room there is in the game. Impression you get once you enter the room is the same if you enter some guys room in real wolrd. You feel the individual style of this guy, you know that this room is his, not the room made by artist.
The locations of the world (parking lot, lighthouse) are awesome as well. Especially it's about the lighthouse and the first time you see the storm. That scene really scared me.
Secondly, the main character. Sometimes when you play visual novels or some other games where you have to make choice in order to push the plot further you can feel that the main charecter is a bit faceless. This effect is made in order to make it easier to asociate yourself with the main character so you want to play more. This game, it doesn't create sunch an effect, it simply doesn't need it. Max is so interesting as person that you want to see the life through her eyes, not yours. The same is also common to games from Grisaia franchise.
In you run-of-the-mill visual novel or something like you asociate the main character with you, in this game you do quite the opposite thing: you asociate yourself with the main char.
Finally, the audio. There is not musch I can say about it. The music and audio effects are picked up really good. The whole atmospere of the game is perfectly accompanied by the audio component.
To conclude the review I must say that there is no way to describe the whole impression I have about this game. If  you're reading this because you don't know if it worth your time and money, you should know one tinhg: it is.

Deciding how much funding you want in each and every little thing...
*Sigh* It's a good time.

With two distinct factions, playing as either a soldier or alien feels very different, and somewhat similar to Aliens vs. Predator (2000) overall. A multiplayer FPS that distinguishes itself though one player on each side taking a 'commander' role. This plays like an RTS, where that player can give orders to other players, and build structures. Upgrades can be unlocked by the commander, using resources gained through capture-and-hold style locations, held by the players. Because of all this, each match tends to play out very differently from the last.
Commanding (marines or aliens) plays like a game of Starcraft: albeit with all the unpredictability and drama "intelligent" units bring to the battle (just be sure to bring a microphone if you intend to command!). When everything goes right, (no small feat) the game mechanics create a fairly unique atmosphere and a strong sense of teamwork. When things go wrong, prepare to lose.. horribly.
I like the idea of a commander, but I feel that too much responsibility and control lies with the one player (commander), for a game with ~6-10 players on each side.

I bought Hotline Miami, got the Deluxe Edition of HM2, I got SpeedRunners and whatever else unlocks content for Payday 2. I personally prefer not having to buy other games for content within Payday 2, so I'm thankful for seeing this as a "standalone" DLC.
All the weapons here feel nice - they have smooth animations, they sound unique and modding them makes them look pretty. They differ a little bit from the stats of other weapons, either found in the base game or by purchasing other DLCs. None of them are great - they're just pretty reskins.
3½ weapons are added to your inventory. 1 Sniper Rifle, 1 SMG and 1 pistol (+akimbo).
The Jackal SMG is a UMP and functions like most other SMGs; it's great until you run out of ammo. There are way better ones out there, should you develop a taste for this kind.
The Contractor pistol looks nice - but in regards to stats the pistol is a down-grade to the LEO and is almost identical to 3 - 4 other pistols.
The only interesting point of this DLC is the Sniper Rifle (Desertfox). With max concealment you can hit 4 detection risk - there are better options out there for crit builds though. And to "balance" it, the Desertfox has very bad accuracy.
Even if you have no DLCs yet, there are better options within the base game, and no weapon mods are added beyond the ones for these guns.
The throwing knives are also a reskin - their function is to deal direct damage to the target you're aiming for - they're a tad slower than the throwing axe found in the Biker DLC, but you get six knives as opposed to the three axes. The thrown Javelin was also nerfed when this DLC hit the store, so I guess there's that.
Purely cosmetic and/or minor aspects of the game.
There's not a whole lot to tell about this DLC. It's one of the worst (so far), and unless the weapons are subject to future changes I don't see them being used very much, beyond the 20 minutes it takes to grind through the 4 added achievements.

Now back to this time SpinTires is now final out, at least with a version with a lot more contenct and objective to it. Now i think it will fallow the same line with Euro Truck with frekvent content updates and pathes for the game. This game is all about driving in very muddiy terrain in the Siberia era. Then when you have planed your route you can take your Truck and do the log delivery from the lobber mill to the objective destination. I hit the spike again while attacking the red skorpians base. A guy asks me to pay tax. It is a small tax. To round this off, if you ever played any of the fallout games, or even the orignal wasteland, this will surely apeal to you. Anyone who loves tactical games, shotguns and not paying taxes? The game where you make the story. The game where you REALLY NEED A MEDIC. SERIOUSLY GUYS, BRING A MEDIC! The game where you obsesively hoard all the junk you can find. Lootboxes - OK lets discuss the elephant in the room here. Lootboxes are terrible and I don't think anyone can say other wise and the way they are implemented into this game is a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ They diliberatly made the later game such a grind so that people will pretty much be forced to buy orcs if they don't want to spend hours getting them normally. I also want to state that you shouldn't JUST hate on this game for the loot boxes as it does do a lot of things really well. The fact that lootboxes don't result in drops of sales is because the games are still good wheather they have lootboxes in them or not and the only true way to kill it is to NOT BUY THEM. If its not profitable they won't try it.
Story/Ending - This was the main reason I played Shadow of War and I have to say i'm pretty dissapointed. The whole story just seems broken as it ends obviously leading to the lord of the rings films which I am not personally much of a fan of even though I have liked these games so far. There isn't a final boss but a MASSIVE amount of defend missions which are all so painful to play through and such a grind. Although we find out Talions fate it just seems rushed and I would of liked to see something more than just a cutscene showing his fate. I also want to say how short the plot is and how I can bassicly just summerize it here. Make ring, loose ring, get ring, take over mordor, betrayal, dead people stuff, defend, ending. The amount of content just really comes from the grind of taking over and defending bases which is a real shame.
World - I really like what they did with the open world in this game. Making it so that there are individual open areas to explore instead of one massive area which unique features to all of them makes it so much more interesting and means your not just running around everywhere all the time. Sadly the generic open world stuff is there like collectables and ♥♥♥♥ING TOWERS to help find the items. Bassicly getting all the items and doing all the challenges is pretty much a waste  of your time unless you want to find out more about the spider (forgot her name already) or your some hardcore completionist like Jirard.
Conclusion - I would not buy this game at this price. Usually the price of WB games drop like crazy once all the content is out so if your that bothered I would buy it then. If this looks like a game you want to play, then it is a game you want to play.
The developers hit all the right notes, especially if you take the time to play into the game's second half. I never played the original (which is included) but its clear this game does all it can to stay true to both the setting and story of that title while creating a modern game of some depth.
If you need your games to be AAA quality, you might take some issues with the graphics or voice acting. The visual design feels rough, though careful examination shows great detail. The voice acting comes and goes, usually introducing a character with a bit of spoken dialog and then going text only.
The story is not exceptional in its overall arc, but the lives of individual NPCs and locations are often compelling and amusing. There is a lot of character in the game with both great NPCs you can join up with and bizarre folks making their way in the wastelands.
Combat is good, though has some rough edges. Armor is fairly pointless on higher difficulties and simply getting the best guns you can find trumps nearly every other consideration much of the time. But there is depth in the skills side that makes character building and development compelling. What is likely a first fight for many groups is exceptionally tough and is not optional. (my hint, bring explosives)  Overall difficulty comes in waves, getting easy when you get some spiffy new guns, and brutal when you wander into a new area and are not ready for  what waits there.
You will be getting a good amount of game for your money. I was worried it was a bit sparse until it became clear there was a second half to the story. It left me satisfied and eager for a second playthrough on the highest difficulty taking some roads not taken the first time around, always a good sign.
Highly replayable, and perfect for those 3-in-the-morning bouts of complacency.

It's definitely a great start to a complete game, although as a huge fan of the developing team and the genre, I do feel a bit let down. The gameplay feels a bit lacking in some areas, such as there aren't many item combinations available and you generally don't carry items around for a long time, you just get them for an area, use them, get the next set. Conversely, there are several areas that are easy to get stuck in indefinitely without seeking help on a tutorial site, which can clog up the fun.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I talk mostly from the perspective of a support class player:
We all agree skill must count. But all "fixes" / "nerfs" / new aditions to the game i've seen recently are just making low dps champions obsolete, aim the only skill that apparently matters & accuracy + dps the main stats to look for in your champion of choice.
In a class based game healing has 4 essential requirements:
- Being aware who needs that heal the most
- Being in range & or sight
- Being on time
- And obviously not having your heals in cooldown.
Then the healer has to make a choice between all the candidates who meet those requirements.
(Meaning usually someone else will be left to die)
In a game where so many champions have close to instakill skills or ludicrously high overall dps, a game where some champions can kill anything but a tank in 2 hits or in less than 3 seconds... the class-based concept evaporates and it becomes a frag contest between hardcore aim gamers playing the "highest-dps & accuracy-champ available".
While obviously healing & tanking are still necessary, anyone can also see that those are the most undesirable choices for most people when matchmaking.
In balanced class based games every class or character has his/her counter.
In Paladins that's not necessarily true.
Likeable characters, interesting story and insight into a angst teen's life, heartbreaking ending... it's just amazing

Man, the game's simply awesome. I can't fully describe the imperession it had on me, though I completed only the first chapter.
It doesn't have any obvious disasvantages, and those which are not obvious are not actually cons.
Firstly, I should say about the visual component. The game is really beuatiful. Every detail is drawn exceptionally good and stylish. You are walking in the Blackwell Academy and you feel like you're in the real high school.
You're lying on a bed in Max' room and the whole room feels like a real hipster-geek girl room. Speaking about room, it concerns every room there is in the game. Impression you get once you enter the room is the same if you enter some guys room in real wolrd. You feel the individual style of this guy, you know that this room is his, not the room made by artist.
The locations of the world (parking lot, lighthouse) are awesome as well. Especially it's about the lighthouse and the first time you see the storm. That scene really scared me.
Secondly, the main character. Sometimes when you play visual novels or some other games where you have to make choice in order to push the plot further you can feel that the main charecter is a bit faceless. This effect is made in order to make it easier to asociate yourself with the main character so you want to play more. This game, it doesn't create sunch an effect, it simply doesn't need it. Max is so interesting as person that you want to see the life through her eyes, not yours. The same is also common to games from Grisaia franchise.
In you run-of-the-mill visual novel or something like you asociate the main character with you, in this game you do quite the opposite thing: you asociate yourself with the main char.
Finally, the audio. There is not musch I can say about it. The music and audio effects are picked up really good. The whole atmospere of the game is perfectly accompanied by the audio component.
To conclude the review I must say that there is no way to describe the whole impression I have about this game. If  you're reading this because you don't know if it worth your time and money, you should know one tinhg: it is.

Well another month, another DLC, this time John Wick has some new guns and masks to show us, but how does it hold up?
During my time playing PD2 I do enjoy the game, especially that it has the one down difficulty I will be spending more hours crying my eyes out until I get all hiests done, but then the DLC fell on my head and here we are, the John Wick pack.
You get:
4 Masks, materials, patterns and achievements
3 new Guns
1 new throwable
and that's it...
With the 3 new guns you get: the contractor pistol, DesertFox sniper rifle and the long waited UMP or Jackal SMG.
Before I start I want to say something, this is probably one of the least unique pack I have seen, Yes you could say that "omg there's a UMP already in the game, therefore it will come" and I did expect it, but honestly it got over hyped. NONE of these weapons don't have a unique personality other than a different reload and has different attachments. Anyways I digress.
Let's start with everybody's favorite, the UMP or the Jackal SMG. The Jackal SMG is... ok. to be honest it is an ok gun when it comes to looks and how it performs, but I'm really disapointed with the gun itself as it has got overhyped to the brim that people wanted this craze more like everyone wanting to have the newest Battlefield 1. And yes I do like the UMP45 IRL as a gun but it doesn't mean that both IRL and in-game mechanics don't have the same expectations, if you were like me and wanting to have unique weapons like a bit of croation or possibly China's weapons, you got to have something that would make it stand out other than the looks and the attachments of it, statistically in the game, most guns share basically more than one gun that it's not even funny and makes the gun play less enjoyable. The attachments are good on the gun however they don't affect the weapon as much, I do like the twinkle grip as it adds another category in the attachments, Which I really want for OVERKILL to add in another section dedicated to foregrips for most guns.
Next gun, the DesertFox sniper rifle. Tbh when I did see the damage, I was excited that it was going to be one of them hard hitting sniper rifles that would beat the veteran snipers like the R93, but when I realised that it literally shared the same characteristics as the R93, I thrown it straight away into the bin. OVERKILL I know you want to make people happy and have more variety in choosing which gun to bring into DW or the new OD difficulty, but having every gun do the same damage as another feels like I'm buying gimmic versions of another gun, again it is boring and is stupid the way it has been dubbed up. What I like about the sniper is the looks and the bullpup design of the SRS, feels unique however when I look back at the R93 or the Nagant, it is embarrasing that I had used a more better looking version than the R93.
Finally the last gun, The contractor Pistol. When I looked at it again, guess what? IT SHARED THE SAME STATISTICS AS THE OTHER PISTOLS IN ITS CLASS. F*cking hell OVERKILL, you make my head explode when I wasted £4 on your product only to have reskins.
I'm not going and can't be bothered to go into more depth into the masks and the achievements but overall, I felt that this was one of the DLCs that everyone felt that they think that "this is the one" but unfortunately its dumbed down weapon balancing just made it absolutely useless. If you want a higher damaging SMG, a sniper and a pistol that does practically the same, buy something else that is cheaper, because I don't think £4 is the fitting price for this DLC, especially that the guns in the game do the same thing as the ones in the DLC. Look I don't want to say, this absolutely sucks, you can buy when you want and I'm not against but I do not recommend you buy it, discount or not it deserves to be known for one of the least good DLCs that I seen, thus I might get a refund for having the same statistics and basically having a DLC that I might never use.

The French have a wonderful word for what I could say about this pack - Bof... - which means it's okay. But it's the forceful 'B' and the finishing drawn out 'f' that make it equal in comparison to a long sigh - exactly what this weapon illicits.
The weapons are beautiful. Overkill's weapon artists shine through in plastic housing once more, successfully translating airsoft replicas into formidable looking weapons of early retirement. Where they fall through though is their performance. Only the Desertfox seems to come out unscathed - the UMP seems entirely too lacking in stamina to get you through any well-playing heist. You'll burn through your Body Expertise augmented initial ammo smattering in the first wave even with first dibs on death goodies. The throwing knife has a throw delay, meaning your well placed shot will miss and your panic knife will be cut short. As for the Contractor, the meta around pistols is well known, the akimbo version is entirely too anemic but the single pistol variant seems competent enough.
If you like the aesthetic, buy it, but you'll be playing Overkill with these weapons, guaranteed. There's little room for these weapons in Mayhem, as they're as I said a bit anemic on the old ammo front, but they DO pack a sizeable wallop.
I mean, sure, you can post a video in which you complete an OD loud heist with John Wick pack weapons but please tell me the number of restarts your crew had to go through so I can laugh at how much time you spent playing the same goddamn heist.

Early in this game's development, it already was an extremely satisfying game to play. The impacts of your actions and the crunchy sound effects added together to make a wonderful top-down experience. It seemed like they already had the "game feel" nailed, and most of Early Access would be focusing on adding more content. And then each update came, week after week, and it continued to just
better and better, and with more content to boot! Any aspiring game developer should spend a good amount of time studying how Vlambeer gets the feeling of their games just right.
The gameplay is fine too. The weapon/character/enemy variety keeps the game interesting for potentially hundreds of hours. The Early Access period also led to some very well balanced generation as well. Each run through the game depends almost entirely on skill alone; it's not often that the game screws you or carries you like in The Binding of Isaac.
Mind you, it's still a difficult game. One moment might be going pretty well until a momentary lapse in concentration puts you from full health to zero. Life is fragile in the wasteland and it takes a good amount of dedication to gain the experience to reliably make it through even the first few areas. But even once you get the hang of it, there's no real skill ceiling to the game. The difficulty past the throne will continuously ramp up to push you to your limit, and those late game situations mowing through massive waves of enemies really highlight the "game feel" that Vlambeer does so well.
A high recommendation from me. Give it a shot if you're up to the challenge.

Microsoft Flight Simulator X was abandoned by Microsoft about 9 years ago. Dovetail Games was given the license to redistribute it, though. This means FSX is a ten year old game that hasn't been updated in almost a decade. It still manages to stay alive by people who just want to mess around. Compared to todays technology, this is a bad simulator. The physics are rubbish, the planes are unrealistic, and the scenery is awful. The thing that keeps it alive is the 3rd party support. There are SO many addons to this game. I have played this game for 200+ hours (including offline time), and I know in order to make this game good, you have to spend hundreds of dollars on addons and equipment. For example, t isn't really worth it to spend $90 on good physics and wind patterns, when they are already in X-Plane or P3D. Things you can learn here are: purpose of different switches and gauges, terrain and radio navigation, communication basics, ATIS & METAR (weather reports). Things you should not think, they are the same (even with best realizm settings) - is flying physics. Yes, it is very close, but not the same. Most surprising difference: amount of rudder input you need, when starting takeoff run in real single-motor plane...

Cessna 172 with round instruments for the beginning and version with Garmin 1000 for later training is best plane to learn basics for future real pilots.
Also I advise to get the book "Microsoft Flight Simulator X For Pilots: Real World Training".

TLDR: Siberian Logging Simulator 2014
Pros:
Best mud and offroad simulation, period.
Excellent models of Soviet-era trucks, suspension and gearboxes all respond in a realistic way
Optimization: On Intel chips, this game can run with basically any graphics set, even integrated.
Cons:
No cockpit pov (though stated by the developers will be added in the future)
That wouldn't be much of an issue except for:
The current camera is the most ♥♥♥♥tarded one I have seen in a game, ever. It's almost as frustrating trying to look at what you're about to run into as getting stuck in the mud is.
Lack of diversity on missions and game modes. Currently hauling lumber from point A to B is the only thing to do on the map, though between the mud, crossing rivers, and running out of gas, you can sink two hours into completing a map easily.
Ultimately, it was worth $30 for me because I've been watching this game for a long time.  If you're looking for a thought-provoking story (or a mindelss one), it doesn't exist in this game. If you're looking for flashy 10,000 point combos and click-to-win type scenarios, this isn't one.
IF however, you have an interest in big trucks, off-roading, exploration, logistics, and physic simulation, all of those things are in this game. The developers have made it clear that this game will be updated and expanded in the future, and though it will never be GTA in the forests of Siberia, it can certainly occupy a space on the "Frustration Porn" section of your games library, alongside Kerbal Space Program and QWOP.

I've not played a lot of this game so far, but initial impressions are of a game that shows promise, but isn't quite finished yet.  Gameplay wise, I can't fault it - if you've played Mafia 1 and/or 2, it's pretty much exactly what you would expect, a well-executed game that is open-world, but very story orientated, with various advancements and enhancements over them.  There is minor things that you could complain about, like the A.I. being a bit stupid, but they weren't exactly geniuses in Mafia 1 or 2 either.
Graphics-wise, though, aside from the minor controversy about the 30FPS lock (now fixed in patch 1.01), they are a little blurry.  This isn't to say they're awful, but you do notice they're not as sharp as you would expect in a totally finished AAA release modern PC game.  There's rumours that this is because the graphics are upscaled 720p, but it could be down to flawed anti-aliasing, as turning down the in-game AA, then using your graphics card's control panel for AA seems to give better results.  There is also the fact that some of the forthcoming content (outfit selection, car customisation and races) smack of things they simply didn't quite get finished in time for launch, but should have been there.
Overall, I do recommend this game, but I would say only buy this game right now if you're content to simply leave it in your library for a while whilst they finish making it.  However, you might save yourself some money by simply waiting without buying it, as there is always the possibility it will go down in price in that time.
