A good timewaster and nothing more.
Unremarkable at its worst, a distraction at best, Fallout Shelter is a great mobile game, but fails to stand on it's own two feet on PC, but is still worth a time, again, as a distraction from the seemingly infinite repetition that is life.
*NOTE: I have played this on Android and on the Bethesda launcher. Playtime here is irrelevant. Also while I like the game, I do have several gripes about the game, mostly about the microtransactions, and lack of content but we'll get to that.
Fallout Shelter is a game where you are the overseer of a vault (Which you can number yourself, I really want a statistic on how many Vaults 69, 420 and 666 have been made) and your job is to build it and make your dwellers happy. The building mechanics remind me of a mobile game by Kairosoft called Mega Mall Story, but the building mechanics are almost the same. Some would also compare this to the classic Maxis game SimTower, which I've personally never played but the gameplay I've seen of that game is pretty similar as well.
Building a vault is as simple as selecting a room and placing it next to an adjacent building. You have 25 floors, each able to hold up to 8 rooms and two lifts. While that sounds like a lot of rooms to max out your vault, you can merge up to 3 of the same room to get better effects. Rooms can do things such as produce Power, Water and Food, which are the basic needs of the vault that will decrease as time goes on, a room to train your dweller's SPECIAL stats (which I'll get into later) and crafting rooms. It is also worth noting that each room has to be unlocked when you get enough dwellers in the vault, and each room can be upgraded twice at the cost of caps to improve said room's stats.
Crafting is a mechanic I have grown to like. Your collected junk ain't junk no more, when you assign dwellers to craft weapons or outfits to equip them with. You can get cool recipes when you adventure and then craft the best items if you have the junk required. (Although how you make a 10mm pistol out a desk fan and specifically that kinda makes no sense if you ask me)
How do you get said junk, either from exploring the wastes or from questing. Exploring basically sends a dweller out into the wastes, collecting resources and gaining xp. Oh yeah, there is a levelling system, each dweller being able to go up to level 50, though you still have to train SPECIAL stats via training rooms. A good SPECIAL rating can max out your dweller's performance out in the wasteland, each stat a modifier as to how well they'll do. Questing is probably my favourite feature, even if it is a pain at times.
Building an Overseer's Office allows up to three dwellers to go on quests, and with it you can control where they go in a dungeon, which really is the most Fallout part of Shelter. While battles are automated, there is a bit of player control in this system, where you can select who or what each dweller attacks, and occasional critical hits, which involves a mouse QTE (I think that's a QTE anyway) to determine how much extra damage you do. The end results could go from common weapons, armour, caps and the occasional recipe and then it's back to the vault with your loot. It has to be noted that while your vault can be attacked by raiders, you cannot select who to attack in defense or do crits, due to the quests actually being an update and Bethesda not updating the new system to the original defense mechanic.
So the game is overall very in depth for a mobile game. Unfortunately, this is PC, so there are a few gripes.
So everything in the game I've said so far sounds entertaining to you? Here is to me the SECOND worst mechanic in a mobile game, WAITING. There is a lot of waiting to do here. Heck, almost everything requires you to idle. Get resources, wait. Craft, wait. Get a freaking haircut, wait. Exploring, wait. And you have to wait another half of the time the dweller travelled for the bugger to come back. Questing? The best feature in the game? WAIT. This game is full of it, and eventually you realise the best thing to do is just let the game run in the background while you are doing something else.
Believe it or not, you couldn't even skip the waiting whatsoever in the beginning. Then Nuka Cola Quantum happened. Which is the typical skip the waiting currency. Now would be a good time to get to the microtransactions.
Now, before anyone says ANYTHING, this ISN'T, repeat, ISN'T, pay-to-win. It's pay-to-be-incredibly-lazy or as I like to call it, pay-for-random-stuff. Unless you are buying Mr. Handys outright (which by the way do nothing but collect the resources for you so you can do nothing even more), you can't control what you buy. Lunchboxes are a blind bag mechanic, where you get 5 random things in game, such as more resources, caps, quantum and new dwellers, weapons and outfits. And you can't choose what you get. This isn't pay-to-win because you can't just buy quantum outright and go all the way to maxing your vault within a week. No, the randomness is like opening a pack of randoms, can be anything. FIFA Ultimate Team Packs, Hearthstone packs, Magic the Gathering, Pokémon TCG cards. That's what it is. Cards. That are completely optional because you can get lunchboxes from quests and objectives. So it's not completely gated off. There are a few problems of course, such as everything you buy is locked to ONE SAVEFILE. So if it gets wiped, goodbye money. This is a bit of a problem to some, but really, since I have never bought anything on this game ($70 for your bloody Fallout 4 Season Pass is enough Bethesda) and just get lunchboxes for free, it's not THAT big a deal to me, though if you do plan to drop money on lunchboxes, this is your warning.
Another thing that grinds my gears is the lack of endgame content. Once you hit the dweller cap or building everything you pretty much have nothing left to do. It then becomes busywork. I myself only play this game in long bursts whenever the game updates or I feel like it.
One more aspect. I know Shelter isn't meant to be canon, but come on. Why does the vault open AFTER the bombs fall? And I'm pretty sure raiders and ghouls can't just break into a vault. And what IS the experiment for your vault? Vault Tec vaults are meant to be very dark social experiment so just... what is it supposed to be. Unless it was meant to be a utopia that also trains the settlers for survival, but that's just to kind of Vault Tec considering their reputation.
Despite these complaints, I have no issue with recommending Shelter. It is a good game, but it can only hold your interest for so long. And hey, kudos to Bethesda for their most stable and crash free game to date. There are bugs (of course) but nothing game breaking for me in about 30 hours of total playtime. It also has a better building sytem than Fallout 4. So there's that.
If you like Fallout or building, or are a newcomer to the series and want a glimpse on what the twisted wasteland is like, give it a try. I enjoy it and I love that this is on Steam.
Also if anyone wants to comment on this, please keep it polite. Don't throw names around and be civil for once please Internet.

Pay attention to your staging, or your will explode and become frustrated. Its not hard to grasp the basics enough to have success in your KSP adventures. Also when it comes to needing to land at a certain spot for a certain contract mission, plan to overshoot by a little bit. Your parachutes will usually put you back on or closer to the target where the mission requires you to exit the vehicle and take a surface sample. A little fun trial and error will prove useful for the next mission. Just keep trying, and even when failing, its still crazy fun.

Just finished Alan Wake and here is my review:
First of all the Level Design is AMAZING! It's a 2012 game but the graphics caught my eye. Not only does it gives you a camping atmosphere but it makes you want to go in a real forest. There are so many details and whenever I played the game, I never used the same path, I never saw the same trees/grass/fallen leafs, there always were new things I missed.
Secondly, not all the textures look great but the LIGHTs made the game look awesome to me. This game is based on light's power, like: kill the TAKEN (the bad guys) with your flashlight / the TAKEN are dead during daytime/ etc so the light's system needed to be at a high level.....and it was. The SUN LIGHT is trully wonderful as you can see the description's images. It gives the game life as well does the sound effects (you can hear birds, river's sound , tree branches moving around, and much more).
Moreover, the story was one of my favourites so far. No need to worry as I won't spoil it. The plot twists were well done, it is continuous and if you read the pages you are collecting during the game, you can know the AI next moves and where the story will be taking you. The TV show is great, really! "Night Springs" is the game's TV show, it's more like a serial if I think again. In each episodes (depending on how many TV you find) is presented a creepy story about a man killing himself in a dumb way, a man who killed his wife in front of his kid (you will know the details if you watch the show entirely as I did ) . For me, the game wasn't a horror one, it was  more like a tell-tale story based game.
In addition to what has already been said, the game COMBAT is pretty fantastic and you will feel overhelmed for many times trust me. As you play the game, the more further you go the more different flashlights you will find (which are more powerful), more weapon choices, flashbangs (my favourite) , flare gun, flares, shotguns, pistols and the ammo for each gun is enough so that you'll never find yourself with no gun ammo and only with your flashligh as you can't use melee attacks. One NEGATIVE aspect I found is that Alan Wake (the protagonist)'s cardio ratio is way too reduced. He's panting from running 15 meters.
All in all and I recommend this game for its level design, graphics, combat, sounds and story which has impressed me alot.
I'm looking forward to seeing more games from its producers !

I didn't buy into the hype around this game, I waited till it was dirt cheap on sale. Now I wish I hadn't waited so long.
I won't oversell it, simply, the game is a wonderful piece of storytelling, and currently 96% positive rating attests to that.
In the adventure games genre, this stands among the best of recent years. It's not about over complicated puzzles, or injecting action mini-games, it's about the story of Max, and that story is worth it.
This is probably the first adventure game where I felt my choices actually mattered, and the level of detail in small lines of dialogue based on what I did put a smile on my face. In spite of some flaws people have encountered (lip-syncing not quite perfect, or the odd glitch) the polish is fantastic. If you want to push on with the story you can. If you want to stop and take everything in you can, but sometimes even this behaviour will be remarked upon, at least I felt it was for me.
The songs are just right for helping to set the scene, of these teenage girls taking in this corner of the world. The soundtrack is perfect at crafting every bit of atmosphere, especially when you sit and take things in as I did. The graphics fit this story, and are easy on the eye.
But, probably most importantly of all, Max feels real, and that is what every writer aspires to achieve with a character.
Max treads that fine line carefully, at least in my eyes, of being enough of a blank slate for the player to settle into their shoes, but also have enough of a personality to feel like a real character rather than a mannequin. It is then those around her that provide the more dynamic explosions in the scenes, and it doesn't feel forced, it works. The cast roster is broader than I expected, with their varying personalities creating the feeling of a bigger world than the game provides, and the interactions between the extended cast and Max compliment the core story. All of this is tied together with spot on voice acting. Not a single character felt out of place.
Not everyone is going to get the same out of this story as a lot of people seem to have. This is about friendship, romance, mystery, grief and loss, time travel and the possibilities it brings. It touches on some difficult subject matter, tactfully I thought without diving right down the rabbit hole, but others may not feel so. It didn't change my life, merely I thoroughly enjoyed the window into this fictional world.
The first episode is free, give it a try, and the game will almost certainly be on sale again. Now, I have to find some way to overcome that feeling when you've read, watched or played a wonderful story- that you can't experience it for the first time again.

An old-school RPG in the style of Fallout 1 or 2 (but not so much 3), Wasteland 2 is a story driven game with an excellent amount of reactivity: even something as simple as the difference between watching a character run off the screen (something that's just for show in most games to allow them to disappear) or running after them to see where they're going can change what happens to them later on in the story. Your actions, or lack-thereof, can change things in unexpected ways as you keep playing. As such, there is definitely a lot of replayability in this game, giving good value for money
That said, while a very good game that is a lot of fun and worth sinking sixty to seventy hours into finishing, the game is not absolutely perfect. The game's most story-interesting sections seem to be stacked in the second half of the game, and the tactical combat (while serviceable) is not as deep as some others. On the whole, though, I consider it well worth the price.

This game has been getting a lot of hate because of the day one initial state of the game, which I agree, wasn't great, but I decided to play on and wait for the patch that was promised. In my opinion Mafia 3 now is a great game, sure it can be buggy but so can everything...
Pro:
- Every scenario is open to however you want to play, stealth (which feels satisfying yet simple), Guns blazing or a mix of the two
- Each style of gameplay rewards you the same, there isn't really a "best" way of doing things
- Seems to always have something to do, from story, to side missions and collectibles
- Story is simple but told very well
- Graphics are great! (now)
- Driving once gotten used to feels great
- weather system is great, including clouds which when covering the sun shadow the area which is cool
- Interesting characters
- Interesting alt story premise (some cutscenes cut to a detective around the 1990s - 2000s talkign about "The case of lincoln clay" which I love)
Cons:
- All of the thugs have only got like 2 - 3 look variations it seems
- Gameplay is simple which may deter some people ( satisfying though which makes you want to play more kinda a pro and a con)
- Some face models in game can look a bit low res from time to time
- Doesn't seem to have many graphics options ( just presets, not found anything majorly specific)
Overall I think this game deserves a buy, great fun with an ok but well told story with really satisfying combat and some interesting characters, don't let the day one hate deter you from a good buy!
NOTE: There may be an fps issue or just because of the graphic improvement it is demanding, I have everything on optimal with a 1080 and get 60 fps max with unlimited fps (sometimes slightly ticks over though)

Look. Nobody likes Loot Boxes. That was dumb. But was Shadow of War a good game?
Yes. It takes the Nemesis System and expands upon it. If you're playing at the Nemesis difficulty, you truly will find yourself invested-yet-frustrated as you try to make your armies work. It's basically Mordor, but with a little added complexity.
SoW's story is a lot more satisifying than Mordor, but that's not really saying much.
The real pride of the game remains playing off the Orcs you meet, fight, die to, and vow a personal vengence against. If you're the type of player who interally roleplays his character's motivations and monolouges it's easy to get lost in the endless sea of loveable Orcs.
The game shows it's weakness, however, when there is nothing left to conquer. I don't mean that literally, but rather once the dust of a new zone clears and the vast majority of the map is under the Bright Lord's Control. You don't feel like you made progress, gazing over seas of hostile orcs in a land in which every freakin' person on the map should be loyal to you. There is little to be done but dodge the now pointless orcs and collect artifacts and complete challenges before running off to the next zone. No advantage to staying, and little reward for complete dominion.
The controls are fine, through detection of when you are trying to flee up a wall or off a cliff is sometimes spotty, resulting in Talion waddling when he should be running. Combat is crisp and clean, and the impact of a rising combo meter feels rewarding, even on the highest difficulty.
The Lootboxes sour my personal opinion on the whole thing, and a part of me felt like merely buying the game was to enable the boxes.... But I am glad I did. It's more of Mordor, and it's a game I am enjoying playing. You don't have to buy the lootboxes to beat the game, thankfully.

Just finished Alan Wake and here is my review:
First of all the Level Design is AMAZING! It's a 2012 game but the graphics caught my eye. Not only does it gives you a camping atmosphere but it makes you want to go in a real forest. There are so many details and whenever I played the game, I never used the same path, I never saw the same trees/grass/fallen leafs, there always were new things I missed.
Secondly, not all the textures look great but the LIGHTs made the game look awesome to me. This game is based on light's power, like: kill the TAKEN (the bad guys) with your flashlight / the TAKEN are dead during daytime/ etc so the light's system needed to be at a high level.....and it was. The SUN LIGHT is trully wonderful as you can see the description's images. It gives the game life as well does the sound effects (you can hear birds, river's sound , tree branches moving around, and much more).
Moreover, the story was one of my favourites so far. No need to worry as I won't spoil it. The plot twists were well done, it is continuous and if you read the pages you are collecting during the game, you can know the AI next moves and where the story will be taking you. The TV show is great, really! "Night Springs" is the game's TV show, it's more like a serial if I think again. In each episodes (depending on how many TV you find) is presented a creepy story about a man killing himself in a dumb way, a man who killed his wife in front of his kid (you will know the details if you watch the show entirely as I did ) . For me, the game wasn't a horror one, it was  more like a tell-tale story based game.
In addition to what has already been said, the game COMBAT is pretty fantastic and you will feel overhelmed for many times trust me. As you play the game, the more further you go the more different flashlights you will find (which are more powerful), more weapon choices, flashbangs (my favourite) , flare gun, flares, shotguns, pistols and the ammo for each gun is enough so that you'll never find yourself with no gun ammo and only with your flashligh as you can't use melee attacks. One NEGATIVE aspect I found is that Alan Wake (the protagonist)'s cardio ratio is way too reduced. He's panting from running 15 meters.
All in all and I recommend this game for its level design, graphics, combat, sounds and story which has impressed me alot.
I'm looking forward to seeing more games from its producers !

The levels contain some secret bonuses scattered around, and that's kind of a good thing, but secrets are best implemented when controls are tight, which is not the case in this game. It could've been a cool little game if it played a little better or had something more to offer, right now I don't think it's worth spending time on.

Hotline Miami is a pixelated, gorey, bloody, messy, and extreme game with such a beautiful and surprising narrative that still resigns with me.

The melee combat and gun combat is VERY thrilling and is rewarding, but also the hardest thing to master in the game and is also the most frusterating mechanic the game has to offer. Enemies are 1 hit to kill, regardless if it's a bullet or a single swing with a melee weapon, but the catch is that you're the same way. 1 hit, 1 kill.
Hotline Miami is one of my most favourite OSTs to this date. It's an exhilarating, upbeat, and brutal soundtrack that goes SO ♥♥♥♥ing well with the game and it's dark tone. I love to search up the playlist for the OST on YouTube and just jam out to it while browsing the web, or just chilling with my Logitech subs. I guarantee you will fall in love with the OST as much as I and the rest of the fanbase has.
While Hotline Miami is
, I still think this game is COMPLETLEY worth the $9.99 price tag that the devs ask for. I felt that this game was hard to get into at first, but if you truly give this game a chance, you will go balls deep into the narrative and just lose yourself. If you are someone who loves retro games, loves top-down shooters, loves beat-em-ups, or hell, even if you're just a person who loves a good story, I think you should give this game a shot. I've only wanted to reccommend a game so much to someone once. That game was The Walking Dead Season 1 and 2. Those games are so deeply close to me, and let me tell you, Hotline Miami is up there as one of my most favorite games. It's one of those games that only happens once or twice. The developers pulled this game off amazingly and I can only simply applaud them for such beautiful artwork they have made with Hotline Miami.

This is an okay game with a nice story, sadly being extended to♥♥♥♥♥♥by repetitive "side-missions" which aren't optional but essential to progress through the story. The first 2h and the ending is very well done and is presented in a good way accompanied with a very good sound track. The graphics looks like♥♥♥♥♥♥and it's a blurry mess. I installed a sweetFX preset which removed all blur and corrected to colours to a less "orange" tint. With this installed the game looks really great, totally on pair with todays standards and the facial animations are spot on. The game doesn't run well though, I get 60fps with everything set on the lowest setting with my i5 4690k and GTX 970 (16GB RAM). This is with the SweetFX installed, but it shouldn't affect the FPS that much.
One thing I do love is the gun fights and the driving. They both feel "real" and not as arcady as games like GTA or Watchdogs. In simulation mode the cars feel heavy and are hard to turn. The recoil is there on the guns and the bots react to being shot at.

Shadow of War is a game stretched to thin.  Your first 20 or so hours of the game will be very fun. You gather your army, you take on the forts, you enjoy your new real estate.
The beginning: The start for the game is going to be difficult. Not having your abilities makes fighting very difficult. You have a talent tree in the game for each time your level up, complete collections, or finish certain quests. You will find out very shortly which talets to pick for your abilities very quickly. This often makes most of the other talents useless. You wont be able to dominate orcs till act 2, Which can take a while.
The middle: So you pushed through and got your ability to dominate orcs and now its time for fun. You find very enjoyable times when you find orcs that kill you, come back, go mad, save you, betray you. Sieging an ai fort is very easy if you control all the captains, You basically walk in press A about 3-5 times in the courtyards and then take on the overlord. The overlord can be the hardest fight you ever had or a walk in the park. Is he arrow proof and beast proof and cant be jumped on? Well arrows and summoning beasts wont do anything. Is he weak to beast damage? Summon a Graug and start decorating your real estate because the graug is op. Your first few sieges will be fun. New environments, doing side quests here and there. That one specific orc npc keeps comming back, great fun for the whole family. If the game ended here it would give it a 9/10. (there are alot of bugs and visual bugs as well.)
The end. I will now refer to act 4. I dont want to give out spoilers so here is a baseline of what you gotta do. Defend. You go back to your forts and level your guys up and defend. Defending is just "kill their attacking captains" Nothing else unique happens. Yea there might be a dragon or a Draug roaming around to spice it up, but you will know how to handle them. Defence will get very boring, very quickly. If they changed it up, where one siege they bring in some tough drakes and they are flying everywhere, might be enjoyable. But it is not. During this time you will be doing the arena alot. Here, you make one captain fight another on 3 different difficulties: maggot, warrior, champion. These will get your very angry quickly. During a normal fight with the player 1vs1 on the captain, the captain will be relentless, constantly attacking never letting up. But during arena aivsai, it annoys you when your captain has the upperhand, is about to kill the other captain, and instead sits back arms out "cheering" the crowd (this does nothing, its just a visual) thus allowing the other captain to get a free hit. Perhaps the enemy captain has a curse weapon, so you send in one that is immune to curse, Your captain loses because rng decided that you will use longer attacking patterns and the enemy decides to use short attack patterns. This gets your captain in a stun lock and he just eventually dies. There is nothing you can do once you send them in. Sure you have a few good matches, but you will remember the bs ones where the rng decided to screw you because your captain decided he wants to boast instead of attack.
The finale. So in the end you will be fully aware of the micro transaction system. They have it there because the grind is so damn big. I dont need to go into this as everyone knows about this dumb system. Its bad, lets move on.
The verdict. The start and middle of the game are great. However the game trips up on the final lap in end game where its the same thing over and over with nothing new. They could have added a quest line or moved a side quest line int he final act to change it up, but they didnt. If you play to final end game, the game is a 6.5/10. If you play to capture the forts and do the side quests (so finish act 3) the game is a 9/10.

Personally, I love this game to death despite its faults. If you played and liked the first game, pick it up, you won't be disappointed. Combat is fun, collecting loot and orcs is fun, and assaulting forts is fun.
The grind at the end is very real, but is not as horrid as I thought it would be, but it is a bit repetative and tedious after a bit.
The nemisis system is leagues better than it was in the first game and is quite honestly the star of the show here. There is so much variety in the personalities of the orcs and I don't think I ever heard repeated voice line thorughout my playthrough.
The loot boxes really are not shoved in your face. I never used a single one and got through the game despire the grind, but I can't blame others for not wanting to deal with it. That being said, I can't condone the use of loot boxes in this game, they have no place in a single player game like this and make little sense because of how personal collecting orcs for your army is supposed to be. You're supposed to be building an army, not buying it. They shouldn't be in this game at all, but at least they aren't as predetory as I feared. If you don't want to buy the game because of the boxes, that is justified.
This was a bit of a ramble but I hope it helps somewhat.

“Broken Age: Act I” by Double Fine Productions is a point-and-click adventure that focuses on two different protagonists in two different stories.  One protagonist is a young female named Vella Tartine and the other protagonist is a young male named Shay Volta.  Vella's story mainly belongs to the realm of fantasy while Shay's story is mainly science fiction.  However, both protagonists and both stories take place within one world, and that's where the game's charm lies.  That's not to say that only the setting of these stories is charming.  Honestly, the whole game is charming in its own way.
The first thing I noticed when playing this game was the fantastic art design.  The art style featured in this game is simple, but how it looks absolutely astounded me.  The animations are practically flawless.  It's insanely hard to distinguish a cutscene from actual gameplay because everything looks so good.  In addition, the environments are beautiful to look at.  Whether the characters were in a forest, in the clouds, or in space, my eyes were more than happy to perceive what I was looking at.
However, graphics don't mean anything if the gameplay cannot back it up.  The player is given a choice between starting with Vella's story or Shay's story.  Shay's story is not very interactive for the first 30 or so minutes.  If I wasn't watching a cutscene, I was clicking something on the screen to start the next cutscene.  To be fair, I'm pretty sure that Double Fine Productions intended the first half of the story to be like that.  Either way, when I was finally given complete control over my character, I never wanted to stop playing.
Even though “Broken Age: Act I” is a simple game, I cannot deny how much fun it was to play.  This, in my opinion, is the best kind of point-and-click adventure.  Every puzzle in this game is actually logical.  In other words, I rarely spent time endlessly trying to combine two different items in my inventory in hopes of finding a combination that would let me continue the story.  Not only that, but every puzzle isn't too hard or too easy.  I rarely knew the correct thing to do right away, and I rarely felt the need to stop playing the game because I couldn't figure out how to proceed.
“Broken Age: Act I” never got frustrating because of the fact that there are two different stories to choose from.  Instead of forcing the player to finish one story before starting the other, the game allows the player to easily change between both stories at the click of the mouse.  No progress is lost, either!  This was a very handy feature for me because whenever I got stuck I simply switched stories.  Whenever I got stuck in the second story, I would switch back to the first one.  By the time I got back to the first one, my mind would usually be calm enough to find the solution rather easily.  This is a simple feature, but an amazing one.  In fact, it's a feature that I wish other point-and-click adventures will pick up.  However, it's a feature that is unique to “Broken Age: Act I,” but that only further proves how good this game is.
Overall, “Broken Age: Act I” was a very pleasant surprise.  It's beautiful to look at and wonderful to play.  In addition, the music this game features and humor this game displays kept me entertained throughout.  Lastly, the story kept me engrossed until the very end.  Very few games have forced me to drop my jaw, but this game is one of them.  I obviously cannot say why my jaw dropped, but I will say that the ending to this game is something to praise.  Not to mention that this is still just the first act of a two-act game.  The first act of “Broken Age” is something to behold, and I cannot wait to see what is waiting for me in the second act.

This game is fun and challenging.
In this game you build a Fallout Shelter. Then the dwellers arrive at your vault door. That is when things start to become a challenge.
You have several things that you need to keep an eye on. The first of these are three meters which measure how much food, water and energy you have in your vault. These are very important. You want to keep them full. If they fall too low, it lowers the overall happiness of your vault dwellers.
The more rooms you build in your vault, the more energy it consumes.
The more dwellers you have the more food and water they consume.
The other things you need to watch for is the happiness meter and the bottlecap meter. The hapiness meter tells you the vault's average happiness and the bottlecap meter tells you how much money you have.
You can also bring up a view of all your dweller's and view their status, which includes happiness, their job and how they are equiped. You can equip your dweller with clothing, weapons and a pet.
Now the most important rooms that you will want to build when you start out are Living Quarters, Power Station, Water Station and Diner. This will allow you to get the first of your dwellers started. These rooms cost bottle caps to build, so be careful of how many you start off with right away. You don't want to use up all of your bottlecaps.
Now will start out with 7 Dwellers at the vault door. You can drag them to the appropriate rooms and assign them jobs. You can determine the right jobs by another meter called the S.P.E.C.I.A.L Meter. Dweller has their own. This meter shows you the dweller's
Strength
Perception
Endurance
Charisma
Inteligence
Agility
Luck
If your dweller is high in Strength you would assign them to the Power Station.
High Perception would be assigned to the Water Station
Agility would be assigned to the Diner.
More rooms will unlock as you play. Each of these rooms will be governed by one of these SPECIAL stats.
Your Dweller's can also produce baby dwellers as well. Baby dwellers happiness will remain at 50% until they are grown and can be placed in a job.
To make things more interesting, your vault can have various disaster incidents occure. It can be attacked by raiders or infested by radroaches or even catch on fire.
Lastly, you can send your dweller out of the vault on quests in which they can fine and bring back various loot and bottlecaps.
It is a fun game and more challenging you might think.

I didn't buy into the hype around this game, I waited till it was dirt cheap on sale. Now I wish I hadn't waited so long.
I won't oversell it, simply, the game is a wonderful piece of storytelling, and currently 96% positive rating attests to that.
In the adventure games genre, this stands among the best of recent years. It's not about over complicated puzzles, or injecting action mini-games, it's about the story of Max, and that story is worth it.
This is probably the first adventure game where I felt my choices actually mattered, and the level of detail in small lines of dialogue based on what I did put a smile on my face. In spite of some flaws people have encountered (lip-syncing not quite perfect, or the odd glitch) the polish is fantastic. If you want to push on with the story you can. If you want to stop and take everything in you can, but sometimes even this behaviour will be remarked upon, at least I felt it was for me.
The songs are just right for helping to set the scene, of these teenage girls taking in this corner of the world. The soundtrack is perfect at crafting every bit of atmosphere, especially when you sit and take things in as I did. The graphics fit this story, and are easy on the eye.
But, probably most importantly of all, Max feels real, and that is what every writer aspires to achieve with a character.
Max treads that fine line carefully, at least in my eyes, of being enough of a blank slate for the player to settle into their shoes, but also have enough of a personality to feel like a real character rather than a mannequin. It is then those around her that provide the more dynamic explosions in the scenes, and it doesn't feel forced, it works. The cast roster is broader than I expected, with their varying personalities creating the feeling of a bigger world than the game provides, and the interactions between the extended cast and Max compliment the core story. All of this is tied together with spot on voice acting. Not a single character felt out of place.
Not everyone is going to get the same out of this story as a lot of people seem to have. This is about friendship, romance, mystery, grief and loss, time travel and the possibilities it brings. It touches on some difficult subject matter, tactfully I thought without diving right down the rabbit hole, but others may not feel so. It didn't change my life, merely I thoroughly enjoyed the window into this fictional world.
The first episode is free, give it a try, and the game will almost certainly be on sale again. Now, I have to find some way to overcome that feeling when you've read, watched or played a wonderful story- that you can't experience it for the first time again.

If you aren't turned off by this game's grotesque art style, you'll find a ton of fun gameplay here. The gameplay is an overhead-perspective 4-direction shooter, and you progress through a randomly-generated dungeon. And I mean very random: Everything is random, from the rooms, to what's in the rooms, to the many unique items you can find. No game is the same, and it will probably take you quite a few tries to get to the end; but if you can get there without giving up, you'll probably want to play through again and again to unlock more stuff and experience the different playstyles that naturally emerge from the different characters and the different combinations of items you can collect.
There's also a DLC pack to basically double the already large amount of content, although I recommend trying the base game to make sure you like it before buying that. In fact, you can find a demo of the game online, so go ahead and try that before you buy the base game.

6 hours in and I can already tell that this game was a good use of my money.
Right from the get-go, I liked it. I have a soft spot for good stealth games, and this game set off on the right foot by following my 3 basic rules for making a decent stealth game:
1. The player must always be aware how close they are to being spotted by each guard
2. There must be many ways to approach one goal in an open-ended level
3. The controls must be tight and responsive enough for the player to have agency in the gameplay
Hotline Miami does all three things very well: each guard dies a bunch, the levels are open-ended and full of extra ways to navigate them, its hard, and the player is simple and fun to control.
A good buy, even when not on sale. When it does go on sale, buy four copies and have fun killing!

Wasteland 2 could be a great game but right now (october 6, 2014) it is rigged with too many bugs and balancing issues. IMHO, this games was not ready for full release.
Pros:
- Dialogues are well written.
- The huge amount of references and nods to the 80s.

Cons;
- Not much strategy involved in fight, enemy AI is really meh...
- A lot of skills feel redundant and artificials (5 of them are just for opening different type of door or container).
- Attributes are balanced for min-maxing character, builds with 2 to 4 dump stats are recommended.
- Weapon balance is terrible: Assault rifles are OP, Sniper and SMG are OK, there's only one good Energy weapon in the entire game, the rest is garbage.
- Too much randomness in loot and skill success, savescumming will lead you anywhere.
- Poor optimisation. For example, any activated alarm makes the game unplayable because of lag.
- Bugs: a lot of bugged quests, inventory management problems (clicking dragging fail 2 times out of 3).
- Lack of meaningfull choice: most quests are one-ended and those who aren't generally only leads to flavor consequences.

Conclusion: this game need either a huge balancing patch or modding tool.

There so many many people giving Paladins a negative review because of OB44 when it was updated.
Just want to clear something up, people. PALADINS IS NOT PAY 2 WIN.
You do not pay Hi-rez studios 0.99$ to get an aimbot headshot on enemies and an instant victory.
It's a GRIND 2 WIN. And that's what people are complaining about now.
People don't understand the definition between a true Pay 2 win and a Grind 2 win.
Warframe is a Grind 2 win, And i enjoyed that game to death because it has a friendly community, good story that livens the spirits of players and keeps the commitment to the game despite its massive grind.
The grind in OB44 is low compared to that of Warframe or even minimum compared to most extreme grind games.
I'm used to grinding in a game so i'm almost immune to grinding in nearly any game i play.
But just because of the grind, most players take it as a reason to give up and not play a good game.
Some also think that the prices on the legendary cards and cards for new players are too high, which on that point, i can agree. It used to be 1200 gold on each card but now it has mixed prices due to rarity of each card, from common to rare.
Legendary cards are 18k Essence each which are obtained from radiant chests you buy using 2500 gold. Say, each chest gives you about 2k essence at best.In total, you would need about 22,500 gold for each Legendary card which is quite a big grind. But for new players, this is a challenge wall they wouldn't touch unless they're a grind gamer which takes the challenge on. The grind is hard but still possible, people who don't want to invest their time in the game would back up quickly but for those who are patient and can appreciate a game like this, will continue playing.
Another thing people complain about is about how this will affect competitive play or Esports Paladins games.
They say that everyone would have an unfair advantage over each other. True that they would but the game still relies on skill, that enemy team may have better legendary cards but it counts on your skill to counter that card. Every champion still gets at least 1 free legendary card per champion they use out of the 3 legendary cards they can choose from.
As for Esports games, what's to say Paladins won't give the legendary cards to the participants for free when they sign up for it, to even the odds when all participants enter the battle?
In the end, it's true that Hi-rez still needs to have a "New player" friendly system but OB44 is not a reason to stop playing. People said the same about other games when a specific update for theirs came and yet people are still playing.
I agree that Hi-rez studios should reduce the grind but i want to say it again, PALADINS IS NOT A PAY 2 WIN.
Please get your facts straight people and don't jump to misleading conclusions.
Like it or not, Hi-rez will still fix it in the end. A free to play game always has time to fix things.

text:
This game.... this game!!! It's really good! It's great! It's awesome! It's colorful!!! It's bright and intense fun and stands out! It's seriously GOOD!
What attracted me to it at first was the irresistable aesthetic. I happened to watch Drive before and I loved the vibes from it. I knew about this game for?? maybe 5 months?? before I actually bought it on sale and during that time I just fawned over fanart, characters, and researched on a game I didn't even own yet lol. I saw it as more of a stylish piece of art and story I hoped to get my hands on (pixel art and graphic violence? ruthless excecutions and cold-blooded killing? SIGN ME UP) than a game. The retro style pixel graphics are sooo neat and it's clear that Dennaton puts a lot of thought into the room designs,it's cool to pick up on little details in the settings.
When HM went on sale I  thought about the gameplay and I realized I'm not even the type to play shooters at all because my reflexes are bad and I'd really suck! I was horrible at it. BUT! These levels. These chapters grow on you, I remember I spent a straight hour stuck on a chapter without even realizing it because it becomes SO much fun. Even if you're usually♥♥♥♥♥♥at these games like myself it feels amazing to get through a chapter and actually notice yourself getting better. HM documentary- "this game makes you feel dirty" and it does exactly that, the mysterious story throws you as a fast-paced killer behind trance tracks where you're dead after one shot. It feels absolutely badass, and even dirty 'cause it feels so GOOD. HM throws you right back in when you die (you're going to die a LOT) from the entrance of the stage, poised to kill all over again. Nothing tedious inbetween your deaths and you're probably itching to try again anyway. Addicting gameplay, It's kind of scary how fast time seems to pass when I'm playing it.
I personally thought the story was well incorporated between levels, but somewhat underwhelming at the end of Jacket and Biker's storylines (but I guess that's why I'm gonna buy Wrong Number now?). Oh, I think we can all collectively agree that the most artfully curated soundtrack Hotline Miami brings is literally half the experience. It's not the same without the synth tunes that get your heart racing when smashing in a skull or ten. El Huervo's "Turf" is the best tbh.
Violence 'n' Gore enthusiasts/fetishists, you'll have fun with this one. Hotline Miami is a pretty, organic, adrenaline-pumping fun time. I got it on sale, but I'd buy it three more times. (serious respect to Dennaton, a two-person team for creating such a masterpiece!)

I have now got 100% completion on this game and feel like I need to make a review... I loved the first game Middle-earth:Shadow of Mordor and completed almost everything in that game as well but This time they really took all of the good stuff from that game and just made it bigger,better and MORE of everything.
The best thing about the game overall is the nemesis-system where you build up your own nemesis-battles and relations with the orc-captains. I feel like the nemesis-system is what really keeps this game floating and I'm suprised no more game-developers have "stolen" this system yet... The only game I can think of that has this kind of enemy-system is XCOM2:s dlc which had some nemesis-elements as well but not as complicated and evolving as this one.
The gameplay and fighting-mechanics feels good and the graphics and technical aspects are good overall with some really good views etc but nothing special or new here.
The cons of the game is the main story which doesn't feel interesting at all... Especially since you know the bigger outcome of the story if you are any involved in the Middle-earth lore which I guess most of the people buying this game will be.
Also I thought the game would have an entire open world but you cant travel between the different zones, instead you have to use the map and "select" the zone you want to travel to. That's a dissapointment for sure...
MICROTRANSACTIONS: If you really like this game like I do you will probably play alot and complete a lot of missions and side quest. Like I said I completed the game 100% so maybe it's a bit extreme but when I got the "true ending" I had 100k silver and 400 gold on my account without spending any extra real money at all on the game. I also bought lootboxes thru the entire playthrough when I felt that I wanted to to get some new loot or good captains(for silver-money mainly and only a couple of the gold-boxes). So if you play the game normally without the need of any "speed-boost" the microtransactions is never something you will even look at. It's just irritating that they put it there in the first place and it worries me what they might use it for in future games since this seems like a new trend even in single-player games.
I'd rate the game 6/10 for good gameplay and funny nemesis-system.
It lacks good story and if they never put the microtransactions in the game it would receive a 7/10.

One of the first games I took to the end credits in a long time.
Deeply atmospheric with an utterly engrossing story, each episode has its own feel and cliffhanger ending without disrupting the narrative. A wonderful homage to horror writers and jam-packed full of pop culture references.

Voice acting isn't perfect and the dialogue is (somewhat intentionally) full of exposition. Combat is fast-paced with some refreshing mechanics, though can become tedious as the game goes on. Luckily, there's enough spectacle to keep things interesting.
Overall, a great game that will keep literary and horror nerds engrossed. Just be sure to pick up American Wasteland as well, for a tidy - if quick - continuation of the story.

When I first got this game it was just a sandbox without a tutorial or any modes of the game. The only way to find out what to do was on a forum somewhere, where I found a list of 'achievements' recreating the space race from the 50s and 60s (in reality it was just some group of nerds who tried to succeed at those tasks in-game and post pics of their results to get respect from the rest). Never before did I have so much fun building and testing stuff in a game, nearly always failing, but winning every so often - but that 'winning', if you can even call it that, felt SO AMAZING that I came back again and again for hundreds of hours, and all when the game wasnt even registering my progress. To have a game give you a sense of such fulfilment without telling you or giving you some arbitrary badge or whatever is IMO KSPs biggest triumph. The Kerbol system is just there... and you have to explore it.
I found myself researching so much about space, orbital mechanics, physics and human cosmological endeavour OFF GAME, simply because I wanted to understand KSP that much more the next time I was playing it. God knows I suck compared with Scott Manley, and I know it, but it has sparked such curiousity in me about the universe that I dont mind murdering vast swathes of little green men just to reach Laythe again one more time. I hope that something like this comes out for my kids when they are older which is this playable so they can have that spark of yearning for science and discovery.

This game will not be for "everyone." I can imagine impatient gamers who are accustomed to fast-paced, action packed games, or games that do not require much thinking or delicate in-game action being (at least initially) quite frustrated with Spintires. Even so, I suspect that, given some time and attention, perhaps even the most impatient "twitch" gamers might enjoy Spintires. It is a rather unique experience, and quite well-done for the purpose it seeks to fulfill.
Spintires is a difficult game to get going with and not what I'd call an "easy" nor fast-paced game. But quite unique and fun. It is in fact, so unique, it is bound to have great promise for expansions and additions that add additional elements. For example, if this game were merged with an engine like Arma or Day Z . . . wow!
Basically, there are maps which seem to generally represent different types of terrain in a sub-arctic region. I suspect it is intended to be far eastern Russia or Siberia, perhaps Finland. The vehicles seem to be Soviet era military trucks, though no weaponry. There doesn't seem to be any fighting or combat in the game, it is strictly focused on driving, navigating rough terrain, and logging.
Good game.
It took me about 2 hours to get a handle on the basics: using the camera, controls like posi-track and 4x, parking brake, the gear shift, judging terrain, using the mini-map, exploring and finding routes around maps that don't destroy my vehicles, using the garage to repair, refuel and augment vehicles.
In total I've played 7 hours, mostly on the "Plains" map (there are I think 7 or 8 maps it comes with: Volcano, Coast, the Hill, Plains, are the ones I can think of but there are at least two more.
I have managed to net three or four achievements: Explore Plains (Remove all of the 'Cloaks' from the Plains level); Sisyphus (Drive a Type C vehicle with the Parking Brake engaged for 300 meters and Diff Lock disengaged); Explorer (Remove all of the 'Cloaks' on any level with the Type A-469 vehicle); Diver (Drive through water so that your vehicle is fully submerged and then escape without the engine stallin).
I have yet to finish any map by doing any logging and transporting the logs to a dropoff. I reckon that will take me another 7 hours. It plays kind've slow, and honestly it is a bit of a 'fiddly' game that an instant gratification gamer might find quite frustrating.
The kinds of challenges you face: Okay, I want to get over there to my northeast to clear that cloaking. I can't go straight at it because there is a forest and a creek. I'll try curving around to the south (20 minutes of carefully, in low gear with posi-track and 4x on navigating around bumps and rocks, and mudholes and trees) . . . nope that didn't work, time to back up and try curving around to the north (10 min of retracing your steps . . . then another 20 min of ambling around to the north) . . . Okay, now I'm in that open area just to the east of the cloaking, but I still cannot see it. Looks like if I go a bit west from here I can maybe get on an old logging road that might veer right and go toward the cloaking . . . (15 min as you navigate across the field, and carefully get onto the road, averting the steep embankment and trees, then another 10 minutes as you follow the rutted road careful to straddle the mudspots where they are bad . . .) Ah! Now I can see the cloaking. But it is in the middle of a pond. How am I gonna get around to that . . . etc., etc.
Probably not for all gaming tastes but a fun distraction if you have patience and enjoy driving on rough terrain. Based on my experience driving in rough terrain, it seems surprisingly naturalistic. It is of course a game, but as games go this might well be the most "realistic" off-road sim so far.
The camera is probably the most frustrating thing and when you get into tight quarters with lots of humps and trees and you
are trying to navigate past an obstruction, the trickiness of using the camera combined with its inherent limitations makes it a bit less than ideal fun.
Using the manual and automatic transmission settings, using the winch, etc., all a bit awkward to figure out, but once you do they are quite useful and allow you to adapt to the terrain much better.

I rate WARMODE a 6.3 out of 10. At the time of writing it is August 29th, 2015, and the game is still in early access and has only been out for a few days. All things are subject to change.
WARMODE is a fast-paced, close-quarters first person shooter game. It's your standard team vs. team deathmatch - it may have some other modes but I didn't put enough time into it to find out.
I'm going to save the best (kek) for last, so I'm going to start with the graphics department.
The graphics are okay; not great but not terrible, and it's got okay optimization. I ran it at about Medium on an Intel HD 4000 (couldn't be bothered to switch to my 650m using Nvidia Optimus), on anything that's more powerful than your standard iGPU you should be able to max it out at 1080p. The game's very playable at the 40FPS I got on my integrated graphics, for as little time as I spent with it, it was completely playable enough to the point where I didn't even bother to change it to my proper GPU. I'd go as far as to say they were "nice" graphics
The sound is okay; it kinda sounds like you're shooting a Nerf gun no matter what weapon you choose, but it's fine. I didn't notice any footsteps but all you hear is gunfire from around the map - good luck soundwhoring Sam Fisher wannabes with all the racket going on making your ears bleed.
Last but not least, the gameplay. The gameplay is fast paced - VERY fast paced. Faster than CoD kind of fast paced. All of the guns are pretty much the same; do the same damage, sound the same, etc. - only difference is range and rate of fire (and ROF only really goes semiautomatic, automatic, or pump action). They're okay guns, but the TTK is ridiculously low. And, if you're moving at all you can barely hit your target... it's worse than the Deagle from CS:GO. However, I do like the crosshair, when standing still, hip-firing feels really nice (even in comparison to other games). Gunplay would be great if they upped the time to kill a lot, made moving much less of a hit on accuracy, and gave an option for a static crosshair.I found myself dying pretty quickly, but it seems that most of the people playing this must have really crappy PCs or something because I spanked everybody and topped the lobby nearly every match... and I suck at FPS games. The weapons are as I said pretty much the same, and some variation would be nice. The maps are pretty bare, some a tad too large for the amount of players, and spawns that are preset and not dynamically changing at all make it a bit of a bore on the larger maps trying to find enemies. I think this is because of it trying to emulate Counter-Strike's spawn system, however with the way this game plays I think a dynamic spawn system would be a good idea. It is in early access however, so this may change. I also did notice that a few times I was getting shot through boxes by people crouching behind boxes not even being able to see I was there theoretically... whether this was a result of wallhacks or just some screwed up playermodels I'm not sure. I'm willing to give the player the benefit of the doubt and say playermodel issues because there is some pretty serious headglitching going on too. It has an in-game store that I didn't even touch but the game surely isn't pay to win at all. TL;DR: Low TTK, weapons are too similar, static spawns + large maps = walking simulator, headglitching. A bit poo in some areas but a fun game to pass time. It feels a bit bare but it is in Early Access; I'm sure that once the game is finished it will be much better.
Now here's the impressive part... it takes up a whopping... 512MB of hard drive space. Get me a flash drive! This would be a perfect game to stick on a flash drive and pass time at work, school, the library, etc... it's a fun five-minute kind of game, good for waiting for another larger game to install, etc.
Overall I'd give it, as I said above, a 6.3 out of 10. Here is my rating in each individual department, out of 10.
Graphics: 6.2
Audio: 5.3
Gameplay Mechanics: 6.7
I'll keep this game installed and play it throughout updates as I feel this game will be getting better. It just released on Steam in Early Access for crying out loud... I am not sugar-coating my review based on that fact but I'm sure, given a few months of development time, this will end up being a really good game.

Just how many Es can you replace with Xes for the title of a video game? Late to the trend of replacing Es with Xes in the title is Xpand Rally Xtreme, a realistic racer that has you competing in off-road rallies and tweaking your car between events. There's a lot of realism here, car damage affects performance and your driver can get injured bad enough that it will end the event. As real as it is, its still fun, easy to play, challenging and a focused experience. Every turn matters, every ding on your vehicle matters. When your co-pilot announces rocks inside, there are major rocks to mess up your car.
I'll start with the negatives and you can compare to see if you find them enough to scare you away. The first is this is a race the clock game that has you racing a ghost rather than against real competition. The game is all about your skill to shave seconds off your time through improving yours and your car's performance rather than playing dirty and wrecking the competition. Other than that, the big negative is a freeze frame split second pause  at many junctures through each race. Even with a modern computer that can handle today's games, this decade old game still flinches and freezes here and there. The load times are long, even when loading cars in the dealership to look at.
You can set the driving to be manual or automatic for the lazy like me. There's a setting for realistic or arcade, the latter of which gives you trolley controls of forward and reverse rather than the former which forces you to brake, then throw your vehicle into reverse before you can back up. All of these styles play well and you have a respawn button if you stray too far off the beaten path. To add to the realism or arcade fun, there are several different camera angles. Chase, close chase, bumper, hood and even the driver's seat.
Xpand Rally Xtreme takes place in Asian countries like Malasia, China and Japan across a few different areas. The career has you participating in blocks of events. Ranking bronze, silver or gold in eight car competition unlocks the next set of events. The events consist of typical races against a ghost, time trials, one-on-one races on closed circuit courses that start one of you at the beginning and the other halfway through the track. There's even a boss fight, which is just a fancy way of saying there's only enough for first place against a single ghost car.
The tracks look beautiful and have a glow about them all depending on your graphical settings. You'll tear across dirt, gravel, sand, water and even tarmac or pavement for each event. Areas feel lush with vegetation and I prefer racing in these areas to those with cold concrete covering everything. It just feels more diverse driving over bridges or along  coastlines. I say diverse, but the sad thing is racing three events back to back in the same area feels like a bit much. The courses change routes, but that's about it. They do their best to block off areas with barricades, so by the time you're out of each set of three events, you'll be ready to leave. Each course has a few details to make the environment feel more alive such as animals running in the distance or men in red shirts scurrying across the track. If you hit these guys, you respawn with wasted time as punishment. Its tough to even hit them.
The events are meaty enough to get some time investment into them, usually around four to six minutes for the early portion of the game. Terrible drivers will soon feel the bumps and bruises of having a door torn off and having to compensate with your car pulling to one side or the other. Its tough to start losing parts though, because with trees and tape, those make for tough targets to bash into. Its a lot easier to lose parts in races that have walls everywhere.
Each of these races gives you cash to spend and the first thing that you'll do is repair your vehicle. Damage is real and it'll cost you, but the choice is yours what to repair and a parentage of just how damaged something is. While everything can be repaired, its the tires that need to be completely replaced. Do you wait until you're at sixty percent or wait for eighty?
You need to be wise with your tires and you're given stats on each course how much is tarmac and how much of it is gravel. In fact the game warns you if you're using the wrong type of tire, but the decision is always up to you. It can be a bit click heavy to go through the menus to get where you need to go and then return back.
These parts all have specifics. I'd normally call them stats, but these are specific numbers and details that you need to look into when tweaking your vehicle. I just go for the more expensive, the better it is approach. There's just too much here for me, but its here if I want it.
You can visit a dealer in the menu that will sell you new vehicles. Some events require specific vehicles that you'll need to buy. Every past event can still be played for more cash, so you will have to grind your way up to earn enough money to purchase a new vehicle or just start selling parts.
With everything said, this is a deep game, but more than just the car mechanics. There are a deep set of options. The controls let you rebind keys for everything but the pause menu. You can use a controller with your directional pad or analog stick and even control the dead zone. I went for controlling with the direction pad rather than messing with the dead zone. The only problem here is if you have 360 triggers for your forward and reverse, they are also your up and down in the menu. Otherwise you can always just use the mouse.
You can set to have your co pilot warn you, along with icons of upcoming turns and even how far ahead they tell you what's coming. There are even performance settings for the ribbon tape physics. There's always a certain something to being told the direction rather than checking a mini map. It keeps your eyes on the action. If you want to turn off the ghost car, the choice is yours. Xpand Rally Xtreme lets you play the way you want to and I'm happy for that.
For anyone that wants it, there's online multiplayer and even LAN support, but with this game being so old, the multiplayer has been dead years ago. There's no split screen either. Heck since you're the only car on the trail, I wonder how they pull off multiplayer. Seeing ghosts of your friends or just seeing their time through each checkpoint.
At a mere $5 this decade old game is worth a risk for anyone that enjoys realistic racing. There are performance issues that make it a tough recommendation, but the game is still an enjoyable challenge for a cheap price.

The one that was lost with the "next gen" era, when the polygon count became more important than the story, when  "Fedex" quests with "GPS assistance" became the norm (this is for you Oblivion/Skyrim, F**K you !). The only half decent RPG we got in 10 years was Dragon Age, and they lost it with the sequel which was an over simplification dedicated to console audience. So 2 years ago when I discovered the wasteland kickstarter, I had to participate, this felt like a last hope to get a real RPG.
And now 2 years later, what can I say ?
THANK YOU BRIAN (and all inxile team of course) ! You made it ! Yes, this game has some flaws (character models are quite bad, basic graphism, some bugs now and then, sometimes too much fights, some very cruel/frustrating gear check along the way in ranger difficulty where your team gets decimated like blood sausages !), but what a game. One where you actually have to look and ask around to solve things instead of following a green arrow, one where what you do has direct and indirect consequences around you, one where the world is not simply divided between good and evil, one where the writing  and the ambiance kept me awake during a few nights these last two weeks. And all these WTF moments :) The "Do you really want to hurt me ?" moment made my day.
I can't recommand this game enough. I have just finished my first playthrough in about 86H and now I 'm already starting a new game (max difficulty this time !).
So if you are a nostalgic of the golden age of computer RPG era, don't hesitate, buy this game !

Xpand Rally Xtreme is a sorta sequel to Xtreme Rally, which is surprisingly realistic, yet saddled with a strange "campaign" engine with "car upgrades" cribbed from far more "arcade" titles that distracts from its realistic car handling and decent terrain engine, ending up with a "neither fish nor fowl" that's neither hardcore nor arcade, and really satisfies neither camp.
Driving sims generally comes in three flavors: pure arcade (turn and burn rubber) such as NFS Most Wanted, hardcore sim (rFactor), or semi-hardcore (WRC games, GRID series). Xpand Rally Xtreme (and its predecessor Xtreme Rally) tries to bridge the arcade and semi-hardcore with choice between arcade and simulation modes, but the "campaign" makes little sense as you have to win money and apply money to repairs and upgrades. Upgrading a rally car, hmmm...
Lack of full controller support (i.e. choose menus with controller) makes actually playing less than pleasurable as one must reach for mouse. it also will not auto-detect my standard Xbox360 controller and I had to map inputs manually.
There are no real cars. The car physical models are based on the real cars, and you can recognize the cars. However, the names are changed as not to offend the original owners (i.e. Ford = Cord)  and minor body work changed as well. Additional car types are introduced in this game instead of just rally cars, grouped into roughly 4 classes.
The rally courses and events are quite decent and long enough (though none of them are super-long). And the cars do handle realistically as they slide and straighten or react to handbrake turns. Driving model is quite good. On the other hand, the setups that you'd expect for rally games, like front vs. rear rollbar, , suspension settings, etc. are hidden via a LOT of icons and such, when they are there at all.  And this is in simulation mode.
Furthermore, you start with a budget. Yes, a budget, 35000, to buy one of the 4 starting cars (approx 33000 or 34000). And you get to upgrade parts like suspension, tires, engine, and so on. For a moment I thought I was playing Flatout, as they involve the same sort of parts: regular shocks, sports shocks, pro shocks, racing shocks, for example.
You may win thousands per race, but you will have to pay to repair the damages, and if you don't finish near the top (1st or 2nd) your winnings may barely pay for the damages, leaving you going nowhere. Furthermore, the idea of upgrading your car in rally, where everybody should be nearly equal, is a bit "hmmmm....".
I wish I can enjoy it a bit more, as I do enjoy rally games, but this game is a bit on the "weird" side.

I have been a Microsoft Flight Simulator enthusiast since inception, and my enjoyment for Flight Simulator has continued to grow as each release corrects bugs, makes improvemetns and provides opportunities for 3rd party support for add-ons.  The Steam Version has made several improvements while keeping the basic FSX concept intact but ignored the one factor that all users face and hate about the FSX franchise - the Out of Memory Error.
2016 brings very powerful CPUs and GPUs to our disposal, and while my PC is at the top Tier in performance, Flight Simulator Steam Edition does not fully take advantage of this power due to FSX 32bit program structure.
Many vendor's add-ons such as ORBX, Aereosoft, and even Steam DLC for Flight Simulator place greater demands on the finite 4GB Memory limits of Flight Simulator.  Thus when using the products with a fully capable aircraft cockpint simulator you will face the Out of Memory (OOM) issue at some point.  It could be 10 minutes into your flight, but more often than not it happens just as you approach that "mega" airport you paid $50.00 for  - resulting in a fatal error,  and the need to restart the program to begin again.
The 4GB memory limit is the one thing that needs to be addressed more so than anything.  Otherwise it is pointless to buy highly detailed aircraft, scenery and airports then dial everything down to bare minimums to avoid running beyond the 4GB barrier causing a simulator crash.
I use a tool called ProcessExplorer to monitor my memory usage during flights, and when the memory usage creeps up to 3.7gb I immediately save the flight because I know what is coming next - this is ridiculous. For everyones edification - Out Of Memory is not a "physical" memory limit but the restrictions of 32bit limits of the program itself, Memory caps out at 4gb regarless of how much physical memory you have installed.
For consideration: Starting up the SIM at a detailed airport with an iFLY 747 you just used about 3.2 gb or Vmemory and as you fly, use the panel cockpit instruments and enjoy the views, the remaining memory will slowly be depleted until your sim crashes - OOM.
Even if developers of this Steam Flight Simulator version produced a tool that automates saving the flight when memory is near the crash limits at least that would be a step in the right direction, but no tool is offered. I guess creating one would be admiting the problem exist and wise folks would avoid the 32bit  franchise all together.
The other issue with this version as in previous ones is Flight Simulator does not properly flush memory between flights, and with each session, the more you fly it too will deplete the 4gb limit eventually,  unless of course you restart the program and waits the 3 minutes for a re-load.
Once again no in game "memory flush" feature for a long known issue.
The one major limiting factor that needed to be fixed went answered: and companies are more than happy to sell you add-ons knowing their add-on products place added demands on the limited memory space of this 32bit program.
Back when Aces was doing the development they would make a statement following each release, "they intentionally build the simulator for the next generation of the PC", WELL here we are, and my system can throw this around at 40+ fps BUT crashes because no one has taken time to address the 32bit limit.  the issue rapidly begain to manifeste  itselft once end users moved up to more powerful systems, and content creators offered "better" higher detailed planes, airports, and scenery.
Moving forward: I would think offering a 64bit release would destroy compatibilty for all those add-ons, and this is the underlying reason the program remains 32bit, to keep the 3rd party suppliers happy more than the end user.
My prediction is this simulator will simply be 32bit forever, and a NEW Flight Simulator will be offered, sold and we enthusist will venture out and buy it, and cough up money for basically the same add-ons to get us to this point in time to facilite the true enjoyment of flight simulation without the OOM crashes. as they say in contracting - you dont make money fixing it, sell them something new.
So how do you avoid all this OOM stuff:  Stick to the basic Flight Simulator and Aircrafts, forgo any add-ons, or at least keep them to the bare minimum. Make your choice- Do you want to look at pretty scenery or have a simulator cockpit experience - with the limits of 32bit program it is difficult to have both.
IMHO it would be best to stick with the basic FSX steam version with limited add-on purchases, and hope the next FXY version will be 64bit.
So how do I like the Flight Simulator Steam Edition - I love it, due to the vast content one has access to, the realiasm, and landclass graphic details frim orbx that can be achieved using new improved land classes, and add-0n airports. but as stated, fatal program crashes will occur depending on your combonation of aircract, area, and detail level settings.
With all the above being said.  Flight Simulator Steam Edition has plenty to offer with many hours of enjoyable game play for all flight simulator enthusiast.

Anyway, it is rare to get a sqad based game ala Jagged Alliance, let alone one set in a post-appocolyptic world.  I did have fun exploring the world despite the bugs.
I would rate the combat mechanics as a 5 on a scale of 1 to 10.  They are servicable and certanly can be improved.
The skill gain system is quite dull, such as the next rank just adds 6% to some ability (hit with a guy, unlock something, disarm something, etc...).
Some of the puzzles in the game are not very intuitive.  I had to google a few of them, but hopefully if you wait a few months, there will be some nice faqs.  Even after reading the solutions to some of them, they are things I would have never figured out.  For in one area you find a screw driver.  In another room there are some odd looking tiles here and there.  No tool tip, just odd looking.  The thing is, there is no hint that you need to use the screw driver on these tiles.  Even given that, if you use the screw driver on the wrong tile (of the right kind) it tells you that you can't use the screwdriver on that.  So that would lead you to think that isn't the right use for the screw driver.  However there is one tile which looks just like all the rest of the tiles that say "You can't use the screwdriver on that" that you CAN use it on, which has the tresure you are looking for.
Then there are other objects you find that have NO CLUE as to thier use, but indeed are useful to someone, somewhere.  Here is a hint, the stuff you get out of toasters IS USEFUL to SOMEONE SOMEWHERE.  It may even be useful to someone in another act.
Anyhow, you might be wondering why I am recommending this to buy with the above said.  Despite all that, it is a fun game.  I enjoyed the exploration and the story.  I did not finish it because it was too buggy in the 2nd act.  Maybe I will someday because I am curious as to how the story turns out.

Building on the classic Civilization II, Civ III introduces several new game mechanics including expanding City borders & also for the first time animated units. The player starts off in the year 4000 BC with a small group of settlers and some basic knowledge of road building, irrigation & farming. After choosing the site of their first City the player then has to explore and expand their empire to other locations. The ideal placement of a City would be close to natural resources & luxuries, this will help increase trade, production & happiness of the citizens. Connecting City's via roads also increases trade and the sharing of resources / luxuries across your empire. During the early game roaming Barbarians may cause problems along your borders and any unprotected units or land will be either captured or pillaged. As you progress through the centuries you will eventually meet other Civilizations. Some of these will be friendly and willing to trade, others more hostile and may attack you completely unprovoked. You have the opportunity to influence the opinions of other empires by your actions towards them, giving them gifts or trading technology is usually a way to get on their good side. Later in the game you can also forge an alliance with certain empires in the form of a mutual protection pact. This is especially useful during times of War to help seal victory over your enemies. The game ends in one of six ways, the most traditional being conquest (destroying all opponents). The Space race victory occurs when any Civilization completes and launches a Space Ship to Alpha Centauri. Other victory types are Cultural, Diplomatic & Domination. If the game ends and no one is victorious by any of these, the game uses a "histograph" to determine the winner by points.
This is one of my all time favourite games, though Civ IV has more depth by adding religion, unit promotions and other special abilities. I still prefer this version to any other.
There are no in game options for changing to widescreen resolutions but if you do the following: goto your Steam/SteamApps/Common/Sid Meier's Civilization III Complete/Conquests folder then find the file called conquests.ini. Right click to edit the file then goto the bottom and add the line Keepres=1 this will force the game to your monitors resolution.
