This game.... this game!!! It's really good! It's great! It's awesome! It's colorful!!! It's bright and intense fun and stands out! It's seriously GOOD!
What attracted me to it at first was the irresistable aesthetic. I happened to watch Drive before and I loved the vibes from it. I knew about this game for?? maybe 5 months?? before I actually bought it on sale and during that time I just fawned over fanart, characters, and researched on a game I didn't even own yet lol. I saw it as more of a stylish piece of art and story I hoped to get my hands on (pixel art and graphic violence? ruthless excecutions and cold-blooded killing? SIGN ME UP) than a game. The retro style pixel graphics are sooo neat and it's clear that Dennaton puts a lot of thought into the room designs,it's cool to pick up on little details in the settings.
When HM went on sale I  thought about the gameplay and I realized I'm not even the type to play shooters at all because my reflexes are bad and I'd really suck! I was horrible at it. BUT! These levels. These chapters grow on you, I remember I spent a straight hour stuck on a chapter without even realizing it because it becomes SO much fun. Even if you're usually♥♥♥♥♥♥at these games like myself it feels amazing to get through a chapter and actually notice yourself getting better. HM documentary- "this game makes you feel dirty" and it does exactly that, the mysterious story throws you as a fast-paced killer behind trance tracks where you're dead after one shot. It feels absolutely badass, and even dirty 'cause it feels so GOOD. HM throws you right back in when you die (you're going to die a LOT) from the entrance of the stage, poised to kill all over again. Nothing tedious inbetween your deaths and you're probably itching to try again anyway. Addicting gameplay, It's kind of scary how fast time seems to pass when I'm playing it.
I personally thought the story was well incorporated between levels, but somewhat underwhelming at the end of Jacket and Biker's storylines (but I guess that's why I'm gonna buy Wrong Number now?). Oh, I think we can all collectively agree that the most artfully curated soundtrack Hotline Miami brings is literally half the experience. It's not the same without the synth tunes that get your heart racing when smashing in a skull or ten. El Huervo's "Turf" is the best tbh.
Violence 'n' Gore enthusiasts/fetishists, you'll have fun with this one. Hotline Miami is a pretty, organic, adrenaline-pumping fun time. I got it on sale, but I'd buy it three more times. (serious respect to Dennaton, a two-person team for creating such a masterpiece!)

So, I got this game on the app store after seeing it on the top charts the other day, and was not dissapointed. I enjoyed playing it for hours straight on mobile for a day before I realized the next day they had a syncing function and you could sync between PC and mobile. I instantly bought Crashlands on Steam and have been playing a lot between mobile and steam. I love this game and would easily reccomend it.
I like the graphics a lot, the cartoony style is really attractive yet easy to run. They don't dissapoint. My computer, which, at the moment has a hard time running games, gets a steady 60 fps on high shaders.
The quests are really fun and you have a ball exploring the open world. The humor of the quests and the way characters speak is really nice and something anyone and everyone can appreciate.
The crafting is very nice, and I love the endless inventory. Only con I can see here is that they ask you to wait a specific time before each item is made. It isn't too bad, usually, but in late game it can take forever, and it feels tedious and annoying. Thats one feature definitely not needed.
Combat is awesome, and doesn't dissapoint. It's very fun to learn opponents patterns and find out tricks and strategies as you go.
The main storyline is funny, fun to play, and very interesting. I have/had fun playing it.
Overall, I'd give crashlands a solid 9/10. It's a great game, but there are a few unwanted features and hinderances here and there.
I think this definitely needs to be connected to the workshop, for sure. I'd love to see what content creators and modders would make and I think it would add a lot more fun and spice to the game. It also needs a console or debug command center, for cheaters and testing and just fun overall. I think all games like this NEED to have a console integrated into the game so the time searching for trainers online doesn't need to be spent.
The time limit on crafting is pointless and should be taken out. It hurts me to say this but its fairly obvious it is just there so that the creators  can have you spend more time in the game. Other than that, it serves no point. At all. Worthless feature which smudges the games reputation and gameplay.
You should be able to view the items in your bottomless inventory. I can't tell you how many times I wanted an item and didn't realize I'd had it, and wasted forever trying to find/harvest it. Thats what the tracking is supposed to fix, but tracking doesn't track multiple recipes, so when you track one piece of armor and keep the other in your head, but then do not have the ability to see if the items for the recipe in your head are in your inventory, it can get annoying. Especially when your very far from home and don't feel like teleporting.

I remember getting controller-throwing angry at games when I was a kid. Sometimes it was because they were too hard, sometimes they were unfair, and sometimes I was just being dumb about something. It's been a long time since I last felt that kind of rage boil up within me, but Nuclear Throne sure does take me back. It has a vicious streak that runs deeper than even its peers on Steam, and yet that might just be one of the reasons I keep coming back to it.
Nuclear Throne is the story of some plucky little mutants blasting their way across an apocalyptic hellscape to reach the throne of legend. There's a whole lot of far less plucky mutants standing in their way, and plenty of guns and things that explode to help you get past them. As a frantic twin-stick shooter you'll be dodging gunfire and explosions while blasting every foe you can find on the cramped, maze-like maps to open a portal to the next murderbox. It's a long journey, fraught with traps and monsters, but loads of secrets to uncover as well. And you're not going to see any of it for a very, very long time.
Nuclear Throne is hard. I'm sure you can name plenty of games that you think are hard or that took you awhile to master, but none of that matters because this one is just going to kick you in the♥♥♥♥♥♥over and over and over. Every new enemy you meet might very well tear your face off instantly and force you to claw your way back to it just to figure out how to beat it. You're going to shoot the wrong thing and blow yourself up despite having full health and plenty of bonuses. Your weapons are going to run dry and your foes are going to laugh as they flay you to pieces.
All of this is by design, because Nuclear Throne is a game that you learn and practice and eventually master to an incredible sense of gratification. Just getting the first few bosses down feels like an enormous accomplishment, in large part for all the things you need to remember to survive. For being such a modern twin-stick shooter this game takes a lot of inspiration from ancient roguelikes that had all sorts of weird, arcane rules to remember if you wanted to succeed. Here you have to know what explodes, what is weak to what, what all the enemy attack tells are, and so on. Forget a single point and you risk instant death.
Does that sound fun to you? It isn't at first, but just like the best roguelikes it instills this dogged determination in you to overcome such adversity. There are a load of characters to unlock, each with drastically different playstyles to learn and master. Seriously, these mutants can eat guns, explode corpses, warp reality, and more. Collecting radioactives dropped from enemies can level you up and give access to powerful mutations but pickups in this game vanish fast, pressing you to play bold and dive deep and probably die again trying to grab some rads or ammo. You can carry two weapons plucked from an impressive lineup of machine guns, shotguns, explosives, beam weapons, and grander things. Finding an effective pair for any situation and balancing their ammo use is yet another challenge to keep track of, one complicated by the single weapon chest in each level you'll usually have to work with. You need to make every shot count, and you won't really have the luxury of avoiding weapons that don't click, at least at first.
If you've gotten this far into the review without running for the hills, Nuclear Throne is the game for you. It's hard, it's cruel, it's relentless, and it comes at you at such a pace that you'll have little chance to prepare or recover. But it's ultimately fair, and the hours of study and practice it demands are rewarded with mastery and tantalizing secrets. I've had a hard time getting into Nuclear Throne because it's honestly not quite the style of roguelike I enjoy. Starting out you're going to be chipping away at the same enemies in the same levels in the same order for hours, lacking any real variation besides the weapons you find and the layouts of the maps. There isn't really any exploration to speak of until you learn what you're looking for, and even then it's just a particular trigger hidden among the scenery. I'm going to keep at it though, because there's a lot to see and do here behind a pretty towering difficulty curve, and I'm just starting to peek at the wonders that lie there.

Well, this is (at the moment) just part 1, and really the game slaps you in the face with that once you reach the end, you think "oh, so that's what... (END OF PART 1)". That aside, it's an old school/new school adventure, with the sweeping and large-ish dialogue trees that you remember mixed up with the really very linear feel, limited backtracking, streamlined interface and simplified puzzles that you'd expect from a new game. Yes, thank you for gently guiding me to the next part of the narrative, I couldn't have managed otherwise.
So it's really a game that you can sit down and finish in one session, and it's a not-unenjoyable ride with a fairly strong narrative. The only element that's specifically dissatisfying is Shay (the boy)'s setting. While Vella gets a pretty dark setting which would not be out of place in a Final Fantasy game, Shay gets something which is like a TV show for under-8s. There is a reason for that (and apparently a meta-reason for the reason), but it's still jarring and awkward beyond the point that any degree of lampshading can fix.

Spending 120 Hours playing Shadow of War, I've been stunned and yet I continue to be amazed at what the Nemesis System can even do at a bare minimal.
(READ READ READ)
Firstly, yes, there ARE "Microtransactions" and "Lootboxes" in Shadow of War, HOWEVER, the only Purchase you CAN make is with Gold - The "Greater valued" Currency which you CAN get in quantities by playing Daily/Community Challenges that are randomated every Day and every Week. The Lootboxes are also barely even affecting, the "Grind" people call which lures them to buy Lootboxes is INFACT the typical RPG Grind, and you don't even NEED to Grind to play the game how you want, the first 20 Levels of the maximum 60 the Player has is easily enough to make your own solid playstyle and you can get the first 20 Levels almost too quickly.
(READ READ READ)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Let's take it from the start: Middle-Earth, Shadow of War is the awaited Sequel to Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor, which was a game about taking the fight in a Backline War with Sauron's Forces in Mordor itself - Killing the ever shifting Captains and Warchiefs of Mordor to ensure that Sauron's Army is delayed in time for the War of The Ring.
You start as a Gondorian Ranger of The Black Gate called Talion - Who shortly after was sacrificed in a ritual by the Black Hand (A group of servants to Sauron) of whom they killed Dirhael, Talion's Son, and Loreth, Talion's Wife. Later Talion is resurrected and Banished from Death by a Wraith that was later discovered to be Celebrimbor - The greatest Smith of the Second Age who helped in a majority to craft the Rings of Power, and was Banished from Dead for his own misdeeds.
Together, Talion and Celebrimbor become the Bright Lord - The counterpart to Sauron, the Dark Lord and they seek the Black Hand, first the Hammer of Sauron, then the Tower of Sauron, and finally the actual Black Hand, of whom in an engaged (Yet sadly a Quick-Time-Event) Manages to capture Celebrimbor and bring Sauron to a Fair Form temporarily, though was pushed back by the Bright Lord Duo.
---------------------------------------------------------------------
And that is where Shadow of War comes in - Where the Bright Lord Duo believe they must craft a new Ring of Power, one born without Corruption and Sauron's Bindings, in order to take on Sauron himself.
With the new Ring of Power, it allows you to Dominate the Armies of Sauron, turning their Captains and in turn their own Grunts against him, you are first set to be shown the fall of Minas Ithil, and engage into a deadly chase with the Nazgul all over Mordor while trying to fend them off and find their weaknesses. All in turn you are also set to capture the Fortresses of Mordor, and will inevitably engage Sauron into a heated Conflict, however, it does not go according to plan, I won't spoiler how.
In terms of what the game is about - The Nemesis System, i'm yet to be disappointed to just HOW much the Nemesis System can create, i've seen Olog-Hai - One of the 2 Orcs in the Nemesis System, that are obsessed with blowing things up, and i've seen Uruks who are called The Machine and are litterally a Mordor's version of DC Cyborg.
The Fortress Assaults and Fortress Defences, while being very simple and subjectively easy, can be in reality a great way to interact with the Nemesis System - That one Warchief who killed you? He'll be there at the gate ready to smack-talk you and tell you how much of an awful fighter you are. See the Captain who is your ally? He'll boast about how cowardly the Overlord is and throw the Dank Memes for you.
The types of Missions Captains can go on has been expanded tremendously, here are some examples:
Trial by Ordeal: Caragors, Ghuls, Graug.
Ambush: (Any Captain can now Ambush any other two Captain's Mission, making a story-like moment sometimes)
Caragor Raid: A Captain will try to raid another Captain's Caragor Pens.
Camp Raid: A Captain will try to raid another Captain's Camp.
Chase: A Captain will try to "run away", luring another Captain into a deathtrap.
Execution: A Captain might of captured another Captain and will Execute him, this Mission too can be Ambushed.
Checkpoint Raid: A Captain will try to hold a "Road" in Lockdown, another Captain will try to destroy the Checkpoint.
And i'm sure there are a few other more rare Missions but those are the ones i've seen the most of, the voice actors for the Nemesis System have almost destroyed expectations - They even have SOME voice lines that referance the name of a Captain and can make a near personal moment.
The types of Captains you can get are too expanded, first you have Tribes, a type of preset that is the first preset to what a Captain can be.
Marauder Tribe - A Tribe that plunders and takes gold and riches in the name of Sauron.
Mystic Tribe - A Tribe that is an occult dating back long ago, collecting mystical knowledge of the Dark Lord.
Terror Tribe - A Tribe that relishes and fantasises Pain, as well as giving it AND recieving it.
Machine Tribe - A Tribe that is like Tolkein's views on Industry: A cog in a War Machine bent on consuming Middle-Earth.
Warmonger Tribe - A Tribe of Orcs who worship the Arts of War and practice all day in the name of Sauron.
Feral Tribe - A Tribe that fantasises, as well as indulge in fetishes of the Beasts of Mordor, adorning oneself fur, claws, etc.
Dark Tribe - A Tribe dedicated to serving Sauron in the Shadows, capable Assassins as well.
DLC Tribes they planned ahead:
Slaughter Tribe - No Details Yet?
Outlaw Tribe - No Details Yet?
You can also have different types of weapons the Captains have, for example you can have an Uruk with a Crossbow who is also a Commander Class, who can call allies into battle to replace his fallen Gang Members, however, Olog-Hai for an example, can only be a Warrior Class but can be any type of Advanced Class.
Firstly, here's a list of Weapon Classes a Captain can be:
Defender - Wields a large shield and a melee-combat Spear
Warrior - Wields only one weapon in one hand, nonetheless a powerful warrior still
Beserker - Wields two weapons at once, a type of Shock-Troop
Hunter - Wields throwing Spears
Archer - Wields a Crossbow - Advanced Class - Marksman (Like a sniper)
And here's the Advanced Classes:
Commander - Can rally the Orcs of Sauron's Army to assist him, and strengthens their morale and power.
Slayer - A powerful warrior who hates any type of gang-conflict, and prefers to duel or fight single opponents.
Beserker - A type of training that allows one to use their Hate as a weapon - extending their bloodlusts
Assassin - Sneaky Orcs that prefer to take the approach of assassination in the Shadows.
Trickster - Unpredictable, these Orcs can use Smoke Bombs and tricks to vanish, disappear and even escape execution.
Destroyer - A heartwarmed Orc who likes to watch explosions, use blasting powder to blow up Middle-Earth.
(I believe there are more other Advanced Classes, but I cannot seem to recall them all, sorry.)
Depending on what a Captain's Tribe, Class and Advanced Class is depends on what their personality would be like, and often even their Titles will dictate on what personality they have, Hoglik The Head-Chopper? He'll be obsessed into executions. Stakuga The Obsessed? He'll be... obsessed into the player's character (Talion.)...
Overall, I cannot say enough to JUST how much the Nemesis System has been improved and it's amazing as ever, you can learn Skills that can allow you to ride Caragors, Graugs and even a Drake (Which replaces the Fellbeasts, even if it's slightly lore-breaking from what I recall).
To properly experience this game, you've got to spend time in the Nemesis System, what I recommend doing is AFTER Act 2 and being given access to ALL Regions, I recommend going to any Region controlled by Sauron of your choosing and spend a few hours just interacting with the Captains, make new allies, be betrayed, end a conflict etc.

This is more of a critique of the game/apparatus than it is of the content.
Spintires is one of those games with the amazing features that can only really define one game or one series of games.  It's one of those games with great concepts, ideas, and potential...but VERY poorly executed upon marketing.
The game is how everyone describes it.  It is great and has all the positive and fun attributes it exhibits in reviews, trailers and demos....
but the developers/marketers have absolutely no idea what they're doing at this stage in the game's time frame.
$30 for pretty much an expedited demo with COUNTLESS bugs, unfinished features and unimplemented concepts.  Honestly depressing how such an amazing game can fall to unacceptable marketing.  There is no doubt that this is the developer's first time in the construction of a game.
It truly is fun, enjoyable and well-assembled, and I do recommend it.  But it is a shame that it is considered a 'full game' and priced at $30 when there isn't more than just a handful of features established than there is in the otherwise free Spintires tech demo.
BOTTOM LINE:  POOR EXECUTION AND NOT WORTH $30.

It's hard not to compare the Witcher 2 to Dragon Age 2 while playing it, though it doesn't really seem fair.  Even though they're very different games, they're both the premier PC Fantasy RPG series at the moment.  Thing is, while you're kind of blindsided by the stunning visuals of the Witcher 2 at the opening, after that, you're a little overwhelmed by the mechanics and density of the lore - and the brilliance of the game takes a while to sink in. The game is quite short and linear, and it doesn't really revolutionize or move the genre, but I still enjoyed it.

Highly recommended if you miss playing Fallout 2, Baldur's Gate, and other iso-view classics. Wasteland 2 has a ton of quests and many of them have repurcussions depending on your choices. Character building is tough because there are more skills than you can master, so it's better to forget about trying to max out in everything.
The dialogue and writing is very extensive and humorous. Arizona is filled with weird characters and location descriptions. Environments are large and it's easy to miss boxes and vaults hidden away in corners. This is the type of game where you have to back track in order to loot and explore everything.
Combat is good enough for what it is, but could eventually become a chore. Other than move, attack, switch weapons, and switch firing types, your only other options are to crouch or headshot. Headshot seems pointless because it's -40% chance to hit, 200% damage, and 0% critical. 0% critical for a headshot? My sniper character has a 25% critical chance, so it's a tradeoff that doesn't seem to be worth it.
Switching items in your inventory and hands doesn't cost any action points, but a "quick belt" for grenades and such would seem handy. Also, weapons jam too much. They SAY the percentages are usually 2-4%, but I would guess they're more around 6-10%.
Weaknesses aside, this is an awesome game with a lot to do. Even right at the beginning is a large decision which affects the later game. I expect replay value will be very high for me.

The third installment in the Civilization series which is getting pretty old these days, with it's successor Civilization IV and V.  This is another one of those titles that you might have grown up with as a kid and have had nostalgic value to you. This is at least the case for me. I remember that the game took a chocking 700 MB of space on my hard disk and it was generally tanking my late 90's computer. I have sunk a huge amount of hours into this game and for me this is the best game in the series.
Civilization is probably the most dominating Turn-based strategy game in the gaming industry. The Total Wars games for example are RTS/TBS hybrids, while CIV is completely TBS. True Civilization enthusiasts probably rank Civ3 pretty low, compared to Civ2, Civ4 and Civ5 which were very well received for their times. For me however, Civilization 3 is the favorite among the ones I've played (Civ3, Civ4 and Civ5). Again - because of it's nostalgic value.
All Civ games start out the same way unless you play a scenario or campaign. You start off with a settler and a warrior of some sorts. The settler can build a city, and as you find a suitable location for your capital - let your Civilization begin! Beware though, once you have started a game you won't be able to leave for at least 4 hours. This game is honestly best played during the night and is mostly a single-player experience.
There is a Campaign/Scenario mode, where you play historical events or just silly settings. As well as a multiplayer mode, but I have never enjoyed these ones at all. Nothing beats that random map mode, select the terrain, the climate, map size and your opponents/allies. Gumboy - Crazy Adventures earns my first negative review.
Let's get started, the protagonist known as Gumboy is a ball (most likely made of gum) that can transform into different shapes by collecting different in game items. There are different story sections of the game: Tutorial, Magic Forest, Bean World, Summer Meadow, Underground, and Caves. Each section is about equal in length except Underground which only has three levels. The tutorials offer a system which allows you to learn the basics of the game before they infuriate you in the actual campaign. Each mission you  have an Astral Guardian who will help you to achieve an objective. Once you have completed the requirements a pollinator (somewhere on the map) will release pollen, you must then using an item offered by the Astral Guardian push the pollen back to the Astral Guardian. Upon completing this a portal opens which you can roll, roll, or roll into. This ends the level and allows you to move up to the next challenge. You can start in the first level of Magic Forest, Bean World, or Summer Meadows meaning there is no real beginning to the game. In fact there is no real story, just simply roll and collect the dust then roll on your merry way.
If you didn’t notice I used the word roll a lot, this is because roll is your only native control. In order to jump you must collect a hiccup seed and it only lasts for a set amount of time. This is fantastic the character can essentially only roll left to right prior to collecting an item, this means before starting a level half the time you have to roll and find this item so you can actually start the level. Not only do you need to find the ability to jump before starting a level, you must then go find the shape transformation items on the levels (this is not optional). You play a character who is made of gum and cannot mold itself or jump by itself. The game continues by making it so the terrain has random bumps in it that block you from effectively moving (half the time throwing me in the wrong way – over and over again). The jump ability only works half of the time and the heights obtained by the jump seem completely random so going from one platform to the other is essentially just luck of the draw. If you could get past the incredibly poor controls, the required transformation changes, the ridiculous requiring an item to jump concept, and the awfully designed terrain you'd still probably not like this game. Gumboy - Crazy Adventures still pushes the boundary with an awful menu interface, rather than being able to simply move the mouse and select to exit a menu you need to roll your character through each menu option where it requires you to stop and wait till the sub menu interface opens. Even the in-game menu works similarly; to exit you have to roll round a huge ball just so you can quit the game. Gumboy – Crazy Adventures is a game that offers very little in the sense of entertainment. Then this game strives for being least interesting game by offering poor controls, terrible terrain navigation, and illogical gameplay.
Overall I would not recommend this game, although seeing as it came with the Indie Puzzle Back I guess you'll just have to have it stuck in your library. Some people would say you could get past all these deficits because the ambience is nice, the environment is pleasing, and the music is soothing. If you want a puzzle game where you are a ball, that offers interesting music, beautiful scenery, and a serene ambiance play influx. It’s the same price, it was made in 2013, and you will not want to kill yourself every time you try and move the character.

Sid Meier's Civilization III, the sequel to the great Civilization II, a game that by some is still to this day considered to be the best of the series, has the heavy duty challenge of not only living up to the standards set by it's predecessors but also to innovate the franchise enough that players of the previous installment can be bothered to upgrade.
It starts out with a somewhat mixed feeling. Some of the great ideas from Alpha Centauri has been brought over creating a much more versatile playing field with a living map and more unique factions but many of Alpha Centauri's greatest assets, such as the ability to build your own units and terrain elevations are notably absent. and others, such as unique factions, are only half implemented.
These improvements however do still manage to increase the interactivity of the game substantially particularly when combined with the many new features, such as culture, that Civ III brings to the table.
Factions are not longer defined simply by their city names but now have a few unique units of little consequence and civilization traits of great consequence. Unique units are simply beefed up versions of regular units that give a faction a small military advantage during the time period in which the unit is present, this can be a nice boost if you happen to go to war in that time but it can also be ignored completely if the time for war is not right. The traits each faction receives now however are of a much greater importance and can range from getting a free technology every age to a half off cost on religious buildings. These traits are big enough in effect that they tend to define your entire game.
A new and important feature in Civ III is culture. Each city generates culture through it's various buildings and the culture in turn defines the size of it's borders. A heavily cultured city can even envelop the city of an opponent and flip it to your side. While the realism or historical accuracy of such a device is laughable at best it does provide players with a new means of expansion and a way to deal with those pesky resource stealing late game cities that the AI is so fond of placing in whatever unoccupied corner of your empire it can find.
Graphically Civilization III is passable as always, the city view is pleasant but the rest of the game gives only a mediocre visual experience. Nothing pretty but nothing that'll ruin your gaming experience either. The soundtrack is still mostly orchestral epics and works very well although the rest of the sound effects in the game are pretty forgettable.
All in all Sid Meier's Civilization III is a good sequel. It doesn't create quite the same feeling of amazement and enjoyment that going from Civ I to Civ II does but it manages to provide a good solid experience with enough innovation to justify the purchase.

This game is a masterpiece. Utilising an intelligent levelling system and perk layout, Nuclear Throne never feels like a waste of time.
The gunplay is superb and you never feel overpowered or at adisadvantage, while still allowing for both frightening battles of survival and massacres of triumph. The variety of weapons also allows for different encounters, forcing player to adapt to the firearms available.
Each character's passive and active skill fit differently into the game, immediately refreshing stages and putting a new spin on a run. While no character is outright stronger than another, their abilities allow them each to dominate a certain situation.
The implementations of Mutations, which allow players to choose from a set of four perks after they level up, allows players to continue having a chance against stronger and stronger foes. Proper choice of Mutations is important, since you only get a certain amount.
Overall, I feel as though I have only begun to scratch the surface of the game, and feel that there are many more hours of enjoyment waiting. This game is a gem, and I would buy it again in a heartbeat. It even has co-op!

Its kind of hard to paint this game in a good light.  Its basically all the same things the original game had to offer with more, but still manages to feel like less.  This is all my personal opinion on the game, so take it or leave it as you see fit.
Pro's:
Its the same combat system smoothed out a bit, which was fun in the first game.  I cant say there was a massive difference aside from the larger pool of skills you can spec into as you level.  I just found myself using the same old things over and over though.
Graphically it looks good, not fantastic, but good.  Regions actually look/feel different.  Well, more so than the first game.
The nemisis system seems to have been tweeked/improved and the variety of foes has been increased.
The game has not crashed once for me.
There are plenty of things to hunt down and collect and different weapons and armour to loot.
Con's:
There is plenty of busy work to get on with hunting collectables. You end up destroying most of the things you loot for in game currency.
Movement can be a bit annoying.  When you try to climb a wall but end up rolling. Using said button any around a orc seems to default to vaulting over them.
Late game is a horrible grind.  With nothing interesting to do except fight, fight and fight some more.  After the first 2 fortresses I found that I just couldnt be bothered to repeat the whole process again.
The above basically leading you to the market place, manipulating you into buying some loot boxes just to speed things along. (I'd like to point out that I did not purchase anything from the market place as I found it distasteful).
I have yet to finish the game despite the number of hours ive put into it, I find I just can bring myself to rinse and repeat these battles or grind out the exp and orcs to progress to the end END game.
As it stands, I cant really recommend this game.  Not taking into account all the bad press leading up to release, at best I can only give it a 5/10.  Which is a shame as I loved the first game.

Dont... just dont. Unless you are planning on staring at your computer for hours waiting for the smallest things to happen,  then selling everything you own, shaving your head and moving to the mountains, then save your money.

This is a game that has really captured the act of driving in mud, over rocks, around and in woodland, through rivers and lakes. It is utterly mesmerising at times to see the level of detail they have captured in this game. Mud will not just part in your wake like so many other games. It will get dug out and pushed aside, forever altering the path you take. In this aspect the mistakes you make can be problematic and also irreversable if you are not careful. If you destroy a path too much, it will mean that you can no longer use it with some of the vehicles and make you take a much longer route to your objective. Thinking ahead to how you should take some obsticles or how to avoid making them worse is an absolute must especially in Hardcore where mistakes are far more costly.
You need to really appreciate the effort that driving takes in this. It's not that you won't get to your destination, but that you may have to fight for every inch of it. That you will spend a good amount of time trying not to stop in the wrong kind of mud. While also ensuring you do not accidently tear up mud that will make it more difficult on the way back. There's the means to use a winch system and with a good amount of practice using it. You can really get around a lot of things you otherwise wouldn't.
The game also features online co-op, which allows you to split the load amongst more people and add a lot more enjoyable elements to the game. Like winching out a friend from a mud hole that leaves them nearly flipping their load and wasting that 20 minutes it took you all to get it there. It's quite a sight to see a convoy of Trucks driving through mud and some river crossing are only truely epic when you can enjoy them with friends.
This is a game that deserves a lot more money than it got for the Kickstarter. It is really well designed and made, optimised really well and is a great simulation for people who enjoy large powerful trucks and driving in mud. The only downside I will say is that the camera is more cinematic/photogenic than it is useful at times and hopefully they will gives us more useful ones soon.

TL;DR
Bugs aside, one of the best games I've ever played. Combat of XCOM meets the post-apocalyptic style of Fallout, with great writing all around and quirky humor sprinkled around serious themes. Worth $60? Definitely. 9.5/10
OVERVIEW
I just finished the game the night before this review, and after putting 27 hours between multiple playthroughs into the beta, I kinda zipped through the first half of the game since I knew what to expect. Still, it took 30 hours to finish the game, and because of the amount of content I realize I missed, it should have taken much longer.
REPLAY VALUE: 9/10
There is a ton of replay value. Often, you are told to choose between sides, whether to save one base vs the other, or keep the current ruling party in power vs replacing them. Sometimes you can negotiate something where everybody wins. Other times, I turned both sides into a bloodbath and skipped away with all of their valuables. After finishing this review, I intend to start a whole new party and go through it again to see how different actions will affect the outcome.
STORY: 8/10
While predictable at times, it was still fun to see how things unfold. Each of the settlements has its own share of problems, ranging from the absurd (giant killer plants attacking us!!) to the exciting (paramilitary team trying to tactfully usurp power from religious wackjobs). While the ending wasn't mindblowing, it was satsifying.
GAMEPLAY: 9.5/10
There are so very many ways to solve problems. At first, the number of skills seems overwhelming, since you only have a limited number of characters to learn them. But if my lockpicker can't open a door, maybe I can have my strength build kick it down. He fractured his leg on it? Hell, let's just blow it off the hinges. Where's that guy with the RPG? Exploring the world is exciting as well. There are plenty of areas that will never get mentioned if you only follow the main storylines, so many hidden caches of weapons to stumble upon. And there's nothing more exciting than going into combat with a brand new shiny weapon. Speaking of which...
COMBAT: 9/10
The combat system is the turn-based strategic grid style that XCOM and Fallouts 1/2/Tactics used. Command your sniper to climb that ladder and watch her accuracy - and damage output - triple. Hide your SMGer behind a wall and order him to ambush anyone who walks by. Why should he walk into harm's way? Put your assault people behind the wrecked car for cover and an accuracy bonus. Doesn't always work, since enemies will still use flanking maneuvers, grenades, and the same tactics as you. If you fall, you'd better hope your surgeon can come fix you before you bleed out. If you're about to fall, send your medic for a quick patchup.
PROBLEMS:
There are a lot of bugs in the second half of the game. For those of us who played it while it was in the Early Access stage, the second half of the game was not available, so once you reach that point, expect typos, a few conversations without purpose, people appearing in two places at once, etc. I personally haven't experienced anything gamebreaking, just frustrating, but the team has been hard at work polishing the game since release.

Sid Meier's Civilization III, the sequel to the great Civilization II, a game that by some is still to this day considered to be the best of the series, has the heavy duty challenge of not only living up to the standards set by it's predecessors but also to innovate the franchise enough that players of the previous installment can be bothered to upgrade.
It starts out with a somewhat mixed feeling. Some of the great ideas from Alpha Centauri has been brought over creating a much more versatile playing field with a living map and more unique factions but many of Alpha Centauri's greatest assets, such as the ability to build your own units and terrain elevations are notably absent. and others, such as unique factions, are only half implemented.
These improvements however do still manage to increase the interactivity of the game substantially particularly when combined with the many new features, such as culture, that Civ III brings to the table.
Factions are not longer defined simply by their city names but now have a few unique units of little consequence and civilization traits of great consequence. Unique units are simply beefed up versions of regular units that give a faction a small military advantage during the time period in which the unit is present, this can be a nice boost if you happen to go to war in that time but it can also be ignored completely if the time for war is not right. The traits each faction receives now however are of a much greater importance and can range from getting a free technology every age to a half off cost on religious buildings. These traits are big enough in effect that they tend to define your entire game.
A new and important feature in Civ III is culture. Each city generates culture through it's various buildings and the culture in turn defines the size of it's borders. A heavily cultured city can even envelop the city of an opponent and flip it to your side. While the realism or historical accuracy of such a device is laughable at best it does provide players with a new means of expansion and a way to deal with those pesky resource stealing late game cities that the AI is so fond of placing in whatever unoccupied corner of your empire it can find.
Graphically Civilization III is passable as always, the city view is pleasant but the rest of the game gives only a mediocre visual experience. Nothing pretty but nothing that'll ruin your gaming experience either. The soundtrack is still mostly orchestral epics and works very well although the rest of the sound effects in the game are pretty forgettable.
All in all Sid Meier's Civilization III is a good sequel. It doesn't create quite the same feeling of amazement and enjoyment that going from Civ I to Civ II does but it manages to provide a good solid experience with enough innovation to justify the purchase.

So after 70+ Hours I think I have played enough of this and gotten the mechanics down to write a review. Now I get this is supposed to be a classic styled game. I loved Wasteland and the Fallout series which is why I had to play this. I went in expecting some pretty decent gameplay ala Fallout 1 & 2 style. While the base game has some decent overtones and it looks extremely polished. The feel and amibiance are fantastic game looks and feels great and just oozes style. However the mechanics are what destroys this title or should I say lack thereof.
Unpopular Mechanics: How the Waste was made.
So lets get this started you have Attributes which give you various bonuses to derived stats and a lot of skills. Every skill or stat goes from 1 to 10 including the  equipped armor stat, but more on that later. Now most of your stats are straight forward extra skill points on level up or higher crit chance on in particular is interesting "Combat Intiative". Seems pretty standard it makes you act sooner in combat right? Well partially right, it allows you to act faster in combat. Meaning you can go two or even three times more then a character with a low score. Making it a godly stat if you get enough of it. Also the average of 13-15 is considered low by the game. Enemies have average 17-19 meaning they go first and sometimes twice before you do.
That leads us into the mess which is Wasteland 2's combat system. Lets start with weapons and see what does what.
Assault rifles: High damage, wonky stats between rifles as some higher tier ones do horribly low damage and most have a solid three round burst mode. This is the go to weapon for most situations the only draw back is they have accuracy penalty at point blank range and if a enemy moves next to you a further aim on all shots is inccured. Also the enemies WILL do this every chance they get to cripple your snipers even if they don't attack them.
Pistols: high crit low base damage. Early ones fire for a pittance of 3 action points a shot allowing you to do some damage. Later higher but not assault rifle damage ones are typically 4 AP a shot. A decent side arm for using 4 ap you can't shoot with a rifle as you switch between guns, not particularly effective though, As you can rarely get a third shot off late game.
Heavy Weapons: These are joke level, they waste huge amounts of bullets to fire large bursts of VERY low damage shots that combine up to equal a couple good assault rifle shots. Bonus joke is you start with a broken M2 .50 caliber machingun rechambered in 5.56 if you select this skill at start. Even though you get .50 BMG ammo later on there is apprantly no real M2 that uses it. To put it in perspective a assault rifle using the same round does 44-70 damage for the 20-30 damage of a heavy weapon. Both of which will be reduced by enemy armor making even a minigun barrages damage miniscule. No mods can be used so they will jam or not have great chance to hit/Hit your own dudes.
Submachine guns: These are to pistols what heavy weapons are to assault rifles. Low damage bullet wasters.
Energy Weapons: Now we are talk here is the games central gimmick and one of things that breaks the game utterly. The more armor the target has the more damage it takes from energy weapons. Late game enemies use energy weapons and melee weapons that go right through your armor. There is a ambush later in the game where synthetics attack you from all directions, I died after 2-3 turns and retried this encounter many times and went back and leveled up and did stuff I might have missed. I was level 34 at my highest character and still died. Solution? I took off my armor before entering the location and the 120 damage hits I was taking turned into 15-20 damage hits. I completed the whole fight with no one under 80% health and having done NO healing during the fight.
Totally disgusting as all my power armor and cool gear I worked for actually slowed me down and made me take MORE damage. Also Explosives do straight damage ignoring armor so a pipe bomb always does 50 damage and a frag grenade does 100.
To reiterate I had to take off all my armor in order to progress through the game or I would die if they I wore armor.
Shotguns: Laughable for a good eighty percent of the game. Enemies will often kill each other with the low damage cone effect. Later ones gain burst fire but insane accuracy penalties where they will either do maybe a shot of assault rifle damage or triple shot remove late game enemies.
Sniper rifles: High damage and long range, Keep enemies back or lure them in for close combat. The best gun in the game is likely the .50 caliber sniper rifle you pull out of the dump as it can and will crit for 250+ oh and like pistols these have a high base crit and rarely miss when in range.
Oh and uh melee weapons: they do more damage based on levels you put into them even though it apprantly doesn't say that. Anything with AP 2-3 is extremly viable especially against rifle using enemies who will run away from you. If you max these out early they are absurd like no other. Especially as later ones have very high armor pen and status effects. Do not trust the listed damage, once you are 6-8 skill points in they pulp whatever you hit, and you can swing multiple times.
Skills or how I learned to extend play time through save scumming. Every skill besides first aid (unless surgery on npc's) has a critical failure. Even a easy 92% check has a chance of going HORRIBLY wrong and maiming your character or breaking whatever you were interacting with. This can straight up break entire quests as you break a lock and are unable to progress in that chain. Frequent saving and loading on critical areas is advised. The game loves to throw critical failures even when its only a 5% chance to hit them.
Weaponsmithing is a mess as it provides a chance to get weapon mods by destroying guns. The random list has older mods which are no longer useful. Though breaking weapons can lead to weapon parts which can be sold at the ranger citadel in arizona for huge profit once you get the basic tier of mods done. Even maxxed out the chances of good mods is not that good unless you have stacks of high tier energy guns and assault rifles. which can instead be sold for bullets and health items better guns.
Theres also a bunch of crazy trinkets that you can swap out for stat bonuses though you will have to save scum when you realize you didn't have your ranger badge on when you needed that extra point of hardass in a conversations as the conversation skill prompts are removed if you quit the conversation or talk about something else no backsies!
Speaking of no backsies, if you pass up a safe or locked item only to come back when you have higher skill. Several times the safes are now "looted by scavengers". Tough break.
The quests, dialog, writng, amibiance, voice acting, art style, animation, story and basically every thing else are top notch. However this game most reminds me of Arcanum with its horrible skill and combat system.
So in summery: Armor kills you and also slows you down, Assault rifles blow basically everything out of the water, even more so when weaponsmithed (save scum those laser sights!), Combat intiative is the best stat next to action points, You can go two to three times for their one and get all your action points each time. Heavy weapons are a funny joke by the devs and are ineffectual unless enemies spam them and even then kinda meh.
Finally, you can't polish a turd but you can sure ruin something trying to polish it with a turd.

I have so much love and for hate this game. And these are the reasons why:
* Free to play. It leaves me more money to spend on Cosmetics because I just love to dazzle people with pretty pixels.
* New characters and skins almost every fortnight now.
* Lovely forum community.
* NO VOICECHATS. Thank gods for that. I'm sick of getting sworn at by 12 year olds in various languages and them telling me they've ploughed my mother.
* Easy introduction into the game for new players. Until you get to level 5, you are playing with bots. That way you get slowly eased into the game and learn the maps and how you handle your Champions until you are matched with real people.
* Everything (apart from exclusive skins and boosters, which are useless anyway) can be unlocked with in-game currency and those things just drop so easily it's ridiculous. Character level up, get gold. Profile level up, get gold. Win a match, get gold. LOSE a match, get gold. Login, get gold.
* Easy objectives. Capture the point, push the damn payload, win. Repeat.
* Easy to understand roles. Tanks tank, healers heal. When Tanks start to flank, flanks start to try and be the tank and cap and healers start to play snipers, things get messy and it rarely ends well.
* The developers actually listen and respond to feedback so much it's spooky.
* Getting blown out of the map by Bomb King's Poppy Bomb.
* Maeve zipping off when you are so close to killing her.
* Comparisons between OW and Paladins.
* Complains about the Legendary cards and the Essence needed to buy them and other loadout cards. Trust me, no one needs all the cards. I played with the basic stock cards for a long time before I went and messed around and made a personal deck. I sucked so hard, I went back to the basic cards for some Champs. The same thing is happening with Legendary cards. Went and bought a few with Essence, hated them and went back to the free ones I was given.
* Playing tank and realizing that my healer is busy trying to be a sniper and is not interested in healing anyone.

What to say about Crashlands? Well i must say that it has consumed a lot of my free time for the past week. The game has a complulsive quality to it. Just five more minutes I tell myself only to quit two hours later. It pulls in ideas from Minecraft, Diablo and World of Warcraft. Yes, its derivitive, but what game isnt these days? It bucks the recent trend for rock hard perma-death games which I find really refreshing. I have always loved rogue type games but of late they have gotten too hard. I like to commit my free time but not to something that wipes out all my hard work when i make mistakes. Starting again from scratch I find far too frustating and I lose the will to play again. I guess the closest resemblance to recent games is Don't Starve, which I found a brilliant idea but ultimately i found it depressing. Quite apart from my character going mad every time it was far too hard and no fun after a while.
Crashland takes all these ideas and re-jigs them and the guys from the briliiantly named Butterscotch Shenanigans have produced a masterpiece (in my humble opinion). They then go one further and pull out yet another brilliant coup - they release it on multiple systems. This means that nerds like me can play the same game, nay the same game save on different systems!! Crashlands is on IOS, Android, Mac and PC. So i can start on my ipad, move to my Macbook Air when I fancy a change, then I can take the same game out on the road on my phone!! Wow!
What else? How long have you got? The game has an unlimited inventory. Collect everything to your hearts content. Want 500 blocks of wood, then go for it. The game also puts the right tool into your hand depending on what you are doing. For example, strike a tree and an axe comes to your hand, strike a rock and you automatically produce a pickaxe, hit a critter and your weapon miraculously comes to hand!
You also dont have to juggle stuff you own. The components you collect from scavanging and killing critters are listed briefly in a text panel over on the left of the screen then that is the last you see of them. You work with recipes instead, 500 of them in all, that are accessed by the numerous workstations that you also make. A recipe might need, ten sawgrass, three waterballoons and some glue. If you have all the components you can make it, as many as you have bits for. If not then the game tells you that you have x of whatever missing. So you go out and find it.
You also find eggs while out hunting. Find a recipe for an incubator and you can make it, then use it to hatch the egg. If you hatch a wompit you can create a nest and put it on it and then milk it! Yes milk it, Eugh! - you milk a one legged dog thing! Why? Because later in the game that milk is a vital ingredient in yet another recipe. The recipes themselves come from randoms drops mostly from kills while hunting. You also get the more important ones from completing quests. These are the workstations, the armour and the weapons and the major tools.
You will note I have said nothing about the plot or the setting. I wont either, suffice to says its ingenius and what starts out simple spins out into some grander. just do yourself a favour and buy it. Now!
To date I have clocked up 15 hours. So that leaves me 45 hours of playtime left according to the developers. I am still in the first map/biome. In one of the dev diaries which you can readily find on the net it takes eight, yes eight hours in realtime to walk from one side of one map to the other side! Thats mind bogglingly big. There are three maps!
I have played, in my considerable number of years of gaming life, very very few games for multiple hours, WOW, Wild Arms, FInal Fantasy games (all 14 of them) and Xenoblade Chronicles but never, apart from Alto, any game for so long on an ipad. Even on Alto i have only clocked up five or so hours. Crashlands has stolen the crown. It really is the bees knees and deserves to be played by everyone.
Are there any negatives? Well its a grind at times, but then I settle into the groove as i inch my way towards 140 blocks of stone and that blasted Wompit essence that was such a trial to get because the goal is so tantilising - a Wompit Garter which turns litle Chomp into a killing machine. So even the negatives turns into a plus.
I could go on, and on but I am feeling the itch to play. I want that level 7 helm but one component, a tiny blue flower bud, is so rare that I am having to trawl the entire map. When I do find it where it grows I will be sure to mark the map so after i harvest it I know where to go when it grows back. And that says it all, the total attention to detail the BS guys have poured into this game across the three years of its development.  Read their story too. Its quite moving.
The game is a wonder - go play.

First off, I have to say this: if you don't like puzzles and story driven adventures, don't pick up this piece. It is an amazing game, but I'm sure many people wouldn't like it. Now then, onto the review.
As many other places will tell you, Broken Age is a puzzle/adventure game telling the story of two characters: a girl named Vella, chosed to be an offering to the monster Mog'Chatra, and Shay, a boy who lives on an overprotective ship and just craves a real adventure. The game allows you to jump between either story at any given time, and honestly, both are highly entertaining. The puzzles the game contains often require a very creative mind, or simply dragging everything in your inventory to see if there is a use for it. Many of the characters are also extremely witty, with many references to popular stereotypes (hint: hipster woodsman). All in all, Broken Age provides a good experience, with the glorious art, engaging puzzles, and fun dialogue. Personally, I can't wait for Act 2 to be released.

Amazing Art Style
Good Puzzles

Engaging Characters
Cons:
Possibly Too Short For Price
Long Wait For Act 2

Do you like Stephen King? Would you like him in a game? Would you like him to take aim?
Alan Wake is not a scary story. It has jumps, and can manage being creepy at times, but is the kind of "safe" horror that King often manages. A spooky, evil presence chases him around a northwest town obviously inspired by Twin Peaks (the developers' previous series, Max Payne, had an outright parody of the series) while he uses a flashlight to banish the evil - and then generally shoot it.
I'm honestly uncertain whether or not this game is intended to have its tongue in cheek, but it's very much self-referential b-movie horror, and in that aspect it actually works quite well. Enemies growl ridiculous one-liners pointing to their former humanity, evil machines menace you, spooky messages from TVs - if you're willing to roll with the odd half-serious flavor and take in all the goofy story chunks, it's solid for fans of the survival horror genre. Mouse aiming makes the game a lot less challenging than I think it was intended, though the difficulty flips when you're outnumbered, as Alan doesn't have a great way to deal with being rushed from three sides, and the camera can definitely work against you when that happens. The way it uses light to relieve and increase tension is actually pretty smart, though the gameplay itself remains simple and somewhat repetitive throughout.
Overall, though, I rather liked it. The story kept me engaged, and the threat ramps up to delightfully farcical levels by the end. It ends on a cliffhanger that leads into American Nightmare, which is interesting and flawed in about equal measure, and the sequel it needs has never materialized out of the darkness. It does include the console DLC that provides more resolution, and though the content in the DLC chapters seems warmed over, it does take breaking the fourth wall to an clever level. Ultimately it's a good romp if you're looking for a 90s b-movie that involves shooting a lot of grumpy, gloomy, guses along the way.

No idea how a game can improve on the original in almost every aspect, and give you a sexy spider (say whaaat?), but still somehow manages to be one of the biggest disappointments of the year.
Mechanically this game is sound. Combat is as slick as an Alaskan oil spill, and traversal about as much fun you can have without landing up in jail - with some exceptions, including Talion's fear of pullies... stops him dead in his tracks. Or slightly raised platforms... oh he hates those.
The nemesis system is back, and boy can you feel the love put into those orcs. Highlights included a shamed captain boasting how he embraced said shame and was a better man... errr... orc because of it, and an unstable cross bow wielding Billy Bob who kept yelling 'I don't know!' over, and over... wait, he betrayed me. Scratch that. He is a low point. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
But alas, all is not well in the land of grog and graugs. I was onboard through out the first Act, but somewhere between breaking into Act 2 and the first siege things turned sour. The pacing of the game can grind to a halt, forcing you to do a LOT of busy work just to build some forward momentum. Tempted to say that some of the Nemesis System being tied to your level was tweaked to encourage a little gold spend... but could also be an attempt to artificially extend the game.
There is also some shoddy environmental texture work that can pop up in the most in your face places. Enough even for oblivious little old me to notice, but not enough to ruin the experience.
Ultimately, Shadow of War is a good game marred by poor pacing and an orc butt filled with fluff. All the little things added up to the point where I gave up. Hence not being able to recommend it. But I do that with one important note: if you don't mind grinding, and find the endless combat of Shadow of Mordor to be a slice of heaven, then more than likely you'll like this game.
*Two further thoughts:
- Turning off the minimap made it a lot more fun, albeit nerve wrecking as all your other bars vanish with it.
- I didn't bother with lootboxes, so no Idea how that influences the game.

Fallout Shelter is the best Bethesda-made (studio, not publisher) game since Fallout 3.
It's a simple, but rather polished idle game, based on managing a Vault from the Fallout titles.  There's three main resource productions to balance, Food, Water and Power, and then Caps is the currency for building stuff, with Nuke cola allowing you to skip wait times.
It's, at its core, a simple time-killer mobile game but that does not make it less enjoyable to play. The animations, personalization, theming and soundtrack are very well made, making you engage in one of those famous reward loops.

Time is the main gate to your progress, it is true that wait times can feel long occasionally, being this a title to be played in a "Pet Game" style, more so than some other idlers or city builders of the genre.
The game also offers the option to explore the wasteland, where you get a log of your pawn's progress delivered through their PipBoy, and the feature of quests, which add some very basic looting, combat and exploration mechanics, that are, however, rather fun to play.
I'd recommend investing some time in this if you are into this genre of games or are looking for a decent time waster.

Welll, I don't know what to say about this one, yet. I do enjoy it, it's basically CS meets CoD, which is kind of a...Bad thing, I guess?
You can buy stuff with the money you get after killing people, pretty much like in CS. You can get better weapons, armor, grenades, lots of stuff like that. Also, lots of weapons from counter strike games appear here, which is a plus.
On the other hand, it resembles CoD, mostly because there is almost zero recoil when you aim down the sights and enemies are bullet sponges. BUT, this game doesn't allow you to go prone, so that's a big ♥♥♥♥ing plus over CoD.
Music is meh, controls are standard when it comes to FPS games, so there is not much to complain about that.Guns are re-skins at the moment, which kind sucks. Just pick the one with the most ammo and the best iron sights.
So far, this game is midly entertaining, albeit kinda generic, gameplay wise. You can buy all the weapons in the game without having to use real cash, which is amazing, so it's definitely not P2W. For an early access F2P game, it's not as bad as I expected, I expected something ♥♥♥♥♥♥ like Tactical Intervention.
Also, I dunno if it's just me, or the game itself, but there's LOTS of lag spikes all the time, even in US servers. I dunno what's this all about. Also, it's extremely easy to spawncamp, spawns are mostly small spaces with two entrances, just put players on each exit and farm kills. That definitely needs to get fixed. I've seen games where one of the teams can't even get out of the spawn, at all. It's fun when you are on the camping team, but if not...It's pretty damn frustrating.
Also, what pretty can kill this game...Sometimes, even if you play on servers close to you, the game's got a serious problem with lag. And with sometimes, I'm talking about 8/10 servers you try to access. When you find a good, not so laggy server, you're all set.
So far, this game is a mixed bag. I do like it, but it gets stale after a while, plus, if you are expecting something extremely good, you will be dissapointed. Just give it a try, see for yourself, it's free to play after all.

This game is amazing. It's essentially Overwatch on the surface, but has a deeper meta. It's free. It's not much of a grind whatsoever. My literal only pet peeve at all is the price of the paid currency. It makes Riot Points look cheap. Anywho...
I'm writing this review at the time of OB44. When there seems to be a large amount of community entitlement for making their game slightly more of a grind. Which they haven't. Not really. Not if you actually consider what this game is like, and how the currency actually operates.
They've added a tertiary currency; Essence. Which is used to buy cards for your loadouts. Essentially, this currency hs caused a great deal of moaning and groaning, and cries of "P2W!". But is it? No. Radiant Chests can now be bought with gems
gold. Gold is extremely easy to earn, and I personally think this game is one of the more "fair" titles out there for people who are on a budget and only able to play mostly F2P games. Within a few wins, you can unlock a new champion, or buy two or three Radiant Chests. Literally less than 10. The games aren't exactly long, either. Most won't generally run over 10-15 mins.
The purported "issue" is that grinding this essence is considered P2W because you can buy Radiant Chests with gems. When in reality, these chests bought with gems confer no extra RNG chance to the essence grind. You just don't have to play to earn them. That's it. Perhaps they increase the chance a little, like any card drop from any Radiant Chest would. Removing a card from the potential prizes pool, to replace it with an essence refund.
Most of the negative reviews you will see here are simply high level players, who have already opened all their levelling chests, who are boycotting the game because they feel they've been duped. They've lost 40+ free chests worth of potential essence.
Absolutely not. Don't let the salt put you off. Try it out, have some fun.
Probably. But honestly, they should already have most of the cards by now anyway, save legendaries. So their grind will be hilariously minimal.

Nuclear Throne is a game in which you select a character and go into the wasteland, hoping you'll survive and reach the throne, along the way, you may mutate yourself to become stronger, along with finding better weapons. The game is filled with secrets, many of which award you with a new character, maybe a better starting gun, maybe a small change to how the gameplay works.
The game has an astounding soundtrack, great variety, great songs.
The gameplay feels sharp, very responsive, each character feels different from the other.
The visuals look great, very good sprite work, good color variety and palettes, the animation is surprisingly smooth, The Palace's Guardian's animations overall, Melting's breathing animation in the character selection screen, the list goes on.
The game's difficulty, however, is not for everyone. Sometimes the game will give you a bad spawn, like in an open corner with enemies around you, enemies which shoot you, a lot, a rain of death which you likely will not survive, or at least, will come out badly hurt, depending on your character and skill/experience, however that's the only ocasion in which bad luck will matter (Lil' Hunter's death pattern might or not have to do with luck) ; Enemies act different one from the other, so learning patterns is a must, the game may not be about luck, but it still has a rather intimidating difficulty to it. Great majority of all weapons are  effective, and the same goes for mutations.
If you're looking for a difficult game in which you gain power ups and better weapons as you go, this is for you, but be warned, it can be very addicting, playing this game for too long... might not be very healthy.
Also there's an online co-op mod. It's fantastic.

Nuclear Throne: A top-down "roguelike-light" shooter that combines the usual trappings (permadeath, randomized levels, character upgrades, loot tables) with crisp retro pixel art, frantic shooting, and teeth-gnashing difficulty. Highly recommended, and here's why.
The world has changed. Once there were humans here, and trees, and things were good. Now there's only the wasteland, the ruins of human civilization, and an awful lot of monsters and mutants. And somewhere, there is the Nuclear Throne. Sitting on it, legend tells, can make things right, and a bunch of determined mutans set out to rest their very backside on that very legendary throne.
Pick a mutant, each with their own unique passive and active ability, enter the wasteland with nothing but a small pistol and some ammo, and say hello to a brutal dry wasteland. You move your potential hero with the WASD keys, aim and shoot with the mouse, and... by now you're already dead. It happens. It will happen a lot. In Nuclear Throne, every single pixel is deadly and wants to see you dead. Getting used to the controls won't take you too long, though, and you *are* always in full control, everything's nice and smooth and precise. As you get a hang of things, you'll pick up better weapons, more ammo, and radiation: That's the stuff that allows you to level up and get new abilities... by mutating some more. Want more speed? Grow some extra legs. Weapons take too long to reload? Get yourself some trigger fingers. Love the shotgun? Get Shotgun Shoulders and see those bullets spray. Like weapons, the mutations you get to pick are randomized, adding some unpredictable element to each run. Across seven stages, things get hairier and more dangerous, always introducing some new enemy, and you also have to make your way past bosses that add some extra challenge.
Nuclear Throne is an unforgiving game. From the get-go, you are outnumbered and underpowered, barely able to take more than three direct hits from a normal enemy before your run's over. Better weapons and a good set of mutations can only get you so far: Your skill at dodging, reading a fight, and reacting within a second to yet another spray of bullets is what will get you further into the game. NC makes it easy to jump back into the fray: One click and you're there again, in the wasteland, and maybe this time...
With a good dozen of different mutants to unlock, with a nice range of little secrets to find, and with a raw, charming presentation, Nuclear Throne is a skill game that will tax your patience but will always see you coming back. There's a lot of satisfying gunplay, there's hilariously overpowered weapons, there's plenty of Yet Another Stoopid Death moments. This game has personality and attitude. It has staying power.
For those who care about this sort of thing, NC was made in Game Maker, and it showcases how to make a good solid game in that toolkit. There are some design decisions that tend to rub people the wrong way, most norably the lack of widescreen support and a hardcoded 30FPS lock, but these decisions are part of the very design- personally I never found any of them being a "bad thing". I'm usually far too busy exploding corpses with my MIND and clubbing monsters with a WRENCH. Through WALLS.
It also has a pretty darn good soundtrack!

If you want to play a game that starts like your typical high school drama crap and then evolves into something that really makes you rethink your life choices, ponder on problems that people around us have, and possibly even shed a tear (or cry your♥♥♥♥♥off, depending on how sensitive you are), then Life is Strange is your game. Download the free episode, give it a try, you've got nothing to lose.
Now, Life is Strange is not your typical adventure game so don't expect it to be one. Here, the primary gameplay mechanic is the protagonist's ability to manipulate time, while the remaining ones, including conversations, plot choices, puzzle-solving, and item-collecting, are subject to it. To be honest, it didn't took a lot of effort to beat everything this game threw at me, and when I actually had trouble making progress, I was either offered an easier alternative or straight up told what to do. And that's fine by me because Life is Strange is about choice and consequence, but not in that terrible, pretentious BioWare style. What I love about this game is that if you feel like you messed something up, you can seamlessly go back in time and do stuff differently -- something you don't get to do in real life. Obviously, some of your actions will have reactions in the future and are not that easy to fix. However, should you REALLY f*ck up and feel horrible about it, you can always restart the game from any major plot point and do things differently. Yes, this is sort of save-scumming but hey, I get enough drama and regrets in real life. Plus, in the end, you don't get to eat a cookie and have a cookie in Life is Strange, so you cannot make a perfect playthrough because there simply isn't one.
Life is Strange may be somewhat interactive-movieish, and it is to a large extent, but the amazing story and its characters make up for it if this is a problem with you. I'd easily recommend this game to the fans of all kinds of story-driven games.
Life is Strange is totally a 9,5/10 in my books. It does have poor voice acting and writing at some (though few) points, lip sync issues, and a bug or two but ultimately delivers one hell of an emotional ride with great plot twists and memorable characters. No doubt one of the best games I've played and a one that entered my personal hall of fame among such amazing masterpieces as Planescape: Torment, Neverwinter Nights 2: Mask of the Betrayer, Deus Ex series, Mass Effect series, and The Witcher series. I salute and thank the developers at Dontnod for this amazing experience that indeed happened at a very strange moment in my life.
