I've been struggling to write a review about Life is Strange for weeks, because I have a lot of conflicting feelings about it. I hate the main protagonist Max, but I love her friend Chloe. I hate the awful pacing of the last episode and the unskippable dialogue, but I love that it's a slow game that invites you to take your time and spend it observing and listening, instead of rushing from action scene to action scene like many other games. And I hate to give a Not Recommended rating to this game, because I love it for what it tries to do, but it just has too many flaws to overlook. Poor quality animation being the most obvious one from the start.
The clunky body animations are not so bad compared to an almost complete lack of facial animations (in some scenes the devs even forgot to animate the lips of the character who is speaking). For a game that relies on building an emotional connection to its characters, it fails so many times due to complete disassociation between the emotions conveyed through voice acting and the blankness of facial animations. Which is why the game resorts to pointing out people's emotional states in dialogue so often. However, after a while, hearing people comment on how Max's face looks "so intense" or similar just draws attention to the shortcomings of the game's animations instead of informing the player of the protagonist's state of mind.
The main protagonist's voice actress is another problem. There are so many scenes where her lines are delivered completely flatly, with as much expressiveness as reading a label off of a shampoo bottle. I get that the developers wanted someone a bit less expressive, because Max is supposed to be a very shy girl (furthermore, her character is less developed in order to allow the player to better identify with her), but I found the voice actress boring just too many times.
Poor animation and voice acting are the main objective reasons why I had trouble relating to the characters. Theme is another, and much more subjective one. If you are not the kind of person who enjoys TV shows or movies about teen drama, you will, like me, dislike *a lot* of this game. I understand that this is not the game's failing, but I simply could not get into it at all. Particularly since I found the game's treatment of certain serious topics, like bullying, to be kind of poor, with the bullying issue glossed over as no-one faces any consequences.
Then there's the writing. The game feels like the product of many writers, not all of whom are equally skilled at writing dialogue. A lot of time the dialogue feels like it's missing bits and pieces in between as characters jump to conclusions based on a sentence or two they are told. (Like in the last episode when Max tells Warren about her time rewind power and he immediately concludes that what she will do next will be "the most important moment in history".) Or the many times where characters heap praise on each other for supposedly being extraordinary, sympathetic, amazing artists, or whatever. It sounds melodramatic and insincere. Things like this might have been written with the idea of depicting teenagers as being overly dramatic or hyperbolic, but it just sounds like normal people would not speak like that.
The unskippable dialogue is another massive problem I have with the game. The only time the player can skip dialogue is when they rewind time and re-attempt dialogue with new information. Restarting from last checkpoint or replaying on another save file will not let you skip dialogue. I am baffled by this design choice. Did the developers of this game not expect people to replay it?
This is the one thing that I probably hate the most about the game, because otherwise I would probably replay it to see how the story develops if I make different choices. But I just don't have the patience to listen to all of it again.
Another thing that was a stupid design choice was forcing a set number of achievements for every episode. Achievements are obtained by taking photos, but due to the structure and events of the last episode, there's not much "downtime" where achievements could be added, and so the photo taking opportunities were put into certain intense situations where stopping to pursue an achievement pulls you out what is happening in the game. This happens at a couple of crucial points when Max is doing something urgent or when the game is trying to impart a message about Max's state of mind, and it breaks the immersion.
[Spoiler warning: some spoilers ahead]
And finally, my biggest gripe: the last episode. The last episode is a mess and the pacing is all over the place, with the first half an hour being almost nothing but exposition that requires almost no input from the player. (Bring popcorn so you have something to do with your hands.) The exposition is followed by an alternate timeline, after we have already established in an earlier episode that these don't work out. Then follows a nightmare sequence in which certain locations from earlier in the game are revisited but are distorted and a new type of gameplay is very briefly introduced focused on evading enemies. And then the episode ends. The player is offered two choices on how to end the game: one choice is emotionally not satisfactory, and the other is wrong. It is obviously wrong because the developers didn't actually bother to make an ending for it. The sole reason this choice is there is because the entire game is about making various (albeit not important in the grand scheme of things) choices that are supposed to impact the progress of the game, and the developers probably felt it would be wrong to rob the players of having a choice at the very end of the game. But everything leading up to the end shows that there should have been only one choice, the one that is emotionally not satisfactory : because all the preceding events and choices in the game served to advance Max's personal and emotional development, and not choosing the "sad" ending undoes all her supposed character growth.
Ultimately, I'm not sorry I played the game. I love that it puts the friendship between two teenage girls at the forefront, that it deals with themes not particularly popular in games (even if a lot of it is teenage drama), that it focuses on developing relationships between characters and encourages you to form an emotional bond with them.
However, right now the game has a 96% recommendation rate on Steam and I had to be a dissenting voice, because despite its intentions, it really is not *that* good.

Fallout Shelter is the best Bethesda-made (studio, not publisher) game since Fallout 3.
It's a simple, but rather polished idle game, based on managing a Vault from the Fallout titles.  There's three main resource productions to balance, Food, Water and Power, and then Caps is the currency for building stuff, with Nuke cola allowing you to skip wait times.
It's, at its core, a simple time-killer mobile game but that does not make it less enjoyable to play. The animations, personalization, theming and soundtrack are very well made, making you engage in one of those famous reward loops.

Time is the main gate to your progress, it is true that wait times can feel long occasionally, being this a title to be played in a "Pet Game" style, more so than some other idlers or city builders of the genre.
The game also offers the option to explore the wasteland, where you get a log of your pawn's progress delivered through their PipBoy, and the feature of quests, which add some very basic looting, combat and exploration mechanics, that are, however, rather fun to play.
I'd recommend investing some time in this if you are into this genre of games or are looking for a decent time waster.

I was concerned about buying this game due to all the negative reviews I saw and video reviews I watched but I finally decided to bite and buy the game.
I'm actually enjoying the game far more than I thought. Everyone seems to be hating on the story but I've been enjoying it for what it is, and not what it could be in terms of canon lore versus non-canon lore. I found running around the map finding lore-items that had small dialogues with some random tid-bit information on places and people of Middle-Earth quite enjoyable.
The gameplay so far is everything I wanted Shadow of Mordor to be, especially with the way time progresses. No longer do you have to pass time in order to get events to progress, instead now they progress as you complete other events which makes everything feel so much better.
I also hear a lot of rants about how the story is slow or mundane but I've put more time into completing the maps and the collectibles and other small goals that I make for myself and when I do follow the story it's really not so bad at all. The pacing feels fine though I should mention I'm not playing mission-to-mission but rather, taking the liberty to explore the maps and do what I mentioned earlier inbetween missions. So I might be experiencing the pacing a little different than others.
Lastly , ofcourse there's a lot of talk about the microtransactions. Having heard a lot about them I just ignored them until around the end of Act 2 (it took me about 20 hours of gameplay to get to this point) and yeah they're not so useful and you can get them for ingame currency (which I seem to have boatloads of) and premium currency. So far I only spent ingame currency and don't plan on buying any premium currency. However it needs to be stated you DON'T have to get the crates. It isn't pay to win. Everything from the crates you can just get from playing the game. Since it's singleplayer you don't really win by getting them either.
I also got a crate from some kind of vendetta mission and I also saw I can get some premium currency from a challenge so it seems to me like this isn't really a huge issue. Unless you want to look at it from a principle standpoint then sure I guess it's kinda messed up.
The negatives:
Feels like Shadow of Mordor because it basically is Shadow of Mordor but designed a bit better when it comes to combat and the sort. Don't expect some revolutionary gameplay because it's basically the same game but on a larger scale and with a few more additions that extend the amount of hours you can put into it.
Controls are a little better but I still get weird targeting from time to time where I want to takedown one grunt but somehow end up taking down a grunt that wasn't even in my vision due to targeting and don't even think about getting into a corner surrounded by Uruks as you'll get stomped while your camera is all sorts of messed up.
Despite the Celebrimbor side-missions being somewhat decent challenges they have no replayability once you beat them fully and the sub-objectives in them to achieve gold rank need to be more creative than just "finish within the time limit" as these just cause me to rush the hell out of the challenge where other more fun sub-objectives could be made instead. Poor design there in my opinion.
Should be said I haven't hit the "grind-wall" everyone talks about and will update accordingly. I did play Shadow of Mordor quite a bit after I completed the story so I can't say if I'll experience the same dislike for it.
Story-wise Talion is stale as ever but it's made up for by other characters having much better voice acting and character depth. However ignoring the non-canon idea behind Shelob I can't believe they overly sexualized her. I really don't see how it matches her characteristics as described by Tolkien. So not a fan of that choice.
Final: Yes I would get this game, even at the price it is now if you feel that you can afford it. If not, we all know it'll go on sale eventually as games do these days. The gameplay is still great and the story is decent enough but not amazing. If the microtransactions bother you, don't use them. You don't have to.
Get it during the sale if you're still not sure.

Huge fan of the first game, but can't really recommend this one.  For some reason it feels more like work than like a game, and I have a hard time putting my finger on why.  There are fun moments, like storming fotresses, but they're surrounded by stretches of tedium.
Anyways, here are the highlights of Shadow of Mordor:
✔️ CONQUERING FORTRESSES:  This is kind of like when you play an RTS and wish you could just be a soldier on the ground storming the castle.  Very much like the pre-launch video, except you're also capturing checkpoints with your orc buds.  Too bad this is only like 5% of the gameplay.
✔️ NEMESIS ORCS:  Dying to an orc really grinds your gears.  Dying twice to the same orc (because of the stupid no last chance trait) makes you want to throw a controller.  Sucks just as much as the first game. Well done.
✖️ CHARACTERS:  Could not be more bored with the main chars, who are predictably bland 1-dimensional tropes that really, REALLY make you hate the bajillion cutscenes.  The orcs with their 15 second intros were more interesting.
✖️ THE LORE:  As pretty much the only new content for LOTR right now, they really dropped the ball.  The giant Shelob spider is a sexy woman ghost?  You're a ranger defeating all 9 ring wraiths at once?  What's in scope for the next game, we falcon punch Mt. Doom into a puddle?
✖️ COLLECTIBLES:  Just... no.  I wouldn't even notice it if some of the upgrades weren't locked behind find all the lost spider memories or some other BS.
✖️ GRAPHICS:  It looks like they didn't really update these. Maybe they have high-res textures now or something, but it looks almost exactly like a game you'd play three years ago.
❌ MICROTRANSACTIONS:  So many times I play single player games and wish I could enter my CC number for cheat codes. /s  But seriously, this is your standard-fare skinner box complete with two funny-money currencies for obfuscation.  Which leads me to...
❌ BALANCE:  To me, this game feels like work.  In the first game, you were a dead ranger haunting the sh!t out of some orcs in Mordor.   That is fun.  Now you're stealth-killing eight archers to draw out the war lord so you can kill'em and remove the fortress gate reinforcement or something.  Wash, rinse, repeat five times.  This game feels less like a game and more like a check list.
❌ LOOT BOXES:  I understand loot boxes.  It's a good way to keep people from gaming multiplayer by preventing them from buying exactly what they want.  Kind of levels the playing field so the 2% of people who buy loot boxes can't get that far ahead of everyone else.  So WTF are they doing in single player?
❌ INVENTORY: I don't remember inventory being so annoying in the first game.  Now you need to destroy all the junk equipment you don't use so you can buy upgrades and crap when storming fortresses.  And why did you need to even add gems?  So you have another collectible to sell 'drop rate increase' boosters in the store?
SUMMARY:
In the original
, I feel like this developer took risks to make a new type of game that paid off as being unique and fun.  Now I feel like
took that original game and slapped on a new layer designed to cater to the 2% of people who pay for microtransactions in multiplayer.
And single player reflects this, because everything is designed to suck you into multiplayer.  There's no army management, just money sinks in defending your fortress against online players.  After you take a fortress, there's no reason to put resources into it since the computer is never going to take it back.
All in all, they've basically pivoted Shadow of Mordor into a multiplayer money pit.  Not recommended unless you get it deeply discounted.

I'm writing this review at the time of OB44. When there seems to be a large amount of community entitlement for making their game slightly more of a grind. Which they haven't. Not really. Not if you actually consider what this game is like, and how the currency actually operates.
They've added a tertiary currency; Essence. Which is used to buy cards for your loadouts. Essentially, this currency hs caused a great deal of moaning and groaning, and cries of "P2W!". But is it? No. Radiant Chests can now be bought with gems
gold. Gold is extremely easy to earn, and I personally think this game is one of the more "fair" titles out there for people who are on a budget and only able to play mostly F2P games. Within a few wins, you can unlock a new champion, or buy two or three Radiant Chests. Literally less than 10. The games aren't exactly long, either. Most won't generally run over 10-15 mins.
The purported "issue" is that grinding this essence is considered P2W because you can buy Radiant Chests with gems. When in reality, these chests bought with gems confer no extra RNG chance to the essence grind. You just don't have to play to earn them. That's it. Perhaps they increase the chance a little, like any card drop from any Radiant Chest would. Removing a card from the potential prizes pool, to replace it with an essence refund.
Most of the negative reviews you will see here are simply high level players, who have already opened all their levelling chests, who are boycotting the game because they feel they've been duped. They've lost 40+ free chests worth of potential essence.
Absolutely not. Don't let the salt put you off. Try it out, have some fun.

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a fantastic, epic spanning RPG, worthy of any PC Gamer’s eye.  Although the game is not without its fair share of technical blemishes Witcher 2 delivers a powerful punch to the player from the moment they click “Play”.  The atmosphere delivered in this title is very engrossing, and as such, Witcher 2 is able to pull the player in and never let go.  The graphics are superb, the art direction is creative and eye catching, and the writing is well delivered, never failing to entrench the player within the game’s vigorously delivered atmosphere.  Although challenging, The Witcher 2 is quite rewarding, delivering an experience like none other.  Most modern RPGs provide the player with two extremes, either absolutely satanic, or non-arguably angelic, and while these games tout their “you write your own story” technique, they fail in delivery.  This is where the Witcher 2 absolutely nails it.  I highly recommend this title.

While I'm a big fan of turn-based strategy games ala Jagged Alliance, Silent Storm, Fallout, etc, I can't recommend this game in its current state.
AI is such that enemies (unless equipped with a sniper rifle) will run straight up to your squad in order to inflict a to-hit penalty on your assault/sniper rifle squaddies, foregoing all cover on the way. This leads to repeated battles in which you move said squaddies 2 steps away, and kill said enemies effortlessly.
Skill points are useless after around level 30 (3/4 through the game), as your specialized squad will have their assigned skills capped, and any more spending only results in overlap.
There are still script/dialogue bugs to be fixed, as well as smaller issues such as items with grossly exaggerated weights.
There are also some poorly-thought out mechanics:
- "Lost Control" - NPCs that join you all have an inherent chance to go rogue, removing your ability to control them and imposing beeline-AI on their actions as described above.
- Leadership skill - gives nearby squaddies a small chance-to-hit bonus within a small area, and reduces the chance for hirees to go rogue within that small area. Move those hirees outside the magic circle, and you risk losing control of them. Exacerbated by melee/ranged.
- Animal Whisperer skill - you can tame animal companions... who don't have enough hp to survive one attack (and they will get attacked), and not only can you not control them, but some will attack, imposing beeline-AI as described above. The result? Expect any tamed companions to die in the next fight.
Shelved until major update.

Yargis – Space Melee is a space combat game with a lot of modes, but it all turns into little more than a jousting match between you and your foes. There’s a quick single player campaign that will teach you how to use the controls and show you just how frustrating it can be to do even the simplest things thanks to the game’s trust controls. You’re flying a space ship, so thrust is always important. You can go forward and strafe side-to-side, but your momentum will slam you into walls and enemies.
The controls seem relatively simple with rebindable keys. Thrust forward, space break, strafe, rotate with your mouse. There’s a button for a speed boost to get you out of a pinch or to break a planet’s gravitational pull. You can only shoot the direction you’re facing, so a lot of space jousting can devolve into butting ships together and hoping to destroy the other one first. Its dull, boring and thoughtless. There’s no grace or finesse to these controls and using a 360 controller is even worse. Even with key rebindings, the right thumb stick is always stuck to zoom in and out as well as thrust forward.
To the game’s credit the single player campaign offers a lot of variety. Death matches, defending planets, rescuing space cattle, collecting ships and dropping them into safe points. The problem is nothing is fun with the controls, even then some of the missions are laughably short and ridiculously easy. Of course if they were any tougher, the controls would be unbearable. It didn’t feel like there was that much enemy variety either and that would have made me feel like I was progressing through the campaign. For every mission you complete, you’ll earn experience and money.
Obviously the money goes to purchase ship parts, and the experience goes to your level which is needed to purchase the parts. You can’t just spend everything you have to get the best armor; the game carefully breaks things down with these leveled parts to ensure you’ll crawl up piece by piece. Different weapons do different things, a gattling gun will fire slower the longer you use it.
The game offers a few items that you can collect, everything from a star pool that acts like a shotgun blast, to health or even walls. I say walls, because walls will crop up in the level. The health is the most valuable out of all the items, but the real problem with the items is the key placement. Relying on four keys to use the items in your four inventory slots. With one hand on the mouse, and another on the arrows, its just difficult in a dog fight to make use of these items. When you use one, the others shift over accordingly. Perhaps the right mouse button would be better to use whatever is in the first inventory slot and shift them accordingly. Rebindable keys to the rescue I guess. Even getting the items in general is tough thanks to the thrust controls that make everything feel like its on ice. There’s no easy way to pull them into you, so you’re stuck relying on luck or moving so slow that you can’t miss them.
One of the major concerns that I have is gravitational pull of planets. It might not seem like a big deal, but it will cause you’re demise if you’re not careful. Under normal circumstances, you can speed boost to break orbit, but if you’re at a dead stop, no speed boost can help you. A death is a death and you have infinite tries for each mission, but it really becomes an issue on the mission select screen. There’s no smooth or easy way to select a mission, you need to fly to it and some of these missions are planets that will suck you in, but not destroy you. Instead, you’ll be asked over and over again to start a mission. Sometimes you won’t be able to break orbit, so then you’ll have to visit the menu and select mission select which respawns you at the start of the galaxy. You’ll then have to find the mission you were at and play it. If you go into the wrong mission, you’ll have to back out. It just feels like wasted time.
Outside of the single player campaign, the game boasts online play and it does have a robust set of modes: King of the Hill, Capture the Flag, Prison Break, Base Conquer (Co-Op), Maze Race (and CTF Maze) and Melee Battle, but the problem is at this price point, there’s no one playing and might never be. To prove it, the game has an intuitive server selection, which all online games should have, so I applause Yargis for that. You can even easily start your own server and have friends join. Its just that over the span of three weeks, I seemed to be the only person trying to play. You can even set up bots and while the maps have good multiplayer designs, its just a dull game to play even if the online has more action.
In multiplayer I noticed some of the bot ships are pitch black with no outline. Since the game is played in space with nothing but a black background, it would make them tough to see if it wasn’t for their health bar. So playing I’d shoot at the health bar.
As for the graphics and music, they feel like low quality. Not just bad, but compressed to make the game take up less file size at the cost of fidelity. I can hear hissing in the music. The music is lack luster and unfitting of a space game. Deep piano backgrounds coupled with the hiss makes me look for the music button, but no I endured it, because its part of the experience.
Also part of the experience is some of the worst voice acting that I’ve ever heard. While I applaud their effort, that doesn’t make it good and yes I’d much rather be listening to dialog than reading it. Oh but I assure you dialog boxes will still pop up obscuring twenty-percent of the screen even at the most inopportune moments. While the voice acting is laughably bad, they can stay, but the dialog boxes need to go. Nothing like being in a space battle, but having to steer off course to press “skip all.”
At the end of it all comes the root of all even and that’s the price tag. While I don’t make it a habit to hinder anyone from purchasing a game based on price, 15€ does seem a bit much for a game of this low quality. I can’t recommend it, because it doesn’t feel like there’s anything redeemable here that people will find fun or engaging.

Broken Age, is a retro-looking point-and-click adventure game, recently released by Double Fine Productions, and funded by Kickstarter backers. It is an absolute feast of an incredibly unique art design, with amazing soundtracks, and a great, great story. Divided into 2 parts, which both are included in price, one is currently available to play, and other one is in progress right now.
(This review is written for people who are familiar with the genre, and have some brief background knowledge about it. I recommend you to pass if you are unfamiliar, since I'll be refering to some classics and relating Broken Age's quality to them.)
I want to talk about the sounds of the game first, since it actually impresses me the most. As expected, Peter McConnell (He was responsible for soundtracks of many LucasArts and Double Fine Productions classics. Creator of that famous Monkey Island loop, pretty nice, eh?) did an amazing job on soundtracks, perfectly reflecting the spirits of places like Meriloft, Shellmound, Bossa Nostra, making you feel like you are actually there. It's one of the best game OST I've recently heard, along with Bastion, Transistor, Braid, and Thomas was Alone OST's. As for dialogues, what you'll encounter is beyond belief, as it was a Kickstarter funded game. Names like Elijah Wood and Jack Black are the voice actors, and they all have done an amazing job, also as expected. You may wonder like, "Where did they found all that money to pay them?", well, they actually didn't! Voice actors were making a huge pay-cut, willingly, just becaue they liked the game so much...
Lee Petty (He was also the art director of Brütal Legend.), working with Nathan Stapley (And he was the art director of Indiana Jones and the Infernal Machine, one of my first action-adventure games (and a pretty good one) after Tomb Raider.) did an absolutely gorgeous job for the visuals, that it's almost as amazing and unique as the art style of Curse of Monkey Island, which I personally consider as the peak of uniqueness. Such graphics will never get old, and will be considered great even after 30 years.
And Tim Schafer, founder of Double Fine Productions, creator of games like Full Throttle, Grim Fandango, Brütal Legend, The Secret of Monkey Island, Monkey Island 2: LeChuck's Revenge...well, I think we don't even need talk about him. An incredible talent, a total genius. A below-decent, and even an avarage story was out of question, all I've expected was pure amazingness, and he delivered just that! Bravo Tim...
Only problem with Broken Age is that, it is kind of too easy for someone familiar with this genre. Yet, it personally doesn't matter for me, since I'm not playing a point-and-click adventure for its ridiculously exaggeratively difficult puzzles (Not like I'm eliminating the ones which has that difficulty level. It just simply doesn't matter.), but for its fluent smart story with a good sense of humor. And, that's Broken Age!
In a nutshell, Double Fine did it again...
Buy this game, buy this game and play it!

Broken Age Act 1 was created by none other than the talented Tim Schafer and the Double Fine crew. This game is a point and click adventure telling the story between two characters seeking whats right for them. Broken Age has a neat feature of allowing the player to switch in between stories and start whichever tale they desire, quick note: it's recommended to just stay on one tale just so you won't forget the puzzle when you return to the next. As always for a Double Fine game, the voice acting is good to catch along with while the suitable soundtrack helps bring life to this Art filled game. It's hilarious even hearing some of your favorite voice actors being featured in this title ( i'm talking about you Jack Black and Richard Horrvits ).
Another side note is that the dialogue with some characters can be a bit unhelpful, i would try to ask as many questions as i can get for better clues of an item i'll need, even though i'll usually just have to ask 2 or more. Honestly this game is incredible in every way, it is pretty pricey but if it's ever on special defiantly download it.

Do
buy this game.
Let me tell you why by first telling you what this game does right. Firstly, the nemesis system is fun. I loved killing an orc, even slicing them in half and them come back as such-n-such the stitched. Was interesting, dynamic, and I think more games need to adopt a similar system.
Pit fighting, also fun. Though after so many, you know what beats what and the surprise is taken out of it. Not all of the orc classes are balanced in pit fighting. Beast masters for example. They could have "epic skill: call graug" or "den mother" but never use it. Also, caragor mounts made pit fighting very dull. Half the time the orc would ride around in a big circle, while gangs fought gangs, and do nothing till every minion was dead.
I (unlike some) did enjoy the story. I know it's kind of dumb; certain aspects. I just liked it. Until it died at the end, which is where this review comes to the "do not buy this" section.
Act IV - The Shadow Wars
Sounds cool af right? Wrong. It may as well be named, "Act IV: Grind your @ss off with no more story or dialogue sans random orc encounters, OR pop out the wallets and buy your way to a half-@ssed cutscene.
They say the store and lootboxes aren't "necessary". They aren't lying, but they aren't being truthful either. The last act of the game is set up in such a way that it blatantly incentivizes purchasing. Because unless you do, then your only other option is to grind and grind and GRIND to get the orcs needed to defend/retake your fortresses.
Then, you have 10 stages. 20 fortress defenses. All of which play out the same. Kill siege beasts, kill warchiefs, your army either keeps bleeding and dying due to you not having the best orcs or best defenses, or they sit and jerk off inside impenetrable walls. Leaving you to hop down solo to kill a bit, climb back in for arrows and health, and repeat the process. 20 times....
It is so boring, and so disconnected from the flow of the first 3 acts, you feel as if it isn't the game you have been playing for 100+ hrs. It FEELS like a game+ mode, where you beat the game and then get the chance to screw around in the world for as long as you want.
I have to add a spoiler section for those that think they are gonna miss something by not playing this. Or ones not entirely convinced by the top reasons. So here goes.
You as Talion, with Celebrimbor, forge a new ring as powerful as Saurons. You then go on a nice journery of doing things. Not gonna spoil everything. You meet characters that literally have no relevance at the end. Humans that just up an leave like you never existed. A tree spirit that has the most interesting story, but disappears once you complete it. Then an elf assassin that has a big part to play in TWO scenes, and then you never know what happens to her.
Ratbag and Ranger, two orcs/olog are like your main story subbordinates but you never actually get to add them to the ranks of your army. Dumb. Bruz betrays you for no reason other than to betray you and show you it can happen. Felt forced.
Then...THEN, final battle time (or so you think, cause stupid Act IV comes after) you go to attack Baradur. To attack Sauron. Celebrimbor betrays you, gives the new ring to the elf assassin. You hate them both, want to kill them both. But guess what? You never get to interact with them again. Instead, you become a ring wraith, have a nice fight with the Witch King, take over Minas Morgal. Then Celebrimbor and Elf Assassin chick fight Sauron, they lose. Celebrimbor gets absorbed into Sauron and they say there is an internal war between them. Dunno. Never shows it, never get to find anything out.
Talion grinds with no story for about 20 hrs to fight 20 sieges, then it shows a recap of the LOTR movies where they add in Talions face on a wraith dragon, and show a light - presumably celebrimbor's spirit flying out of a dying sauron into mount doom. Whatever happens to the second ring and the elf assassin, no one knows. You just get a cut scene of Talion tossing his armor and weapons into a field, and walking off into the sunset.
Totally not worth the grind and all the money one has to put into it.
First 3 acts are fun. I enjoyed them. Last act and ending are BS though.
So I repeat, do NOT buy the game. Not worth it. Get it at a discount if anything.
Lot of potential squandered on trying to incentivize a loot box system.

If you want to play a game that starts like your typical high school drama crap and then evolves into something that really makes you rethink your life choices, ponder on problems that people around us have, and possibly even shed a tear (or cry your♥♥♥♥♥off, depending on how sensitive you are), then Life is Strange is your game. Download the free episode, give it a try, you've got nothing to lose.
Now, Life is Strange is not your typical adventure game so don't expect it to be one. Here, the primary gameplay mechanic is the protagonist's ability to manipulate time, while the remaining ones, including conversations, plot choices, puzzle-solving, and item-collecting, are subject to it. To be honest, it didn't took a lot of effort to beat everything this game threw at me, and when I actually had trouble making progress, I was either offered an easier alternative or straight up told what to do. And that's fine by me because Life is Strange is about choice and consequence, but not in that terrible, pretentious BioWare style. What I love about this game is that if you feel like you messed something up, you can seamlessly go back in time and do stuff differently -- something you don't get to do in real life. Obviously, some of your actions will have reactions in the future and are not that easy to fix. However, should you REALLY f*ck up and feel horrible about it, you can always restart the game from any major plot point and do things differently. Yes, this is sort of save-scumming but hey, I get enough drama and regrets in real life. Plus, in the end, you don't get to eat a cookie and have a cookie in Life is Strange, so you cannot make a perfect playthrough because there simply isn't one.
Life is Strange may be somewhat interactive-movieish, and it is to a large extent, but the amazing story and its characters make up for it if this is a problem with you. I'd easily recommend this game to the fans of all kinds of story-driven games.
Life is Strange is totally a 9,5/10 in my books. It does have poor voice acting and writing at some (though few) points, lip sync issues, and a bug or two but ultimately delivers one hell of an emotional ride with great plot twists and memorable characters. No doubt one of the best games I've played and a one that entered my personal hall of fame among such amazing masterpieces as Planescape: Torment, Neverwinter Nights 2: Mask of the Betrayer, Deus Ex series, Mass Effect series, and The Witcher series. I salute and thank the developers at Dontnod for this amazing experience that indeed happened at a very strange moment in my life.

Yargis is an old styled action space shooter. You meet the world of Yargis in front of the conflict and you're the only one who can sort it out.
You start the game as a beginner and learn how to control the ship and guns :) Your main task is to flight from the space and fight with the enemies. Throughout the missions you're challenged with flying through labirynths and completing the objectives in certain missions. It's not always about eliminating enemies, but sometimes you need to collect parts or survive the level. The levels in the Story mode are not very difficult but you need to upgrade your ship by buying new guns or armor from the money earned by completing levels. The offline mode is a little bit more challenging so you need to care about upgrades more than in story mode. It was designed to be the training mode for multiplayer so it's obvious.
I really enjoyed how the ships are controlled. At first I had some troubles with discovering how to brake the ship but the Space button on KB is really helpful. The way how the ships are behaving is really nice and feels realistic. For example if you fly close to planet, your ship is affected by it's gravity. Therefore if the planet grabs your ship, you need to use boost to counter the force of planet's gravity. I was very satisfied with the graphics. The details of space and planets are really fantastic.

I backed Wasteland 2 as soon as it was announced on Kickstarter, so I was pretty excited when the game finally released after following it for so long.  Wasteland 2 is a large CRPG set in a post apocalypse world.  The game is amazing from beginning to end and I enjoyed every moment, but it is not without faults.
The character creation is brilliant and let's you create a diverse group of people to start your adventure off with.  The first thing to realize is that Wasteland 2 is not a game where you control a lone wolf, it is a party based game where you have a team with each person having their different uses.  You have a lot of skills and attributes to choose from which help you out along the way.  You use computer skills to hack doors, reprogram robots, and access computers.  Lock picking picks locks, dialogue skills like smart♥♥♥♥♥and kiss♥♥♥♥♥open different avenues of dialogue, perception allows you to notice things you normally wouldn't, animal whisperer lets you manipulate or get assistance from animals, and so on.  You have weapon skills so if you give a character points in bladed weapons, you cannot just give them an energy weapon and expect them to be accurate with it.  One thing I was not expecting was how important some skills would be, like medic or surgeon.  While I knew having a medic or surgeon would be important, I figured there would be items to compensate somewhat but that just is not the case.  Without the proper skills you will be watching a party member bleed out pretty early in the game, and there is only one item you can use to restore health without a medic which would get expensive very quickly.
The biggest problem with the party/team/characters is that I really felt no connection to them during regular gameplay.  They felt like an assortment of tools I used to complete the objectives, which kind of sucks considering that I rather enjoyed creating them and thought I would become more attached.  The only time I felt a connection was during combat where they each had their specific jobs that made them feel like more than a collection of skills.  Combat is done through a pretty simple turn-based setup, where the order of turns is displayed on the top of the screen, and action points and costs detailed when required.  Action points are what you use to shoot, heal party members, use skills, and move around the map, and they are in short supply so you have to be careful how you use them.  Thankfully killing things is a lot of fun, because there is a LOT of things to kill.  Like I said before, combat is simple, but it's just complicated enough to create tension, and fun where it needs to be.
The atmosphere is wonderful, and had enough character that I never really got bored of traveling in a desert where most everything looked the same, and when I just started getting bored of that the game takes a big turn and you end up in wildly different areas.  There was a whole lot of story and dialogue which I rather enjoyed.  There is a lot of people and story you can miss out on though by not visiting every nook and cranny which makes the game a completetionist's nightmare, but it's fun nonetheless.  The thing that surprises a lot of people is that despite the grim setting and horror all around you, the story can be pretty playful at times with enough dark humor and offbeat jokes to keep me wanting more.
Despite the few glaring negatives the game felt really good, was a lot of fun, and I really recommend playing it.  I plan on playing Wasteland 2 again very soon so I can explore the things I missed, and I will definitely be playing it a lot more once the mod tools are released.

I'm writing this review at the time of OB44. When there seems to be a large amount of community entitlement for making their game slightly more of a grind. Which they haven't. Not really. Not if you actually consider what this game is like, and how the currency actually operates.
They've added a tertiary currency; Essence. Which is used to buy cards for your loadouts. Essentially, this currency hs caused a great deal of moaning and groaning, and cries of "P2W!". But is it? No. Radiant Chests can now be bought with gems
gold. Gold is extremely easy to earn, and I personally think this game is one of the more "fair" titles out there for people who are on a budget and only able to play mostly F2P games. Within a few wins, you can unlock a new champion, or buy two or three Radiant Chests. Literally less than 10. The games aren't exactly long, either. Most won't generally run over 10-15 mins.
The purported "issue" is that grinding this essence is considered P2W because you can buy Radiant Chests with gems. When in reality, these chests bought with gems confer no extra RNG chance to the essence grind. You just don't have to play to earn them. That's it. Perhaps they increase the chance a little, like any card drop from any Radiant Chest would. Removing a card from the potential prizes pool, to replace it with an essence refund.
Most of the negative reviews you will see here are simply high level players, who have already opened all their levelling chests, who are boycotting the game because they feel they've been duped. They've lost 40+ free chests worth of potential essence.
Absolutely not. Don't let the salt put you off. Try it out, have some fun.

To say that this game is unrefined is like to say that rule of Adolf Hitler raised certain controversy. You are not wrong but description does seem a little lacking.
Where to even begin? Legends of Persia is a hack’n’slash game by Iranian developer Sourena Game Studio creators of titles such as… Wobbly Jungle and that’s it as far as Steam is concerned. Legends of Persia allows you to embody persona of a Persian Paladin (which is puzzling enough in itself). Who are you precisely is a mystery because story is a haphazard nonsense, mostly devoid of any “cause and effect” connection. Cutscenes constantly introduce new characters and threads, leaving most of them unresolved, making the whole thing confusing in the absolute least. So the player is left stranded without clear motivation or objective, probably asking themselves why are they even playing this.
Every aspect of the game is a mess. Gameplay goes down to running from one monster to another and holding down right mouse button until it dies. Process is occasionally interrupted by a skill activation and potion consumption. What might seem as remarkably crude description of hack’n’slash genre in case of Legends of Persia is left without any finesse most of its competitors hint. Fighting system lacks any form of complexity or balance. You cannot dodge and majority of skills have unjustly long cooldowns. Character development fails to visibly alter gameplay since it doesn’t affect skills and all equipment is available for pickup at any time regardless of skillset. What may seem curious, different movement animations (comparably wooden) of 3 avatars to choose from, results in one character either move or attack noticeably faster than the other.
Most of the game you fight against 5-6 different enemies regardless of whether you are protecting peasants’ fields from monsters or conducting a war against opposing nation’s soldiers. It’s still the same skeleton archers. Furthermore item drops appear to be fixed, meaning that every playthrough specific mob will drop exactly identical item on death every time. Introduction of more powerful items and stronger enemies later in the game is probably the only sign of progression.
All of the above at best dubious development choices were parts of the game that were meant to be. But there is much more to it for it has all kinds of lovely bugs and they are numerous. I brought myself to beat the game twice which took me roughly 5 hours and in the meantime I experienced enemies losing textures on hit, mobs getting stuck on thin air, sound missing after loading, a few crashes and my personal best: during my run with permadeath mode on I suddenly turned invulnerable after entering the village halfway through the second level of the game. Changing level, nor restarting the game affected this state and since autosave on checkpoint is the only option available, there I was stuck with being immortal for the rest of the “hardmode”. Convenient.
Game is riddled with a number of flatout mistakes too. Wrong spelling in item descriptions, persistent use of continuous tense in objectives, mixed soldout health and mana potion notifications and I could carry on but all of the above truly suffice to make the point.
The point being that there is no redeeming quality about this game. It’s plain horrible and there is no reason to ever come into possession of it, in any other way than as a mandatory part of some bundle. Legends of Persia is gaming equivalent of an african action movie and some, of peculiar taste, might find it “so bad that it is good”. I have to admit that playing it does put things into perspective and leaves me wondering how in the wake of fierce competition of modern gaming industry such oddities come to be.

I've been struggling to write a review about Life is Strange for weeks, because I have a lot of conflicting feelings about it. I hate the main protagonist Max, but I love her friend Chloe. I hate the awful pacing of the last episode and the unskippable dialogue, but I love that it's a slow game that invites you to take your time and spend it observing and listening, instead of rushing from action scene to action scene like many other games. And I hate to give a Not Recommended rating to this game, because I love it for what it tries to do, but it just has too many flaws to overlook. Poor quality animation being the most obvious one from the start.
The clunky body animations are not so bad compared to an almost complete lack of facial animations (in some scenes the devs even forgot to animate the lips of the character who is speaking). For a game that relies on building an emotional connection to its characters, it fails so many times due to complete disassociation between the emotions conveyed through voice acting and the blankness of facial animations. Which is why the game resorts to pointing out people's emotional states in dialogue so often. However, after a while, hearing people comment on how Max's face looks "so intense" or similar just draws attention to the shortcomings of the game's animations instead of informing the player of the protagonist's state of mind.
The main protagonist's voice actress is another problem. There are so many scenes where her lines are delivered completely flatly, with as much expressiveness as reading a label off of a shampoo bottle. I get that the developers wanted someone a bit less expressive, because Max is supposed to be a very shy girl (furthermore, her character is less developed in order to allow the player to better identify with her), but I found the voice actress boring just too many times.
Poor animation and voice acting are the main objective reasons why I had trouble relating to the characters. Theme is another, and much more subjective one. If you are not the kind of person who enjoys TV shows or movies about teen drama, you will, like me, dislike *a lot* of this game. I understand that this is not the game's failing, but I simply could not get into it at all. Particularly since I found the game's treatment of certain serious topics, like bullying, to be kind of poor, with the bullying issue glossed over as no-one faces any consequences.
Then there's the writing. The game feels like the product of many writers, not all of whom are equally skilled at writing dialogue. A lot of time the dialogue feels like it's missing bits and pieces in between as characters jump to conclusions based on a sentence or two they are told. (Like in the last episode when Max tells Warren about her time rewind power and he immediately concludes that what she will do next will be "the most important moment in history".) Or the many times where characters heap praise on each other for supposedly being extraordinary, sympathetic, amazing artists, or whatever. It sounds melodramatic and insincere. Things like this might have been written with the idea of depicting teenagers as being overly dramatic or hyperbolic, but it just sounds like normal people would not speak like that.
The unskippable dialogue is another massive problem I have with the game. The only time the player can skip dialogue is when they rewind time and re-attempt dialogue with new information. Restarting from last checkpoint or replaying on another save file will not let you skip dialogue. I am baffled by this design choice. Did the developers of this game not expect people to replay it?
This is the one thing that I probably hate the most about the game, because otherwise I would probably replay it to see how the story develops if I make different choices. But I just don't have the patience to listen to all of it again.
Another thing that was a stupid design choice was forcing a set number of achievements for every episode. Achievements are obtained by taking photos, but due to the structure and events of the last episode, there's not much "downtime" where achievements could be added, and so the photo taking opportunities were put into certain intense situations where stopping to pursue an achievement pulls you out what is happening in the game. This happens at a couple of crucial points when Max is doing something urgent or when the game is trying to impart a message about Max's state of mind, and it breaks the immersion.
[Spoiler warning: some spoilers ahead]
And finally, my biggest gripe: the last episode. The last episode is a mess and the pacing is all over the place, with the first half an hour being almost nothing but exposition that requires almost no input from the player. (Bring popcorn so you have something to do with your hands.) The exposition is followed by an alternate timeline, after we have already established in an earlier episode that these don't work out. Then follows a nightmare sequence in which certain locations from earlier in the game are revisited but are distorted and a new type of gameplay is very briefly introduced focused on evading enemies. And then the episode ends. The player is offered two choices on how to end the game: one choice is emotionally not satisfactory, and the other is wrong. It is obviously wrong because the developers didn't actually bother to make an ending for it. The sole reason this choice is there is because the entire game is about making various (albeit not important in the grand scheme of things) choices that are supposed to impact the progress of the game, and the developers probably felt it would be wrong to rob the players of having a choice at the very end of the game. But everything leading up to the end shows that there should have been only one choice, the one that is emotionally not satisfactory : because all the preceding events and choices in the game served to advance Max's personal and emotional development, and not choosing the "sad" ending undoes all her supposed character growth.
Ultimately, I'm not sorry I played the game. I love that it puts the friendship between two teenage girls at the forefront, that it deals with themes not particularly popular in games (even if a lot of it is teenage drama), that it focuses on developing relationships between characters and encourages you to form an emotional bond with them.
However, right now the game has a 96% recommendation rate on Steam and I had to be a dissenting voice, because despite its intentions, it really is not *that* good.

I would first like to start out by saying that Butterscotch Shenanigans has quickly become one of my favorite video game producers to date. It is made up of three brothers that have shared their life story of their interest in video game design in their brief documentary called Dev Diary, which I highly recommend.
This is a group that knows how to make games, simply put. The combination of strong story-telling, logical game structure, and just the right amount of humor and wit makes any game they create a masterpiece in my eyes.
Now to Crashlands:
Crashlands is a Survival Action RPG with elements of Terraria's complexity, Don't Starve's play style, and the kind of awesome creativity that only Indie game producers have.
You play as Flux Dabes, an intergallactic shipment shipper who, after having her ship destroyed by a megolomaniacal alien by the name of Hewgodooko, finds herself stranded, along with her trusty robot sidekick, JuiceBox, on a planet called Woanope. Here, she must use here intuition and stick-to-it-iveness to fight, craft, and build her way back to the Bureau of Shipping to get her packages delivered!
One of my favorite parts of Crashlands is the combined elements of both RPG and Survival. As you traverse the alien planet, you will find numerous quest givers that are in dire need of your help, in return for a small reward, of course. Completing different quests allows you to craft new and more powerful items. This allows you to explore new areas, defeat new creatues, and climb up the seemingly never-ending tech tree towards victory.
TL;DR
If you like good games, good art style, good story, a good challenge, or even just good-old-fashioned fun, buy Crashlands. It is completely worth it.

This game really takes me back when i was just a kid and my dad had dumped a big pile of dirt in our back yard for me to play in. I had all sorts of little toy trucks and hotwheel cars and i would just sit in that dirt pile all day playing with my trucks and even pouring water in it to make small streams and mud. Holy crap this game is like the super advanced version of that! The terrain deformation is fantastic. I really appreciate stuff like that especially when it's well done. I have been following the developement of this game for about a year now and i am very happy with where it is at right now.
Pretty much all of the trucks are Russian based. That's cool, i can live with that although it would have been cool to see some German, Japanese, or even American trucks but then again that's what the modding community is for. The vehicle models are very well done and very detailed. The tire deformation is VERY impressive also. Pretty much everything that needed attention to detail was given. Nothing was overlooked in my opinion as even the environments are very pretty (for mostly bieng mud).

The camera...eh...well it's generally agreed that the camera sucks. I really don't think it's that bad although i play this game with an Xbox controller and controlling the camera using an analouge stick is MUCH easier than using a twitchy mouse. Now controller support is pretty good. Everything works and the developers were even nice enough to add vibration support which i personally appreciate very much. It just adds a more satisfying feel when you shift down into first and feel the engine vibrate in your hands as if you were feeling it through the steering wheel in the truck. Well, it's not THAT immersive it's still a nice bonus that i wasn't expecting.

Performance wise the game seems very well optimised. I have the visual settings cranked all the way up and my computer doesn't even seem to be breaking a sweat. I am sure lower end PC's should have no problem running this game at lower resolutions.

Multiplayer is pretty well done actually. Although you are to 4 people per map i don't think that's a huge limitation. My biggest gripe with multiplayer is that you can't save your game. To be honest i'm not sure how they would even to be able to do that in the first place so i can't blame them for not having the ability to save. It's still something that is to be desired and maybe sometime in the future we will have that ability (although i doubt it). Oh, and most people online that i meet only speak Russian. That is a little annoying when i want to communicate with other players. I wish there was a region option where i could select which country of people i would like to play with. Nothing againt Russian speakers, i am sure they would prefer to play with people who could communicate with them as well. This really isn't as big of a problem am i am making it out to be though. As most people will probably be playing online with their close friends using skype or teamspeak. Single player is just like multiplayer except you are by yourself...obviously. Single player is fun it just takes longer to get things done.
That's really all i have to say about Spintires right now. I only have about 11 hours logged into it and i will update if anything changes.

I was excited for this game. I loved the first two, replayed Mafia 2 a few times, when they announced the third one, I was heavily excited. I was skeptical of course, a brand new studio working on this, despite drawing established people from other studios was still a tough pill to swallow, but I followed the game. The amount of pre-release videos drew me in, normally there was never that much pre-release gameplay shown so I figured the game would be alright. Boy was I wrong
It's obvious from the moment you enter the menus that this is a console port. I was expecting this but what I wasn't expecting was the general lack of care and polish put into the PC version. Options menu is pretty barren with very little options, not even a texture quality selection. Audio options are standard but not a big issue. Controls are where I have an issue. Rebinding is not great, and is one area where it's apparent it's a substandard port. A lot of pc players have mice that have more buttons and yet the game doesn't recognize these, can't rebind anything to them. Can't rebind any actions to clicking the mouse button either. You can always tell if a developer put effort into the pc port by the options menu and it is heavily apparent, they did not.
Now, onto the game. First off, when you change your resolution, it uses upscaling, instead of putting in the effort to make  proper options, they went the lazy route. Texture quality is crap and they intentionally hide this via blur effects.Graphics are crap, even on what they consider max settings, changing graphics options does nothing, fairly impressive PCs are struggling to hit 30fps, frakking 30!! That shouldn't happen on a game that looks this bad.
Now the sad part is, this game could be good. The gunplay is satisfying, driving can be fun, and the story is really damn good. But, I don't know whether this was developer laziness or whether the publisher imposed deadlines on them that required corners cut, all I know is that the first game out of Hanger 13 is not great at this point in time.

The first game held my attention long enough for me to beat it. Let see if the sequel surpass it.
Story:
You play as Talion, a ranger risen from the dead who took revenge on the Black Hand of Sauron in the first game. With the elf spirit, Celebrimbor, you forge a new ring to destroy Sauron once and for all.
Lore wise, it not the friendlies game since it take a lot of liberties to bridge the gap between the Hobbits and the Lord of the Ring. After all Shelob, you know the giant spider that tried to eat Froddo, takes the form of a woman and is given a more tragic fall from grace. It just feel strange, and I'm not even a huge fan of the lore and I can tell they take liberties with it. But despite that, I found the story more entertaining then it was in the last game. But it may be because they used so many recognizable characters and creatures than they did in the last game.
Gameplay:
If you ever played the previous game then you know what you're getting. This is a 3D open world with a combat element similar to games like Arkham series. You have your attack and a counter button. These are you bread and butter of combat. Counter incoming attack, and attack them back. The combat was tight in the last game and feel the same in this game.
There is also a nemesis system. Basically you have the ability to bring enemy orcs to your side. Orcs captains have unique strengths weaknesses  and you want to get some of the best on your side and pair them up to assassinate or fight those who have weaknesses to their strength. This is the real fun of the game. You get so many stories of Orcs captain who you've defeated, or possibly killed, returning to get vengeance on you. It really fun and memorable to be traveling when suddenly you ambushed by the blood brother of a Orc you killed. You call one of captain to help you and he betray you and then suddenly when you feel that all hope is lost another Orc shows up to help you out. These moments really make this game shine. Combine this system with the ability to lay siege and take enemy fortress and you got a fun time.
Now this game have one huge weakness is the loot boxes. Now before people start lighting up torches, the loot boxes are not need to complete this game. And frankly I went through most of the game without ever even touching them. Basically you can buy loot boxes with in game money or real money to give yourself better gear or even better Orc captains. Really this feature could have been left out of the game and I would have never even noticed. This feature only really become a nuisance toward the last act of the game when you get to a grindy part of the game. You're force to defend your fortress from multiple sieges and these enemy armies don't have push over Orc captains. And if you haven't been leveling up your Orcs, you may find quite of a few of them dying during the siege.
Final Comments:
This game would easily be a 9/10 game for me. But the loot boxes when combine with a final act that almost seem to encourage pay-to-win mentality just don't sit right with me. The final act take the feature I love about the game, sieges, and put me through siege after siege after siege after siege. It just get tedious. Too much of anything can become a nuisance real soon and that what happen in the final act. All in all Shadow Of War is a great sequel but is under siege from loot boxes and repetitive final act.

I recommend when you install this FSX, that you make it a clean install making sure that you removed all the left-overs or remnants of the (Boxed) FSX, if you had one; this includes cleaning up the Registry. Not doing so could run you into working problems with some of your (Boxed) FSX addons. This happens because FSX:SE was re-designed to work in dual with the older (Boxed) version if chosen to, and this causes the install program to name the FSX:SE folders to FSX:SE rather than FSX, and this is where problems can occur.
Go for it and get this newer version, I think you will be satisfied as I am. Since I moved over their have been two updates; which happens automatically when you boot-up your computer.

I've poured hundreds of hours into this game on other platforms and all I can really say about the Steam release is, "Why now?"
At first, the game seems fun. It's very new, still got that new car smell, and you're figuring out all the features. Once you've hit 100 dwellers and created all the rooms, you still want to snag all the achievements, right? So now you're building multiple skill-up rooms, more living quarters, more Nuka-Cola rooms, more power plants. You're still interested at this point, but you're losing it slowly. You've now found a routine, where you hop on the game for short moments at a time now. You complete the skill-ups that are waiting, you send some dwellers out for a quest. Your interest is still slowly dropping, but you're invested in it enough to continue playing at least once or twice a day for about five minutes at a time, not including quest time. At this point, you realize how inconvenient the game has become. You're still trying to finish each session more quickly with each passing day. You're a busy person, you have other, better games to play, but you dropped some money on this game months ago and you don't want that money to go to waste now, do you? Only now you really do know just how inconvenient the game is since you've been trying to only get in a few minutes at a time each session. Every time you log into the game, you're now trying to complete your tasks as quickly as possible in order avoid the elephant in the room. You've finished your task, you're hitting the Save option and you're about to exit the game when it finally happens: Random deathclaw attacks.
You say to yourself, "You kidding me? I was a half a second short from exiting the game and doing anything else and NOW I need to spend another 5 - 6 minutes here to deal with this crap?" I mean, you need to kill the deathclaws at some point. You could just go ahead and quit the game, but they'll still be there inside your vault when you log back on, so you might as well keep playing to make sure your dwellers aren't killed.
That's pretty much how I feel about this game right now. Just one more inconvenience, but I'm invested, I spent the time and the money, so I might as well keep playing so I can at least get my money/time's worth.

In my honest opinion, I don't know if this is a popular opinion here, but I believe the BEST version of this game is the Windows 10 version for two reasons.
The Windows 10 version included gamepad support (only handy if you're on a laptop and don't have a mouse) and it included Xbox Play Anywhere. Xbox Play Anywhere is a feature on the Windows 10 version that allows your save data to be shared in the cloud with your Xbox Live account so that you can play the game on your Windows 10 desktop or laptop and take your save data with you to your Xbox One console, hence the gamepad support. There aren't too many times when I'm playing the Xbox One instead of the PC version, but this also allows me to take my save data with me from my desktop to my laptop. For this very reason, I'm NOT leaving a positive review for the Steam version.
If you don't need the additional Windows 10 features, or you just can't stand the thought of using UWP games (how dare they, I know) or you've never played Fallout Shelter before, then by all means, check out the Steam version. Just keep in mind the inconveniences of this game. Again, I don't know why it took so long to bring this to Steam. This was the only game I even booted up the Bethesda Launcher for. =/

Edit after a few more hours of play
Backed on Kickstarter with BG2 nostalgia. Too much of a mixed bag for me.
- Writing, atmosphere and emotional engagement
Let's be clear, that's why we're here. Boy have I missed playing a squad of lively characters with believable, coherent personalities (yeah I'm looking at you Bethesda). You start with 4 PCs and can have 3 NPCs at a time. The writing is good but very unequal from zone to zone, sometimes great, sometimes annoying.
- Strategy, tactics and intellectual engagement
Tactics are OK but get boring quite quickly. More complexity and diversity would have been nice, like with expanded science/crafting/mechanics skills and lots of consumables and craftable devices to adapt to each encounter (to have something akin to the wizards in BG2).
Strategy is annoying. Your choices are too uninformed early on ; for me the beginning was very hard whereas it got too easy after I got the mechanics. Non-combat skills are universally unnerving. They are designed so that you can only get a fraction of the game per playthrough, unless you save and reload a lot, so you are left to pick between playing the game 15 times or reloading all the time.
- Design and engineering
I haven't played the beta. The game is fluid and bug free on my 64-bit Ubuntu rig (still looking at you Bethesda). I initially had 1 glitch in 40 hours, but then there was a bug that made me lose 4 hours of play and that's kind of a dealbreaker for me. Loading times could have been faster, and the UI could have been better (more visible highlight mode, unified and codified representation of possible interactions (wasted one real-life hour in highpool because the highlighting of the Surgeon skill is different form that of Disarm), a panel with all the skills from everybody ...).
- Graphics
Let's be clear, that's not why we're here. Isometric 3D works for me, other than that, don't care. Sometimes it's too 3D : stuff gets in the way and it's hard to click where you want (whatever).
- Sound
Music OK but not memorable - would have loved some epic music. Voice acting sometimes dull, sometimes great, sometimes non-existent.

The AI is replete with bugs and are highly inconsistent, making most tactical decisions irrelevant. Sheer firepower is the only thing that gets you through the firefights. Your sniper can be crouching in an elevated position and blocking the only way up, and the enemy WILL run the equivalent of 30 odd action points to circle the position just to stand beside your sniper. Likewise the AI npc follower WILL make the same circuit just to stand in front of the enemy to die. Doesn't help that the AI followers have 1 or 2 bullet shot's worth of hp and can't be healed. Even under normal circumstances depending on the AI's whim and fancy they ocassionally develop a sudden ability to produce more ability points than otherwise deemed possible so that they can come and hug your characters in a loving embrace. The AI npc inconsistency has the potential to utterly ruin your attempt for a perfect quest clearance for at least one of the compulsory quests.
There's a general lack of ammunition and medipack drops at the start of the game, so each encounter has to be carefully planned and executed. Unfortunately, in the early parts of the game, much of the available ammunition can only be found in locked/trapped safes/chests/boxes, which require a significant investment into the necessary non combat skills, which affects the distribution of limited stat points for combat skills, further wasting limited ammunition. Not a bad thing in itself, but would require careful planning.
A corollary to the above is, on the long run characters starting with high intel and charm will significantly outstrip all other characters in every single way. One of the earliest followers you can get is characteristic of this. Low intelligence results in inadequate points to spread amongst auxiliary abilities, which results in bombs exploding, locks breaking, alarms ringing, bone fractures, skipped conversation choices and blue screens of death, and crucially, low supplies.
Other than this, an excellent, excellent game. The story is brilliant and the choices you make in the game have implications and depth, though a number are more akin to morally abstract implications.
P.S. There is a hidden choice at the start of the game, though it makes your playthrough a little harder than the standard choices. And remember to pick up the damned shovel.

There's really no polite way to put it.  This game is horrible.  Which is a pity because it almost wasn't.
It would be possible to overlook the Dungeon Siege 1 era graphics, the generic, repetitive music and even the shoddy user interface if the game-play was good.
But the game-play is not good.  It's buggy and derivative.
Straight off the bat the first achievement I got was for killing the second boss.  The first boss never appeared.
It doesn't seem to be possible to transition back to previous locations which is a problem because that means one can't ever go back to the merchant to buy more potions.  Or sell the huge amount of cruft that gets picked up (assuming you can find the tiny off-center click point to pick up objects).
This is practically game ending because there are no real save points.  The restart point of an area could be after a merchant.  If you didn't have the gold to buy health potions.  Or simply didn't realise the difficulty was going to ramp up then that's it.  You're done.  You will not have enough health to continue.
Compounding the poor object picking - including clicking enemies - is that walking seems to work erratically.  Generally holding down the left mouse button makes the character walk but sometimes no amount of releasing and clicking will get them to move.  It's minor but adds up to be quite annoying.
The combat.  The combat is really all there is to Legends of Persia and it is it's major flaw.  Slow attack animations with no ability to doge makes for boring ping-pong sessions of sword play.  It's a game of attrition as you hold down the right mouse button.  And press 1 occasionally if you've upgraded stun (stun being the only useful upgrade).
The sound effects are either very muted or just don't exist.  They added nothing to the game and music is only slightly better.
The user interface is a mess.  Different fonts.  Text not sitting in windows.  Items getting stuck to the mouse cursor in the inventory.  The truly enormous warning message text.
Legends of Persia feels like the developer was told about Diablo 1 but had never played a game before coding it.  It's boring, repetitive and makes amateur mistakes that should have been simple to fix. Seriously, avoid.

I was excited for this game. I loved the first two, replayed Mafia 2 a few times, when they announced the third one, I was heavily excited. I was skeptical of course, a brand new studio working on this, despite drawing established people from other studios was still a tough pill to swallow, but I followed the game. The amount of pre-release videos drew me in, normally there was never that much pre-release gameplay shown so I figured the game would be alright. Boy was I wrong
It's obvious from the moment you enter the menus that this is a console port. I was expecting this but what I wasn't expecting was the general lack of care and polish put into the PC version. Options menu is pretty barren with very little options, not even a texture quality selection. Audio options are standard but not a big issue. Controls are where I have an issue. Rebinding is not great, and is one area where it's apparent it's a substandard port. A lot of pc players have mice that have more buttons and yet the game doesn't recognize these, can't rebind anything to them. Can't rebind any actions to clicking the mouse button either. You can always tell if a developer put effort into the pc port by the options menu and it is heavily apparent, they did not.
Now, onto the game. First off, when you change your resolution, it uses upscaling, instead of putting in the effort to make  proper options, they went the lazy route. Texture quality is crap and they intentionally hide this via blur effects.Graphics are crap, even on what they consider max settings, changing graphics options does nothing, fairly impressive PCs are struggling to hit 30fps, frakking 30!! That shouldn't happen on a game that looks this bad.
Now the sad part is, this game could be good. The gunplay is satisfying, driving can be fun, and the story is really damn good. But, I don't know whether this was developer laziness or whether the publisher imposed deadlines on them that required corners cut, all I know is that the first game out of Hanger 13 is not great at this point in time.
