Before i begin let's make some things clear. Kickstarter backers of Wasteland 2 , both those that played the original and those that didn't, knew exactly what inXile was about to deliver. Through the development and stages tests (alpha, beta) there was always a constant stream of communication between producer and consumer. Thus the majority of them had a good idea of what to expect and if they would be satisfied from the outcome or not. So that leaves the rest of the world. Can W2 be a game to a newcomer and non-backer? Can someone that doesn't know the Adam of post-apocalyptic games find true love? Let's find out.
Game starts as your typical party based tactical isometric RPG. You choose a party of four, either pre-generated characters or create ones from scratch. There are no classes in Wasteland 2. You character type is the result of the skills and attributes you choose from a list. From you typical weapon skills , either long range (rifles, smgs ) or melee (blunt weapons, or brawling ) to dialog skills (smart♥♥♥♥♥ bad♥♥♥♥♥ . Yes those are the actually skill names. Game is full of humor , some times dark , and you'll never feel down the mainstream rpg river without a good laugh or chuckle every now and then. Game also lets you pick your character's attributes (strength, speed , coordination and the like)  which in turn translate to in-game mechanics, like available action points (you spend those for every action you want to do during combat) to critical chance, hit chance and so on.
The story is the continuation of the original wasteland 1. Yea, that one that came in Commodore 64 , Apple II and PC DOS (no, those aren't spaceships, nor we are invaded by aliens, don't interrupt me please) back in 1988 (yes, Earth existed back then, you are not the first generation in this planet, now will you stop interrupting me?)  So those that need to grasp the entire story and lore you have to at least read some background info of the original one , or the outcome of a game through. Of those oldies that we actually played the original  prepare for the feels train , because some characters are back (and some not :(  ) again after 15 years of various events in the desert of Arizona. If you loved the atmosphere of Fallout games (Interplay's or Bethesda's) you will feel right at home. Dust and bones, sand and rust, blood and raid, mutant animals and humans, crazy robots and half-robots , lunatics of the mushroom cloud that worship their god Titan (an actual nuclear missile) who self-detonate even for the slightest reason hoping to join the Great Glow after their 'holy sacrifice' all welcoming the player in a dystopian world that reason has left people's minds while they struggle to survive a hostile post-apocalyptic world. That is immediately visible for the player and the feeling grasps the newcomers right from the start : Your team starts with limited resources, no funds , few bullets and their starting guns (depending on the weapon choices you made at creation, it may be a melee weapon) attending to Ace's funeral (an actual follower of the original team of original wasteland) , having valiantly fell under mysterious circumstances in the harshness of the Arizona. General Vargas (one of the protagonists of the original team), the boss of the Ranger Citadel ,hands you your first task as new recruits in citadel task force and 1 flask of water. Welcome to the desert Rangers.
What it may happen after this , is completely at player's hands and free will. You may go searching right away for clues to what happened to Ace, you may wander around the desert to discover new locations and people, or you may clean the area of raiders and thugs earning precious xp . Don't overdo it though. That flask of water Vargas gave you? Yea , it wasn't for the looks only. You see , game plays in two modes. The map mode where you moving your team around discovering the whereabouts around Ranger Citadel, and isometric team mode . Wandering around you need to worry for 2 things. Water, which constantly consumed by thirsty mouths under the hot sun, and radiation which in some areas they formed 'hot zones' making them impassable without proper protection...okey you have to worry about random encounters too, mutated creatures, raiders, crazy psychos, robots, mutant crazy psycho robots raiding and little kitties (these last two compete of which is actually the most terrifying to face, although recent researches incline for the later) but heck, you are in a post apocalyptic world that everything went hellish way so you did expect that didn't you? Every skill and attribute you spend on your team now has to pay off. You can avoid encounters by having someone with high outdoorsman, you can persuade someone to agree or become friendlier by using your smart♥♥♥♥♥during conversation. You wont last long if you shooting thin air , the result of a low coordination ,nor missing someone with the ability to pick locks which will return valuable ammo from the random lockers and containers. Every team must be complete, having as many skills as possible. Don't fret if you can't take everything from the beginning though. You will encounter NPCs that, will the proper motive and persuasion, (helping them at their problems, or kissing their asses) can join you adding their own sets of abilities to team's repertoire.
Second view mode, apart from map view is the isometric team view. You move around all your squad together, or each one individually. You can talk to NPCs (according to prom video game contains more than 550k words...i am speechless) , use your skills to discover hidden stuff in the dirt, unlock chests , locks and containers or do some traditional kick butt turn base♥♥♥♥♥whipping combat. When you initiate this though, the free movement ends and the fun begins. Every character has action points and every action he or she wants to make consume some of those. Those that have played jagged alliance, or original fallouts know exactly what i am talking about. Tactical decisions during combat are fairly limited. This is part to inXile wanted to make the game more fast, more quick paced which is fine. Sometimes you wish you HAD some alternatives though, specially when things get ugly (lots of enemies, few bullets) . You can move around, shoot or seek for cover . Cover is terrain oriented . You gain 50% evasion bonus if you cover behind a box from the PROPER side against an enemy. You do gain 10% increase to hit against all enemies. Boxes and other fragile objects can break though. Yes there is a certain level of destructibility on the environment. Some things break. You can also crouch or prepare for an ambush (W2 variant of overwatch) . Swapping weapons or inventory gear is free action . The best is to have a team with as many diversities as possible. This includes weapons. Smgs are fast, shotguns shoot in a cone, heavy weapons suppress enemies, sniper rifles shoot from afar and so on. Weapons can be moded also (yeaah!)  , altering their stats using your weaponsmithing skill. Generally don't expect huge depth or variety in combat, but it surely serves its purpose . Its a fast (for turn based game at least) guns blazing, explosion ridden  , brain splattering , limb chopping fragfest . Yup, game contains violence....and strong language and tons tons of humor also.
Speaking of which, don't get the game if you want to see super graphics (it HAS great audio and soundtrack though). Get the game for the story instead. Post apoc lovers will love it. Party based RPG funs will adore it. W1 fans (yes those two of you that have left) will drop a nostalgic tear or two. And everybody that admires well written scenario and story will embrace it. Prepare for hours of fun, prepare for the wasteland...

I love this game and have been playing it religiously for the past months. The core gameplay was fun, and the emphasis on movement was great. And the buisness model was wonderful.
The loadout cards were locked behind gold at a very reasonable rate. Attainable after a reasonable grind for a F2P game. I expected them to charge us for the skins, mounts, poses and what not. Cosmetic stuff. Sounds cool right?
But then ob44 happened.
Then the essence system happened, locking core gameplay mechanics in a huge grind. Even guys like me, who've played for a long time are having trouble getting enough essence to unlock enough legendaries to be competitive.
Imagine going into comp and having to play a chamipion because the team composition demands it, but you don't have the best legendary for that champ. It's very frustrating, and comp was bad enough as it is.
The game no longer feels competitive or fair thanks to the essence system. Even in casual matches.
Unless they fix this system (or remove it completely, yeah right, as if they'll do that), this game is not a good investment of your time or money.
I can see the legendary card system working though, after some balancing (a lot of balancing).
And the ttk has been increased, turning a stragetic fps experience into a twitch-shooter experience, which i think is the wrong direction for the game as a whole.
EDIT: Hi-Rez have reduced the grind for essence. But every other point here still stands. All in all the changes have been good, and more changes are promised in the future to help with essence.

Play Van Helsing 1/2 first. Play Torchlight 2 first. Play Grim Dawn first. Play Path of Exile first. Play Diablo 3 first. Now my opinion on this game is both good and bad because this is both extreme ends of the scale. I played this game for a while on most of the game modes and stacked up just shy of 40 hours game time so I hope my opinion on this isn't dismissed lightly. Anyway, Orion: Dino Horde is both a great game but it needs a large amount of tweaking before it is worthy of its famed rating. It has great content with weapons from a basic .45, fully auto or duel high powered pistols. A good variety and mix of guns including Light Machine Guns (LMG's), Sub-Machine Guns (SMG's), shotguns and sniper rifles, and not to mention the high grade adrenaline weapons to add some bang to your buck. There are some awesome perks to that give various boosts and  take the game to a whole new level of entertainment.
Now onto the maps. The maps are epic to say the least, they have a great range with all varieties from night to day and even frozen varients, some are even on an enormous scale taking 10 - 20 minutes just to get from one side to the other while at the same time avoiding or killing dinos as you go. The community on this game is great and all are very welcoming and just make this game that much better, a big shout out for them.
Overall Orion: Dino Horde is a rollercoster ride of fun, planning and a rush of excitment when the going gets tough!
But as all games do they have room for improvement so now I shall speak of the down sides.
Firstly is the most dominant of the problems, the lag. Despite this is a great game all round the lag really dents its rep and causes it to become almost unenjoyable and in some cases unplayable do to whats known as a "rubber band effect" which causes peoples eyes to hurt from the lag on the screen. This is a server issue with the game and once its gone will be a huge improvement to the quality of game play.
The next issue would be dino controls in rampage mode, using the dinos is fun but is almost impossible to use them to any effect, in all my dozens of games I only met one person who could use the horde dinos well. If they were given an aimer to help guide biting, grabbing, throwing and spitting it would make it so much more fun but at the same time the dinos do seem a little over powered as they are but if the human's were given the option to spend money on guns or perks instead of a set class loadout it would level it off nicely.
Finally to my personal suggestions, these are neutral what I feel could spice things up.
More guns! currently there are:
6 pistols
2 SMG's
2 shotguns
2 LMG's
1 Assult rifle
3 sniper rifles
and 1 sword
(excluding adrenaline weapons)
Although this is a great range of guns I think it would be nice if we had more of each type and if the stats were tweaked because SMG's are actually better than LMG's and LMG's are a support weapon designed to use high .cal bullets with a large mag, not as a controlled weapon like an SMG. But more assult rifles would be first rate with me, I personally am a fan of assult rifles and was quite sad to see only one of them to use so adding more would be a big boost to weapon selection.
My last suggestion will be a more base function that is currently missing from the game as a whole, a tutorial. When you start the game your thrown in the deep end and I personally dont mind because I catch on quickly but others might not and would take a while to learn the game. Adding a practise mode with a built in tutorial showing all the game funcions and what all the buttons are and how to use all the equipment to its fullest would be a big improvement. Not only would it leave less questions but give a direct insight into how to better play the game.
This is all I have to say on the game at the moment so based on my experience this is a great game that has lag issues and needs improvement but has amazing potential to become a truely epic first person shooter.

After everybody telling me how similar this was to the Telltale games, i knew i would like it. I loved the Walking Dead games, the stories really sucked me in and made me care for the characters. However, even then,  i was not prepared to what level this game affected me.
Life Is Strange, to me at least, is a masterpiece of storytelling. It makes you feel and be Max Caulfield, shy Photographer-to-be, nerd-wannabe, time-traveller by accident. This calls back to landmark movies like Back to the Future or Groundhog Day (and calls out to them plenty of times), but it goes so much deeper. It tackles issues like bullying, insecurity, internet culture with incredible care and accuracy. And it makes us question our place in the cause and effect of all that goes on around us. Oh, and there is a bit about climate change too.
When Max (never call her Maxine) Caulfield returns to Arcadia Bay, after five years of following her parents to Seattle, she is coming home, but it is all new and strange to her. Being back in her hometown, because it has one of the best photographer programs, makes her reminisce about how she wasn't a real good friend after leaving her BFF (who says that anymore?) for Seattle, and that she should come out of her shell more. After a class of her professional hero, Mr. Jefferson, star photographer, Max has a weird life (and time) changing experience. What can she do with this newfound power.
This journey through time and emotions, where every decision does indeed matter, left me often speechless, and many times teary eyed, but i also shouted out "YES" with Max, when something went our way. And yes, after just a few short episodes with her, i felt like i am there with her, choosing not only her fate, but also finding out a lot about myself in the process. Actions demand reactions, choices have consequences, and even rewinding time can not stop emotions.
This is one of the best time travelling stories i have ever experienced, and while there may be some very minor glitches in gameplay to some, i love the art, the message, the choices, the emotions. I love everything about this game.
It IS a heavy game. You will cry a lot (or if you do not, well, you are a more hardened soul than i am), but if you like to be on an emotional rollercoaster, this and the Telltale Walking Dead games are the best out there.

The best off road game I've ever played. Where other off road games miss the mark Spin Tires is able to excel. The core gameplay is phenomenal. They perfectly captured the feel of the trucks and environment. The physics engine forms the off road simulation back bone of this game. Getting from point A to point B alone provides a challenge as it should in this kind of game. The trucks handle realisticly and each offers it's own advantages and disadvantages meaning you won't just be spending all your time driving one. A fully loaded truck feels and handles completely different making the gameplay that much more engaging.
The multiplayer is fun and requires team work to accomplish objectives but can be quite the time sink. I usually only bother to join a lobby if I have a decent chunk of time to dedicate to playing.
Overall there are a few bugs and at face value it may seem to be lacking content (number of maps and trucks) but at it's core the simulation portion of this game is rock solid. With this well established base I can only imagine the kind of things that could be added in the future. As it sits now it is well worth the price tag if you're a sim or off road fan. I'll be putting many hours on this title.

After playing through it three times, it still doesn't fail to leave a lasting impression on me. LIS is a weird game to categorize. It does not really feel like a game in the first place, but rather as an interactive movie of sorts. I could write long paragraphs about why I love this game, but I'll just list what I think are the strong and weak points of the game (all subjective, of course.) Beware of minor spoilers.
Positive:
+ Interesting characters. Many of them start out as (American) high-school archetypes, but the game deconstructs these archetypes and the characters themselves as the game progresses. Good voice-acting helps to bring these characters to life.
+ Amazing soundtrack that fits seamlessly with the scenes you find yourself in.
+ Being a choice-based game, your choices bring about a lot of changes. Some are big, some are minor. The many nuances, changes to scenes further down the line and extra dialogue that occurs through these choices make the game feel rather life-like.
+ The game is very interactive. You can interact with a lot of objects and characters in the game. A part of the game and its characters' stories are told through these little random interactions, which give the game's world a deeper dimension. Never just rush from one objective to another, there's a lot to explore and discover! There is also Max' diary, which is an entertaining read on its own and serves as a recap of what you've done in the game thus far.
+ The overal atmosphere, compounded by the soundtrack, voice-acting, visuals and interactivity of the environment made for a very life-like experience that tugged on my heartstrings in ways few games manage to do. The game gets close to you, and it shows.
+ Replay value is high with all the little and big choices you can make.
Negative:
- While the dialogue is good overal, it's quite clear the developers went a bit overboard with trying to make the teenager characters sound ''cool'', which results in some awkward and outdated use of of words and dialogue.
- A major part of the story is never truly resolved/its origin is never explained in satisfactory detail.
- While there are many choices to make in the game, and they do have impacts, the final scene comes down to a binary choice between two endings. Most major choices in the game have no effect on this final scene. Furthermore, while one ending is satsifactory in light of the game's narrative (if predictable), the other one seems grossly out of place and lazy.
Mixed:
+- Suicide, murder, sexual assault mentions and severe depression occur as themes in the game, which may make it unsuitable and possibly too personal for some people to play. Bear this in mind.

Introduction
Life is Strange is a very story rich game in which the choices you make throughout matter.  You play as an 18 year old female,Max Caulfield, photography senior who finds out she has the ability to rewind time and change what happens in the past, and as she does so she realises that she changes the future.  This game is a masterpiece and in this review I will explain why.  (Note - At time of writing this review I have only done one playthrough and will probably go through again to make some different choices)
Episode One
The first episode of Life is Strange is actually free and I would highly recommend you download it and give it ago.  That way you can tell if you think this game has a remote chance of making you spend money on it.
Story
Life is Strange has a beautifully written original story which captivates you and leaves you want more after every episode.  I played through this game in one sitting all because I wanted to know what the ending was going to be (I was very lucky and knew nothing about this game).  The basic premise is that you’re characters, Max Caulfield, she finds out she can reverse time by saving her friend Chloe Price.  I will leave it at that so I don’t spoiling anything since it is best to go into this game blind.
Visuals
This game released in January of 2015 so don’t expect amazing next level graphic.  Something I did admire about this game is the style it used.  Cartoonish to an extent with some dark themes.  I did not find myself saying that the game looked bad or that it aged poorly.  The graphical art and style of the game is very suiting to the world and the characters within it.
Music/ Soundtrack
One thing that people might not think about when they are playing a game is what music they are hearing and how it sets up or suits the situation you are in.  Life is Strange has one of the best soundtracks that I have heard from any video game.  Not only is the original music suiting of the game but, for me, it truly is the licensed music.  The music that Dontnod used in this game is phenomenal and suits the game and it’s themes so well.  The first song you hear really sets the tone for what this game is about.  A young woman learning about something she thought is impossible.  At no point throughout the game did I think “This music does not suit this scene” because I found that whatever was playing was chosen very carefully.
Mechanics
Being able to reverse time is not an everyday thing.  Not even in video games.  Of my own personal recollection, without searching online, I can not think of any games that have this type of mechanic.  “Reversing makes the game too easy, the decisions mean nothing” you might be wondering; and to that I say you are wrong.  I found that it made the choices harder.  Because you might say to yourself I will change that and then do it and realise “Wait maybe the other choice was the best”.  At some point you have to settle and reversing time makes it a whole lot harder.
You may have realised that all that I have said is positive about this game.  While the game is very well made it is not perfect.  I feel like that when the characters move sometimes they should be saying something but instead you have to wait for the game to focus back onto their faces to carry on the conversation; it almost feels like body language and speech are almost separate entities and should not be combined which I think is a shame.  Another annoyance I have with the game is once again is to do with speech, in that the characters facial animation and their vocals are out of sync which can bring you out of the moment for a second.  While none of these are deal breakers they are still gripes that should be recognized and spoken about.  Now the the next issue is a spoiler, so read at your own risk.  While I have heard people complain about this I did not find it as big of a deal, others might disagree.  *SPOILER WARNING*
That is my review of the masterpiece that is Life is Strange.
This game is honestly one of the my favourite games of all time and I don’t know if anything can compare to how it made me feel emotionally.
I truly think that this game should be played by as many people as possible.

A lot of people might disagree with me on this review, but I think this game is awesome. For many games, I would agree that when the same game mechanics are used in the sequel, it usually means that the developers were lazy and couldn't be bothered to polish it. For SoW, I think it works. The developers have taken the original gameplay, and managed to build on it. There are more skills and more opportunities. They have taken the core gameplay and improved.
It really pisses me off that people are complaining about the microtransactions. There is no reason to buy them, and there is no part in the story where they are necessary.
Personally, I think they did a brilliant job with the grinding in this game. So far, I haven't gotten bored from grinding (and I'm in Act IV, the grindiest act of the game).
The story in this game is a huge improvement from the first one. There are multiple quest lines, and the characters managed to grow on me (especially Bruz). I thoroughly enjoyed the questlines (although the Spirit Of Carnan quests were a little tedious) and when the ending came around,
It made me emotionally attached to the characters through good character development and great story development.
All in all, I think this game is brilliant. I think the nemesis system is brilliant, I think the story is brilliant, and I think the gameplay is brilliant.
I am very happy to recommend this game, and hope that others enjoy it like I have.

Hotline Miami is a top-down shooter game with stealth elements. This game isn't mindless running and gunning, but rather requires quick planning and strategy in order to succeed, which makes the game all the more fun and unique. The base game is about 6 hours worth of play time, (at least for me) not counting bonus levels.
The story is decent, and features characters that have more depth than those of any young adult novel.
Note that the game is very bloody and gory and at some parts quite innapropiate, though I don't care I know there are some who do, and there are no options to play without this.
Pros:
-Silenced pistol is actually useful
-Different unlockable "masks" which give different abilites to fit different playstyles
-Unlockable weapons that I believe are just reskins (tell me if I'm wrong)
-Lots of base weapons
-Variety of enemies
-Good amount of content
-Boss fights
-OST is great
-Tutorial that doesn't overstay itself
-Secrets/easter eggs
-Game often introduces new mechanics on the fly to keep the game fresh¹
+/-:
-The AIs and Weaponry in the level are somewhat random
-The art is both good and bad at times, though most of it is just artistic choice
-Game is somewhat difficult
Cons:
-Some deaths feel cheap because of the random AI and weaponry
-Some things are hard to understand, chiefly some boss fights and some complicated levels
-Game crashes more commonly than most other games I've played, this usually isn't disasterous but can mean you having to repeat a level
-Limited option menu (THINK OF THE COLOR BLIND)
-Some rare bugs
-¹:The mechanics are often barely or never revisited
Final verdict: 8/10, buy it for yourself if you enjoy any type of fun challenge

Achieved 100% both in-game and in terms of Steam achievements (as of Oct 23rd, 2017). I'll assume you've already played the first part of the series (
), please note that this review compares certain features to the previous game.
If you liked the first game of the series, you will most probably LOVE this. All the good stuff, like the nemesis system, skills and inventory have been greatly enhanced (hell, I'd killed an orc captain by shooting down a Morgai Fly nest upon his head, and next time I've visited the place, he cheated death, becoming a legendary nemesis "half-orc, half-poisonous-fly-nest thing", THAT KEPT CHEATING DEATH AND AMBUSHING ME EVEN ACROSS DIFFERENT REGIONS OF THE MAP. HOW COOL IS THAT?!). Want to be a classic, Skyrim-like Poisoning Stealth Archer? DO IT! Want to fight in the frontline as a pyromaniac warrior, blasting everyone - including yourself, for a damage boost of course - with flames? DO IT! Want to be the local serial killing nightmare, terrorizing orcs and killing the hierarchy from inside with the help of some spies? DO IT! You can build a large amount of character types, just as you want.
They mixed the base recipe with an above-average story and some interesting plot-twists, but that certainly doesn't add as much to the replayability of the game as the enhanced nemesis system and the new loot system.
As for the lootbox system, deemed so controversial by the public: in my experience, it doesn't subtract, nor add anything game-breaking into the frying pan. I've barely unlocked 4-5 free boxes during the campaign, only to find myself with more than 100k silver (with investing in all four forts with maximum upgrades) in the ingame. I've used around 30k silver from that amount in the late 95-100% completion to get an exact type of orc for 2 achievements, which again, is not a must-have thing, I just wanted a clean plate. Oh, also, I've also achieved a rather high rank in the online system, without investing anything (I've come across the ocassional "all my warchiefs are legendary" kiddos, but they only delayed the inevitable (7 minute siege instead of 5 minutes). It certainly helps during the endgame to have a full set of legendary captains in sieges, but they are just as much susceptible to death as any other common captain when it comes to a wall destruction or a giant ball of fire. They do help though, when you are stuck in a difficult part of the game, but that amount of lootboxes can easily be obtained from gathering silver during the campaign, there is definitely no need of investing real money.
The only problems that occured to me was that sometimes the cloak of Talion clipped in a funny way, making it look like as if a stool was under it, but moving a few steps, waving around the cloak made it disappear. Also, there were obvious graphical optimization problems, mostly when traveling at high speeds (caragors, drakes) or entering detail-rich areas, but these small FPS drops didn't make the game uncomfortable at all. Also, the graphics sometimes felt decent, but a bit outdated (obviously, don't expect Crysis or Batman-like supercharged graphics).
The other negative that I could emphasize was that the end-game (20-30 hours) is rather "grindy" and repetitive (dominate captains, level them up, defend fortress, move to next region, repeat), with only a short, extra cinematic at the end.
All in all, I'd give it a solid
for being just as innovative as its predecessor, and having a good 60 hours of fun with going for 100%.
- the enhanced nemesis system provides hours of fun and great replayability
- the new loot system and overhauled skill system make the overall gameplay more enjoyable
- the story continuing Talion and Celebrimbor's bond keep you enterained while you are at more grindy parts of the game
- the last 20-30 hours (a.k.a. the end-game) is quite grindy and repetitive
- minor optimization problems (graphical and rendering issues here and there)
- the supplementary lootbox system triggered quite a few people, though they are much more annoying than the lootbox system itself, which is only an extra boost if you are having trouble

Hotline Miami is one of the hardest games I have played in my life. While the game may differ from many shooters in the sense that 1 bullet, or swing from a melee can end everything, the games are extremly enjoyable.
The Great Level Design Compliments every play style that can be associated with one of 26 masks, 23 of which provide a gameplay changing aspect or weapon to start out with, and no weapon in the game is considered overpowered or underpowered.
The game also has a kickass soundtrack that makes the atmosphere of every level enjoyable.
Of course, there is a couple of cons that many players have to consider. Right out of the tutorial, the game doesn't hold your hand. In fact, it takes a hammer and a nail, and smashes it into the joints of your fingers. The game is extremly difficult, and you as a player has to have cougar like reactions. Sometimes, it is insane how fast enimies react. If you are a player that can't keep up with Bruce Lee reaction times, than do yourself a favour and not waste money on a game you will probably never pass the 3rd chapter.
There is another problem with hitreg for melee weapons. I really wanted this game to be good, but sadly, it is quite primitive and lacking for its price.
You can clearly tell the game was designed to be played on a phone. The menus, combat, crafting, and gameplay are overly simple and leave a lot to be desired.
- With no skills and just basic items, the combat gets old within an hour or two.

You have to click an item to view its properties or what it is (You also can't hover over items in your tracked craftables, there also is no hotkey to move back in a menu, you have to press back). You also have to be at a crafting station to see what materials you have to craft with.
- Quest log is primitive and often not always clear what you're supposed to do.
- Crafting is on a time-based system. Appropriate for a phone maybe, but a waste of time and design on the computer.
- Combat is so basic that it becomes easy to master within minutes and never die.
Overall this game is probably fun if you spent $2 on it and played on your phone, but as a full-fledged steam release I expected more and feel underwhelmed and accepting of my loss of money.

Fantastic new school version of old school games like Zelda 1 mixed with Smash TV. The gameplay is pretty simple. a 3/4ths top down shooter that allows you to shoot in 4 directions. There are also alternate power ups and bombs to use. Really simple controls like Smash TV mixed with Zelda. You are Isaac, stuck in a multi leveled dungeon. Each one of these dungeon levels is in the old Zelda 1 style where each room is 1 screen. The dungeons / basements are randomized, every room and enemy combination is randomly generating. The gameplay is fun and addictive. The only downside is no lives, no continues. There are tons of quirky weapons, enemies, power ups and bosses. Everyone should spend the $5 to play this game.
I can understand if its not for everyone, because it is an arcadey retro Zelda 1 meets Smash TV sort of game. The graphics are cute and charming, but portray horrifying things like if you were to ever see a doodle of a fetus or a doodle of someone coughing out flies and poop staining the floor. Like a sad disparagingly sort of awesome. You play as Issac who basically has to get out of randomized Zelda style dungeons. There are dozens of unique enemies with different attack styles. Few enemies seem to have predictable patterns. There are also plenty of boss battles.
The controls take some getting used to, but they are basically Smash TV controls. You use your directional pad, then you use an attack direction. So you can move right and shoot left or up, or down or right. You have a bomb button, a special findable item and an auxiliary power up button for things like pills. The main attack are bullets... which are really tears. Bombs sit, but you can push them, pills do good and bad things. Some items / power ups give you dolls for extra weapons, or a dead cat gives you 9 lives but the catch is you have 1 heart energy per life. You can also get metal hearts, that count as energy, but once they're gone you can't get them back like normal heart healths.
You play through 'basement' floor after floor marked with a boss at the end. You find keys, bomb walls, kill enemies, gamble, visit stores, danger rooms and so on. Just like Zelda 1. The only thing is that it is all randomized. The room layouts are randomized, the rooms themselves are randomized, the stores, the weapons, the items.
It is all randomized, so you'll never play the same game twice. This isn't a story based game, so it won't appeal to everyone. Its highly entertaining especially in short bursts of play. For that price, you can't miss this game.
I highly recommend the game for its gameplay, cheap price and its never the same game twice with the random dungeons.

Alan Wake is a great mixture of both storytelling and action horror. You'll feel as if you're in a Stephen King novel with pistol in one hand and a pen in the other, and that's the point. Alan Wake, the protagonist of this story admits several times he was inspired by Stephen King. In a truely bizarre mix of story telling, Alan Wake is everything. He is your narrator, your hero and your player character. He is you trying to survive in a story taken over by unknown forces which use a strong control over the darkness to grow ever stronger and remove you from it's sinister and cruel plan.
With nothing to stop you from being swallowed into a violent, angry and endless void you must run until you can find a means to protect yourself from a world being torn apart in the black of night. Nothing can help you and nothing will help you, except for the light. Dawning a flashlight and the knowledge of how to finally fight back, you become the champion of light. You begin to shape destiny again. You become a hero.
With your new found power and in a desperate race against time, you must find your wife who was inexplicably swallowed by the darkness. You must convince yourself that you're of sane mind, when everyone else is trying to convince you otherwise. You're a hero, who will fight endless legions of the Taken inorder to reclaim the one you love and care for the most. The only question though, is how?
I've found out the answer to this over five times on Xbox 360. Yes, the story is that good. Yes, maybe I should play something else. Yes, yes and yes. Get this game.

I’ve only played the Original Wasteland game very briefly a long time ago, however I’ve spent countless hours playing the pre-Fallout 3 Fallout games on PC which were inspired by Wasteland. Now I’ve played Wasteland 2 for around 7 hours, it’s not a fast paced game, this has only been enough time for me to complete one of the first main missions.
- Overall I was very happy with the game, personally it was awesome to see a modern Fallout-like game with a traditional isometric view and detailed text descriptions of everything seen and done in the world.
- However I found that I spent way too much time having to loot one loot container after another as well as sometimes fighting identical enemies repeatedly.
In the character creation the graphics aren’t very appealing. However when you actually play the game you don’t usually view things so closely.
-----Generally the actual graphics looked good in my opinion. But personally I’m satisfied as long as it’s a competent modern three-dimensional adaptation of Wasteland and an adequate improvement compared to the two-dimensional Fallout titles.
-----What I was really impressed by was actually the textual description of entities and objects in the game. They provided more interesting details about everything you see.
-----I also really liked the text dialogue that my companion expressed during combat rather than being mute. It really made the character seem more alive.
-----Most of the character models looked fine, especially humans who featured a lot of variety. But I really got tired of seeing the same unimpressive giant bunnies again and again.
-----There were also a couple of locations which I was not impressed by. One area was just a big empty square. While another fenced you into lanes which I don’t think fit well into a world that I believe should feel very open.
-----But I was really impressed by many of the other environments that I saw. I liked how you could rotate the view, this would reveal objects you couldn’t see previously.
-----Many environments looked handcrafted and irregularly shaped. I think this platform has a lot of potential even for other games with a fantasy theme.
I liked the character attributes and skill system. However the benefits of investing into some attributes didn’t seem worthwhile. Likewise investing in combat skills seemed to suffer from strong diminishing returns.
-----I set out to play this game in an unusual way. I didn’t want to micromanage a squad. So initially I took only one ranger. This didn’t work out so well initially.
-----So after playing for an hour I started over and I redesigned my starting character. This time I created a more intelligent character so that they could multi-skill and thus take on multiple roles.
-----Early on there is a high level character who you can recruit named ‘Angela Deth’, I took her along with me because going solo with a low level character is actually very difficult. So the game almost let me play the way I wanted to because I didn’t have to take a whole squad.
-----I don’t mind the turn based combat, but it’s one of the reasons the game is slow paced. I knows it’s more traditional. But I would have preferred a real time system where you could pause and redirect the action.
-----Occasionally my companion would go out of control in combat and make actions without me directing her. How do I make her do this all the time? I’d rather my NPC teammates were more autonomous. I don’t want to have to tell them to do every little thing.
-----Outside of combat for the first several hours that I played, I couldn’t move my characters individually for some reason. So I wasn’t able to rearrange my character before entering combat
-----This was a bit weird. I don’t know why this happened but eventually I was suddenly able to direct them individually.
-----In games like this I feel compelled to search every nook and cranny in a level for loot. Especially because you really need to do so in order to scrape up enough ammunition to fight and enough medical supplies to survive.
-----I know it’s a post apocalyptic game and scavenging may be the ‘thing’ to do. But I think I easily spent half of my seven hours of game-play looting and managing my characters’ inventories. That was tedious.
-----Why do I have to ransack the property of people who I am supposed to protect? How do my characters carry all those guns and where do they keep them, just to sell at a vendor?
-----I wish there was a better system for acquiring better gear. Perhaps credit towards an interchangeable load-out based on each characters rank and experience levels?
So yes, I definitely have my gripes about this game. But I was very happy to play it. This game proves that Fallout 3 didn’t have to make the shift to FPS. Not sure that I will have more time for Wasteland 2 though.
-----I’m happy that the price has come down. The previous $60 price tag was a major reason that I had not purchased this game quite some time ago.

After 1000 hours of playing, I have planets yet to visit, places to still explore and station upgrades to make.

Just getting 100% exploration of of your home & its two moons is a great achievement and dozens of hours of play, and to do well you'll want to have communication satellites and space stations pieced together over multiple launches, a small maneuveable lander, a heavy mining lander for fuel, or maybe even a mobile surface base that does it all but creeps slowly across the surface on solar power... once in place you use them and explore each area as a mission itself. Then take those lesons and do it again on an interplanetary mission with different gravity and different atmospheres.
Throw in the career mode and now you're doing the whole thing with budget considerations.
Its a beautiful game, easy to play and maybe impossible to master. It is my favorite game, and has been since early access.

If you purchase this game expecting Diablo III or Torchlight II set in a Middle-Eastern world, you will be horribly disappointed. I backed the game on kickstarter thinking it would be exactly that - a mid-east Diablo II clone. Initially I was put off by what seemed to be an overly simplistic game, as everything seemed to be rather generic. However, if you play on, the game gains more complexity - equipment gains stat modifiers for example. Legends of Persia is actually a fairly decent ARPG.
The graphics are not great by modern standards, but they are not as terrible other reviewers say. I guess people tend to forget that many of the games people loved that influenced this game (Diablo I & II, Divine Divinity, Siege of Avalon) look horrible by modern standards. In a forum I saw someone compare this game to RAW. This game is no where near as bad as that turd.
While I like the game, I believe that the average steam consumer probably would want to pick this game up when it is on sale because it does not compare favorably to some of the other games available on steam in the same genre.
What is interesting to me is that the game studio is based in Tehran. The story is based on a legendary prince of ancient Persia. Personally I believe that cultural engagement with the Middle East is important, and do not at all mind having paid full price for this game. I also believe that this game studio is capable of improving and doing better. Instead of giving up on the game after 10-15 minutes, play the game and give the studio constructive criticism.

I enjoyed the game, but not as much as I was hyped. Please note, I RECOMMEND this game at a lower price, but at full? God no.
I felt there wasn't much I haven't already done in other post apoclyptic games, or RPGs for that matter. The story was good all the way up until the end, where it fell flat and felt very rushed. The fact that the main antagonist was recycled once more from the previous iteration was neither suprising and also extremely eye rolling.
The freedom of 'choice' seemed very bare bones, making me feel that there was only a few ways to solve problems with each branch just ending up at the same point. It suffers from the 'amusement park' effect of most RPGs, (which needs to stop). Where, sure there are many interesting areas to see, but once you've more or less tied everything up at that area, there is no need to return to it, ever. There is no real sense of a vibrant enviroment around you, you just go from A to B to C to D, only really back and forth to replenish/sell/top up your water and some few quests. There wasn't much dungeon raiding or exploration, I may have missed a few - and if I did that's on me.
I thought all of Los Angeles was super rushed and pretty crummy, with exception of Rodia which was kinda when I got my second wind, only to be really kinda drained by the lack of really anything interesting going on. With each stop after rodia easily tied up and finished within a hour. The last two hours of the game dragged on with combat and really bad black and white choices.
As when I played it (I hope it gets patched for whomever is interested) a lot of the sidequests were really broken or dead ended if you did specific things in a different order. Which sucks if you have no idea - I would make sense if it was specific to something you dead, but sometimes it uses a character that isn't relevent anymore, but since you already did something related to another quest with them, their dialog wheel is a bust. (McDade im thinking of you as well as Maggie).
The combat was awful, straight awful for the first bit - however once I got so overpowered from overlevelling (due to so much travel and map combing for areas) you smash through confrontations, and after doing massive criticals did I really start getting excited to do battle. Once you hoard RPG/Rocket launchers, did it really get fun too. Only problem I have is the weapon jamming was pretty broken. I jammed so many times, I never had a real issue with missing, I would just CONSTANTLY jam, it only made fights more longer, I was never really in danger.
----------
The only really things that was consistent and what I enjoyed, was the followers. They always had something relative to say, and for every quest/event etc. Scotchmo and the tryhard rebellious LA punk were my favourite. They all have little bios you can read. There are some good dialog trees but they are few and far between, I again felt that with all of the chest thumping and crazy black or white decisions you had to make, people kinda didn't do anything about it unless it was to -try- and kill you, face forward. Which is a dumb way to resolve anything.
I did enjoy the customization of my characters, and the idea of spreading out all of your wanted perks over 4 characters. I could roleplay 4 different people rather then being a jack of all trades. Which was a shame, because nobody really noticed or reacted specifically to any individual of my group specifically. It might've well of just been one person, shame.
Overall I'd rank it a 6.5/10. It started off strong but towards the end I was writing it off. I  really love the post apocalyptic genre, and I could never get sick of it. The controls and interface were crisp and steady. Unity was a poor choice, but acceptable. I just hope they do not get discouraged or blame fans if they didn't enjoy their return. I hope there is turn based wasteland game to come.

Part 1 review: I liked this gentle scifi comedy. I've heard of complaints that the puzzles are too easy and I'd disagree, though unlike some games, if you use the spanner and then the bucket on an item to try to solve a puzzle, it will often give you a hint that you need to use the item on the bucket then spanner, rather than keeping you guessing at every possible combination for hours on end. I liked the riddle, mainly because I didn't have the item in question and only by working it out did I know where to go to solve it.
Part 2: the problems definitely ramp up in difficulty and, though I liked the challenge, I have a beef with some aspects of this. MINOR SPOILER AHEAD Several problems rely on using information one of the characters you control discovers with the other, but, in some cases, there's no way the information could be passed on. Sort of like a game in which a person in England in the 1870s discovers a diary entry which gives the combination to a safe which is then used by a character you control in the revolutionary America. No internal logic to justify the transfer of information. They might at least have hinted at some sort of telepathic link between the two or something but if they do, I missed it... This irks me. Possibly unnecesssarily, and the rest of the game is great, it's just that this makes me go Hmmmm. A lack of care in game design.

My all-time favorite pixel-style arcade shooter right here!
It's simple and fun, easy to jump in for a few quick rounds of blowing up baddies. There are times where it can be frustrating due to the difficulty, but it's hard to get too mad because that's the idea behind it all. There are no save points or anything to hold your hand. It's up to you to keep trying and learning new techniques if you want to advance.
I love the charming pixel-style graphics for one, even though it may be a bit over-done in the current market. The music and sound effects are well done even if I play my own music for background noise. Overall it feels like a solid product with no glitches either that I've seen. Part of me doesn't want to reach the Nuclear Throne since I thoroughly enjoy just jumping in and playing for the heck of it. It's not a game one would spend hours at a time on, but it's works so well if you want to kill some time in short bursts. It's like my fun alternative to playing Tetris (any platform really), Space Invaders, Binding of Isaac or Geometry Wars. Definitely will be playing this one for many more hours to come!

The game is pretty much a visual novel. There's very little to no gameplay making this barely a "game" at all. In the story you navigate as either Shay or Vella depending on the story you choose to start with. As these protagonists you must solve "puzzles" or dilemas you face with cunning and use of your environment.  Neither story is repetitive at all and each are unique so it's reccomended that you play both stories to get the full value of the game. The art style is relatively unique and playful, similar to if Tim Burton stopped using Grey and Black for every pallet. After everybody telling me how similar this was to the Telltale games, i knew i would like it. I loved the Walking Dead games, the stories really sucked me in and made me care for the characters. However, even then,  i was not prepared to what level this game affected me.
Life Is Strange, to me at least, is a masterpiece of storytelling. It makes you feel and be Max Caulfield, shy Photographer-to-be, nerd-wannabe, time-traveller by accident. This calls back to landmark movies like Back to the Future or Groundhog Day (and calls out to them plenty of times), but it goes so much deeper. It tackles issues like bullying, insecurity, internet culture with incredible care and accuracy. And it makes us question our place in the cause and effect of all that goes on around us. Oh, and there is a bit about climate change too.
When Max (never call her Maxine) Caulfield returns to Arcadia Bay, after five years of following her parents to Seattle, she is coming home, but it is all new and strange to her. Being back in her hometown, because it has one of the best photographer programs, makes her reminisce about how she wasn't a real good friend after leaving her BFF (who says that anymore?) for Seattle, and that she should come out of her shell more. After a class of her professional hero, Mr. Jefferson, star photographer, Max has a weird life (and time) changing experience. What can she do with this newfound power.
This journey through time and emotions, where every decision does indeed matter, left me often speechless, and many times teary eyed, but i also shouted out "YES" with Max, when something went our way. And yes, after just a few short episodes with her, i felt like i am there with her, choosing not only her fate, but also finding out a lot about myself in the process. Actions demand reactions, choices have consequences, and even rewinding time can not stop emotions.
This is one of the best time travelling stories i have ever experienced, and while there may be some very minor glitches in gameplay to some, i love the art, the message, the choices, the emotions. I love everything about this game.
It IS a heavy game. You will cry a lot (or if you do not, well, you are a more hardened soul than i am), but if you like to be on an emotional rollercoaster, this and the Telltale Walking Dead games are the best out there.
10/10

At this point, I might as well proclaim my undying love to Tim Schafer. It seems every title I've touched with him behind the director's chair reminds me why I love video games.
Apparently 16 years since his last point-and-click adventure game, Grim Fandango, and the man still knows how to work it. I mean it's not like he wasn't doing anything, with Psychonauts and Brutal Legends druid-plowing themselves into my favorite's list, but point-and-clicks are very different from your normal genre. Practically visual novels; if the story or context doesn't hook you, there's nothing to go back for it aside from meager puzzles.
Luckly Broken Age hooks you from the start with both, and beautiful artwork to boot. Shay and Vella's story is nothing new, something we've seen or read plently times before, but Tim Schafer's spin leaves it refreshing. For example, Shay's situation is entirely understandable, where he puts a mental barrier between him and the "Computer" who is taking care of him. Although never brought up by Shay or the game itself, it's likely only programmed to take care of him - it isn't true love and concern. Yet all it takes is some lovely voice-work provided by the ever awesome Jennifer Hale and a small story toward Shay, and I can't help but feel sad for "Computer". Damn you, Shay, just call her "Mom" for once.
Contrary to what I'm saying above, the game is light-hearted. Vella's story about sacrificing maidens is not as grim as you'd imagine it to be. No blood or gore, just a small glimpse of a body as it's devoured by a giant species of monster called a Mog. Yet that's part of its charm. Combined with its watercolor artwork and peaceful soundtrack, it's as if I'm reading a children's storybook. Then you eventually come across someone whose name is shortened to Ch't.... heh-heh.
All and all, I am very looking forward to Act 2. Having started Shay's story first, I thought I had an idea of where his story ended when I was nearing the end of Vella's. The end of Act 1 practically told me "Nope," punched me in the face, and jumped off a cliff. I'd pay again in order for it to come sooner, but like everyone else, I'll have to wait for the free update... whenever that is.
C'mon, Tim. Don't do this to me, man. I needs it. I needs it now~

I'd highly recommend Spin Tires to anyone with an interest in realistic physics, off roading, rock crawling, mudding and orienteering.  If you're looking for high speed off roading, this is not your game.  You need to choose your best line and constantly evaluate your situation, as things can get messy in a hurry.
Pros:
deformable terrain
accurate simulation of suspension flex, locking differentials, and all wheel drive
amazing detail - mud collects on tires, diesel smoke billows from exhaust, the list goes on...
engine sounds are good - trucks sound like trucks, not toys
winching/logging and exploration
Cons:
camera limitations - this is my biggest problem with the game.  It is truly unique, and I understand that with an off roading game, you need a 360' view of your surroundings.  But I often feel like I can't zoom out enough.  The view dips in and out, and it can really test your patience
draw distance - it's a little dissapointing that you can only see about 200 yards out
map variety is lacking - maybe jungle, desert or arctic terrains could be a future installment
Overall, I really like this game.  No other off-roading game comes close.  If you ever wanted to be a lumberjack and learn how off roading works, it'll be money well spent.

It first came out for mobile, and it sure seemed to be designed for it. You make a vault, gather resource and wait. Oh yes, there is a lot of waiting in this game: You wait for your resources, crafting, going to the wastelands, etc. The good thing for mobile is that you can open the game anytime, anywhere. This is obviously not the case for PC.
Also, your save files do not move over to different platforms. All vaults have their individual save files that are saved locally. This means, whatever progress and in-game purchases you made STAY ON THAT VAULT AND ONLY THAT VAULT. I don't know about you, but to me that seems to be an absolute waste of money. There are ways to import save files across mobile to PC, but really who would waste so much effort just for that. If they supported automatic file sync across platforms, this game would be much more enjoyable.
Don't misunderstand, I love Fallout Shelter. I have over 80 dwellers in my phone and it took a lot of time to reach that level. I just feel like playing the game on PC would be a waste of time since you can't sync your files anywhere else; it just stays there.
First of all, a lot of you guys seem to think that I don't know that the save files can be moved from different devices. It is, in fact, possible and I acknowledged it in my review. There are dozens of websites that guide you on how to do it and even a Steam guide on that topic.
Second, I marked this review negative not because I don't like the game nor the PC port; both are great. I'm did this because having played it on mobile for months, I just feel like the waiting and low maintenance made it seem like a mobile game. If you like to play idle/waiting games on PC, then this game is for you.
I spent months playing this game on mobile so I don't see a reason to suddenly move to PC just because it is released here. I've grown comfortable playing with my phone and I've decided to stick with it. I have moved my save files to PC just to try it out and it really works, but still not enough motivation for me to switch platforms.

HiRez may very well have fixed the glaring issues with OB44, but I'm going to leave this review as it is for posterity.
Once upon a time, this was a fun game. back when I started in early October, I found this game to be a nice reprieve from the typical fast-paced, low time-to-kill shooters that one tends to find. I remember all the fun things like how Drogoz could fly at sonic speeds, and all the bad things like Skye's inescapable time bomb. I still flinch a bit when I hear the phrase "Time's Ticking!". Unfortunately, time and time again, HiRez have shown that they intrinsically do not care about people having fun.
Drogoz' speed limit was the first sign that things were going downhill for me. Instead of incorporating this fun little exploit into his kit, HiRez insisted that everybody has to sluggishly hover about in midair, becoming prime prey for all the hitscan champions out there. This, of course, is the wrong way to go about things. Multiple developers have taken quirks in the code and blown them up into full features, like rocket jumping in Quake, or the genocidal warmonger Gandhi in Civilisation. To me, this change just felt like HiRez were becoming the anti-fun police.
Last month, they introduced a new champion, 'Maeve', whose arrival significantly shifted the game's dynamics. Whereas most flankers can be easily dealt with if not caught off-guard, Maeve is so stupidly agile that hitting her is nigh impossible on a champion that doesn't have constant hitscan weapons, not to mention the effective HP that she has from all her health regen cards and her insane damage output. However, the biggest issue with her is that she has rendered Skye completely and utterly obsolete. There is absolutely no reason whatsoever to play as Skye anymore. HiRez have killed a champion that his been in this game since the closed beta, yet they've gotten away with it.
And now, we've just gone through the 'Season 1' update, wherein they may very well have just signalled this game's death.
Firstly, they did not sufficiently test this update; the developers promised a second round of testing on the public test server which never came. And during that sole round, I found that choosing the champion Barik would cause the match to never load up. How have HiRez solved this? By just disabling the champion.
And then, there's this god-awful crafting system that they've just introduced. Prior to the update, you could just go ahead and buy cards with the gold that you can grind in-game, but now, the only way to get cards is to unbox them or use 'essence' to purchase them. How is essence obtained? By getting dupe cards in the chests. This makes the game incredibly inaccessible to new players, as they are completely dependant on RNG when it comes to creating a new loadout, and keep in mind that there is 22 champs, with 16 cards each. That means that there is a 1/352 chance of getting the card that you want.
Or, rather, it would be that, if there weren't also emotes, poses and sprays in this chest, further decreasing the probability of getting anything useful, never mind the 66 legendary cards, which were just introduced, that can severely change the way a character plays. Now, here's something interesting; before the update, people extrapolated from the costs of the standard cards that legendaries would probably cost 10,000 essence. Despite this being used in calculations all over the place, HiRez decided it would be a good idea to make them cost 18,000 instead. It costs 792000 essence to unlock all the non-default legendary cards. I, a person with most things unlocked, probably average at about 1,500 essence per chest. It is inexcusable how the game has locked away playstyle customisation,
, behind what is essentially a paywall, since you're going to have to buy boosters if you want to grind for gold, or even just directly pay for the chests.
And that's just about the game itself. I could probably go on for a while about the general attitude of the members of the dev team that hand public relations, like one particular fellow who called people that didn't like the old Time Bomb 'noobs' (despite it being a guaranteed kill in a massive range), and how he seems to have disregarded all crticism on Reddit since it's just a 'hole for whiners'.
I've seen this level of greed kill a fair few games in my time. I don't want Paladins to die, but at this rate it is going to die a very unceremonious death. Of course, it wouldn't be HiRez' first failure. Just look at Global Agenda and Tribes: Ascend.

Alan Wake is a strange beast, it does some things very, very well and some other things horribly bad.
To start off with the good stuff, the game has an amazing story. It's suspenceful, fresh, unpredictable and full of twists. It can be a little confusing and weird at times, but at the end of the day it wraps up things well.
Amazing atmosphere thanks to the wonderful graphics, light effects and good music, the woods give an eerie feeling and you almost could feel the night breeze on your face, along with the sense of insecurity coming from wandering a forest at night, with enemies hiding in the shadows of every tree.
The gameplay it's very good in my opinion. All enemies are shrouded in darkness and you must cast the darkness away before you can harm them. You have a small amount of tools to succeed in your goal. The first and most basic is your flashlight, it acts both as a shield remover and as a crowd control measure, by staggering your targets for a couple of seconds every time you light them up. It has unlimited power but it will take some seconds to recharge or a new battery after intense use. It takes some seconds to drain away their shields with the flashlight though so you will have something better to deal with a large group of enemies. The flares help you in that kind of situation, by keeping your opponents from enter their area of effect and also draining their shields. Then you have two "I win" buttons: flasbangs and flare gun. Both instantly kill most enemies in their blast radius, the big difference is that the flare gun has more range and it leaves a flare burning on the ground after the initial blast. Then, once their shields are down, you have to use guns to finish them off. Unlike in many games where you reload in a split second by just changing magazine, here your character inserts every single round in the weapon, taking quite long, so tactically choosing when to reload is crucial to succeed.
AI is quite good, it constantly tries, and often manages, to flank and sorround you. It uses the environment, the trees and rocks to close distance in the safest way possible. As said, AI tries to get melee range by default but it can also trow projectiles, often you'll see enemies covering the advance of other enemies with their projectile weaponry.
Unfortunatly, from the gameplay also comes the game's greatest flaw: its EXTREME linearity and monotonousness. The game starts very fresh and very fun but after some chapters it will feel like a chore that you endure just to see the ending of the story. You have one single tipe of enemy, a humanoid figure that wields various kinds of work tools as weapons, with two variants: a brute variant that can soak more damage and has better shields and a fast variant, that moves around very fast and employs hit and run tactics against you. You also have to deal with some environmental hazards that can be destroyed with light. These enemies are the same from the first to the last chapter, you meet them very often and you fight them in the same way, with the same weapons and in the same setting almost every time. Encounters WILL become extremely repetitive, monotonous and tedious. Also, it's quite annoying that the game spawns a lot of enemies right behind you as a cheap way to increase difficulty.
Controls and camera are really bad. Your character moves slowly, takes some time to start moving and recover after a hit and gains momentum, meaning precise movement is hard to achieve. The camera is set too far to the left (or the right) of your character, making you essentially blind in a side or the other that, coupled with the AI's tendency to flank, will make you take a lot of free damage. Those flaws may be intentional, but they are really annoying making some fights artificially hard.
One other thing that really annoyed me is that at the end of every level you are stripped of all your weapons and items, there's nothing more irritating than collect a lot of good stuff and save a lot of resources just to have them taken away from you.
I would give this game a 7/10, and recommend it if you don't mind monotousness and enjoy atmosphere, story and are looking for something fresh and new. Definitely buy if you can find it on sale.

This game is amazing. It's not super realistic, but it is realistic enough for you to get an appreciation for how hard getting anywhere in space is. So instead of wasting time and words telling you what KSP does right I'd like to take some time to highlight its very few flaws.
- Planets are extremely barren. This seems to be a problem endemic to any game where you can go down to a planet's surface; I first noticed it in the original Mass Effect, then in KSP, then later in Space Engineers. While getting to the planet is fun and challenging, there is very little to do once you actually get there.
- To really enjoy KSP you have to find your own objectives. Once you start recognizing how samey the contracts can be you need to come up with your own project, or perhaps impose restrictions on yourself (no reloading failed launches!), and I find that a lot of people don't have what it takes to entertain themselves in a sandbox this large.
- There's no cute girls in it waaaaaah
- It is tempting for the more chaotically-minded among us to forego launching rockets and just making things explode in ways that glitch o ut the physics engine. This is never a thing I found very fun but hey, the odds of you being me are less than one in seven billion so maybe you'll think different.
Overall this isn't a game for everyone; if you don't think you can tolerate a thoughtful, meditative experience you should probably go back to Dark Souls or Call of Battlefield or what-have-you.

Alan Wake is most likely the best game I've played thus far that combines psychological horror with a heavily plot-driven storyline that leaves much to the players' interpretations. While it is true that other games have accomplished one or the other on their own, very few have successfully combined both for a lengthy gaming experience - with the only others in my mind being Fatal Frame and the early renditions of Silent Hill. If played on a higher difficulty, one truly experiences the definition of psychological horror: a feeling of helplessness against the might of Alan's dark enemies. The somewhat painful (in a largely bad sense of the word) sequences in the forests are offset by very great moments of the game, such as the concert and Night Life in Bright Falls. While the combat will eventually feel lacklustre, Alan Wake never fails to deter the suspense and interest that a game of this genre and caliber should generate.
On a side note, I felt the change of gameplay and plot focus in American Nightmare to be quite refreshing. Sign me up for Episode 2.

If you hate dinosaurs, then this is your golden opportunity.
Jokes aside, it's no doubt worth the money. It provides exciting and sometimes terrifying (spinosaurus, deinosuchus, t-rex) combat against various kinds of dinosaurs. You get to use many types of weapons and other tools of destruction such as VTOLs and tanks.
Pros:
- Surprising amounts of depth and customization via classes, their weapons and augments that let you play the way you want
- Unreal engine means it runs smoothly and provides great visuals
- Voice commands and taunts to help you communicate and annoy easily
- Gigantic (and smaller) dinosaurs with very impressive animations and diverse approaches to combat
- A leveling system to give you a feel of progression and achievement
- An open-world game mode which I've not yet tried but sounds very interesting
- The developers seem committed and appear to release updates frequently

First, I am gonna say about the game itself. It's bigger and better compared to Shadow of Mordor. As someone who was a fan of Assassin's Creed and currently loathed Ubisoft to the max, this is a good reminiscene of what I love before. Of course there's no Frigate we can play with in the ocean but a Drake can be a nice substitute while capturing enemy fortress with your army of Orcs. Discovering maps are fun too as now we have more regions to be explored and conquered. More interesting Captains and Warchiefs to be found. I like the artisty ones like Poet and Singer. Their attributes and skills are more menacing now as they leveled up. Weapons, armors and rings can be easily acquired through drops from Captains. While gems can be socketed and upgrade which dropped from certain orcs. The story is also nice and while others might questioning why there's a black man in Gondorian ranks, there's a nice story behind it and plausible for Lord of the Ring universe. Empowering women is not new in the lore and Idril is a very strong Gondorian soldier with high spirit. There are many women characters in the story although not playable.
On the cons side of this game, currently there are bugs occured. Quite frequent as of writing but no crashes so far (unlike what I heard from others on Youtube). So far, the bugs didnt stop the game completely but quite annoying when happened. Such as the banter when a Captain or Warchief encounters you, they-didn't-say-a-thing bug where Talion having a quiet staring contest with them. Sometimes happened when Talion capturing a fortress, happened to me twice. While the game is quite repetitive, it's not in a bad way tho for me, the most annoying part would be when you're gaining higher levels as the Captains and Warchiefs getting more troublesome. They will quickly adapted to your attacks and gradually you have lesser way to attack them. It's very challenging especially when you encounter more Orcs ambushing or even betraying you. I have a hard time fighting a Captain that has Commander attribute (call in more orcs reinforcement) plus Beastmaster attribute (call in caragors or Graug). Not forgetting his immunities and whatnot.
While I do recommend this game for others if they still hesitated due to microtransactions, it wasn't a big deal. I wonder why WB put it in in the first place considering most of the lootboxes are kinda useless when you attain higher level as it's according to your levels anyway. Because you dont even need to spend any to play the game. I think, the only thing that really help quickly to proceed to the end game would be the EXP Boost thing. That's because of gaining what kind of Orcs you want anyway since by level 20 (and doing side quests), you can get all basic Skills to be unlocked plus several secondary skills. The real use of your levels is to get higher levels of Orcs. The Orcs that you get from lootboxes are usually not good enough compared to the one you can get whom you can level them up yourself. It's okay if you think this Microtransaction is ethically wrong, it's up to you.
Overall, I give this game 7/10. Would love to give it an 8 only if the bugs were fixed.

Hotline Miami is one of the hardest games I have played in my life. While the game may differ from many shooters in the sense that 1 bullet, or swing from a melee can end everything, the games are extremly enjoyable.
The Great Level Design Compliments every play style that can be associated with one of 26 masks, 23 of which provide a gameplay changing aspect or weapon to start out with, and no weapon in the game is considered overpowered or underpowered.
The game also has a kickass soundtrack that makes the atmosphere of every level enjoyable.
Of course, there is a couple of cons that many players have to consider. Right out of the tutorial, the game doesn't hold your hand. In fact, it takes a hammer and a nail, and smashes it into the joints of your fingers. The game is extremly difficult, and you as a player has to have cougar like reactions. Sometimes, it is insane how fast enimies react. If you are a player that can't keep up with Bruce Lee reaction times, than do yourself a favour and not waste money on a game you will probably never pass the 3rd chapter.
There is another problem with hitreg for melee weapons. At some moments, you clearly can see your melee attack connect with the enemy, but the game sometimes disagrees and acts as if you never hit them in the first place.  Of the time of this review, I have 1400 hours of the First Person game "Team Fortess 2", and the hitreg in that game  is horrendous, but hitreg in this game just comes close to that.
My last gripe is boss battles. These battles do add diversity from the regular kill everyone on the map, but they are extremly difficult for first time players. There is no big hint  to beat the enemy (other than small arrows that point out weapons for some bosses), so it is up to you to figure out the stradigy. If  you are stuck on a boss for about 5-10 minutes, I suggest looking up the stradigy online or on steam community guides.
