Taken at face value, this game provides hours of fun by interacting with the much-loved nemesis system which has received a hug update but, having sunk a considerable amount of hours into this game, I feel like I should give you a heads up before you even think about buying
Pros:
Updated nemesis system with a significant variety of orcs: the tribe of the orc influences their abilities and playstyle in interesting ways
Orc Pokemon arena: you can send your followers into battle to level them up or, if they die, recruit a new and improved orc (the one who defeated them) - gotta catc em all
Siege mechanic is promising (but serious flaws)
Nice animations
Dominated orcs still maintain their personality - they're not just zombies anymore... sort of
Cons:
Tribe system and various abilities of orcs are totally ignored - I thought tribal mechanics would pave the way for intense rivalries, but it feels like an entirely missed opportunity. WB said that picking your overlord would change the landscape to reflect their tribe but it is entirely negligble and goes unnoticed
Orc Pokemon: cool idea of leveling your followers but immensely frustrating. Super clunky mechanics and you may find your overpowered legendary orc being inexplicably steamrolled by a weak orc. Sometimes they just stand there without attacking (not to do with their weaknesses/fears etc just bad AI/programming).
Story:
- the story is abysmal which is surprising because it had so much potential. Each storyline feels entirely disjointed and you feel no sense of accomplishment and feeling unsure at what point you were supposed to complete each mission
- the Gondor missions are reskinned slave missions from the first game: "go to point X. Free X amount of soldiers. Fight enemy warchief guarding them" rinse and repeat
- each individual story feels unfinished and ends abruptly - probably because the content was either removed or will appear subsequently as paid DLCs to justify the season pass price (which did not come with the already exhorbitant price of the Silver or Gold editions)
Super Cons (skip here):
- same as all other reviews: microtransactions. WB claimed that it wouldn't be required to play the game but the way the game was structured begs to differ: the most insulting was when a particular warchief blatantly tells you to visit a certain orc to help build your army and that orc is the one you see when you enter the marketplace. So not only are microtransactions implemented into a single-player game, but the actual characters in the story encourage you to enter the marketplace and buy lootboxes which is totally immersion-breaking and infuriating
Act IV: without spoiling too much, the game finishes in Act III which was actually interesting. However, Act IV is a pure grindfest. There is absolutely zero story (no exaggeration) - you have to defend your forts 20 times against progressively overpowered enemies who way outlevel your orcs, forcing you to grind to level yourself up so you can either dominate them or build up your own powerful army. This shoehorns in microtransactions and encourages you to buy XP boosts or additional orcs from the marketplace. The only shred of story after Act III is a short video which i recommend just looking up unless you're a completionist
No endgame: having endured the prolonged grindfest of Act IV, there is nothing to look forward to. Sure, you can play online sieges but it's more or less the same thing and, of course, you soon hit the paywall with that too. After winning and increasing your siege attack, you run into super overpowered legendary orcs with no weaknesses and each having super attacks and abilities (such as "no chance") and the game expects you to take the fort in 10 minutes or you get little reward for your effort
Complete disregard for lore: I would be ok if WB straight up admitted that Shadow of War was LOTR fanfiction but instead, they try to tell you that this is how it happened and basically forcibly insert their own lore (see Act IV ending) which I woudln't really mind but is kind of eh. Another example was how they claimed that Shelob and Gollum were the unsung heroes (but I won't spoil anything)
Also: Mirian disappeared from my game - I sold a bunch of gear and continued playing, only to find after I completed a siege I had lost 40,000 Mirian which had been reduced to 836. I'm not alone in this issue and it is frustrating when you earn all the mirian to buy loot boxes only to have your money taken from you. I'm definitely not spending real money on this ridiculous market
Summary: I wanted to love this game but the nemisis system was entirely overshadowed by the lack of compelling story and the Act IV endgame grindfest just shows a blatant disregard for the gamers/customers by replacing what should be interesting story to encourage you to finish with microtransactions in an annoying, pay-to-win fashion

Shadow of War is a tough one to review. Its basically a game that has some love in it wrapped around some really terrible packaging.
The jist of it is this. The actual combat and the Nemesis sytem are incredibly well done. It offers a lot of scenarios in which the player will find himself in them, such as getting ambushed by an Orc's blood brother you killed hours ago and then you summon your bodyguard at which point he also betrays you. The Orcs also have this abillity to adapt to your skills especially the tougher captains. At one point the legendary orc I was fighting has adapted to every single attack I had and the only thing I could do was run away and stealth attack him over and over since that was his only weakness. The voice acting of all the captains is purely well done and not just the orcs but the main characters as well. It all feels high quality.
Sadly thats all the good there is and while some may find that enough, others will despise everything else that is bad. The first thing you'll notice is that the game is stuck in the past with the same open world formula Ubisoft games had in the past. Tedious collectibles that are mandatory if you wish to gain skill points, repetitive and boring main quests that feel like they are just markers on your to do list. It can get boring incredibly fast. Capturing forts while it feels great at first, also becomes repetitive. The worst conteder though is the final act which puts you in a series of grinding that its hard not to quit. I personally gave up, after 30 hours of gameplay that I spent capturing all the forts and doing all the main quests and most of the collectibles I was not going to spend another 20 hours of the same thing just to get a 3 minute cinematic that reveales the faith of Talion which let me tell you, its ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. It will somehow tie things with The LOTR. I'm not entirely sure that was a good thing or a cheap thing to do.
Would I recommend this game? On full price, no. I'd say given the negatives and positives of the game, a below 30 euros price would be a better fit. Overall a 7.9 out 10 game.

Alan Wake is an interesting little piece. For a horror game, it's not particularly horrifying. For a shooter, it's not particularly innovative. Yet, in spite of these things, it's still quite entertaining.
The game's primary focus is the rather bizarre story and how it is told. I'd best describe it as a video game version of a Steven King Miniseries...and frankly I think the game would too. The entire game is told from the perspective, or rather, narrative of the titular Alan Wake, a very popular horror novalist with some deep rooted issues and typical famous-person life problems. When I say narrative, I mean it quiet literally; the story is told to you mostly through novel-style narration; as if what is happening is all just a book that Wake is in the proccess of writing. He regularly cites Steven King as his favorite author, and compares much of the darkness and chaos around him to the happenings of King's books.
Again, a Video Game Steven King Miniseries. Not only is the theme accurate, but every segment of the game begins and ends as if it were a new episode of a television broadcast, even going so far as to include "Previously, on Alan Wake" followed by replaying things that you quite literally just went through. The game's commitment to style is...admirable?
Either way, it works in my opinion. Don't take "Steven King Miniseries" as a criticism; that theme is much of what makes Alan Wake entertaining in spite of being relatively poor as far as "horror" goes. The game does good to leave out all of of "King's Tropes." No blood-sucking christians, one-dimensional bullies or ham-fisted political contexts to be found here, just otherworldly weirdness and a poor, hapless sap stuck in the middle of it all.
I found myself very much enjoying Alan Wake, even though it didn't give me the spookenings that I was initially hoping for, aside from a couple of "oh♥♥♥♥♥♥oh god what do I do" moments until you realize that whatever you are afraid of is rather easily dispatched with a flashlight and a shotgun.
If you aren't interested in story, don't play Alan Wake. There are far better horror games to spook your socks off to. If I were to have another criticism, it would be that the controls do suffer a wee bit from Consolitus. If you're the kind to use a gamepad in a shooter, you won't have any problems and I'd recommend it. If you're a K&M purist like me however, it WILL take some getting used to, though once you pick up on it you shouldn't have any problems.
All and all, as a story I highly recommend Alan Wake. It's just surreal and intriguing enough to keep you playing, and the action can be fun, if not rather derivative.

Fallout 1 and 2 remain favorites of mine. While the FPS updates of Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas were great in their own way, inExile's Wasteland 2 is the true "successor" to Fallout's vibe and gameplay.
This makes sense when you realize the Fallout universe was created as an IP-claim-avoiding homage to the original Wasteland.
Many of the great people that worked on Fallout 1 & 2 have returned to make Wasteland 2, including great work from Chris Avellone on writing and design and the return of Mark Morgan's beautiful ambient music.
It's worth noting this is game is thematically dark, with far less of the goofy humor that started to undermine the Fallout series. There's swearing, sex, drugs, lots of graphic violence, and many, many morally ambiguous choices.
I haven't even finished the game yet, but I am already planning a second trip through the wastes.
Highly recommended for fans of Fallout 1 and 2, Torment, Baldur's Gate, and post-apocalyptic fiction.

I wasn't really a committed fan of the original Wasteland - by the time I had heard about it, the first Fallout game was released so I played Fallout instead. It was one of those things where I would have been terribly addicted to the original...if I had a computer back when it was released.

Stick with it...it'll draw you in and suddenly it'll be 3am on a work night. As it has to me the past week or so of playing it. At about 70 hours, I still know I have a fairly long way to go to finally finish all these missions.
I'm going to take inXile's word that the game will be moddable. It definitely should be! There's a lot of empty space on the maps that could use something interesting. There could definitely be something that could be done with some of the loosely affiliated raiders in the area, too. It would also be nice to have more situations where those robot parts would come in handy. The robots/synths are really more nuisance than fun to beat...they don't really drop a lot of loot. You'd think, considering that the robots scavenge for equipment everywhere that they'd have something at least besides the servo or optics that you tore out of their frame. I think a talented modder could go crazy with this.
I know there are a lot of different endings based on your choices in the game, though sometimes those choices felt like they were more as a result of impatience about having to run around and do chores in some small town oppressed by thugs that you want to be on the good side of and wind up wiping out those who gave you the chores. Not sure how that plays out, but it'll be interesting. That sort of replayability puts it on par with anything out there right now.
I also felt there could be a little more depth with the squad based combat. Sure, you get a bonus for hiding behind a box or a car hulk...but always the same bonus? Sometimes you can shoot through something that seems like a wall and have just as high a hit percentage as if you could if you were totally in the clear. There's an effect if an opponent is too close to you and you only have ranged weapons equipped, but that seems like it would effect a sniper rifle far more than an assault rifle or a shotgun. As in, you need to get back at least x number of spaces to clear that effect.
Also, the guns jamming. Ugh. It's enough to make you want to cheat and give yourself enough anti-jamming mods to stop it from happening. It definitely seems to happen far more to your team than it does to the enemy. Even if you have a 4% jam rate, it seems to happen early on at closer to 20%. If I have a 0% jamming rate from weapons mods, that gun better not jam. I've seen those guns jam. I know they sort of nerfed it in the new patch, but it's still somewhat more frequent than you'd expect. It could have been tied to weapon maintenance, which would be part of weaponsmithing...it would be nice to use that skill for something other than adding mods and taking them off.
That said, this is a fantastic game. It's more stable than pretty much any game I've played in a long time, which is a testament to how hard inXile worked at testing and fixing it throughout the beta phase. There is a lot here to work with and it has all the little things that really make it a great one to play. This is the first game I think that could occupy all of my allotted gaming time since I started playing Skyrim a couple years ago.

Spintires is an off-road simulator. It's a very niche genre without a whole lot of competition. In fact, the only game you can compare Spintires to on Steam is probably "Off-Road Drive", which is also a great game.
As an avid off-roader IRL (as they say), I can attest to this game's ability to scratch that off-roading itch a little bit. Only the real thing is better. The mud and water deformation is amazing (an apparently, award winning). The physics of driving a vehicle off-road is as close to the real thing as I've ever seen in a video game; there is no going fast in this game. The fastest you can go is maybe 20 MPH if you find some paved road (which is rare) and shift it into high gear. Ostensibly, the game is about logging. More accurately, hauling lumber through the Russian backwoods.  That's it, haul lumber from point A to point B, alone or with a "crew" of up to 4. Of course, you could just ignore all that and just go hit the trails, which is also really fun.
That said, this game isn't for everyone. My wife watched as, for 15 minutes, a buddy and I struggled, trial-and-errored and fought a piece of terrain which was only about 10 feet long. Let me be clear: 15 minutes to go 10 feet. She couldn't understand the appeal of that, and I can totally understand why many would be turned off by it. But you know, THAT IS OFF-ROADING. That's how it goes down in a real life, sometimes even longer to go an even shorter distance! But off-roaders live for that sort of thing. I absolutely love the technical ability and intestinal fotitude needed to tackle terrain like that. By the way, the winching system is stellar! Since the game is so good at capturing that, this is not an easy game. On top of the technical challenge of maneuvering an 8x8 monstrosity towing a trailer full of long logs through tight slush, your truck has both limited fuel and hit points. Yeah, here comes the pain.
There are cons however, ones that luckily can be remedied fairly easily.
- The damage model is inconsistent and frankly a bit harsh. I'll be driving my little UAZ 4x4 in some gummy muck, hit a rock a bit larger than my vehicle likes, take it right in the undercarriage and I'll do about 1-7 hit points of damage. Then I'll hit a tree barely any larger than a sapling with my front bumper going slower than when I hit the aforementioned rock and cause 25-55 points of damage! Quite a bit when you have 200 HP. This damage model also COMPLETELY negates using 4WD high; when you find a bumpy but solid road, not a whole lot of mud, you'll be tempted to put it in high to get a little more speed. WELL DON'T. Those tiny little bumps will start hitting you for 10, 15, 25, 50 or more hit points even if you're hitting them with your tires. Found a paved road? Think it's time to shift it into high gear? WRONG. I tried this with on of the big hauler trucks, gathered a decent amount of speed, hit a dip and BAM! 200+ damage in one hit! Why am I being punished for driving 25 MPH on a paved road? I don't get the logic there. I'm not sure what this is supposed to be simulating. Maybe these Russian trucks are made of glass?
- The maps. There about 5 or so maps and they are quite large and can take quite a while to explore. However, let's be honest Spintires fans, they're all the same. Yes, some have more water than others, one even has a volcano, but at the end of the day you're spending about 80% of the time driving (and getting stuck in) mud, 10% in water, 5% in dirt and 5% on rocks and other rough terrain. The majority of these maps are covered in impassible forest, with trees so close to each other there's no way to squeeze between them. Also, all too often the terrain texture is grass or dirt, then when you drive on it, it ends up being mud. Deep, gummy, unforgiving mud.
- I don't understand why there isn't an official sandbox mode. It seems to fit this game perfectly. The logging and hauling is great. Tons of fun. A great challenge. But sometimes I just want it to drop me on a map, infinite fuel, damage turned off, let me choose ANY truck in the game and just let me GO, with friends too!
- Excuse my language, and I'm sorry if this offends anyone, but the only trucks in the game are Russian sh*tboxes. Gutless wonders, every last of 'em. I don't know if licensing Jeeps, Toyotas and Land Rovers was too expensive or what, but we need something different. Even the big diesel trucks feel way too large and heavy for the amount of power they have, which is probably what it's actually like in the real world. The UAZ is a tiny Jeep imitation, it doesn't need much power, but they give it to you with placid, pizza cutter tires. Imagine taking THAT in the mud. Yeah, you get real cozy with your winch. Broncos, Blazers, Hiluxes, CJs, Wranglers, Patrols, FJ40s... gimmie gimmie gimmie!
Finally, this game was born to be modded and has a large and healthy modding community. It's just a matter of time before all of the above gripes are addressed (Workshop integration would be amazing!) So for now, this game is great, but given time, Spintires will become the greatest off-road sim of all time.

Secondly, the freaking cross platform play is absolutely wonderful but no where necessary to fully enjoy the game. The fact that I can lay in bed and continue playing is huge and seemless. I couldn't have expected more for the total of $20 I paid for this game and appreciate the vast amount of fun that it has given me.

First, I am gonna say about the game itself. It's bigger and better compared to Shadow of Mordor. As someone who was a fan of Assassin's Creed and currently loathed Ubisoft to the max, this is a good reminiscene of what I love before. Of course there's no Frigate we can play with in the ocean but a Drake can be a nice substitute while capturing enemy fortress with your army of Orcs. Discovering maps are fun too as now we have more regions to be explored and conquered. More interesting Captains and Warchiefs to be found. I like the artisty ones like Poet and Singer. Their attributes and skills are more menacing now as they leveled up. Weapons, armors and rings can be easily acquired through drops from Captains. While gems can be socketed and upgrade which dropped from certain orcs. The story is also nice and while others might questioning why there's a black man in Gondorian ranks, there's a nice story behind it and plausible for Lord of the Ring universe. Empowering women is not new in the lore and Idril is a very strong Gondorian soldier with high spirit. There are many women characters in the story although not playable.
On the cons side of this game, currently there are bugs occured. Quite frequent as of writing but no crashes so far (unlike what I heard from others on Youtube). So far, the bugs didnt stop the game completely but quite annoying when happened. Such as the banter when a Captain or Warchief encounters you, they-didn't-say-a-thing bug where Talion having a quiet staring contest with them. Sometimes happened when Talion capturing a fortress, happened to me twice. While the game is quite repetitive, it's not in a bad way tho for me, the most annoying part would be when you're gaining higher levels as the Captains and Warchiefs getting more troublesome. They will quickly adapted to your attacks and gradually you have lesser way to attack them. It's very challenging especially when you encounter more Orcs ambushing or even betraying you. I have a hard time fighting a Captain that has Commander attribute (call in more orcs reinforcement) plus Beastmaster attribute (call in caragors or Graug). Not forgetting his immunities and whatnot.
While I do recommend this game for others if they still hesitated due to microtransactions, it wasn't a big deal. I wonder why WB put it in in the first place considering most of the lootboxes are kinda useless when you attain higher level as it's according to your levels anyway. Because you dont even need to spend any to play the game. I think, the only thing that really help quickly to proceed to the end game would be the EXP Boost thing. That's because of gaining what kind of Orcs you want anyway since by level 20 (and doing side quests), you can get all basic Skills to be unlocked plus several secondary skills. The real use of your levels is to get higher levels of Orcs. The Orcs that you get from lootboxes are usually not good enough compared to the one you can get whom you can level them up yourself. It's okay if you think this Microtransaction is ethically wrong, it's up to you.
Overall, I give this game 7/10. Would love to give it an 8 only if the bugs were fixed.

I first picked this up for android while waiting for Fallout 4, since this was launched in the meanwhile as part of the hype. It has always been free, and is now available on Steam as well. Compared to other free tablet ports this is pretty decent, but it's nothing more than a timesink, to be honest.
Basically, you get your shot at constructing your own Fallout vault. A variety of rooms provide different bonuses or resources, and 4 main resources are needed: power, food, water and caps. What this game is about is pretty much down to expanding your vault while making sure you have the resource needed for it.
As such, this is not a game that will challenge your intellect that much, neither will it require cool nerves or lightning reflexes, it's more about planning, building and then waiting while your resources stock up. The waiting I figure is part of making players buy certain add-ons, wich are sold in-game, but these are not necessary for the game, it just makes progression quicker. If needed you can also do quests to gain additional resources, and belive it or not, but the quest stories are sometimes better than the ones in Fallout 4.
All in all, as a timesink and considering it's free, there's worse alternatives out there, and for someone that's a fan of the Fallout franchise, this is a good way to quickly kill a few minutes when needed, or even an occasional hour.

Taken at face value, this game provides hours of fun by interacting with the much-loved nemesis system which has received a hug update but, having sunk a considerable amount of hours into this game, I feel like I should give you a heads up before you even think about buying
Pros:
Updated nemesis system with a significant variety of orcs: the tribe of the orc influences their abilities and playstyle in interesting ways
Orc Pokemon arena: you can send your followers into battle to level them up or, if they die, recruit a new and improved orc (the one who defeated them) - gotta catc em all
Siege mechanic is promising (but serious flaws)
Nice animations
Dominated orcs still maintain their personality - they're not just zombies anymore... sort of
Cons:
Tribe system and various abilities of orcs are totally ignored - I thought tribal mechanics would pave the way for intense rivalries, but it feels like an entirely missed opportunity. WB said that picking your overlord would change the landscape to reflect their tribe but it is entirely negligble and goes unnoticed
Orc Pokemon: cool idea of leveling your followers but immensely frustrating. Super clunky mechanics and you may find your overpowered legendary orc being inexplicably steamrolled by a weak orc. Sometimes they just stand there without attacking (not to do with their weaknesses/fears etc just bad AI/programming).
Story:
- the story is abysmal which is surprising because it had so much potential. Each storyline feels entirely disjointed and you feel no sense of accomplishment and feeling unsure at what point you were supposed to complete each mission
- the Gondor missions are reskinned slave missions from the first game: "go to point X. Free X amount of soldiers. Fight enemy warchief guarding them" rinse and repeat
- each individual story feels unfinished and ends abruptly - probably because the content was either removed or will appear subsequently as paid DLCs to justify the season pass price (which did not come with the already exhorbitant price of the Silver or Gold editions)
Super Cons (skip here):
- same as all other reviews: microtransactions. WB claimed that it wouldn't be required to play the game but the way the game was structured begs to differ: the most insulting was when a particular warchief blatantly tells you to visit a certain orc to help build your army and that orc is the one you see when you enter the marketplace. So not only are microtransactions implemented into a single-player game, but the actual characters in the story encourage you to enter the marketplace and buy lootboxes which is totally immersion-breaking and infuriating
Act IV: without spoiling too much, the game finishes in Act III which was actually interesting. However, Act IV is a pure grindfest. There is absolutely zero story (no exaggeration) - you have to defend your forts 20 times against progressively overpowered enemies who way outlevel your orcs, forcing you to grind to level yourself up so you can either dominate them or build up your own powerful army. This shoehorns in microtransactions and encourages you to buy XP boosts or additional orcs from the marketplace. The only shred of story after Act III is a short video which i recommend just looking up unless you're a completionist
No endgame: having endured the prolonged grindfest of Act IV, there is nothing to look forward to. Sure, you can play online sieges but it's more or less the same thing and, of course, you soon hit the paywall with that too. After winning and increasing your siege attack, you run into super overpowered legendary orcs with no weaknesses and each having super attacks and abilities (such as "no chance") and the game expects you to take the fort in 10 minutes or you get little reward for your effort
Complete disregard for lore: I would be ok if WB straight up admitted that Shadow of War was LOTR fanfiction but instead, they try to tell you that this is how it happened and basically forcibly insert their own lore (see Act IV ending) which I woudln't really mind but is kind of eh. Another example was how they claimed that Shelob and Gollum were the unsung heroes (but I won't spoil anything)
Also: Mirian disappeared from my game - I sold a bunch of gear and continued playing, only to find after I completed a siege I had lost 40,000 Mirian which had been reduced to 836. I'm not alone in this issue and it is frustrating when you earn all the mirian to buy loot boxes only to have your money taken from you. I'm definitely not spending real money on this ridiculous market
Summary: I wanted to love this game but the nemisis system was entirely overshadowed by the lack of compelling story and the Act IV endgame grindfest just shows a blatant disregard for the gamers/customers by replacing what should be interesting story to encourage you to finish with microtransactions in an annoying, pay-to-win fashion

Alan Wake is an interesting little piece. For a horror game, it's not particularly horrifying. For a shooter, it's not particularly innovative. Yet, in spite of these things, it's still quite entertaining.
The game's primary focus is the rather bizarre story and how it is told. I'd best describe it as a video game version of a Steven King Miniseries...and frankly I think the game would too. The entire game is told from the perspective, or rather, narrative of the titular Alan Wake, a very popular horror novalist with some deep rooted issues and typical famous-person life problems. When I say narrative, I mean it quiet literally; the story is told to you mostly through novel-style narration; as if what is happening is all just a book that Wake is in the proccess of writing. He regularly cites Steven King as his favorite author, and compares much of the darkness and chaos around him to the happenings of King's books.
Again, a Video Game Steven King Miniseries. Not only is the theme accurate, but every segment of the game begins and ends as if it were a new episode of a television broadcast, even going so far as to include "Previously, on Alan Wake" followed by replaying things that you quite literally just went through. The game's commitment to style is...admirable?
Either way, it works in my opinion. Don't take "Steven King Miniseries" as a criticism; that theme is much of what makes Alan Wake entertaining in spite of being relatively poor as far as "horror" goes. The game does good to leave out all of of "King's Tropes." No blood-sucking christians, one-dimensional bullies or ham-fisted political contexts to be found here, just otherworldly weirdness and a poor, hapless sap stuck in the middle of it all.
I found myself very much enjoying Alan Wake, even though it didn't give me the spookenings that I was initially hoping for, aside from a couple of "oh♥♥♥♥♥♥oh god what do I do" moments until you realize that whatever you are afraid of is rather easily dispatched with a flashlight and a shotgun.
If you aren't interested in story, don't play Alan Wake. There are far better horror games to spook your socks off to. If I were to have another criticism, it would be that the controls do suffer a wee bit from Consolitus. If you're the kind to use a gamepad in a shooter, you won't have any problems and I'd recommend it. If you're a K&M purist like me however, it WILL take some getting used to, though once you pick up on it you shouldn't have any problems.
All and all, as a story I highly recommend Alan Wake. It's just surreal and intriguing enough to keep you playing, and the action can be fun, if not rather derivative.

Warning. This review contains **SPOILERS**.
I was asleep, next to my computer, which was running Mountain. I love the ambient music and sounds, as well as the little piano note that sometimes appears whenever "The Mountain talks". So, yeah, I decided to let it play as a background music while I was sleeping.
After a few hours, at 2am, I heard a very strange music in my dream. I eventually woke up, but I was still half asleep. I tried to open my eyes, slowly, and I saw a gigantic pyramid dashing to my Mountain. The music, man... The music was scary. My screen started flickering, and as I was kinda still sleeping, it felt as like some kind of spirit had entered my computer and was haunting it, just to kill my dear little mountain. As the bloody pyramid came closer and closer, the screen started to turn red, while still flickering, then... Then... A flash. An explosion. Then, the silence. My mountain was destroyed, killed, annihilated, by the bloody pyramid.
20/10.
Actually, I wasn't aware of such a thing, I didn't know we could "lose". I thought Mountain was just a non-game about... well, watching a mountain with some nice ambient sounds. But nope. It's more than that. Or maybe it was just a dream after all. ;D
Anyway, a good non-game worth trying, even just for fun. Or a good background music. :)

I so want to like this game... The story is nice, the writing is good, but the combat is awful. The gameplay is dated, maybe it can appeal to retro gamers or people who mistake boring mechanics with hardcore. There is a lot of boring combats, which is slow and crappy.
The hard consequences that the game touted are...subpar so far. Fallout New Vegas felt more alive and your actions had more weight than here.
To talk in details about the combat system, think fallout without any combat options (no called shots) and moronic AI. You just trade blows with hard-hitting melee sprinters or eagle eyed ranged NPCs that suffer from a preference to eat lead by leaving cover if someone is next to them. It's turn based, but with no tactics (you could call the cover system tactical if you were very nice) and as such it ends up being slow.
The character creation system is poor and having no perks and lackluster attributes leave not so much to the imagination. The skills are varied and made necessary if you don't want to trudge throught the combats.
The dialogues are sometimes a tad strange and you end up with some stereotypical NPCs. They try to put a veneer of gray on your choices with cynicism and "realism", but it often fall flat IMHO due to the comedic nature of some situations.
A lot of the quests are fedex quests made painful by the lack of fast travel, slowness of movement and the ubiquitous boring slow combats.
The so-called inhospitable wastelands are filled with oasis, making the presence of the water mechanics... strange to say the least as it never occured to me I could lack water.
The "open world" is level locked, so even though you could probably go wherever you want, the choices are often limited.
If you have most of the skills (and with the 3 NPCs you can recruit, it's easy to keep nearly all of them maxed) you'll be rich and never have to worry about ammo.
I understand the devs wanted to cater to the nostalgics of Wasteland 1, but gaming has evolved and some mechanics are better left dead in the 90s.
In short, a promising game with crappy combats

If I had any one desire, it'd be deeper, more interesting combat - especially given how common combat is! - but while it's not going to match XCOM: Enemy Unknown in that area, it's not *bad*, either.
Wasteland 2 may not appeal to everyone, but if you're interested an old-school, turn-based CRPG, this'll scratch that itch for you.

Remember the 90s, when you played a game called Fallout? It was supposed to be the sequel to one of the most amazing games ever - Wasteland.  So we played it, it was great, it had a sequel - Fallout 2 - and that was great too. But it was missing something.
Then a big name company tried to revive Fallout. Fans rejoiced. More changes were made, and Fallout 3 was that game that almost killed the series. Not a bad game, but should have been named something else. Maybe "Fallout - Tales from DC" or something. Then New Vegas came out, and brought back the nestalgic feeling we all knew from the original series.
Then, something magical happened. In 2012, Brian Fargo announced he wanted to recreate the classic that started it all. Wasteland 2. We were skeptic, but we tossed our money at the idea anyway. A few of these Kickstarts failed (or close enough to call a fail) - and a few of them saw the slight success they wished for, while others got forgotten about by all but the most die-hard of fans. Then Wasteland 2 came. And blew them all out of the water. Mr. Fargo listened to his fans, and instead of selling out to major companies, keeping the project quiet, or hiring expensive actors, he instead used the money wisely and created a game better than most major games out there. This is the game we should have gotten in place of Fallout decades ago - and it couldn't come at a better time.
The graphics are amazing, and in a retro-new-age sort of way. The game play is simply amazing, requiring you to actually think instead of just jump in guns blazing. And the best part is the fan's opinion mattered. Even in a lot of indy projects, you don't see this anymore - a lot of people see what works in a different game and go there, instead of creating fresh ideas. But instead, Mr. Fargo ignored all the other games, went back to his classic roots, and made the game we wanted to see, not just another "Minecraft with zombies and aliens and 1st person shooting."
If you love RPGs with a rich story and puzzles, games that make you think of your choices before you act, and games that require you to assess a situation before charging in head first, this is for you! If you want a boring game about shooting anything that moves that has a story so generic that the main feature of the game is online multi-player? Go wait for the next Halo or Call of Duty. But give this a try while you wait, you will be hooked!

Tl;dr: A VERY niche game that won't appeal to many people, but is suprisingly good in it's execution and what it sets out to do.
I've only played the first level of the campaign, but had to write a review to say... that was one of the best intros I've seen in a while. Love the art style, and while this gave me the first impression of "random nonsense humor" which I generally don't go for (since, you know, I'm over 13), this felt thought out enough to go from that first impression to just plain ridiculous surrealism (and awesome) after about 15 seconds. I was not expecting to go into this game and have it transform me into a kid blown away by a badass saturday morning cartoon. I would totally watch the s**t out of that show, and it left me wanting to play it just to find out more about the different factions and characters.
Gameplay is odd, for sure. It definitely feels and plays like a flicking game (which is a thing, I guess?), and should be treated as such first and foremost. If you suck at flicking things, you're probably going to hate this game. Aiming isn't too rough though, as you have a ring around your ship when you flick it showing how far your ship will go. The main difficulty comes from the pressure of managing multiple ships in a real time environment. In my hasty flicking, one of my first moves was destroying my entire fleet by flicking it too close to a planet, sucking it into the atmosphere (I still came back and won though, they take it pretty easy on you on the first level). I can see this game getting difficult quickly as you progress.
The odd inclusion of RTS seems to work well and adds a suprising amount of depth for a mechanic that you wouldn't think you could shove depth into, but already from the start on top of the basic expected units there's stealth ships with cloaking and torpedos, and freighters that can carry other ships via tractor beams allowing you to move large fleets over long distances. I'm sure there will be more ships with different abilities as the game progresses.
All in all, it's a very weird, niche game that's a combination of two niche genres. The gameplay is all about the flicking and that's the main appeal, so if you came to this game mostly for the RTS aspect you'll probably be disappointed. The atmosphere and depth just scream RTS though, with the story and even the menus reminding me more of RTSes than a casual flicking game, so it's not really for the casual gamer either. It's a combination that is not going to appeal to very many people (myself included, honestly. Two genres [is flicking a genre?] I don't really care much about.), but it is well done in it's execution. There is enough here for there to be a good chance for me to actually play this again, though it will probably just taunt me from within my massive backlog.

Shadow of War is a tough one to review. Its basically a game that has some love in it wrapped around some really terrible packaging.
The jist of it is this. The actual combat and the Nemesis sytem are incredibly well done. It offers a lot of scenarios in which the player will find himself in them, such as getting ambushed by an Orc's blood brother you killed hours ago and then you summon your bodyguard at which point he also betrays you. The Orcs also have this abillity to adapt to your skills especially the tougher captains. At one point the legendary orc I was fighting has adapted to every single attack I had and the only thing I could do was run away and stealth attack him over and over since that was his only weakness. The voice acting of all the captains is purely well done and not just the orcs but the main characters as well. It all feels high quality.
Sadly thats all the good there is and while some may find that enough, others will despise everything else that is bad. The first thing you'll notice is that the game is stuck in the past with the same open world formula Ubisoft games had in the past. Tedious collectibles that are mandatory if you wish to gain skill points, repetitive and boring main quests that feel like they are just markers on your to do list. It can get boring incredibly fast. Capturing forts while it feels great at first, also becomes repetitive. The worst conteder though is the final act which puts you in a series of grinding that its hard not to quit. I personally gave up, after 30 hours of gameplay that I spent capturing all the forts and doing all the main quests and most of the collectibles I was not going to spend another 20 hours of the same thing just to get a 3 minute cinematic that reveales the faith of Talion which let me tell you, its ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. It will somehow tie things with The LOTR. I'm not entirely sure that was a good thing or a cheap thing to do.
Would I recommend this game? On full price, no. I'd say given the negatives and positives of the game, a below 30 euros price would be a better fit. Overall a 7.9 out 10 game.

TL;DR : Bad PR, fun game....A must buy IF you liked Shadow of Mordor. Above average if you don't. AVOID ACT IV IN STORY MODE. Reasons below.
While I seriously hate the lootbox microtransaction stuff they are trying to pull , but the generally postitive feedback for the game from the players have pushed me over the edge into buying the game since I loved Shadow of Mordor and I was really sad that they did all that. And after playing the game,it is actually pretty great.... until the story reaches ACT IV.
Allow me to explain why act 4 is total garbage first before all else.
ACT III changed the whole game and it's enviroment without a way to switch back and forth after that.
The siege defenses are a reeeeeeeeeeally long grind. With increasing attacker levels each stage (total of 10 stages before you get "true ending") which requires you to go do open world busy work to level up that only gives a slight bit of EXP again and again which was really boring to me, and I liked playing around in the open world with the nemesis system in the first game, that's saying something.
On top of that, to defend against said sieges you will be constantly in need of new uruk captain recruits. Now recruiting uruks isn't that hard but it certainly takes a long time AND (from what I've noticed) New Uruks captains that spawns in ACT IV have significantly higher chances to have traits that makes them un-recruitable (Iron Will , Unbreakable), which makes the grind even more painful and long.
The main quests take about 10-12 hours to complete at most but the grind known as ACT IV is easily 3 to 4 times longer(without buying lootboxes), which lead us to the biggest problem and the most controversal topic related to this game, microtransactions and loot boxes.
ACT IV is without a doubt designed so that it tempts the player to buy lootboxes to skip the process of recruiting uruks. You might say people can just play the game instead and grind it out but seriously no one with the right mind let alone has time to sit around grinding for 40-50 hours just for a true ending (which is just a 3 minutes long cutscene btw lol)(idc if this is considered spoiler or not but imo is definitely not worth the time) and some gear. NO. This has the end here, or else we will be playing singleplayer elder scroll games with lootboxes soon enough. DO NOT support this.DON'T BUY THE GOLD LOOTBOXES, PLEASE. It's a net negative on the consumer's side.
What about the rest of the game?
Gameplay wise:
It's definitely more fun to play, Talion feels alot weaker than he did in the first game which is a welcome challenge.(He could execute 2 uruks after landing 2 hits AND heal himself in the process with the right build if you didn't know. The dude was basically invincible.)However it kinda breaks the immersion that why did he forget things he could do in the first game and had to relearn them, it felt odd.
Uruks are more random in voices,appeareance and combat capabilities. Yet just like in the first game, if you don't die to them there aren't much personaility to speak of since unless they come back to get killed again, all we get to hear is the line when he sees you and the one when you kill him. There are new enemy types like Olog-hai and Drakes, they are tougher to take down than the rest and they mix up with the already present enemies like uruks and caragors quite well.
The assassin's creed/arkham style combat paired with expertly crafted animation makes combat very satisfying. Against weaker mobs of uruks,Talion leans towards quicker kills rather than all out brutality seen in the first game makes the combat alittle smoother, although against captains his executions can still be extremely brutal and long, which makes the kills seem more personal and stood out. I like that.
There are more variations of nemesis missions as oppose to the previous installment (Duel, execution, betrayal, hunt), now there are more types of the same genre of mission, for example , when you send a dominated captain to kill the other captain , it won't just be duels , it could be a supply raid , a chase or ambush etc. It makes the game feel more alive as if they do have stuff to do instead of standing around talking about how they would've killed the Gravewalker or complaining about almost got set on fire the other day.
Sieges are fun, for the first few times, the online modes are tac-on and obviously pushing for more lootboxes sales(sigh). I enjoy online vendatta missions though , averaging other players deaths feels great. But unfortunately, there are no depths in these online systems , there's no point to keep playing them after getting the legendary gears from the challenges.
And oh yeah , the fight pits. Have you ever wanted to be a pokemon trainer? The bright lord has you covered as you pit your precious uruks against random challengers to level them up... or get chopped to pieces infront of your very eyes. Exactly like pokemon.
The tutorials were way too long and could be a drag to play through them. There's also a difficulty option now. I recommend playing on Nemesis difficulty since as I mentioned , if the uruks don't kill you their personalities don't flesh out.
Story-wise :
First I have to mention , at the start of the game , how does NOBODY mentions or recongize what Talion and Celebrimbor did to the black hands of sauron in the first game , they saved alot of people from being enslaved and gave hope all across Mordor yet nobody seem to notice Talion is the legendary Ranger or rather it seems the news haven't reached the city yet...? I mean if they knew someone like this exist , and seeing a guy came out of nowhere, teleporting , flying across the city cutting down uruks like vegetables they should know or suspect that he is the gravewalker?
The characters are alot more fleshed out than SoM, the writting is better since there's more tension to the story than fighting afew warchiefs that you can kill with like 2 hits. Talion and the bright lord often face foes way out of their league and it's quite an exciting experience. BUUUUT it kinda goes down hill after afew hours as the quest branches out to different parts and the characters just disappears after you complete their specific quests. It feels rather seperated and empty. The Plot twists are okay.
Can't say if the story goes well with the lore since I am not a LOTR fan so no opinion on that.
Techinal-wise :
The game looks pretty great but with varying performances on different PC setups. Graphical options are customizable and detailed.
Sound designs are similar to SoM and it still holds up , pretty great. A few dialog audio glitches where they overlap and can't hear what the characters are talking about.
A few bugs and glitches here and there, the mouse sometimes just dies and doesn't move for some reason (alt tabbing seems to fix it) , died afew times after getting hit or pushed into the terrain and Talion just dies without any last chance or anything when there's still health left, and one time i got stuck hanging off a market stall while the uruks just keep smashing my spine in like they are chopping off pieces of ham off from a BBQ'd pig leg, that was fun.(it's not)
Overall:
A potential GOTY but held back by terrible business practices , pointless grind and medicore story. It's definitely better than Shadow of Mordor and it's one of the better open world games on the market right now.If you enjoy games like Witcher 3 or Breath of the Wild than this game will deliver, but just the delivering, no surprising.
I give this game 46 Bruz's / 236 Ratbags.(idk what does this mean but hey , no scoring is the best scoring)

An overall improvement over SoM. You have lots more options for handling orcs and situations and adds new things that keeps the fights from having you do the same thing when you come across the tough orcs. If you want corpses to explode half the time or summon Graugs with sappers or your bodyguard who regenerates against everything when you are fighting captains, you also have matching sets of equipment that provide more bonuses for you to abuse. You can slot gems into equipment and switch them around to further customize your options to have your weapons hit much harder, have orcs take half damage, to getting up to 50% more XP for killing stuff, or even leveling captains when you dominate them.
Rush through the boring first act and progress to where you can dominate captains and invade forts. Advancing the game opens up new things and lets you unlocks skills faster. Do weekly community challenges that give you boxes of captains and equipment based around your current level. Do daily challenges and get enough gold to buy discounted packages of several boxes or goods based around your level when you open them.
The microtransactions improved the game for me since it provided all the extra stuff I needed to get past the boring parts and get to do pokeorc battles. You get boxes for doing almost anything. Avenge your friend and get fixed level boxes, do that enough times and get loot boxes that could increase your point gain or double your XP boost. They also get point towards those same loot boxes if you succeed and they are endless and varied challenges. Do online conquests to get boxes for speedrunning and get another boxes by doing enough of them. Invade your friends and not worry about losing orcs. Just walk up to them and revive to full health. I have enough money just playing the game to get dozens of boxes of captains to throw away.

My first impressions of Mafia 3....
It’s not that easy to look “neutral” at such a game like Mafia which offers also an open world experience like GTA 5. I don’t want and can’t compare those games because we see here completely different scenes, times and stories, that’s just to clarify that I don’t want to denigrate Mafia!
I start playing it last night after it was released (yes, I stayed awake and was waiting for it :-P)
The really first cool and for me “goose bumps” experience was the music which is offered in this game. The launcher is easy to handle and I’d like to do already some settings without starting the game. What I don’t really like is, that if you have already started the Story, there is no possibility in-game to access the settings without clicking on “Continue”…. that’s a little bit annoying – probably I haven’t found it, correct me in this way please.
Let’s have a look at the settings of the game. For my taste they settings are smart and quite clear. The only thing what I don’t really like is the really bad possibility to handle the graphic settings – I would like to setup the view distance etc. to myself but that’s just a personal taste…
Graphics:
After the first impressions I got shocked… unfortunately in a negative why and I was a little bit unsure if this is now just the “preview” scene…. The graphic of Mafia III is for my taste not a graphic which you will expect in 2016... I have tried to adjust the (smart) graphic settings to get the picture sharper but I failed. The only thing I found is, if you turn the AA settings to “low” the picture looks a little bit sharper. I don’t know which graphic engine is used here, but is that FXAA which is causing that behavior? I had problems several times with that FXAA setting… also in other games. The whole game looks blurred and “not sharp” on my screen (GTX 980 Matrix latest nvidia Driver) – no other game has this issue.
I also need to getting used to the Sky (Clouds) and lightning. It is really cool and I am impressed that it’s added a dynamic lightning system affected by cloud moving, but this doesn’t look really good for my taste. The weather system itself is also not really clear for me. The weather changed a lot of times in the last 4 hours gameplay.
Game General:
I was really excited as I heard that there will be a new Mafia game and I know, that we for sure have not found out what the game offers to us. I got a little bit confused by the mini-map. There are no icons on the map where all the “special” places are. What I also don’t see is, where my “home” is, where I can put my money back into the vault. (Probably I just only stupid and can’t see it…).
I haven’t found out yet if there is the possibility to use the public transportations like Taxi or trains. I haven’t seen one yet. The “drive-feeling” is for my taste really cool the only thing I need to getting use to it is the crash simulation, but for me it’s funny :) I also found a “bug” today.
As I walked between two cars which are crashing, I was smashed into the Air and fall down again, and stayed alive :) (Probably I am the Superman of Mafia 3 :-P).
Weapons:
Can’t review this in detail what are the possibilities here. The Menu shows a lot of locked slots – don’t know what happened here.
What I don’t like is, that you can only have 1 pistol and 1 bigger weapon (no Shotgun and Machine gun at the same time) but probably that will be a possibility if the slots gets unlocked in the future game experience. Sound of the Weapons are ok for me :)
The Radio, to call “help” is a cool feature. I only can call the “weapon shop”. Looking forward what will be provided in the further gameplay :)
“Movie Scenes”, Characters:
I am really the person who is skip just scenes BUT in Mafia 3, I am really impressed. The Characters and the graphic in the scenes of the skins and so on are incredible! In the beginning it’s a little bit confusing if the scenes are switching between the story but if you know what’s going on, it’s really cool! I like this it!
What I would really like to see/find out is:
- Better Graphic Settings, no blurred graphic, sharper graphic
- If the possibility is given, public transportation to use
- Mini-Map rework, I am really frustrated if nothing is written and marked on the map. (expect the things you have already discovered…)
- Some rework for the lightning system and clouds if possible
- Weather Settings/Engine should be a little bit adjusted that it doesn’t change so often
- Legendary Taxi Mission, Side Missions, Doing some “little jobs” in the city.

A design aspect I DO have a lot of problem with however is that the enviroment doesn't fade when it's between the characters and the camera. Spintires isn't for everybody and its not perfect. Lets get the problems out of the way straight off the bat.
1. No fixed camera, no interior camera, fairly poor camera placement and controls.
2. Not a whole lot to do in the game.
3. Some bugs and in some ways feels like an early access title.
Now onto the good.
1. Fairly realistic fluid displacement engine, you create tracks in the mud and if you're not careful you will find yourself bogged very fast.
2. Co-op multiplayer, its always fun playing with friends.
3. Nice graphics engine and Truck models. While it isn't the best game graphically, everything comes together well, the game runs great and looks nice in most parts, the Truck models are top notch though.
4. Several different trucks with different attachments. This means you and your friends can set yourself up with the perfect trucks for any given situation and actually use teamwork.
5. A winch system! You can winch yourself and friends out when they are bogged, you can winch yourself to a tree to pull yourself out if no one is around to help, lots of fun and very cool.
I could write far more about this game, but if the idea of 4WDing around several big open world maps is appealing, just take the plunge and make the purchase, you won't regret it.

Do you know what a locker is? Does the term 'UAZ' mean anything to you? Did you try recent 'off-road' 'sims' such as Off-Road Drive, then sigh and go back to Screamer 4x4? If you answered yes to the above then this game is for you!
The terrain deformation that put this game on everyone's radar a few years back is still present, and the world doesn't just reset after you leave the area or even reload the game! Repeatedly take the same route through a soft paddock and you'll soon be fetching a support vehicle or left scratching your head whilst staring at an overturned log truck. It's challenging alright, even on the 'casual' setting, but it's also a lot of fun and very rewarding when you get things right.
The visuals are incredible considering the relatively low specs required - with max settings I'm getting 60FPS @ 1920x1200 on a 3.6GHz i5, GTX460 and 4GB RAM. The lighting is stunning and it actually gets properly dark at night, which is all too rare in games.
Like most games though it is far from perfect-
-The camera is great...until you try to move it. It feels like it was designed by Satan himself and is easily the worst part of the game
-Controller support needs work. Can't configure buttons and you need to keep KB&M handy for important things like map navigation and using truck mechanisms (eg- winches). The use of analog triggers is also poorly implemented and trucks jump to about 50% throttle at the slightest press.
-There is only autosaving and it only saves when you go to the main menu or quit. This means if the game crashes you can lose hours of progress, and you also can't have multiple simultaneous games going.
-At time of writing, no mod support
If you can see your way past the above then you could have a lot of fun with this game. Definitely worth the $30.

It's a must have for the serious gamer. And if you've never played Natural Selection before, this game will open up a whole new world to you with unprecedented possibilities, and it will definitely blow your mind.
Although, if you've been an avid Natural Selection fan in the past, it's unavoidable to find the pace of this remake quite low, so prepare yourself for a little disappointment... Just a little though..

Hotline Miami is a fast, brutal, tremendously satisfying game. It has the Super Meatboy quality of being ruthlessly unforgiving of mistakes, but the checkpoints are freqent enough and the levels short enough that this is never taken to a place of being frustrating.
The campaign is short, but it's as long as it needs to be for this sort of game. 5 hours for me, but of course I died a lot. The plot is weird too, revolving around the main character's steadily deteriorating mental state. It's something vaguely to with your character killling off the Russian mafia in 1980's Miami, but we have nobody's word for it on who exactly he's killing or why. One scene suggests the character is on drugs and this is contributing to his mental decline. The ending is a slightly unsatisfying conclusion to this intrigue, but the game is so fast paced it doesn't register as that much of a problem with me.
Again, this is quibbling. The game is good, it goes on ssale a lot, if you get a chance it's worth playing it.

I just finished and loved Broken Age (Act 1, of course).
The grapics and art are absolutely stunning, and the story... it's just captivating. I would hesitate to call this a game, though, as it is more of an interactive movie. I've read many reviews stating that it was dry, or too easy, but the reality is that is entirely encompasses the viewer. As the story unfolds you are confused and intrigued. You are brought further into a story that seems to spiral into itelf. The wonderous thing about this is that you don't have to be in a high intesity mode. I found that after a hard day at work I would want to just play a little bit more in order to advance the story line, to learn more, to understand what was happening. It was relaxing and charming and whimsical. It encourages creativity in it's puzzles, and had the cutest elements of humour.
My only quam with it is that I found it too short. It took me somewhere between 4 and 5 hours to complete. And when I got to the end I was so upset to learn that it was over... but it's not over. Based on the length and the cliff hanger ending, I'm glad that I didn't purchase it at regular price.
But seriously. Absolutely beautiful. I would say it's great for anyone and everyone.

Welcome to Alan Wake, also known as STOP TAKING MY ♥♥♥♥ING GUNS!
Sam Lake, who wrote the original Max Payne and Max Payne 2 is back with several other writers to create a world where a best-selling thriller novelist has his wife kidnapped(?)/killed(?)/abducted by a supernatural entity(?).  He is either battling this supernatural horror, dealing with these kidnappers, going insane, or possibly just dreaming the entire time.  If you like your endings with a fair bit of bioshock infinite or a hint of Inception, this is probably your game.
The story is well-paced, well-written despite some holes, and solidly voice acted.  Looks pretty good too, with an appreciable sense of detail.  It's everything else the game kind of has problems with.
While the game isn't on rails, it's pretty linear.  The environments are reasonably beautiful, but you simply spend too much time in the damn woods.  When you start hitting enemies in open turf, you'll realize that the whole lost in the woods act was really the only way the devs could figure out to make the game intense.  You'll frequently venture laterally to pick up goodie caches located by marks that only show up with a flashlight, but that's about it.
Enemies, whom you must first de-cloak the darkness from via a flashlight, have very little variety.  Perhaps maybe five types in the entire game.  Between tracts of tromping through the woods fending off cheap, boring enemies with a prodigious amount of ammo (on Normal), you'll get sucked ino the story in several other environments.  Between these areas, even between combat areas you will conveniently lose all your ♥♥♥♥ing gear almost every single time, with the game's occasional narration (Sam Lake really held himself back!) even pointing out the fact just to aggravate you all the more.  I can't quite call it a survival-horror game as it is an action third-person shooter.  It's actually better if you simply shoot everything in the face rather than trying to hold back.
The controls are squirrely at best on a keyboard.  If you have a controller, use it.  Alan  has simply awful cardio, enemies can run faster than you even while sprinting, and the default dodge controls are not particularly guaranteed.  I say that even while having the dodge achievements.
To be honest, once you've sorted out most of the aforementioned mysteries, the latter half of the game is quite a slog.  The game reveals its hand too early, which only leaves five enemies in various combinations for the rest of the game.  Light or even simple time restores your health, but you'll reload frequently, usually due to cheap shots from behind.  This is clearly a story-driven piece, so if you're looking for enjoyable combat, you'll have to look elsewhere.

Crashlands, or Don't Starvbound of Isaac Crashers
An isometric survival game with RPG elements, where you fight strange creatures and use strange tools to fortify against the dark and harsh world? Isn't that Don't Starve? Well, there's tiered crafting with space-y themes and all manner of useless decoration to clutter your stuff, plus it can get a little grindy. Oh, so you mean Starbound? Well, it's got a rather perverse art set and sense of humor, with strangely proportioned and overstuffed chibi-esque art... Ok, look. Imagine, if you will, that Ed McMillien led The Behemoth, and they wanted to mash the best parts of Don't Starves exploration and crafting through the RPGish parts of Starbound, all within a rediculous adorable world. Combat is quite skill based, with widely telegraphed attacks that hit like trucks and all sorts of status ailments and special items. Inventory is managed for you, and you can always warp back home from anywhere. Multiplayer looks like it'd be a blast, so grab it and lets adventure through jellyfish infested wastes together!

If the name of the developer-publisher, Artifice Studio, rings a bell for you then that is good, it should. Artifice Studios shocked us back in 2013 with their debut game, Sang-Froid – Tales of Werewolves. That game was held in extremely high regard for its fascinating and thoroughly well executed combination of action, strategy, RPG, tower defense game play. It was certainly among my favorite indie games developed that year. It took the studio two and a half years to release their second game, but again it is a deeply interesting game, in Conflicks – Revolutionary Space.
I’d like to highlight the points of the game that I perceive to be a negative first. The game is played in a real-time fashion with a flicking mechanic. The flicking mechanic takes too long to do that at higher levels and harder difficulty settings so much is happening at once that it becomes incredibly difficult to keep up. The inability to pre-order moves on the pause screen only adds to this frustration. I can understand that the devs may view this as a level of cheating but it’s more of an unfortunate reality than a cheap way to win. What this means is that the difficulty level increases on an artificial level rather than a natural one. Rising rates of difficulty should almost always be natural. It should never be because the game is broken in any way, shape or form. Unfortunately, that’s what has happened here in my opinion. The game would have worked much better as a turn-based game with the utilization of the flicking mechanic. It really would have transformed the game for the best and made it a much stronger title. There are other issues that I have with the flicking mechanic as well. Far too many of the abilities rely on this mechanic. This again not only slows the game down because moves cannot be pre-ordered
It’s not all bad. In fact, I do believe that Conflicks is quite a solid title that could have been much better had better game design decisions been made. The highlight of the game for me is the overall presentation. This comes in the form of the graphic novel style approach to the narration of the story and the fantastic character writing especially that of the charming, talking owl Unlucky Locke. I couldn’t help but feel immersed in the game world. The campaigns serve as great tutorials to the multiplayer game. Unfortunately, there are very few players playing but the two multiplayer games that I managed to get into were entertaining battles let down only by the flick system. The presentation, however, mostly made up for that system and enabled me to have a good amount of fun.
If you own Conflicks or intend to purchase it or end up winning a copy from Steamified please hit me up. I’d love to play a game or two with you!
Conflicks is a flawed game but one that has a lot of charm in the presentation. It’s certainly worth some of your time so I urge you not to ignore this game.

Tiddlywinks in space. This won't revolutionize space battles. I really wanted to like this game; as others have said the art style and humour is great. Pythonesque with Douglas Adams influences amongst others.
However, I find the game mechanics completely unplayable as a real time strategy. The focus is on flicking one ship at a time, or moving ships linked together with a frigate. The linked ships can't use their abilities whilst still linked by tractor beam to the frigate. Meanwhile the AI is sending multiple ships at you (and around your defences) from multiple directions. Your ships don't move on their own at all. Lots of micromanaging but only 1 unit or linked group at a time. It takes a few seconds to line up and judge a flick, rushing it could send half your group into an asteroid or the gravity well of a planet. I also found that by the time I had flicked a torpedo action at a target, the target had already flicked itself out of the way, been destroyed by conventional weapons, or my torpedo ship had been destroyed.
In the end, I resolved myself to producing a load of small ships to scatter about and delay the opponent whilst I control my attack group to attack the enemy's flagship.
I also had a little trouble understanding the resource flow of the game. Metamatter. You collect it from planets with henships, or collect the glowing baubles left in the debris of destroyed ships. There's a bar on the bottom of the interface that tells you how much of it you have in total, how much you're currently using and how much you have unassigned. I'm still not sure what makes up that locked overhead metamatter cost. The metamatter cost of an action isn't always obvious, and the yellow dots signifying unit cost is tiny in the flagship and battleship production interface.
I understand that the creators wanted to create a sense of urgency and panic, a mad click-and-drag-fest to match the mad theme of the game, but it just felt frustrating to me that I had so little control over the situation as a whole. If you enjoy 'Tiddlywinks', you may enjoy this game a lot more than I did.

I was at first turned away by the strange setup and cartoonish characters, however I quickly grew past it as I began to play. This game is by far the best rogue like I have ever played, with its amazing replayability, multitude of weapons that make you feel like a badass and cool character abilites. Each character gives a new ability that augments the base playstyle quite nicely. They do not drastically affect the gameplay but change it just enough to be interesting and fresh. Additionally, if you are looking for a big change in the game, or greatly increased difficulty, never fear, for there are many different modes for that. In conclusion if you are a fan of Rogue-likes, this game is a MUST HAVE. On the other hand if you have never tried Rogue-Like's then this is the perfect game to get started with.

One of the best top-down shooters ever created, Nuclear Throne is a challenging, fast-paced ♥♥♥♥-'em-up that makes every run intense. With procedural generation and a wide variety of characters and weapons, and the goal of always getting further even once you've beaten the throne, it never gets boring. The post-apocalyptic style is awesome and everything is designed really well from both gameplay and design standpoints.
My only gripe is that lategame (loop 2+) could have been balanced better, it usually becomes a massive bullet spam that forces you to either always have a melee weapon to clear projectiles or hug corners and slowly get rid of enemies, which kinda whithers down the shoot em up aspect for me. Regardless it's still incredibly fun at this point and pushes you to keep trying to get further (which is still very hard).
I highly recommend trying this game at some point, it's definitely worth it's full price.

Conflicks - Revolutionary Space Battles is a really unique game in my opinion. Renaissance in space is what it comes down to. In this alternate history humans discovered  a new, powerful form of matter inside the yolk of hen eggs. This led to a technological singularity that catapulted humanity into space in the 1600- 1700's. Humanity is now among the stars with the help of this chicken egg matter, battling not only themselves but also sapient, sentient chicken mutants who have suddenly evolved.
Gameplay wise most combat will involve flicking ships through the battle map (pulling back on them and launching in a certain direction). This is also how most abilities work, from missiles to tractor beams. There are a handful of different ship classes from small fighter/scouts to behemoth capital ships and all sizes in between. Your capital ship usually acts as your base and primary shipyard for creating more units.  There are also a variety of factions but with the time I got to play Conflicks I did not experience most of them. I also did not get into any detailed multiplayer, having spent most of my time in the single player campaign.
Overall I enjoyed what I did play, and thought the art style was pretty enjoyable and definitely unusual. I recommend the game to anyone looking for a new indy game, or anyone who is a fan of space battles. Conflicks is not a mobile game but I would recommend mobile fans play it because of its movement style.

This game is super good. Combat is like X-Com light and is servicable but pretty simple. The story and world is pretty generic, but there's a ton of stuff to do and things to read, with over 800,000 words total (!).  The game really rewards exploration, as a result, it's very nonlinear and there are a bunch of secrets. There's a lot of cool faction stuff, plenty of choices that determine the fate of each area, and a pretty insane level of detail to boot. Probably the best Kickstarter game I've played yet.

Overall, the game is pretty good. I think that the turn based combat was better than XCOM, and fans of group-based tactical RPGs should enjoy it. However, being an old-school RPG, there are some old-school prolems that I ran into that ruined the game for me.
My first issue with the game was weapon balance. I tried to research ahead of time and pick weapons that weren't underpowered. While researching the shotgun, all of the complaints seemed centered on it causing friendly fire. I picked it for one of my characters with the intent of using positioning to avoid friendly fire. I was able to do that effectively, and rarely needed to be in a position where I would hit my own teammates. However, the shotgun is greatly underpowered, especially at the beginning of the game. The damage per AP is low, the armor penetration is low, and the range is low. The only real advantage is that you could potentially hit multiple enemies, but there is little to nothing that you can do that will put enemies in a position where they are grouped up. Shotgun characters will spend most of their time hitting single targets for low damage. Shotguns get better mid-game when you start to get shotguns with longer ranges, but their damage still does not compare well to other weapons.
Halfway through the game I felt like my shotgun character was just dead weight in my party. With 30 hours in, it felt too late to reroll my characters. Just like old-school RPGS, be careful about how you spec your characters or you risk being stuck with underpowered characters.
The second issue was the annoying bugs. If you handle something in the game in an unconvential way, expect it to bug the game, forcing you to re-roll. Luckily, do to was auto-saving and quicksaves work, it's easy to get back to a save game before you encountered the bugs.
Finally, don't be scared away by people who say that the game is too hard. Go ahead adn play on the second highest difficulty setting. I found that the game was not challenging at the third highest setting. The highest difficulty setting is for people who hate themselves and want to constantly reload the game.
