The yes/no recommendation is a bit difficult on this one. A solid 5/10 "you tried" for inxile's kickstarter game. It's a functional tactical RPG that doesn't do anything
wrong, just... rough. Combat tends to be a stand-and-shoot affair. Cover is sparse and inconsistent; X-Com this isn't. Every map in the game needs a thorough rebuild of the combat grid. Level design is half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and feels incomplete on all but the Ag Center map, which is what they put together to showcase the game six months ago, so of course it got three times the effort. ... still horrible about cover, though.
Equipment balance is all over the place. Entire weapon classes that do jack-all (smg, lookin' at you), and assault rifles that out-range and out-hit most sniper rifles. And of course, a separate skill for every minor weapon type rather than classes of weapon (three different melee skills). But then bafflingly, no skill at all required for explosives, rocket launchers, etc.
Character design is limited and ugly, with no cosmetic appearance for armor. And it's almost insulting how so many of the unique appearance items like "top hat" or "chef's cap" have generic models if you put them on a female character. Women too hard, guys? Echos of Ubi here. You can even see it in the character creator, too, where it seems like you have to double-click to move to a new appearance, but you're really just cycling through identical options that look unique on guys. Skill bloat runs rampant, with things shoehorned in to force replays. Three different conversation skills? Really? FIVE different "open the box" skills? C'mon.
And despite it all... I've had a fair bit of fun. The game has its frustrations, sure. It's a bit disappointing after all the excitement. But that's Kickstarter for you. In the end, there's a lot to enjoy, and that doesn't have to be drowned out by the flaws.
Buggy, lack of character depth, weak combat system... this game feels like the hated Fallout Tactics.

Ignore the hype, the history, the legacy.  You only really need to know this:
Wasteland 2 ~= Fallout 2 + Jagged Alliance 2

As of writing this review, I have about 90 hours spent onto the game, about 40 of these in the beta. The game has recently come out and received one patch. So that's the state I am talking about. I'll put my conclusion first for those that just skim reviews:
Would I recommend to buy the game currently? Nope.
Would I advise people returning from the beta to start playing now? Nope.
But I am pretty sure if you
, you'll have a good game in the visual style of Fallout 2 and with the writing of the original Wasteland.
Why would I not recommend this game now? Too many things are broken: Quests are a core issue in an a Fallout-inspired game, right? Sadly, a lot of alternative quest solutions are either broken or the feedback is not present -- so you keep wondering whether what you did had any effect. And it is even less reassuring when NPCs texts ("You doomed us all") do not match the quest summaries ("You saved everyone"). So you are currently not roleplaying, shaping the world by your interactions, you are tip-toeing around, trying to find a way to solve specific quests that does work. And hopefully the result matches your expectations.
Would I recommend to
, say in the beginning of 2015? Yes, probably.  Quests, story development and game balance are all fixable. Still, I beleive it will only be a good, not a great game. Why? It does feel sloppily made. And I my doubts that a software that started with little care about quality will become perfectly polished by the same team. Now what do I consider sloppy but hard to fix? Some examples:
Recommendation: If you have not played the recent Shadowrun RPG yet, buy it instead (it's cheap). The story telling mechanism in SR is similar, but the game was designed around it. The actions are very limited, but the story flow is so much better. The combat uses a similar, probably also XCOM-inspired cover system. And the feedback about whether you are on the right track is much more direct. Enjoy it and come back to this game somewhere in 2015.

Alan Wake is another stunning example of a stylish cinematic (and yet rich in gameplay) narrative experience that has become a trademark of Remedy Entertainment. Following the story of a writer who may or may not have found himself inside a horror novel he has been writing, this game is a delightfully postmodern journey that constantly makes the player doubt his perception, and the reality of time/space. What is true, what is but a dream, is the protagonist a "real" man or a character - but wait, isn't he the character of a game that you're playing? Drawing heavily on the style and works of Stephen King and David Lynch, Alan Wake leads you through a dangerous track of uncertainty, and through that achieves genuine tension. It may not be a very scary "horror game", but it definitely is filled with anxiety.
Another highlight of Alan Wake is its unique multi-layered narrative - one that can only be found in the art of interactive media. The plot unfolds simultaneously through a variety of sources: the actual story experience, pages of an in-game novel that the player collects, occasional radio broadcasts, the timely use of licensed and original music, episodes of an in-game TV series... *and* the TV series that the game pretends to be with its episodic format! It's clever, it's ever dynamic and it is also a smart instrument of manipulating our fears. Every now and then the games "spoils" an event to come  - for example, by revealing an attack on the protagonist with the next page of a novel - yet it deliberately omits the circumstances, the "where" and "when", thus driving the player to assume that the said event might happen anywhere and at any time during the episode.
With Alan Wake, Remedy Entertainment also re-establishes itself as one of the leaders in video game art direction. While it's simple to say the game is a beautiful one - and remains so even even now, at the dawn on the new console generation - it is first and foremost *effective* in employing colors, character and location design and, naturally, light and shadows to affect the player emotionally. Like any good horror story, Alan Wake builds up tension not as much through confrontation with "scary stuff" as it does by visually dividing safe areas, small and well-lit, and the vast dark misty territory of the unknown dangers outside. The game encourages exploration through various collectibles, yet here exploration require courage.
In the world of Alan Wake, every step is not taken lightly - and thus matters all the more. This game is an engaging experience with a complex story, fascinating characters (all the more fascinating because of how they might not be real), outstanding game design and a sense of dread that is sure to cling to you for days to come, making your heart skip a beat every time you find yourself on a dark street with only a faint light of street lamp in the distance.

A fresh take on the Survival Horror Genre.
A psychological manipulator that has wit, innovation and integrity.
Play as writer Alan Wake when he awakens in a world full of mystery and full of darkness.
Travel through wicked territories and face terrifying creatures in order to rescue your girlfriend from the demonic forces.
Light is your only friend and is the only thing that can help you on your journey. In order to cause damage to any demon you must first purge them with light to break down their protective barrier. Use a flashlight, street lamp, torch, explosive barrel - any resource available to illuminate the darkness and defeat the demons.
10/10 - Highly recommended to fans of the Survival Horror Genre.

With this game on a big sale right now, there are certain to be people on the fence about buying this game.  I thought it is time for me to write a review on this game.
Over the past year, I have tried all of the current "big three" sims: FSX (got it 75% off), X-Plane 10, and Prepar3D v3.  I also have Dovetail Flight School and even FlightGear.  Out of all five, FSX:SE is by far my favorite.
Yes its technology (32 bits and unfinished DirectX 10) is aged by today's standards.  However, I myself am a diehard retro gamer and I am able to overlook its age to make the most of a sim that is still relevant in today's market.
Its greatest strengths are:
-Diversity in gameplay.  You can take lessons and try to pass checkrides, fly in a variety of missions, or go on a solo or multiplayer free flights.  The game has GA aircrafts, airliners, a helicopter, a glider, and a few other aircraft types right out of the box.  Even if you don't feel like flying, you can read its vast in-game library to learn about the game and the planes' different features and how they are used in real life.
-Expandability.  The default terrain is a a bit bare (but still waaay better than FlightGear).  There is a good number of add-ons available through Steam, and around 75% of the add-ons designed for boxed FSX still work for FSX:SE with no or only a little tweaking.  The default game will keep you busy for many months and the add-ons will keep you busy for YEARS.
-User friendliness.  Almost everything works right out of the box.  Yes there are a couple of bugs that DTG unfortunately cannot fix due to its distribution agreement with Microsoft, but some of them can be fixed by the players with the right amount of research (and back up all originals!).  The in-game options, AI planes, ATC, dials and gauges, four seasons landscape, real-time weather, map, flight planner, rewards, and frame rate all work.  You can start on the runway or at any of the parking or gate area in the game's 20,000 airports.  You aren't given a million options to choose from just so you can set the game the way you like it and take to the skies.
People very new to flight simmings or to aviation in general will not have their hands held - they will still need to take the lessons, read the library, do additional research online, and invest in at least a cheap joystick to make the most of their experience.  That is where many would-be simmers give up.  If you want to fly as soon and as easily as possible, this sim is not for you.  If you want to learn how to fly and enjoy the rewards out of doing so, this sim is for you.
Will FSX:SE be our go-to flight sim forever?  Maybe not forever, but for at least for the rest of this year, yes.  Prepar3D (based on FSX) is still boring and built on old technology despite its price tag.  X-Plane 10 baits and switches for sales and still can't offer detailed airports, good ATC, and the four seasons right out of the box.  Dovetail Flight School is missing too many features for serious simming, but the upcoming Dovetail Flight Simulator may be FSX:SE's rightful replacement.  FlightGear is admirable, but it is freeware for a reason.
So in short, if you are interested in aviation and you are willing to learn, then take advantage of this sale.  FSX:SE, sale or not, is an affordable and accessible entry point to the wonderful hobby of flight simulation.

Just like the CRPGs of yesteryear. It's hard as hell, with regards to both the learning curve as well as the game's difficulty level. I'm playing on the lowest difficulty setting and it's still giving me trouble. And it's hella long, too. At this point, I'm 20 hours in and I'm just now getting to Damonta. That being said, the story, which is the most important part of any RPG, is fantastic. It kind of reminds me of Fallout: New Vegas with the Wacky Wasteland trait enabled. Little touches here and there of dark humor work well to distinguish Wasteland from its successor series.

For isometric RPG veterans like myself, this is a game I have been itching to play ever since the Baldur's Gate re-release reminded me why this genre can be so great. Wonderful writing, haunting atmosphere, a universe that straddles the line between believable and silly (though the use of CDs as jewellery is a bit much) and the satisfying sound of a bullet (or bullets) tearing through some schlub's skull make this a must for those craving a hit of old-school Fallout.
Even better, if you remember the original Wasteland, there's tons of lore call-backs here to reward your playtime. Knowing the exact details of Highpool or Base Cochise isn't necessary, though - exposition galore takes care of that for series newbies.
I would like to see skill use streamlined, through. It feels like a few clicks too many just to perform a hack or lock pick.

Wasteland 2 was a bit of an impulse buy for me. Because it inspired the fallout series, i was expecting something a lot like Fallout 3. Boy was i wrong. What this game actually is, is something closer to the old style random Encounter RPG's you remember from Final Fantasy. But mixed in with the Overhead Tactical Combat.
As soon as i loaded up the game, my first thought was. "What the F*** does this do? How is this important? What do i Choose?" That was the character creation screen. Now, this is what really makes or breaks the game. If you make the wrong decision here, you will not survive long in the game. (Testimate to my 4 Party Creation attempts). Once the game started, i realised something. This game does NOT hold your hand. It does not explain anything to you about the game, instead you have little tutorial pop ups on the side of the screen.
My first experience with Combat, was terrible. I hadn't selected any weapon specialities, so i went off into the Wasteland with sticks. Boy was that a mistake. My second experience, my entire party got killed by a mutant frog in the first area. But once you get used to playing with the layout of the land, and being able to plan ahead and scatter your party for combat, the game gets a lot easier, but also interesting.
Being partway through the same, it becomes blindingly obvious that Assault Rifles are the only weapon worth investing in. But, due to the limited ammo, it pays to diversify.
All in all, i would rate Wasteland like this:
Story: 10/10
Game Play: 8/10
Originality: 9/10
Mechanics: 8/10
Visuals: 6/10
For an overall Rating of 8.2/10

Crashlands is a humorous and well-done large world RPG set on an alien landscape. Combing elements of survival, story, and humor to create an amazing title. I will add a TL;DR at the end.

You are Flux and you are handling a urgent delivery with your robotic companion Juicebox. Your ship is destroyed by quite the purple head thingy... yeah.  You are now stranded on an alien planet and have to try and establish communication again and survive on the planet with its hostile environment.
The controls within this game are fairly simple using the mouse to either click and you will move there or hold it and you character will move where your mouse is. Crashlands also utilizes the A S D F and C V buttons as quick buttons, the A S D F buttons can be changed to quickly use your items while the C and V buttons are for your wonderfully murderous pet. The game mechanic is done well and I can see how easily it is converted to its mobile counterpart. Crashlands has a large amount of customizable floors and walls with useless furniture to behold. The game does a nice job of guiding you through everything and learning the game with rather comedic moments with Flux and Juicebox whether it be between themselves or the non-hostile inhabitants of the planet. The combat mechanic in the game is very fun as it requires you to be intelligent about you approach with every creature you see, which wants to kill you.... which is almost the entire planet. This game also removes the hassle of having to manage you inventory because apparently you have black hole pockets, just don't question it and be happy. Other than the expected do quest, get gear, and farm stuff mechanics you would expect of an RPG you can also rip the eggs from the creatures you kill and then raise their baby to murder their past brethren, overall very nice as long as you don't think too much on how STWOMPY (My personal Wombit) killed over 100 of his own kind already along with other creatures (so proud). The only problem is having to go back to old areas to remove bits of black so I can see the whole map, as it's quite the long process.

The graphics are cartoonish and more innocent than anything else. They are polished and very smooth and the evolution screen while you evolve your pet is quite majestic to watch. The music is alright and the sounds match the creature well.


+ Great survival element
+ Good amount of customization
+ Large game allowing you to play for hours on end
+ Cross-platform saves

- Annoying to have to go back to previous areas of the map to fill it out without black areas
- Moments where a crafting recipe I was tracking is replaced by a quest item track when I talk for the quest (slightly annoying, perhaps an option to not automatically change the tracked recipe?)
- Grinding is existent and prevalent within the game

These are my personal suggestions that I feel would improve the game.
- With the editor major update (when it is released) there should be an option to create custom player models and creature models to help create a true sense of freedom through customization in the update.
- If the created creature is hostile the ability to select its attack patten would be amazing
- Workshop for maps and mods with the large scale update
- Ability to have "Vanity items" meaning that you could be waring one item for stats, but you can use another item that you prefer visually to be seen on you
- Ability to see pet stats. To be able to see stats such as growth (Ex 26/100 and when it is evolved #/300), damage, and unique attack chance.
- Future Co-op feature

I played Don't Starve and it was nice, but it wasn't my cup of tea. Crashlands however dragged me in and keeps me there. The game is fun and even though it is meant more for a mobile platform with its control scheme it does not take away from its value as a game in itself. It's a challenging game and makes you a bit more alert as you try not to get stomped out of existence. I love Flux and her attitude along with Juicebox and I think this game is something I could easily recommend to those who like Don't Starve but want something different and a bit more lighthearted. Also the trailer is just perfect.

The game is a more lighthearted version of Don't Starve and is able to keep you in a way Don't Starve couldn't. The game has mobile controls but it really doesn't hurt the game as a whole. There is a large amount of customization and the RPG element is great. This allows for the game to be a large, more open world, RPG survival game. It's actually cool that the main character is a female and the interactions she has between the non-hostile inhabitants of the alien planet, or her robotic companion Juicebox are very humorous at points. There are not many issues I am able to find as I play through the game. The only issues I see people having is that there is a grinding element to the game and that there are times on the map where you have to move to previous areas to have a fully exposed map without any black spots. I would definitely recommend this to people who want a different take on the Don't Starve survival technique or simply want to try something new and love an RPG element with customization.

Do I recommend this game?
No.
Why?
Because in 2016, you don't roll with an AI as dumb as this one. Oh forget about the graphics. Unless you have one of those highly calibrated eyes that can see the non-existing flickering of a TFT screen or the screen tearing of a non G-Sync display running with v-sync off, you will not find it any worse than all the other decent AAA titles out there.
There are a few visual glitches and a rather annoying sunrise/sunset glare that makes you wish you wore shades, generally low res textures even on high, but that's besides the point here.
It's the AI (or the lack of it)
This game tries to be about storytellin' and all, but what kind of stories can you tell with 2bit brain less automatons running around the world? Let me tell you: the ridiculously weird kind. As it is the case with the ridiculous, it soon becomes boring and annoying, rather than funny.
I would whistle in amazement over how dumb the AI is, but that would painfully remind me of one of the most annoying and stupid gameplay features ever invented to demonstrate pathetic AI, luring the enemy in with whistling.
You can whistle, which will cause nearby enemies to be alerted and go to check out the source. Now you would think that its a bad thing, but its not. Since our anti-hero is a friggin terminator, he can just gut, behead, skewer or simply choke anyone to death that gets within 5 feet of him. He can do this from literally any angle and height as long as the enemy is not aware of him, or after throwing a few punches if the enemy is somehow aware.
So what does our dear boy do? He whistles, mobsters come and die.. one by one or in groups. The only real problem is when enemies further away actually notice him and start shooting, but thats rarely the case.
As luck would have it, mobsters are not quite bright, so only a few of them know how to use the phone and they are extremely proud, so they rarely call for help or fall back. For most of them, killing or dying is a matter of honor and running away would be considered worse then death.
This must be why they will go check out the whistling behind the crate swimming in blood and surrounded by gutted bodies of their comrades, just to die in a few minutes and add to the body count.
Pedestarians? No better to be honest. They don't care bout traffic or eachother the slightest. They have their own little lives and unless you unconvenience them somehow, like spilling blood on their shoes, they will ignore pretty much everything - sans the odd uni grad, who knows how to call the cops.
As much fun it was at first, as boring it is now. That plus the missions being all the same, repetitive n stuff.
The story started out awesome though and I was hoping it to continue in that style, but I'm not sure I will have the patience to grind through all the padding to enjoy it.
I also quite doubt that the AI will improve a lot. AI is not something thats fixed easy in complex games like this. Maybe with one of the first expansions or DLCs, they will roll out a better one. I might wait until them and frankly, I sugges you do too.

OK... so now I have a decent amount of time in game so I can write an informed review.

Please do excuse my English and any possible mistakes in text :). During the review I'll make some comparisons with Mafia 1 and 2 (more with 1 because 2 left a "smaller mark" on me - it was too short too make a big impression).

STORY + IMMERSION:
As far as story goes I personally love it overall. I feel like it developed too fast (the number of missions until the plot twist (at least the first one... did not finish the game so there can be others coming) was relatively low) and the begriming is a bit forced but that's the only bad thing I can say about it so far. I love the way things are narrated (from different ppl. point of views, like a documentary). The characters have depth and react as expected (ironically I find the main character to be the one with the least depth - personally I would've love to find out more about his life before the war, or during the war - maybe this happens later, at least I hope so).

About immersion... well... I feel like Mafia 1 was better at this but considering I got old since I played that and thinks impress me way less I'll conclude that Mafia 3 is ok at this point also (I did play for 5 hours without break without noticing it so... yeah, I think is ok).

Really liked the fact tutorial is not separated and is included in story. Also like the fact it has a connection with Mafia 2 (I recognized a character pretty close to start - I'm expecting him to come back later in the story).

Even though the subject is common (big bad hero has friends killed), the way is presented is awesome. Congrats for the story. At least so far... I do hope I won't get hit by a disappointment later.

GAMEPLAY:
The mechanics are good and nicely balanced. Weapons are variated enough without being to many. LOVED, just LOVED the "screaming doll" or however is called that attracts "weak minded" ppl. The step of the game is rather alert. Way more fast than its predecessors (personally I find it a bit too fast but I guess many other ppl. will like it more).

The feeling is somewhere between Mafia 1 (or 2 - it felt rather similar to me) and a GTA game (close to San Andreas actually - there are territories, you take over them, etc.). For example traffic rules and cops do exist but is much easier to escape them. You don't have speed limiter and apparently speeding is not a problem any more. There are even mechanics like scaring informers by "driving like a madman". Imo the partial lack of liberty from old Mafia games was good for immersion but again... there are new mechanics based on this new liberty so is not that bad it changed.

The surveillance mechanism is a really good idea - so you don't have to spend hours by checking every corner for a collectible (I am a bit compulsive and tend to do that - it bugs me). Collectibles are nice (especially the playboys - the first collectibles I actually watch; no... I'm lieing... I also watched the witcher collectibles :P).

The whistling was also a nice idea and deserves a note (but I've seen it in other games so that's why I was not so blown away by it).

Driving has 2 modes (normal and simulation) but I don't find them so different - a bit of a wasted opportunity here.

As a bad point... enemies are kind of stupid. I killed a guy right next to another and the second guy was just looking at me. I was thinking "SHOOT ME GOD DAMMIT... I'm killing your friend here". He didn't. I play on normal difficulty, maybe they are better on hard (have no idea). Also... I think they can't hear right. Apparently they can hear a gunshot on the other side of the street.

Overall... the game is fun. Nothing revolutionary (except maybe that surveillance I talked about) but well done.


GRAPHICS:
Well... this is a bit of a problem. I see hundreds of bad reviews because of graphics (90% of those are because of the fps lock). Mafia 3 is not the "most beautiful game ever created". It is decent/good though. It lacks the wow factor on graphics, especially on closeups and dark rooms. The 30 fps that everyone complains about is a minus but when I see posts like "30 fps - my eyes" my first reaction is to hit something. Yes, it is noticeable and yes it may tire your eyes a bit if you play for hours but that's just about it. No, you will not die because in that exact millisecond when the low fps "gap" (for lack of a better word) happened a bullet was shot towards you. Is not a multiplayer competitive shooter where even 1 fps matters. Is a story based game just enjoy it. In the 8h I played so far I think I had about 3 "big" shootouts. Rest I played "stealth" mode (actually I should have put this as a plus at gameplay... if you prefer not to shoot ppl but to sneak around and ninja them it is possible). Anyway, point is... stop being spoiled brats. I also invested a lot in my pc and being stuck on 30 fps bums me but really... be real about it and HAVE FUN (that's the whole reason you are playing something right?).

To sum it up (because I started ranting a bit)... graphic is ok. Day/night/rain/sun/blabla effects are nice. The game could look better but is not that bad (can't wait for the patch though).

AUDIO:
While the graphics are not that awesome sound is. Voices are well chosen, music is awesome. When you get out of a car if you don't close the radio you can hear it from the outside like you would in real life. I love that detail. I actually park my car close to the missions so I can hear the music for a while more :). Anyway... really good job here.
BUGS: I've seen a lot of ppl. complaining about this. Yes, bugs do exist (I encountered one in the first mission for example (a guard spawned somewhere where I could not kill him and could not continue mission - loaded last checkpoint and was ok). But are not that many and most of them are barely noticeable.

I'll update the review after I finish the game. So far... I loved it.


STORY: 8/10 (so far)
GAMEPLAY: 8/10 (so far)
GRAPHICS: 6/10
AUDIO: 10/10

OVERALL: 8/10 (so far).

I have to admit that it is good. I haven't got nearly the same amount of add ons, or DLC's as they are called here, as I do on my original MS version, but I have NEVER seen or had frame rates so high as on the Steam Edition.
I am taking advantage of this Summer sale while I can, as I think this may be the way forward. The old FSX is languishing with more and more addons, all having a hit on frame rates, but no one, before Steam, has taken a proper GRIP of FSX and made some very basic changes to the insides that we, the Flight Sim Community, have been crying out for, for years!
So firstly, congratulations to Steam for tackling this monster of a Simulation Product. When you have time there are so many little things that need tweaking and updating in FSX, please get around to them as well, because so far it is certainly not what I expected and absolutely stunning. In my opinion of course, their will be those that moan and groan, but this is far easier to control the addons that you use, half of which were just to update FSX itself and the majority of them not doing a very good job!
So far things are looking very good indeed. Had MS not ditched the whole subsiduary company that made FSX for them, I guess it would look something like this now!
What a loss for MS and such a huge gain for STEAM.
When it comes to numbers of players, we are not a huge base, but we are loyal, it is a very adictive simulation and the more you use properly, and learn about the larger commercial craft or whatever is your "thing" and do it properly, the better it will be.

Too much clicking/flicking and micromanaging... not my cup of tea...

I love the art, setting, and storyline so far. However, the controls are unnecesarily difficult. There are simply too many options and you have to micromanage each ships abilities.
-Things like building new ships should not have to require selecting the capitol ship, selecting the ship to build, and then using the flicking mechanic to initiate the build. To many steps for something that can just be attatched to a number key and auto built.
-The flicking mechanic is cool, and I like how it moves the ships. However, you can only flick one ship at a time. In order to move a fleet, you have to create a specific ship, activate its tractor beam mechanic, initiate the machanic using a flick, then double click the navigation guide computer so you can see exactly where you will end up, activate the move ability, flick to move the ship which tractors all the fleet with it, then finally deactivate the tractor beam because the other ships can't use abilities with it on. In a RTS one should be able to just select all units and flick them as a group. The tractorbeam mechanic is a very bad idea that convolutes a process of movement which sould be stupid simple and easy to implement and instead makes it difficult to just play and enjoy the game. Instead you spend all the time of the attack micromanaging movement from point a to point b. Just NO! Bad!
-I love the planet capturing mechanic, and it's cool that you have to aim the hen ships just right so they don't get caught by the planets gravity.
-Mechanics like the corvette's spike ability which gives it extra ramming damage should just be automatic! It just adds another unnecesary step onto the pile of unnecesary steps already.
-A lot of these abilites should be automatic. Cloaking should not be a thing you need to activate. It should just deactivate when you enter battle or use an ability. Henships stealing metamatter with the drone ability from other ships should just be an automatic timed event. It should be a penalty for going to close to a henship which is pretty defenseless anyway.
The activated torpedo mechanics where definately cool, and the astroid physics were really fun. That is what makes the flicking mechanic so unique and they did a good job at it. However, the flicking mechanic is way overused for too many mundane unnecesary tasks to make up for it, and it feels like these mundane convoluted actions were included to slow the game down so the players couldn't rush too hard, or overwhelm too easilly. However, instead it's really game breaking in that it gets boring way to fast, and worse obnoxiouse. It really ruined the game for me even though I wanted to experience the rest of the cool, if a bit cheesy, storyline.
Game have very good presentation, but when you start playing the gimmicky flicking mechanic is a deal breaker. It looks like this game was designed for mobile phones.
I don't like it, don't waste your money on this sh*t. -rep

I thought this game was a joke when I first saw it appear on Steam. Driving trucks through the mud for $30? Pfft! Get out of here.
Then I tried the tech demo and was instantly hooked.
This game has a lot to offer if you're looking to be entertained. There aren't really any objectives, but the maps are interesting to explore and the physics are hilariously fun. Who knew Russian logging could be so interesting?
Pros:
-Surprisingly good graphics
-Deformable terrain and off-roading goodness
-WINCHES
-Varied and useful "attachments" that can be loaded onto your vehicle at a garage
-There is a considerable challenge in just navigating the terrain, from towing a log trailer through deep muck to navigating river crossings that can easily flood your engine or tip you over
-Multiplayer!
-Heavy modding community presence
-Terrain remains deformed between saving and loading your save back up. You can create trouble spots for yourself if you're not careful.
-Refreshing gameplay, who else has made an offroad simulator even close to this?
Mixed:
- Camera is extremely robust, the developer knew players would need to see their vehicles from all kinds of wonky angles. This also makes the camera difficult to control/learn to use, however.
- You can only control 1st and 2nd gears along with reverse. In order to reach gears 3+ you must shift into "automatic" meaning the subsequent shifts aren't under your control. This can be a problem, if say, you wanted to cruise along the road at the speed offered by 3rd gear but the transmission shifts itself to 4th and continues accelerating.
- Wooded areas can be too dense. You may want to take a shortcut through some trees to avoid a muddy area you know you aren't able to surpass, but oftentimes you can't because the spacing between trees is too tight for your vehicle. This makes it VERY easy to trap yourself in a cluster of trees, especially on an incline.
Bad:
- Lack of objectives can be a turn-off for many players
- Small selection of vehicles (though there are dozens available with mods) and they are strictly Russian.
- Very narrow focus (Russian logging) which could easily have been expanded to other areas of the globe.
- No independent saves. If you want to switch maps you must delete the save for the previous map you were on. It really makes no sense why the developer chose to do this.
- There are some graphical glitches here and there, though nothing too serious
- Random bugs. None that are game-breaking, but they can be annoying

Ever since playing the tech demo, this game has been on my radar and has been something I've been waiting for. Now having played the game I can say, Oovee hasn't let me down. Getting stuck in the mud while carrying a load of lumber has never been so much fun.
Spin tires is a open world sandbox style game with objectives, either being clearing blacked out spots on the map or delivering lumber to a sawmill. All while fighting your way though the earth of Russia. In the game, mud behaves like you'd expect it to. The ground will deform and break under you anywhere on the map, well besides paved paths that is. The trucks range from a little 4x4 landrover style to a 8x8 Missle carrier (Missle not included). With these trucks you can wench and tow them, you can rip trees from the ground (With enough power of course), you can cross rivers (if you dare). On that note, the  game probably has one of the best vehicle engine sounds I've -ever- heard. Hearing a that diesel wind up though a 5.1 headset hasn't been more sexy.
The game is beautiful as well, almost everything acts and reacts like it should. Leaving ruts in the mud is such a pleasing thing when your driving a truck. Everything from the exhaust smoke to the bits of mud that fly off the tires is just eye candy.
Performance of the game is astounding, while only being 500mb DL at the time of writing, the game will run flawlessly on max settings on my computer which is: (Simplifed summery)
Intel core-duo 3.0Ghz Wolfdale.
4 gigs of ram.
ATI 4870 1G XFX Edition.
1 TB 7200 RPM Seagate Harddrive.
Which is a old computer pushing almost 6 years at the time of writing.
So, if you like driving offroad, getting lost in a giant forest while listening to the birds and the sweet sound of a diesel rumbling though your headphones, I would highly recommending getting this game. Oovee has stated they are fully supporting this game with future content and mod support. The game only has one direction and that is up and I fully look forward to the direction this game is going and will be along for the ride the whole way.

I reached the "true ending" tonight and while I admire their attempt to tie the game into the canon of the LOTR universe, I just feel like I have been cheated.
The last 10 hours of this game (which is about 1/3rd of my playtime mind you) is a meaningless grind that adds nothing to the story nor is it a particularly fun experience to go through gameplay-wise. Then, when you're finally done, bam! Cutscene "true ending" that so badly ties up the game that it makes everything you've done from the start of the first game meaningless. You can't help but feel bad (and not in a good way like Spec ops: the line for instance).
The game wasn't bad (except the last act) but it constantly gave me the feeling that if I kept playing, I would get some kind of pay-off (be it new powers or a cool story). About 2/3rds in you've seen every cool bit there is to see and the story just dies off.
Now if I had to say something positive about the game, it would be that loot chests are definitely not required to play the game in single player. You can easily play the game without dropping a dime on it by doing what you did in the first game: killing and dominating orcs.
If you liked the first game solely because of the gameplay, I'd say wait for a sale and grab it for like €15-€20. If you're in it for the story I wouldn't touch it with a 10ft pole.

Wasteland 2 might not be for everyone, so I would definitely recommend doing a little research about the game before making a hasty purchase.
With that being said, this game is excellent. It has the classic RPG feel, reminiscent of the original Fallout games. The turn-based combat system, along with the addition of environmental coverage points, allows for clever tactical takedowns. However; the wide range of skills also provides the player an opportunity to approach encounters and conflicts with more intelligence and diplomacy. The grim, post-apocalyptic atmosphere pulls the player into the Wasteland, while the fleshed-out characters and story firmly root the player in this universe for hours on end. While adventuring in the Wasteland, the player will also face moral dilemmas with consequences that follow the player throughout the game. (It also provides great replay value.) Overall, Wasteland 2 is an excellent game, and I would definitely recommend it for purchase.

Broken Age is the return of the Point and Click genre from fantastic developer Double Fine. With humor, great gameplay, and an even better story, it's hard not to recommend this game. Just be ready to be hit with a giant cliffhanger at the end of Act 1, which is all that is released at the moment.

A true Desert Ranger, what a journey it was to become one. Wasteland 2 has captured the essence of computer role playing games, the best indicator of which is the giddyness you'll feel when you think about doing another playthrough. It has an astounding wealth of good writing in it, so many encounters, quests and dialogues that are simply joyous to experience. The best thing is, that so many of these things can play out differently, depending on your party and your actions. A reactive world with a deeply emotive story.
On your adventures through the sands, towns and cities, the game accompanies you with amazing music and visual style. The art and sounds immerse you, creating an atmosphere, that is both truly gritty in its post-apocalyptic splendor and darkly humorous with countless references and jokes. It's a world you want more of, a world you want to experience and are constantly thrilled to see what comes next.
Combat is tactical and bloody, you will be able to attain all kinds of weapons, hilarious and deadly, and the death animations with the combat action descriptions make it purely Wasteland. Thoroughly enjoyable action from beginning to end. Different playstyles are well taken into account, playing with a bunch of melee bruisers or a squad of dead-shot riflemen, it's all equally satisfying. Though let's just say, that my favorite remains pummeling four raiders into red mist with a single well-placed burst from an automatic shotgun. Brutal and awesome.
You will be creating characters of any variety you wish, and you will fall in love with them. The attribute system, skill system and a cool variety of cosmetic customization are a joy to tinker around with. As you play the game you will learn more about how the game progresses with the type of characters you've created, or NPCs you've recruited, and you'll be excited to try out different things next time. It's a game that keeps on giving.
Do yourself a favor, if you've liked the 90's cRPGs, and play this game. It has been a long wait, but we finally got a game worthy of being up there at the top, with the best cRPG classics. Many games fail to deliver memorable moments, but this one, just like the good ones before it, has you fondly thinking back at the great things you've experienced with it.

It's a fresh way to do real time strategy with a great sense of humor and a good art style. You control ships by "flinging" them which is basically hitting 1 and pulling back so that the ship flys forward. It's a nice concept but it does lead to a lot of micro managing. Although, I don't feel like this destroys the game because of the simplicity that the game offers and because the first few missions give you time to get used to the system, I don't think it's a problem.  The physics system is rather refreshing too. Launching a missle at a meteor will send it flying depending on where you hit it. I feel that this adds some depth to the game. The game does feel aimed towards a younger audience and I think the typcial RTS player may find it boring or simply dumb as the way you control your ships is far from standard.
Over all, it is a good game with a lot of creativity in it. It has some issues like ai not being as hard as you may want but I feel that because of to control system, this game was never meant to be hard but fun because of the wacky things you can do. I recommend this game because it is simply and fun to play.

This game gets 10/10 for the intro video, story and concept and I really wanted to like it but I got frustrated within a matter of minutes of playing the first mission. This game simply doesn't work as an RTS with the flicking mechanics. It needs to be turn based.
Out of a desire to give it a second chance though I attempted to play multiplayer but when no one showed up in the lobby I ended up launching the game against AI instead. I'm glad I did. Playing against a real person would have been a nightmare. The AI isn't remotely challenging - the challenge is simply in navigating anywhere on the map without crashing into something and exploding.
After colonising the nearest planet I set my sights on the nearby enemy planet. I spent a couple minutes building units, linked them to a frigate and flicked them across space... only for an outlying torpedo ship to clip one of the cheese moons and send the entire fleet bouncing wildly in the opposite direction and straight into the gravity well of a planet. Survivors: 0.
So having discovered the... excessive physics properties of these moons I rebuilt the fleet, launched more carefully and avoided the moons... only for a wormhole to appear in front of me and result in the entire fleet crashing headfirst into a planet on the other side of the system. Survivors: 0.
Unsure how I was expected to know that was going to happen or what I possibly could have done about it I tenuously rebuilt the fleet again, this time split and linked to two separate frigates on the basis that surely at least one would not die horribly and unpredictably. I flicked them carefully again and promptly crashed into an enemy ship that just happened to choose that moment to cross my path. Half the fleet was immediately sucked into the nearest planet having lost most of its momentum whilst the others ended up drifting idly into the nearby mothership. Survivors: unknown.
Rather than attempt to flick these units to safety one by one I decided to make the best out of it and send the other half of the fleet in to attack. In my haste however I failed to notice the small half dead patrol ship left in my path from the first failed attempt which the fleet promptly crashed into before bouncing off, hitting a cheese moon, then a second, then a third before finally crashing into two of my henships, knocking them into the planet and getting sucked in themselves. Survivors: 0.
At this point I was beginning to question the strategic nature of this game.
Since two of the AI players had spent the entirety of the game thus far with an equal number of henships perpetually colonising/sterilising the same planet I was, remarkably, still in the lead. However the victory bar was less than half full and I didn't much fancy the prospect of building another dozen ships with a shorter life expectancy than the Titanic so I decided to concede my victory. Well, I say 'concede' I actually just ordered my mothership to fly directly into the nearest planet and take all my henships with it convinced this would be the surest way of ending the game.
Unbeknownst to me however the game just replaces your mothership almost immediately. It just never ends...
If you are unsure if you will like this game then try to imagine playing your favourite RTS only where half the units you build instantly die and the rest can only be moved via a slingshot every ten seconds. If that sounds like your idea of fun then you should probably get this game.

Well I did come here to post about OB44 (Open Beta 44) and how it absolutely destroyed this game but it seems many have already beaten me to the punch.
So ... I will try to do what most don't do: Give you a basic synopsis of what happened in 44 and why it made so many leave.
The big reason why people loved this game is simple: Cards and F2P. There are not many quality F2P FPS games on the market and this is one of the few. Sure the graphics aren't anything to write home about but that is what makes it accessible to everyone.
On top of this, the cards and loadouts give so much more complexity and depth to the game that it is hard to put into words. You want to spit rockets constantly with Mr. Dragonboy there? You can do it! You want to be a really fast sneaky assassin with Skye? YOU CAN DO THAT TOO! You want to be an incredibly elusive, dodgerolling crossbow wielder? SURE CAN!
There's literally LOADS of ways to build and customize your champions and in a way that games like Overwatch cannot compete with as they do not have the systems in place. Tie all this up with a game that IS LITERALLY FREE and you have a fantastic idea my friend.
Then came the terrible concept of OB44.
So ... changes to the game were pretty massive:
***** Removed many high quality cards and turned them into 'Legendaries' which are extremely powerful cards that tweak how your character is played. You get to select from 3 and can only have 1 the entire game.
For example: Grover is a sentient tree that throws lumber axes (I know, hilarious) and his three legendaries are pretty neat: A. His crippling axe (applies cripple to enemies for 2s, cannot use movement abilities) now also roots. B. His heal gets stronger. C. His axes get stronger the further away the enemy is.
Awesome, right?
Except, you only get the root one at first. Others are locked behind a third new currency, which brings me to:
***** "Essence"
For some reason they didn't feel like keeping just gold and gems (the premium currency) so they added in essence.
Now how it USED to be is you got about 400-500 gold per match and you got gold from duplicate drops in loot boxes.
Now, you still get that level of gold but can only buy cards and legendaries with essence which does not drop from anything BUT DUPLICATE CARDS IN CHESTS. NEW PLAYERS, YES I MEAN YOU! THIS SUCKS FOR YOU. Because this means you have an insanely large amount of grinding to do before you can start 'buying' cards. You need to unlock them via RNG chests before they start giving you essence for getting them again (and that is IF YOU GET THEM AGAIN)
Now get this:
***** LEGENDARIES COST 18,000 ESSENCE A PEICE
This means that if you wanted to get all legendaries it would take almost 800,000 essence. Considering you're lucky to pull 400 from a chest (THAT'S IF YOU'RE A VETERAN, NEW PLAYERS ARE JUST SCREWED), and chests cost 2500 gold.
You'd need to play 225 games really well before getting enough essence to get a legendary. TWO HUNDRED AND TWENTY FIVE ♥♥♥♥ING GAMES.
And add in the fact that you can even get duplicate legendaries in chests, INCLUDING THE ONES THE GAME GIVES TO YOU FOR FREE. Why the HELL would a chest give me something the game KNOWS I have?
Last but not least: The bugs. Jesus Christ the bugs ....
***** THE BUGS
Barik (A tanky dwarf with shields, turrets and a death dome as an ultimate) is no longer playable. Bugged out.
The new survival game mode that everyone was excited about is bugged out and disabled.
People cannot play in groups as the leader is the only one who joins games, the rest are kicked.
Competitive games are crashing at the end and givign losses to those who disconect.
These are just a handful of the bugs I've found by myself and from others.
All in all, Hi Rez is a horrible company who will eventually turn greedy. I highly reccomend that if you do try this game, try it with the understanding that it was not always this horrible. This game used to be amazing.
Now ... it's just a grindfest P2W game like any other...

Since I've played it quite a lot now and know what I'm doing I'd say this is quite a decent little game. Build up your vault, go on quests, get loot, craft stuff, make children and that's about it. Pretty simple but since its all fallout themed its quite a nice game.
There are some problems with it for example in a single room you can't have two people both with pets, zooming in & out and moving the camera with the mouse is a bit annoying, especially when you keep accidentally grabbing a vault dweller instead of moving the camera. The graphics aren't good, could atleast make it look a bit better for the PC verison. The elevators aren't realistic, a character can go down an elevator right after another one just went down. After a while you see every location in the game and stuff just repeats, would be better to get a bit more of a variety. Perks/skills don't work like they do in the main games, you can have a level 50 dweller with the best weapons and armor and still have a bit of trouble killing high level enemies, whereas in the main games you just 1 shot everything at that level. There's also a lot missing that are in the main games, not many enemies, locations, items, or characters aside from the legendary ones. Hope they add more to it eventually.
Since its a FTP game it does take a long while to do things like beat quests and pretty much everything else, you'll probably just keep going back to it once or twice a day until its all done however its not a pay to win game although there are micro transactions. You can easily get everything done without having to pay a cent. Just takes a while.
Overall a decent little game. I'd give it a 8/10. Needs more content really.

TL;DR: I don’t want to sugarcoat things here, so it would be fair to say that I loved this game *in spite* of its flaws. Read on if you want to know why…
I’m giving this one a thumbs-up, but that’s not without caveats. Shadow of War is a bigger-better-faster-stronger successor to Shadow of Mordor in virtually all respects, but that’s also a mixed blessing.
SoW has a single brilliantly-executed and enjoyable idea/element – the Nemesis System (NS) – that serves as *the* core mechanic around which everything else revolves. Regardless on your thoughts on combat, the writing, loot and itemization, the grind, siege/army management, or anything else, the NS in all its enhanced and expanded glory infuses this game with a kind of chaotic dynamism that drives everything forward. The Middle Earth setting, while fun and well-drawn, is still just wallpaper. The setting is enjoyable but incidental; the NS defines the play experience at almost every level, regardless of the “who” and “where” of things. Full stop.
If the prospect of an endlessly-changing, procedurally-generated roster of villainous orc captains, war chiefs, and overlords that you must kill or dominate and then use to lay siege to, capture, and eventually defend a series of forts sounds like fun, then you might like this. Things can get pretty grindy, and many of the menus for managing the various pieces – questing, army and siege management, loot, etc. – feel unwieldy and far too busy, but there is still an awful lot of fun to be had here.
Sieges and fort defenses are tedious to setup but an absolute blast to partake in, combat is fluid and fun, and your skills are varied enough and really make you feel downright superpowered as you murder-bot your way through a surprisingly varied series of adversaries and regions. Movement and targeting controls can still feel frustratingly imprecise at times, and especially in larger, chaotic battles and when trying to be in any way accurate with your double-jumping antics or beast-riding. But growing in power and advancing the narrative as the ultimate Third Age anti-hero was generally a blast, and the cartoonish villainy of the NS and its many voiceovers and encounters never lost its magic for me.
The story will rake Tolkien purists over the coals with its creative and borderline-ridiculous embellishments and retcons, but it’s hard to complain too strongly when so much of the overall experience is so viscerally satisfying. Without getting too specific, the story was fun but also very uneven for me personally. I’m a fan of the books but don’t begrudge Monolith for taking liberties with the Middle Earth property, but with that said the first two acts are *really* strong and then things advance at breakneck speeds to a poorly contextualized false ending that serves as a pretext for the *real* ending that is essentially gated behind a truckload of additional siege defenses and everything that entails. Now I generally *liked* leveling up and killing/dominating orcs in the first couple acts, so this isn’t bad per say, but it’s important to note that I plan on going through Act 4 at a much slower pace and eventually “finishing” the Shadow War part over the next few weeks. I’ve watched the video of the hidden/secret/real ending cinematic on YouTube, so I know what’s coming, but it’s a major misstep that the devs chose to gate that experience behind such a huge and unnecessary grind. I imagine that many players won’t even bother to finish once they realize how many flavor-free hours will be required to “earn” the real ending, since there are no more story missions or the like after Act 3. I hope that future updates move the final cinematic to the end of Act 3, thus removing the *need* to grind through the Shadow Wars if you don’t want to while still letting those that want to continue mucking around in the NS sandbox do so as much as they’d like post-game.
And finally, the gripe that everyone seems fixated on: gimmicky DLC offerings and microtransactions in a AAA game that already cost $60-100 depending on the version you bought. Woof.  There are three parts of this debate/issue for me: communication, cost, and content.
Cost: Full disclosure, but I bought the $100 Gold version thinking that was essentially the same thing as pre-buying the Season Pass, and since I had a 20% coupon from GMG, I went that route. I *believe* that is still true – that I’ll essentially get all the extra story DLC and additional tribes – but I’m no longer certain of that (more on communication later). To be clear, I’m not averse to paying top dollar for a very rewarding and complete gaming experience, and aside from the SNAFU with the staging of the base game’s ending, I got (and will continue to get) my money’s worth. However, the pushy prevalence of loot boxes in this kind of game left a bad taste in my mouth. I agree that they are not necessary and that you can beat the game without ever touching the stuff, but it’s also clear that the for-pay loot boxes would reduce the grind/tedium by immediately giving you seriously OP gear ahead of the curve (the game gives you enough Gold to buy one of the high level chests, so I waited to cash mine in until the end of Act 2 and was surprised by how powerful my new kit was. I replaced almost everything I was wearing just from that single box). It all feels at least a little pay-to-win, which feels very odd to say for an almost entirely single-player game.
Communication: WB has done a shoddy job communicating the realities of the story DLCs and how they relate to the base game content. Are the Eltariel and Carnan quests in the base game the actual DLC content, or is there additional story-driven content coming that relates to those two storylines? It sounds like the new orc tribes are coming in standalone DLC, but will that integrate into the base game or will they be confined to other unreleased DLC packs? How does the season pass stack up compared to the Silver/Gold versions of the game? Again, it’s possible I’ve missed something obvious, but WB seems to have dropped the ball here by not going out of their way to make the differences between all these variants clearer. Getting answers to questions like this should not require research and the scouring of message boards.
Content: This is a bit more zoomed out and critical of both WB and the gaming industry overall, but I miss the days of these big AAA games being a complete experience out of the box. Or, at most, going with the base game plus a big, meaty expansion pack 6-18 months later that gave you enough new content to make replaying the whole thing worthwhile. I don’t even object to DLC per say, since that can be an efficient way to create big, new stories for an existing gaming world that is financially viable – like with The Witcher 3 and its two excellent paid-DLC packs – but I find the larger trend toward excessive and borderline scammy monetization in modern games to be frustrating and disheartening. I want to support devs and even some publishers that I love by buying their games as early and as often as I can, but it’s getting harder not to just wait for the inevitable GOTY edition or for a steep discount in the following year or two.
To conclude, this was an enjoyable and sufficiently conclusive end to Talion’s story. It integrated well into the canonical events/world state of Middle Earth, but in the way that great fan fiction manages to invent enough space for itself to live without actually disrupting core characters or events in an established world. The NS is back and better than ever, combat and sieges are fun, but there’s still a tendency toward unnecessarily bloated systems and unwieldy UIs for managing them. There’s also all the grossness of excessive monetization through pay-to-win microtransactions and confusing DLC plans.
Again: I don’t want to sugarcoat things here. I loved this game *in spite* of its flaws. Maybe you will, too.

Abstract
0. Background: 70h of gameplay on normal difficulty, all quest lines completed (100%) including the true ending, game progress 98%, ZERO money spent on microtransactions
1. General technical aspects: Good
2. Steering and gameplay: Cumbersome in certain situations, but overall acceptable
3. Story: Uninteresting and forgettable
4. Lootboxes: Absolutely no need to shell out real money for them, game is fun without them
Verdict: I liked the predecessor Shadow of Mordor, and I enjoyed this game here very much.
Following is the detailed review:
I play(ed) the game on an i7-4770 with 16 GB RAM and a GTX 1080 graphics card connected to a gaming monitor (144 Hz refresh rate). I bought the gold edition of the game and the forthog slayer DLC; the latter was refunded automatically. However, I never saw the forthog slayer in the actual gameplay (I was sometimes saved by other friendly orcs). Only in the "true ending" credits movie I saw the forthog.
1. General technical aspects:
The game runs performant on my system. I use high to ultra settings and the high resolution texture pack. Most of the time, I get 100+ fps, seldomly dropping to 80 fps in highly dense situations. It feels fluent all the time. Loading times are short, and I never had a crash or a hang. Only the brightness setting seems to be bugged, because everytime I restart the game, I have to set the brightness again.
Concerning antialias settings, there is FXAA, which doesnt help against the jaggies in the far background, and TAA, which gets rids of all graphical jaggies but blurs everything that moves to a degree that I dont like it. My solution to this was to slightly oversample / overscale render (there is a settings for that) and use FXAA as well, which is a good looking compromise.
2. Steering and gameplay:
It does its job somehow, however it gets cumbersome and clunky in narrow places when you try to fight lots of enemies with lots of friendlies around, for example in a siege situation. Your attacks will hurt your allies (and their attacks hurt you as well), because it is impossible to target a certain enemy with the sword. This problem also applies to enemy orcs / enemy and friendly AI, I have seen mini-cutscenes of one enemy captain killing his allied captain in such crowded environment. Only the bow has pinpoint accuracy. Many keys have multiple functions, for example the key to heal your fallen comrades is the same that you need to use to brand / domninate enemy orcs (and even more functions). While in less dense combat situations, this works well, it fails in situation where in front of you are both friendlies and enemies, and both normal orcs as well as captains, because all of these different combinatins will result in different actions depending on the target (friendly/foe, normal/captain). When trying to dominate a specific broken enemy captain, I often end up branding another enemy orc instead or start to drain life from a comrade. Likewise, trying to heal a friendly captain with lots of enemies around needs several retries until you finally snap on the intended target and do what you want to do and not something else to the rest of the orcs that are staying around. This multifunctionality of keys isn't only a problem for the attacking-healing-brading-complex that is bound to only one key, it also applies to the multifunctionality-complex of dodge/run/jump over orcs, parry an incoming sword / use the bow etc. pp. Overall, it seems the steering and input methods are generally aimed at controllers and not for mouse and keyboard. Menus and other UI elements could be controlled easier if the mouse would have been taken into account seriously. On top of that, using the mouse to look around has an inbuilt mouse smoothing that you cannot disable.
Mini-cutscenes when a captain is killed are nice, however they disorient the camera and interrupt your action. Such a cutscenes stops you in your place to watch it, and might leave you disoriented after that. The rather small field of view doesn't help that either, escpecially if the camera tries to zoom in when you are backed up against a wall.
Also, sometimes it is not entirely clear what is a mini-cutscene, normal gameplay or QTE-minigame. Once the game threw me into the "last chance" minigame without me noticing it, therefore the typical button mashing (and hoping it will target the intendend orc) lead to my instant death because I was in that minigame that gets you killed if you press a wrong button or too early.
Leaving this shortcomings aside, it was stil fun to play, and mashing lots of orcs and seeing funny accidents happen all over the place or happening to me was good. Yes, while I list problems with the steering and camera movements, overall I am still enjoying it. Epic batlles are epic because of their chaos. You don't lose much if you die, because you just respawn and can try the mission again. And if you lost a siege over your castle, no problem, you can regain it (and attacking castles seems to be a lot easier than holding them). The only fights I needed several tries where the Nazgul enemies, those should be toned down a bit, in my view.
3. Story: Uninteresting
There is a spider woman and another woman and an elf and another elf and they have some problems with each other or you or want something from you or each other. Or something. I did not really dig the story, I could try to retell it here, but I don't want to, because killing lots of orcs was/is more entertaining. You can think of the story in this like a story in a pron movie: There might be such, but nobody cares. Additionally, the movie cutscenes look worse than the acual rendered ingame scenes.
4. Lootboxes:
Totally ignoring the microtransactions does not impact the game in a negative way. Maybe it's the opposite, but I don't know, because I didn't buy any of them. With the gold edition, I got a golden whatever lootbox at the start, and a sword because of preoder. But that sword was level 5 and I soon had a better one looted from normal gameplay, and opening the golden box didn't get me something good because the orcs you get from the boxes are your level or below, so that wasn't much of a help as well. The preorder bonus and the box (or boxes, can't remeber really) you get from the gold edition might help a bit in the beginning, but are soon forgotten and replaced by the stuff you get by normal ingame mechanics and playing the game.
Overall, I never felt like I had to do microtransaction or would have more fun if i did. I made enough ingame currency from playing the game. You don't need legendary orcs in your army to play the game and get to the true ending. And for me, it didn't feel like grinding, I had my fair share of fun killing lots of orcs. That is what the game is about. Maybe if you don't take active part in sieges you must use legendary orcs, but I don't know, because I was doing fine with the four or something legendary orcs I got from normal gameplay.
So, the necessity of lootboxes bought with real money / microtransactions to avoid a tedious grind in act IV is a lie, in my view. The game is definetly balanced without the microtransactions. Maybe the reviewers that state the opposite have to gid gud? I mean, I don't think I am a pro gamer (normal difficulty in Fallout 4 was too hard for me), but this game here was fine for me on normal, so I don't get why some reviewers claim that the endgame is pay-to-win or whatever.
Don't get me wrong, I am in no way defending the microtransactions, rather the opposite. I am wondering why they are even there, and it's a bit annoying and tedious to have to go through the same place (the market) if you want to spend the silver you earned ingame. But it pretty much didn't affect me.
Verdict:
Overall, I had lots of fun with the game and am looking forward to the story expansions. Meanwhile, I will probably doing the online vendettas or sieges or whatever it is.

It's like being back in primary/elementary school playing with marbles, only now the marbles have guns. Artifice Studio, after creating Sang-Froid,  pulls of creating another mind-boggling genre hybrid, as fleet engagements are basically a giant game of Strategic snooker, or tactical péntanque, which is awesome.
I'm not much for multiplayer, but as someone who loves the campaign portion of RTS, great atmosphere, novel mechanics and lovingly made products, I'd like to reccomend this game on those merits alone when you can get it for 10 quid or less.
I had a wonderful time with the campaign. As you can tell from the intro, this is a strange beast in many ways, but the campaign's storyline is an honest and charming collection of 18th century tale telling. You've got your love-lorn British Privateer who will do anything to win the heart of his love, A Loyal French Female Musketeer looking for her father and a time traveling Spanish Monk who repeatedly tries to save his brother, while revolution is brooding. The drawings and artwork are fantastic and the voice acting cleverly replaced by striking sound effects. Love this game.
Other than that, it has all the depth I need out of my RTS. There are no less then 4 different factions, each with a good variety of ships. Each of these ships have their own abilities. British ships can armor up, have blast weapons to knock enemy ships away. French ships are strong at area of effect abilities. The Spanish can warp and teleport both themselves and others around, while the Ottomans can clone and duplicate. There is great potential to stick to theme and come up with something interesting.

A realtime strategy space battle game where, instead of directly ordering ships to move, you "flick" them like rubber bands. The setting and art are very unique, but...
This game is a laundry list of "it could have been good if..."
if they had ditched the gimmicky flicking and just made it a standard RTS
if it was turned based instead of real time so you could manage all the crap (it actually seems like it was meant to be turn based but was changed at the last second)
if you could actually issue orders while paused
if the controls weren't so choppy that you end up deselecting the unit half the time you go to "flick"
The end result is just a mess of fiddling with the annoying flicking mechanic while your ships are shot up in real time with no real ability to pause because you can't pre-order flicks while paused. There are special abilites that differentiate the ships, but most of them also require flicks and aren't worth the hassle. Both building ships and using abilities take the same money resource, but you recover money so quickly that it's never a factor. The only limiting factor is the player's time and attention flicking ships one at a time. Special abilities aren't worth using because that's time you could have spent building more ships (which also requires a flick on the contructing ship) and flicking them towards the enemy.
This could have worked turn based. This could have worked without flicking. This could have worked with the ability to issue orders and flicks while paused. But none of those are true so the game just plain doesn't work. It's a shame because from an artistic standpoint it's great. The gameplay is just horrid though.

I couldn't even bear to finish tutorial, that's just how stupid it was. It asks too much of a micromanagement in a too short time frame. It is obvious that this game was initially developed as turn-based, but for some reason became real-time. Graphics are  good, but gameplay? Total crap.
1) This game uses flicking, which is effectively drag&drop on mouse. Now go look at how similar games are made and in what manner they are different. Right, most of them were initially developed for touch screen. And succesful PC ones in general try to limit number of times you have to drag&drop because it is very taxing on hand compared to regular mouse movement.
2) Micromanagement here asks you to manually control each ship, and do regular flicks to be successive because in most cases you can't flick ships far and travel often requires more than two flicks.
It would all be okay if it was turn-based giving you time to catch a breath, but it is RTS, so 1) + 2) combined means what I said earlier: too much actions to do in too short time.
Combine it with heavy stress on arm = bad choice. Me, with mild CTS limiting how long i can stress my arms with KB or mouse won't be able to play this game for any prolonged period of time. That's why I say NO. If you like that ridiculous challenge - okay, it's a good game for you. But not for me.

A fantastic (but short) atmospheric game relying on its strongpoints of storytelling to make up for what can be seen as shortcomings in the action sequences. A great deal of effort is put into engrossing the player in its world, setting up th e game as an episodic miniseries, complete with intros, recaps, and outros, as well as plenty of collectibles and side tihngs to find that expand on what's happening. The game plays well, but unfortunately combat can fall short and become repetitive, since the tools at your disposal are few and mostly upgrade in pure numbers. It's tense enough to keep you on your toes, but playing on normal/hard, i never felt truly stretched for resources except once during the game. That said, the presentation of the game, and the story it tells make up for the difference in spades, and it's a shame the game only got two small DLC episodes instead of the true "second season" it deserved.
Would definitely recommend to fans of the thriller/mystery genre, as long as you're OK with never really finding out what happens after the end.
