A bit rough around the edges but with some tweaks and changes can be the perfect off-road simulator.
The world looks excelent and reflects well onto your vehicle such as mud being kicked up or being washed off with water and the effects on your vehicle are just as detailed and beautiful like the plumes of desel smoke coming out of exhausts and across the ground.
Unfortunatly the same cannot be said for other players vehicles which lack any effects visible
to you and also do not share terrain deformation which leaves them feeling more like ghosts in your world rather than active participants.
The lighting in the game is a mixed bag. Normally its very well done but at night the world is far to bright except when you turn on your headlights which changes the lighting completely and makes the night feel much more realistic but sadly as other players headlights do not effect your game its left to be a mainly cinematic option as turning them on only cripples your vision.
The water in the game is well worth mentioning as it looks amazing and makes the world feel much more alive.
Weather effects freshen up extended time play in the game by varying the conditions of the world but unfortunatly they seem to have no impact on the world which is a huge missed oppertunity and a rain effect is blindingly missing.
This game is the closest experience to real world 4WDing I know of and its a joy to simply traverse the maps in the multiple vehicles provided but one of the most infuriating problems with the game is that most of the ground is far too slushy and appears deceptivly solid on observation.
Areas that should without a doubt be solid ground, such as around trees and on high ground, can inexplainably be as liquidy as water, which gives an unwelcome randomness to the game and leads to traversing neccesary areas using only your winch, from tree to tree.
Winches being as required as they are are inexplicably limited in length and more often than not when truly needed lack the length required to be used or used effectivly and are also limited in that you can only have one winch deployed at a time.
Vehicles also lack appropriate winch points to recover them after rolling over so unless you play in the casual mode that allows automatic vehicle recovery you will need to spend up to an hour or so trying to get your vehicle right side up.
Water features become incredably difficult to traverse when you are faced with not only extremely unpredictable ground, and no way to check water depth but also water currants far too unrealisticly strong and the overly dangerous water itself as when water reaches a certain height on your vehicle it will start to take huge chunks of damage and eventually cripple your vehicle.
The camera (while currently being addressed) uses an AI that is absolutely horrible and will constantly make changes to your view that are more often than not extremely unappreciated and with no way to lock the cameras position you will not only be battling the terrain but battling the camera to show you what you need to see.
There Isn't enough content in the game at launch with only a handfull of vehicles and appreciated but limited customization options for each.
The game needs more variety, especially in the lower size of vehicles aswell as vehicles that promote interaction with other players and with the world itself.
There is no variation in the objectives in the different maps which is another of the games great missed oppertunities where the game is expressly directed at the transportation of lumber to the exclusion of all else save for fuel and repair vehicles which facilitate the lumber transport.
The damage system in the game stands next to the watery mud as one of the most unrealistic and annoyingly broken mechanics in the game as an subtle bounce along an otherwise prestine road can severely damage your truck and hitting unimportant parts of your truck without much force also eats away at your damage threshold very quickly in trucks without much ground clearance.
Unfortunatly there is a lack of mod support for the game at launch but hopefully full mod support and steam workshop support will be implemented.
Server hosts lack any options to customize the map and would greatly benifit from being able to edit the types of vehicles at each vehicle location, an option to remove cloaking and the ability to kick and ban players from their game.
There are many other key features missing such as muting players, VoIP support, a chat log, saving progress for players during a hosts session, transfering host duties when a host leaves a game, a drop in drop out connection.
The chatbox also dissapears randomly and pressing keys to type a message will sometimes trigger their bound action in the game.
Players have next to no interaction with each other except for fullfilling objectives such as revealing cloaking.
Towing players is near useless as the physics engine makes the experience jerky and feel extremely heavy compared to towing your own vehicles.
Other players vehicles are strangly still somewhat interact with your unoccupied vehicles through physics while able to move through them and not see your unoccupied vehicles while not being effected by them at all.
Unoccupied vehicles need to either be visible and interactive with other players or non interactive and not visible to other players.
The game is alot of fun and with the right support can become the best off-road sim currently available. Definitly worth the purchase if you want to experience off-roading at home.

I don't usually care much for story-driven games, but Alan Wake is an exception. It's basically "Stephen King Book: the Game" (it even mentions him by name a few times in the dialog - heck, his name is the first two words spoken in the game!).
The plot revolves around the title character going on vacation with his wife to the town of Bright Falls in the Cascades of WA (close to home!), only to end up with her disappearing. After Wake suddenly comes to in a crashed car and realizes a week has passed of which he has no memory, things start to get weird: people go missing and turn up in the woods attempting to murder Wake; apparently his wife was kidnapped, and the kidnapper is demanding a certain book manuscript as ransom, but Wake is certain he never wrote the manuscript being demanded; and the cabin he and his wife were staying at was apparently destroyed nearly half a century before their arrival in a volcanic eruption, meaning they'd been staying at a litreal ghost house. As Wake stumbles through the woods trying to figure out what's going on and how to get his wife back, things just get weirder.
The game itself is set up to look like a TV miniseries, with six "episodes" each ending with a fade to the game's title on the screen accompanied by end-credits-y music, and the next one starting with a "Previously, on Alan Wake ..." segment recapping the events so far. It works well for the way the story plays out.
Gameplay consists of wandering through the woods along vague paths (you have a radar that points you in the right direction, so getting lost is never a problem) while fighting off shadowy people known as the Taken. The Taken are people from Bright Falls who have recently vanished, now somehow appearing as corrupted, dark versions of themselves bent on killing Wake. Your only weapons are a flashlight, which removes the shadowy "shield" the Taken possess when they first spawn, and whatever guns you can find, with which to shoot the de-shadowed Taken - even when the flashlight is used on them, they remain hostile, so you have to get rid of them. The combat is unfortunately a bit limited, and is the game's weakest point: there are only four different kinds of guns and two kinds of throwables, and most aren't available at most times (you lose your previous equipment frequently due to various story circumstances, such as falling off a cliff). There are occasional places where the environment provides other tools that can be used for combat, such as aiming a spotlight as a giant flashlight or running over Taken in a truck, and minibosses pop up from time to time, including a couple of possessed bulldozers. Still, it gets a bit monotonous hiking through the trees and shooting the same Taken over and over. Apparently the woods around Bright Falls were filled with mad meathook-wielding joggers ripe for possession.
PROS:
+The story is excellent for anyone who enjoys Stephen King books - it feels like something he could have written
+The episodic format makes for nice breaks in the story, and each episode ends on a cliffhanger to keep you going
+Some nice songs on the soundtrack, including one that's used cleverly for story exposition and guidance towards the next objective
+Collectibles and achievements add a bit of replay value
+An entertaining and ever-shifting cast of characters
+A few very annoying characters got what they deserved
CONS:
-Exploring the woods gets old after a while, especially since interesting landmarks stop appearing after a while (early chapters have campsites with tourist-y stuff to explore)
-Combat is repetitive with only a few weapons, most of which aren't available at most times
-Wake himself doesn't really develop as a character, which leads to his attitudes and monotone voice getting a bit tiresome
Overall I'd recommend Alan Wake for anyone who enjoys Stephen King's work and doesn't mind rather simplistic gameplay if it means getting a cool story.

Well I did come here to post about OB44 (Open Beta 44) and how it absolutely destroyed this game but it seems many have already beaten me to the punch.
So ... I will try to do what most don't do: Give you a basic synopsis of what happened in 44 and why it made so many leave.
The big reason why people loved this game is simple: Cards and F2P. There are not many quality F2P FPS games on the market and this is one of the few. Sure the graphics aren't anything to write home about but that is what makes it accessible to everyone.
On top of this, the cards and loadouts give so much more complexity and depth to the game that it is hard to put into words. You want to spit rockets constantly with Mr. Dragonboy there? You can do it! You want to be a really fast sneaky assassin with Skye? YOU CAN DO THAT TOO! You want to be an incredibly elusive, dodgerolling crossbow wielder? SURE CAN!
There's literally LOADS of ways to build and customize your champions and in a way that games like Overwatch cannot compete with as they do not have the systems in place. Tie all this up with a game that IS LITERALLY FREE and you have a fantastic idea my friend.
Then came the terrible concept of OB44.
So ... changes to the game were pretty massive:
***** Removed many high quality cards and turned them into 'Legendaries' which are extremely powerful cards that tweak how your character is played. You get to select from 3 and can only have 1 the entire game.
For example: Grover is a sentient tree that throws lumber axes (I know, hilarious) and his three legendaries are pretty neat: A. His crippling axe (applies cripple to enemies for 2s, cannot use movement abilities) now also roots. B. His heal gets stronger. C. His axes get stronger the further away the enemy is.
Awesome, right?
Except, you only get the root one at first. Others are locked behind a third new currency, which brings me to:
***** "Essence"
For some reason they didn't feel like keeping just gold and gems (the premium currency) so they added in essence.
Now how it USED to be is you got about 400-500 gold per match and you got gold from duplicate drops in loot boxes.
Now, you still get that level of gold but can only buy cards and legendaries with essence which does not drop from anything BUT DUPLICATE CARDS IN CHESTS. NEW PLAYERS, YES I MEAN YOU! THIS SUCKS FOR YOU. Because this means you have an insanely large amount of grinding to do before you can start 'buying' cards. You need to unlock them via RNG chests before they start giving you essence for getting them again (and that is IF YOU GET THEM AGAIN)
Now get this:
***** LEGENDARIES COST 18,000 ESSENCE A PEICE
This means that if you wanted to get all legendaries it would take almost 800,000 essence. Considering you're lucky to pull 400 from a chest (THAT'S IF YOU'RE A VETERAN, NEW PLAYERS ARE JUST SCREWED), and chests cost 2500 gold.
You'd need to play 225 games really well before getting enough essence to get a legendary. TWO HUNDRED AND TWENTY FIVE ♥♥♥♥ING GAMES.
And add in the fact that you can even get duplicate legendaries in chests, INCLUDING THE ONES THE GAME GIVES TO YOU FOR FREE. Why the HELL would a chest give me something the game KNOWS I have?
Last but not least: The bugs. Jesus Christ the bugs ....
***** THE BUGS
Barik (A tanky dwarf with shields, turrets and a death dome as an ultimate) is no longer playable. Bugged out.
The new survival game mode that everyone was excited about is bugged out and disabled.
People cannot play in groups as the leader is the only one who joins games, the rest are kicked.
Competitive games are crashing at the end and givign losses to those who disconect.
These are just a handful of the bugs I've found by myself and from others.
All in all, Hi Rez is a horrible company who will eventually turn greedy. I highly reccomend that if you do try this game, try it with the understanding that it was not always this horrible. This game used to be amazing.
Now ... it's just a grindfest P2W game like any other...

But the way the missions take place leave so much to be desired. In the main AND side missions you are doing the same ffing thing over and over and over again without the feeling of progress.
I have 12 hours on record and I don't know how, I don't feel like I have achieved anything. The first few hours were amazing but the rest is starting to feel like a waste of time. Now I don't know how far I am in the story but I do know that I have lost interest in driving from point A to B and kill a bunch of people, then driving back to point A to tell them I succeeded in killing a bunch of people. This game made me wish for a quick travel option..
Am I really the boss in this game or am I still a puppet with strings being played?
Haven't we learned from far cry 4 that the hero is often just a slave to the side characters?
How (in)appropriate for this game, atleast we got to shoot them kkk members so it's worth am I right?
Why can't I buy clothes? Oh you are going to add 'costumes' in a later patch? Which you probably have to acces via the start menu just like switching between lethal an non lethal kills eh?
Why can't I go to a car dealer and buy cars? I get a set of cars picked for me? For free? Jolly good, such choice.
Why don't the police mind me speeding? Do the police even give tickets? What is their use other then being just another gang. Why is the entire police system a downgrade from mafia 2?
Why are the lockpick mechanics a step down from mafia 2? I could see the freaking lock in that game, even opened cars that way. Now i just bash a window and jump in gta style.. is it cause I'm black?
What happend to the licenseplate system? Yo, that was cool.

In the end I even had unopened Vendetta lootboxes and sat on over 36.000 credits ingame currency.

ORIGINAL REVIEW.........................................................................................................
Since I started The shadow wars I just defended every fortress with the orcs it happened to have.
If that meant going with my level 30s against level 50s, I fought it anyway, but the difference in attacking and defending strength doesn't make it impossible to win.
In fact I'm now in Shadow War Stage 9 and have only lost a fortress 3 times (disregarding the one time you loose it in the story).
And I haven't bought a single war chest either, I just upgrade my fortress by dominating the attackers.
And even if I wanted to buy war chests, I could, because I'm constantly at 20-30k Mirian, since you just get so much of it.
I feel like the idea that lootboxes "could" have influenced this part, makes people give up already at the moment they see their fortress under attack by a stronger force, while its really easy to swing it in your favor just by dominating a couple of them.
Honestly, I feel like this part is even a little bit too easy, even with big level differences and on highest difficulty,
But it's fun and gives me something to do. Something that I didn't have at this point in Shadow of Mordor.

Don't get me wrong, Wasteland 2 is not a bad game. The problem is that it's not a good game either. At the beginning It definitely gives you that sweet feeling of an old style RPG, but as you go deeper into the game, you start to realise that it's just the surface and Wasteland 2 is pretty dull at the inside. It's not about some major issues, the problem is that there are huge number of small ones.
1) Game mechanics is not transparent. Do you know that high combat initiative allows you have more than one move in a turn? Do you know how luck affects drop rates? How charisma works, is it party-based or character-based? Do you know that formula for action points is (STR+INT+SPD)/4+CRD/2. Sure, you can dig forums and find answers to most of your questions, but you can't find them in game.
2) Boring levels. Maps are quite big and full of hidden crates and containers. There are no shortage of mobs as well. It makes progression tedious and dull.
3) Most skills are poorly designed. Computer science, demolitions, lockpicking, safecracking, toaster repair - in 95% of the situations you use them to get access to some loot. And you really need that loot and those skills, because ammo is sparse. I found that Mechanical Repair and Animal Whisperer to be enjoyable, just because they are not used routinely.
4) There are dosens of crates, safes, and blah-blah on the map. Almost all of them contains some junk, a little bit of ammo and tiny amount of money. It makes the gameplay grindy and tedious. Instead it would be much better to remove 90% of the crates and fill remaining 10% with cool items, and give the player feeling of the accomplishment.
5) The storyline is not engaging and full of cliches. It really fits theme of original Wasteland, but what was good back in 80s is boring and repetitive now. It reminds me of Fallout Tactics, which is not cool. To be fair, there are good things about the story as well: i really like emphasis on hard decisions and "you can't save em all" attitude.
6) There are times when game really breaks the immersion.  First time you see a honey badger - it's really funny. Second time, it's ok. But when you see a whole valley full of them, you just facepalm. There are no day/night cycle (fallout 1/2, arcanum, hell - even Ultima 7 had that). And yeah - dosens of crates full of staff in what was supposed to be a wasteland.
7) And list goes on and on.
Note, that none of these issues are gamebreaking or something. They just take away some satisfaction of the game. So if your are a fun of post-apocalypse theme and turn based combat - by all means get it, but wait for the sale. Otherwise - avoid.

I don't usually care much for story-driven games, but Alan Wake is an exception. It's basically "Stephen King Book: the Game" (it even mentions him by name a few times in the dialog - heck, his name is the first two words spoken in the game!).
The plot revolves around the title character going on vacation with his wife to the town of Bright Falls in the Cascades of WA (close to home!), only to end up with her disappearing. After Wake suddenly comes to in a crashed car and realizes a week has passed of which he has no memory, things start to get weird: people go missing and turn up in the woods attempting to murder Wake; apparently his wife was kidnapped, and the kidnapper is demanding a certain book manuscript as ransom, but Wake is certain he never wrote the manuscript being demanded; and the cabin he and his wife were staying at was apparently destroyed nearly half a century before their arrival in a volcanic eruption, meaning they'd been staying at a litreal ghost house. As Wake stumbles through the woods trying to figure out what's going on and how to get his wife back, things just get weirder.
The game itself is set up to look like a TV miniseries, with six "episodes" each ending with a fade to the game's title on the screen accompanied by end-credits-y music, and the next one starting with a "Previously, on Alan Wake ..." segment recapping the events so far. It works well for the way the story plays out.
Gameplay consists of wandering through the woods along vague paths (you have a radar that points you in the right direction, so getting lost is never a problem) while fighting off shadowy people known as the Taken. The Taken are people from Bright Falls who have recently vanished, now somehow appearing as corrupted, dark versions of themselves bent on killing Wake. Your only weapons are a flashlight, which removes the shadowy "shield" the Taken possess when they first spawn, and whatever guns you can find, with which to shoot the de-shadowed Taken - even when the flashlight is used on them, they remain hostile, so you have to get rid of them. The combat is unfortunately a bit limited, and is the game's weakest point: there are only four different kinds of guns and two kinds of throwables, and most aren't available at most times (you lose your previous equipment frequently due to various story circumstances, such as falling off a cliff). There are occasional places where the environment provides other tools that can be used for combat, such as aiming a spotlight as a giant flashlight or running over Taken in a truck, and minibosses pop up from time to time, including a couple of possessed bulldozers. Still, it gets a bit monotonous hiking through the trees and shooting the same Taken over and over. Apparently the woods around Bright Falls were filled with mad meathook-wielding joggers ripe for possession.
PROS:
+The story is excellent for anyone who enjoys Stephen King books - it feels like something he could have written
+The episodic format makes for nice breaks in the story, and each episode ends on a cliffhanger to keep you going
+Some nice songs on the soundtrack, including one that's used cleverly for story exposition and guidance towards the next objective
+Collectibles and achievements add a bit of replay value
+An entertaining and ever-shifting cast of characters
+A few very annoying characters got what they deserved
CONS:
-Exploring the woods gets old after a while, especially since interesting landmarks stop appearing after a while (early chapters have campsites with tourist-y stuff to explore)
-Combat is repetitive with only a few weapons, most of which aren't available at most times
-Wake himself doesn't really develop as a character, which leads to his attitudes and monotone voice getting a bit tiresome
Overall I'd recommend Alan Wake for anyone who enjoys Stephen King's work and doesn't mind rather simplistic gameplay if it means getting a cool story.

Wasteland 2 is a very, very strange game.
It feels polished, refined, old-school one second, and completely like shaite the other.
It's all there. You have a party, you have a world (to save), you have a story, you have a huge world to explore (larger than Fallout 2, as far as I can tell - that's a lot of gameplay hours)...
You have weapons, and you will be working with them a whole lot. Yes, working - finding new ones, adding attachements, all the glorious micromanagement (and I like it).
It all goes south when you go east - literally. Before a certain point in a game concerning a very messed-up canyon it's all good. Even perfect for completionists like me.
BUT AFTER... the location is so convoluted that playing a good guy becomes a chore. You fail if you shoot up bad guys. You fail if you don't. You fail if you did not level particular skills up. And you can do pretty much nothing to change the situation, because you can choose between a lame and stupid status quo (with a SUDDEN TWIST), a change in management that makes it no better, and a free-for-all deathmatch.
At this point inExile fails good storytelling forever.
And don't get me started on dialogue tree lockouts. And the CRAjunkP you have to lug around. And on companions that do nothing or suddenly explode with no explaination. And endgame companion choices. And a skill system that suffers from underdesign and overdesign at the same time. And lame-butt character graphics (is it just me or do they all look malnourished?). And no beautiful armor actually appearing on the character models when you do equip them with armor.
And on top-tier armor setting you at a disadvantage against high-level weapons (no, really?)...
I'm deleting the game now and settling in for another long wait. Here's to hoping they WILL actually fix at least some of this madness.

Alan Wake starts of with a fairly long back story intro that sheds light on Alan's history with his writing, and his relationship with his wife. Then the "accident" happens and all kinds of weird and bizarre stuff starts happening. At this point, I wasn't sure how the story was going to progress but I found myself day after day while at work wondering what's going to happen next.
Throughout the game I was continuously impressed with the dialogue and voice acting that added a lot to the ambiance. There are radios and TVs scattered throughout the game that have a sometimes creepy "Night Springs" TV show, and the radios are a continuous radio broadcast hosted by Pat Maine who sounds like a nice, small town radio host. All the different characters were all quite believable, mainly because the actors did a great job making me feel like I was actually lost in the woods, or walking through the police station, or mowing down some Taken. Definitively one of the better games in which the main character does have a personality and his decisions never had me yelling "why the F would you do that?!" at the screen.
The combat isn't anything special, there's a slow-mo dodge that evades any incoming attack as long as you time it right. Alan's flashlight is the main weapon against Taken, using it to burn off the "Darkness" that... well.. took them. All the enemies have melee weapons and can be easily dispatched with a few quick bursts from the flashlight and 2-3 shots from the pistol. Occasionally there's a Taken that throws a hammer or knife at Alan, and there's the really big guys that take a bit more from the flashlight and a few more bullets. I didn't bother trying out all the secondary weapons and hardly had to use FB grenades or flares, since the combat is REALLY predictable once I got the hang of it. There's quite a few weapons to choose from, but the pistol and hunting rifle are all I used. Again, it's not about the combat, its about the story. I started to think about the combat as being more like interactive loading screens between character dialogue. Occasionally the Darkness inhabits objects like barrels, boxes, cars, trucks and just about anything actually. They get hurled at tremendous speed, but as long as there's something in between Alan and the "Poltergeist", even a plastic cup, it's enough to stop the weight of a charred tractor. So there's that.
I found the end of the game right where it should have been, it didn't seem rushed like Michael Bay movies. I liked how the old woman would sometimes scare the hell outta me with a fullscreen flashback that was made to seem like she was in Alan's head. So there was no way of knowing when it was gonna happen, just an old scary♥♥♥♥♥lady would pop up and say something in a weird voice, like 50 people talking at once. There were only a few jump scares, the aforementioned old witch lady being 95%. There wasn't a typical boss at the end of the game, more like a weird vortex thing. I liked the VERY end, as it sets up for the second game.
I'd recommend it to people that like a good story that's quite psychological. It's has basic combat, lots of stuff to listen to, and awesome character development.

It's something vaguely to with your character killling off the Russian mafia in 1980's Miami, but we have nobody's word for it on who exactly he's killing or why. One scene suggests the character is on drugs and this is contributing to his mental decline. The ending is a slightly unsatisfying conclusion to this intrigue, but the game is so fast paced it doesn't register as that much of a problem with me.
Again, this is quibbling. The game is good, it goes on ssale a lot, if you get a chance it's worth playing it.

KSP is already a singular construction and simulation title that is unforgettable for a large portion of its players. However, the developer has a rare opportunity to make this one of the all-time great games. Further improvements will solidify it's position in the gaming zeitgeist.
I understand that KSP is a complex game that won't ever appeal to everyone, but smoothing the difficulty curve would help more players enjoy this unique title. It's a rare occurrence to have developed an all-time great game -- I'm hoping Squad isn't too anxious to abandon it for the next big thing. This isn't a game.  What this is instead is still the glorified tech demo with a "game" sprinkled (poorly) over the top.
While this game is pretty, and the physics are impressive, this isn't a foundation for a full game.
I've never encountered a driving game with a "fog of war" style mechanic, and a game that focusses on difficult, technical driving makes this massively frustrating.  If this is trying to be a simulator, I can't possibly imagine anyone driving off road without a map and a plan of the terrain or route they're wanting to follow.  Realistically, on any level, the first "objective" is to clear all the fog of war, just so you can see the damned map and where you're going to do the main objective.
The driving is also frustratingly slow primarily due to the vast amount of mud and mud deformation used which will bog down nearly any vehicle incredibly quickly and the constant rescuing/winching rapidly grows tiresome.  While this is an off-roading game, even the "main" roads are rutted so heavily that any form of progress is also painfully slow.  The mud is also so prevalent that there is no reason to ever turn off the all-wheel drive or the diff-locks as it's virtually impossible to make any real progress with these turned off.
The vehicles that i've encountered so far include a small jeep, which will also get stuck incredibly easily and even on the main roads, a rear-wheel-drive only truck which again gets stuck far too easily, and several larger 6 and 8 wheeled trucks that you'll end up using for pretty much everything, including basic scouting.
Vehicles can be customised to a basic extent with the addition of repair kits or additional fuel tanks which can then be used on the truck to which they are applied, or to other nearby trucks.  The fuel tank add-ons are incredibly annoying as the basic garages at which you select the upgrades, and of which there are generally only one or two on a map, do not fill these fuel tanks.  Instead, you must take these tanks to a dedicated fuelling station which are usually a long distance from the starting garages and again assume that you've removed the fog of war on the map to actually see where they are and so you can plan a route to them.  Worse is that the main objectives of lumber delivery usually has you travelling a long way to get from the starting garage to the lumber yard, and then an incredibly long way to the final delivery point.  This distance is usually so great that it's impossible to do this journey on a single tank of fuel.
While on the subject of objectives; Fog of War only removes at specific map locations and there are approximately 10 of these points per map.  Garages require special points to unlock which are in the form of an upgrade to a truck that acts as a "load" that needs to be delivered which i've found to take 2 journeys to unlock (I realise there is a larger trailer that should do it in one journey, though again this gets stuck far too often), and the main lumber delivery objective which as far as i've encountered, also requires two full journeys to complete.
A typical playthrough of a level will consist of: starting, driving forward 10 yards and getting stuck, turning on the all-wheel drive, and the diff-locks and then leaving them on for the remainder of the game.  Next, open the map, set a market for one of the fog of war checkpoints, head towards it and promptly get stuck, faff around for a while trying to get unstuck, get within 100 metres of the checkpoint only to find there's no access from that direction, try and go around, get stuck, more faffing, eventually find the checkpoint, get stuck or roll over just outside the specific zone required, faff trying to rescue the vehicle, reset, start again.  Repeat this for each of the checkpoints and then try and do similar for the actual "main" objective.
Generally the vehicles control reasonably well; there's a weight and momentum to vehicles, although a frustrating and clumsy camera system makes it very difficult to properly see what's going on in certain situations.
TL:DR?
Pros:
Pretty visuals
Good vehicle physics
Cons:
No actual gameplay, still just a tech demo / showcase for mud deformation
"Fog of War" for map in a game emphasising navigation
Vehicles get stuck far too easily

Conflicks is a Phsyics Focused real-time strategy game, with quirky humor and it's fair share of yolks.
Overall, the game is good if you enjoy physics puzzlers, as you will need to get used to the flick mechanic to function in-game. The main litmus test I would present to anyone curious if they should buy this game or not: "Would this movement system hinder your enjoyment of an RTS?"
Main reason for presenting it like that, is you use flick for almost everything, it's like a rubber-band shot, and would transition exceptionally well to mobile devices if the devs ever decide to go that route. As for doing it with a mouse, I felt it was just kind of "meh" to control my ships like that.
Let's look at the rest of the game though:
Pros:
- Quirky and fun story, a little dry at places, but enjoyable none the less (sometimes get a "trying too hard" vibe)
- Aesthetic is pleasing, and holds an almost "Monty Python Animation" feel to it.
- The Vocals and audio assets are well done, adding to the atmosphere of the game.
Neutral:
- Simple strategies, but overall necessary due to the involvement of physics as a core mechanic (though the physics are strategies in and of themselves)
- Ships have a movement cooldown, so your aim better be good.
- Movement, Actions, and Unit Generation all utilize one core resource (it regenerates quickly, but you can create a big ship and be caught by not being able to move another ship for a moment).
Cons:
- Some of the animations are too long, almost grindy feeling. While a lengthy animation can add impact, when it's key animations or ones you see frequently, it can get inhibiting to the player.
- Hard to use complex tactics because the flick mechanic can act as an inhibitor, you're not going to be doing near as much micromanaging here as in, say, starcraft or C&C.
Note:
- You learn about 'pausing' in the campaign, a few chapters in, It would seem like this should be in the basic tutorials or first story mission.
- The tutorials themselves are unnecessary, you actually have most of what you need explained to you via the campaign (and it gets redundant if you do the tutorials first, then do the campaign)
Overall, I can recommend this game, provided it passes the litmus test for you. It's a good game, just definitely appealing to a niche audience in the physics aspect.

A fascinating blend of launch style physics game play and RTS mechanics.  Players use meta matter top preform all actions in the game.  From creating units to "moving" units by dragging and launching them through various effects.  Ships can also use meta-matter to preform a number of special actions based on their faction and class.  Meta-matter its self is generated by both the players flag ship and as well as captured planets.   The mechanical base is fairly compact but offers a wide range of depth with the interaction of various space hazards and ship abilities.  Matches tend to be shorter (15-30 minutes) this is nice if you don't want to spend hours playing "sim city" which can happen with some RTS games.
The single player story is both humerous and compelling in its absurdity.  Both strange and unique, the game is set in a sci-fi post-renaissance (the late 1700s or so) with an art style the matches its mood.  Players will encounter various historical figures and anologues.  The missions feel varied enough but not overly difficult for an experienced RTS player.  The single player does its job though in both being a good introduction to the mechanics of the game and entertaining with its characters and plot.
Currently there are not many people in the multiplayer which is unfortunate as there is little doubt abilities will need tweaking and balancing, not to mention that the multiplayer maps seam well designed.  Multiplayer games are a bit different from the single player in that each person plays to a score limit.  Score (as far as I can tell) is given for destroying ships, building ships and capturing meta-matter.  Destroying an enemies flag ship is worth a great deal of points but they do appear to re-spawn after (this was my experience fighting AIs in the "friendly" multiplayer mode).
I got this game with the two for one value and at 10 dollars I feel it is worth the price.  The single player alone was highly entertaining and the potential mutliplayer strategies promise to be fun.   I do hope this game gets more attention so there are more players online, but if not you can always get together with friends if you have a few to game with.
One last thing to note is that ships improve in power based on accomplishing some of the single player campaigns and by using them in multiplayer.   Given the low number of players online it is hard to tell how much of a good idea this is.  While progression can be distracting it may be problematic for the balance of new players vs old players.

A funny and yet compelling game base on the simple concept of flinking your ships to position rather just point and clicking your way towards the destination.
The art style and humor of this game keeps is separated from the competition while the flicking mechanic makes it intriquing and compelling enough.
Even though the campain can be challenging [God damn it Antonio!!!!] it dose a good job at introducing the players to the faction mechanics before dropping litterraly all that you have just learned towards the end.
The gameplay by design is more focused on the micro management since you simply can not flick more then one ship at the time unless you use a Frigate, and even that is not exacly macro gameplay, you just attach your ships to one and shoot them into space in hope a vessel dosen't bump into a rando asteroid and blocks your entire ball.
Even though the ships by them self have the same base stats, it's the skills that each one posses that can change the flow of the battle. For exemple I found that if the AI leaves the mothership alone for a good amount of time, taking a Greater Britan corvette with the shield on can cause as much damage as a well dispached torped, just distract them long enough for the bigger guns to move in.
The physics are just the ice on the cake and good players will be able to make the best of it while also efficently using all the skills in your arsenal and constantly pouring out new ships to send to the frontline.
Moving each ship can be, however, frustating or stressing simply because you have to aim each and every one of them in order to not screw your self by bumping your own troops into their doom.
Not much to say on the options since it's a 2D game with a cartoon art style the only effective change to the quality is the screen resolution.

The developer has already said they're working on a patch for framerate issues. That shows that they care and that they listen to the feedback. I saw a lot of reviews saying "come on, this is Mafia!", and those are right. This is Mafia. This isn't Call of Duty. The devs weren't going for screaming frame rates and super high quality textures. They weren't trying to tax your gaming rig to its limits.
So what does the game have?
I'm about an hour and a half in it's clear the devs put a lot of love into this. This game has a lot of love, and it shows.

Please keep in mind this is all my personal thoughts about the game and because I can - I will compare it to the other games available on the market to give other players a little information of what they may expect.
NO SPOILERS.
First thing you will notice is that...yes - no third parties applications needed to run the game! Thank You! No useless ubi...or ms or club crap applications - compared to GTA IV - I was so disgusted. Even Blizzard decided to abandon their app which was so painful and useless. So HUGE THANKS FOR BEING SMARTER than other greedy companies. Gamer community doesn't want to pay for some crap - we want to play! Is this important? Maybe not, but it might be annoying.
Game Interface. Simplicity. If You think about percentage of your money being wasted on game interface maybe you will agree with me that gamer doesn't need game interface to be fancy so much to even crash the game (Ubisoft for example - just review Splinter Cell series through out the history - game interface now looks like a Christmas tree).
Mafia III - simple, accessible, clean.
Game play, story line...just wow. Amazing. Twists and surprises. You can really see how much time and effort was put to make this game as good as possible. No unnecessary PR with some overwhelming trailers etc. I don't want to tell too much but I was really pleased finding out after about 2 hrs of game play that actually game starts only now. Game is simple without some stupid elements that would get your attention away from the story line ( GTA V wtf :( another fail after IV ) - making whole game really unique. However, I must admit that for some reason, overall image of presented world wasn't exactly how I would expect it to see. Roads wildly wide everywhere...just very little details of surrounding houses etc...just too simple and a bit empty. Map is however impressive and huge.
Difficulty. You will actually get frustrated with some missions what is actually quite nice. Nice work.
Programming, FX etc. This is a point to be a bit disappointed. Flickering textures, NPCs. NPCs are often not behaving properly trying to walk through objects etc. IT DOESN'T happen often - but it does. Within one hour of game play you will be able to see quite a few bugs or visual-bugs. Looks like there wasn't enough time spent for game testers. All bugs are minor and I wasn't able to crash the game or bug it so much to make it unplayable but there is just way too much minor issues within the game engine, textures and AI. First of let me just say this before I even start listing the good and the bad;
Those who been saying about Microtransactions please just stop because you are embarrasing yourselves here. the microtransactions in this game can be earned using the games currency and points that you get when you do Vandetta's. Also note that there is no exclusive items that cannot be obtained without purchasing the chests using real money. You can get every item using in game currency.
The Review;
Shadow Of War is a perfect addition into the Middle Earth franchise. Shadow of Mordor is definately still a good game but this game expands what the previous game could of done better. The Nemesis system has been expanded and more diverse than the original also it is important to command your orcs before taking a fortress. Talking about Orcs, the captains in Shadow Of War drop currency and loot. You can also grab currency or gems from the loot orcs that have a sign above their heads. Currency is used to purchase loot boxes that drop random loot from common to legendary and guarantees a Rare. They are also cheap. You can also buy the loot boxes that contain Orcs and you can kill those Orcs through the Market menu to gain gear as well.
Performance is not really an issue but please not when bumping up to 4K with a GTX 1080 it does get harder to run, my system can only handle medium/high settings not achieveing a solid 60fps. I have not had any issues with the 4K Cinematic Pack either. The game looks stunning, it is a very detailed and beautiful game to play.
Combat system is till styled like the Arkham franchise but combat still gets challenging with the more different types of Orcs coming in later in the game and Orc captains can adapt to some moves that you can repeat. None of the less it is still a fun game to play even though the combat gets boring quite quickly.
The open enviroments are really large and contain alot of collectibles. The Open environments in Shadow Of War really makes this game fun in a sense as these different zones have alot of high up and low down terrain that its possible to stealth from point A to B really easily. Also you have to take these Orc outposts that are like the Far Cry outposts but instead of killing all of the Orcs in the area you have to do an objective to kill/dominate the captain who rules that outpost.
Story is where it falls. I dont understand why Shelob is a sexy looking female in this game when in LOTR films and books Shelob is a massive spider. Some story elements get confusing and the story is kind of split between different characters. The whole premise is to kill the Witch King and stop Saurons forces from taking over Mordor which is to take over the main fort in every zone.
Overall if you really enjoyed Shadow Of Mordor or WB's Mad Max or Batman Arkham franchise you will deffinately enjoy Shadow Of War. In the time of this review I have 22 Hours in and Im not really getting bored of the game at all. Really looking forward to the later updates and DLC that gets released for this game.

Shadow of War is a repetitive, faux-deep game.
The combat is neat, but there's only so much you can actually do. The boss fights are fun enough, but the majority of fights aren't boss fights- and simply involve fighting endless amounts of Orcs until you can't fight anymore, and you have to run away.
The Gondorian soldiers on your team all look+move exactly the same, which really detracts from the realness of the game. They have literally 1 character model- even the leaders.
There are tons of different missions/quests- but I'm not really sure what many of them do. The quests lack any real feeling of depth for me, and they're hard to navigate.
The inventory/loot system, while ostensibly beefed up, feels contrived. Each piece of gear has 1 stat on it, and I just don't really care when I get something good. I can't see how much damage I'm doing per hit, or how much damage I'm taking- which makes it hard to put a finger on the impact items really have.
While the Nemesis system is a really cool idea, it falls short in practice. Killing captains feels like I'm just churning out bad guys, because they always get replaced when I die or time advances. While this makes sense, it makes it feel like nothing is permanent/ I didn't really progress.I really like the idea of the Nemesis system, but it just doesn't seem very impactful to me. If I control a good Uruk, he may just betray me at any time- which is fine, they're orcs. However, it lends to that feeling that nothing really matters. Fortresses are nice, and sieges are pretty fun- but in an 'RPG' like this- I'd expect conquering cities to feel a little more satisfying. Instead, I just capture them, make a grandiose speech, then go on to the next thing.
I'm a big UI/UX guy, so I have to include this: even the menus seem clunky. Game Settings and Marketplace shouldn't be located in the same spot as in-game elements, such as Inventory, or Index. One of the reasons I have trouble with the quests, is because I have a hard time figuring out what to do- or when to do it. DISCLAIMER: I received this product for no cost for the purpose of reviewing. However, this does not affect my views and opinions of the game.
Peak Angle: Drift Online is a pseudo-online multiplayer racing game. The title is unique as in it's not a conventional sort of car race. The challenge of the game is not to get from point "A" to point "B" the fastest, but instead; who can accumulate the most "drift points" or score within the allotted amount of time. In this regard the game feels more arcade-y. The game is online only, though the opponents appear to be ghosts of real players completing their own runs on the same map. This also makes it so collisions between vehicles are not possible. The game is recommended to be played with the steering wheel controller, though using the keyboard or a game pad also work.
--------

The graphic assets of the game are quite good. Bigger racing titles do have a bit more polish to their graphical fidelity though considering this is a small title by a small studio, the 3D models are decent for what they are. The game's physics and movement of the cars are very standard. Again, not as  defined as other titles, but it does get the job done. There are quite a bit of visual customization options within the game and a decent amount of playable cars. All cars are based off of real-world models, although named differently. In addition to this, there are a good amount of maps to race on albeit they all look somewhat generic. The game is surprisingly not that demanding and should run fine on any lower tier - mid tier CPU and graphics card. Playing around with the graphical options is also recommended as the default settings may not be suitable for all setups.
--------
The sound and music assets are all very generic. That being said, the game does a good job with it's soundtrack. The themes are all fast-paced and blood-pumping tracks, which is what is to be expected from a title like this. The car noises are not too far off from sounding authentic and all the audio within the game does get annoying or tiresome after long game sessions.
--------
The game's mechanics are solid and the concept is quite simple. The player will choose their car and navigate through a stage with other players' ghost's, to compete for the highest score. Score is obtained by drifting. The longer and more frequent the player drifts, the higher their score will be. Points will not be counted if the player hits a wall or environmental hazard while drifting.
In terms of upgrading and customization, the player can buy upgrades and new cars. Upgrades can increase horse power, steering power, and other handling options. In game currency is earned by taking part in matches. The game also has various tuning options for cars which can be accessed in the car options menu.
--------
The game is has a unique but simple concept, and I've never played a racing game in which the "race" was to accumulate more points than the other players. I feel like the ghost multiplayer is sort of a double edged sword; there will always be a match ready for you, but you may never have the experience of REALLY playing with other people. Though considering that the player count of the game is low, this may have been the right move for the development team. Maybe sometime in the future they will be able to implement true multiplayer.
I feel like people who don't take racing games too seriously, and those who would enjoy a casual "drifting" game, would also enjoy this title. I personally couldn't find my bearing with the game's controls though that's more of a personal gripe gather than one with the game's actual controls.

Thanks to the devs for giving me the opportunity to review the game, as well as anyone who took this review into consideration, I hope it helped.

Regular track racing is what I am most familiar with. GT, Indy and Oval is what I consider regular. There is only one professional grade simulation solution when it comes to regular racing. Difting now has a professional level simulator. Peak Angle is for those that want to drif and only drift. With either a controller or steering wheel (I know keyboard works but have not tried it) You can slide around varous circuits across the globe. Do not judge this by my video below. I did not know what I was doing. Since that video I have gotten better at this and that has translated to other non-drift focused titles. There is a different side to Peak Angle that I find almost as much fun as drifting. That is making the car look the way I want it to look. If You have the time and the creativity, You can make a almost any vector graphic in full color on Your vehicle. I had neither so there is just preset text on 2 of my cars. I recommend this to everyone who has drifted on purpose in their current racing title(s) of choice. Have You ever wondered why some people have wheels that poke out at the bottom of a car that looks too stiff and low to drive? Peak Angle will explain it. Do You know the difference between drifting and getting sideways? Here is a hint: Some of us can drift in a straight line while using the driver (or passenger) door to see straight ahead. Peak Angle. You will learn not only about drifting but about setting up the car to handle/perform accrding to your tastes. Do You wrench on Your tuner in real life? Why not test some setups in here before you go burn the clutch in that RX7 you just modified for competition? Do You just want to enjoy a few slides without the reckless driving ticket? I recommend this to anyone looking for fun behind the wheel.

Alot of love has gone into this game. You can tell this by the attention to detail the devs have put in. The water moves as you push forward into it, the mud sticks to the wheels and sprays backwards as your tyres spin furiously to gain traction, the gorgeous visuals coupled with immersive sounds of a wet muddy forest filled with wildlife and the vehicles you use to drive through all this makes for a unique gaming experience.
There are 5 maps to explore, all of them are hidden beneath "cloaking" points that need to be unlocked in order to reveal the areas hidden beneath them. You do this by driving around the map in a variety of vehicles that anyone who's played Dayz mod will instantly recognise.
The main objective of the game is to collect and deliver lumber. This is done by hauling small, medium or large logs around the map to a pre determined point. Youll drive through impossibly deep mud, fast running rivers, tall thick forests and still tranquil lakes. Youll also need to negotiate steep inclines, often muddy wet steep inclines that will require some measure of fore thought before attempting. If you get stuck you can always fall back on the handy winch feature that attachs to any nearby tree, enabling you to pull yourself out of trouble, which is inevitably where you'll end up.
Other vehicles aid you in the completion of this objective such as repair and fuel trucks. These all need to be driven by the player by swapping from one vehicle to another as they become unlocked on the map.
The one thing that lets this game down is the camera. You follow vehicles from an off centre perspective that works well when youre on the wider areas of the map, but as soon as things get tight the limitations of this become apparent. Trying to see where you're going when the scenery closes in, or when your're trying to save yourself from toppling  over on one of the many steep inclines that run out of deep water crossings, can be frustrating. Thankfully this doesnt hurt the game to much but it does take something away from the gaming experience.
There is also a multiplayer option that enables you to basically do whats done in single player only you get to drive around with friends as well.
I like this game because it's challenging and is gorgeous to look at. It is one of those games that just grows on you the more you play it and the challenge to deliver those logs to there destination while negotiating the steep, muddy, rocky, wet, uneven and trecherous "roads" you travel along,  make for a rich and rewarding gaming experience.

SpinTires is a quick and easy game to get into if you want some aimless fun exploring the map in a truck. With mud. And Trees.
Add in the 4 player multiplay and hilarity ensues as you bump someone off an embankment into the water, or get serious and work together to unlock all of the garages and trucks.
If you've ever wanted a free-roaming, off-road game with no timers or vehicles that require hours upon hours of grinding to unlock, then it's a solid price point.
SpinTires has not changed very much since the demo release a couple of years ago. What you get in the released game is multiplayer, 5 new maps, half-a-dozen or so new trucks, new addons for the trucks, one objective to strive for (lumber transport) and some garages to unlock that are places around the map.
is probably the biggest addition to the game which gives it some longevity. It's a basic lobby system where the game creator becomes the host of the game. While this works OK with your friends, it falls down when you join a random game. Unfortunately, all of your hard work will be undone as soon as the game host wants to leave. There's no saving, there's no swapping hosts or log out timers. It's just a sudden, and jarring disconnect from that game. The best advice would be to organise your own group of friends to play the game with.
The multiplayer chat is very basic and somewhat buggy. The default key for chat is Y, and sometimes when you're typing out a message, the chat bar will randomly disappear. Also, pressing Y to initiate chat will stop your truck. This can be very frustrating when you want to simply type "Yes" or "Thanks" and your truck stops dead. Opening the map also does this and is just as frustrating. There is no minimap and the compass is pretty useless. You really need the map to navigate efficiently, but doing this will also slow you down since it stops you in your tracks. A minimap would be ideal, or an option to have a transparent map overlay showing while you drive.
The next major additions are the
and the trucks. The 5 maps included are all the same size, each with it's own theme. Volcano, The Plains, The Hill, etc, are all what they say. However, all the maps are just muddy tracks and lots of trees. They all look the same in colouring, textures and details. The short view distance and draw distance do nothing to help the maps look any different from one another and if you were put in a randome spot on each map, the likely hood that you could which map it is would be pretty high.
The
are all highly detailed and functional. There are some awesome addons for the trucks, particularly the crane which would have to be the best. You can fully operate the crane to pick up logs and load them into another truck. You can operate stabilizer bars to give your truck that extra stability it needs. The crane has full movement up and down, in and out and is trully a great addition. Log trailers are also pretty cool, adding a whole new level of skill required to take them through the tracks to a lumber yard. Once you load up a log trailer, you can immediately tell that you're carrying a lot of weight. The trailer is prone to tippping over a lot, so you have to drive slowly and skillfully. Reversing trailers has never been a strong point of mine in real life and I'm just as bad in SpinTires! Oh yeah, the trucks sound pretty good too.
is nice, but can be a little unpredictable and I think the damage model needs to be tweaked down a bit. It's very easy to damage your truck by hitting a bump in the road a bit fast. hasn't changed since the demo except that there is more of it. There's also
to contend with. One of the maps, The River, has.. would you believe it, a large river running through it, separating the map in two halves. Inevitably, you're going to have to cross it. In reality, your truck just takes damage to the point where it no longer functions. It's nice though, it really adds a sense of urgency to get across. It's probably one of the only times where your butt grips your chair in the game.
The
are standard fair. Keyboard and Mouse, or, Xbox 360 gamepad. There is no steering wheel support at present, but Oovee have seen the requests for it and I believe they are looking at adding support later on. There doesn't seem to be any rebinding of the gamepad buttons allowed yet. Hopefully, this will be patched in. Currently, if you're using the Xbox gamepad, your also using the mouse and the keyboard, too. Thats 3 peripherals folks! Yep. It's awkward and unintuitive but that's the design. Ideally, you would play SpinTires with keyboard and mouse only, as then you can do everything fairly easily. But I love kicking back with the gamepad and being able to finely adjust my steering with the thumbstick. Where it becomes clunky is, I have to put down my gamepad and use the mouse to operate the UI. So if I'm stuck, I have to put the gamepad down, grab the mouse, click the screen to get the cursor, click advanced, click a winch point on my truck, click a winch point on a tree/truck, then press 'F' to winch in (because I cannot bind winch in to the gamepad) and then, if I need to steer while winching, I have to try and grab the game pad and manouver with it awkwardly while holding F. can, and will be, annoying. The camera.. works. Some people like it, others hate it. I hate it. Wanted to like this but the -creative- control mechanic isn't a -good- control mechanic. Flicking the ships around is slow, which would be tactical except they damage each other in real time and the computer is less slow so can sneak several ships up on you while you're trying to maneurve a harvester (sorry "henship") all the way across the map to the tiberium (sorry "planet"). It's like trying to play subbuteo in boxing gloves. Every ship has a special ability - but I found it was pointless using any of them because they are as fiddly as the movement and the time taken to do it would be better spent manually pulling another ship out of the construction yard (sorry "flagship"), or manually moving another ship another few inches toward whatever it was supposed to be doing. The special abilities are also the only distinguishing difference between the 4 factions, so the movement mechanic ends up limiting even that.
If it had been turn-based a lot of the frustration wouldn't have arisen, but I guess they must have discarded that idea for some good reason or other. The humour deserves a mention - but the joke (alternative history with chicken powered space travel) wears thin quickly, and they fill several screens of text with it at the start and finish of each mission.
I played about 6 missions and quit after spending an hour on a map only to then flick my mothership through a wormhole that just dumped it onto the side of a planet where it crashed. (Wormholes are random to make everything even more laborious.) I couldn't take any more after that.
I'm not angry with it as a purchase or sorry I bought it, it was worth experimenting with. It's clearly been developed in a polished, professional way and they might well tweak and improve it somehow. Maybe it should be touchscreens-only. Maybe it should have a 4x grand strategy layer also controlled by ludicrous flicking. Maybe it would be more fun if you couldn't really tell where the ships were going to land. I don't know. It just isn't for me.

Ready for a novel?
Inspired by Alan Wake here comes my best attempt.
I bought Alan Wake two summers ago on the Steam sale, thinking that it looked good, it had an interesting story, and it wasn't a typical horror game. So you might ask why did it take over 16 months to finish? Was it because I was super busy with life? No, not especially as I can always find a few hours during the week. Was it because there are other games that took up my time. Yes, but not because I valued them over good old Alan.
You see it took me only about 2 minutes of the game to realize that this would be a struggle the likes of which have rarely been seen outside of Star Wars. To begin, 3rd person games have difficulty with their camera controls most of the time. Alan took this to the extreme with its constant cut scenes which change the angle and expect you to turn and adjust within half a second of regaining control. The camera control improves when the game gives you access to vehicles. Mostly because the camera becomes static and you're too busy struggling with the driving controls of the cars.
But the thing that caused me to quit playing the game 4 times was the decision to give Alan the stamina of a 400 lbs 70 y/o grandma. Some of the fun of a game is finding your own way to solve the puzzles, or to deal with the boss fights. But with Alan Wake you were forced time and again to have to kill every single bad guy, every single time to progress.
So why did they limit your character with such abismal stamina? Was it staying true to the setting? "Alan is a writer, he won't be in very good shape" Maybe, however, you'd think that in an scenario where your wife has been taken and weird shadow-ie things are chasing your with axes you'd be able to sprint more than 10 feet. I'm in pretty lousy shape most of the time, but the two times a year where I attempt to start an exercise routine I am able to run 5 or 6 blocks before I collapse.
Were the developers trying to give the player a better experience with the limited stamina? Maybe, but there were so many other issues: camera, driving, dodging mechanics, overly exact looting, etc that made the game difficult to enjoy why would they waste their time on stamina?
So, was anything in Alan Wake done right? Yes, the cinematics were great, the character modling was awesome. The story was fresh and interesting. I particularly enjoyed the sweeping camera shots and the seeing the layout of the city.
Excellent framework for a game, I just wish they had put in a few more weeks work to tighten up all the shoddy bits.

This ain’t your colonel’s chicken
This game is currently in Early Access, With time the review could change along with the game.

This is a game that knows full well what it is.
Bordering on breaking the 4th wall, and never taking itself seriously this game tells a story of love in space, with chickens thrown in to spice things up.
Merging time periods, with a unique art style and game play, and as someone on another review I had read said “Monty Python in space” I’ll take it, and not only will I take it, I’ll love it.

At the time of writing this I’ve only played some of the story for one of the four factions. But hands down this is one of the best strategy titles I’ve had the pleasure of reviewing.
I’m not going to touch much on the story itself, as that should be experienced to get the full impact of the humor as well as delivery of it.
But the gameplay, well, that’s awesome too. The game is top down strategy/RTS. You take planets, and you use resources to build ships and move them. No resources, you’re not going to be going anywhere.
The best way I can describe the game mechanics is think of the “board” as a big pool table, in space where there are chickens. The physics react kind of like that. Smacking a ship with another will send it tumbling about, sometimes (even your own ships) smashing into a planets surface to it’s fire filled end. Just think of the chickens won’t you?
From the developers website
“Our intention is to combine the chaos produced by the laws of physics governing the movement of many ships at once to the depth of a good RTS in order to create an accessible game experience that can also turn into something quite challenging for more involved players.”
They succeeded. This could easily be one of the top time sinks of 2015 for me due to the ease of access as well as the depth that it can hold.
This game takes strategy and turns it on it’s head, and makes it a blast to sit down with. My son was walking by and he saw it and had to comment about the chickens and how much fun it looked to play.
I’m not sure if it is or not, but this is a game that I could see being put onto mobile, or tablets. The gameplay begs for it with the “flicking” mechanic. With this you click and drag and a line appears that shows you roughly where your ship will go/fire. You release and then there goes your ship. It doesn’t always work in your favor and sometimes you’ll end up a little close than you wanted, or really far away.
Despite this the game isn’t broken, the physics become another contender in the fight and there is no side that is super-powered death machines of feathers. It’s fair combat, which is refreshing. You can manage to start out the gate behind, but pull ahead because of your tactics and using the battlefield to your advantage. One of the issues I have with strategy games lately is that if you mess up early, it’s nearly impossible to come back from and you get steamrolled quickly. Thankfully this game actually tried to be a strategy game, and depending on your usage, less can be more. Often games will take the route of zerg rush = game win, we don’t need more of those. We need more space chickens.
Last topic would be the soundtrack is glorious. Epic and campy, I would often find myself sitting on the menu while the game ran just for the music even when offline (steam has not correctly tracked my playtime).
My only complaint, and it’s nothing against the game is that none of my friends have this. I would love to zip around in space with them either as a team, or just to see who can knock the other out of orbit.

As of now, all I can say is this is a game that you need to have in your library. Humor, tactics, immersive, Artifice Studio’s my top-hat is off to you.

Alan Wake is a "linear survival horror" game, I guess you'd call it.
The premise is that Alan Wake is a writer. A horror novel he doesn't remember writing -while he's in a dry spell and on vacation- suddenly becomes his life, with him as the protagonist fighting a formless evil that possesses objects and the minds of others while they are in the dark.
This game is a repurchase, from when I owned it initially on Xbox 360.
This game is very very well written. Characters, plot points, villians, etc. Good sense of timing and pacing.
Let that sink in for a sec, because it's the most important part of this game.
However, the plot is presented in a very cliche episodic format. (Video games aren't good enough on their own without also being TV shows, apparently.) There's a "Next time on" and "Last time on" every end and beginning of a chapter, just like marathoning a TV series. While the episodic structure is really more of a throwback to TV series with similar theming in intention, I think it kind of misses its mark on the referential and is simply annoying.
There are other references it makes to the genre that do it justice and are appreciated, like the Night Springs TV show within the game and several more clever nods to horror novels.
Besides all of the Stephen King stuff they throw in your face as if he's Jesus himself, the realistic topics are also somewhat uncomfortable (This is a good thing in this instance). With /just enough/ understanding of the perils an artist of any kind can face in their career, it is self aware and handles these subjects with respect.
Liked all the characters. Alan Wakes agent gets a special mention.
Enemies can be dull for a game with supernatural horror, but the game is mechanically very well rounded.
Runs well on my PC as far as I can see, no complaints there.
It's a good game. I enjoyed it, and I can recommend it easily to fans of the genre.

This isn't exactly a review, but a game-site forum-post I wrote about the game in April 2016.  I think it expresses some feeling I have about the game.  My actual review is: great game -- buy it.
===
Best early access game ever. A great success for early access as the developers roused player feedback and fostered a mod community.
I know that there is always pressure to sell the next big thing, but this developer, Squad, should keep working on Kerbal Space Program. Refine it, expand it, and improve the gameplay elements. I'd like to see this get more story-driven and add competitive elements.
KSP is already a singular construction and simulation title that is unforgettable for a large portion of its players. However, the developer has a rare opportunity to make this one of the all-time great games. Further improvements will solidify it's position in the gaming zeitgeist.
I understand that KSP is a complex game that won't ever appeal to everyone, but smoothing the difficulty curve would help more players enjoy this unique title. It's a rare occurrence to have developed an all-time great game -- I'm hoping Squad isn't too anxious to abandon it for the next big thing. So far Squad has been tremendous in supporting KSP, I just believe it would behoove them to stick with it a while more.

I gotta say, this game shocked me. It really did something Im not to used to seeing in most games, especially one that did one thing; and I say one thing lightly, this game really did something unique while still falling
short of its full potential.
Alan Wake was one of the best written games Ive personally played in a very long time. It featured a story of fully believable characters, and a tone that set the atmosphere perfectly. It captured its players in a story that was meant to make you feel something , and set out to do it in a wonderful way.
It placed heavy empahsis on its moments of combat to futher those means of driving you deeper into this world that they've written. A world like ours, but dark, mutilated, disrupted. It captivates its audience using heavy visual cues, and sounds, and gameplay mechanics to give you a sense of this obstacle, this presence looming over your every turn, watching everything you do, while you do it.
Its menacing to honestly try and think about that, while not psyching yourself out. Go on. I dare ya.
Anyway, without rambling, and without sounding stupid, though Im honestly just trying to give you my thoughts on what I noticed, hopefully so you can appreciate the game like I did, this game is unique in a sense that its a story. Its really nothing more. Its a game used to deliver a piece of work that was honestly meant to be more of a story than an experience. A tale in the long list of works by Stephen King nonetheless, but still a very unique and wonderful story.
Without spoiling the story for those who are hopefully reading this, and havent played the game yet, the story is really straightforward. It really stayed true,
somewhat, to a horror technique that Im familiar with, but not in the slightest am I truly knowledgable, so bear with me as I try to explain, Tension and Release.
This concept of horror is used to scare people using a method of building suspense without actually scaring you. It comes in a variety of ways. sound, the rocks you see falling in front of you, or the ocassional barrel or chair flying through the scene, a large object falling in the distance and so forth. Its that flickering light you see in a otherwise normal scene, but seeing it flicker just lets you know something is wrong.
(If you want to know more about this kind of method of horror, and how its applied to games more deeply, I highly suggest you check out Extra Credits video on it linked here >>>
The gameplay attributes to this too. At first it may seem hard, but when you start getting a feel for the game, you realize, almost everything Alan does is slow, or cumbersome, its a chore getting into a fight. Im serious, almost every time it happened, I honestly said something along the lines of  "well great, there's 6 enemies and more on the way and I have 3 batteries, 19 bullets and no Save Haven in sight to save me." They did this on purpose. Its similar to the idea in The Evil Within, but I may be wrong, Ive yet to play the game myself. I only gathered this from what Ive seen of the gameplay, and asking people about their experience. The reason the combat is so difficult is because they want you to feel helpless. They couldnt really scare you if you had all the weapons with a light that never died. You would look forward to the fights, expecting them to be more rewarding than finding out more about the lore thats happening right in front of you. in essence, it would kinda be Resident Evil 6. And we dont want that. We wanna be scared guys.
Also, before I wrap this up, I wanna mention the story, but Im only going to say what I felt about the story, not how the story took place. This story is amazing because, as a piece of work, being just a story, it stands alone its own. Truthfully, you couldve released this as a book, and it would have been just as great as the game, I'll be damned to say if it did, I would be ♥♥♥♥ed if Hollywood didnt do a movie on it. Its job was to scare you, and as a story by itself it does just that. It scares you and it scares you good.
I didnt really touch on this, but real quick, I just wanted to point out, for a game that filled with a lot of gripes from people, its pretty obvious the developers cared about this game. There are alot of things that you noticed playing that let you know this, one of them being this game jokingly trashes video game developers constantly (you'll see why *laugh* seriously). But they game came across to me as too good. Its not a gem, but Ill be damned if I wont reccomend it because of that. The story, the gameplay, and the mechanics were damn near all perfectly aligned in this one.
Not to sound conceited or anything but if I had to rate it, I would give it a 6 out of 10, but that is only including the story.
If you liked what I had to say, leave a comment or something so we can talk about it more, comeon guys, I need people to talk about game design, this stuffs really fun!!!
