In this game, you control a custom robot, and fight in team fights (1 life per match) which feature objectives like capture the flag, plant the bomb etc...but they are mostly negated because you can finish the match by simply killing the enemy.
Pros:
- good robot customization, you can build your own robot from scratch, make your own custom weapons and other robot parts, it most fun part of the game, using and testing different loadouts
- ladder and ranking system, your robot reaches higher rank by upgrading its gear
- not great, but good graphics (they are cartooney like borderlands, there are black edges around models)
- nice looking themed maps
- there is also some cosmetic customization like hats, profile pictures and masks which you can earn by doing achievements; you can also change robots' colors
- you can earn everything for FREE, it just takes time, you can earn exclusive currency (the currency you usualy need to pay with real money in other games, you can earn it in this game), by completing achievements and doing daily missions
- nice achievements to earn
- there is tutorial
- even though population is small, you still can find the match if you search for minute or two
- it seems that some of the players are acctualy bots, although game doesnt state them as such, this of course, boost number of matches played
- friend and guild system in game¸
- you can play minigame while you are searching for match
Neutral (things i like but other people might not) :
- you get only 1 life per match and matches are really short, thing about this is that this system allows more players to play, since matches will be done in couple of minutes, maybe 5-10 minutes at most, and players will search for another match so new players wouldnt have to wait long to play; if matches were longer,2-3 groups of 10 people would play matches for more 30 minutes which will mean other players probably wouldnt find anyone to play with and would just quit
- there are consumables and more powerful ammo you can buy before the match, even though you can buy it for free, i dont like this system
Cons:
- devs are trying to resurrect this game (they havent updated it for more than 1 year) using indiegogo site so players can fund the game... however it seems that project is failing ( they have raised 180$/50000$ only)
- i dont think there is that much skill included in this game, basicaly only thing you need to do is make a good robot, and you will kill anyone with weaker one, no matter how hard they try
- robots could use more functions, like jumping
- only three game modes : capture the flag, plant the bomb, and basic elimination; however most of people ignore them because you can consider each mode as elimination mode, when one team gets eliminated they lose
- this game could use casual servers where you can pick which one to join, also you cant pick mode you want to play either
- playerbase is small, under 50 players at the time
- it seems that most players are children, i dont blame them however, it is game for them, but still, adults can enjoy it aswell
- robot making can be confusing for new players at start
- there are inventory slots, which are very annoying even despite the fact that you can unlock them for free
I recommend you to try this game as soon as possible, because it will probably get closed very soon.
Why did i vote no? Well simply because there was nothing that lured me to play the game again, after i quit it.

Most emotionally impactful game that I've played. Next closest would be something like Bioshock Infinite, but it's not comparable.
On a scale of 1-10, this is a solid 11.
Game offers:
• a plethora of characters all with their own compelling story, intervowen with the main narrative,
• "tough" choices that matter, affect the course of the game, and that don't have an obvious best/good outcome either gameplay or ethics wise
• this is true to the point where the distinction between antagonist and perfectly relatable secondary roles can disappear
• absolutely outstanding voice acting and dialogue,
• fitting & beautiful soundtrack
• interesting main plot which can neither be ignored, nor does it push itself on the player in a way that would marginalize sub plots / side quests too much
• exploration of the setting with lots of interactable objects, locations, dialogue
Cons (if I'm forced to come up with some):
• game can feel slow if you want to exhaust every exploration option and not leave any information behind, and that the main plot especially starts out strong but then has a kind of lull until it picks up again in the last two episodes.
• lip syncing isn't flawless; there's one scene in particular where one of the participants doesn't show any lip movement at all
• very rare audio bug in which character voice playback stops and you can only rely on subtitles (hasn't happened to me, but I've seen it elsewhere)
• Some people have described the game as "angsty". I can see that if and only if the themes/topics the game touches upon are boring to you (target audience), and if you listen to every piece of voiced commentary that the characters make - which is something you can control and cut short to your preference.

In the Book of Genesis, Abraham is called upon by God to sacrifice his only son, Isaac, to prove his faith. After climbing a mountain, Abraham turns on Isaac, binds with rope, and places him on an alter. Before he can bring the knife down, God stops Abraham, telling him that he has indeed proven himself.
So what happens when "God" calls on this Isaac's mother to do the same and doesn't call off the ritual? You get this wildly inventive top-down shooter of sorts.
You play as Isaac (there are other characters, but good luck unlocking them), a small boy that escapes his doom at the hands of his zealous mother by fleeing into his basement...only to encounter horrors beyond belief.

-Weapons

for my NVIDEA users with that cancerous stutter
=======================================================
0
A FANDOM User • 05/21/2016
1. Open your Nvidia Control Panel. Not Geforce Experience, Nvidia Control Panel. Type it into your start menu's "search programs and files" bar if you have to and start it from there.
2. Select "Manage 3D settings" in the side bar, then click the "Program Settings" tab.
3. Click "Add", find the Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor program, and select it for customization.
4. Once selected, scroll down the feature list until you find the "Vertical Sync" setting near the bottom. Change it to "Adaptive". Just straight-up Adaptive. This will activate the Nvidia-exclusive Adaptive Vsync on your GPU, which should be what fixes your issue.
5. Click "Apply", then close out of Nvidia Control Panel. Start up Shadow of Mordor and turn off the game's regular Vsync. This last one is important, you might have issues if you leave it on.
With that, you should be done, and your slowdowns should be fixed.

I've played for about an hour on Android and decided to purchase it for PC as well. So far I'm really enjoying the game. The developers seem very active on Twitter and you can tell it's a definite labor of love.
Only an hour into the game I can't comment on longevity, but the humor in the first bit has been great. It doesn't bash you over the head with punny humor that'll get stale the first time through, but it's definitely there to help bring a little fun to the story. So far the story seems fairly minute, which is fine for a game like this. Terraria had almost no story, but is a game you can easily dump a few hundred hours into.
The gameplay seems solid so far. Loot seems somewhat varied, with different crafted weapons and armor having a variety of stats. At this point I'm unsure there will be "rare" qualities to items, but I'm engrossed enough to keep playing and find out. Combat seems simple with a couple of elements of nuance. Fairly early on you get a Wrench to bash enemies on the head with and stun them. It seems there will be a few mechanics to combat that will add depth that some building/adventure games like this lack.
The comparrisons to Don't Starve are very accurate. It definitely resembles Don't Starve while being much more forgiving and not having permadeath. I think the game can definitely be summed up the good parts of Diablo, Don't Starve, and Terraria.
If you're at all a fan of Don't Starve I would definitely give this a shot. I'm not sure if it will have the exploratory feeling of Terraria, or the loot pinata feeling of Diablo, but if you're interested in 2 out of the 3 I'd definitely give it a shot.

Alan Wake is the video game embodiment of the B horror genre. Awful acting? Check. Laughable plot? Check. Low production values? At times (though the final quarter of the game is pretty impressive.) In spite of all this, or perhaps because of it, the game is a surprisingly charming gem for the genre.
My only real complaint with the game is how the designers chose to constantly revoke your stockpile of weapons at every turn, instead of taking the time to balance progression properly. One of the first rpg's I ever played was Wasteland 1 as a youngster (Either first or second). I have great memories from it, at the time it was something very new and different. Years past by and when I was a bit old Fallout 1 came out, while not the same it was great to play a game with the same "heart" as my beloved Wasteland 1. Then came Fallout 2 which was even better and Fallout Tactics which was alot of fun to. Years later Bethesda does a new "next gen" fallout game with fallout 3, which while good for the mainstream and new players to the series, to vets it just wasn't the game we had hoped it would be. It didn't have that fallout (or wasteland) feel to it, the story was crap, most the characters extremely dull and overall a game that just realy felt like Oblivion with guns (as annoying as that saying was to me before fallout 3 came out, it did ring true for me after fallout 3 came out and I beat it).
Thankfully Obsidian came to save the day and released the wonderful Fallout New Vegas. I was excited by this, Obsidian has alot of old Black Isle devs (guys who made fallout 2) and sure enough the showed Bethesda how to do a proper fallout game with there engine. A bunch of factions helped, Obsidians wonderful writing for the story helped, the dialogue was well done, interesting characters, great voice work (John Goodman? Hell yes), it felt ALOT more like the early fallout games (it just had that fallout feeling, something fallout 3 just couldn't nail)..
After all that we have Brian Fargo bringing his talents to Kickstarter and getting Wasteland 2 kickstarted. What we have here is a wonderfully crafted game, jam packed with content, Wonderful writing (characters, story and dialogue), tough choices that matter (best since Alpha Protocol and New Vegas decisions imo), great atmosphere, fun gameplay, Controls are good and a great job of balance (especially in the skills and character builds you can do). For new comers asking "What is this game like? I never played wasteland or Fallout1/2!". Well it has a bit of Wasteland 1, a bit of fallout 1/2 and a bit of xcom all mixed together. The turn based combat is a joy to play and doesn't get boring as each battle can be different then the last.
You're choices actually matter in this game, you might make a decision and not think about it, only to have it come down on you later as it shows the consequences of you're choice. The game does a wonderful job in the writing department as I said above, having Chris Avellone from Obsidian helped in this aspect and it shows. Characters you meet are interesting, the dialogue is very well done and the story keeps you very interested. The game world is harsh and unforgiving, you better make you're decisions wisely, always make sure you have ammo and medical gear and be on you're toes. You will thank me later :)
This game is deep, complex and I friggin love it. The game has come a veyr long way since it was in alpha, at first the UI they had was terrible and I was worried this was really going to take away from my enjoment of the game. Thankfully though the developers tried some new versions, listened to fans and in the end made the UI a ton better. Alot of missions have multiple ways of doing them, you will find yourself either playing the game 2-3 times or saving the game and seeing how different decisions or actions effect the game and the world around you later on. Sometimes I find I have made the right decision at first and then hours later you might hear of bad things that happend because of what you picked.
The game is not perfect, there is a few bugs, I wish there was more visual customization for characters and the graphics are not the best, but the good far outweighs the bad in this  new modern crpg. If you are looking for a new rpg that has hundreds of hours of gameplay, great replay value, wonderful writing, nice atmosphere and great gameplay give this game a go ASAP. You can really tell that this game was crafted with love, no publisher telling them to get it out early or telling them what to add to make it more popular. This Brian Fargo and his team at there best and this is a testament to old school rpgs and doing kickstarter/early access the right way.
After spending 100+ hours on this game (and plants to play atleast another 100-200 ours), I can say it was well worth the wait, it is one of the years best games and that I am very excited to see what InXile comes with next for there new Torment game. If it is as good as Wasteland 2 we are in for another treat and another resurection of a charished old school rpg. 26 years after I first fell in love with Wastelands charm we get Wasteland 2 and Inxile sure did deliver, this game rocks boys and girls. There are a few things I wish where in the game and a few negatives but 95% of this game is a masterpeice I must say. As someone who has been playing rpgs for 25+ years, this is just what I wanted from a Wasteland sequel, good writing, fun gameplay, interesting characters, tough choices and tons of content. In a day and age where old game series get new reboots and games totally different from the original games, it is a breath of fresh air to have a sequel to an old game be JUST what the fans of the original want.

Alan Wake is a "linear survival horror" game, I guess you'd call it.
The premise is that Alan Wake is a writer. A horror novel he doesn't remember writing -while he's in a dry spell and on vacation- suddenly becomes his life, with him as the protagonist fighting a formless evil that possesses objects and the minds of others while they are in the dark.
This game is a repurchase, from when I owned it initially on Xbox 360.
This game is very very well written. Characters, plot points, villians, etc. Good sense of timing and pacing.
Let that sink in for a sec, because it's the most important part of this game.
However, the plot is presented in a very cliche episodic format. (Video games aren't good enough on their own without also being TV shows, apparently.) There's a "Next time on" and "Last time on" every end and beginning of a chapter, just like marathoning a TV series. While the episodic structure is really more of a throwback to TV series with similar theming in intention, I think it kind of misses its mark on the referential and is simply annoying.
There are other references it makes to the genre that do it justice and are appreciated, like the Night Springs TV show within the game and several more clever nods to horror novels.
Besides all of the Stephen King stuff they throw in your face as if he's Jesus himself, the realistic topics are also somewhat uncomfortable (This is a good thing in this instance). With /just enough/ understanding of the perils an artist of any kind can face in their career, it is self aware and handles these subjects with respect.
Liked all the characters. Alan Wakes agent gets a special mention.
Enemies can be dull for a game with supernatural horror, but the game is mechanically very well rounded.
Runs well on my PC as far as I can see, no complaints there.
It's a good game. I enjoyed it, and I can recommend it easily to fans of the genre.

I gotta say, this game shocked me. It really did something Im not to used to seeing in most games, especially one that did one thing; and I say one thing lightly, this game really did something unique while still falling
short of its full potential.
Alan Wake was one of the best written games Ive personally played in a very long time. It featured a story of fully believable characters, and a tone that set the atmosphere perfectly. It captured its players in a story that was meant to make you feel something , and set out to do it in a wonderful way.
It placed heavy empahsis on its moments of combat to futher those means of driving you deeper into this world that they've written. A world like ours, but dark, mutilated, disrupted. It captivates its audience using heavy visual cues, and sounds, and gameplay mechanics to give you a sense of this obstacle, this presence looming over your every turn, watching everything you do, while you do it.
Its menacing to honestly try and think about that, while not psyching yourself out. Go on. I dare ya.
Anyway, without rambling, and without sounding stupid, though Im honestly just trying to give you my thoughts on what I noticed, hopefully so you can appreciate the game like I did, this game is unique in a sense that its a story. Its really nothing more. Its a game used to deliver a piece of work that was honestly meant to be more of a story than an experience. A tale in the long list of works by Stephen King nonetheless, but still a very unique and wonderful story.
Without spoiling the story for those who are hopefully reading this, and havent played the game yet, the story is really straightforward. It really stayed true,
somewhat, to a horror technique that Im familiar with, but not in the slightest am I truly knowledgable, so bear with me as I try to explain, Tension and Release.
This concept of horror is used to scare people using a method of building suspense without actually scaring you. It comes in a variety of ways. sound, the rocks you see falling in front of you, or the ocassional barrel or chair flying through the scene, a large object falling in the distance and so forth. Its that flickering light you see in a otherwise normal scene, but seeing it flicker just lets you know something is wrong.
(If you want to know more about this kind of method of horror, and how its applied to games more deeply, I highly suggest you check out Extra Credits video on it linked here >>>
The gameplay attributes to this too. At first it may seem hard, but when you start getting a feel for the game, you realize, almost everything Alan does is slow, or cumbersome, its a chore getting into a fight. Im serious, almost every time it happened, I honestly said something along the lines of  "well great, there's 6 enemies and more on the way and I have 3 batteries, 19 bullets and no Save Haven in sight to save me." They did this on purpose. Its similar to the idea in The Evil Within, but I may be wrong, Ive yet to play the game myself. I only gathered this from what Ive seen of the gameplay, and asking people about their experience. The reason the combat is so difficult is because they want you to feel helpless. They couldnt really scare you if you had all the weapons with a light that never died. You would look forward to the fights, expecting them to be more rewarding than finding out more about the lore thats happening right in front of you. in essence, it would kinda be Resident Evil 6. And we dont want that. We wanna be scared guys.
Also, before I wrap this up, I wanna mention the story, but Im only going to say what I felt about the story, not how the story took place. This story is amazing because, as a piece of work, being just a story, it stands alone its own. Truthfully, you couldve released this as a book, and it would have been just as great as the game, I'll be damned to say if it did, I would be ♥♥♥♥ed if Hollywood didnt do a movie on it. Its job was to scare you, and as a story by itself it does just that. It scares you and it scares you good.
I didnt really touch on this, but real quick, I just wanted to point out, for a game that filled with a lot of gripes from people, its pretty obvious the developers cared about this game. There are alot of things that you noticed playing that let you know this, one of them being this game jokingly trashes video game developers constantly (you'll see why *laugh* seriously). But they game came across to me as too good. Its not a gem, but Ill be damned if I wont reccomend it because of that. The story, the gameplay, and the mechanics were damn near all perfectly aligned in this one.
Not to sound conceited or anything but if I had to rate it, I would give it a 6 out of 10, but that is only including the story.
If you liked what I had to say, leave a comment or something so we can talk about it more, comeon guys, I need people to talk about game design, this stuffs really fun!!!

I'll make this quick, Alan Wake is not an easy game to play and it does have a few things that can frustrate the player but the story here reminds you of Silent Hill. It's not a Silent Hill clone per se, but a fresh take of the horror genre even though there's not much horror here.
Gameplay:
Enemies here are called the Taken. They are essentially human beings that have been taken over by the darkness. Unfortunately, they are practically invincible. You can't kill them with gunshots if they still have darkness within them. Here you will quickly learn that your worst enemy is your flashlight. To kill the Taken you have to shine your light at them making them vulnerable to gunshots. However, if you run out of batteries (which will happen often even on the normal setting) you are almost guaranteed to die. The dodging mechanic doesn't really help you much because as soon as the enemy hits you, you are unable to do anything. They pretty much stun you into submission and this will happen a lot when the game decides to throw groups of Taken at you. There are tools that can help you evade these groups such as the flares, flare gun and the flashbangs. These are uncommon but very useful items. The game forces you to create a tactic in which you decide whether you want to run or fight. This game is definitely not easy and during my playthrough (on normal, which is the hard mode of this game) I died at least 7-10 times.
Graphics:
The graphics here are nothing special but the scenery and the mountains will take your breathe away. Remedy has put a lot of attention to detail in the way they create this world and the little town of Bright Falls, and even to the surreal world of the Dark Place. The characters you encounter have their own set of personalities which sets them apart from any other characters. They aren't just NPC's here, they actually feel alive. More often than not, they will actually help you survive groups of Taken in some Episodes. Let me tell you that they don't miss!
Controls:
The controls feel stiff and that really doesn't help in surviving the night. As I said before dodging kind of sucks as Alan will only take two steps the the direction you want to dodge and if you don't time it right, the enemy will hit you. In fact its better to fight from a distance. Stay away from large groups! There is no reticle for aiming so you will miss a couple of shots. This isn't a first person shooter and therefore you can't look down the barrel of the gun. Running also can kill you if you run out of breathe. No stamina means that Alan will walk slower and aim his flashlight much slower. Another thing too is that running is pointless since the Taken can run much faster than you. Unless you are standing 5 feet from the next checkpoint, running away is near impossible.
Overall: Did I say I was gonna make this quick? Ooops....
Alan Wake is not for everyone. It is definitely not an easy game to beat and the controls don't help it much. It is clear that Remedy has put a lot of thought into the mechanics of the game but I felt like I was being hindered which in this case as a survival horror game it did well to keep me on my toes. Every death felt cheap but not cheap enough to get me to rage quit. Eventually I understood why I died and I grew to like this game even more. Now the story portion is what attracts everyone to this game and I'm glad to say that it did not disappoint. Alan Wake is an episodic adventure and it was meant to be treated as such. If you like a good challenge and a good story, then this is the game for you. However, that being said expect a lot of deaths and instances of frustration!                                    -7/10

In the Book of Genesis, Abraham is called upon by God to sacrifice his only son, Isaac, to prove his faith. After climbing a mountain, Abraham turns on Isaac, binds with rope, and places him on an alter. Before he can bring the knife down, God stops Abraham, telling him that he has indeed proven himself.
So what happens when "God" calls on this Isaac's mother to do the same and doesn't call off the ritual? You get this wildly inventive top-down shooter of sorts.
You play as Isaac (there are other characters, but good luck unlocking them), a small boy that escapes his doom at the hands of his zealous mother by fleeing into his basement...only to encounter horrors beyond belief.
As you fight your way through multiple rooms (that change in every playthrough) you'll find various power-ups, pills with random effects, and tarrot cards to help you along your way...and you'll need all the help you can get because it's back to square one upon your clumsy, easily prevented death.

If you're looking at this game because you played FSX and are getting nostalgia for it again, you'll find everything is exactly how it was on the original CD release. All the control mappings and defaults are the same. Flight controls are the same. Missions are the same. It's the same simulator that Microsoft released a full 10 years ago. The scenery is that outdated look and the engine still has the same fun problems (except for some compatibility issues, see "Steam Edition"). The plus side is the base package can be run on max settings from even mid-range laptops with integrated graphics.
Let me explain just why this game is now available on Steam. Dovetail Games (a pretty bad developer who sees itself as the god of sim-games) bought the rights to distribute FSX 2 years ago so they could make their own flight simulator. What they did for FSX was quickly patch some issues with compatibility for Windows 8/8.1 devices (and probably W10 too), so that it could run on Steam users' current PCs. Then they released it into the wild to earn cash to fund their development project for a new flight sim. I don't think they've touched it since.
Lots of add-ons for MFSX will not work with the SE version for a number of reasons. The most basic is that an add-on refernces the standard installation directory, which is not where the SE version is installed. There are other reasons, but I can't really explain them.
While Dovetail
fixed some compatibility issues with newer operating systems, they certainly didn't fix all of them. In addtion, there are some things they should have fixed before re-releasing this on Steam. For example, the mission compass is still really stretched out on a monitor that isn't at a 4x3 aspect ratio. If you use DX10 rendering (better performance), you will never be able to go near an airport because of the horrid texture clipping that occurs. Every line and every asphalt surface that overlap encounter the WORST texture clipping with the DX10 engine. And if you go back to the default renderer, DX9, it then becomes impossible to see some pause menus (for example, rebinding keys mid-flight). Instead all you see is a black screen where you know there should be a menu. At that point, the only thing you can do is close the program externally. So you're basically forced to have massive texture clipping.
While I miss the days of FSX when it was new, I definitely am not reliving those now. The software has so many issues relating to newer operating systems that it makes the game unplayable on any modern platform (especially on the Windows 10 that Microsoft has been shoving down our throats). If I had a computer running Vista or XP (both no longer supported by Microsoft, fyi), this would be a worthwhile buy. However, to get this playable on a modern system requires you to dig around the web for solutions that involve manual edits to the game's source code/installation files. It's just not worth it.
Dear Dovetail: how is it when you're given only a handful of things to do that you still manage to fall short? Even a cash grab should be well patched to work on a modern system. And you saw that your new flight sim/school was targeted at the wrong audience (I mean, what did you expect? The last good flight sim at its release was THIS, in 2006, or XPlane, which is quite a bit more complicated to use. Of course we're first in line for a new flight sim). And can we talk about how all of your other sims seem to tank in the reviews as well? You're not
for anything, and the only thing you're
for is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥people off with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ simulators. I.E. your train simulator should still be in the oven for optimization fixes. Your new flight school still has a lot of artifacts from the FSX engine like details popping into view and it's only got 2 planes. From all I've seen, you're one of the worst developers I know of. I WANT to enjoy a new flight simulator. Don't push out a release too early when you build the full thing. GET IT RIGHT. It's so frustrating when a developer is desperate for cash so they push a game out before it's ready. Then it never gets fixed and everyone hates it. Thing is, this is what it feels like you, Dovetail, are doing with EVERY SINGLE THING YOU MAKE.

Imagine if Don't Starve and Terraria had a child. Now imagine that child grew up and got hours more content than its parents, and got rid of all the emotional "inventory management" baggage their parents were carrying. Then he joined a comedy club and acquired an actual storyline that doesn't suck.
He also saw his parents involved a lot of walking across half the procedurally generated map just to collect a few things or to retrieve your inventory after dying, so decided you can teleport freely wherever one of the generously spaced warp pads are, and that death (which if you're playing on Insane, will happen A LOT) doesn't mean dropping literally everything you own.
The child then decided being only on PC sucked, so it visited iOS and Android and was smart enough to get vaccined against the dreaded "IAP" disease that was endemic there.
That child is Crashlands.
It has a few flaws (like why don't more people know about this game aaargh) and minor bugs, but this is one of the most flawless indie sandbox releases I have seen on Steam, especially with all the pre-alpha early access nonsense going on lately. Right off the bat it has content rivaling Terraria and Don't Stave, with combat and gear resembling an aRPG, without the micromanagement chores of either (although if you are playing on higher difficulty levels and want to min-max your gear you will have to grind some).
It has an infinite procedural map, easy building, tons of crafting recipes, sensible progression, a long storyline, quests and side-quests, farming, fishing, pets, interesting combat, boss fights, rare loot and unique legendary gear, a unique social platform called BscotchID, achievements that unlock side-content IN OTHER GAMES, and WHY ARE YOU STILL HERE GO BUY IT ALREADY AAAAAHHH.
This review alone doesn't do this glorious child-comedian-genius justice so check out the other reviews if you're not yet convinced.

Let me begin by saying that Wasteland 2 is not like Fallout outside of the post-apocalyptic theme, and a few design choices. Wasteland 2 is a great game, but it is not as good as Fallout 2.
The game is a good squad-based RPG that reminds me heavily of those old Fallout games, though. And indeed, I love this game much the same. There is a variety of ways you can solve most of your problems, and because of that, this game has consumed what has to have been over 10 hours of my life already.
There are some problems I have with the game. And if this game were made by any other unknown indie developer, I would have rolled my eyes and moved on. But this game was made by Brian Fargo, with help from several other veterans of good old RPGs that we knew and love, so this makes me disappointed at a few design choices.
1. A few skills are a bit too divided. Unnecessarily so. Why is Safecracking and Lockpicking two different skills? Why not just make Safes harder to lockpick? Why are Blunt Weapons and Bladed weapons separate? What was so wrong with a general "melee" skill? Why is there a skill just for modding weapons? Who in their right mind would put skill points into Toaster Repair? While some skill divisions made logical sense -- obviously, in a squad-based RPG, a generic "guns" skill would be broken, and speech is basically divided into what you want to accomplish with words (Reasoning, Seduction, or Intimidation). But I honestly think Weapon Modding should have been covered by Mechanical Repair, and Safes should fall under Lockpicking.
1a. And while I am at it, what is the point of the Demolitions skill outside of trap disarming? All explosive weapons are disposable, one-use items (REAAAAALLY dislike, by the way), and none of them are affected by your skill at handling explosives. Instead, grenades and bombs are handled XCOM: Enemy Unknown style -- click where you want the bomb to go and the character tosses it, with little chance of error. Now, I loved XCOM, but what the hell? No grenade launchers with appropriate ammo? No rockets for your LAWs and RPGs? No mines? (well, the ENEMY can place mines, but you can't). No C-4? Why have Demolitions at all, outside of defusing the numerous (frankly obnoxious) traps inside every other box of loot?
2. No Stealth mechanic or skill. This hit me pretty hard when I realized there was no stealth in the game, because I am all about conflict avoidance in RPGs. I am the kind of guy whose priority in Fallout New Vegas was getting my speech to 100 -- the fewer bullets I fire during a quest, the better. Not to mention there were several situations I ran into that practically BEGGED for the usage of stealth, and yet, it simply wasn't possible.
Aside from that though, the game seems to be doing well in the "cause and effect" aspect that many RPGs sorely lack. There are tough decisions you will find yourself making as you journey across the wasteland. The best solutions that benefit everyone often require large amounts of skill in the required talents -- Unless you specialize your rangers, you aren't going to do many great things. It's a good RPG. And honestly, it has me hooked. But damnit, I DID expect better.
I do recommend it though, despite its flaws. The game itself is good, it's just that I did not expect to find the flaws I did from veterans of the industry. If you liked Wasteland, and you liked Fallout 1 and 2, check it out. Of course, I must stress this -- it is NOT Fallout. Don't get the game expecting Fallout.

This is a very interesting game. Definitely very accurate and detailed on the physics side of things; tires adapt to the surroundings, terrain deforms, trees bend, the truck suspension moves realistically; I would expect to see this leve lof realism on a real vehicle, not a virtual one. Great job on that!
SpinTires is certainly not an easy game, because you constantly have to look where you're going and plan ahead. Depending on the route taken, fuel consumption needs to considered and active diff locks and all wheel drive certainly increases that amount of fuel used. Given the detail I would definitely rank it among the best simulation games I have ever played so far.
The overall gameplay is based on unlocks on a specific map, and there are a number of ways to complete the objectives and side objectives. You can rescue a stranded truck by supplying it with fuel, or "teleport" it back to a garage; at least in non-hardcore mode. That's no fun though. Much more rewarding to fight your way to the truck with a cistern trailer full of fuel. You can also unlock additional garages that can serve as outposts along the way by supplying parts ("garage points") which gives you more places to repair damage on your vehicles.
The main objectives right now are hauling logs. Short, medium, or large ones, depending on your truck and specs. The longer the logs, the more points you get. Hopefully more objectives will be added in future, and ways to repair the roads etc. There are plenty of awesome suggestions in the developer's forums, including for vehicles with tracks!
I definitely do agree with others though as far as the camera is concerned. It definitely needs improvement. It gets stuck at odd angles and it's almost hard work having to coerce it into moving around the vehicle you're driving; especially in tough spots. It's OK most of the time, but there are some situations that require a more precise camera perspective, and that's almost impossible to achieve.
I can thoroughly recommend it though, and if you like simulation games of any kind, then this is for you. The price is also fair considering the fun you get out of it!

Most emotionally impactful game that I've played. Next closest would be something like Bioshock Infinite, but it's not comparable.
On a scale of 1-10, this is a solid 11.
Game offers:
• a plethora of characters all with their own compelling story, intervowen with the main narrative,
• "tough" choices that matter, affect the course of the game, and that don't have an obvious best/good outcome either gameplay or ethics wise
• this is true to the point where the distinction between antagonist and perfectly relatable secondary roles can disappear
• absolutely outstanding voice acting and dialogue,
• fitting & beautiful soundtrack
• interesting main plot which can neither be ignored, nor does it push itself on the player in a way that would marginalize sub plots / side quests too much
• exploration of the setting with lots of interactable objects, locations, dialogue
Cons (if I'm forced to come up with some):
• game can feel slow if you want to exhaust every exploration option and not leave any information behind, and that the main plot especially starts out strong but then has a kind of lull until it picks up again in the last two episodes.
• lip syncing isn't flawless; there's one scene in particular where one of the participants doesn't show any lip movement at all
• very rare audio bug in which character voice playback stops and you can only rely on subtitles (hasn't happened to me, but I've seen it elsewhere)
• Some people have described the game as "angsty". I can see that if and only if the themes/topics the game touches upon are boring to you (target audience), and if you listen to every piece of voiced commentary that the characters make - which is something you can control and cut short to your preference.

Most shooters of recent times never seem to catch my eye too much. Many of them feel like the same thing over and over again, such as the Call of Duty series. There are, however, a select group of games that classify as shooters that I can thoroughly enjoy. One of those is Guns and Robots.
Where do I start with this game? The basic idea is that you assemble a robot and send it out into battle against other players' robots and try to complete an objective. Whether that's delivering and planting a bomb whilst stopping your enemy from doing so, or just good old fashion 'last one standing wins', Guns and Robots gameplay is very simple to get used to.
One of the key selling points to this game (despite it being free for the most part), is how the actual robot is built. You can purchase a variety of different parts that you must assemble in order to build your perfect war machine. There's also the case of needing to repair damages and resupply your ammo which is a nice little touch. Lastly are the weapons, which are split into light, medium and heavy categories, and each has a very familiar feel. There are quick firing weapons, explosive weapons, laser weapons, sniping weapons and even a flamethrower, all of which you can slap onto your bot and use to your heart's content.
The game's physics engine is another praise point I have for it. Your robot does not have a healthbar, but instead, the damage to each body part-the head, torso, both arms and the chassis-is shown instead. Losing your head causes your controls to act funny, losing your chassis makes you immobile, losing an arm means losing a weapon, and if your torso is destroyed, you are basically dead and eliminated from the round. I found this especially interesting, as a player now has the ability to strategize which parts they want to eliminate. You can aim for the chassis and turn your enemy into a helpless turret, blow their head off and watch them dizzily stumble around, remove their weapons to make them helpless, or you can aim for the torso and watch them go boom. Strategy is something we don't often see in your typical shooter. Not even Team Fortress 2 is so strategic.
As a final note, I do love this game for what it is, and what it does, and my only advice to the developers is to continue to bring us new and interesting content to play with. There are only so many customization features, and only so many game modes and maps. Keep pumping out the goods, and we will stay loyal, and bring more gamers to love this game.
Final Mark: 4.5/5

If you liked Shadow of Mordor - you will love Shadow of War. It really is that simple.
Yes, the game has flaws - I think everything about loot boxes has already been said. And in some instances I find the graphical fidelity a bit lacking. Even with the high resolution textures playing the game at 2560x1440 some parts look a little blurry. Also compared to the previous game the model of Talion's face this time around is just.. off. He looks like an Action Man.
With that out of the way - everything else has improved. The new loot system has created a new level of depth possible with builds that you simply couldn't get in SoM. Difficulty has been ramped up massively - playing on top difficulty I'm still getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked frequently by Uruks even after unlocking the vast majority of Talion's skills. A much welcome change of pace given that in SoM once Talion had most of his skills you could just steam roll the game.
The nemesis system is so much wider in scope now that it's hard to know where to even begin. The Uruks interact with each other so much more, some Uruks will actively hunt you down or try to catch you off guard. You can make your Uruks fight in the pits against other Nemesis Uruks. These pit fights are surprisingly gut wrenching, especially when it's an Uruk you've spent some time on the battlefield with, or who's helped you take over your latest fortress down there in the ring fighting for their life. The new difficulty means that dominating a whole army is much more difficult than it was in the previous game - which in turn makes Betrayals, Ambushes and Revenge plots much more meaningful, another welcome change.
Combat also gains more depth thanks to the new damage types, glaive moves, and the choice between hammers and bows as ranged weapons.Aside from these, much is familiar here - attack and counter gameplay with a hitstreak counter with some special moves thrown in for good measure.
Over 20 hours in to the game and I'm still being surprised and challenged by Shadow of War.
All in all - good stuff.

The games learning curve is a bit hard for the first few stepts, but onces you get past the tutorial/basics you wont have any issues picking out how to approach things.
One of the games very interesting points it has is perma-death in it, not to where oh you got a random head shot you're gone for ever, but if you don't use the revive skill on someone after a set amount of time they will be gone and your now short a member. however they do have npcs you can recruit in some towns as well as some story npcs if you save them to give you more members.
If i'm giving points my overall arbitrary number would be above 75's but below 90 out of a full 100, the game is good and would say its worth while to play, but the thing that really pulled me in was the nostalgia of playing an updated Fallout 1/2. Combat consists of clicking on the enemy then clicking on a safe patch of land when they attack.
Due to their fast attack speed you will only get 1-2 hits in before you have to move.
So you're constantly clicking from side to side.
Combine this with the fact that some enemies have an enormous amount of hp that takes a few minutes to wear down, and abilities that kill you in 1 shot, and you have a very frustrating experience.
Further combine with with the fact that you only have 1 other ability (a short stun on a long cooldown), and combat gets very tedious very quickly. You can craft bombs that do 75% of your damage which is useless on single targets (and you can't fight more than one with the speed of their attacks and the dodging required).
The rest of the game is running around collecting things and crafting.
That's literally all there is to the game.
Tedious oversimplified combat and lots of padding.
There is no real game here.
The humor is great and really drew me in, and there is lots of grinding/padding/crafting/upgrading to keep players looking towards the next big thing, but the game itself is not fun to play.
Also, the game suffers with controls designed for mobile.
I didn't have any crashes and the graphics are colourful, although there is almost no variety in the ground types or mobs. and no real biomes to speak of. I ran south for 1 hour and everything was basically the same except some of the mobs changed colour and got larger. In terms of stability the game is mostly good, but it does freeze for up to a minute when you open the map if you have not opened it in a while which is really annoying.
Overall, the game is polished, looks nice and has humorous elements, but is a padded grindfest with no real gameplay to speak of and ultra tedious combat.
Grab it on sale to relax with but don't expect too much.

As a Kickstarter backer I got this game for $15, but if I had paid $40 for it I probably wouldn't be happy at all.
The whole way the game interacts with you is ripped out of 1987 in the worst ways.
There's no fast travel, you watch your party walk for ages, because that's the only way out of the labaryth maps, walking back to the entrance, slowly. And there is plenty of mandatory back tracking.
The combat is boring, and the RNG makes it an annoying chore, but most of the time you can't avoid it. Put points into outdoorsman and flee every random encounter.
There's no cool stuff like reverse pick pocketing a land mine into someone's back pocket, or shooting their legs off so they can't flee. Just aim, and miss or get jam or whatever.
The character creator is super unintuitive and weird and kind of horrible. INT doesn't help with "wisdom skills," charisma has nothing to do with your ability to influence people in dialog, and strength has no bearing on your ability to break down a chain link gate. Why not? Because!
There is an over-world, but don't think that it's open, you need to follow the linear plot.
There is lots to see, but the game moves ridiculously slowly, ie level 5 and done with the first dungeon in ~12 hours.
The story is really decent and the game delivers a lot of it's "old school" promise, but honestly most of that is the bad things from the old days that should have been forgotten. For $40 I wouldn't buy it, and after my $15 I'm not sure if I will have the patience to finish it, even though I like the story.

Having tried the "tech demo" last year, I was excited to see Spintires arrive on Steam. What might look like a boring truck game for some, is actually an impressive and extremely detailed game. The physics are mind blowing and the detailing is awe inspiring.
Trees and shrubs bend in perfect contact with your truck. Mud deforms under your wheels and gets stuck to them. vapor comes off your engine when you cross a body of water. cross deep rivers with a truck of heavy logs and watch as the water sloshes over your hood and under your trailer.
And getting stuck doesn't mean game over. Winch yourself out of sticky situations and if you're playing multiplayer, your friends can winch you out too. Did you manage to flip your logs and now your precious cargo sits in the middle of the path? Get a crane and load them back up! Get the job done!
A beautifully crafted game. It looks pretty, it feels pretty and it's super fun! Definitely recommended!

I backed this game because I am a huge fan of Fallout 1, but after a few hours I can't be bothered to play it. Everything seems unfinished and generally rough around the edges. The engine is garbage and the graphics are ugly even at maximum setting. And I'm not talking low-definition ugly - the whole look of the game is just a big mess. It's all pasted together and no details seem to stand out. The UI is abhorrent with a ton of wasted space, which is not acceptable in 2014.  Navigating around the place is a pain because there aren't any proper map markers like in Baldur's Gate, for example. In fact, various caves and other area transitions are so poorly marked that they are hard to click. The camera is beyond terrible and adds to the unfinished feel of the game. On one map there was a tall tower that got in the way of the camera while I was in combat and I spend an ungodly amount of time trying to see around it. This is simply not acceptable in modern games. And don't get me started about combat, such utter rubbish! The guns feel like little slingshots and at times it seems more tactically sound to just come at the enemy bare handed. The combat is so boring and broken I don't even have the space to get into it. This is just one of those games that you want so much to like but the more you play it the more everything bothers you until you just decide enough is enough, close it and then uninstall it. I really don't know what the developers were doing but no one is going to convince me that this pile of garbage is the result of over 3 million US dollars and countless unexplained delays by the developer. My department just finished coordinating a 1.5 million international research project and if we pulled things like inXile we would in all probability be sued into utter oblivion.

I remember when the game was first announced and had me eagerly waiting only to be let down by the X360 exclusive release of 2010. Being disappointed by Microsoft's decision I kept my distance from that version in hopes of a later PC release, which eventually happened after two years. Even though I didn't get my hands on it until 2014, having read the overwhemingly positive reviews from both users and critics, my expectations were still high.
To me a good game is a game that you feel like playing again shortly after you've finished it. Unfortunately, this was not the case with Alan Wake. It's not like the game was a disaster but, given my expectations, I found it to be a rather mediocre title.
The story is compelling and well-thought but it failed to get a grip on me faster than the dull and unimaginative gameplay got me bored. The mechanics are repetitive and the level design pretty straight forward. You don't get much of a variety of weapons to defend yourself and the enemies can be dealt with in one and only way. Aim flashlight, wait for the darkness to weaken then shoot. You get to solve a few puzzles every now and then but they never become much of a challenge. Most of the time you'll spend in game you'll be wandering around the woods of Bright Falls at night. The atmosphere is ominous and dark but it's not really frightening. Some times the darkness will overwhelm the player, forcing him to run for his life, but in my case it didn't feel scary as much as it felt frustrating. And speaking of frustrating, I have to mention the few sections of the game where the player has to get in a car, in order to cover the distance, which were absolutely horrendous. The vehicles' handling was pretty much terrible and no fun at all. On the bright side, broken into 6 episodes, the game's story unfolds in an interesting way and with nice pacing although the shallow gameplay makes getting from point A to point B feel like an eternity. The characters have depth and the voice acting is excellent although I could not develope any kind of sympathy for Alan for whatever reasons. Maybe it's just me. Aside from the storyline, a strong point of Alan Wake was the sound and music which were perfectly tailored for the game's setting.
Overall, the game was a sour experience and I can not recommend it. I'd give it a 5 out of 10 at best.

Any other PC drifting games with low-to-med spec requirements?
I don't think so.
Pros:
+ Very nice drifting physics
+ Quite a lot of cars, many still in development though
+ Not Pay2win
+ Vinyl system encourages creativity and allows you to replicate real life liveries (although with fictional aftermarket logos)
+ You compete against other people's ghost record = no lag, no sync error, you can pause mid-match
+ Money farming isn't tedious and slow
+ Car customization: body kits, rims, spoilers, vinyls and decals
+ Fine tuning option is one of the best and most complete among lots of racing games.
+ Perfect for both casual drift players and hardcore drift enthusiasts
+ You can play this using keyboard (now, think about how many drifting games impossible to play on keyboard.. and then there's Peak Angle, which is comfy on keyboard!)
Cons:
- You compete against other people's ghost record = not 100% multiplayer, but hey, I'll still take it
- No car performance downgrade feature (yet).
- Many of the cars still don't have customizable body kits (many visual models are still in development, so this makes sense).
Controversial topic:
The developers have recently decided to put three-quarter of the total car amount into DLCs. Now, before everyone goes crazy, I'd like to inform that all players who have accumulated over 500.000 Credits (Cr) at any point of their gameplay get free access to all DLCs; they can buy the cars in-game without having to purchase the DLCs.
On the other hand, new players who buy the game after the DLC update are left with only 7 cars. Although this game is not pay-to-win at all, this renders all newer players unable to collect cars without buying DLCs.
However, are the DLCs worth the money? While most people will answer "No", I leave the answer to all of you. One DLC contains 2 to 4 cars, some even with a body-kit set unlock. Surely, if a player likes the content of a DLC, they will definitely buy it. But, with the price of the DLCs right now? I can say that most people will choose other games, and I agree. However, this is due to the fact that many of the game's cars are still in development.
Therefore, I can conclude that this DLC implementation is rather too early as the game itself still doesn't have enough cars.
Conclusion:
A perfect drift game for both casual and drift enthusiasts. Although the game is still in development, it is really good in terms of physics and customization. If you don't have a really beefy PC but want a nice and non-demanding drifting game, you should really consider picking this one up.
NOTE:
After the Version 205 update, the game connection might've been bugged a bit. At the moment, players might experience an issue in profile saving.
However, FEAR NOT! The devs are the kind that listen to the players! They're active on the forum and take suggestions, as well as answer players' questions. Additionally, they always try to provide solutions to players' problems.

This isn't a review just for the game per-say, this is more orientated towards the reviewers themselves also.
If the game isn't up to the spec as other games that were released before it (Mafia 2 being prime example), then why do I see 2K apologisers and, for lack of a better word, "fanboys" of this series claiming (in brief) "The game is not about the graphics, its about the story".
I'm sorry but, its 2016. We've had games come and go in the last few years that were spectacularly produced and ported without much of an issue. Did we have a 30fps cap on Witcher 3? No, it was optional. Did we have blurry vision in GTA V? Only when drunk. Did we get pixelated textures in Fallout 4? Well yeah, we did. But at least the anti-aliasing was good.
Now coming to a point that I'll probably get poked and prodded about, "Did the devs say they were going to do any of this?". No, they didn't. But when you've come this far down the timeline in the game industry, you expect a certain quality. When you expect quality and don't receive it, its going to get messy no matter how you try to fix it. First impressions are vital.
Now to conclude my little review here. So far I've tried to enjoy the game with its current "features", and yet I can't because my game crashes 4 minutes into the game (2x 780 ti aren't powerful enough for you?) but from those 4 minutes I've played I could tell what the devs were trying to accomplish. It looked decent, if I squinted hard enough through the forced gaussian blur. The cars were there, the people were there, the protagonist "Harambe" was there if a little rigid in his bank guard costume.
I hope the devs figure something out in the next few days, otherwise I'll start regretting my purchase.

for my NVIDEA users with that cancerous stutter
=======================================================
0
A FANDOM User • 05/21/2016
1. Open your Nvidia Control Panel. Not Geforce Experience, Nvidia Control Panel. Type it into your start menu's "search programs and files" bar if you have to and start it from there.
2. Select "Manage 3D settings" in the side bar, then click the "Program Settings" tab.
3. Click "Add", find the Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor program, and select it for customization.
4. Once selected, scroll down the feature list until you find the "Vertical Sync" setting near the bottom. Change it to "Adaptive". Just straight-up Adaptive. This will activate the Nvidia-exclusive Adaptive Vsync on your GPU, which should be what fixes your issue.
5. Click "Apply", then close out of Nvidia Control Panel. Start up Shadow of Mordor and turn off the game's regular Vsync. This last one is important, you might have issues if you leave it on.
With that, you should be done, and your slowdowns should be fixed.

The best 'game' I've ever played.
Even though it originally came out in 2006, Flight Simulation X still holds up as a truly amazing simulator.   The Steam Edition has made improvements to the performance.
The base simulator covers the entire globe, has flying lessons built in and also many missions to complete.
A word of warning though, if you end up getting into flight simulation, it may end up costing you a lot more as there are some amazing addons to pick up.
I'm a photoscenery fan, as I like to know that what I'm flying over is an exact replica of what I would see if I was really flying.  Plus it can be used to navigate accurately.
If you're new to flight simulation, here are my recommendations, bearing in mind I'm a GA flyer:
Firstly, buy the book FSX for Pilots- Real World Training.  It is the perfect way to learn how to fly using the simulator.
Essential Addons:
General:
REX
FS Global (preferably ultimate editions)
Natural Tree Environment X - not essential but I like it.
Accu-Feel - Makes the default planes feel more realistic.
If you're not into photoscenery:
FTX Global
FTX Vector
If you prefer photoscenery, then it might not be worth getting the two FTX products, as your photo scenery will overwrite them
UK Photoscenery:
VFR Generation X v3
Revolution X ( a criticism levelled at photoscenery, is that they can appear flat, however this adds loads of autogen andis fantastic).
UK2000 UK airports
These titles are amazing.  So realistic.
USA Photoscenery
Megascenery Earth
TreeLines (like Revolution X, but only includes trees.  Works well though)
Night Environment for each state where available.
Airplanes:
The default ones are ok, but there are better ones out there.  For GA flying I love the A2A Piper.
Traffic:
Ultimate Traffic 2 is a good one.  Makes things a lot more interesting with other planes flying around.
Finally, I recommend a decent PC to run it on, and a decent yoke and rudder pedals.  I use the Saitek products.
You might want to try a few tweaks too.  I recommend Frooglesims youtube video called 'VLOG: How to get better FSX performance' and the tweaks referenced in the Megascenery manual.  Matt Smith is also a good user to watch youtube videos on.
As I said, beware, because if you do get hooked, you may end up spending a lot (of time and money) on the hobby. Time and money very well spent though.

Not too sure why people are slating the Dev's for giving us 'More of the same' ??? Seems like people just expect a complete rework of engines and such when a new title is released. Expectations have risen too unrealistic amounts these days. This is a good game, and in no way a BAD game. It has it's flaws; microtransactions being the biggest one, but that's not a decision made by the developers. The story, whether you think it's good or bad is actually presented quite well, and while this is an alternate universe of Tolkien's lore, its a great addition to Middle Earth. Fun to play, lots of initial mechanisms to learn, controls are intuitive, and the nemesis system allows for wide replayability. However, it must be said: I fkin love anything even related to Lord of the Rings, so take what you will from this review.
On a serious note though, critiques of games are too harsh these days, coming from what I assume the majority of people don't know how game development really works (including myself). The technology involved with this game is AAA and as far as i've seen has not been replicated in any other AAA title. Everyone loved the Arkham series, and that was 'more of the same' so I don't know what kind of salt people are eating in modern times, but too much salt ruins everything.

So,I just want to state that the first thing I did was to play multiplayer, and it was within the first 10 minutes of playing the game, that I learnt just how far a soft suspension truck is supposed to tilt.
I roll to the bottom of a hill, on my roof, helpless with a stalled engine, and no idea how to get out of the situation I had just created.  Laughing at the same time at how I could go and♥♥♥♥♥♥up so fast.
Anyway, I do what anyone would do, I hit every key looking for the chat button, "Ah, it's Y", I think to myself.  I then proceeded to plead to my comrades to save me!
In the effort to save me, my friend Crevarski gets pulled over the edge of the hill and ends up stuck at the bottom of it, ensnared by all the surrounding stones deeper in the pit.
This was, as you might assume, was unbelievably hilarious.
We then both proceed to beg for the random player to save us.
In his attempts to save us, he is then also pulled off the cliff, just to roll onto his roof on top of me.
This led to tears of laughter on my end.
Within the first 10 minutes, I knew my money was well invested, just because I've never laughed so much at having a lack of understanding the game.  The game is just hilarious as you go from blunder to blunder, stalling engines in every possible way possible for the first few hours.
Once you're past that part of the game, and you start getting good at traversing the environment in your behemoths, it occurs to you that 1 truck is not going to cut it when tackling this unforgiving terrain!  Leading you to try and get a team sorted, where you'll have to assign everyone a task.  Such as 2 log haulers, and the other 2 as the support, dealing in the winching, repairing and refueling!
(For those of you that don't enjoy multiplayer, you can switch to any truck unlocked at any time to go and save the one you just drowned in 'quick-mud')
Anyway, this game is so unbelievably addictive, not just for the strangely addictive gameplay, but for the amount of teamwork that is required for a driving simulator, that even the 'crème de la crème' of driving games manage to skim the surface of.
Plus, with the game being relatively new, I will ignore its minor flaws, such as the camera being annoying at times, and a few missing options that would of been nice, but aren't exactly going to ruin your time, as I'm sure most of these annoyances will be addressed very soon!
I would
recommend this game to anyone that is interested in off-roading '
' games like Euro Truck Simulator.

This game is great! A rich back story that draws on a lot of Twin Peaks, a little Stephen King, and that special Remedy touch that made the first two Max Payne games so good. Subtle, creepy horror with a handful of jump scares.
I started out on normal difficulty but I found that dying really interrupted the flow of the story. By the third chapter it really started to drag. Normal is not especially difficult, but it does involve the usual amount of trial and error which can really distract you from the story the game is trying to tell. The action mechanics aren't very satisfying so this combined with regular death interruptions makes it seem like the levels are really dragging on. The first time I played this game I ended up giving up on it halfway through episode 3.
I decided to give the game another shot for my Halloween 2014 horror pick. This time I scaled the difficulty back to easy and WOW! It was a whole new world. Suddenly the game was like a thriller you can't put down until you reach the last page and the morning sun is streaming through the windows. The drag of the levels practically vanished, and a number of action sequences could be dealt with by a panicked thrill run to the next light source instead of a drawn out fight, which really added to the suspense.
I still found myself in a few tight spots - just enough that it felt like I was still working for it. Fights with a high number of enemies were still a bit of a challenge, and were often followed by panic when I realized I was out of ammo with no idea what was ahead on the trail. But like the thrill-runs to avoid the smaller fights, that anxiousness only added to the suspense of the story.
This game isn't about the action, it's about the story and the atmosphere. You aren't missing anything by putting it in easy mode and letting the story play out. From my experience I'd say you're missing out by NOT playing it on easy. The action really takes away from the atmosphere - scale the action back, and the creepiness factor increases. All of the thrill with none of the frustration.
Overall, highly recommended!

Time, patience, skill and the heart to watch your truck and payload rollover into a ditch without throwing your computer out the window are what you'll need to play this game. It's brutally hard and unforgiving but an extremely satisfying offroad simulator. The premise is very basic. Explore and unlock (or decloak as they call it) the map to reveal hidden vehicles and structures. Collect them and then proceed to deliver loads of lumber to the designated sites. You can customize your vehicles loadouts and tools at garages you've unlocked and use the map and compass to plan your route. You'll need it, plan or drive poorly and you'll be rewarded with a mouthful of mud/water and trying again.
There are repair trucks, refueling trucks, winch/rescue trucks and loading cargo trucks some even with their own fully operable cranes. There are also smaller scout vehicles like jeeps for mapping and finding the points of interest. Escort your delivery trucks with the needed support vehicles to ensure they arrive safely at their destination. The game support mulitplayer sessions as well and this is where it really shines, allowing you to form offroad convoys with your friends and help each other out, each person filling a needed roll in the convoy.
Its sandbox style maps allow you to go anywhere and do anything at any time. My only gripe is the game lacks a traditional save/load feature. It saves continously and automatically saves as you play and you can quit at any time and can continue later where you left off. But you can't save half way through an attempted delivery or before a risky maneuver and then reload if things go horribly wrong (which they frequently do). This means if you screw up, you have to either reset your vehicle and try again or attempt to winch yourself out of trouble and continue the fight. This can be both intensely frustrating or satisfying if you're really hardcore about it. It certainly teaches you to be careful and not drive with reckless abandon. Regardless, there needs to be an option for it IMO.
The devs have promised regular updates and content additions in the following months which is good and we'll see. But for a kickstarter backed, small dev project it's remarkably polished and delivers alot of offroad driving pleasure.

Let's get the quibbles out of the way first: It's not immediately apparent why Vella needs to do what she does when she gets to Shellmound, and the occasional lack of variety in "I can't use these things together" messages is jarring when considering the great variety on other occasions.
That said, Broken Age is a fine throwback to the era of the adventure game.  If you grew up on Monkey Island, you'll find much to love here.  If, however, this is your first foray into the genre, I can think of no better introduction.  Control is simple without invoking a dozen or more arcane verbs, puzzles are mostly intuitive, and hand-holding is minimal unless you go out of your way to prolong certain stages of the game.
Plus, it has the best Quaker Oats Guy I've ever seen, viewable in my screenshot gallery.

A pretty cool little time waster. Of course sometimes you'd want to waste 20-30 minutes and accidentally waste an hour and a half, but it's not a game you can just binge play. In any case, the physics are simple enough, the game countersteers for you. It's  a simple to learn, difficult to master type deal. For physics download the demo it'll tell you everything you need to know.
Note - not all cars have changeable bodykits, not all bodykits can be bought with in game currency (which is VERY difficult to win in daily challenges). Same goes for wings and wheels. On that note it's not pay to win. The multiplayer aspect is... well as far as I figured it out you play against ghost replays of other people online, which is a good way to exclude lobbies, lag, griefing, and many proper online problems. On the other hand it's not really online, but I do not care much about that. All in all is it worth 12 eur? Well, you decide, at first I thought not, then I got into it and I thought "yes, probably it will be a good value for money, since it will bring a ton of playtime over time"
Now that time has passed, it deserves an edit. The servers are pretty much empty, you'd be lucky if you get into a drift lobby with more than 1 other player (and with the system the way it is, it just means there's pretty much ONE PERSON EXCEPT ME who is playing this).
The developers have decided to also NOT finish the game and to NOT add the missing cars, which is logical, as the sales dropped, the revenue stopped and nobody wants to work for free... but you DO need to keep the game relevant and updated to get the revenue stream going and not stopping. Something the developer seems to be too lazy to do.
The new game by this developer is stated to be "THE COMPLETELY NEW GAME", and it is exactly the same game, judging by the trailer (it's not out yet), and it already has DLC listed. So this will likely be abandoned very soon (Actually this was abandoned some time ago), and the "Furidashi" game which is "totally not this same game with a new name" will be sold for money. Honestly, I feel cheated by this.
Verdict? Get CarX instead

Short: A good game to waste away some time. Aside from controls, I see no difference between the PC version and the Mobile version of Fallout Shelter. Which ever device floats your boat.
Long:
1. It can be played via Keyboard, Mouse (my method) or controller(*).
2. While you can make purchases, you do not need to spend any money to progress.(**)
3. Most of the excitement, for me, is in the overwatcher's missions.
Alright, first keep in mind that this came out first as a mobile app. The graphics are simple and cute. The playstyle is also fairly simple and does not really offer anything 'new'. But it is a good game to play if you have a few minutes to waste but cannot or do not want to get invested in another game. OR if you want to multi-task for some reason. (Window-mode movie watching or working on homework/projects.
Keep in mind that boxes earned in a game (the free boxes) can not be opened in another save. But you can get pets and Mr. Handy from them. You get one box every 7 days you check in and you can randomly get a task that rewards with a box as well. (Same with the overwatcher missions. Some times they reward boxes, pets, outfits, etc.)
Customization mostly comes later in the game, but you are free to re-name the people as you get them (or randomly during play). Once you unlock (via x amount of people living in the vault) certian facilities, you can alter their hair style/color and make clothing/weapons without relying on chance. Dinners and living quarters also have themes (fairly new) which auto change during certian events. You can also collect themes to change it anytime you want.
Holiday events are enjoyable enough without feeling overwhelming. But you will find lots of slow periods while playing. Especially on Survival mode where building up too quickly has deadly drawbacks.
(* Not sure if it auto detects for a controller, as I rarely use them on PC gaming.)
(** That being said, progress can be very... very slow at times. It is a pay to be lazy mechanic more than anything.)

This game is great! A rich back story that draws on a lot of Twin Peaks, a little Stephen King, and that special Remedy touch that made the first two Max Payne games so good. Subtle, creepy horror with a handful of jump scares.
I started out on normal difficulty but I found that dying really interrupted the flow of the story. By the third chapter it really started to drag. Normal is not especially difficult, but it does involve the usual amount of trial and error which can really distract you from the story the game is trying to tell. The action mechanics aren't very satisfying so this combined with regular death interruptions makes it seem like the levels are really dragging on. The first time I played this game I ended up giving up on it halfway through episode 3.
I decided to give the game another shot for my Halloween 2014 horror pick. This time I scaled the difficulty back to easy and WOW! It was a whole new world. Suddenly the game was like a thriller you can't put down until you reach the last page and the morning sun is streaming through the windows. The drag of the levels practically vanished, and a number of action sequences could be dealt with by a panicked thrill run to the next light source instead of a drawn out fight, which really added to the suspense.
I still found myself in a few tight spots - just enough that it felt like I was still working for it. Fights with a high number of enemies were still a bit of a challenge, and were often followed by panic when I realized I was out of ammo with no idea what was ahead on the trail. But like the thrill-runs to avoid the smaller fights, that anxiousness only added to the suspense of the story.
This game isn't about the action, it's about the story and the atmosphere. You aren't missing anything by putting it in easy mode and letting the story play out. From my experience I'd say you're missing out by NOT playing it on easy. The action really takes away from the atmosphere - scale the action back, and the creepiness factor increases. All of the thrill with none of the frustration.
Overall, highly recommended!

Bryan Fargo presents: Bryan Fargo's Wasteland 2 eschews almost every major game design improvement of the last thirty years for the cause of nostalgia. Combat is simplistic and enemy difficulty scales purely by turning them into bullet sponges, and any 'set piece' fights can be negated by having one party member trigger combat and then run back, drawing snipers from towers and cover to chase them down on foot.
Attributes are completely disconnected from skills simply because that's how it was done 20 years ago; as a result, two of your *seven* attributes are dumpstats and may as well not exist (Luck and Charisma), and since Coordination is a meaningless concept when divorced from fine manipulation skills, it may as well have been folded into Speed. The modified ASSI system would be in fact, far less so than the current CLASSIC set-up.
However, if you do want to choose Charisma on a character, do not level any social skills with them whatsoever! Charisma's only real benefit is a set boost to all XP gained that scales with how high the stat is, and all dialogue skills grant experience to the entire party when used. Active skills such as the two redundant Lockpicking skills, Demolitions, Mechanical Repair and Computer Science, et al, only grant experience to the user. As a result, your Charismatic character should be highly Intelligent in order to gather as many active skills to benefit from the experience stat. As a result, none of your other three characters really need high Int; 4 or 6 should suffice. Your ideal party should be a beautiful Adonic IT guy who can't tie his own shoes and can calculate pi to the first 200 decimals without paper, and three semi-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ punch monkeys who kill or sweet-talk everything between them and victory.
The game is riddled with minor bugs, which would be expected of a newly released game, except every higher-tier Kickstarter backer got the questionable reward of becoming QA-tester for
the majority of the development process. Unless you got a copy of the game for participating in the Kickstarters of other Interplay alumni, I guess. Currently, keeping any allied non-party NPC alive is terrifyingly difficult as they're often equipped with pistols, and since you can't control them, gleefully run into the firing arcs of any Ranger they can see to maximize their self-harm. But they will duel you to the death if you accidentally clip them, which results in the player having to utilize amazingly unorthodox tactics. Prepare to think outside the box!
I've played through the original Wasteland multiple times, as well as Fountain of Dreams, Wasteland's toilet baby. It's not that I hate this game, or even dislike it; in fact, it's exactly what I expected when I put $60+ into the Kickstarter. I've privately bemoaned streamlining game mechanics in favor of overall experience, and it's almost cathartic to have the inevitable conclusion of that flawed ideal thrown in my face. I'm not a
, but there have been a lot of general QOL improvements to RPG and strategy gameplay mechanics that an entire development team had to put horse blinders on to avoid.
