Let me tell you about Wasteland 2.
I was out on a mission after having managed to strike a truce with a potential enemy who'd already flattened my crew more than once. The guy who tried to land the Desert Rangers in trouble with them is scared for his life because I dobbed him in as the true culprit - even after he helped me put things right, even after I said I wouldn't. He runs off to get his scaly mates all wound up and ready to make trouble.
I think about it for a split second then headshot the stupid bugger. He can have his little hissyfit, but there's no way he's stuffing up this unexpected and welcome truce, Not while my sniper's rifle is loaded.
Then I realise the effect this game is having on me. I'm horrified with myself. I rationalise the decision: the guy was too dumb to live; he'd have only got more innocent people killed; he was trying to covertly start fights he couldn't finish; at least if I put him down like this the other mob wouldn't torture him to death or something. I'm even more horrified at the rationalisations. I wonder if the game even has an event path for what I just did. Would his friends jump me next time because of a bug, or did he need to actually make it back to his friends to trigger that situation? Would there still be a truce when I got back? Did I really take care of the problem?
The problem. Huh. That problem had a name. And friends. Possibly a family.
This game is getting me to play like an amoral hardcase for the first time ever (usually I do my best to be a good guy) - and I simultaneously love it and fear it for that. Not because it's fun but because everything is a moral grey area, every success has a bit of failure in it, and it's rare for everyone to make it out alive and unscathed.

Once, long ago, I played a game called Wasteland that forever changed how I would view the way games should be played.  It was the basis by which many other post-apocalyptic titles (such as Fallout) and essentially solidified the turn-based strategy genre.  Playing Wasteland now, years and years from when it was first published, is a frustrating experience; but nonetheless, I still feel a little of the magic I felt back then as a kid playing something that was so cool and so new for its time.
Wasteland 2 does not disappoint.  I will readily admit I'm the type of player that hypes himself up too much before his first minutes in a game and leaves disappointed because the experience did not coincide with his images of it.  However, given a few hours of effort and attempts, I find that Wasteland 2 is a deeply satisfying sequel to one of my favorite games of ages past.
For those unfamiliar with old-style turn-based games, this game is DIFFICULT.  You will not be a battle that you don't have the potential to lose.  Even the most soft of the game modes is has some extremely difficult battles in them.  Chance can and does fail you.  That chest which probably has some decent loot more often than not will be permanently broken instead of opening for you.  Your gun will jam at the most inopportune times and a number of enemies will be sufficiently higher level than you to make your first couple of fights in each new map be an extremely cautious experience.  You will be required to use all of the skills available to you to effectively fight battles.  In higher difficulties, it is highly possible to design a character that is completely unusable past a certain point in the game.  Not to mention your characters are capable of being permanently dead.  Resources are limited and you'll find times when you run out of ammo (make sure you bring spare weapons).   However, if challenge suits you, this is the type of game you should play.  The musical score is very well thought out and after a few hours the story becomes very engaging.
Some problems, like most reviews I've read, have more to do with nitpicking bugs or GUI designs instead of something that is truly gamebreaking or experience ruining.  The graphics are awful for the current generation of games, but the environments are well thought out enough to really ignore that type of problem;  besides, as one review pointed out, if you're playing this game you aren't playing it because it's pretty.
Other issues include complicated inventory management, the inability to adequately group characters (there are several points in the game where you have to break up your team to manage certain areas) and a 'sluggish' interface (usually due to abundantly clicking a certain NPC or area).  Additionally I was disappointed that the voiceovers were pretty limited, usually first lines of a dialog, but to be honest I got over that pretty quickly once I settled back into my old-school RPG mood.  One really delightful element to the game is that I feel that each skill tree is actually worth investing in, even if some are more influential than others.  I don't feel like another round of Diablo where there are 3 specific builds worth doing and everything else is trash.  If you play, I highly recommend diversifying your skill sets (stick to roughly 4-5 per characters, exceeding that you'll become a jack of all trades and a master of none) and get close to maxing your intelligence (skill points per level are awarded based on int, 8 for 4 points, 10 for 5).
All in all I would rate it an 8 out of 10, most of my complaints are polish and general clunkiness.  But, as expected, I found no lack of enjoyment thus far in engaging in the post-apocalyptic world of southwest Arizona, a member of the Desert Rangers once more.

Have you ever put down a good psychological horror book and wished you could experience similar thrills in video game form? Well, there are plenty of options for that, but here is Remedy (developer of Max Payne and its sequel The Fall of Max Payne) and their take on the genre. While far from a horror classic, Alan Wake provides enough thrills and atmosphere to prop up the mysterious, and rather compelling, story.
The player controls titular character Alan Wake, a successful novelist who finds himself traveling with his wife Alice to the Pacific Northwest in order to break a drought of writing inspiration. The setup instantly draws comparisons to other works, such as Twin Peaks and The Shining, giving the game an instant feeling of familiarity, yet still retaining that feeling of mystery and intrigue. What follows from this setup are even more recognizable tropes (quirky locals, mysterious woods, marital disagreements) which all come together to form an impressive and memorable narrative, however forceful and contrived it gets. The game splits itself into "episodes" (ala a tv show, complete with previously ons and next time ons) which allows the game to set into a nice pacing, however predictably each one has to find new ways to throw Alan into the woods to contend with evil forces.
The gameplay continues the trend of familiarity, borrowing heavily from other shooter/horror games. The gunplay is recognizably Resident Evil 4, however looser and faster. Alan Wake may be a writer, however he seems to know his way around firearms quite extensively, though it's only through the game's sole unique mechanic, does he shine. In order to mow down enemies with your arsenal of guns, Alan must make use of his trusty flashlight (powered by real brand Duracell batteries!) and stun enemies with it until their shroud of darkness disapates, leaving them open to bullets. If low on (Duracell brand) batteries and (non affilated brand) ammo, Alan has the option of dodging enemy attacks and running in the opposite direction, however on Normal difficutly, with enough exploring and well placed shots, one should never have much issue with lack of resources.  While fun and novel at first, the game never really adds anything past the flashlight mechanic, which after its surprisingly long campaign (11-13 hours), it starts to see diminishing returns rather quickly, thus the game loses quite a bit of tension and becomes more predictable.
Originally an XBox360 exclusive, the game was ported to PC several years after its release (in order to recoup a 5 year development budget), including all the the DLC. The game seemed well optimized and I ran into minimal issues in terms of bugs and graphical glitches, as well as an acceptable amount of graphical options, which is always appareciated in this day of rushed and shoddy console ports.
While flawed, Alan Wake is ultimately a game worth picking up, even at its full price. While the gameplay begins to stale in the later hours of the game, there is always a well done cutscene or interesting collectable around the corner to alleviate some of that boredom. If anything, its another portal into the mind of writer Sam Lake (who also was the creative mind behind the first two Max Payne games), who proves to be a capable and inventive storyteller.

You really have to break this game down into categories to give it an honest review. All of this is an objective opinion in the end though.
10/10  Audio - The music is amazing I need not say more. The choice of music is fitting for the era the game is placed in. The tracks are fitting in the scenes they are placed in and all in all truely awesome.
4/10 Graphics - If you look past the blurry textures there is a large amount of detail in the world to be seen. It is unfortunate that it was released with the texture quality that is present because I think it really dosen't do the game justice. I wish the open world could look even half as good as some of the cutscenes do honestly.
??/ 10 Performance- They weren't lying it really does run at a rock solid 30 FPS lol. This will be patched though so really its a mute point.
8/10 Story - I am loving the story so far. Theres grit, drama, passion (not in the love sense from what I've seen so far), and brutality. Can't wait to delve into it even more.
7/10 Driving - Im enjoying the driving so far but I am using the Simulation mechanic located in the menu. Bigger cars have more weight than smaller cars and you can feel it while driving. Cars with more horsepower feel like they have more horsepower than ones with less. Its kind of hard to describe but I like it.
7/10 Gameplay Mechanics - Shooting feels good as guns provide good feedback for what they are, ie shootguns pack a punch, rifles and submachine guns provide recoil, pistols provide accuracy up to a certain range. Moving with lincoln is a bit clunky using mouse and keyboard so some may prefer to plug in their controller for this one. I have not messed around with rebinding as I have read about peopel not being able to get them working after doing this. A good couple key rebinding and the controls would probably be a lot more fluid thought honestly.
All in all I would recommend the game due to the story (so far) mainly. If some of the other issues can be patched I think It would honestly do the game more justice. Having better textures in the game would do the game a whole lot from the cosmetic standpoint. I think its a fun game so far and am enjoying it up to this point. I will probably hold off until the patch hits to really get in and try the game out.

I'm giving a thumbs-up but this game is definitely not for everyone. There isn't a story and even though the music fits the game, it's the same few scores over and over. Amazing Adventures: The Lost Tomb is for those looking for a challenging hidden object experience. They really cram a ton of items into each scene and many are well hidden. I guess they don't call it hidden object game for nothing. :p  So the game is basically just many many HO scenes with puzzles inbetween each one. Jigsaw, Memory Tiles, and Spot the Differences. The game gives you 20 "missions" and each one is an ever increasing number of said HOs and puzzles. At the end of a mission, you'll get a fact about Egypt and part of a manuscript. I'm assuming you assemble the manuscript at the end of the game. I haven't got there yet. I still have 10 missions to go and I have a feeling it's going to take awhile. One thing about The Lost Tomb that I REALLY like is the bonus you get if you find a scarab in each of the 21 HO scenes. You'll then be able to play each scene and find EVERY item. (When you find an item on the list, a new one will pop into its place). There is a huge satisfaction in completely clearing a scene. I wish other HO games had this feature. So in closing, only buy this if you're up for a challenge, don't mind the lack of a story, and can deal with some repetition. It's a good game for HO fans who need a break between other things. :)

If you liked Shadow of Mordor - you will love Shadow of War. It really is that simple.
Yes, the game has flaws - I think everything about loot boxes has already been said. And in some instances I find the graphical fidelity a bit lacking. Even with the high resolution textures playing the game at 2560x1440 some parts look a little blurry. Also compared to the previous game the model of Talion's face this time around is just.. off. He looks like an Action Man.
With that out of the way - everything else has improved. The new loot system has created a new level of depth possible with builds that you simply couldn't get in SoM. Difficulty has been ramped up massively - playing on top difficulty I'm still getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked frequently by Uruks even after unlocking the vast majority of Talion's skills. A much welcome change of pace given that in SoM once Talion had most of his skills you could just steam roll the game.
The nemesis system is so much wider in scope now that it's hard to know where to even begin. The Uruks interact with each other so much more, some Uruks will actively hunt you down or try to catch you off guard. You can make your Uruks fight in the pits against other Nemesis Uruks. These pit fights are surprisingly gut wrenching, especially when it's an Uruk you've spent some time on the battlefield with, or who's helped you take over your latest fortress down there in the ring fighting for their life. The new difficulty means that dominating a whole army is much more difficult than it was in the previous game - which in turn makes Betrayals, Ambushes and Revenge plots much more meaningful, another welcome change.
Combat also gains more depth thanks to the new damage types, glaive moves, and the choice between hammers and bows as ranged weapons.Aside from these, much is familiar here - attack and counter gameplay with a hitstreak counter with some special moves thrown in for good measure.
Over 20 hours in to the game and I'm still being surprised and challenged by Shadow of War.
All in all - good stuff.

Shadow of War is one of 2017’s biggest disappointments for me. While its Nemesis system is better than ever, the rest of the game provides a flawed and repetitive experience with some unpleasant practices integrated into the menu.
Imagine a single player game that advertises its microtransactions and season pass every time you pause. That may not sound too bad, but I easily spent at least forty percent of the game digging through the bloated and slow menu system. I must have seen them hundreds of times. In addition to that nonsense, you have the (microtransaction) Market section, filled with Gold and Mithril Chests that promise epic or legendary items and orcs. Other things you can spend your premium currency on include experience boosts and Featured Friday Chests™.
Not everything requires real money in the Market. You can spend your Mirian (in-game currency) on somewhat useless Silver Chests and redeem rewards tied to the online component of the game (Online Vendettas and Sieges). Those delicious rewards trigger a glowing circle right next to the Market in the menu, you know, to make you click on it. That way you can be exposed to more of their premium offerings since they’re all mixed in together. It’s just the other way the game is engineered to advertise its boxes to you. There is some serious free-to-play mobile game design philosophy wrapping its glistening, bulging arms around Shadow of War.
Now that we’ve covered that nasty part of the game, let’s talk about the Nemesis system. It’s good and the orcs make it fun and interesting. You’ll run into and be killed by poet orcs, orcs that don’t know how to stay dead, and orcs that will save you time and time again (to my horror, which I’ll go over later). Their responses to the numerous situations that can occur within the game impressed me. The voice actors put in some great performances as the orc and olog captains, especially when you earn the ability to shame them into insanity (highly recommended).
Unfortunately, the game overstays its welcome with its forgettable story and unlikable protagonists. The elf ghost seems unable to say anything that doesn’t involve the word Palintír™ and Talion doesn’t really develop or seem interesting. Shelob is apparently eye candy with her fine humanoid form and has a unexpectedly dumb storyline tied to her memories (one type of collectable in the game) that becomes apparent when you gather all of them. The other characters in the game are a slightly better while the orcs are #1. They have much more entertaining and interesting personalities than everyone else.
The other big problem with Shadow of War comes in the form of highly repetitive and somewhat frustrating gameplay. If you’re the type that can’t help collecting collectibles, then you’re in for a boring and tedious ride. One of the worst parts about hunting them down is having to climb a tower that activates a mini-game that involves scoping out the territory until your crosshair shrinks enough to discover it when you’re close enough. Some of them have interesting lore pieces attached and others, not so much.
The combat varies greatly in its quality depending on the encounter. You can easily find yourself spamming dodge or counter for extended periods of time if the captain has the right combination of immunities and traits. Some enraged captains will endlessly lunge at you if they’re Enraged leaving no room to do anything else until they chill out. Sometimes you’re stuck kiting the enemy or you’re facing a tank who keeps healing over and over again (don’t waste your time and run away until you’re at a higher level). Other times, you’re being clever with all your tools and feeling pretty great about your conquest. Then again, you could end up becoming uncomfortably intimate with the game’s horrible targeting and wasting a powerful attack on an unintended victim. It’s a somewhat common occurrence with groups.
Other issues involve traversal and glitches. Talion seems to have a fetish for climbing and will lovingly attach himself to any surface that’s nearby when running around. I’ve accidentally started climbing up a wall, pillar, or structure when just trying to travel from point A to point B. This problem happens frequently and with mounts too, especially graugs. However, the inclusion of the double jump was a very good choice and was fun to use. As for the glitches, I fell through the world once, witnessed silent speeches, and more. For the most part, my 33 hours didn’t have many technical problems and the loading times were fantastic on my HDD.
The mission design could have used a better touch too. Too often would I be going out of bounds in an open-world game. And it’s not a matter of running 1000m in the wrong direction, the arbitrary boundaries are poorly placed to the point of causing mission failure and having to restart. It’s aggravating to see that message pop up and doubly so when it causes a restart. Let me use the environment to my advantage instead of forcing me in a weirdly confined space in a game where you’re normally able to move freely. Since orc speeches are unskippable, you can expect to hear plenty of repeated dialogue if you happen to run into a very difficult fight.
The game has a weird grind going for it towards the end. Recruiting orcs means not collecting sweet loot off their dead bodies so each one has an opportunity cost between an item or convert, making the purchase of chests more attractive. I’m glad I got the Act 1 Starter Pack for 50% off with the 500 real currency Mirian which helped me stay geared up. Leveling up slows down too so again, I’m glad I ended up with a handful of 2-hour 100% experience boosts.
Lastly, I don’t understand the balance in this game. The combat balance seems off when it comes to the difficulty level. Normal is too easy and Nemesis removes nearly all the hitstun that Normal difficulty has. I found Nemesis to be an exercise in frustration since some missions could end up turning into huge difficulty spikes while repeating the mission on Normal made it a cakewalk. You can tune the difficulty at any time, but nothing can fix that weird gap between the two.
I lied, one more thing, before I forget. That heroic orc that kept saving me wasted my time. The upgrade system for items involving fulfilling some requirements that function like a mini-quest of sorts. The legendary ones tend to favor recruiting very specific orcs of a certain level, tribe, and class. This means staring at the Army section of the menu and going through the orcs until you find the right ones. You might even have to pass time if you don’t see any available. However, this one orc I recruited could not resist saving me and when he did, he delivered a one hit killing blow.
In conclusion, the Nemesis system and great orc voice acting carry this game hard. 2.5 out of 5 stars would be awarded based on that and the positive aspects of combat alone. Numerous things rubbed me the wrong way though and I cannot bring myself to recommend Shadow of War to anyone. Maybe at 40-50% off. It’s a horribly bloated experience with a sluggish menu. They needed to trim down a few things and go with refinement instead of having such a busy menu with too many functions. Oh, I do like the Photo Mode. Make sure to give that a “shot.” Hyuck.

Alan Wake is a game. At the same time, it is a mind-bending experience that asks the player to question every section of their journey. Is Alan experiencing reality? Can any moment of his story be taken for granted? If so, who is your friend? Who is your foe? Why are things happening this way? Can there be any happy resolution? None of these questions are hand-fed to you by the game; it is up to the player to ultimately make a decision as to what he thinks is truly going on.
Alan Wake, from a gameplay perspective, is a tense third-person shooter. By keeping the camera close to, but still over and pulled back from, Alan's shoulder, it allows the player to feel the tension and intensity of the situation. Each engagement has a simple system to follow: Use the flashlight, or any device that creates light, to burn away the shield of darkness that prevents Alan from harming it. Then, light it up with a variety of tight, responsive, and powerful weapons. The enemies of Alan Wake do not use intelligence or tactics to overwhelm the player, but sheer numbers and individual brute force. It is up to the player to use the environment and the equipment they retrieve tactically to defeat the horde, and in a worst-case scenario, know when to sprint straight for the nearest safe haven.
Alan Wake is a deep game; it's meant to be played multiple times. The story, while indepth and well structured just in the pacing of the game in of itself, contains many hidden facets found in its collectables that add depth to what Alan is experiencing, as well as the history and unseen events that occur in Bright Falls, Washington. Radio broadcasts, mysterious manuscript pages, and even the music itself all are important clues as to the truth of what is happening.
Without a doubt, Alan Wake is a game I'd recommend to anyone. It plays tight, it has a deep, dark mystery that holds the attentions of its players, and it is a fascinating experience that always lends a new clue into the truth every time one plays it.

This is a brilliantly constructed horror-themed game. Now mind you, when I use 'horror' I'm talking more like a Stephen King thriller novel. It's not terrifying or gruesome and probably won't leave you awake through the night wondering if that creature under your bed or in your closet is going to come out to drag it's nails across your eyelids. Instead, this is a well-written story very much in the same vein as many famous 'horror' writers, told in an interactive way.

It's very much a survival game that will leave you desperately budgeting your ammunition and light source and hoping you can dodge and run your way through packs of monsters. The combat is clever, although I did find it hard at times and found myself repeating areas with some frustration. The graphics are beautiful and our byronic protagonist evolves through the game as the events unfold around him, leaving you surprisingly attached to someone who seemed initially so unlikeable. Many of the mechanics are clever and unexpected, particularly in the DLC.

Overall, I enjoyed this game thoroughly and it stands on my shelf as one of my favourites, next to the likes of a completely different take on horror, Silent Hill 2. The story is intriguing and the world is immersive and filled with nods to horror stories most of us know at least enough to get the reference. I eagerly await the next installation.

I quite liked this - the story is solid, and does make it feel pretty much like you are the protagonist in a Stephen King novel or similar (especially with you being a frustrated author). The mechanic of having the enemies damaged/stunned by the light helps the atmosphere, and gives plenty of excuses to have you creeping through darkened houses, woods and abandoned industrial buildings, which always makes for a good basis for a horror game. The third person over the shoulder perspective is personally not something I favour generally, as it always feels clunky and unimmersive to me, but I didn't find it as bad as many other games that use this perspective at least.
The game works especially well in the beginning when the enemies are sparse and new. As the chapters of the story pass however, the combat/non-story related parts of the game become less compelling and a bit more "filler" like - this is obviously a common issue with horror themed games, whereas in a 90 minute movie or a book you can have just a few attacks on the protagonist, a game like thus runs much longer and you end up having to deal with many more rounds of threats to deal with.
Once you have killed dozens of the same shadowy crazed attackers it does turn the game into a bit of a chore - the story remains solid enough, and progresses reasonably until you get to a combat section where you have to grind your way through a fairly boring stretch of road/woods/whatever dispatching wave after wave of now tedious enemies you have seen a hundred times before, just to "earn" the next interesting bit of story advancement.
Still overall worth playing, but a shame that the promise of the early sections of the game is spoiled by this method of stretching out the content.

I'm not giving this game a positive review to show the devs I don't support these kinds of ports. It's sloppy and lazy.
Let me go by naming a few:
-Capped 30FPS (of course I had to say it)
-Really low quality textures
-Objects clip into eachother
-The view distance is tiny
-The environment in general seems blurry
-Floating bottles
-1080p is blatantly an upscaled 720p (which is the main cause of many of these problems)
-Stuttering framerate
-When the game launches, it doesn't close the launcher, forcing me to go into task manager and close it because it plays music
This is unnacceptable. This shouldn't become the norm for Triple A PC Releases. This is abhorrent and ridiculous. Hangar 13, I know this is your first major game (I could be wrong), but that doesn't mean you can do this to your PC community. You know damn well that a huge amount of PC Players can run this game so much better than you're forcing the entire community to play it at. Fix it, and fix it quick. Once the patch comes out, I'll edit my review depending on what happens.
EDIT: Now that the game has been patched, the game runs better now, but it's noticably poorly optimized. Even with the low quality textures the game has, it only gets like 57 fps. It's ridiculous. Also, the only other thing they changed was the keymapping. There's still no ability to change graphical settings. You can still only change post processing. Still not recommending.
EDIT 2: After playing for over 10 hours, I think I have a rough idea of what this game is. I thought this was going to be a successor to Mafia 2, but looking back at things, Mafia 2 is eons better. This game is watered down with the same rinse and repeat missions. The main story missions are few and far between, since you have to gain control over an entire territory to unlock it. It's frustrating and makes this game burn out fast. This game should have been worked on longer. They should have added more main missions rather than the side missions you're forced to do.
EDIT 3: Well, I beat the game. Can't say I feel accomplished. Story was alright, but way too overrated. I have no interest in playing afterwards. I feel like I wasted my money and I'm never getting it back. Devs released another patch that fixes blurry upscaled resolution, but it did nothing. I genuinely enjoyed the entirety of Broken Age--when I wasn't smiling I was laughing out loud from the absurd characters and their energized dialogue.
Pros:
Snappy adventure gameplay
Beautiful art style
Zany characters
Cons:
Short playtime
Predictability
There are plenty of unusual situations and puzzles, and the puzzles were sensible enough that none of them sent me to Google to solve. Also, if you dig its art style, you'll enjoy many of the set pieces with great camera direction. The characters are often memorable and almost always slightly off.
Unfortunately, Broken Age is still only Act I, so the playtime is about 4 hours. They're great hours, but they go by fast. The other caveat is that it seems to target tweens, and so many of the plot beats are predictable. There were definitely a few unexpected twists, but the hints leading to the big reveal were as obvious as a camera zooming on a shifty-eyed dog, ahem, which might have taken all the wind out of its sails were it not for a brilliant red herring leading up to the climax.
Overall, Broken Age is a joy to play, and I'm looking forward to Act II when it is released, which I suspect will have the opportunity to add a great deal of depth now that the stage has been properly set by the events in Act I.

First few sections of the game felt pretty solid, but the second half of the game in particular really seemed to drag on. Worse, bugs started cropping up more and more often. NPCs getting caught on objects mid-movement in combat causing the game to become stuck permanently, cutscenes playing off-screen, broken quests, typos in the dialog, redundant quest items wasting inventory space (mostly the rad suits - how many times is the same plot point going to be a major quest line?), fairly weak voice-acting (Matthias in particular), and just a slew of "little things."
There was never really any point where the game grabbed me, which was probably its biggest failing for me. There wasn't any story or dialog that blew me away, and the combat never grew into anything special. It just felt like they took what they did in the first game and made the safest possible sequel they could. I constantly had a feeling the developers saw what they had and said, "Eh, close enough" and called it a day. I can't even remember a point where any of the voice actors really raised their voice beyond speaking volume.
I'm sure patches will clear up a lot of the technical issues and typos, but the underlying problems are probably going to last.

This is not a very good game. The NPCs and their dialogue are boring and lack character, they're little more than placeholders to guide you to the next quest, which is unfortunate because Fallout 1 and 2 had such interesting NPCs and conversations.
There is no perk system. Attributes other than strength and intelligence are pretty pointless. Levelling isn't exciting since there's no reason to diversify your skillset, so you wind up dumping all of your skill points into one or two different skills.
There is WAY too much combat. In fact, this game is almost exclusively combat focused, in my time playing it is very rare to move the story forward without a lengthy combat sequence. While this isn't ideal, it'd be fine if the combat were at all interesting. There's a cover system, but it's hardly used and most combat takes place without being around any cover. There's no bonus to pincering an enemy, so there's not much point to moving around during combat. Gone is the Fallout system of targetting different body parts to cripple them, or make them drop their weapon, the only option you have now is to take a headshot for two extra AP at -50% chance to hit for 200% weapon damage (which is never worth doing since your chance to hit will never be above 95%). The jamming system has replaced the critical failure system. Now you can have a weapon that has a 1 in 10 chance to randomly jam up, wasting your turn.
Using skills is tedious. After combat you will want to heal your rangers, which requires using first aid. Each use of first aid requires watching a cross fill-up over 5 seconds, and most rangers require two first-aid packs to fully heal. With a party of 6, healing after battle requires about a minute of not being able to move around or do anything else in the game. Almost every loot container is locked or booby-trapped, oftentimes both, which requires watching some other animation that lasts 5 seconds to fill up. Waiting for animations to complete gets very tiring.
One of the strangest design choices was to have a rotating camera. The camera is VERY annoying, you'll frequently miss important items, people, and entrances and exits because your camera wasn't pointed the right way. Designing the levels from the ground up to have a fixed camera perspective would have made a lot more sense.
Lastly, the game just doesn't have much character. So far it's a lackluster wasteland without the zaniness, wonder, and humor of the classic Fallout games.
I hope they do a lot better with Torment...

A free game which is designed for mobiles and tablets.
It is enjoyable if you are the type of person that enjoys clicking repetively on rooms to collect power, food and water, which in turn slowly builds your bottle caps (money) allowing you to expand your base over time.
As per usual with these type of games, they make it relatively easy in the beginning so that you feel you've accomplished something, some form of base which you're happy with, just before the real slowness sinks in, and the possibility of your wallet feeling the weight of your growing lack of patience kicks in.
To speed the game up, which is another typical feature of mobile games, it has got a 'pay to win' system where you can buy additional lunch boxes to collect junk, food, water, power and those trusty bottle caps. Without these purchases you may experience boredom and even death due to the extremely slow and grindy nature of the game.
What's a couple of pounds/dollars here and there? Nothing until you realise you've lost track of how many small purchases you make and you end up living a real life desolate waste land experience in an alleyway out the back of Burger King.
I write this review from my friends couch, as I suffer paranoid flashbacks each time a bottle cap drops or a lunch box rattles.
I would recommend this to achievement hunters or people with bad computers, otherwise there are definitely better games to spend your time on.

Truthfully, I didn't know what to expect when I first got into Alan Wake.  It looked like your standard "point-flashlight and run" sort of horror game.  I was pleasantly surprised, however.  Here is my rundown:
Graphics:
I am getting this out of the way as quickly as possible.  The game looks absolutely stunning.  The atmosphere is great, and the lighting features are wonderful.  You instantly know where to go when you see lighting.  I loved how this game looked.
Gameplay:
Very unique.  Unveiling messages with the flashlight was a great idea.  Likewise, certain puzzles were done fantastically.  That being said, these unique ideas constantly were redone in some fashion or another to where it started to feel very overdone by the end of the game.  However, it was an enjoyable experience, even up to the end of the game.
Storyline:
Pretentious.  Very pretentious.  However, Alan Wake is a writer.  He will never let you forget that he is a writer, so the player shouldn't be surprised when the game has a very overly-artistic and dramatic feel to it.  It's annoying, at times, but not overtly so.
The game is great for what it is.  I'd highly recommend it for a playthrough.  You might find yourself getting tired of the repetition towards the end, but the payoff is very worth it.

This FPS is a mix between Counter-Strike mechanics and Call of Duty fast gameplay, wich makes this game pretty fun.
The game suffers of a lack of quality as it looks, but the final product can give you some hours of fun with friends and skirmishing alone.
It has microtransactions as it is a F2P, but the most noticeable difference wich makes this game pretty balanced is all the available weapons are usable for everyone when you first enter the game, giving you the opportunity to get them with In-Match currency that you earn by receiving frags and assists. That's right, weapons are earned by In-Match money, similar to Counter-Strike. The only thing purchable on the store are badges and masks for your character.
Gameplay is fast paced, aim mechanic is a mix between the Dynamic Croshair from CS and Aim-Down-Sights from CoD, wich makes this game pretty unique and fitting to all kind of FPS players. But, lacks of in-game tutorial, wich is simply a screen with all the button layout, wich for efortless players wanting to play the game right away is a bit overwhelming.
In conclusion, the game needs a bit more love by the developers and players, it's not a bad game, it's not horrible, it's not the best FPS but it's fun, playable and can run on Low-Class PC's. What more do you want? Give it a try and download it. You won't regret it!

You can go level and get your items up in singleplayer, learn the story about the game and  it is possibly a time spender. Each campaign mission are repeatable and can be done in 3 different difficulties where the rewards and difficulty increase. Pros:
+ Game that goes straight to the point by starting a tutorial when you start the game for the first time. (Steam only I guess, I wonder how I connect my account to my mobile app...)
+ Tells clearly in singleplayer campaign when you meet a new enemy with new abilities.
+ Automatic play button, let the AI play the fight for you.
+ Quaranteed elite character with random properties is under massive paywall of 100 euros.
+ Battle skills can only be used once in a fight. It's nothing major, but can turn the tide.
+ Starting characters have a good variety of skills, level them up to evolve them to get more item slots.
+ You can delete unwanted character you get and get boost that you can use to level up your favorites. However your fighters need a break at some point.
+ Fun animations and campaign story.
Cons:
- Battle girl doesn't have victory animation (Tumbles and straights then swings a sword to shoulder, while knight hurrays and mage plays gitarr with his staff).
- Repeating background music (You will turn it off at some point).
- Finding right items for your build is time consuming.
- Should have general tips so people could find some more options to manage their gameplay more casually.
- Fighters could have fighter types so people would realise if this fighter is focusing more into defense than damage, control or healing.

So far, I have enjoyed the first episode. Granted, I had a harder time understanding where to get the items I needed to progress on the girl's side of the story. The boy's side was easier for me, but that might be because I played his side after I finished with hers.
Both stories, however, are equally interesting plot-wise. They are both struggling with their surroundings, trying to step out of the "fate" that has been woven for them. The end of the episode was an interesting twist that left me wanting for more. I can't wait to see what happens to our protagonists, and what the consequences of their actions will turn out to be.

The game seemed very interesting at first. I like the art style, the animations and effects all seemed pretty cool. However, after an hour and some minutes into the game, it started to feel far too grindy and I would spend too long doing the same things with very little variation. It might just be the case that later into the game things got less grindy, but reading some reviews it led me to believe that they wouldn't. The game shows a lot of potential, however, it needs to tone down on the grind and increase variety. For the whole hour I spent with the game, I killed the same monters (2 types) and chopped the same resources, over and over.
I think this is the product of having only resources you can collect and monsters you can actually defeat near your "current level area". This means, since you need to gather that item or fight this monter, you'll see almost exclusively those types of elements as you progress through the tiers, creating a feeling of "too much of the same, over and over".
In short, I think the game is fun, but to me, too repetitive.

There should be a word that combines grind and slog so I can use it to describe Wasteland 2. In the before time, there was gaming, and whatever it was, we don't remember it now because in the intervening decade and some, we grew up and so did gaming. We learned that telling tales of "how hard game x was" to be far more entertaining than actually doing it. We learned how to design levels and create meaningful narratives and games that were fun to play, not just fun to have played. Oh, and we learned how to find voice actors. Wasteland 2 is probably faithful to its spiritual predecessor. I wouldn't know, because I wouldn't play that now either. The bones of a decent tactical rpg are there, but the level designs don't reward you for making use of them. Similarly, the bones of a good story rpg are there, but the disconcordant voices muddy the experience. Much like, "an arrow to the knee" cried out for a mod to stop, Wasteland 2 needs some serious fan love to be worth playing. Until the need to wander around the desert, grinding out raider encounters to level up is gone, I suggest you give this a pass and stick to New Vegas.

So I watched and waited eagerly, I played the early access, I tested every build. And I got exactly what I paid for in the end. This was a good throw back to the golden age of gaming, and I hope Wasteland 3 is more than a teaser.
Gameplay wise, the game starts off simple and ends simple, the combat can be challenging but after a bit of playing you'll get the hang of what works and what does not, you should expect to reroll probably once. The story may be a bit generic, but it's well told again and has a few curve balls I didn't expect so I was really pleased.
Now for a more detailed review of the mechanics in the game.
Combat.
Combat is done in turn based model gameplay, you have your tile grid for movement and what not and Action Points which dictate how much you can do per turn. This game does support min maxing in particular and punishes those who don't take the path of least resistance often in terms of combat.
Weapon choices are a bit iffy, after playing through the game having 1 energy weapon user was a core requirement, having more than one will definitely let you scale into the end game well.
-Sniper Rifles felt rather weak, they scaled all the time and their final weapon was impressive.
-Assault rifles are a great weapon all game long.
-Shotguns can be a massive game changer and scale well.
-SMGs start off ok, and end .. ok.
-Heavy weapons start off terrible and pretty much will be terrible until end game.
- Handguns are better than heavy weapons for some reason until very end game, where they die off almost entirely.
-Grenades and explosives work wonders all game long, and i suggest having 1 rocket launcher at all times for when things look grim.
-Weapon Modifications are critical. The biggest game changer is the ability to remove jamming early game and that can be more important than you'd ever imagine.
Anyway I can't go into more detail about Combat without spoiling the game entirely so I'll now jump onto the next part of the review, Stats and Skills!
--------------------------------
Stats
Coordination - The true dump stat in this game. Hilariously, a sniper doesn't even really need much. I had started the game with 4 and the action points every 2 points was not as impressive as the combined AP given from INT and STR. I dare say you could drop Coord to 1 on every ranger you start with and just use the bonus points for more INT to get the bonus ranged TCH from leveling skills faster.
Luck - A semi important stat, you only really need 1 really lucky guy, and he'll be the primary looter if you do. I'm unsure if it's true that luck makes a guy find better items, but when my lucky guy was looting I kept getting good loot. Also in the description it said it did affect loot so I dunno. I'd highly recommend this on a sniper, as that weapon is basically all about crit chance.
Awareness  - The second most important stat in the entire game, some will argue the most. This boosts your combat initiative, high enough and you can have a few turns in a row over some enemies. Golden rule, never have less than 4, and 6+ is recommended.
Strength - Strength is an important stat for looting, health and AP. It's recommended to have 3 at the minimum on most characters. If you ever see a character cappable of getting an extra AP from investing in STR, i'd recommend it.
Speed - Can be a dump stat, but it does affect combat movement and combat turn speed. Snipers generally won't need much speed at all because they can start fights and have other rangers shield them. But naturally Melee and Shotgun/ Smg users will want speed to close distances.
Intelligence - The most important stat in the entire game. I'd recommend 8 as a minimum on all your rangers that you create. Intelligence gives you AP and extra skill points, since this game is a VERY LARGE SKILL CHECK game having more SKILLS LEVELS is demanded of you. If you want to access all of the content in the game, loot pretty much everything or want to not suck in combat, you'll need a large sum of skill points and 8 int gives you 4 points, which is good for level by level skill ups. You can go as far as int 10 for 5 skill points, but 4 will be more than generous enough.
Charisma - Not a dump stat, jesus christ do not even try to dump this stat. Have at least 3 on every ranger for decent XP gain, I would recommend 1 dedicated ranger to having charisma 10 at some point due to the fact it synergies with LEADERSHIP, which is a game changing skill. Charisma also locks you out of content and some followers, so try to have decent sum to not be shunned by some of the  more interesting NPCs.
Now onto skills.
---------------------
This will be heavily generalized due to many skills falling under the same category.
Weapon skills - I'd recommend only investing in 1 tree of weapons for MOST rangers, definitely would suggest Shotguns or SMG dual classing for Heavy weapons and Energy weapon users, as they are better LATE game in comparison to EARLY.
Medical skills - There is no passive healing in this game. You will most of the time only need 1 medic, but you should have an additional surgeon in case your medic gets gunned down. I kept the most low level medical supplies for this purpose on all my rangers near end game.
Conversation Skills - Naturally keeps these as high as you can manage without compremising combat ability. They open up the world and give EXP rewards when executed.
Looting skills - Very important to maintaining your squads supply of explosives, ammo and new gear. Locking and Safe cracking can get you into certain locations elsewise locked off.
Hacking skills - VERY IMPORTANT. Hacking works on robotic enemies which turn them into allies for the combat duration, alarm disarm can be used to open electronic safes (so can computer science but eh.)
Repair - Not used often, but worth investing in having. They can repair your ♥♥♥♥ed up attempt at lock picking, and allow you a second shot. Generally worth it.
Explosives - Demolitions is super important if you don't want to die. Put it on the guy with the lowest charisma and he'll have a steady supply of bonus EXP to keep up.
Barter - Not an important stat. Very mild benefit, would recommend leveling a NPC follower for it if you want it.
Animal Whisper - Surpringly robust skill early game, dies out throughout the game but can make a lot of fights easier.
Perception - Super important. It helps you find secret loot, lets you see hidden traps. Definitely a must have.
Brute Force - Semi imporatnt. Early game it's kind of a very important skill for a few areas but end game I found it was more or less useless.
Weapon Smithing - Use this if you want to have not ♥♥♥♥♥♥ weapons. Seriously, it's god damn important.

Leadership - Only useful on a charisma ranger, Gives bonus TCH and lowers Rogue chances for NPCs (important.).  TCH bonus is massive.
----------
Onto the story portion, I won't say much. In fact very little at all. The game has many endings and has a good range of choices for you at any given point. The biggest warning I can give is, don't just click the buttons in the conversation list for no reason. There are some very deliberate negative tokens, even special text ones can set off some horrible misunderstanding / wrong intents.
-------------
Ending summary
This game is very recommended to those who enjoyed the old Wasteland 1 game and were fans of fallout 1 and 2. The game is challenging, at least it was for me on Ranger difficulty.
This game is NOT recommended for those who lack the ability to critically think. Seriously, it'll punish you.

If one's goal as a developer is to revive classical game mechanics, one has to be sure of actually improving upon them.  Wasteland 2 is ultimately a pale imitation.  The Unity engine powering WL2  performs poorly, looks bad, and is accompanied by fairly unimpressive audio throughout.  The crux of the game, combat, is unbalanced and uninteresting.  But for all its faults, is Wasteland 2 worth a play for true fans of the long-dormant genre?
A big part of making a believable wasteland lies in making sure the details standout.  With few exceptions, WL2 fails to create the visual and audio cues necessary toward really immersing the player.  Instead of supplementing the audio/visual presentation of an area, WL2 instead opts to incessantly hurl descriptive text.  What would have been a charming callback to games of yesteryear is instead used, endlessly, in an attempt to cover up lackluster design.  Environments and the denizens therein are hopelessly underdeveloped, with the biggest culprit being the severe lack of character portraits.  I've met no fewer than three distinct characters all using the exact same portrait.  In a game prided for its community support, surely the developers could have reached out to fans for some more variation.  Character models themselves are messy, blurry, blocky affairs complemented by unnatural animation.  But enough about presentation; true fans of Wasteland, Fallout et al would never disparage a game for not looking like it was developed by Crytek.
They would, however, disparage a game for playing poorly.  Right off the bat, player creation hammers the player with boundless stats whose longterm value is questionable at best.  How does .1 combat speed affect units?  How about +1 initiative?  What's the difference between selecting 4 intelligence and 5?  It is all too easy to hamstring oneself out the gate because the game does a remarkably poor job explaining all this.  The value of character skills runs the gamut, as well: after selecting a Mechanic skill for one of my units, I progressed through the game  almost never having been able to use it.  Why is lockpicking separate from safe cracking?  Why is alarm disarming separate from trap disarming?  Why can virtually any character, regardless of skill, use the supremely powerful (and rare) explosive weapons to perfect effect?  The skills screen tells me ammo for assault rifles and sniper rifles is more expensive than for handguns and submachine guns, and yet later on in the wastes the opposite holds true.  When the absolute basic mechanics at work in a game are flawed, the entire experience suffers for it.
Speaking of flawed mechanics, how about that combat?  In a word, it's broken.  There's a slew of weapon types from which to choose, but some end up being significantly stronger than others.  Player characters never have quite enough skill points to be godlike killing machines, and if you've chosen poorly, there's no way to get those points back.  For a great stretch of the game my party featured two melee characters, but the few weapons available to them put said characters at an enormous disadvantage.  The heavy armor you'd expect to pair with such combatants instead hampers their movement to such a degree that they may spend half the battle simpliy shuttling between enemies.  And the enemies?  In a game featuring up to seven player-controlled characters (Take that, X-Com!), competent AI is a must.  Unfortunately, and this is the absolute biggest thorn in WL2's side, the AI is consistently absent.  The tactical combat WL2 aims to deliver flies straight out the window from the outset.  When combat begins, rather than units flanking, sniping, crippling, and controlling one another to sweat-inducing effect over the course of several nail-biting turns filled with careful planning and deliberate execution (ala the recent X-Com game), it devolves into one amorphous blob of units colliding with another amorphous blob of units until one blob lies dead.  Mainstays of tactical combat such as cover systems, range limitations, flanking, unit position, fields of fire, suppression, crippling wounds, stealth, targeted shots, etcetera etcetera are either completely absent or barely qualify as being in infancy.  Without fail, combat begins with enemy units covering several screens worth of distance on the first turn to stand directly in front of my characters.  How such tragically broken combat (in a game filled to the brim with it) made it to release is beyond me.
So, the bottom line: is Wasteland 2 worth playing?  This is a tough.  On the one hand, as a gamer who grew up on Fallout, Jagged Alliance, Silent Storm and, yes, the original Wasteland, the prospect of an old-school video game renaissance thrills me.  The relative success in crowdfunding of Wasteland 2 and similar games proves I'm not alone in wanting
of its ilk.  Anything is better than nothing... right?  On the other hand, as somebody who puts Fallout 1 and 2 (and yes, even Tactics) up on a pedestal, looking past Wasteland 2's myriad faults becomes too difficult.  On its own, it may be an acceptable diversion.  But next to developer Brian Fargo's previous masterpieces, it simply doesn't hold a candle.  Significant patching and/or modding could remedy or obscure some of the more fundamental issues, but in its released state, I can't recommend Wasteland 2.

A brief warning up ahead - i have not yet finished the game nor am I entirely sure I am ever going to finish it.
Secondly this brief review only portrays my own personal opinion and therefore is not universal for all kinds of people and especially fans of the original Wasteland.
And on a final note I have not played Wasteland 1 so I can not speak to the connection between the two.
So now that we have all that out of the way here we go:
------------------------------------------------------------------
Wasteland 2 is a decent to good game but boy oh boy does it make me feel sad almost every step of the way. The two words most fitting Wasteland 2 at the moment are "wasted potential". So many of the mechanics are servicable and many things make you smile for a while but still there is that lingering feeling of squandered potential and the feeling that this game could have been so much more if given more time or more care.
Almost every aspect of the game is flawed in some major or (mostly) minor way, which accumilates to the above mentioned feel of dread at the unused potential of Wasteland 2.
Character creation seems vast at first but quickly desolves to bare bones customization. The lack of customization on a visual level is almost an insult to most games (even old classics). Characters can be depicted as drawn portraits (from a very limited and often reused pool of portraits) or by a 3D rendered model of your customized avatar that honestly looks kind of dreadful.
Which leads to the graphics, I mean don't get me wrong, I like Unity games and the Unity engine is a viable alternative to high priced alternative engines, but man does this game look ugly in places. It gets me kind of angry actually now that I write about it, because I see good art direction and interesting locations that are all sold short by the half baked graphics that look very unappealing and clunky from mid to close distances.
The camera is also god damn TERRIBLE. It obscures important items or dangerous traps which can in terms lead to your party walking in mines, cutting your adventure short.
This is especially sad since "IF" the game was designed isometrically it would have been completely unaffected by this problem but it had to be rendered in full 3D with a half baked camera pan that obscures something more or less important at almost any time.
But all could be well if besides the technical shortcomings there was the hyped up, vast and immersive gaming experience that was advertised and propagated by the media and other reviewers but *SPOILER* it isn't.
And this..this just hurts me the most. The game propagates that you have choices and a connection to the world around you but thats only kind of half true at best. The few choices you have ultimately lead to the same outcome and only shape your way to said outcome. And even worse all the locations remain stagnant and dull after you "complete" them.
So for example i saved Highport and with that, I doomed the AG Center which felt awful and shows a GLIMPSE of how good the game could have been. But this is just a one and only occurence in the grand scheme of things, there are no consequences to either choice, it just dissolves into person X telling you how you dommed your food or your water support in regards to which location you saved. Thats it. Really.
So Highport is save now but nothing happens there either. Vendors don't replenish. No new quests pop up. Dialogue is exhausted. Its practically as dead as it would have been if I did not save it. Basically I could delete the location and never return since there is nothing there for me to RETURN TO! It just serves as an replenish point for water while being sorrounded by two additional oasis' to replenish said water so...thanks..i guess.
The bright side is that combat is actually pretty fun. Weapons feel good and useful, visual impact of hits taking off legs and popping heads like watermelons is satisfying. But ultimately the combat system is pretty shallow, with few combat options (Headshot,kneel/stand/Fire Mode/Overwatch/Reload) and even fewer options for cover. Also the system seems fundamentally flawed in its design by providing evasion and bonus to hit even if your cover is flanked by an enemy or right besides the enemy itself.
The combat system is pretty much the only saving grace of Wasteland 2 and seperates it from being a bad game since you are going to fight A LOT and with that I mean literally almost EVERYTHING has to be resolved by shooting someone in the face with your revolver. The few places where you can negotiate or even talk to someone in the first place often lead to shooting someone else later anyway.
The writing is decent, not great but by no means bad. But it suffers beneath the stagnant nature of the game. Once you talked with someone you exhausted his dialogue and there is in the rarest of occasions a reason to come back and talk to him ever again.
One aspect that is not fun in the game in general is how it artifically ramps up the difficulty and punishes you for EXPLORING. Yes you read that correct, the game that boasts it lets you explore and make choices punishes you for doing so by stomping you into the ground by throwing almost impossible to defeat enemies in your way if you decide to go off the beaten and ultimately linear path of the game.
For example i managed to fight off the Raiders in the prison area of the game, which was not that easy to begin with but doable. A Raider has somewhere around 80-120 HP and does variable, but ultimately manageable damage. Then i explored and stumbled across a giant robot with 500+ HP that could literally jump right next to me and laser my entire team to death, but hey it's just one right? I surely can overcome this "challenge"? Nope. Three of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s magically jump besides me and stomp me into fine dust.
And that is just an example of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t the game can throw in your direction and that is not mentioning the randomnes of the combat itself with weapons with literally two percent chance of jamming, jamming 5 times in a row, or shots with 99% accuracy missing their mark in several occasions, which seems to corelate to bugs inside the system if the patch notes are to be examined.
All in all it's by no means a bad game, but it's not nearly as good as it could have been nor is it as good as people make it out to be.
It is great fun at places and even creates great moments of simple joy as you find a small amount of ammo for your favorite weapon or find a hidden cache and stock up on valuable grenades.
But ultimately it is pretty shallow in many places where it boasts it would not be shallow. The game could have used a lot more time and effort for sure allthough I appreciate the initiative to bring back old CRPGs and their style of gameplay, but that does not justify the many shortcomings of this game.
6/10
Buy it if you are a hardcore fan of CRPGs or Wasteland. Everyone else should wait untils it goes on sale for 50%-75%

Hello, here is my little Wasteland 2 review.
The game is a turn based squad based tactical game with roleplaying elements. It plays in Arizona and LA after an nuclear&chemical apocalypse. So you will have to deal with Raiders, Bandits, giant animals, killer nuns, robots, cyborgs and other stuff.
The production value and grafic quality is abysmal. The character models look atrocious, the level maps are bland and uninspired with next to unique landscapes to discover.
The combat system has not many options to it. You have 2 skills to use in battle. Crouch and headshot. Your combat performance is calculated by your attributes, ranged weapons coordination, melee weapon strength. Your action points are calculated by speed, coordination and intelligence. Your weapon skill in blunt w, bladed w, smg, hand gun, energy weapon, assault rifle, heavy w increase your hitrate. When maxing your preffered weapon skill you can't improve your character anymore. The only thing to do are distributing attribute points. You get 1 for every ten level extra to spent. Now that is not really very exciting. You have no special skills beside animal whisperer and computer science to use in battle. those are used to hack robot or befriend animals to fight a short period of time on your side.
Combat AI: All battles play the same, the AI enemies rush into maxrange or into melee range and start shooting hitting your characters. You do the same. I found no unique encounters beside one battle against tinker the cyborg in Damonta. The only thing you do there is hack some terminals before combat to safe a girl from dying. The AI melee fighter can run all the battle map to your characters in one turn. They can bypass your melee front fighters and attack your ranged characters. You can not block them, tackle them, stun them to help your ranged out. The only thing is to take them out really quick with all of your characters shooting them.
The level design is really simplistic. The maps feel boring and bland. The only thing to explore are containers squattered over the map. For these containers you need your 5 "roleplaying" skills, lock pick, safe knacking, demolition, computer science and brute force to open them. The loot inside the containers is randomized. Most of the time you only get some ammunition or random vendor junk stuff to sell out of them.
The social interaction with npc in the world is rather simplistic too. You have 3 social skills smart♥♥♥♥♥ kiss♥♥♥♥♥and hard♥♥♥♥♥to manipulate npcs with predefined keywords, but only the first time you see the keywords. When you close the social interaction screen the unused manipulation keywords just disappear.
Crafting: Weapon smithing is the crafting in this game. When your weapon smithing skill is high enough you can disassemble weapons into different kind of things, a high chance for weapon parts and a lower chance for weapon improvements like a barrel, a new magazin or a scope. Weapon parts can be sold at ranger citadell. You can not use all enhancements items on all weapons.  That is as simple as a crafting system can get.
The story is mediocre at best. Some unkown individuals make threats over radio. Your boss Vargas is scared. So your job in the first part of the game is to install 3 radio repeaters on radio antennas to triangulate the signals origin. You do so traveling to 5 locations on the Arizona map. Then you fly to LA and have to establish a base and do some good things so the people of LA recognize the Desert Rangers as the new power in the area. I call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t about the upholding the Law, when all you do is shooting people who do not live according to your morale standarts. In LA you help or destroy some locations or factions and then go off to fight the big baddies in the game.
Fun stuff are the radio messages from the different faction leaders. They comment on your behaviour directly after the event. They make propaganda against other factions and the desert rangers over the radio.
Another thing are the different factions. They are not new or unique but have all a different flavor to them. The red scorpions in arizona are just bandits in red uniforms, with a dogloving commander. The Children of the mushroom cloud ♥♥♥♥♥ship an atomic bomb. The church of hammer wants to kill everyone in the world because they are all sinners. The Mannerites want to kill all people that are impolite or unclean. Mathias and his cyborgs want to transcend into artifical humans. The robot Durgan wants to eleminate all fleshbags.
I have to force myself to play the game. 90% of the game is combat, and that is so mindnumbling simplistic and boring that i can only bear it for an hour.
The game is only for people who really like postapoclyptic games and are resistant to the boring combat system. You will have to read one or two pages of text too. If you do not mind the simple gameplay mechanics, boring combat and simple level design you will have the game of your dreams. But don't come back to me, i did try to warn you.
Have a nice day.

Truthfully, I didn't know what to expect when I first got into Alan Wake.  It looked like your standard "point-flashlight and run" sort of horror game.  I was pleasantly surprised, however.  Here is my rundown:
Graphics:
I am getting this out of the way as quickly as possible.  The game looks absolutely stunning.  The atmosphere is great, and the lighting features are wonderful.  You instantly know where to go when you see lighting.  I loved how this game looked.
Gameplay:
Very unique.  Unveiling messages with the flashlight was a great idea.  Likewise, certain puzzles were done fantastically.  That being said, these unique ideas constantly were redone in some fashion or another to where it started to feel very overdone by the end of the game.  However, it was an enjoyable experience, even up to the end of the game.
Storyline:
Pretentious.  Very pretentious.  However, Alan Wake is a writer.  He will never let you forget that he is a writer, so the player shouldn't be surprised when the game has a very overly-artistic and dramatic feel to it.  It's annoying, at times, but not overtly so.
The game is great for what it is.  I'd highly recommend it for a playthrough.  You might find yourself getting tired of the repetition towards the end, but the payoff is very worth it.

Episode One - From the beginning, this game certainly leaves an unsettled feeling with you, and as far as episodic play goes, it cuts out at the right moment.  The gameplay was pretty straightforward, but the "boss" at the end did make things a bit challenging.  The dream nature of the game leaves the player with a lack of control, which may be an appealing concept to some, but I suppose isn't something that draws me to video games.  If I wanted to feel like I was only observing, I would have watched a movie.
Episode Two - The gameplay didn't change much with this episode, though the story telling took the front seat in more ways than one.  The vehicle segment toward the end is something to look forward to, and had some of the most accurate driving controls I've seen in a while.  The birds fight at the end, was frustrating and underwhelming when complete, but the cinematic at the end was a nice cliffhanger ending, and did encourage the player to keep playing.
While I found myself drawn in by the story of this game, the drawn out segments of stumbling through the dark did not create much of a draw for me to keep playing.  I was honestly expecting more of an adventure game, and not really a survival horror game.  Perhaps this expectation has created some of the disappointment for me.  Unfortunately, the repetitive nature of the enemies, and consistently dark tone of the game did not create a world that I wanted to return to explore past Episode Two.

Shadow of War's predecessor, Shadow of Mordor, was a great open-world action game that came out of left field.  Its Game of the Year edition is an easy recommendation to anyone new to the series at $20.  Shadow of War offers a few minor improvements, including some passable new story missions and several excellent new settings.  However, the main direction that they chose to expand the game was with a "fortress siege" system, which primarily involves grinding to add captains to your army and then performing the same attack and defend missions over and over again.  It was obviously developed in an attempt to sell additional loot boxes for real money - taking a page out of the book of predatory mobile game monitization schemes.  It's a shame to see a series with such potential run into the ground by a greedy corporate publisher.  It also still suffers from many of the original game's shortcomings. The storyline progressions feels odd and disjointed.  A few characters and orc designs are interesting, but most characters feel one-dimensional and sometimes cringeworthy.

This is one of those games that has an alright idea (take weapons and characters similar to Counter Strike and merge it with Call of Duty-esque gameplay) but it struggles a lot due to the bugs and the quality of the game over all. I have a lot of issues with connecting to servers and most of the time I get audio errors which cause all my sound in game to be delayed.
The core mechanics of the game could use a lot of work as well. The price of some of the guns are very steep compared to how much you earn per kill, enough so that if you want one of the better sniper rifles you will be running around most of the game with a pistol trying to kill people with AK's and shotguns just to try and afford it. However some of the most powerful weapons are priced extremely cheap. The Spas hits like and absolute truck (argubly overpowered, you can snipe with it) and you can buy it as soon as you get in the game. The price of some of the guns also causes you to be stuck with whatever gun you buy the entire game.
The movement feels very floaty and you never really feel like your character is touching the floor as well as the aiming just feels off at times. Characters often bug out and will run through walls or completely disappear. What I have ran into a lot has been seeing enemies who appear to just be running, they are not aiming at me at all and don't appear to be looking at me, just to have my character randomly die from them.
There are a ton of bugs in this game at the moment and it really feels borderline unplayable. However with that being said the game is in early access and it's clear to see what the developers are trying to do with the game. There are a lot of small things in this game that I think they're doing well. It's a simple design, the game doesnt feel cluttered and over complicated. The idea of a kind of CS meets CoD type FPS is intriguing and one that I think could be executed well with the right team behind it. I'm going to recommend this game even with it's faults under the assumption that the developers really put the time in to cleaning the game up and improving on it, It's very rough around the edges right now but the potential for a really fun game is here.

I have been giving this game a try and the result is this is absolutely Pay to Win, in the second region of the Campaign with several levels ahead of the monsters, I can barely make it thru, its absolutely Brutal. Considering you can pay to buy gems to buy random boxes for gears, chars and battle boosts... well that says it all, its a Pay to Win game, where if you don't pay or get unspeakably lucky, you won't be able to progress in either online or offline, because the enemies in the Campaign are OP and the only players to progress to the higher tiers of the Arena are payers.
Now I know people will say you can win gems and thus buy some of those boxes... you win a gem or a couple per first wins in the Campaign at each of the 3 difficulties, and the match I did fight in the Arena I won 1, otherwise you get a few by completing achievements, the char box cost 200 gems, and the gear box cost 25 for a cheap one and 200 for a good one... and all of it a random boxes, so obviously you have low chances of getting anything descent and high chances of getting crap, you can't buy any chars or gear outside of those boxes which basically bind progress in large part to how much $ you are willing to throw at the game. So this game is going to quickly go nowhere for any Free Players, and considering I know how much those random box crap work from other games that all embraced that crappy gimmick, Payers are still likely to have to pay several hundreds of $ to get anything good.
Also said gear not only you again need to get lucky to get the good stuff, but also once equipped you can't unequip it without paying gems and if you don't know that and you try to replace the gear, it delete the one you used to have equipped... nice to learn wasting a blue 1 star item because they didn't say anything about that, considering again how rare those bleeding gems are... it would cost 50 gems to unequip a blue 2 star item from one of my char... which is twice the price of rolling the cheap random box... or a quarter of rolling for a char or good random box... how nice.
Also if your chars die you can either pay with those rare gems to revive them in battle, for 25 gems for all if all your chars died and to continue said battle, or after battle for a couple of gems each, unless you go back to your Barracks and pay gold... which while better if you got 2 chars killed you can say goodbye to quite a cut of your gold earned in that mission.
