Hello, here is my little Wasteland 2 review.
The game is a turn based squad based tactical game with roleplaying elements. It plays in Arizona and LA after an nuclear&chemical apocalypse. So you will have to deal with Raiders, Bandits, giant animals, killer nuns, robots, cyborgs and other stuff.
The production value and grafic quality is abysmal. The character models look atrocious, the level maps are bland and uninspired with next to unique landscapes to discover.
The combat system has not many options to it. You have 2 skills to use in battle. Crouch and headshot. Your combat performance is calculated by your attributes, ranged weapons coordination, melee weapon strength. Your action points are calculated by speed, coordination and intelligence. Your weapon skill in blunt w, bladed w, smg, hand gun, energy weapon, assault rifle, heavy w increase your hitrate. When maxing your preffered weapon skill you can't improve your character anymore. The only thing to do are distributing attribute points. You get 1 for every ten level extra to spent. Now that is not really very exciting. You have no special skills beside animal whisperer and computer science to use in battle. those are used to hack robot or befriend animals to fight a short period of time on your side.
Combat AI: All battles play the same, the AI enemies rush into maxrange or into melee range and start shooting hitting your characters. You do the same. I found no unique encounters beside one battle against tinker the cyborg in Damonta. The only thing you do there is hack some terminals before combat to safe a girl from dying. The AI melee fighter can run all the battle map to your characters in one turn. They can bypass your melee front fighters and attack your ranged characters. You can not block them, tackle them, stun them to help your ranged out. The only thing is to take them out really quick with all of your characters shooting them.
The level design is really simplistic. The maps feel boring and bland. The only thing to explore are containers squattered over the map. For these containers you need your 5 "roleplaying" skills, lock pick, safe knacking, demolition, computer science and brute force to open them. The loot inside the containers is randomized. Most of the time you only get some ammunition or random vendor junk stuff to sell out of them.
The social interaction with npc in the world is rather simplistic too. You have 3 social skills smart♥♥♥♥♥ kiss♥♥♥♥♥and hard♥♥♥♥♥to manipulate npcs with predefined keywords, but only the first time you see the keywords. When you close the social interaction screen the unused manipulation keywords just disappear.
Crafting: Weapon smithing is the crafting in this game. When your weapon smithing skill is high enough you can disassemble weapons into different kind of things, a high chance for weapon parts and a lower chance for weapon improvements like a barrel, a new magazin or a scope. Weapon parts can be sold at ranger citadell. You can not use all enhancements items on all weapons.  That is as simple as a crafting system can get.
The story is mediocre at best. Some unkown individuals make threats over radio. Your boss Vargas is scared. So your job in the first part of the game is to install 3 radio repeaters on radio antennas to triangulate the signals origin. You do so traveling to 5 locations on the Arizona map. Then you fly to LA and have to establish a base and do some good things so the people of LA recognize the Desert Rangers as the new power in the area. I call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t about the upholding the Law, when all you do is shooting people who do not live according to your morale standarts. In LA you help or destroy some locations or factions and then go off to fight the big baddies in the game.
Fun stuff are the radio messages from the different faction leaders. They comment on your behaviour directly after the event. They make propaganda against other factions and the desert rangers over the radio.
Another thing are the different factions. They are not new or unique but have all a different flavor to them. The red scorpions in arizona are just bandits in red uniforms, with a dogloving commander. The Children of the mushroom cloud ♥♥♥♥♥ship an atomic bomb. The church of hammer wants to kill everyone in the world because they are all sinners. The Mannerites want to kill all people that are impolite or unclean. Mathias and his cyborgs want to transcend into artifical humans. The robot Durgan wants to eleminate all fleshbags.
I have to force myself to play the game. 90% of the game is combat, and that is so mindnumbling simplistic and boring that i can only bear it for an hour.
The game is only for people who really like postapoclyptic games and are resistant to the boring combat system. You will have to read one or two pages of text too. If you do not mind the simple gameplay mechanics, boring combat and simple level design you will have the game of your dreams. But don't come back to me, i did try to warn you.
Have a nice day.

Crashlands rocks.
I tested this for around 60 hours before release and can say that the game delivers on it's promise.  The sorta isometric view seems to make everyone mention Don't Starve (damn it.  I just did it.) I see it.  Crafting, weird creatures, item drops, etc...  It's all there.  But the games are very different.  Don't Starve is a grim bizarre survival game that will murder you often as you discover your randomly generated tale.  Crashlands has a scripted story that pulls you through the colorful, randomly generated terrain of three biomes as a super powered interplanetary delivery person. The whole "kill, pick up drops, craft materials, become more badass" loop is super tight. I've spent way too many late nights scouring the savannah for one more essence to give me one more shot at making an epic weapon.  There is some dark compulsive magic at work here.
The actual combat is interesting because it works well on a tablet or on a PC, and it seems right at home on both devices.  That's cool.  The pc feels comfortable in the whole Torchlight/Diablo format and the approach works well on tablets as well, which I found really surprising.
Crafting is super with the infinite no-fuss-no-muss-none-of-this-stupid-encumberment system.   The Butterscotch Shenanighans crafting slot machine is one of the games best features, and finally getting a great weapon or embiggening a pet is super satisfying.
I love games with pets, and the whole raising, fighting and embiggening of pets is a great addtion.  Pro tip:  If you're as terrible as I am, you can make your pets pretty powerful and let them do most of the work.
The story is funny and warped and weird and emotional and exciting.  If for some reason you don't like having fun, ignore the story and get back to hitting things really hard.  The game won't penalize you.  If laughing hurts your soul, the gameplay will pull you through.
This is a really good game.  Just buy it.

Pros:
- Good writing. It's believable, the people act like they realistically would. There's good attention to detail; for instance, if you recruit a companion and bring them to someone else they'd know and ask them about said companion, the person will acknowledge their presence and say 'Uh, dude, I'm not gonna talk about them when they're right here.' It may not seem like much, but little things like that really add to the immersion. The writers put a lot of thought into what they were doing.
The dialogue system is functional, and I really like that they added the ability to type in your own keywords which harkens back to Fallout 1 and allows you to discover hidden dialogue, rewarding players paying close attention. Unfortunately, this is used far too infrequently and I've only discovered a few hidden dialogue options with it. Granted, one of those was very significant and completely changed the outcome of an important quest.
- Good combat. Not amazing, but solid. Like most aspects of the game, it's similar to Fallout 1 and 2's combat with action points used to shoot, swing with melee weapons, move squares and reload. In theory it's much more simplistic, because you can't target individual body parts. But in reality, you only ever went for eye shots and chest shots in Fallout 1 and 2... just like in this game where the options are headshots or regular shots. It has just the right amount of tactical depth, I'd say - any more with the amount of combat this game has and the size of the party you have would siginificantly add to the tedium.
Difficulty wise, I'd say it's close to right - I've been playing on Ranger which is the 2nd hardest, and it's been a bit too easy but not easy enough for me to want to increase it further. Some fights have been very challenging, party members having to be revived is common.
- Good map design. The maps in this game are huge and wide open with many nooks and crannies to explore. In comparison to many other modern RPGs like Shadowrun: Returns it's incredible how large and open this game feels; it's very easy to miss things, making subsequent playthroughs more rewarding.
- Good interface and options. There are a variety of 'quality of life' changes over classic RPGs to reduce tedium. For instance, when you loot a corpse it doesn't just loot the individual corpse any more. Instead, it will loot all corpses in the general area saving you the hassle of walking to and looting each of them. When you sell items to vendors, you can click the 'sell all junk' button. The inventory could be better however. There are things called 'trinkets' that you can equip to give you small bonuses such as +3% critical hit chance, but their icons look very similar to junk items so you often have to spend time mousing over each item to find items to equip. Similarly, there are books that increase certain skills, but they can easily be confused with lore books you pick up that exist solely for you to read backround information and stories. Items should've had a border colour based on their item type, you should've been able to search your inventory and there should have been more filters.
Cons:
- Lack of skill checks. In games like Fallout 1 and 2, Planescape: Torment and so on you'll see skill checks depending on how you built your character. For example, you might be exploring a town and find a farmer's crop field. Your character has an extensive knowledge of science, so a skill check like this might appear: [Science] "Your farming method is inefficient. Let me explain crop rotation to you." Things like that, in my opinion, greatly enhance the role playing experience and add importance to the way you built your character. In Wasteland 2, the only ones that matter for dialogue are three skills: Smart♥♥♥♥♥ Kiss♥♥♥♥♥and Hard♥♥♥♥♥ simplifying the process considerably. It's much less engaging and too simplistic.
- Bad quest design. Not all of them, but most are very simple and only have one solution. You enter a town and someone needs your help to become mayor. So, can you side with the other mayoral candidate and help him instead? No. Can you at least choose the way you go about helping the other person become mayor?  Can you bribe the people into voting or threaten them, etc? No, you simply have to complete all the quests in the area. Also, tying into the criticism directly above, your skills (almost?) never play a role in completing quests: you find a guy who is a huge fan of energy weapons. You have a maxed out Energy Weapons skill, so can you impress him with that and get him to do what you want to do because of it? No, as your character's skills are never relevant in that way. Attributes are VERY rarely useful outside of combat, with Awareness and Charisma very rarely granting you more dialogue.
I found many other issues of varying severity. Many times where you'll accidentally skip ahead to a later stage of a quest by accident and the NPCs don't acknowledge it at all, times when quests are abruptly cancelled for no reason as the developers decided to arbitrarily set a point where they were no longer completable, stuff like that.
- Somewhat bad skill/attribute system. So you create a big ol' brute with 10 Strength. You come across a merchant who has gotten his cart stuck. You move it out of the way with ease, right? No, it's tied directly to your Brute Force skill and doesn't interact with Strength at all. In my opinion skills like Brute Force and Perception should be tied directly to your attributes - instead of being a 12% chance to move the cart with Brute Force level 1, it should be calculated as Brute Force lvl * 1/2 of Strength or something. Again, I feel like this adds to your character creation and makes for a better, more believable role playing experience.
- Bad balance. Melee characters are blatantly terrible in comparison to ranged characters. Not only do they have the disadvantage of having to get up close making them vulnerable and out in the open, but the actual damage of melee weapons usually pales in comparison to their ranged counterparts, which is unforgivable. For putting up with the inherent disadvantages of melee, they should do MORE damage than ranged weapons. They do generally use less AP, but even taking that into consideration the overall damage is still far too low. Shotguns suffer similar issues, as do pistols to a lesser extent.
- The game rewards save scumming. With the skill Lock Picking, for instance, instead of having a system where with level 1 you can open level 1 locks, with level 2 you can open level 1 and 2 locks and so on, it instead has a system where with 1 point you can open level 1 locks with a very high chance, level 2 locks with a medium chance, level 3 locks with a low chance, and level 4 locks with a very low chance or something to that effect. This greatly encourages you to put in 'value points' - just enough points to have a chance at opening the current level of object you're coming across currently. This is made worse by the fact that you don't have to immediately spend points when levelling up and can hoard them for when you need them.
- The world lacks believability to some extent. Endless chests and safes are scattered around the wasteland. Good weapons are far too easy to come by; you'll be stocked up on all kinds of high tech gear within the first 30 minutes. It doesn't feel like you're surviving in a post apocalyptic world a lot of the time. Also, screw boobytraps - they're everywhere!
Overall, though I've been quite negative in this review, I really like the game and I feel that the good outweighs the bad by a large margin. Wasteland 2 is a worthy successor to Fallout 2 (I can't speak for the original Wasteland) and is the best RPG in quite a few years. If you have any interest in classic CRPGs then you owe it to yourself to at least try this game. Here's hoping that InXile iron out the creases and make a truly amazing game next time.

I can't believe it. For once in years, a triple A title is actually packed with content and things to do.
Many complain about the microtransactions and I fully agree, they're absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s for putting that in. I'm 100% sure they're doing this to pacify us and make releasing singleplayer microtransactions the norm.
HOWEVER
I cannot ignore the fact that the developers really put their soul into the game. It really doesn't hold your hand like the Assassin's Creed games. It's truly a difficult game but it can be overcome with some wit. Unlike the AC games, the combat is amazing. You get a bunch of skills that are reminiscent of the first Fable game in 2005. There are so many unique skills that are unlike each other and each one gives you an advantage but not enough to make you overpowered.
Also unlike the AC games, the parkour mechanics are horrid. Often clunky and unresponsive on mouse and keyboard, I find it difficult to steer Talion to where I want him to go. I normally had no problems with this in Assassin's Creed. It's also difficult to target which enemy you want to use your dominate ability on (turning them into your soldier). This often lead to me dying as I wasted time charging up the ability on the wrong person only to be attacked from the back.
Story-wise, I won't lie, it's hard to follow. I'm not an avid Lord of The Rings fan and I can't quite wrap my head around the universe. All I know is the 'bad guy' took something and we have to get it back through conquering territory. That's the gist of it.
Speaking of conquering, let's talk about the war system. Each region has a fortress that you ultimately want to lay siege to and take. To properly do this, you will need orcish companions that work for you through defeating them in battle. I fell in love with this system because each orc is truly unique. Each one has their own personality, voice, and lingo. I've played almost 20 hours so far and I haven't experienced repeat dialogue with an orc.
Keep in mind: the amount of orcs you can conquer is literally unlimited. This means there is an unlimited variety of personalities out there (and that you can't capture them all as I made the mistake of trying to do during my first 5 hours of play).
Was this game worth 80 bucks Canadian? Hell yes. I believe this is the game of the year.
Is the loot crates in-game worth paying for? Hell no. Steer clear of that garbage. You can fully experience the game without having to do so. Paying for their loot crates is telling them you like having microtransactions in a single-player experience.
I give this game a 9/10.
It lost the 1/10 for all the issues I outlined in this review. If they can make parkour and combat less clunky/frustrating, I would give it a solid 10/10. It doesn't feel like they cut out content to make way for DLC.

Understand first and foremost that this is a niche simulation.  If you have no interest in large industrial trucks, off roading, and a little vehicle management then this is not the game for you.  While the screen shots and trailer show you all of that goodness, they dont show you the subtle complexity of the maps.  Think of this like a game of Klotski, the block puzzle game where you have to slide varying shaped and sized blocks inside a rectangle to get a colored block out of the rectangle.  The trucks are the regular blocks, you move them around the map to get the colored block (lumber) to the objective.  It sounds easy, but if you have played the block game then you know that sometimes it takes many moves to win.  You will have to set up your trucks with right attachments at the garage, and position them on the map accordingly, so that you can move the lumber.  The devs have made every map unique, from swollen deep rivers to little paths through the hills to highways of mud, there will be obstacles all along the way.  Count yourself lucky if you find a paved road, it saves you fuel and damage to your truck.  Those are two factors that have to constantly be managed.  After a while you start finding yourself considering every turn and path to see how not to get stuck axel deep in a quagmire.  So there are two levels of complexity, simply navigating your vehicle, and the working the vehicles in concert.  Keep in mind that nothing about the gameplay is fast.

UPDATE:
Sound/Music:
Great soundtrack with some of the best songs from the 60s. The radio, including the custom DJ lines is only adding to the overall 60s athmosphere.
Gameplay:
Gameplay is quite repetitive. There are towers analogies (Junction Boxes) and multiple resources/collectibles that takes a lot of time to be collected.
Many times player will need to clear up the same place twice. More times if they already by chance decided to clear it off the mission.
There is a lot of mindless driving just for the sake of driving from one part of town to another (e.g. get from the mission starter to the contraband boat). Nothing interesting happens during these drives at all.
I like the stealth mechanics. It is fun to clear out the enemies one by one by just luring them away.
Shooting is not so fun. Enemies are not very smart and their actions are very predictable.
The "ablities" (moving armory, reinforcements, etc.) are interesting addition to the gameplay. Though I've found myself constantly saving them for later (not the free ones).
Graphics:
The main consern. 30 fps lock on launch (fixed now) is unacceptable for PC.
The textures are blurry. The lighting is buggy. The overall optimisation is just bad.
I'm getting 60fps on maxed out graphics (1080p), but the game doesn't look good at all.
Plot:
Pretty simple revenge plot. Nothing fancy. I wouldn't say that it is too far from the Mafia 2. But it is definitely not on the level of the original Mafia.
Suggestions:
1. I feel that the game should reward player for actions. For example if the place has already been cleared out off the mission, the objective should be completed when the mission is received. No need to do it one more time.
2. Resources can be placed in more convenient places, so the player would be close during the mission.
3. Instead of driving to get the mission, in some cases simple radio communication would be enough or a taxi service would be nice.
4. When the racket income is maxed out, the mission giver can say that no more trucks/boats are needed at this time. Otherwise it is confusing.
5. Give Lincoln the ability to climb non horizontal surfaces (e.g. railing on the stairs).
6. Optimize the graphics. More clear textures.
OLD:
Real console experience.
30 fps lock and bad graphics (even maxed out) just makes it. Developer really needs to step up and fix it.
This is unacceptable for a game of this level.

So far the story is amazing! I mention the story first because that's the entire reason I purchased the game and it does not disappoint. I couldn't care less about FPS, as long as it's at least 30, the FPS patch will be nice, but it's really of no concern to me. I, fortunately have not had any crashes with everything on high. Now... back to the story; it's gritty, raw, and realistic. It feels like you're actually the south of the United States in the year 1968. Lincoln Clay, the main character, is vicious, brutal, and honestly, I don't like him, but that only makes me love the game even more. Who says a main character has to be likeable or redeemable? That is completely unrealistic, and I praise Hangar 13 (the developers) for making the provocative choice. There is nothing politically correct about this game, and it's a credit to the developers bravery to really tell it like it was for a black man, in the Deep South,  in the late 60's, after returning from
Vietnam. Thank you Hangar 13 and 2K! I will be updating my review as I play more.

I have put about 80+ hours into this game before its steam release and I have to say it's fantastic. I haven't bought all the cars yet but the four I have (MK2, S13, GT86 and of course the Hachi-Roku) are all different in their handling and drift style/physics.
There are three main game modes
A quick race mode where you can select your track and if the other players are same the league (license) or free for all (no limits on league or car spec) and one for cars of similar spec. This is where you get your rating up, to gain higher leagues/licenses (you also earn money and experience)
Then there is the global championship where you bring your own ride to the party. The course for the championship changes each day and there is a ranking system where the top 5 each day win credits. (I have managed a 4th and a 5th in my time in game so far woot hehe)
Also there are daily events which give you a predefined tuned car (that you can't tune or fiddle with yourself so we are all on an equal playing field bar skill) so you do get to try a lot of the cars before buying them. There is also a ranking system in this mode where the top 5 get credits too.
You don't earn rating points in the championship and event modes but you do make good money and experience.
And there is a practice mode for getting your tuning sorted and learning tracks or trying new lines.
The livery system is good and there is a nice selection of body kits (for non premium cars), spoilers, exhausts, rims and paint options.
The tuning system is top notch and very tweak able.
The game itself runs fantastically on my system (i7 950, 12gb ram, gtx970) at 2560x1440 DSR, max settings and AA, with the only issue being stupid high frame rate when loading the game and maps that leads to coil whine. (vsync or frame limiting fixes that though)
The only bad I can come up with is that all the car models aren't in game yet and the multiplayer isn't yet proper PvP. But these are coming so I'm not to fussed about it.
All in all if you like drifting this game is bloody awesome. It has even pulled me away from The Crew Wild Run which is quite a feat, well done guys!!.

Phenomenal. This is what happens when you let talent of the likes of Brian Fargo and his dream team of writers and designers (and Mark Morgan) create the game they wish to make: a love letter to classic CRPGs full of rich descriptive text and atmosphere, amazing depth in options, laugh out loud ridiculousness, and several truly chilling moments. In an age of gaming where we've grown tired of pressing the win button, Wasteland 2 throws hundreds of possibilities in your direction and doesn't even pretend to try to hold your hand, allowing you the joy of discovery and surprise as your decisions often leave no clear cut winners.
You'll often find yourself under-equipped and struggling to keep your party members alive, tossing those last few rounds of ammo to a teammate and praying for their 35% hit probability to go your way after enemies have left you devastated. And right when you think you've gotten the hang of things, new scenarios will put you firmly back in your place.
Wasteland 2 is a shining beacon of what games once were, and a sensational example of what they very well can be today when the fans - and not profits - come first.

Okay...I watched all the preview videos-just like you I thought, "What a silly game."  I moved on without a second thought.  After becoming ever frustrated with hours of playing games Elite Dangerous, I thought, "maybe I NEED some silly."  I bought it.  I did the responsible thing and did the stock tutorial, you know, "How To Blah-blah-blah".  Got on the launchpad and lifted off.  Holy Crap!!!!!  Son.  This ain't your Dad's Oldsmobile!!
First off, the sound is bang on.  The whistle of the air as its passing over the airframe, mixed with the slight camera shake as the engine thunders...the sudden silent whistle as the air returns.  The first stage has flamed out.  Separation.  POW.  A kick in the pants! PHWOOOSH as the next engine ignites.  Vapour trails stream over the airframe as you stab through the dense atmosphere, too fast everything turns red and blowtorch flames.  Damn, too fast!  Throttle back and finally...stars, blackness of space, peace, tranquility.
Yeah, you can say i'm hooked.  The launch is just the outer skin of this onion, and yes, you have to master it.  Once out in space you deal with true Newtonian physics that make shows like Star Wars and Star Trek laughable as there are no straight lines in space-you'll see.  In fact you will be amazed just how much you can learn of Orbital Mechanics, Thrust-to-Weight ratios, Celestial Navigation and have fun doing it.  There is a huge following of this Indie jewel, we are talking engineers who are calculating Delta -V's (speed and directional changes) using the same rocketry calculations as NASA.  And there are those , like myself who just enjoy the esoteric experience and let the game mechanics do all the work.
I have gamed for over twenty years, and nothing matched the sheer gratification I felt on my first successful moon landing or after a nail biting rendezvous and docking.  The game has missions or sandbox where you can just go out and do.  Myself, I need goals, so I play on career mode- a parallel to the NASA program relying on reputation, funding, and cost control; where you start from getting a man to orbit then finally to the moon...oh yeah, and back!
In short, if you pass up this game--you are passing up a lot!
Cheers fellow Steamers and Gamers alike!

This game isn't so much 'wasteland' as 'wasted opportunity'.
Where Fallout/F2/FTactics were self-explanatory in regards to mechanics and tactics, this game mistakes 'complexity' for 'depth'.
I play tactical turn-based (TTB) for the pleasure of planning and setting up effective ambushes and assaults and despatching enemies efficiently. It is this element that is at the heart of all turn-based tactical games, from Silent Storm and Jagged Alliance through to the original Fallouts. Wasteland 2 throws this aspect of the genre out altogether. What is not clear is whether this was intentional, or just the result of really incredibly poor game design and a lack of knowledge of what the genre is all about. Remember, Wasteland was an RPG, not a TTB, and Wasteland 2 has not made the transition well. It's not RPG enough to be an RPG and not TTB enough to satisfy the TTB grognards.
The combat system is borked. There is no tactical complexity to the combat at all. In all real combat, the side with the initiative tends to win. In this game, initiative automatically goes to the enemy. No setting up mutually supporting arcs of fire then luring the baddies in. No, you set up your mutually supporting arcs of fire, fire a single shot, then the baddies swarm you.  You only get to try to gun them down when they're next to you. They are able to run across the map to get you.
My 'leader' toon has an assault rifle. When he fires a single shot to initiate combat, enemies (even those outside his range of fire) have the opportunity to run fifty or sixty yards and initiate hand to hand combat before he can fire a second shot. It's ludicrous to include a semi-automatic rifle in the game that fires the equivalent of once every fifteen seconds. A hundred years ago, soldiers with bolt-action rifles were firing aimed shots every two seconds. Does InXile understand how firearms work?
The probability engine is also borked. It's not uncommon to miss 5-6 60% shots in a row. This also extends to other skills such as lockpicking or safecracking. Many other people giving negative reviews have also commented on this.
The presence of indestructible objects (ie, the vines in the Ag Centre) that block progress until other goals are achieved is inexcusable, especially considering the confusing and unclear mission objective system. You literally cannot approach a mission in any way other than that deemed appropriate by the developer.
The character development process is bizarre. Your Strength stat has nothing to do with your strength-related skills. Your Charisma stat has nothing to do with your social interaction skills. You may as well put all your points into Intelligence to maximise stat points on level up and enough into Agility to maximise your action points in combat. To reiterate: no matter how rubbish your stats are, as long as your skills are high enough, most of the stats really don't matter.
I completed Fallouts 1 and 2, and got as far as I could in Tactics until the bugs killed the game, and never felt as frustrated as I have with this game. The fact that I have 20 hours invested without even completing a single module says a lot about the game.
The graphics are, to my mind, no better than we saw in Fallout nearly twenty years ago.  But I could forgive that if the core gameplay was there, but it's just not. The tactical aspects are ruined by an idiotic system that ALWAYS gives the enemy the initiative. The mission log system is unclear and confusing. There are booby traps on at least a third of the items, doors and chests EVEN IF THERE IS NO REASON FOR IT.
I applaud the attempt to bring Fallout-style gameplay into the present day, but this game is just a wasted opportunity. I wanted to believe, and instead I just wasted $40.
What a tragic waste of time and money.

The only thing funnier than how bad this game is, is the number of people who keep comparing it favourably to Fallout 1/2/Tac (bearing in mind those games are 10-15 yers old).
The only thing more tragic than a wheelbarrow full of cute puppies on fire is the number of fanboys who cruise the negative feedback section giving 'not helpfuls' to people trying to steer unsuspecting buyers away from this piece of crap.
It's just sad.

Kerbal Space Program is essentially a physics simulation using rockets that you build, piece by piece, from scratch. It is a sandbox game without any real set goals, though reaching other worlds and landing on them is an obvious motivation. Utilizing the mechanics of the game to get a craft into orbit or sent to other worlds requires experimentation, research (a lot of which has real-world basis), and clever engineering. For learning the basics of rocketry and aviation, this game is an amazing learning tool.
It has a career mode which adds several progression mechanics such as research (achieved by reaching different parts of the solar system and transmitting data back to your home world, or collecting samples and bringing them back for an even greater bonus), money (collected through randomly generated contracts), and astronauts themselves (which can be obtained through missions or by hiring with money). Though these added mechanics aid a player to slowly experiment with limited sets of technology and gives motivation to avoid disastrous problems (especially losing your precious Kerbonauts), it isn't balanced particularly well and can't be taken too seriously. It is basically a tutorial for new players, though I still prefer it over sandbox mode. I recommend playing on the mid-level difficulty with undo-function disabled for a decent, but not too punishing, experience.
There are some pretty glaring flaws. The learning curve is extreme and some of the rocket building tools aren't very intuitive. The game provides tutorials that help explain the mechanics, but further research from YouTube will be required for more advanced things. Also, atmospheric aircraft have extremely finicky physics. If you play career mode, I recommend you skip any long-range aircraft missions on Kerbin. These missions can take a really long time since time acceleration messes up the physics even more. Also, the game is lacking in N-body physics, which detracts from the complexity and educational value slightly.
Overall it's a wonderful game if you have the patience, and there is a free demo available to try (though it's way out of date last I checked). There is also a thriving modding community that can extend the complexity and fun. Although people often talk of the extreme difficulty of the game, it makes the achievements very satisfying. Plus, I guarantee you'll feel much smarter once you figure it all out.

However, the main direction that they chose to expand the game was with a "fortress siege" system, which primarily involves grinding to add captains to your army and then performing the same attack and defend missions over and over again.  It was obviously developed in an attempt to sell additional loot boxes for real money - taking a page out of the book of predatory mobile game monitization schemes. Game is awesome, totally free roam with lots of challenges, but no closed Circuit, no point to point racing.....actually no racing at all, its all about trial and error where error spells disaster so u end up stuck, too damaged or out of fuel and hence u will soon enough learn to drive very carefully, just like u would irl.
The physics are superior to every other driving game ive ever tried (ive tried quite a few), Spintires has all the things we always wanted in an offroad game, manual diff lock, enable/disable AWD, winches and cranes.
You can even winch out ur fellow driver if hes stuck somewhere, bring fuel and/or repair his truck on site.
There are however some things that needs to get sorted, like the camera, its a chase-cam that can be moved a little using the mouse, but it acts in an annoying way that prevents u from seeing what u r actually looking for, because it centers the truck that makes it obstruct ur view.
Controls aren't always all that easy and not really explained anywhere in game, well some controls are, but things like how to operate the crane isn't, ive been struggling for 20 mins with it as it wont let me control one piston at a time, hence it moves both pistons in or out at the same time, making it impossible to use.
Theres nothing to find online, Ive googled several times for several things about the game, simple things like "Spintires How to use the winch" aso., but I get zero results that has an actual answer, so it goes for the crane control, all I get is a video that demonstrates how it can move (controlling one piston at a time) but nothing about how its actually done.
So better/more extensive in game help (maybe even a tutorial), rewrite of the camera so itll move "freely" and with the option of a wider perspective.
A fully manual gearbox would be nice too, so far u can choose from 4 gear lever positions 'Auto, 1st, rev' and a position that makes the engine stall.
Also manual reduction gear would come in handy a lot of the time, especially when passing over rocks where too much speed (approx. >3 km/h (1.5 mph)) will cause damage to the truck.
It would be good for going down steep hills as well, where ur truck otherwise gets some heavy dmg when u hit the bottom and for these things, even 1st gear allows for too much speed.
Despite these issues, I still think its incredible good quality compared to the issues we normally experience in other games just after release.
Ive been playing for a few hrs straight and never do I experience any lag or similar issues, everything just runs super smooth all the time, gfx are set on max all the way and im even on an old GF GTX470 gfx card, so the games graphics are indeed very light to run and I can see on my NVidia monitor, that it takes up about 500MB of VRAM, which isn't much by todays standards.
As far as for realism, ive never tried driving any of the vehicles irl, but I can say that driving that 6 wheeler in this game, is very much similar to driving the Hydrema 922 dumper, in the sense on how it handles at different speeds, going thru rough terrain etc., so ill say the game feels pretty real for most parts.
One thing they shd consider imo, is the rocks, they have weird physics and doesn't feel like rocks, also the truck tires has very little friction when passing over rocks which seems wrong and the rocks doesn't get squeezed into the mud when passing over them in well, mud.
All in all, if u like free roam off roading, buy the game, u wont regret it. :-)

Back in 1999, when I was just 15 years old and didn’t know any better, I went on a school trip to Germany.
I never took German at school and to this day I can’t speak any German, so it’s a genuine mystery to me as to why I went there with the school at all but I did and whilst there, I visited my very first modern art gallery. I’m not sure why we were taken to a modern gallery.
Maybe it was an attempt to widen our cultural horizons or perhaps the teachers were just stumped for ways to keep us busy and so just signed us up to any old rubbish in a desperate bid to kill half a day. Whatever the reasons it really doesn’t matter because I can barely remember the place or any of the art that we saw. I can vaguely remember that one piece of art was a rusty piece of metal welded to a chair. The other piece I can loosely recall was just two steel or iron girders placed on the ground end to end with just an inch or so separating the two and there, sat in the gap, was a sponge. Like the sort of sponge you would use in the shower.
Of course after 15 years there’s no way to tell just how accurately I am remembering these but suffice it to say they had very little impact on me.
But there is one thing I remember with a crystalline clarity and that was after we had all left the museum and our teacher, a man named Mr Tarrant, asked us for our thoughts on what we had just seen. He wanted to know what we made of it all. Had we enjoyed it and had we been impressed with all the lovely art that we had seen?
Round the group he went and one by one my classmates all spoke warmly and enthusiastically about the pieces they liked best and how impressed they had been with with this piece and with that piece. Round the group he went, one by one until he reached me. And I opened my mouth to speak.
And I lied.
I pretended that I had really enjoyed the gallery and that I had understood what I had seen. I lied about how interested I had been in this piece and that piece. I was 15 years old on a school trip to Germany and there, outside a modern art gallery I lied to my teacher and to all my classmates because I was afraid of looking stupid. I was scared of looking as though I just hadn’t been able to grasp whatever it was that everyone else had managed to get. Even worse I was scared that maybe the art had been amazing and i just hadn’t been smart enough to get the point of it. So I lied and pretended I had gotten it. I pretended I had loved it.
But here’s the real truth. As the years have dribbled by, I have gotten older, I’ve gotten more cynical, I’ve seen more and I have become more and more convinced that in fact everyone in that little group huddled outside that modern art gallery 15 years ago was in fact lying. We just didn’t want to look stupid in front of our mates and our teacher. After all, nobody wants to be the first person to put their hands up and say “actually, I don’t understand what the hell this is supposed to be”.
For some reason when I was reading through the many glowing reviews of this new ‘game’ Mountain from David O’Reilly, I was suddenly reminded of that time we spent huddled outside that modern art gallery in Germany, 1999.

Mountain is a dollar well spent.
For those saying its just a glorified screensaver, to each their own. But make no mistake, there is actually quite a bit to do in Mountain.
Looking out on the abyss in which your mountain floats is serene. Sometimes, terrifying, if your annihiliation is slowly flying towards you.
Yes, it's not as flashy as COD, but I would take this over COD anyday. Just the quiet ambience, and the occasional lone, melancholy note signalling that your Mountain, this huge, hulking Mountain, has thought of something. Sometimes it reflects on the weather. Other times he expresses sadness and memories long forgotten.
Controls-wise. Well, the music you can play. You can activate raging firestorms, fish, frogs, hearts, coins, or even blood. It all comes raining down upon your Mountain in a way that can be truly terrifying, engaging, or beautiful. Every now and again, your Mountain experiences a bit of cold weather, and snow comes down upon it, coating your little objects in white fluff. You can zoom in to examine these objects, these stray pieces of someone's or something's life, that come crashing into your Mountain from the cosmos. You can then move these objects, or feel joy/sadness as you purposefully/accidentally send them hurtling back into the void. You can express your distaste at clouds by waving your mouse wildly in defiance.
The game is meant to be played when you want. I recommend checking up on it occasionally, but not actively playing if you don't feel like it. Check back if you hear the telltale ping of the Mountain's thoughts.
The Mountain is thinking. The Mountain is waiting.

Still got a couple more missions to complete, and much more contents to explore but I want to point a few things out for those struggling on whether you should buy it or not. It has so much potential, and in terms of the time frame New Bordeaux is in, it is portrayed excellently through the story and soundtrack. First, it feels somehow incomplete; due to graphics issue people have mentioned so far, and the texture scales being grainy and bugs here and there. 30FPS DOES SUCK but it's bearable to a certain extent. I haven't had any issues with the game crashing as of yet (running it on GTX 860 with Windows 8.1) and I will update my progress as I go much further into the game. Gameplay might feel repetitive for some people (drive here, grab this, drive there, kill x/y) because it reminds you of the ordinary grinding to progress through the game. I found it repetitive myself a bit, but you need to submerge your mindset to the era you're playing in so you give a bit of an understanding to the game itself. Repetition is balanced out by how characters' lives are introduced through cutscenes and gameplay so if you're the curious George type, you'll enjoy fulfilling mission requirements to unlock cutscenes and conversations. Sure, patches will be out soon but I feel there is much work that must be done. Don't expect much from the game as of now because graphics and other bugs must be addressed first. Controls are a bit clunky if I should comment on it; though if you adjust your sensitivity settings you'll be fine. Key mapping is strange to jump back and forth (stuff like driving with directional buttons but using C instead of H for horn or using DELETE key to whistle to get the AI's attention). Combat system is interesting since it has a good mix of stealth and brute force all in one package. For my tech savvy gamers out there who have strict guidelines as to what a perfect game of 2016 must be, I feel you should be patient with the 2K's progress with patching and addressing issues, and at the same time must anticipate great gaming experience once they address the issues they've complained about. I'm a graphics freak especially when anyone can clearly see the difference between a game from 2016 and from 1999, so I wasn't happy with this game too. But give it a bit more time, and it's never too late to do what we gamers are proud to do should the issues are not properly addressed: provide constructive criticism and hate the dogs**t out of it till its fixed lol

I can't believe it. For once in years, a triple A title is actually packed with content and things to do.
Many complain about the microtransactions and I fully agree, they're absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s for putting that in. I'm 100% sure they're doing this to pacify us and make releasing singleplayer microtransactions the norm.
HOWEVER
I cannot ignore the fact that the developers really put their soul into the game. It really doesn't hold your hand like the Assassin's Creed games. It's truly a difficult game but it can be overcome with some wit. Unlike the AC games, the combat is amazing. You get a bunch of skills that are reminiscent of the first Fable game in 2005. There are so many unique skills that are unlike each other and each one gives you an advantage but not enough to make you overpowered.
Also unlike the AC games, the parkour mechanics are horrid. Often clunky and unresponsive on mouse and keyboard, I find it difficult to steer Talion to where I want him to go. I normally had no problems with this in Assassin's Creed. It's also difficult to target which enemy you want to use your dominate ability on (turning them into your soldier). This often lead to me dying as I wasted time charging up the ability on the wrong person only to be attacked from the back.
Story-wise, I won't lie, it's hard to follow. I'm not an avid Lord of The Rings fan and I can't quite wrap my head around the universe. All I know is the 'bad guy' took something and we have to get it back through conquering territory. That's the gist of it.
Speaking of conquering, let's talk about the war system. Each region has a fortress that you ultimately want to lay siege to and take. To properly do this, you will need orcish companions that work for you through defeating them in battle. I fell in love with this system because each orc is truly unique. Each one has their own personality, voice, and lingo. I've played almost 20 hours so far and I haven't experienced repeat dialogue with an orc.
Keep in mind: the amount of orcs you can conquer is literally unlimited. This means there is an unlimited variety of personalities out there (and that you can't capture them all as I made the mistake of trying to do during my first 5 hours of play).
Was this game worth 80 bucks Canadian? Hell yes. I believe this is the game of the year.
Is the loot crates in-game worth paying for? Hell no. Steer clear of that garbage. You can fully experience the game without having to do so. Paying for their loot crates is telling them you like having microtransactions in a single-player experience.
I give this game a 9/10.
It lost the 1/10 for all the issues I outlined in this review. If they can make parkour and combat less clunky/frustrating, I would give it a solid 10/10. It doesn't feel like they cut out content to make way for DLC.

Its not often I do reviews, though seeing as how much hate is being thrown towards the title for its poor optimisation for some customers, i figured I'd throw in an actual finished review.  I finished the main game in around 19 hours, If you enjoyed mafia 2, i'd say youre in for a good time with this, though if anything Mafia 3 reminds me more of the old Godfather video games more then anything else, as you focus on bringing down the Marcano Crime Family by targetting their lower ranks and infastructure, and working your way up the chain until eventually reaching Marcano himself, where as Mafia 2 was a very linear Story driven experience.
I've seen some people hating on Mafia 3 for not allowing much customisation towards Lincoln Clay or having a multiplayer feature, and whilst those would be nice, its not expected. The Mafia series has always been a story driven experience in an open world setting. There is no 'benchmark' of expected features all open world games have to feature. I believe 2k are going to be adding in several outfits for Lincoln in the months due to the large request for customisation regardless, which is good to hear, but if you want heavy character customisation alike GTA, this isnt for you.
Whilst playing, my game crashed once and aside from that and the mentioned locked 30FPS (which personally matters very little to me), I had no issues of note with optimisation.
I found the gameplay to be great, Lincoln is built up to be a badass and it feels satisfying plowing through mobsters via takedowns, guns or explosives. The majority of the gameplay plays out with taking over the districts of the city to hurt the Marcano family. Each district is headed by a different Capo or Lieutenant, and each of these has 2 enforcers under them. Once you disrupt each enforcers operations in a district, they'll show themselves for oyu to take them out, and once both enforcers are gone, you can claim the territory from the current Capo or lieutenant.
Once the district is yours, you decide who you wish to hand it to from your selection of underbosses. Vito and the Italians, Cassandra and the Haitians or Burke and the Irish. Each Underboss has their own benefits and perks, though without spoiling anything, I found several descisions to be easily one sided.
The game has several expansion packs planned, aswell as free content such as the customisational outfits previous mentioned and things such as a golden weapon pack i believe (not sure of details), which should all be rolling out in the coming months. The expansions sound interesting, and hopefully wont be another 'Joe's Adventures', which many found to be lackluster in Mafia 2. Overall, I found Mafia 3 to be a great experience, which was what I expected of it, it may not of had as strong of a story as Mafia 2, though the additional gameplay elements make up for it in my eyes.

I could go on and on about the story, the characters, the studio, the mechanics, etc. but you've probably already read about all that.  If the waterfall of those positive reviews hasn't sold you yet, though, this probably will:
Check out the hours of record for the reviewers.  (At the time of this review, I've put in 46 hours: 15 on laptop, 41 on mobile.)  And I'm one of the light-weights.
The fact is that this game has crazy playability, which is rare for an indie title.  Most indie games that get noticed, much like independent films, tend to have tons of artistic merit and critical acclaim but nevertheless lack the plain fun and replayability of big studio productions.  CRASHLANDS IS DIFFERENT.
Part of what makes the game hard to put down is its balance.  Good games strike a magic balance between challenge and reward, giving us that wonderful sense of satisfaction and accomplishment.  For me, at least, Crashlands hits a sweet spot.  Whether I was Level 1 or 31, I always had a good mix of easy, challening, and just-out-of-reach objectives.
Another thing making the game hard to put down, is, well, how easy it is to put down.  With the "crossplatforminess" between my laptop of phone, I've played Crashlands in 2 minute spurts and evening-sucking marathons.  Although the game has dozens of hours of content, cloud syncing and that great balance of objectives makes it easy to fit that playtime into your schedule.

The last Tim Schafer game I played was back in the 90's with the Monkey Island series along with the Tell-Tale refreshed versions (all of which are good games and highly recommended), so when I found out that Tim Schafer (along with some help from the creator of the Monkey Island Series, Ron Gilbert) created a Kickstarter to create a new adventure game, I jumped on backing it.  It was a great decision.
When Broken Age was finally released, the amount of time and effort spent into creating and polishing the game was apparent throughout my entire play through.  The humor is great.  The story is solid.  It's very well-animated and the voice acting really brings you into the game.  The puzzles are a bit simple compared to other adventure games (however some of those suffered from convoluted solutions or the problem of hunting for hard-to-see objects), but Tim Schafer said the difficulty will be bumped up in Act 2.  All things considered, I would recommend getting Broken Age.  Act 2, a free update that completes the game, should be coming out later in the year.
***
What I would recommend just as much is to get the documentary on the making of the game.  To me that is a true gold nugget.  Most documentaries on making of games I've seen are very short with quick interviews, and are understandably made that way because developers' focus are on the games and the behind-the-scenes footage are considered bonuses.  On the other hand, when Broken Age was on Kickstarter, the creation of a documentary by a professional team was a huge selling point.
As of June 2014, there are 15 episodes, the earlier episodes being around twenty minutes long and the later episodes being about forty minutes, detailing the creation of the game.  The documentary isn't just cameras sitting behind people and silently recording their work big-brother style; it's the team interacting with each other, discussing their thoughts.  Sometimes they have troubles and talk about how to solve them, and other times they make something really cool and want to show it off.  If you've been following Broken Age in the news and heard about mishaps, such as the developers needing more money from backers (while they did need more money than the Kickstarter funds they had to complete the game, they were talking about brainstorming for ways to get additional funds, not getting more from backers) and the NDA debacle on official reviews near release (which was an unfortunate side effect of letting backers get the game earlier than the official release date), then watching the documentary will enlighten you on those problems.  A great part of the documentaries is that there are no spoilers (except in the latest episode where it states at the beginning that Act 1 should be played before watching the episode).  There are some mentions of the characters to be in the game as well as some of the locations, but nothing that I've heard that would spoil the game.
Since only Act 1 has been released, there will be more episodes in the future.  In addition to these episodes, there are also episodes called side quests, fifteen released so far.  These episodes are more focused on people in the team, such as the music director or a programmer, and each of these are also twenty to forty minutes long, all of them interesting as well.  I'm hoping that when the game is finished, the documentary would also be released on Steam because it truly is worthwhile for anyone, gamer or not, to watch.  But if it doesn't get released, you can head over to the Broken Age website and get the documentary.  I'm not sure if you get immediate access to the available episodes now, but even if you don't it's worth the wait when it gets released.

I wasn't sure what to expect from this game.
Whatever it was I was expecting, this game FAR EXCEEDED my expectations.
This game is fun. It oozes a special something, and it just makes me happy.
You can tell this game was made by people who love games.
It respects your time. There's no level grinding. There are generous teleport pads across the open world, and you can teleport to any of them at any time (once you've discovered each one).
You have infinite inventory, so you never have to worry about managing what to collect or not-collect. You want to just collect everything.
The game lets you play however you want, at your own pace.
There's no penalty for dying. You WILL die. You will drop some of your items when you die.
Simply go back to where you died, and you instantly pick them all up again. You move on.
This game is about enjoying the world that has been created by the team at Butterscotch Shenanigans.
The story seems really large, with many side-quests. It's all open world, so you can complete anything at any pace you want, and any order.
The game just feels good.
I also recommend picking up the mobile version of the game. Your save will automatically sync between both versions of the game, so you can always play wherever you go. That's another sign of a game developer who truly cares and respects the player!
If you're looking for a game to get lost in, this is the game to be playing.

For a simple reason really.
Fallout Shelter is a mobile game that has been ported to pc, problem being that when detracting this game from the mobile "ecosystem" you essentially missed out on any incentive to keep playing it, just try it for a while and you'll see it's true, and it's for a basic reason, it's simply easier to give a follow up and a check up in the phone that you don't use always for games or work, than it is to give that kind of attention and consistency on the pc.
Pair that up with the fact that since it is a "free to play" title, the game obviously has in-game transactions, something that's no bother, makes sense really, but again, the incentive for even paying for this transactions goes out the window when you take into consideration the simple amass of trainers, as well as memory editing tools that are out there.

Just like any other mobile "free to play" game this is nothing more than a successful attempt from Bethesda to create a game that essentially uses the already amazing Fallout popularity as a pedestal in which to have a name, but besides the superficial similarities don't think you'll get more from this than you will get from any other "free to play" game, you'll enjoy it at first, then you'll stop playing it after spending some cash on it, or cheating to give yourself everything, making the game in whichever way you choose, redundant, and a dull experience in anyway you see fit.

After playing KSP for quite awhile I would like to go back through and state my problems with the game more clearly.
First off, I have fun playing this game.
Its one of the few games that have made me actually yell "YES!" when I complete a complicated manuever successfully; which is why the limitations of the game are so frustrating.
The Engine.
KSP was developed in a realistic physics engine designed to accurately simulate the way a rocket (or space plane) works, both in atmosphere and in vacuum. However, there are two points when the physics of the game is "eased" and both have directly resulted in erratic bugs that make the game unpredictible in a very bad way. During this physics easing, all parts that have physics applied to them jump and/or wiggle in a way that has resulted in:
Sudden destruction of previously undamaged, well built craft.
Death or disappearamce of kerbals.
Destruction of objects attached to the ground (while playing with mods)
Yes, mods do exist to somewhat allieviate this problem but depending on the community to supply fixes for your game is not good development strategy. Unfortunately it is one that Squad heavily relies on.
The Learning Curve.
Other reviews have gone into a lot of detail about this so I won't expound too much, but KSP is literally rocket science. Sure, it's dumbed down to the point that even I can do it, but rocket science nonetheless. The tutorials and information in the game are wholly inadequate to the task. Even simple info points like part tooltips don't always provide the information necessary to actually use the part. A player actually has to exit the current game to even look at keybindings.
Again, Squad relies heavily on the community to provide the tutorials and knowledge necessary to play the game to its fullest, and not be frustrated while doing so.
This is a RECOMMENDATION not a thumbs up or down on whether I like the game, or have fun playing. Obviously, I went through all that I've listed and still played the game for nearly 300 hours. However, I would not recommend it to most gamers I know. Kerbal could still be a great game. Honestly, it would not take very much tinkering to do it. In its current state though, It still feels like it could be in beta.

Alan Wake is a psychological thriller that continuously bends the rules of reality. Incorporating third-person shooter mechanics with a story that continues to give more questions than it answers, Alan Wake is a game that takes psychological manipulation to a whole different level. However, Alan Wake suffers from almost a lack of identity. It tries to do too many things at once, and sometimes falls flat on its face.
__________
Synopsis:
Alan and his wife Alice take a vacation to Bright Falls. Soon after arriving, Alan learns it was a ploy by Alice and his agent Barry to help Alan get over his writer's block. Furious, Alan temporarily storms off, but returns when he hears Alice screaming. Being sucked into the lake by an unknown force, Alan dives in after her, but fails to come back up. Waking up, he's in his car, as he seems to have driven it off the road and gotten injured. When he returns to town, no one recalls seeing Alice or even hearing about her. Plagued by strange interactions with the psychotic, shadowy figures of Bright Falls, and having recurring nightmares, Alan must navigate his way through the seemingly infinite series of nightmares and alternate realities to understand and overcome the evil forces that plague Bright Falls.
__________
Story: The main plot of Alan Wake is like a road that twists and turns, then flips upside down. While it is engaging and suspenseful, there are quite a few times where the plot fluctuates in periods of dull segments and seems to lack consistency at holding onto the excitement the story brings. Coupled with sections that are filled with unpredictable and random humor, the game suffers from a lack of seriousness that most would expect of a mystery/horror game, which sometimes compromises the integrity of a game that so heavily relies on its story to drive the point home.
Graphics and Environments: Using towns and environments that are more spread out than most, the game gives a certain feeling of freedom during combat and exploration without being too open or too enclosed. Visually appealing landscapes also incite you to take in the view. Furthermore, the game does an excellent job of instantly shifting from what seems to be a harmless open field into a fear-inducing cage.
Functionality and Gameplay: Mechanically, there is nothing wrong with Alan Wake; the controls are fluid and the usage of weapons and gadgets is simple and effective. The weakest point of Alan Wake is the combat; and it is unfortunately a very big, yet small part of the game. Defeating enemies requires you to shine your flashlight or other sources of light on them to dissipate their black shadowy shields, followed by laying into them with bullets. The game imposes upon you a sense of haste: Quickly dispatch these enemies, or be overrun. Often enough, you are forced to constantly kite enemies and run in circles to further increase your chances of not dying. Furthermore, the amount of enemies are in over-abundance, losing their effective scare-factor by the second time you encounter them Thus, for how much of a psychological thriller the game tries to uphold, it's constantly under minded by the combat system.
_________________________
Overall, this is a story-based game. Combat is simply a filler to get you from one area to the next. Removing the combat completely or giving the player limited combat options might have made this game into a much more solid contender in the mystery/horror genre.
I recommend you buy this game on sale.

Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

It is now time to land the review for this game after having finished it at 100%.
I know a lot of reviews are talking about the loot boxes and how they should not be there but i wanted to finish the game to see how “needed” the loot boxes are in the game to finish it 100% (online high level play excluded of course)
I will talk about all aspects of the game first and not mention them. In the final chapter of the review i will explain how the loot boxes play a role and how necessary they are.
If you are pretty much familiar with the workings of the game and just want to see the loot box conclusion and the general conclusion of the game scroll down to the bottom. It is a long winded review
Having finished it completely and dabbled in online play I enjoyed the game quite a bit. If you played the first game (Shadow of Mordor) and enjoyed it then you will enjoy this as well. The gameplay is not that much different from the first but with some more polish. Of course with the now newly added content of fortress defending and attacking which will play a major role in the last act of the story. Next to that every area has its own share of collectibles in the form of memories , artifacts, poem verses for items and of course missions of the past (where you play as Calibrimbor)
I shall refrain from any spoilers of course but i can tell that the game offers about 4 to 5 different story lines you can explore that track through different zones. If you are a hard core lord of the rings lore fan you might have some questions about the story decisions they made here in reference to the movies/books but they gave it their own spin. if you don't take the books/movies too serious then the quests are quite entertaining and intriguing.
[h1Combat[/h1]
In contrast to the first game the combat has not had any great significant changes.  If you have never played the first game the feel of the combat can be compared to games like Assassins Creed or the Batman Arkham series.
In this game you get a Large skill tree where you can spend points in that you earn through leveling or completing certain objectives. Skill are divided in different categories like combat , predator , ranged etc where everything has 1 “main skill” and 2 or 3 “flavor skills” which alters the main skill in a way that will fit your play style. Only 1 flavor skill can be active though but once it has been unlocked once you can toggle it on or off or switch to others whenever you want (even in the middle of fighting something).
Besides the skill system this game now also offers a Loot system where you can equip 6 different item slots On higher rarity items a item can have a sort of mini challange to “unlock” some extra buff or power on the item. Its minor enough to be ignored though but a fun little addition to this all.
The biggest Unique point of this game is of course the Nemesis system which they have also expended on.
If you don't know what this is basically all orcs have the potential to become more significant to your world by developing a personality.That random orc that just happens to kill you that one time is now promoted to a captain and you can ambush him or enlist him in your army later on. Every orc has its own personality trait which can be sadistic ( “I just want to rip you apart!”) or silly ( like a bard orc who started to sing to me when he attacked me) or just weird ( an orc who only moans. or repeats a certain word or phrase repeatedly. just weird stuff ) but it makes every orc unique it its own way.
Well these orcs can develop relations to you or with each other. for example if you kill a captain somewhere maybe in the middle of a different fight or quest somewhere you get ambushed by another captain who comes to seek revenge for his fallen blood brother. and many more interactions like that. The orcs are not always bound to what you do but can choose to Ambush or betray you as well. every playthrough different things will happen.
Shadow of war does not know a “real” online multiplayer mode but it is more of a social aspect. There are 2 different ways of going online. “Online Vendetta” and “Online conquest”
Online Vendetta missions are mission to avenge other players in the world. You get send out to kill a captain that killed another player. They are quick and easy and reward “Spoils of war” and a loot chest . I shall expand on this in the lootbox section. but they just contain some gear that is around the level you do them on.
conquest is the fortress online mode of the game where you can attack another player's fortress. It has a ranked version and a friendly version with people on your friends list. Now 2 important things I will put here since the game is a tad vague on it.
The orcs you take along with you on the attacks can permanently die in your game world as well. so be careful on who you take with you. The defending player does NOT lose any orcs. so don't feel bad for killing his precious legendary warlords. they won't loose them. In the friendly mode you will NOT lose your attacking orcs.
I think this is the chapter which kind of ties it all together. Sure there is a long story. lots of collectables and fortress defending and attacking to be done but how necessary is the lootbox system in all this. are you messed over with your gear if you don't buy “legendary” items from the story. or are you doomed to fail in the end if you don't have max level legendary captains on all your fortresses?
There are boxes you can buy and boxes you can earn in game. with all different levels and contends. The boxes you can earn in game are
Vendetta loot box
Conquest loot box
Spoils of war chest
These boxes mostly contain gear for your character. the Spoils of war chest is obtained after earning 1000 spoils of war from playing online and contains orcs  and follower upgrades as well. but these can not be bought in the store.
Store bought chest are chests that contain 3 to 4 orcs at a time where you have the in game currency version off and the premium version off. where the premium version of course gives guarantees on epic and legendary orc drops.
well… no..
I have played this game on the nemesis difficulty ( the highest) and have used NO boxes in anything that involve the market. I might have used a for gear items from vendetta chests i got but besides that i never used it once. So that is good news of course. Having seen the entire game it makes me wonder why the loot boxes were there in the first place of course but at least it did not mess up the game drops in any way. I got flooded in so many orcs and items i did not know what to do with it sometimes. Even the “gind part” of the final part i did not do ANY grinding whatsoever. So as far as i am concerned no extra money is needed to finish the game.

If you enjoyed the first game than this game will certainly not disappoint. the improvements on the nemesis system and fort capture is a good addition to everything.though of course it has its “open world busy works quests” but luckily that is all optional stuff. So, here is the thing, I really enjoyed the first one, Shadow of Mordor, and this game is pretty much the first one, just with a bit of new content. The problem is that here you are forced to either go deep in the Nemesis system, grind for levels by playing the same missions over and over again, or by using the market to skip the repetitive, boring grind.

The other issue is that the combat is not as satisfying, but remains as easy as the first one. Another complain the first game had was that the fights were to easy. I understand where that complaint is coming from, but it was still fun to carve your way to the end. Unfortunately, for the sake of variety, they have introduced new enemies, and some combination of enemies force you to use crowd control and focus on a few set of enemies. With the weird spawn mechanics, you can end in situations where you are fighting one or two types of enemies that keep getting replenished, amid a sea of grunts. It is easy but boring work, so I find myself avoiding 90% of the fights. Even against captains, I rather weaken them using environmental hazards before dominating.
