As someone who loves dinosaurs and violence this game is the saddest creation on Steam.  Not worth the .99 nor the time to install a free trial.
The game has horrible matchmaking connectivity, match sizes are too small, and invites from friends don't work reliably.  The lobby menus are bloated with an obvious cash grab shop and "look at me" achievements.  After finally getting into the game the environments are so empty.  Sad textures on bland geometry.  The objectives are agonizingly simple, go here, push button, await dinosaurs.
The AI has simple charge maneuvers with little variance.  Other game modes offer different playstyles, but those are just as droll.  Playing as a dinosaur should be an exciting encounter with you as a 'boss' monster, instead you get mown down in seconds by standard weaponry and vehicles.  The bigger dinosaurs available are sluggish and their hit detection leaves you wondering if you're playing on the same map.  How did the developers attempt to balance smaller dinosaurs against their totally-not-spartan soldiers?  They've strapped 'dino-mite' (oh god this is probably what they called it) onto the back of Compy and Pterodactyls.  Orion: Dino Horde is supposed to be a dinosaur game, or at least about dinosaurs, but there are only two decent selections in the multiplayer.  It is more rewarding to be a faceless marine than the game's namesake.  I would call that a failure.
Speaking of "original" protagonists.  Models, animations, and even the physics feel so similar to Halo titles it is like the budget was spent paying Bungie's royalties, as if they could afford them.  The guns are such obvious plagiarisms they appear to have been stripped from Halo 2 and altered in the simplest ways.  Round a barrel here, recolor there, different gun!  The worst example is the tank.  It is the Scorpion from Halo shamelessly reused.
Orion: Dino Horde is a decent concept, horribly executed.  The developer must be trying some last ditch effort to squeeze money out of the dying player-base.  I've found out there is another game in the works, an open world dino warfare game.  I can only hope that they've learned from their mistakes and attempt to make something different from Dino Horde.
Despite all that I've said I did play this game, I did laugh at it with friends, but I still feel shorted. I spent .99 on this game and I wish I could have it back.  It is that bad.
TL:DR = One of the worst things you could play.

Gad damn where do I begin??
At the beginning I suppose...
It all started back when a buddy of mine [Mr. Food] invited me to the St. Louis IGDA (International Game Developers Association) which is basically an awesome group of like-minded people that get together once a week and talk about games and more specifically game development (tips, tricks and tools). It's really awesome, check out:
to see if there is a chapter in your city (If there isn’t one, you can start your own!) The very first time there- two cool dudes took the stage, Sam and Seth Coster…
and they proceeded to describe an amazing game that they were working on and I remember thinking to myself holy♥♥♥♥♥♥that would be incredible!
Well guess what???
THIS IS THAT ♥♥♥♥ING GAME!!
And it truly is everything the Super Coster Bros described that fateful day.
From a story aspect:
Right off the bat, the dialogue will make you laugh out loud (LOL) and the humor never fails to deliver throughout the game! It’s much more story driven than the majority of crafting style games out there. It is filled with cute (and sometimes dangerous) little creatures and the NPCs you meet along the way really breathe character (pun intended) into the game (love that Juicebox). It really sucks you into the world. Also, the title is a great little pun (that you Crash-land, but you probably already noticed that).
From a gameplay aspect:
I’ve never played a crafting game with such smooth functionality, everything is so polished and the controls feel so… natural! I didn’t know if I would like that almost everything is mouse controlled (except for some quick select buttons) but they’ve integrated the majority mouse control style so well that I don’t miss the keyboard! (It appears to be very touch-screen ready, which will be fun to see if Crashlands makes it onto iOS and Android, and to have a ‘Deepworlds’ kind of situation where you can switch from playing on your computer to on your smartphone seamlessly). The combat is some of the best I’ve ever seen in mouse-only control scheme (really, the mouse movement does not hinder you at all), the enemies will show their red [damage] ring and you can dodge out of the way quite nicely, however it’s not that easy, every enemy has their own attack personality and you will find yourself getting to know each enemy on a personal level! The build mode is also really well designed, you can lay down floors, walls, etc with serious ease! Heck, just listening to the build mode music is worth it! I LOVE that you can “recycle” tools, weapons, buildings basically everything, and it will give you the resources back! Another great thing is finding schematics, you never know where or what you’re gonna find; all I can tell you is you will get super excited every time you see a crate! It gives you just enough to make the crafting aspect fair and actually enjoyable (it doesn’t feel so much like a chore, but more that you want to cut down♥♥♥♥♥♥) but it doesn’t spoon feed ya either!
From a aesthetic aspect:
(I’m not sure if I’m using that word correctly, what I mean to say is graphics/sfx/music all that audio/visual stuff) From the start you notice that Crashlands has a graphical style all its own and it is truly the trademark Butterscotch Shenanigans style that is unlike any other. (In fact, Sam did a presentation on how he uses Inkscape to make his awesome little creations) I find it refreshing to see these kind of unique graphic styles (don’t get me wrong, I love pixel art but it’s nice to see something new once in a while) there is a sort of ‘brutal cuteness’ to Crashlands and it fits the game’s personality like a [Wompi]glove! The music is excellent, composed by FatBard (another cool guy who did a presentation on game music at IDGA St. Louis) from the upbeat daytime music, to the soothing nighttime track and even the awesome build mode elevator muzak; it compliments the graphic style so perfectly! In fact, I feel as though the music is audible version of BScotch’s graphics (if that makes any sense at all). Everything down to the adorable little beeps and boops that characters make when you talk to them, to the epic “TOOL INTEGRATED” splashscreen, to just the quirky flavor-text of the items and tools (Baconweed™ is good for me!) everything ties together so magically delicious(ly).
All-in-all:
Even though I might seem biased because I’ve met the Coster brothers (and they are REALLY AWESOME guys, super nice and funny, as you can imagine!) Crashlands really is an incredible little game (actually it’s not little, in fact the world is quite huge!) At first glance, it may seem like it shares many similarities with Don’t Starve, but the second you start playing you will find that Crashlands is such a unique and fun experience all its own. It is a testament to the true indie game; handcrafted by real-life brothers, who poured their hearts into this sweet little baby… And it shows!
Best of luck BScotch Shenanigans, and CONGRATULATIONS on an awesome game!

KSP is one of my all time favourite games. I got it a few years ago when it was first released on Steam, the devs have put a lot of time into this game and I am glad to see that it is still being worked on. You can tell how much I love this game by how many hours I have in it. As much as I love it, KSP is not a game for everyone and doe have some faults, as well as some things you should know before you get it.
1) KSP has a sharp learning curve, I played the game for a year before I even got to space.
2) There are some confusing aspects of the game, so I strongly suggest playing all of the tutorials, starting with a sandbox game, and reading the description of all of the buildings.
3)DO NOT FORGET TO CHECK YOUR STAGING!!! YOU WILL EXPERIENCE A HORRIBLE MESS IF YOU DO!!!
4)Read the engineering report to check if you are forgetting something
5)Use the KSPedia for help
6)You have to manually install mods, so create a shortcut to your gamedata folder
7)Mods are hard to find and having to many will crash your game
8)There is re-entry heating, remember your heat shields and parachutes will break if you move to fast
9)Different planets have different gravity and amount of atmosphere, prepare for this as well as planets moving and closing transfer windows
10)Use the CoM(Center of Mass), CoL(Center of Lift), and CoT(Center of Thrust) tools
11)Different engines use different fuels and have different thrust to weight ratios
12)Jet engines only work in an atmosphere
I will continue to update this review with more things as I think of them.

So, here is the thing, I really enjoyed the first one, Shadow of Mordor, and this game is pretty much the first one, just with a bit of new content. The problem is that here you are forced to either go deep in the Nemesis system, grind for levels by playing the same missions over and over again, or by using the market to skip the repetitive, boring grind.
The biggest problem Shadow of Mordor had was that most missions were variations of the same thing, and Shadow of War suffers from the exact same problem. In fact, becasue the game is longer, it feels worse, because you are repeating more cycles, even if the cycles are made up of more components.
The other issue is that the combat is not as satisfying, but remains as easy as the first one. Another complain the first game had was that the fights were to easy. I understand where that complaint is coming from, but it was still fun to carve your way to the end. Unfortunately, for the sake of variety, they have introduced new enemies, and some combination of enemies force you to use crowd control and focus on a few set of enemies. With the weird spawn mechanics, you can end in situations where you are fighting one or two types of enemies that keep getting replenished, amid a sea of grunts. It is easy but boring work, so I find myself avoiding 90% of the fights. Even against captains, I rather weaken them using environmental hazards before dominating.
I'm on the third 3rd (4th?) area, and taken over 3 fortresses and I think I am done with this game. I might come back when there is nothing at all to play, but for now I don't see any point in playing anymore, I am not having fun.

This is a must-have for anyone looking for a flight sim.
FSX is a very old simulator though (I myself have used this for the best part of 10 years), and its age is now showing.
I will warn anybody looking to buy this that you are probably going to have spend a hell of a lot of money if you want to make it look and feel realistic. The simulator was developed in 2005/2006 and now requires DOZENS of add-ons to bring it up to todays standards.
Be warned, You will require a high-end PC to run it on high settings. And will spend countless hours tweaking your settings and config files to get those all important frame rates to a reasonable level.
Personally I think FSX days are numbered.
It is time a simulator was developed with the same user-friendly interface (sorry, x-plane just does not cut it...) but optimised and developed to today's standards.
Until then, FSX (+addons) will have to do.

I've already spent almost 100 hours playing this game on the Windows Store, and I have to say that it's one hell of a time waster. Fallout Shelter doesn't have any specific goal in mind, so you can spend your spare time increasing your vault's population (and have your own Gary-themed whacko-fest); training your dwellers' SPECIAL stats for gameplay bonuses; or send them all out in the wasteland, and battle a dozen Deathclaws, for that chance to find a rare item - just remember to send them back to the vault if you're going to exit the game, because the timer keeps ticking even when you're out, and reviving a dead vault dweller costs a lot of caps. Tip for new players: a high food level keeps everyone happy and smiling in the face of danger; therefore, invest in it early in the game (or send the useless dwellers out to die in the wilderness), because it dwindles fast if you have too many people.
Overall, a fun casual game. There are microtransactions available, but your vault can survive even without purchasing any of them. You might have to spend more time playing and managing if you want some of the loot that can be purchased in the store, but a day or two of waiting wouldn't hurt.
And there you have it.

Act one serves as a good introduction, act two features you conquering mordor by mind controlling everyone, act three is the strongest hour of the game narratively, in my opinion, and act four is dragged out far longer than it should've been, culminating to an ending that tries to tie the game into actual lore while not satisfying me as much as I wanted. Fortress assaults are not what was seen in the first 20 minute gameplay trailer, but still have their moments. Overall, a great game with several overarching problems with storytelling and pacing. I would reccomend buying it when it goes on sale, but if you really loved the first game, go ahead and get this whenever you want. NOTE: Used or felt the need to use lootboxes approximately zero times in the entirety of the game, and I played on nemesis difficulty with counter and detection indicators turned off the entire time.

Let me tell you the tale of "Pushkrimp", a lowly grunt that got lucky one fine Mordor day. About how, in the chaos of battle with a undead Ranger, he managed to land the fatal blow. From that day on, he became known as "Pushkrimp Tark Slayer". He was a ferocious Orc, weilding far more damage output than most, a berserker with a gaggle of savages following him around after he murdered his old captain. He was angry at the world for not recognizing his greatness, and he never gave his foes a second chance, if they even got so lucky.
Pushkrimp became the focus of one particular undead Ranger, the lucky blow not going forgotten. So an ambush was arranged to have him assassinated for his insolence. Pushkrimp laughed at the pathetically underprepared Ranger and his crew. Murdering the Rangers thralls quickly, before killing the Ranger in a single blow. A sign of things to come. Now... Pushkrimp had the Ranger in his sights...
For the next few days, Pushkrimp would lie in wait and ambush the Ranger, mercilessly murdering him again and again with his savage blows and inpenetrable armor. Twice, he suceeded in killing the Ranger, and twice the Ranger fled in horror as Pushkrimp gained more power than even the Ranger wielded. But the Orcs savage reign of terror was not to last forever... or was it?
Amonst fiery pits, the very war machine which Pushkrimp guarded, he again ambushed the weary Ranger. An epic battle ensued that climbed the heights of the scaffoding and confused orc workers. Above the pits, Pushkrimp and the Ranger did glorious battle one more time. Clashing and dodging the Orcs vicious blows, the Ranger stabbed where he could, keeping his distance despite his arrows being useless (even though Pushkrimps sole flaw was ranged attacks). Near death, Pushkrimp raged at his fall from flawless victories, and quickly began recovering health, wildly swinging his one-hit-kill axes at the Ranger. His fury was his mistake.
Near death, enraged, and too close to the edge of a bridge, the Ranger saw his moment, his chance at victory. He drop kicked Pushkrimp from the bridge, breathing a sigh of releif as the Orc that caused him no end of suffering plummet to his doom into a pit filled with lava. The Ranger fired arrows into the screaming Orc as he burst into flames, just to be sure the meance was gone forever. It wasn't until the screams died away that the Ranger felt safe again, the top predator in Mordor.
Leaving the fields of lava, the Ranger plotted his next move. Who was to become his new thrall, how he would conquer the looming fortress... then a axe whizzes past his head! Ambush! There... his armor and hair burned away, skin melted, and body charred... stood Pushkrimp! He challenges the Ranger, chastising him for his confidence, before raising his axes declaring he has become "Pushkrimp the Flame of War" as they burst into flames. The Orc cackles maniaclly as he twirls his flaming weapons, the Ranger terrified.
The undying Orc rushes the Ranger, another epic battle ensues, but no lava pits to unexpectedly lend assistance. The Flame of War demonstrates his newfound strength in rapid regeneration as well as enhanced resistances. He has become a true monster, enraged, unkillable, and very lethal. He tackles the evasive Ranger in a fury, and caves his head in with his bare fists. The Ranger dies again, and terrified of the monster lurking in that region, flees to another.
Time passes, the Ranger grows in power, all while avoiding the hunting grounds of the Flame of War. Soon, the Ranger feels he is strong enough at last to defeat the now surely weaker Orc that gave him trouble so long ago. He returns... to desolation...
The captains that once swarmed around the fortress: dead. The Warcheifs that served the Overlord: dead. It was as though the Ranger need not invade the empty land at all... save one Orc standing fiercly at the top of the fortress... There, in command of the land of death, stood... PUSHKRIMP!!! The new lands Overlord had mounted a staggering one Orc assault on the fortress, annihilating all in his path. Worse, forged in war, The Flame had gained still more power than the Ranger by a wide margin. Facing him would surely mean death.
Nevertheless, the fortress defences down, the Ranger trained until he matched the Orc in strength... theoretically at least. Pushkrimp had made the fortress his home, stringing up his old commanders as decorations for his walls. His strength was on full display. He had no need of Warchiefs, so he assigned none even as the Ranger assembled his armies and mustered his power.
The assault on the fortress came as planned, the walls falling quickly, but none of that was the true challenge. Pushing open the metal doors of the keep, the brutality of The Flame was on full display, his piles of bones, and traitors of particular note hung from the walls. There... upon a throne of skulls sat The Flame. He welcomed the Ranger, thanked him for giving him the confidence to rise through the ranks. Then, he asked for one more favor: that the Ranger die once again to solidify his place as top Orc. The cordality of the meeting distracting from the horrific scene the Orc chose for himself.
They clashed, the lesser minions meaning little as they fell quickly from the sparks flying between the two old rivals, none could stand between them. The Flame himself rend his minions if they interfered, their assistance more interference. The battle ascended the steps to the throne, and the duo clashed before the throne of bones long after any battle should last, the Ranger forced to avoid any blow from the wicked fiery axes. Then... the Ranger fell, Pushkrimp catching him on a backswing.
All was lost, The Flame was too strong. Mordor would forever be strangled under his shadow. The game would end. Then, a ray of light as one of the Rangers loyal commanders tackled The Flame before he could land the killing blow. The battle resumed, the weakened Ranger trying his best to protect his friend. "No! He's too strong for you! Retreat!" the Ranger wanted to yell, but he knew his ally was the sole bulwark between him and death. Still, death came. And again, an ally saved the Ranger. So it went, three more times, until the Five Ranger Commanders and the Ranger himself stood before The Flame in glorious battle.
Still, sorrow filled the ensuing melee. The entirely competant fighting force crashed against Pushkrimp like angry waves against a seawall. The furious Orc ducked and dodged, struk and withdrew with the finesse of a seasoned warrior, his health wildly swinging between full and none. Then... the Rangers allies began to fall, one by one. First was the brute Oolog the Ranger relied on as his shield. Then, his archer commander fell. Then his frontline commander lost his head to a flurry of blows... it was looking grim as the unnatural Orc Overlord slew all the Ranger had arrayed against him.
Finally, the Rangers last two allies, another berserker and a heavily armored defender, did the unthinkable. While the berserker at long last broke The Flames will, the Defender threw himself in front of a ferocious spinning assault that would have surely killed the Ranger. Mogzu One-eye... we will never forget your sacrifice. In that moment, The Flame grinned a wicked grin and mocked the Ranger for his weak allies. That was when the Ranger struck in the moment before Pushkrimp once again would enrage and regain the hard fought health robbed from him.
In a blur of blue magicks, the Ranger threw out his hand in a desperate hope of ending the madness, forgoing the thought of killing the Orc, fearing such a assault would fail... leaving The Flame as strong as ever. The Flame falls to his knees, roaring in rage, cursing the Ranger as his burning eyes of hatred turn blue... then submissive. "I am yours to command..." he growls, almost with resentment. The Flame became the terror of the Bright Lords armies... an unstoppable force.

I am not terribly far into this game as of yet, but I am far enough to say I cannot, in good conscience, recommend this to anyone at all.
You see, if you liked Shadow of Mordor, the gameplay is more of the same.  There are some differences, like the fact that, instead of simply enhancing your weapons with runes obtained from killed orc Captains and Warchiefs, they actually drop equipment you then use, including new armour and cloaks, and the skill tree is changed quite a bit.  You might be thinking why I cannot recommend this, then.  The answer is one word:
Microtransactions.
Not only is there microtransactions in this game, you are actually pushed towards them in a fairly aggressive manner.  When you start the game, you are asked to accept the End User License Agreement, and specifically accept a clause stating that you agree to Warner Bros providing 'personalized messages' based on your game play experience, use your device information for analytics and transferring your data to the US.  You can choose NOT to agree to this clause, and you are warned that this locks you out of online features, including the in-game market, where you buy the microtransactions, and asked if you're really sure you want to do this.  However, the game only accepts you not agreeing to this temporarily.  Any time you get to the main menu, either by quitting the game whilst playing it or by starting the game to continue playing it, you have to go through this process again, so it feels like the game is badgering you to accept it.  In addition, on the main menu, there is a fairly large chunk of the screen taken up with advertising stuff you can buy in the market.
Basically, if you buy this game, it feels like you have paid money for Warner Bros and/or Monolith to badger you into paying them even more money, with a game attached as a secondary consideration.  This means that the fact this game is actually quite good, even without shelling out more money, feels like it isn't actually something that is entirely intended by the developers and/or publishers.

It's the most fantastically frustrating game I own, where when I see a "81% to hit" stat I can safely assume I'll miss, or the gun will jam, or I'll hit a friendly... or any other number of things that will go wrong.
Because in this game, if it can go wrong it absolutely will.  Guns with a 1-3% jam rate seem to jam every other turn.  Squad members with excellent skills in markmanship (handguns/etc.) will miss far more often than they hit.
In Wasteland 2, you will spend 10 minutes disarming a trap and unlocking a safe only to find absolute junk inside.  Reload to try it again and you'll find a shiny new sniper rifle instead.
It's hilarious: I've never been so frustrated with a game that I couldn't stop playing.
As addicting as Fallout/Fallout 2, as frustrating as trying to tame a hyperactive six year old in a toy store.
Guns jam with staggering frequency.  A gun that says it has a 5% jam rate?  Try 45%.  Seriously.  In one firefight, where each of my squad members had a 75% or higher change to hit, not a single round hit the enermy... FOR THREE TURNS.  It was incredible.  I've never seen such a ridiculous display of gunnery incompetence...
Until my 98% to hit point-blank pistol shot went awry.  Not once.  Not twice.  Thrice.
Wasteland 2 will punish you for even thinking that you have a chance.  If you don't learn that F9 must be pressed before ANY action you will not progres.  Your characters will miss the enemy, repeatedly shoot themselves, and somehow manage to catestrophically fail digging up something from the ground... resulting in two fresh bodies for the Arizona wastes to reclaim.
You will quickly learn that the only thing that Wasteland 2 is honest to you about is that there are a lot of things out there trying to kill you, including the mechanics of the game itself.
But it isn't all bad.  When things go right it can be a lot of fun.  The graphics are pretty good.  The story is even better.  And hey, you're playing a RPG about a post-apocalyptic America- no kidding your guns are going to miss every other shot.
Short, not scary and needs a save feature... 3/10

As a huge fan of Shadow of Mordor, and the middle earth universe in general, I have been waiting 3 years for the sequel to SOM to come out, and whilst its not a bad game (I actually think its better than SOM), I don't feel that I can recomend it, at least now, based of the large number of issues I have with the game.
First of I will start with the positives
+ The game is much larger in scope than SOM with more areas to explore (Five in total, compared to SOM's two)
+ A much better loot system that replaces the runes of the last game. There is now armor and weapons.
+ A better story, which feels more Lord of the rings than SOM's story
+ More varied orcs with new attack patterns and new olog-hai (trolls)
+ Large fortress battles
+ A few new skills and improvements to the SOM formula, like auto picking up arrows and double jump
Now sadly onto the negatives, and I have alot of them :(
- The game is very buggy at the moment and as far as I am aware there has not been a single patch released for the game on PC (I am not 100% sure)
Twice have I failed fortress assaults because my character has glitched into the enviroment and I am unable to move.
- The maps are actually smaller than the ones in SOM (but the total mass of all 5 maps is bigger than the 2 in SOM) and they just arn't very memorable. Appart from the forts which vary a bit, 4 of the 5 maps are basically the same, with different skins over the top. There are pretty much no memorable locations on any of the maps except the Minas Morgul map.
- The controls still feel clunky, and the gamepad controls have too many actions on too few buttons. For example, on an XB1 controller, A is to sprint, jump, climb jump, roll, volt over an enemy and a few more moves. This means that when you are in combat you end up doing the wrong moves, like trying to volt an enemy instead of dodging an attack. There are also too many enemies at once and its pretty much impossible to attack a certain one, the game will just attack anything it wants.
- Far too many reused assets. As a huge AC fan, I am used to seeing alot of reused assets going from game to game, and I don't have a problem with reusing assets, as long as there is enough new stuff to make it feel fresh. The problem is that this game doesn't have enough.
The combat animations are 95% the same as SOM, the background music and combat music has been copied over from SOM, one of the 5 regions of the game is in the same region as one of SOM's maps with alot of reused textures and models.
As someone who played SOM for over 200 hrs between PC and Xbox, I have to say this game starts to feel stale way to fast.
- The end cutscene is hidden behind a grindwall. To access the real ending of the game you are forced to defend your fortresses 20 times in a mode called "shadow wars" at the end of the main story. After 2 or 3 assults it starts to get boring real fast, and every single attack feels pretty much the same. Since it's the end of the game there is nothing left to do except repeat the fortress assaults, and when there are bugs like the ones mentioned above it really starts to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off.
- The loot boxes. Like I said above the ending of the game feels purposely hidden behind a grind wall to make the player want to buy loot boxes. There are also adverts all over the main menu and the pause menu and even pop-ups on the army screen telling you to "buy" new orcs from the market.
- Poor optimisation on lower end PCs. My Rig is running a 1080Ti, so I have not experienced this one first hand. That said, many friends running lower ends cards, as well as other reviews I have read say that the game doesn't run that great on lower end PC's. I wasn't going to add this since it hasn't effected me, but I decided to just to keep people informed.
- Alot of the orcs use the same dialogue, which was never an issue in SOM (for me), and it makes alot of the enemies you face feel the same as other enemies you have already killed. I have run into 7 orcs during my playthrough which all have the same story about how they were bitten by a spider and they all look the same, with the same orc character model with a spider web stuck to their faces.
- The orcs talk too much during sieges, let me explain what I mean.
Like in SOM, every time you run into a named orc from the nemesis system, the gameplay will pause and the orc will talk to you for 10 - 20 seconds, usually saying something about how hes going to kill you and eat your face. The problem I have is that when you attack an enemy fortress there are usually 6 warchiefs in charge of the fort that you will have to kill. Each warchief usually has 2 bodyguards, which means there are about 18 nemesis enemies in total in every fort. Every time you run into one they will start to talk to you, and there is nothing you can do while they talk to you for 10 - 20 seconds, and there is no way to skip it. This means that during every fortress assult you have to listen to 18 orcs telling their boring stories about how they are going to kill you. This really ruins the pace of the assults as they are ment to be huge scale battles with tonnes of enemies to kill, and having the game pause once every few seconds as you run into another orc captain really ruins the pace. Simply adding a skip dialogue button would fix this problem and I don't know why the devs havn't done this.
To summarize, I don't think this is a bad game. I even think this is a better game than SOM. But sadly the game has too many problems and not enough new things for me to recommend it at the £45 / $60 price tag. If the game is patched and some of the issues are fixed I might change my review to a positive, but as of now I honestly cannot recommend this game.
Im sorry if this review comes across as very negative, but its because I had really high hopes for this game and I want to see it succeed. It just has too many problems for me right now :(

Again, overall, it was great!

Back to her Hometown in the outback of the State of Piaui – Brazil, Maria came to visit her mother, who was ill, and finds herself trapped by a legendary local curse. They said that the curse will finish only when the beast successfully catches and kill seven Virgin Mary, but maybe there is another way to defeat this terrible beast.

There are 5 different endings, you have to restart and do all of them to fully complete the game. Part of it is a ritual you have to perform to reach most of the endings. The storyline is above average for this type of thing, probably due to the fact that it's a real legend and the game has been built around it rather than some lame tale made up by the developer and stuffed into the gameplay just-because. It's a Brazilian legend so the narration is Portuguese (with English subtitles) which I think adds to the atmosphere.

A very compelling, classic, post-nuclear RPG with highly satisfying turn based combat in between. Wasteland 2 got a pretty cool flair to it, rough and sometimes weird characters. Lots of text, which you actually have to pay attention to - really nice to have something like that amidst the dozens of games requiring nothing of you but to look at the minimap and the HUD telling you to what to kill and how many of them.
Pretty good integrated tutorial function, which holds your hand if you want to but you can also just go ahead and figure out most of the mechanics by yourself. Either way works. Skill system is deep enough but not overly complex and the story kept me hooked most of the time.
The only thing that is not quite favorable are the graphics - and that is coming from someone who usually doesn't give a rat's♥♥♥♥♥about the looks of a game. And I'm not talking about polygons or explosion effects. It just seems a little bit too blurry in some scenes, the colouring is very desaturated and without a lot of contrast, sometimes making it hard to spot certain things like crates or objects related to quests.
Other than that, if you like the style of games like XCOM, the Fallout series, maybe even S.T.A.L.K.E.R. (even though that's an FPS) you might just dig Wasteland 2.

The game doesn't have any major glitches or problems. It just has forgettable characters, a storyline that fails to hook the player in (I never cared about who I was saving or why), and a rudimentary combat system (you tell your guys to point and shoot and that's about it [assuming they have ammo, which is sparse - something a person find appropriate in a post-apocalyptic wasteland, but it's only appropriate if the melee mechanics balance with the ranged mechanics]). But my biggest gripes are with the journal system and "the chance to fail."
Journal system - if an NPC gives the location to something important, I want it saved in a journal, along with relevant information. This isn't the 90's and I don't want to have to carry a pen and paper just to understand what I am doing and why. It's also difficult to keep track of who is who and why they matter without a reference - at least for myself.
Chances to fail - I don't mind failing in games. The problem is when I "critically fail" at opening a door (a door that MUST be bypassed to continue the game) and then wander around the complex, going through all the adjoining branches of the dungeon for two hours, only to discover that I'll have to reload a save from two hours before in an attempt to bypass the door I jammed shut. My time is very valuable to me and I don't have enough of it to waste my time by restarting from such an early save. I'm not a fan of roguelikes for this reason, and the fact the game put me through this has completely put me off of it. I might try it again months or even years from now. But I am totally disappointed at this point. The fact everything else about the game is simply "good" or "ok" but not "great" doesn't help (in otherwords, it's not worth the frustration).
Bonus complaint: apparently EVERYONE in the wastes has explosives... and uses those explosives to booby trap EVERY FREAKING DOOR! My number 1 use of med packs isn't during or following combat - it's healing from traps - traps that remain invisible despite high perception skills and the ability to disarm them.
I cannot quit playing this game.  Somebody, send help.

As someone who loves dinosaurs and violence this game is the saddest creation on Steam.  Not worth the .99 nor the time to install a free trial.
The game has horrible matchmaking connectivity, match sizes are too small, and invites from friends don't work reliably.  The lobby menus are bloated with an obvious cash grab shop and "look at me" achievements.  After finally getting into the game the environments are so empty.  Sad textures on bland geometry.  The objectives are agonizingly simple, go here, push button, await dinosaurs.
The AI has simple charge maneuvers with little variance.  Other game modes offer different playstyles, but those are just as droll.  Playing as a dinosaur should be an exciting encounter with you as a 'boss' monster, instead you get mown down in seconds by standard weaponry and vehicles.  The bigger dinosaurs available are sluggish and their hit detection leaves you wondering if you're playing on the same map.  How did the developers attempt to balance smaller dinosaurs against their totally-not-spartan soldiers?  They've strapped 'dino-mite' (oh god this is probably what they called it) onto the back of Compy and Pterodactyls.  Orion: Dino Horde is supposed to be a dinosaur game, or at least about dinosaurs, but there are only two decent selections in the multiplayer.  It is more rewarding to be a faceless marine than the game's namesake.  I would call that a failure.
Speaking of "original" protagonists.  Models, animations, and even the physics feel so similar to Halo titles it is like the budget was spent paying Bungie's royalties, as if they could afford them.  The guns are such obvious plagiarisms they appear to have been stripped from Halo 2 and altered in the simplest ways.  Round a barrel here, recolor there, different gun!  The worst example is the tank.  It is the Scorpion from Halo shamelessly reused.
Orion: Dino Horde is a decent concept, horribly executed.  The developer must be trying some last ditch effort to squeeze money out of the dying player-base.  I've found out there is another game in the works, an open world dino warfare game.  I can only hope that they've learned from their mistakes and attempt to make something different from Dino Horde.
Despite all that I've said I did play this game, I did laugh at it with friends, but I still feel shorted. I spent .99 on this game and I wish I could have it back.  It is that bad.
TL:DR = One of the worst things you could play.

After flying on the original MS FSX before the Steam Edition came out, it was a no brainer for me to pickup the Steam version, it definitely does run slightly better than the old boxed version however not by much.
FSX:SE is still FSX which means that, to get the best experience out of it, not only will you need to invest in a lot of 3rd Party addons such as Scenery, Aircraft, Traffic Packs etc, you'll definitely want to be looking at the ones that aren't listed on Steam as "DLC" such as UK2000/Aerosoft/PMDG/OrbX etc.
Again, just like FSX, a lot of tweaking within the config files is needed to boost its performance or low fps / crashes become common, luckily there is a lot of information on how to tweak your configuration file and what modifications do what, it just takes time and patience to get the right balance as required.
Overall, it really depends on what you want to do, if you'd like to fly in a more "Arcady" setting then using Default FSX will probably be enough, if like myself you want to go down the full realism route, then add-ons and tweaking are definitely required.  I would still recommend this, however, other sims such as P3D (which is effectively a re-released FSX but with more tweaking done under the hood) and X-Plane we may soon see FSX become a thing of the past.

In the first few episodes I thought this was one of the best games ever created. As the game progressed though it showed its faults.
The game looks visually stunning, runs well and it even has very good sound in it. Surround sound is working great here! The story of this game is so captivating, it always kept me playing, wanting me to know more about the dark secrets of Bright Falls. Character development and the relationships between them is well explained. You can see TV shows, listen to radio stations and it contributes greatly to the atmosphere.
Also the pacing of the game started out as ideal. An ideal mixture of a few action packed scenes and much exploration where you feel the threat of the darkness. No scary effect has been used twice. It was impossible to predict what was going to happen, where fights occur and so on. A thing barely any horror game gets right. This game really scared me to death quite a few times.
But the game continued and showed faults, ridicolous ones at times. Episode 3 felt stretched like chewing gum, barely  any story progression at all and an absence of introducing new gameplay mechanics.  Afterwards the pacing was all over the place. No time to feel the fear, everywhere action, combat and even more combat. Sometimes it felt like Left 4 Dead in a 3rd person perspective. Combat itself is mediocre at the very best. Few guns, even fewer enemies. Repetition comes into play and frustration. Dodging attacks is difficult, sometimes even impossible at times. Why is run and dodge bound on the  same button? Quite annoying.
Then the level design quality started dropping. The forests were so repetetive and the "go over small ledge, unable to go back"-element has been abused to death.
And the last driving scene made me almost quit the game. Seriously. I thought it was some twisted test by GladOS. Driving -> Artificial Barrier -> Pass through on foot -> New car. Rinse and repeat. Half a dozen times.
There also  collectibles, in the form of interesting manuscripts, but also coffee thermos. Coffee everywhere, why? Why Remedy? Glimmering objects destroy immersion, especially if the game doesn't even try to explain the reason of them being there in the first place. Sad fact about collectibles: As soon as you start exploring the levels you realize how small the level design is. Invisible barriers and doors impossible to open.
Another concern is the UI of the game. Minimap in a horror game with pretty straightforward level design, really? And why does the game tells me the whole time what to do, I wonder why it didn't tell me to breathe? Reading those manuscripts, or signs scattered throughout the game opens a rectangle with the menu font. Not very immersive at all.
The last very ridicolous thing is the inventory management. Sometimes you just lose all the stuff you had for absolutely no reason. Frequently you hit the maximum amount cap of a certain item. This is atrocious game design.
In the special episodes they show off how good level design could be. Crap was that all scary. You really felt the nightmare. I just wished there would have been more of that.
If it wasn't for the great story, atmosphere and the really great episodes 1,2, 4 (esp. beginning) and the two specials, I probably wouldn't recommend it. If Remedy just cut the game shorter by about 4-5 hours, this could be really epic.

Downloaded Early Years of Flight add-on.
Early impression: how did the industry get off the ground with those aircraft?
Further tinkering was required but here's what I got so far:
1-Mixture set lean gives just enough boost to stay airborne once past the ground-effects lift.
2-The realism setting on FSX required unchecking the "stress causes damage" to allow the overspeed indicator to come up, allowing climb as these motorized box kites were waay prone to stalling out.
3-Flying around obstacles as opposed to climbing was the rule here.  Any gain in altitude required a very shallow angle-of-attack.
4-Best visual aid is to set the POV at a point where a feature on the aircraft corresponds to horizon enough to prevent over-zealous climbing, compensating for the lack of instrumentation.
With these in mind, I was able to complete a traffic pattern at Friday Harbor airport with the Wright model B, Louis Bleriot, and the Handley-Paige.  The Wright took about 5 attempts, but getting her down on the runway without cracking up imparted a major thrill of victory.
I nominated this for the "Best Game I Utterly Stink At" award because it's a terrific game with fun controls and interestingly varied character playstyles that I still can't get past level 5 with.

Fallout Shelter doesn't have any specific goal in mind, so you can spend your spare time increasing your vault's population (and have your own Gary-themed whacko-fest); training your dwellers' SPECIAL stats for gameplay bonuses; or send them all out in the wasteland, and battle a dozen Deathclaws, for that chance to find a rare item - just remember to send them back to the vault if you're going to exit the game, because the timer keeps ticking even when you're out, and reviving a dead vault dweller costs a lot of caps. Tip for new players: a high food level keeps everyone happy and smiling in the face of danger; therefore, invest in it early in the game (or send the useless dwellers out to die in the wilderness), because it dwindles fast if you have too many people.
Overall, a fun casual game. There are microtransactions available, but your vault can survive even without purchasing any of them. You might have to spend more time playing and managing if you want some of the loot that can be purchased in the store, but a day or two of waiting wouldn't hurt.
And there you have it.

The Battle of Mogadishu, more commonly referred to as Black Hawk Down or, locally, as the Day of the Rangers (Somali: Maalintii Rangers), was part of Operation Gothic Serpent and was fought on 3 and 4 October 1993, in Mogadishu, Somalia, between forces of the United States supported by UNOSOM II, and Somali militiamen loyal to the self-proclaimed president-to-be Mohamed Farrah Aidid who had support from armed civilian fighters.
A U.S. Army force in Mogadishu, consisting primarily of U.S. Army Rangers from Bravo Company, 3rd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment; C Squadron, 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta (1st SFOD-D), better known as "Delta Force"; as well as Air Force Combat Controllers and Air Force Pararescuemen and helicopters from 1st Battalion, 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment, attempted to seize two of Aidid's high-echelon lieutenants during a meeting in the city. Shortly after the assault began, Somali militia and armed civilian fighters shot down two UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters. The subsequent operation to secure and recover the crews of both helicopters drew the raid, intended to last no more than an hour, into an overnight standoff in the city. The battle resulted in 18 deaths, 73 wounded, and one helicopter pilot captured among the U.S. raid party and rescue forces. One Pakistani soldier and one Malaysian soldier were killed as part of the rescue forces but other resources claim there was greater loss of life. American sources estimate between 1,500 and 3,000 Somali casualties, including civilians; SNA forces claim only 315 killed, with 812 wounded. The battle is also referred to as the First Battle of Mogadishu to distinguish it from the Second Battle of Mogadishu of 2006.

The game is horribly optomized.  The framerate can stutter like crazy.  The graphics aren't even anything to be overly impressed by even if you zoom all the way in.  It doesn't use the strongest, most vigorous, or even most stable engine.  The minimap is fairly bad, with no capability to zoom in or out or mark waypoints.  There are also lots of bugs.  More UI issues than you can shake a stick at.  Enemies who can run all the way across the map to you in one turn.
But none of that matters.  Because the game is wonderful.
First, the game assumes you're a competent human being.  There are tutorials and there are waypoint markers, but it doesn't hold your hand for every step.  You're expected to balance your party.  If you don't want to have to do it yourself you can look up a good party on the internet, but the game makers don't spell it all out for you.  It's easy for you to mess up, but it's not too hard for you to plan carefully and do just fine.
Second, the story actually has depth.  Characters can have complex motivations, and past actions have consequences.  Some of these consequences aren't obvious for quite some time, but when they come up you'll recognize them.  For the most part they're not just cheap shots.
Third, combat is fun.  It doesn't have the depth of x-com or Fallout 1 & 2, but it has a lot more depth than most modern games.  Weapon types are all quite different, and building a diverse team is encouraged through limiting ammo of each type.
Fourth, there is often more than one way to solve a problem.  You can unlock doors with your lock picking ability, brute force, or even spare explosives you have lying around.  Sometimes different approaches to the same problem can be easier or harder.  Which path you take is your choice.
Fifth, they're continually improving the game.  New patches are coming out after the game has been released.  In a few months, who knows how many of the complaints at the top will still be accurate?

This won't be an extensive review, simply addressing some of the criticism that the game has gotten that I feel has been unfair.
First micro-transactions. I agree with most people on this issue that the addition of micro-transactions in this game was unnecesary and just seemed like a way for a dodgy publisher to make more money of the back of a popular release; that being said I don't agree with many of the people who say that they are forced on you or that you must purchase them to progress in the game. The micro-transactions are stupid, they appear when you open up the market icon, but in 35 hours playing this game, not once did I ever feel the need to purchase anything and I have been manipulated by micro-transactions in the past with multiple games (including the Shadow of War mobile game). This game is NOT designed to make you purchase the market items or manipulate you into doing so, if you really think it is then you must never have been exposed to freemium mobile games.
Second the story. I can't really comment on the accuracy of the story with regards to the overarching lore, but disregarding that I can't see that there is much wrong with the story itself. I agree it isn't fantastic, the characters are not given enough "screen time" and story threads don't amount to much, yet there are some great moments with regards to the story as well as some amazing scenes that really immerse you in the world. Even if the main story isn't that great, there is still the nemesis system which creates an additional stories that happen all the time whilst playing through the game.
Third the positives. They listened to the critisisms of the first game and I don't see many people talking about it. Everyone hated the terrible boss fights of the first game and so they made them better. Everyone said that the first game was too easy and so they made it harder. Everyone loved the nemesis system and wanted more, so they gave us more. They messed up some things coming into this game but they learned from Shadow of Mordor, I think its worth at least some credit.
Final side point, Shelob. Why does everyone hate women? I never thought I would be saying this as someone who laughs at modern day feminism but wtf. As soon as the character was shown all I saw was "why is Shelob a sexy lady?!?!?". The whole point is that she wants Talion to trust her, wouldn't it make more sense that she made herself into a woman rather than a massive, terrifying spider? And I am aware that it might not be entirely canon, but of all the things that are inaccurate, Shelob turning into a form that would be easier to trust is the one that you are all mad about?

Where to begin...
(I'll avoid spoilers)
This is a episodic game in the form of a telltale game sorta. Your choices will effect your playthrough and the world around you. However different from Telltale games is that This is set on a original, built from the ground up, World.
It's set around a High school where you play as a Teenage girl named Max. Who comes back to her hometown, Arcadia Bay, Oregon, on a scholarship to Blackwell. A school for talented students. Early on in the game due to events you learn that Max can rewind time. With Max's new power, and some shady♥♥♥♥♥♥goin on around Arcadia Bay. It's up to you and your old childhood best friend Chloe, to figure out whats going on.
Right off the bat, yes. This game has some really cringy dialogue. I get the whole going for the "teen girl talk" effect, But in reality, not alot of teenagers talk like this. But If you can lower your expectations on it like I did after I heard reviews when Ep 1 came out, then it won't bug you so much.
The gameplay like I said is your standard point and click game almost. It's your job as the player to of course decide which choice you wish to go with or how you play. What dialogue options you'll take, What easter eggs and hidden collectibles you'll find. etc... Added with the time rewind thing, you'll also have to take into consideration how to use your power. You can redo a choice that you really didn't like to do, Talk to a character then do a complete rewind and use info they gave you in the past conversation, and use it on them for the new present conversation. The player will have to think carefully with their choices along with what they use there power for. Breaking open this door, will get you inside but if you forget to rewind, that door will remain busted and it WILL effect your playthrough. Just a example of that.
The visual art style and graphics are very Beautiful. From the scenery, to the in game photos, and the Breathtaking End Episode Cinematics.
The emotional impact this game had on Many players and I included. Is massive. The Game starts off strong a first two episodes. I feel like Ep 3-4 kind of start to lose the magic but there still fine and enjoyable episodes. Ep 5 is just a big ol WTF simulator (I mean this whole game does have to do with time travel, what did you expect?) Characters like Chloe and Max, make them very memorable and probably some of my favorite video game characters in recent years.
The Ending feels somewhat very underwhelming and powerful at the same time. It's definitley a strong emotional ending (regardless of which one you choose) But I felt like the episode was almost rushed and not given enough thought to with the Whole Time Travel thing. Some things happen that make no sense in terms of Time Travel sense, and you start to feel like your not accomplishing anything in the episode.
The Soundtrack alone is a 10/10 it picks up at the right moments and the Song choices for each episode are brilliantly done. You'll probably find yourself listening to it, well after you've beaten the game.
In the End Life is Strange is a Beautiful, Emotional, Breathtaking adventure game That is definitley all about Enjoying the Journey, rather than the Destination. The Dialogue is cringy so lower your expectations.Though the Characters, Soundtrack, and world of this game make it a must buy. I look forward to coming back to this title many times in the future and sharing its praise with friends. Bring on Life is Strange 2.

I really like this game because it manages to do one thing very well that only few games can do. That is connecting narrative, design, and gameplay. The narrative is set during the 80's so the design in the enviroments is vibrant and bright. Plus the pumping soundtrack just yells 80's. For most of the game you are sent by an underground mafia to commit mass murders while high on drugs. So the gameplay is very violent, free flowing, loose, and fast paced. It's easy to lose yourself and you'll probably die alot of times. But at first I was thinking tactically about taking out the room in front of me and after being killed 10 times, I just started wildly swinging a baseball bat around until everything was dead. Suprisingly the latter option worked out alot better than you would think. The gameplay ties to narrative because it really captures the bezerk rage of being drugged up and sent on a sucide mission (which is what the story is about). I also like the fact that you can die instantly but respawn within seconds. Not only does it keep the gameplay fast paced, it also makes you feel like you're expendable which in the context of the story, you are. The narrative is ambiguose but it conveys how dazed, confused, and insane your character is, as the lines slowly blur between hallucinations and reality. This ties into the design in the enviroments because they're surreal and colorful like you're experiencing them through a psychedelic haze. Then you wake up the next morning and your apartment is designed with darker brown colors and everything is messy and scattered almost representing the visual state of having a hangover. Narrative, design, and gameplay all go together to capture the lucid high feel of the 1980's which I love. The only negative is the ending sucks.

Hotline Miami is a top-down shooter set in the 80's with a great style choice and music to match.
by looking at gameplay footage and screenshots you would think this was a fast-paced shooter like Quake, while it is a play style you can choose, you'll be surprised to know that "running and gunning" is actually the most riskiest option, because you die in one hit, making gameplay strategic with the likes of Abe's Oddysee (another game where you die in one hit).
this makes you very vunerable to enemies, and it's recommended you plan out your attacks.
As you might already know this game is quite gory, which in my opinion adds to the charm and satisfying gameplay like 'Soldier of Fortune' being able to dismember your opponents is always great fun to watch, as wrong as that sounds.
The first annoyance I discovered was the controls, these do take time getting use to and trust me you will have to master them, especially in the later sections of the game.
Other annoyances would obviously be the one-hit kills, however this wouldn't be a problem if your enemies weren't so cheap!
Yes, most of the time they are aimbot hit-scanners that will never miss encouraging stealthy and strategic gameplay.
This is a game you'll be replaying over and over again as it is a true challange, especially to newcomers.
However, as cheap as the bots are some of your deaths are a bit unfair, like for example your weapons won't register on the enemy, they hit you with a far hit box, stuff like your enemy's getting more advantages over you.
This game isn't as nearly as difficult as Super Meat Boy, but it's a game that'll make you rage quit or break into violent matters.
So the main goal of each and every level is murder everyone and to make it in one piece, there are some boss fights you won't see coming but I won't spoil anything.

Would I recommend this game, yes go ahead but be warned by the annoyances but I can't garantee anything as I don't know what hardens your fist.

So after a year I decided to play this game again, nothing much has changed since back then.
The graphics are outstanding as always and so is the gameplay. Assemble your robot and launch your attacks against the enemies. Play with strategies or just go for the kill. I have 2 videos, one is team deathmatch and the other capture the batteries. There is also a third game mode, plant the bomb, I will post a video about it on here some other day.
In both I was talking through skype with my mate so we played it organized.
TDM:
CTB:
Unless you squad the teams are pretty balanced! Which is hard to find in any other pvp based game out there. You don't get matched with or against players that are more than 1 rank higher or lower, unless you squad ofcourse.
Being in a squad brings a lot oppertunities and dissadvantages. You know your mate that he won't mess up and it's easy to talk to (no russian language or an other which you dont understand) and you can use certain tactics to win. HOWEVER you can also get matched up against players ranked higher than both of you. Especially if the gap between you and your mates robot rank is big. So keep this in mind.
Now the question might arise, what is this rank that I keep blabbering about? It outputs the strength and agileness of your robot in a simple number ranging from 1-10. Keep in mind that the differences are HUGE. A rank 3 robot can kill a rank 1 robot in 1 hit. A rank 5 can do the same to a rank 3 etc. Ofcourse this isn't always the case, but that are the differences. So yes the games are very balanced.
For once this game isn't pay to win, you can pay for buffs or you can earn them ingame with the special buyable currency known as sparks. They are easy to collect or pay like 1 buck per 100 sparks. This brings buffs such as more xp for your character or double golds from games or 3 way squads. Or you can buy cosmetic stuff, shortly said, the gameplay does not get ruined by peoples with a lot money.
If you have watched the short videos you will have a rough idea by now about what the game is. I highly recommend you to at least give it a try. The tutorial pretty much covers the basic gameplay and play 1-2 rounds online. Most of the players (that speak english) are very kind and will help you rightaway if you're stuck with something. A good community for once in an online game!
The game is free to play, but those game are 9/10 times better than the game for which you pay 20+ bucks.
The sound effects are also superb. With a surround system you can hear where your enemy is walking and act according to their position. For example you don't move and flank them when they get close.
Visual, graphical, gameplay and community wise I give this game a well deserved 9. There are some minor buggs but they won't ruin your gameplay unless you have invested 50+ hours. Then you might be able to spot the first bug ;)
Oh also they have easter eggs in the game! Found a dutch add in the garage.. after owing the game for a year or so...
Hope to see you in game <3

Crashlands starts out of the gate with a good sense of humor, and takes you on an adventure that I enjoyed despite some of my problems with it. The game is very basic in the action RPG genre, and it shows some of its mobile elements (as the game is also available on mobile devices) with some of the control elements and mouse drive controls. With that said, the combat can give a challenge with its sorta give and take gameplay, and it's complemented by a crafting system that has some depth to it. It's a game that took elements that I normally don't enjoy, like “home building” systems, and made them enjoyable for me. It's got a good sense of humor with its small jabs and wit here and there, and the game comes together well as an overall package to deliver a fun experience. I've got 10+ hours in it, but I've seemingly only scratched the surface, as while the game can get repetitive, it definitely delivers on the content in terms of items to collect and craft. Whether it be on Steam or on the mobile platform (if you have something like a Galaxy Tablet, it definitely works well there) (and there's cross platform play), Crashlands is a fun time all around, and is best suited for the kind of adventuring player that wants to take in the sights, and enjoy the trek along the way.

Nuclear Throne is like Binding of Isaac, but faster. You kill more enemies faster, and you die faster. Since enemies drop much-needed health, ammo, and xp pick-ups on death, you can't hide behind cover, you have to move forward constantly.
Skills and weapons combine to create completely ridiculous loadouts. My favourite skills are "Shotgun Shoulders", which makes shotgun pellets hilariously bounce all over the screen, combined with "Impact Wrists", which makes fresh corpses hilariously bounce all over the screen. Melee combat is surprisingly satisfying, with melee weapons reflecting enemy projectiles, and a combination of animation tricks makes each swing feel shockingly weighty for a 2D isometric game.
This game is really ♥♥♥♥ing difficult. There is only one ordinary skill (and no pick-ups) in the game that increases your maximum health, and you have no invincibility frames when hit. Enemy attacks do high amounts of damage. Thankfully, even in later stages, enemies do not feel bullet spongey, but the sheer number of them, with some enemies firing either extremely accurate shots or spraying their attacks everywhere, poses a significant challenge.

Considering it's free, this game's not bad.  You've got to keep in mind it's also an early access game, so there's bound to be some glitches, backdoors, and so on that'll be abused.  It's a good concept and I think in time it has the potential to be a fun game.

After being in the Flight Simulation hobby for nearly 15 years and using flight sims from the 90's to Microsoft's final release before it was bought out (FSX Boxed Edition) I must say FSX-Steam Edition is a BIG improvement over the former boxed version.
As  you can see at the time of this review I have 912 hours logged on the steam version, but off steam I have logged over 12,000 flight hours in nearly 15 years of all flight simulators since I have started this hobby. I have to say that Dovetail did a pretty good job with this release.
They fixed allot of the issues that made the boxed edition horrible. With this version from Steam you no longer have the dreaded low fps (Frame Rates). You no longer have the OOM's (Out of Memory) Errors. You are able to run the graphics at Ultra without any hickups, even in the high end payware VC's (Virtual Cockpits).
Over all this is one major improvement! If you are a Vet Flight Simmer you know what I mean. And if you are new to the hobby, you would be doing yourself a big favor by going with the Steam Version, if you choose the boxed version, you will see why so many if not mostly all boxed users have made the switch to the steam version.

Delta Force is an oldschool budget tactical shooter franchise and Black Hawk Down is the 6th installment. Team Sabre is a big expansion pack set in Colombia and Iran. The core gameplay stays the same, but the locations and the difficulty has increased.
The Visuals.
Same as in BHD. BHD has it's own engine and runs at DirectX8, 4:3 aspect ratio resolution. I managed to get it up to 1200p, it refused to go above. All widescreen solutions stretch / cut off the screen. Considering that it's budget titles made in 2003 the visuals are fine. Decent textures, fine poly count and nice drawing distance (like in every other DF title). Framerate is unlimited. Game is compatible with pretty much all Windows versions.
Considering this is an expansion the mechanics and AI haven't been upgraded and are pretty much the same as in the main game. The only minor complaint is that some objectives are buggy and there are some minor friendly AI bugs.
The Audio.
Just like BHD Team Sabre offers nice background music and nice team dialogues.
The Gameplay.
With the expansion you get 5 missions set in Colombia and 6 missions set in Iran. Some new weapons have been added. Unlike in the main game these missions are way longer and more difficult (you get less saves too). The shortest mission is around 10 minutes and the longest one is half an hour+. Missions include village, airfield, jungle, island, oil rig, oil pipeline and even stronghold raids with various insertion methods. Some of these mission offer far more complex maps with lots of buildings and enemies which easily makes this far more interesting than the main campaign itself.
If you liked Black Hawk Down then you'll most likely will like this expansion even more.

When it comes to the mechanics, they are okay.  Talion controls better than in the original game, there are more animations and the variety of orcs has been turned up to ten.  But ignoring whether or not microtransactions are 'required', the game is simply exhausting to play.  I fully understand why the loot boxes are there, and while yes their inclusion offends me, what offends me even more is that they are ingrained into the play experience.  It's not just pay-for gold boxes, it's that acquiring orcs is time-consuming, albeit fun, and losing them is not.  My first three dominated orcs took me about 40 minutes to acquire and then one of them betrayed me, killed the other orc and my last orc died when he came to my rescue.
It's certainly an interesting game and the moment-to-moment gameplay is quite fun, honestly it is.  But the overarching concept is far, far too drawn out.  The personalities and interesting stories are stretched too thin, the side activities too numerous, and as stated: the gathering of orcs too slow.  What's the solution?  Loot boxes of course.  Rather than spending twenty minutes dominating two orcs, you can get them right now from a silver box!  Sure, that's an in-game way of getting what you want but if the solution is to just hand them over then maybe the fun way of getting them, stalking and domination, could use some work.  Like any modern AAA game there is ten hours of content here being stretched over 40 or more and that just dilutes what fun there should be.
So while I do think you can get your money's worth out of this, keeping in mind it is 100$ for the full experience, do I really recommend a game that is designed to wear you out and rely on instant gratification to make up for it's shortcomings?  No.  The game was designed with the loot boxes in mind.  Progression is deliberately long and tiring enough to make even the silver ones tempting.  I know: if you decline the data policy you have to play the game offline (like that's a minus), but it lets you see squarely how the game is 'intended' to be played.  And it's quite evident once you have a taste for the silver boxes, that's what is meant to make you more pliable for the cash money ones.
And that's just not an experience I would recommend.  I bought it, the gameplay is fun in small doses but I doubt I'll ever see the end of Talion's story because the game is too long, too grinding and too exhausting.  The gameplay is wholly designed to push you into the marketplace to buy loot crates, of any kind, to make an advance on the time you would've spent otherwise.  Without them, who knows how long the game is but I know this: too long.  What's on offer here is not a 100 hour journey I would want to take.  If EXP boosters and 'free' loot and orcs doesn't highlight how the game is designed to be played, well: give it a try.  Because without the loot boxes it's a slog, and to me at least, that only makes it seem worse.

Almost exactly a year ago, when Philip Seymour Hoffman haven't yet died, defending New Zealand from Attila the Hun's ressurected zombie hordes, I got my hands on tech demo for Spintires for the first time. I haven't been the same person ever since.
Upon my birth Reptilians have planted a device in my head that lets them read my thoughts. For a reason unknown to me they established Oovee Game Studios (oh come on, doesn't THAT sound Reptilian?) and used all the information they gathered to create a video game of my dreams.
In Spintires you assume the role of a Soviet truck driver in 1980's Siberian woodlands where a concept of "concrete roads" is considered an imperialists' attempt to weaken the USSR.
Your main task (and by far really the only one) is to pick up wooden logs from point A and deliver them to point B.
Easy, right? Well... IT'S♥♥♥♥♥♥♥NOT.
At the beginning you get max 2 vehicles - usually a jeep and a small truck. Jeep is purely for exploration purposes, in which it excels, while the truck, in theory capable of delivering small logs, is best in support role as it doesn't even have an all wheel drive. To be able to complete your task you have to start with exploration.
Your minimap is full of dark spots which you uncover driving near their centers. Knowing the terrain is critical in planning the route. Even the biggest trucks won't go through rivers and dense forests. You have to drive smart. But even the best route available won't promise you success if you don't have the right equipment. More trucks can be unlocked the same way as minimap which is driving near them.
All vehicles can be customised in garages, though the options available vary for each vehicle. Your trucks can carry spare parts (as trucks can be damaged), fuel (as some trucks may use even 20+ liters of fuel per MINUTE of driving), trailers for wooden logs in different sizes (there are 3 sizes of wooden logs). If your main truck is badly damaged or runs out of fuel you can use the other one, with proper equipment, to save it.
Whether exploring or completing the delivery your greatest enemy is Russia itself. It does what Russia does. It kills you. It devours you. It consumes both your truck and your very soul. This is where the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥gets serious. Physics in the game are simply marvellous. Trucks react to every bump, each wheel's suspension is independent, tires deform. Terrain is also gorgeous. Mud deforms under your wheels in real time and it stays deformed for as long as you play on the map, water behaves in a very natural way and you can mow down small trees.
The game is pretty difficult and it favors patience. Moving through the mud is slow and painful. More than once you will find yourself stuck or flipped upside down. In many times you will have to use the winch (it's a really helpful tool) or revert your truck back to garage (but only in casual mode. In hardcore mode if you're♥♥♥♥♥♥♥then you're♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The game is also moddable. First mods were released for closed beta which sounds promising for the future of this title. There's also multiplayer.
There are some downsides as well. Graphics are good but not the best, the only real task so far is delivering wood, the game saves your progress only on one map at once (if you want to play on another map all your progress is lost), maps are similar in many ways, draw distance could be better, lighting at night is pretty awkward AND THE WAY CAMERA WORKS IS A REAL BUMBERFUK. I don't want to sound like a fanboy (even though I am one) but I believe many of those problems will be fixed as both developers and community do their best.
You can download tech demo
to see if the concept of Spintires seems to be appealing to you as I believe it will not be to many. Many of you fukers will be disgusted by it.
So should you buy it then?
Because in the end the money you give to the developers, if not you, will at least benefit me, and honestly it's all that really matters.

There is a statue in the game, which says "i wish they'd use Unreal Engine". Wasteland 2 looks really ugly, i mean, it doesn't look like you would expect game to look in 2014. Graphics are bad both tech and design-wise which is something you cant possibly fix with patches. Some questionable game-design descisions, like placing explosives on everything (including piles of Cow♥♥♥♥♥♥, making enemies with tons of durability AND damage AND speed at the same time and all in the same encounter, difficulty spikes (even if you take away the fact that difficulty levels themselves are poorly balanced, basically, supreme jerk means you deal 50% less damage, but take 100% more). Somehow restricted character development which may seem complex and can even make you sit in character creation for at least an hour, but when you hit the actual game you probably will be dissapointed. Like, you expect charisma or intelligence to have some affection on conversation options(since it was like that at least in Fallout games, right?), but charisma wont affect anything except leadership skill aura and XP gainings (there is also hidden stuff like some number of potential companions wont join you if you dont have certain ammount of party charisma, basically you need to have total of 25 to be able to recruit every potential candidate). Intelligence doesnt affect anything except skill points per level and some action points. For extra conversation options you have 3 skills that are not affected by any of the attributes. Combat system lacks complexity, it is even less complex that recent XCOM remake, which was pretty simplified. It is even less complex than Fallout 1-2 or Fallout Tactics and it is not what you may call "different concept", it is just dumbed down and badly designed system. There are also some annoying bugs, especially in second part of the game (i assume it wasnt part of the community beta).
I Could spend all day listing all of the downsides of this unrefined gem, but it wont be necessary because i got what i expected - an interesting and massive storyline, where even "postal" side-quest may have unexpected options with unexpected results. Rock-solid writing literally for everything and everyone in any part of the game. If you ready to suffer just to get what this game realy good at - then get it. I've been addicted to Spintires ever since the first tech demo that came out around the time of the kickstarter.
I can honestly say that I've never played another game like it, and even though I've played for a few hours I still haven't delivered a single load of lumber.  There's something really relaxing and satisfying about driving these big trucks across muddy roads, and through shallow rivers.  The nature sounds and the roar of the engine are all you hear (no music) and it really feels like you're cruising through the back woods of some forgotten old socialist republic.
The huge 6+ wheeled monstrosities really feel huge when you're driving them, the physics and simulation are superb, and all in all this is one of the greatest and most unique games I've ever played.

Over all, its an ABOVE AVERAGE game and should be priced at $ 30-35 $

Broken age is a point and click adventure game that is challenging to the point that you will probably pull out your cellphone to look up advice a few times when you get frustrated at not progressing. As with most point and clickers, you will find yourself doing a lot of detective work. Running back and forth, trying different combinations of things, throwing everything at the wall and seeing what sticks. Some people don't have the patience for this type of gameplay, so be aware of that before picking up this game.
The story is split in two halves, featuring a boy and a girl living in different worlds. You can jump between the two character at just about any time, which is helpful when you come across those "I'm stumped" moments that you want to move on from. The female story happens to be the more interesting of the two, but both stories seem to be worthwhile. The characters that you come across are all lovable with great dialogue and voice actors, which helps when you're playing in a genre that requires a lot of trial and error by talking to NPCs.
