5 out of 5 space scientists recommend you play this game before you try to apply at NASA.
The game has a somewhat steep initial learning curve, specially if you're not a wannabe space scientist / engineer / astronomer already.
Not that you can't learn it by pure trial and error - it's just that you're gonna kill a lot more little green creatures that way. But you'll kill them sometime anyway!
It is also a very good sandbox, and a game about using your imagination and creativity. Besides a good reason to learn something about space and physics.
Designing and building is like building stuff out of Legos, except the stuff you build can leave atmosphere and enter orbit.
Most spaceship parts in the game are inspired on actual rockets, planes and spacecraft modules, like those used by NASA. So you can build things similar to the Saturn V, the Space Shuttle, Apollo missions, Falcon 9 rocket, or any design of your own that you can think of.
The stock game is already cool, and there are LOTS and LOTS of mods that add much to the base game. The mods aren't fan-made hacks, they are inherent to the design of the game - there's a "mods" item on the games main menu! The modding community is very active and encouraged, and there are mods for various styles of gameplay.
From improved graphics to a full scale real solar system with 9 planets (including Pluto), it's one of the most modable and actively modded games out there. All for free.
Just look at how many hours I spent playing it. It's currently (at the time of writing this) the most played game in my list, and beats every other game I have hands down, in hours played per buck. Totally worth it!

The little back story on this would be that I found out about the soundtrack of this game before I ever owned the game itself, do yourself a YouTube search and you'll get the score. I loved the hell out of it and I found myself listening to while I played other games like Minecraft, KSP, or AI War. It's fast, energized, frenzied, and sometimes rather calming with it's more toned down tunes. So that said, I eventually owned the game...
First off, the music fits. It's a furious play through as you sociopath your way though buildings and slaughter their inhabitants after receiving cryptic messages from your voicemail. The neon haze of the '80s era of living creeps into your subconscious as you blitz through doors taking no prisoners. I had read that stealth was involved, but I honestly found to be quick reactionary style game where you bounce from victim to victim, and if you die, you're immediately start over to try again with slightly different timing from the previous attempt. Weapons vary, but give me the knife any day as it has the quickest draw-speed compared to the other weapons and honestly, I didn't have to guess of it's effects. Kill the thugs and make you're way to the boss if there is one. It's a pretty straightforward game that ranks each performance and rewards you with different masks that provide benefits of bonuses.
I can't help say something about the controls. The screen is already disorientating at times as it zooms in and out on it's own and swivels and gyrates as if the camera has seasickness. This on it's own fuels the blaze of your fury as you proceed through each level, and it's great! But it mixed with the controls is very aggravating because often I lost where my cursor was and I found myself facing the wrong was as I ran up to my enemies to attack (obviously you need to be facing forward to attack what's in front of you.) The movement controls are independent from the direction in which you face. Having tried this with keyboard and mouse first, I found impossibly difficult, and I bought myself a game pad specifically so I can trying using the dual stick controls.
Though using the game pad was better, it still made it difficult. I'm running that way, my character should already be facing that way. I don't know a man alive who can run full sprint forwards while swinging a bat out of his backside. That's the crux of this experience. I loved the graphics, the flow, the music, and the energetic feeling it elicited from me. But the clunky control format made it really hard to keep that momentum up and I usually quit out of frustration more than dislike of the game. It's a mixed bag, so I only recommend the game if you have a game pad. Otherwise I'd skip it.

Anyway I hope they do the right thing over the next year and patch or turn it over to the community; for me the ending was mass effect 3 cringe worthy and I hope they have better ideas for Torment.

Mafia III will and always will have a very split audience. The game to me is very interesting so far, open world and many things to do but it doesnt quite live up to the expectations I've had from the pre-order.
First off, if your playing it for the story you will really enjoy this game. Between the characters, interactions, cutscenes and map diversity you truly feel like you are in the late 1960s. The styling was done correct as well as the enviorment, due to the lowlying lands of 'New Bordeaux' it gives you a down south feeling in the late 60s where race was still a major factor. It really has you on your toes the whole time when walking into the wrong part of town. The storyline itself is very interesting and keeps you wanting more, the cutscenes dont get old and repeditive seems like there is always something new and interesting to get you excited to play again and try new things. It does feel like you are really living the life of the main character and put back into a specific date and time, driving around in a car through racially devided towns listening to some of the best music from the 60s. You can feel the emotions of the character which gives you the drive to play more.
On the other hand, the game has all of the shortfallings of earier games.
-The driving still seems really rough, and the same cars are seen around every corner. I prefer running almost everywhere when not on a mission or going long distances.

-Ive played the game on hard mode and its extremely easy to stealth most missions, sneaking around and taking out enemys one-by-one because they pace the same spot back and forth.
-The lock-pick setup seems really dull and pointless, its almost impossible to NOT pick a lock. The method of breaking the lock seems to have nothing to do with how its actually done rather just 'do this right and the lock is broken'
-Every collectible is easy to find, after preforming specific actions you can see them on your map. Essencially giving you the locations of every item in game.
-30 FPS lock, leaves you feeling the game is at a constant slower-speed and for everyone with a higher end system.
All in all, I enjoy the game, if you are someone who is interested in a games story line then you will too.
With the shortcomings in the game and the only REAL positive being the storyline missions it leaves you questioning what will there be to do after the game is completed? Will the game sit in your Steam library forever never to be touched again? After the first playthrough will there be anything else interesting about the game, or will you be left driving the same cars, doing the same things, aimlessly? Time will tell.
Worth the buy if you are looking for a story to follow and something different. If you are looking to cruise around a late-60s racially devided city looking for trouble or truth trying to fix corruption while getting your hands dirty. This is the game for you.
If you are looking for a GTA style game, this is not it. The driving makes you feel uncomfortable, the weapons have terrible accuracy. The police chaces will actually make you want to lose the police and run away rather than have an all out-vendetta.
I would have personally waited a little while till the price of the game came down, im on the fence if I really want to give the game a positive or negative rating. But it did deliver what you would expect from the Mafia series. A game with a great storyline, and okay-ish functionality.

Story - 10/10. The story of Alan Wake is a masterpiece. Little bit of Hitchcock, little bit Twilight Zone, lot of Twin Peaks and Stephen King. Everything is extremely well written and flows together perfectly.
Presentation - Again 10/10. The game play and story flows together seemlessly. It plays out not so much like a tv show or movie, but like a miniseries. It's very distinctive. That's an impressive feat. The camera angles, the story arch, the presentation in general, it's almost tv worthy. The setting is amazing. It pulls you right into Washington state, with all of it's beauty and isolation.
Gameplay - 6.5/10. (That's not a bad score. I'm a tough critic. I know I gave the story and presentation 10/10, but I believe It's brilliant. Best of any game I've played.) The game plays well. A few quirks here and there. The combination of flashlight and gun works well, keeping you at a cautious pace. If you were able to blaze through it with guns popping, it would take away a lot of the suspense. They also give you just enough exploration and collectibles to keep you from complaining about it. I would like to point out that I did not feel like I had to "endure" the gameplay to get to the end.
Music - 10/10. Not just the song choice, but the use and placement of the music is just superb. This is one of the unexpected high points of the game.
All in all, this one is a gem and I was lucky enough to pick it up on a whim. It's so much more than a game, it's entertainment. If you love Twin Peaks and video games, this is a dream come true.

This isn't exactly a horror game. Lotta jump-scares, and hella dark atmosphere, but this game is more action than horror. Every single part that takes place in the dark woods with scary♥♥♥♥♥music always makes me wanna go and cry in the corner, though, so I would have to say that dreading every single step you take before taking another step into the dark is a very good way of capturing the suspenseful atmosphere.
Some may say this is a story-driven game, but I never really felt connected to Alan or Barry. The quips Barry consistently made were out of place and didn't feel natural. I know, he's supposed to be coping with the situation by making stupid jokes and trying top get his mind onto anything besides the impending doom. That doesn't make the SHEER AMOUNT of jokes he makes any less annoying. Or the jokes themselves any less ♥♥♥♥♥♥.
My thoughts about the plot started to turn around in the later half of the game, when the things start to connect. It probably wasn't influenced at all by recently watching in The Mouth of Madness and loving the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of that movie. Nope, not at all. Anyways, the whole plot suddenly became interesting as I start to wonder about the 'what ifs' and wondering what happens next.
Of course all the hope that the story might be interesting was immediately dashed when the climax came. No spoilers here, but it really felt heavy handed and very much like a cop-out from the writers.
The gameplay wasn't original, but it was executed rather well. As someone who likes to play on the hardest difficulty from the get-go, though, I felt like the challenge was in how many enemies you could run past in order to conserve all your ammo and batteries. Which isn't bad at all, a lot of good horror games are designed to be this way (ala Resident Evuil and Silent Hill.) The problem with this is, you're encouraged to go Rambo on everything. Which is counter-productive to how you play (or at least how I played [which was like the chicken I am]) The result is that I end almost every single level with a large surplus of supplies, happy that I used almost none of them through the level except for the parts where you're forced to fight.
I used a keyboard and mouse for this game, so I'm not entirely sure how the controls handle there, but on the keyboard they were simple and tight. At least from what I remember. It was rather difficult to turn around quickly, something that is imperitive when dealing with enemies that LOVE LOVE LOVE to jump out behind you. The length of how long Alan can sprint often gave way to much frustration.
So... I can't really think of anything else to talk about? OH, the collectables are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Why the hell would you put collectables that are only available from a difficulty that you have to unlock after beating the game? A few of the easter eggs made me chuckle. Uhhhh.... that's about it.
Conclusion: 6/10

The LastNightMary is less-than-great horror point-and-click, its major flaw being the unintentional (I guess) aesthetical similarity of most areas in the game. Still, it manages to create a ghastly atmosphere in which one never feels entirely safe; a surprising achievement for such a low-budgeted indie game.
Positive aspects include carefully crafted close-up screens and local folklore elements, all working together to make this short game an unique experience. Some Brazilian players may also find the voice acting a little exotic, as Piauí's accent (from the same province where the Cabeça de Cuia legend originated) is not often heard on mainstream media - an aspect that helps to enhance the overall mood.
All in all, this videogame may be compared to Zé do Caixão (Coffin Joe)’s movies: technical limitations are part of its DNA, and otherwise it wouldn’t be half as interesting as it is. I'm glad to hear that a new game from the same developers is already on the way.

This won't be an extensive review, simply addressing some of the criticism that the game has gotten that I feel has been unfair.
First micro-transactions. I agree with most people on this issue that the addition of micro-transactions in this game was unnecesary and just seemed like a way for a dodgy publisher to make more money of the back of a popular release; that being said I don't agree with many of the people who say that they are forced on you or that you must purchase them to progress in the game. The micro-transactions are stupid, they appear when you open up the market icon, but in 35 hours playing this game, not once did I ever feel the need to purchase anything and I have been manipulated by micro-transactions in the past with multiple games (including the Shadow of War mobile game). This game is NOT designed to make you purchase the market items or manipulate you into doing so, if you really think it is then you must never have been exposed to freemium mobile games.
Second the story. I can't really comment on the accuracy of the story with regards to the overarching lore, but disregarding that I can't see that there is much wrong with the story itself. I agree it isn't fantastic, the characters are not given enough "screen time" and story threads don't amount to much, yet there are some great moments with regards to the story as well as some amazing scenes that really immerse you in the world. Even if the main story isn't that great, there is still the nemesis system which creates an additional stories that happen all the time whilst playing through the game.
Third the positives. They listened to the critisisms of the first game and I don't see many people talking about it. Everyone hated the terrible boss fights of the first game and so they made them better. Everyone said that the first game was too easy and so they made it harder. Everyone loved the nemesis system and wanted more, so they gave us more. They messed up some things coming into this game but they learned from Shadow of Mordor, I think its worth at least some credit.
Final side point, Shelob. Why does everyone hate women? I never thought I would be saying this as someone who laughs at modern day feminism but wtf. As soon as the character was shown all I saw was "why is Shelob a sexy lady?!?!?". The whole point is that she wants Talion to trust her, wouldn't it make more sense that she made herself into a woman rather than a massive, terrifying spider? And I am aware that it might not be entirely canon, but of all the things that are inaccurate, Shelob turning into a form that would be easier to trust is the one that you are all mad about?
Fight or flight, I chose flight.

Life is Strange is one of those choice-based story games that is in the same vein of Telltale games. It stands out as a top-tier title in this niche genre for its high concept story, which was met with surprisingly fluid game mechanics and a multitude of choices that have lasting consequences. Though the genre suffers with only a few choices really mattering in the grand scheme of things, Life is Strange does a terrific job of carrying changes over into other episodes with unpredictable consequences. While the mechanics allow for you to entertain the consequences of all options, you are ultimately tasked to select one before progressing. But knowing the reactions ahead of time allows for you to make a more informed decision without having to replay the entire game or episode over in full length.
As for the story, I'll just say that an ordinary teenage girl gets the power to rewind time and uses it to cope with life in a small forest-y town. Despite the cringy dialogue and out-of-date memes that accurately described adolescence years ago, the sheer mystery of character motivations will keep you going through the episodes. The writers also went to a great length to pace out the storylines - nothing ever felt rushed. If anything, you might feel that you wished that there were more opportunities to connect with minor characters. I guess that's what fanfic is for.
TL;DR - Life Is Strange is an outstanding game in the Telltale-like story rich genre for it's near-perfect triangle of mechanics meeting original storytelling that shares a good balance of gameplay with the cutscenes. You may feel a little off-put by the environment and some characters, but you'll always want to know what they're up to and what role they have to play in the story.

Mountain is a semi-interactive screensaver masquerading as a game worth 99 cents.
I say ‘semi’ interactive because while the game’s world—comprised of a single mountain dotted with trees, boulders, and random objects—can be spun around, examined from different angles, and viewed from the starlit vastness of space, I always felt distant from what little action I witnessed. The weather shifts from snowy to rainy to sunny whether you’re watching or not; random objects appear without any personal context (I received two trash bins, a bed, and a padlock, amongst others); and when Mountain expresses its thoughts, it does so with little to no awareness of my presence as a player.
But according to Mountain’s developer, David O’Reilly, this is sort of the point: “It's designed to run in the periphery of your life,” he writes in an August 2014 update. “You can play Mountain while playing other games. If you are not playing it, it will play itself.” In other words: You don’t really HAVE to play Mountain. Its contents are so inconsequential that it requires only a tiny fraction of your attention. It matters that little. But give me a dollar anyway! Thanks!
(Ironic side note: For a game meant to run serenely “in the periphery of your life,” Mountain is a noticeable CPU hog that will likely overheat your computer, especially if you’re using a laptop.)
The only thing about Mountain that I found interesting or entertaining was how oddly bi-polar it was. In my hours of game play (or non-play), I began to notice that Mountain’s musings fell into distinct categories, ranging from Dalai Lama-esque mindfulness:
“I see great purity in today’s utter perfection.”
“I feel at one with the universe inside this foggy winter night.”
“What is sadness?”
…to a teenage girl’s volatile ‘feels’:
“I’m super into this dreamy night.”
“I couldn’t care less about today’s rain.”
“Maybe I am alone because my rocks are ugly.”
…to the nagging of a self-absorbed ex:
“I’m a total babe.”
“Helloooooo?”
Sorta cute, but ultimately, things most people will hear for free. While, you know, living their actual lives.
At the end of the day, Mountain falls in line with dozens of other titles lauded by some for pushing the boundaries of what a game can be and crucified by others for daring to call itself a game at all. I tend to side with the latter, though less harshly, as Mountain did serve as a pretty background time-waster for the few hours I played it. Mountain will definitely appeal to collectors of snow globes and people who like half-heartedly watching ennui-rich land masses against a faint ambient soundtrack. A niche market, for sure, but an “experience” some may enjoy.

I haven't played the original Wasteland or Fallout 1 or 2.  My introduction to Fallout was through Bethesda's Fallout 3 and then Obsidian's Fallout: New Vegas.  I fell in love with the post-apocalyptic wasteland instantly and craved more.  Years later and I find this game on Steam.  Looking into it more, I realize this game sounds great.  My friends have always talked about how great the old Fallouts are, and I've always wanted to play them, but just didn't have access.  So with this game out, I decided I would not only get to play a more modern isometric Fallout, but also an updated classic cRPG that is part of what Fallout was entirely based on.
I'm only a few hours in the game, but don't plan to stop anytime soon.  I'll be completely honest, it's a flawed game with bugs applenty (none-game breaking) and with a kinda wonky interface that takes time to get used to.  It's a super slow game that takes time to get into and that doesn't have an overload on story (no SAVE THE WORLD kinda plot here, it's smaller and a more personal story).  But if you like in depth RPG's and love Fallout/post-apocalyptic wasteland games, this game might be for you.  It's a story customized to your choices and where you feel that your choices matter.  On the other hand, your choices will let you know that no good deed goes unpunished, as all choices have consequences and no matter what you do, by helping someone, you're going to either hurt someone else, or let them get hurt.
Also if you like Baldur's Gate or Dragon Age, or D&D, this is pretty much a post-apocalyptic setting D&D in the real world gameplay wise.  So there is that.
Overall, I do recommend this game.  It's a flawed product, but I appreciate it for what it is, and how much work has gone into it.  It's an accomplishment in the gaming industry to see such a successful Kickstarter for a game that has been so deserving for so long, and if you are able to accept it's bugs and problems, you will be rewarded for your adventures!

I was gripped by Alan Wake's presentation during the first hour of playing: gorgeous but ominous scenery of remote mountain-top villages hiding secrets that disturb the senses, psychological horror narrative that plays with perception and a sensitive inspiration from Stephen King's works and Twin Peaks that was well-thought and in good taste.
But then the game drowned itself in a sea of subpar shooter gameplay.
Warily, dreading the unwelcome diversion from a story I had just taken a liking for, I trudged on through the countless identical encounters. It can't be long, I thought, it's just an early combat level to satisfy the shooter crowd and then I'll get back to the good parts. It's not that bad, maybe I'll be able to avoid most of the encounters if I try - and just look at the pretty scenery oooh.
Three hours later I was still in the forest repeating mandatory shootouts while slowly forgetting what Alan had seen or was trying to achieve in his arc. With sadness I had to contend that I would need to abandon Alan Wake to the forgotten part of my Steam library, its secrets forever unexplored.
Maybe I should recommend this game to people who are bigger fans of action-shooter genre games. There might be moments in life when I can enjoy a shooter, maybe even one as clunky and dull as the parts I mention in this game. However, the mindset that one must be in when I desire to play Alan Wake - a mindset so tastefully enhanced and sustained during the exploratory/narrative segments of the game- is so dissonant from the mindset of generic shooting, that I feel it doesn't let one enjoy either aspect. Story detracts from gameplay and vice versa. Such a shame that one cannot turn the combat off.

I always get excited when we get horror from unexpected places. Zombies and vampires and long-haired Asian girls have pretty well run their course, but when was the last time you encountered a creature from Brazilian myth? The Last NightMary is just such a tale, pitting you against a bulbous, scampering thing in a deadly race against time. And just like a lot of races, it'll be over before you know it.
You play a young woman named Mary, fresh off a troubled past and now stuck in the wrong place at the wrong time. The entire game takes place in fields of tall grass by a river and the one dilapidated shack out there, all of which factor into the story of the thing chasing you. I'll keep it vague but there's a thing you need to do to keep it from killing you, and it's steeped in mysticism you'll need to collect a handful of notes to understand.
The Last NightMary plays like a first-person adventure game. Each scene can have elements to look at, items to take, and points to use those items on. However, much of your time is going to be spent scrambling around the fields, which form a maze of very samey clearings with the occasional point of interest. The one structure in the game is only four rooms as well, so in the end you're not going to be finding much to puzzle out. As a matter of fact I think there's only 10 or so items in the whole game. Also, I'm going to avoid spoiling anything about the monster but its effectiveness is short-lived once you puzzle out the simple mechanics behind it.
You might be thinking this doesn't sound all that great, and indeed I was on the fence about recommending this game. The Last NightMary was the product of a game jam and it shows, being easily beatable in 20 minutes even on your first attempt. And yet I stuck with it for longer, poking into the details and corners and finding little secrets there. There are a mess of endings depending on what you find on your way to the conclusion, and a secret ending that takes plenty of effort to get but will please the Silent Hill fans in the audience.
The art is perfectly serviceable for a game of this scope, especially the monster which manages to unsettle in his aggressive loping. The sound design helps with the proper horror moments, thanks to some clever tracks and well-placed stingers. Again, it's an incredibly short game with few hurdles to clear, but I enjoyed my time with it. There's more to unpack if you start delving into the many achievements, and even if you don't it's a fun, sometimes tense ride the first time through. Any horror fan looking for something new will get some mileage out of this lean little tale.

This is a point and click game with no animations, not even in the cutscenes, so if you're looking for fast-paced action move on!
You go from clearing to clearing in the long grass searching for clues and bodies, trying to avoid the monster constantly appearing. It makes you panic a bit trying to click the right spot to escape and it still got my adrenalin pumping now and then well into the game.
There are 5 different endings, you have to restart and do all of them to fully complete the game. Part of it is a ritual you have to perform to reach most of the endings. There seem to be no clues whatsoever to get the correct combination and I've calculated that there are 720 possible permutations. In my opinion that's unfeasible without consulting a guide. Perhaps I missed some vital clue but I don't think so - I have all achievements and seen everything there is to see in the game.
The storyline is above average for this type of thing, probably due to the fact that it's a real legend and the game has been built around it rather than some lame tale made up by the developer and stuffed into the gameplay just-because. It's a Brazilian legend so the narration is Portuguese (with English subtitles) which I think adds to the atmosphere.
This is an achievement hunter's dream. There are 45 of them, many of which have to be specifically attempted rather than just following the normal game progression so a big thumbs-up for that. 7 trading cards too.
A couple of hot tips for you:
Despite the limited play area there's several hours of gameplay if you go for all the endings and chase the achievements, especially if you do it without reading a guide. I got it on sale and was very satisfied with it but not sure if I would pay full price.

Nuclear Throne is an action packed roguelike developed by Vlambeer that takes place in the apocalyptic future. You find yourself playing as one of 12 mutants fighting to stay alive long enough to reach the fabled Nuclear Throne, a device that is said to be able to revert the world to what it once was. This game is sure to keep you hooked in a love/hate relationship with its frustrating but rewarding gameplay, many characters that offer a different style of playing each, variety of weapons (over 100 in total,) and seven playable areas with many other secret areas to discover.
-Beautiful art drawn by Paul Veer
-Music that captures the mood and environment perfectly by Jukio Kallio
-Addicting and challenging gameplay
-12 different characters that allow for a different gameplay experience every time.
-Over 100 different weapons that are satisfying and fun to use. Ranging from a simple Revolver to a Double Minigun and a Super Plasma Cannon
-A wide variety of enemies that are sure to test your worthiness of the Throne
-Cooperative gameplay: local and a fantastic mod that allows you to play online with a friend developed by YellowAfterlife
-The game is locked to 30FPS
-It is also drawn at a 4:3 aspect ratio because it "prefers vertical movement"
-Some aspects and enemies are a tad
challenging for a game that plays at 4:3
-The developers have stated it will
go on sale. Even for its low price, sometimes I feel as if it isn't worth the price
-Infrequent updates: The developers often delay updates for months, the most recent of which has been delayed 307 days since its announcement (as of Nov. 23, 2016)
After all is said and done, I feel Nuclear Throne is an excellent game overall, but no game is without its flaws, especially this one; but I would certainly recommend it to anyone who enjoys a challenge.

The little back story on this would be that I found out about the soundtrack of this game before I ever owned the game itself, do yourself a YouTube search and you'll get the score. I loved the hell out of it and I found myself listening to while I played other games like Minecraft, KSP, or AI War. It's fast, energized, frenzied, and sometimes rather calming with it's more toned down tunes. So that said, I eventually owned the game...
First off, the music fits. It's a furious play through as you sociopath your way though buildings and slaughter their inhabitants after receiving cryptic messages from your voicemail. The neon haze of the '80s era of living creeps into your subconscious as you blitz through doors taking no prisoners. I had read that stealth was involved, but I honestly found to be quick reactionary style game where you bounce from victim to victim, and if you die, you're immediately start over to try again with slightly different timing from the previous attempt. Weapons vary, but give me the knife any day as it has the quickest draw-speed compared to the other weapons and honestly, I didn't have to guess of it's effects. Kill the thugs and make you're way to the boss if there is one. It's a pretty straightforward game that ranks each performance and rewards you with different masks that provide benefits of bonuses.
I can't help say something about the controls. The screen is already disorientating at times as it zooms in and out on it's own and swivels and gyrates as if the camera has seasickness. This on it's own fuels the blaze of your fury as you proceed through each level, and it's great! But it mixed with the controls is very aggravating because often I lost where my cursor was and I found myself facing the wrong was as I ran up to my enemies to attack (obviously you need to be facing forward to attack what's in front of you.) The movement controls are independent from the direction in which you face. Having tried this with keyboard and mouse first, I found impossibly difficult, and I bought myself a game pad specifically so I can trying using the dual stick controls.
Though using the game pad was better, it still made it difficult. I'm running that way, my character should already be facing that way. I don't know a man alive who can run full sprint forwards while swinging a bat out of his backside. That's the crux of this experience. I loved the graphics, the flow, the music, and the energetic feeling it elicited from me. But the clunky control format made it really hard to keep that momentum up and I usually quit out of frustration more than dislike of the game. It's a mixed bag, so I only recommend the game if you have a game pad. Otherwise I'd skip it.

I 100%'d this game in 44 hours without spending a dime more than the base game costs. There is no grindwall, there is no paywall, and overall it's a very fun Arkham style action game.
You're handed tons of tools to kill orcs, and you can do so however you please. The improvements from Shadow of Mordor are great, and make it feel like a true sequel. Enough to resemble the first one, but tacking on so many more abilities, movement options, mounts, and equipment.
The Orcs have such personality and each one feels pretty unique to the last. You could easily get lost in building the perfect army. My main gripe is that you can't skip their intros, which later in the game when you're facing 7-12 orcs at a time, you kind of start to suffer as you sit through 5 orc intros, move two feet, and get greeted with another 3. It gets old fast, especially when they can trigger mid combo.
All in all, Shadow of War is Shadow of Mordor turned to 11, and that's just what I wanted from this game. It's worth the 60 dollars for the base game, and I definitely recommend picking it up if you can spare it. If not, 100% grab it on sale.

I guess this could be called
– at least in the way that it basically is on the same level as
when it comes to quality and dev effort, so definitely not your average
type of deal.
In short, it's a great offroad simulator. You drive on muddy stretches that used to be roads and try to avoid getting stuck in the mud, or you drive around the roads and try not getting permanently wedged between trees. Along the way you transport logs, unlock things and go exploring blindly on the blacked out parts of the maps.
Lasting power can probably be compared with Euro Truck Sim as well. You don't have the long term business objective of ETS2, but finishing all the maps in Spintires will take enough time to get your money's worth. The different maps feel a little more varied than the stretches of Europe's highways as well.
The lack of cabin view is a disappointment, but on the other hand you'd probably need at least three screens and Track IR or probably Occulus to get a good enough sense of what's outside the truck to see the heck you're doing from inside the cabin anyway. External camera works usually well, but I just spent 15 minutes getting unstuck from a tree because the same tree prevented the dynamic camera from letting me see the best suited winch mount...
Physics wise there's not much to complain about, and same goes for handling. The trucks are nicely rendered and the types behave differently enough to keep interest up. The environments are kind of pretty but a little lifeless. I saw a bunch of flowers that made me go "ahh" at one spot, but if there's any wildlife I haven't spotted any yet.
It's still a little unpolished but the devs seem commited, so I'd say it's 5/5 for offroad driving fans and simulator freaks with a wide taste in general. For someone like me, who likes to try something different once in a while, I'll give it 4/5. For anyone else, I probably recommend finding a friend who'll let them try it out first. I'd say it's well worth the full €25 considering the fact that it's a well developed niche game.
Oh, and it lacks a shovel. I've heard from IRL off-roaders that that's the most important accessory for a truck... but maybe that would have made things too easy?

My Feelings are kinda mixed on the game so i'm gonna make a pro/con system with my review. Here goes:
Pros:
The Gameplay:
As Far as gameplay goes, it's decent. The game itself isn't long enough to find too many repetitive segments. Allthough if you want more than 35hours out of the game you'll have to do some tedious repetition. Most of the game time is spent on quests and not so much hunting for orcs and upgrading your army, which brings me to my next point
The Story:
I liked the story, despite all it's lore breaking things events and characters that just arn't right. But from a storytelling standpoint, it's good, I really liked it.
The Microtransactions:
If the only thing stopping you from buying this game are the microtransactions then ignore it and buy the damned game. Microtransactions, granted, should not be present. That being said, they are also completely unessary. I went through the whole game without spending anything on microtransactions and frankly, spending would not have impacted my gameplay. Simply put, the differency between normal. epic and legendary orcs isn't big enough for you to need then to enjoy the game at all. And I encountered my fair share of legendary orc and gear without having to resort to throwing my money into a cashgrab system. The encounter rate of the legendary orcs and loot is good as it is.
Cons:
The Gear:
Don't get me wrong, the gear is good, but that's just it.... Ther's an easy 5 minutes per area little hunt you can do and get a full set of legendary gear. Or you could do vandetta's. basicly get into another player's world avenge them and if you complete an extra requirement, boom, legendary peice of armor. Frankly, within 2 hours of gameplay into act 2 I had a full set of legendary gear and the rest of the loot was just extra money for crates, which always give an epic follower so i guess thats good? But then again, why have a gear system if nobody's going to use it in game. Best thing would of been to keep the runes and have ocasionnal set peices drop
The nemesis system:
I was dissapointed by the nemesis system. My whole playthrough i only had 2 orcs come back from the dead, and i don't even remember either of their names. Nobody standed out, no followers were even fond to me except for one, who isn't even a follower he's just part of the story. This might just be because i didn't spend much time recruiting orcs i just did the normal dominate every captain and assault the fortress strategy. Most exciting moments were when forthog came to save me and i have to chase this legendary captain and lower his level 3 times to remove his iron will perk.
Conclusion:
All in all, the game was good, but kind of dissapointing. The nemesis system was overhyped, from me at least, and most of the new assets were useless. I equipped gems once and upgraded them in the start of act 4 (which is just an endless mode concealed to boost hours) After act 3 you should just go online and watch the "true" ending (also lorebreaking) I posted the review because from what i've read, my opinions are kind of opposite the the rest of the community.
Verdict:
Story:8/10
Gameplay:7/10
Nemesis system: 4/10
Gear/Follower system:5/10
Total:6/10

Mountain is a semi-interactive screensaver masquerading as a game worth 99 cents.
I say ‘semi’ interactive because while the game’s world—comprised of a single mountain dotted with trees, boulders, and random objects—can be spun around, examined from different angles, and viewed from the starlit vastness of space, I always felt distant from what little action I witnessed. The weather shifts from snowy to rainy to sunny whether you’re watching or not; random objects appear without any personal context (I received two trash bins, a bed, and a padlock, amongst others); and when Mountain expresses its thoughts, it does so with little to no awareness of my presence as a player.
But according to Mountain’s developer, David O’Reilly, this is sort of the point: “It's designed to run in the periphery of your life,” he writes in an August 2014 update. “You can play Mountain while playing other games. If you are not playing it, it will play itself.” In other words: You don’t really HAVE to play Mountain. Its contents are so inconsequential that it requires only a tiny fraction of your attention. It matters that little. But give me a dollar anyway! Thanks!
(Ironic side note: For a game meant to run serenely “in the periphery of your life,” Mountain is a noticeable CPU hog that will likely overheat your computer, especially if you’re using a laptop.)
The only thing about Mountain that I found interesting or entertaining was how oddly bi-polar it was. In my hours of game play (or non-play), I began to notice that Mountain’s musings fell into distinct categories, ranging from Dalai Lama-esque mindfulness:
“I see great purity in today’s utter perfection.”
“I feel at one with the universe inside this foggy winter night.”
“What is sadness?”
…to a teenage girl’s volatile ‘feels’:
“I’m super into this dreamy night.”
“I couldn’t care less about today’s rain.”
“Maybe I am alone because my rocks are ugly.”
…to the nagging of a self-absorbed ex:
“I’m a total babe.”
“Helloooooo?”
Sorta cute, but ultimately, things most people will hear for free. While, you know, living their actual lives.
At the end of the day, Mountain falls in line with dozens of other titles lauded by some for pushing the boundaries of what a game can be and crucified by others for daring to call itself a game at all. I tend to side with the latter, though less harshly, as Mountain did serve as a pretty background time-waster for the few hours I played it. Mountain will definitely appeal to collectors of snow globes and people who like half-heartedly watching ennui-rich land masses against a faint ambient soundtrack. A niche market, for sure, but an “experience” some may enjoy.

I played all episodes on the PS4 cos they gave away the whole thing to PS plus owners (i only have the first episode on PC), so that's why i don't have any achievements on PC and the hours are low.
I enjoyed it but not as much as a lot of other people seem to have, i played the first ep and it didn't pull me in that much, it took me a month or 2 to finish the rest of the eps so i could clear space off my PS4. It gets more interesting later on in episode 3 onwards.
I realise i'm not the demographic for this, i'm not a teenage girl so i didn't connect that much with the main characters. You play as a girl called Max who for some unknown reason gains an ability to manipulate time, or like rewind time. Through the game you are tyring to uncover a mystery about what happened to a missing girl who your best friend Chloe knew.
The thing is a lot of the impact of the game seems to hinge on how you feel about Chloe, and i didn't care for her character. The way she behaved through the game is really annoying, hot-headed and stupid and she said "hella" every other word, i f*cking hate that word lol i remember before it was popular i had heard Cartman say it on South Park, and that was taking the p*ss out of his character, since then i associate anyone who says that with that South Park episode.
I did like how they reference real time travel movies and books and things in this, usually in a lot of games they will have fake media and films so it grounds it more when the characters mention The Time Machine or Donnie Darko.
There is actually a time travel mechanic they do in this game that i don't think i've seen before in other time travel media where Max is able to for instance blow up a door enter the room and then rewind time so she is still in the room before she ever blew the door open. I guess that would work maybe....cos you are travelling through space and time? i dunno, can't test it cos time travel isn't real but that actually made me think like wtf is that a thing? lol
In episode 5 toward the end it seemed like one stealth section was just there to pad the episode out, that was annoying, but i did like the very end of the game and the song used. It is similar to The Walking Dead though where there's only ever 2 outcomes you can get from changing time so you don't really feel that much ownership over how things ultimately turn out.
Infact that reminds me that towards the end in episode 4 or 5 there is one section where you already know you have to rewind time again and erase that timeline but you can still effect and watch other characters shocking choices and actions even though it's now pointless cos you already know you have to change things again.
I did like how three dimensional some of the secondary characters were like Frank and David. It's weird actually cos i did like Max and how nearly everyone else was written apart from Chloe. There's a thing with Chloe i can't mention for spoilers sake that sort of fleshes her character out and gives her more depth, but i dunno her character was still just too unlikeable, i get she was the edgy teen and everything but... *shrugs*
It surprised me that in the prequel you play as Chloe, i guess it's to make her more fleshed out so she has more of an arc, but i think they shoulda really done it in this game rather than have to add it in retroactively.
I still enjoyed the game in spite of Chloe, i think it would actually be cool to play a true sequel where you are an older Max f*cking with time again, but i don't think that's gonna happen cos the main theme in this seems to be you should just accept the past and not try and f*ck with sh*t so much lol

Having had a long, wonderful history with the old Black Isle games (Fallout 1, 2; Torment; Icewind Dale; Baldur's Gate; etc.) I jumped at Wasteland as soon as I read who was developing it. With 20+ hours of gameplay so far, I'm enjoying Wasteland 2 more than I have any other RPG in years -- more than I have any other game I've gotten from Steam in a long time with the exception of Civilization releases.
Wasteland 2 is engaging, thought-provoking, well-written, intellectually stimulating, and even educational. Every battle is a new puzzle. No amount of playing can make the player impervious to what may come next. The writing is superb (surprise, surprise) the music is great, the graphics are beautiful -- although not a selling point -- and all in all this game is easily a 9/10 in my book, and it's not even selling at a triple-A title price (just 40 USD on release day).
Negatives: people say there are bugs everywhere. I have encountered one. It was not a game killer and I expected to see more bugs than one within 48 hours of release.
People say it is too hard. If you were born after 1990, you'll probably hate even the normal difficulty and very likely the game altogether. There's plenty of reading to do and very little hand-holding. I don't mean to be guilty of ageism, it's just that games have gotten far, far, far more user-friendly since the days of Atari and Infocom. The truth is, Wasteland 2 has 1/10th the difficulty of Wasteland, and W2 is catering to the same crowd. In short: this is a *compromise,* and InExile Ent. isn't apologizing.
Conclusion: if you loved the Black Isle games and are on the fence about W2, don't be. I'm hardly through my first sizeable misson and I haven't relaxed so deeply into a game in years. It's like all those comfy afternoons playing Baldur's Gate, except new and improved and back in the Wasteland I spent my 20s in. Quality game development in my book, through and through.

This isn't only a great survival horror game, it's a great game period. While it has a few minor flaws they are easily overlooked because what it does right it does near perfect. The game looks outstanding and ran well even on my old GTX260. Aside from how good it looks the audio is of very high quality too.
The pacing of this game is fantastic, it's always pushing you forward but letting you catch your breath at just the right time. While the scares aren't quite inline with the likes of Silent Hill 2 the story and the pacing of Alan Wake won't disappoint and provides enough chills and thrills to keep you hooked.
The only gripe I have is that it took me awhile to get use to the controls as they weren't very intuitive (I use a Windows 360 controller) and combat I also found using the mouse and keyboard rather weak and laggy, if you have a controller use it.   I also found easy mode a bit too easy and normal mode a bit too hard, I can't imagine what hard difficulty is like.
All in all Alan Wake is a great game with beautiful visuals, a very entertaining story, quality acting and sound, and satisfying game play.  It's also one of the best PC ports you'll ever find.  If you like survival horror or 3rd person action games you can't go wrong with this.

Best of the turn-based RPGs I've played this year.
This tickled my turn-tactical bone in the same way X-Com Enemy Unknown did. Now that I've played it through I enjoyed the general story arc, it felt like you were bringing law and order to a land full of people clammoring for it. Gotta love the Star Trek-esque takes on alternative societies as humanity claws its way back from the grave.
It isn't perfectly open ended, but you have a lot of freedom to accomplish goals. I ended up doing a lot of quest lines backwards by outright murdering individuals .. which inadvertently solved quests later. A lot of times you're forced to take 'sides' in conflicts between factions, but you can just obliterate both of them if you so choose. In certain cases that may even be desirable, we're talking about some odious people here.
The gameplay is pretty solid. Investing in social skills heavily can pay off in several questlines later. There's plenty of skill objectives in every map, making it feel rewarding if you invested in something as seemingly irrelevant as Toaster repair. The various weapon types all feel useful in different ways, forcing you to seriously consider if items are up upgrades to your playstyle or not.

This game brings a whole new meaning of being afraid of the dark. In the small town of Bright Falls, writer Alan Wake takes a vacation for a first time in a while after his tour of his new book. Not having written anything in two years, he goes to clear his head with his wife to enjoy so peace and quite. Once the couple reach the town, all hell breaks loose that revolves around Alan. After a car crash, Alan wakes up to find out that he can't remember in the past week of being in the town. After soon finding out that his wife is missing, Alan does everything to get her back again, even if it means going to hell and back again. With the plot of the story revolving around Alan's missing wife, Alan must face the demons that he has created from a book he doesn't even remember making.
Over all, this game is really good when it comes to its story. The style of telling it from an almost 3rd person omniscient point of view really makes it interesting. The gameplay of the game is good as well; it's very fluid with the controls. Graphics wise, they could be a little better, but if you get invested in the story, you don't care about how the game looks; you just want to see how it ends. There are also very little to no bugs that appear as well. The only bug I had was when you're in an elevator and one of the npcs kept on running in circles the whole time. Other than that, nothing went wrong with the game.
I would have to give this game a 9/10. The storyline is very immersive, and the whole idea of the game is really interesting. With having no main complaints about the game, I would have to say, this game is one of my favorite horror games there is. The only thing I would have to say negative about this game is that the graphics could be a bit better (I don't really care about it that much to go into depth on the topic) and difficulty curve of each setting could be a little less drastic. Other than that, this game is one that should be on everyone's must-play list.

My Feelings are kinda mixed on the game so i'm gonna make a pro/con system with my review. Here goes:
Pros:
The Gameplay:
As Far as gameplay goes, it's decent. The game itself isn't long enough to find too many repetitive segments. Allthough if you want more than 35hours out of the game you'll have to do some tedious repetition. Most of the game time is spent on quests and not so much hunting for orcs and upgrading your army, which brings me to my next point
The Story:
I liked the story, despite all it's lore breaking things events and characters that just arn't right. But from a storytelling standpoint, it's good, I really liked it.
The Microtransactions:
If the only thing stopping you from buying this game are the microtransactions then ignore it and buy the damned game. Microtransactions, granted, should not be present. That being said, they are also completely unessary. I went through the whole game without spending anything on microtransactions and frankly, spending would not have impacted my gameplay. Simply put, the differency between normal. epic and legendary orcs isn't big enough for you to need then to enjoy the game at all. And I encountered my fair share of legendary orc and gear without having to resort to throwing my money into a cashgrab system. The encounter rate of the legendary orcs and loot is good as it is.
Cons:
The Gear:
Don't get me wrong, the gear is good, but that's just it.... Ther's an easy 5 minutes per area little hunt you can do and get a full set of legendary gear. Or you could do vandetta's. basicly get into another player's world avenge them and if you complete an extra requirement, boom, legendary peice of armor. Frankly, within 2 hours of gameplay into act 2 I had a full set of legendary gear and the rest of the loot was just extra money for crates, which always give an epic follower so i guess thats good? But then again, why have a gear system if nobody's going to use it in game. Best thing would of been to keep the runes and have ocasionnal set peices drop
The nemesis system:
I was dissapointed by the nemesis system. My whole playthrough i only had 2 orcs come back from the dead, and i don't even remember either of their names. Nobody standed out, no followers were even fond to me except for one, who isn't even a follower he's just part of the story. This might just be because i didn't spend much time recruiting orcs i just did the normal dominate every captain and assault the fortress strategy. Most exciting moments were when forthog came to save me and i have to chase this legendary captain and lower his level 3 times to remove his iron will perk.
Conclusion:
All in all, the game was good, but kind of dissapointing. The nemesis system was overhyped, from me at least, and most of the new assets were useless. I equipped gems once and upgraded them in the start of act 4 (which is just an endless mode concealed to boost hours) After act 3 you should just go online and watch the "true" ending (also lorebreaking) I posted the review because from what i've read, my opinions are kind of opposite the the rest of the community.
Verdict:
Story:8/10
Gameplay:7/10
Nemesis system: 4/10
Gear/Follower system:5/10
Total:6/10
